A solid platformer at a good price. The game reminds me of a variety of things; perhaps the best summary is something like "Symphony of the Night meets Dark Souls". There are two gameplay modes (survival, which plays more like a roguelike apparently and classic which is a more traditional Metroidvania) and three difficulties for each which provides a decent array of challenges for any player. Boss fights require pattern recognition and decent skill, and searching for upgrades, which are scattered throughout the maps through hidden "souls" and in shops, with a variety of upgrades and tools you can grab to either make fights easier or explore faster. There are a variety of skills that can enhance your base abilities, with a passive bonus for points in each tree supplementing the individual elements of each tree. Dying costs you all your money (by default, which you can mitigate with starting money found through upgrades) and shunts you back to a 3D printer to respawn. You can travel between these, which alleviates the walking required, and save your upgrades and loot here (on Classic).
You can acquire a variety of primary weapons and quite a few different sub weapons, which provide a variety of strategies ranging from beam weapons to deployable drones. You can also do your traditional movement upgrades to move more quickly and reach new areas, though these are mostly optional (I'd recommend them though). There are plenty of secrets scattered throughout the various maps, some with great benefits like more HP or ammo and others that are just easter eggs. The writing is decent and the voice acting, while not perfect, is fun. The subtitles are not super accurate, but item descriptions are satisfactory and overall the game's sense of humor lasts well through the end, leaving me wanting mroe.
The boss fights are decently clever, and there are various mechanics that force you to adapt and use different weapons and strategies for each fight. None of these fights are too rediculously hard, and sometimes they can be a bit too easy, especially if you've gotten as many upgrades as you can. Unfortunately, these can't be repeated in the course of a story run, and if there's a boss rush mode or a way to repeat the fights I missed it. More interesting are arena fights in the form of "alarms". These are either triggered as you progress through areas or as optional encounters off to the side in areas. As you repeat alarms, the difficulty level increases, resulting in more (and often times more dangerous) enemies.
The soundtrack, while not phenomenal, is solid and immersive and doesn't get annoyingly repetitive, unlike some others. The sound design is nothing extraordinary either, but things sound like they "should" based on other games, so it's nothing to worry about.
Now for a summary:
Pros:
Cool upgrade system that encourages collection and synergizing.
Gameplay is solid and difficulty is neither too hard nor too easy (based on a medium playthough).
Story is good and compelling.
Writing and humor are engaging and amusing without becoming heavyhanded. (I was surprised by the ending, which is rare, although it's not the most unique ending I've ever seen.)
Cons:
Too short; I could stand twice as much content easily (again, it's worth the price, but I liked it so much that I'm left wanting more)
No new game plus; even if just repeating with your unlocked "geekies". it would be nice to play through again, even if just with a few nods to your previous run.
Difficulty is middle of the road, but some segments may be too difficult/frustrating for some players or to easy/repetitive for others.
Don't let the length of the "Cons" section fool you; I recommend this game readily, and look forward to more content from this indie developer.

(EDIT: Due to the high level of knee-jerk downvoting I've noticed as I happily play via emulator after my steam refund, I thought I'd explain a little something: I adore FF VIII (otherwise why bother even warning people about how wretched this port is?), it's my favorite PSX Final Fantasy and my 3rd favorite, full stop. I know I use big words, but you do yourself a disservice when you don't read to the end of a document - reading is a big part of JRPGs, after all)
FF VIII is a deeply misunderstood Final Fantasy, probably because it breaks with so many series traditions and has a mechanics system based around stat management. This requires more responsibility on the part of the player than a lot of JRPG fans would probably prefer; you don't just gain levels and skills, it's on you to figure out how to develop your characters the best way. But there has been plenty written about the gameplay and storyline on both sides - I would like to focus on the Steam port.
You'll notice on the store page that you're also required to agree to a Square-Enix EULA. This may not seem like a huge deal, just hit "accept" and agree not to basically break down and resell the game, right? If only. You'll first be required to make a separate account, log in via their website, confirm again via email, and then enter a setup window.
Here you can arrange the buttons for your controller, and here is the ultimate deal-breaker for me. Hope you arranged everything exactly as you like it, and never want to change anything, because in-game your controller buttons will be referred to by their device names, that is, B1, B2, B3, etc. This isn't so difficult until you consider that a number of characters' limit breaks and other attacks rely on timed button inputs - hope you don't ever want to play as Zell!
Also, every time you start the game you'll need to use your keyboard. You cannot boot it up, grab a controller, and go. You know, the implicit promise of a console game from the PSX era.
Couple this with MIDI music left over from the 15-year-old PC port and you're left with the option of spending hours installing mod after mod to (supposedly) get the game to be (maybe) playable, and I'm forced to say that once again, Square-Enix has shown itself to be the animated zombie corpse of Squaresoft. What a mess.

This is not a declaration of whether this game is good or bad, but rather, whether or not I recommend it based on what I did and did not like about this game. Here we go~
First, let's discuss the port. I played the PC version of this game that came on four discs quite a few years back, and I found this Steam version to be superior. Its graphical quality seemed slightly better, though I didn't screen capture to confirm, I'll admit. The greatest thing about the Steam version of the game, though, is high speed mode. With the exception of tutorials, you can press F1, and the game goes around 5x as fast. This means that the draw system can be dealt with much, much, much faster. Dealing with the most boring thing to me in this game in a drastically smaller fraction of the time was ever so satisfying. With this being a PC game, of course, folks have put out mods/updates for graphical improvements and music improvements.
The only downsides I came across in the port were that the high speed mode will take a single button press as multiple button presses at times, which can screw up drawing the right spell or using the wrong spell/healing the wrong team member. High speed mode is still great for drawing magic out of enemies, and would be superb for simply grinding with strength as high as you can set it and constantly just spamming "Attack." Oh, and I searched multiple Steam and Game FAQs discussion threads about how to use the "Boost" ability with GFs, and despite equipping Quezacotl on Squall after fully learning Boost, no combination of buttons I pressed would work; even holding 'J' and hitting every other button that was mapped. Furthermore, the summons take forever and a day and are incredibly boring, so even if I did get the Boost buttons to work, high speed mode wouldn't be an option for fights where I need the GFs to do legitimate damage in the early game (because I'd get in less real-world button-presses while the game moves at 5x speed). Later in the game, I found that summoning GFs was a waste of time because your characters' magic and normal attacks/limit breaks deal more damage faster.
That's all I have to say about the port. I love high speed mode, though it does have a few caveats, and the issues with boosting not being labeled properly and possibly not even working for some users is rather irksome.
Final Fantasy VIII (FFVIII) or was a graphical leap forward from its predecessor, FFVII. In FFVII, character models in battles looked like the characters were intended, albeit very basic due to graphical limitations, while outside of combat, all character models were incredibly basic to the point that I found them cringe-worthy. I felt the SNES FFVI sprites were easier on the eyes. FFVIII, however, gave characters appearances out of combat which matched their appearance in combat as well, and I much appreciated this graphical enhancement. The "movies" in this game are still decent-looking today, and there is a fair amount of attractive things to see. The world map is a bit crisper than FFVII's, and it does the job. Easier navigation of the world map is opened up by a small number of transportation options, and although they're alright, FFIV on the SNES remains my favorite for world map vehicular traversal. Most probably like FFVI and FFVII's airships better, but my sense of direction when my POV shifts is just terrible.
Every song I heard while playing the game again today was very nice. I'd forgotten how good some of these songs are, like the fire cavern music. The battle theme is alright, which is good, since you'll be hearing that music more than any other in the game, since this -is- a Final Fantasy game. The boss music is okay as well; better than I remembered it being.
The combat itself is good enough. It's pretty standard fare for a Final Fantasy game, with the exception that instead of summons being very powerful beings you spend typically high amounts of MP to summon them like in earlier titles, in this game, summons (GFs) are free to cast, can be used every turn, are ridiculously overpowered at the beginning of the game, and peter off to the point that they are usually worthless to use. I mentioned earlier that GFs take forever to animate their attack, but you need to hit buttons to Boost the damage if you want to have them be worth using around the middle of the game, meaning high speed mode won't help you when it comes to summoning GFs against all but the early game common enemies. Also, limit breaks are very high damage attacks your characters use when their health is low, so beating most bosses in the late-game tends to be based on deliberately getting your health low, then repeatedly using limit breaks with every character until the boss is dead.
As aggravating as the Draw system can be for collecting spells from enemies, it does have alternatives a little later in the game (converting cards into magic spells), and the high speed mode makes that better as well. However, -the- most bothersome thing for me in FFVIII is the bizarre micromanagement this game employs. The Junction system lets you stick GFs on each of your characters, which let you stick spells on each of your characters to boost their stats. You unlock new abilities and junctions for each GF by getting Ability Points from winning battles, and can choose the skills each GF is learning over time, which I really love. However, the Junction system itself is where almost all stats in the game come from. In most JRPGs, if you're having trouble with a boss but you already have the best gear and spells, you just go grind to level up, come back, and do better because your stats will have improved. This would be the case in any other Final Fantasy game.
However, in FFVIII, enemies scale close to your party level. This means that if you aren't good at the game and have the best gear/spells you could have, you would be making a difficult battle -harder- by leveling up, because the boss would level up as well, and I have read that enemies' stats go up significantly more per level than characters' attributes, so leveling is often counter-productive. This leaves me dumbfounded and irritated just on principle. Also, if you Junction a spell to a character's stat, that character can't use that spell without lowering their stat each time they cast it, meaning you have to go Draw more of that spell from enemies or turn more cards into magic. This discourages players from ever using the best spells in the game since they tend to Junction for the highest attribute bonuses.
There is a card game in FFVIII called "Triple Triad." It's kinda awesome until really annoying rule changes get introduced later, which require that you do a lot of annoying busy work to change the rules to rules you prefer. It's one of the most memorably excellent things in this game, and I would have adored Triple Triad if not for what I felt was going overkill on having rule changes that turn a fun game into a real pain in the ♥♥♥♥♥♥. Despite this, I prefer it over Tetra Master, the FFIX card game, which is pretty impressive since you would expect the sequel to improve upon the original card game, but that's not the case.
Lastly, the story and world...it's insane. Not a Sam & Max good kind of crazy, but it lacks any real sense. Sure, it's fantasy and these games do weird stuff, but aside from a few plot/logic flaws, the bare bones world should make sense. However, in FFVIII, the first few hours show a teenage

Unlike other games in this genre, Paradox has created an inflexible game that as you progress increasingly becomes more and more boring due to limitations they built into the game on purpose.  What limitations?  (1) The larger you get the more your tech advances cost, and if you get ahead tech wise your tech costs go up again.  This effectively keeps most players within a narrow band tech wise, as Paradox hated the whole idea of people trying to race up tech trees to gain advantages.  You can't do that here.  (2) The game always has to be played with some type of advanced tech alien in the game (fallen empires).  And these empires have ships so in advance of you that you have no hope of beating them until very late in a game.  Plus if you settle to close to them they get upset and attack, forcing you to destroy the settlement + one or two other worlds as punishment.  SO while you can't race up the tree, you have an enemy you have to avoid in order to survive.  (3) Limited world control.  Oh so sorry, you can only directly control 5 (or a few more with tech advances) worlds at a time.  The rest have to be assigned to sectors and controlled by the (dumb AI) computer.  And just to force you to keep to that mechanic, it will cost you precious admin points to remove a world from a sector (so no moveing worlds in and unless you cheat and give yourself admin to make up for this stupidity).  (4) No way to break up alien alliances.  Once they form they are more solid than diamonds.  All you can do is get in your own alliance and both sides can stare at each other daring one to cross the border.  Hence mid game and later becomes massive wars where you are depending on your computer allies for any success .. and if they screw up, you are so screwed.  (5) Late Game boredom.  And this is the reason you see so few games of Stellaris being posted on the net .. people have quickly tired of the game.  If you want to win a domination victory, you usually have to go to war alliance to alliance, and target only a few planets each war.  If you try for more, since they can jump around in space, you usually end up in a trading game of you taking planets while their fleets take your planets and neither side advances war wise.  So the game bogs down into go to war, take a couple planets, end war, get planets out of resistance, go to war again .. over and over and over while you try to advance on the domination victory mark.
I could keep going on and on with all the issues and errors in this game.  it's one of the worst I've purchased and I'd return it for a refund if I could.

Another bare bones game rushed out the door. This one already had a DLC tab on launch.
A poor combination of Distant Worlds and Galactic Civilizations.
The game tries to limit you as much as possible to still be playable.
I was frustrated with the game, can't do this, can't do that, can only play it a certain way.....
Played it enough to figure this out:
All you do most of the game is survey stars and build mining/research stations.
Another game where the AI plays the game for you since you can only directly manage 5 colonies in your empire. Anything beyond 5 has to be AI controlled. And it will replace buildings you don't want replaced with other buildings (it's rather dumb to the point that it won't upgrade any buildings it's built).
It has lots of broken game mechanics. (i.e. click on planet, click colonize = nothing happens, all the unassigned colony ships just ignore it).
Broken quests. (A few you can't complete because there are no objectives or are blank).
Popups on top of popups. The popups you need you never get (i.e. research completed, war declared, etc).
The popups you do get are repetative, the game will tell you you found something, a short pointless narrative and then you click either fascinating, amazing, or interesting. But none of these actually do anything for you. But they are annoying and they freeze the game.
You can't queue your research, and since you don't get a popup for it, you'll often miss that it was completed. What you will get is a small bubble icon at the top of the screen that disappears rather quickly.
A leader died? Another small bubble icon at the top of the screen (if you're not watching for it you'll miss it).
War was declared? Another small bubble icon at the top of the screen (all the bubble icons have a limited delay that isn't changable).
Shows planets that are colonizable (green circle = desirable), but you can't actually colonize them since you haven't researched that technology yet or your race really doesn't like them.
If your race likes (i.e.) tropical and you conquer a primitive race that lives on a turndra, then every tundra planet on the galactic map will have a green (desirable) circle next to it. Sure, makes sense, it's inhospitable, but desirable.
Every AI empire you meet will hate you. Where's the "Advanced Diplomacy system worthy of a Grand Strategy Game."
Due to border friction, it's impossible to get anywhere with dipomacy. And they'll constantly ask you to turn over border planets. Saying no = war.
War = You've just conquered 5 AI planets, but you can't annex them, only cecede one of them to end the war (based on warscore earned and government).
Over-powered enemies. (i.e. Advanced established empires (overwelming compared to you) that always seem to declare war on you when you're barely getting started). No option to disable them.
Very limited leaders (10, 3 of them must be for research, the other 7 will be on science ships). Why even have the option for governers, generals, or admirals?
Combat is just graphical, you can't control anything. After the first few battles it gets boring to watch.
No option to see all your ship commands, so you end up sending ships on the same missions over and over.
All space stations build ships at the same pace regardless of what size it is. The only point of upgrading to a larger size is to build bigger ships. And each station can only build 1 ship at a time.
No option to sort ships. Ships, fleets, planets are all on a the same scrollable side bar (lots of scrolling constantly)
Pro's?

Abzû’s story peaks in what’s meant to be a grand catharsis, but I was tempted to roll my eyes. It works better as an impressionist piece than a directed experience, which is where it clams up for me. The story is simple: a ruined underwater civilization that once lived in harmony with nature lost sight of that relationship and started exploiting the creatures it once worshipped. Technology rolls in, cast as an industrial menace and does its destructive thing—it’s a story I’ve heard many times before and a familiar one for a studio with the same creative director behind Flower and Journey. Personally, I agree with its argument—yes, let’s be better to this earth—but any direct attempt to ‘say’ something feels hamfisted.
But when Abzû doesn’t paint silly expositional hieroglyphs on the wall, when it presents me with beauty and behavior and lets my mind go where it will—that’s when I felt most affected. Who knew doing a barrel roll on a humpback whale through a fish tornado would choke me up?
Despite the forced narrative, there are few games quite as curious and beautiful as Abzû, and fewer of its kind on the PC. It’s a short, dense journey filled with intense wonder and inherent beauty, and every inch is worth seeing.

This is a First Person Brawler with a simple combat system, original and out of the ordinary art style. Featuring a 2-3 hour story mode and another hour of challenges.
The game uses the Source engine (Half Life 2) so it has limited but memorable scenes. The art style is astonishing and  aestheticly looks like a wierd dream.
I really want to see the concept arts or a sketchbook from the creator. Technically the game looks okay. There are low res textures, jerky shadows and low poly stuff. But the caracter design, the weapons and the environment...man this game looks and feels really uniqe.
The music just like the graphics fullfills this wierd dreamy athmosphere. There are many memorable moments thank to the great combination of them. Voice acting is cheesy but funny. The dialogues are genuinely funny and serious at the same time. The sound effects are basic public domain stuff.
Gameplay wise well... it's simple. The main scenario is arena fight. You get to a locked area and you have to defeat all the enemies. Imagine these like nodes in a graph. These nodes are connected by edges that are basically linear paths. And overall the game is linear and the level design is linear too.
There is a turret section as well but still has the stong dreamy athmosphere so it's okay. You will encounter little enemies, normal enemies, normal enemies with weapons (melee, ranged), brutes and bosses.
The little enemies are crabs, chickens and those big rabbit thingys. I think most of them just spit you acid liquid. Normal enemies are basically fighting partners. These guys can pick up weapons as well. Enemy vaiety is nice here because there are different models and fighting styles. Brutes are big, tough enemies and you better kill 'em with melee weapons. They take multiple hits as well. Bosses are easy battles, just like old times: wasd 'em and shoot 'em.
You can shoot only in ADS otherwise you swing the weapon towards the enemy. You can throw the weapons as well. Mechanically these are the same as in other games but they feel strange and uniqe in a positive way.
The melee system is simple and easy to learn. There are basic combos and advanced combos. The game does a good job teaching you these things in the tutorial sessions. There is a challenge tower for pro players. It's basically a fight fest. You have to climb the tower and defeat all the enemies. Things could get hard here... :)
As I mentioned the Singleplayer story mode is linear and each replay will be the same. But if you liked the story and the wierd things in it, I'm sure you'll give it another go. However the Challenge Tower is pure gameplay and fun and absolutely replayable.

At first glance Magicka will look like a fun button mashing experience to have with your friends. If you look further you will see that there is more enjoyment to experience from Magicka than you could ever see from the trailers and screenshots. Magicka has created something that no game had ever done before (at least not well). From just a combination of buttons you can create powerful spells that bare strategy behind them. Of course there are a number of downsides and bugs to this game that when overlooked barely interfere with the gameplay at all and will usually result in a laugh. Make no mistakes, this game is for pure fun and joy.
If you are looking for a game to play with your friends then look no further because this game is precisely what you need. You are getting a lot more fun out of this game than the price would intend you to believe. At such a low price you get hours of gameplay excluding all of the tremendous amount of downloadable content. Magicka is a co-op game that brings out the evil inside you and your friends. You can be on your way to defeating the infamous Grimnir when out beaming behind you is a beam of arcane from your companion aiming directly for you. Magicka really brings out the troll in most people and with countless of opportunities to kill you your friends will never get bored killing you and reviving you, killing and reviving you, killing and... yeah.
For the serious competitors that don't like the limitations that Magicka: Wizard Wars gives you but are still interested in the humor and game mechanics of Magicka then the pvp or challenge modes will prove to be very effective gamemodes. As stated before Magicka has a very diverse field of strategy. For example someone will be coming at you with some fire so you have to quickly decide to cast a fire shield onto yourself to become immune to fire and then come at them with the most unexpected attacks in order to win a player versus player match. Challenge mode also includes some strategy and competition. Once you die in challenge you're done for and must start from square one. This means you can compete against your friends and see who is the greater wizard.
Now I bring you the bugs, glitches and problems this game faces. The bugs in this game are usually hilarious to see happen to someone you are playing with and usually funny to watch when they happen to you. These are the small bugs that don't affect you in a huge way when playing Magicka but through your playthrough it is not unlikely to come across a big glitch that will require you to restart the game and have you go back to the last checkpoint. Another thing that could be considered a problem in this game is it's massive amount of downloadable content which could possibly be a deal breaker for you if you just hate paying just a bit extra for a full package. What I must reassure you with is the fact that none of the extra content is required to feel whole although it is a bit depressing when you look at your robes and see a horde of robes unable to play with. When it comes to actual level and gameplay dlc Paradox have done something I must praise them for. When playing online only the host needs the downloadable content in order to play it so essentially you could play every dlc level without ever paying a cent.

i dont typically write reviews for games, but whenever I see game made by basically one person that is this fun, I gotta give em props. I am a sucker for old school games, But I hate people who think nostalgia alone is enough to act as a hook. That is not the case with Bot vice. The game does a good job of making fun of old school games and the corny stories that they follow, while also making the game adicting and fun! If you make a light parody/homage type game, this is the way to do it.
Next off lets talk about the game play. This game does a great job of establishing all of the controls and power ups from the very beginning as well as the maneuvers. The controls are simple and tight and the game plays like a cross between Sin and Punishment, and  Wild Guns (not a bad combination at all!). My only real gripe is that I wish that there were more guns ! I don't need like 20+ but maybe 3-4 more would do it for me.
Moving on I will cover  the games look and design. I love the variety of bot designs and bosses, They are nicely animated and have a vibrant appeal to them. The baddies also have an array of attack styles that make you have to adapt accordingly, usually by waiting for an opening (Snake bot I'm looking at you!) The satges also are beautifuly designed! each of the stages look unique and have interesting gimicks that can add to the mayhem, such as trains ramming through the stages, armored trucks launching bombs every where.or even Robot trash bugs chasing  you out of trash cans!
My final talking point is music. I love video game music and music and general so For me a games soundtrack appeal is crucial to my desire to want to play a game. I believe that A games soundtrack should enhchance and support the overall game. This game nails it! I love the Megaman and TMNT esque soundtrack that this game delivers! the 80's and 90's synth fit the homage style and each stage has it;s own theme! No reused songs except for the bosses at the end of the main levels, but each boss specific stage has their own high octane but kickin background theme! I only wish that the Music was dlc :D
My only real gripes are that I wish there was more guns , that there were a co op, and that the game innovated a little buit more in establishing its own Identity. but judging by the ending, I am sure we will see more from the creators one day! and I look forward to it! Get this game if you like frantic high octane shootouts and a cast of corny quote spewing enemies with laughable voices!  For a Arcade game 8/10
Also when you beat the game be sure to check out the extras, because the fun truly begins there ;)

Ghost 1.0 is a new entry to the metroidvania genre, and it comes with smooth controls, intense fights and a selection of different game-play choices.
Read more...
Fran is the main developer of Ghost 1.0, with only receiving assistance for art, music and sound effects leaving the remaining to him. Ghost has been in development for 2.5 years and was released on Steam on the 7th of June 2016.
The game begins with two hackers who are hiring an agent called Ghost (the player) to sneak into the Nakamura Space Station and once on-board, to begin searching for anything which would display their secrets. Your tasks become clearer as the story develops and you discover the entire space station.
Unlike the usual type of game where you'd just control one character and shoot everything in-sight, Ghost works differently as she has a special ability to leave her body, which is a drone, and control any other drone she pleases to help her accomplish the mission in a safer and easier manner.
In this game you'll continually be harassed by drones, turrets and lasers as you move swiftly from room to room, you will constantly need to focus on dodging incoming attacks while shooting your own shots, waves, beams and bombs.
Ghost 1.0 Pipes
Ghost 1.0 is a game where you may find yourself continually grinding waves of enemies in order to accumulate high amounts of currency to purchase upgrades and guns which is vital for boss battles. There are over 300 rooms to explore, 35 weapons to purchase and 40 upgrades, items and power ups. There's a lot to collect and purchase.
There is a skill tree which doesn't work in the same RPG element as the game states, instead you'll slowly build up these points as you explore and find pickups. There are over 60 different abilities which the user can put points into but each run they can only utilise 20 of them and there's also no resetting your point selection, so chose wisely.
Once you've completed the initial classic game mode you can also select to play survival, where the gameplay runs at a much faster pace but is much more harsh in terms of punishment for death.
The graphics in the game are extremely well done in cut scenes and gameplay with a fitting selection of voice acting, music and sound effects which give the game a professional and completed feel.
Ghost 1.0 Header
Eventually during the game it may feel over repetitive as you search for items which you found a different colour of earlier, but as you move to the different sectors of the space station the gameplay doesn't specifically change, but it adds a new objective like completing mind-boggling puzzles or collecting plant extracts. It's a nice variation of tasks.
The controls of the game are very smooth and feel natural but if there's a problem it can easily be redefined or even countered with a controller connection. There's a whole host of options including sound, video and languages too.
The developer, Fran, is also working with the community in order to fix bugs that arise and also problems that a high percentage of the community have, since it's release on Steam it has received multiple updates which are all requested in the discussions.
Overall, I feel the game is a completely amazing product which is fun to play and doesn't leave you brain-dead and constantly shooting, instead it forces you to think for yourself at points.
10/10

Truly an incredible game. I can't say tho which one is better, this or 7 ... but I'm sure this is one of the most underrated Final Fantasy game. Maybe because it was released almost instantly after 7? I don't know but you really won't go wrong if you start playing this.
Also Squall was kinda closer to my heart than Cloud. His personality is something I can relate to but also the fact that character development has a bigger focus in this game than in 7.
It's hard to talk about the story without any spoilers but I've really liked it. Even the ending which is something "controversial" or at least heavily debated by the fanbase.
Obviously the game is almost 20 years old so the graphics are a bit dated but that doesn't take away anything from the experience.
But it's highly recommended to use some mods to make the game better. Here are the ones I've used:
1. Tonberry: Ehanced. You need that for modding.
2. SeeD Reborn. Full menu overhaul.
3. Roses and Wine. Full high quality PSX music instead of the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ MIDI music we got with the PC release.
4. Xbox360 controller icons. That's optional ofc but I recommend to play with a controller.
Also this is not a hard game but it can be difficult! The game is kinda vague about what you should do (there is no quest system!) so I highly recommend to use a non-spoiler walkthrough
That leads to the biggest con of the game. It's not the story, the art, or the characters... it's the fact that the game is mechanically broken. Basically imbalanced. By the end of disc 1 (which is still the early game) you can max out your GFs, all your party members can have 5k HP and one shot every enemy. And don't even mention the infinite money glitch. I don't say it's bad but in the end it makes the game really easy (much easier than 7). In the other hand you can ignore these things but it's in the game, in front of your eyes. Hard to pass it when otherwise you would need to grind the same NPC for hours just to get the desired loot. It didn't take anything away from the game for me but it has to be mentioned.
Also don't ignore the Triple Triad card game! Collecting cards is fun and the game is also fun to play. The best game inside a game ever.
I recommend to use Gamer Corner FF8 database for researching items and cards (what to refine to what, where to find X items and monsters etc.)
Also it has a nice Junction Workshop where you can optimze your GF setup
What else to say? A great game. Just go and start playing it. Now!

All in all, it's an amazing game. I recommend it wholeheartedly, for old fans and newcomers alike, especially if you can get this when it's on sale!

This game is great.  It's the best 4X game I've played since MOO 2.  The universe is huge, and it's easily manageable.   The AI acts like I would expect.  Some games are brutally short, some games are epic.  There are even some games that drag out into a huge stalemate of politics.  Pretty realistic.  There are flaws in the design, but Paradox seems to be addressing those pretty quickly.
There are some complaints about the ship design having no impact.  Yes, the tactical combat can become something of a slugfest early on.  But by mid-game having a balanced fleet can really impact your battles.  Make some heavily shielded/armored ships with short range weapons to act as tank, use some point defence ships to stop missles, build some bigger snipe type ships for the rear.  These can make a significant difference in combat.  Paradox has addressed some of these concerns in the latest patch, extending the range of weapons causing the ships to stand off more during combat.
Also, they addressed the empire management so that the AI governors more closely do what you expect of them.
There's some more work to do, but the scope of this game is amazing.  It's definetely a huge step in the pausable RTS, 4X generation.  There's tons of races, tons of techs, and amazing graphics.
There will probably be a better game to come along in the future, but it probably won't be for many years.  I'm happy I pulled the trigger on got this in my Library.  It will be remain on my hard drive for a long time.

ABZÛ doesn't feel like much of a game at first to be honest, because it's mostly linear, you can't really die, and the goal is basically going from point A to point B, 'til you complete said chapter, and then go to the next. It doesn't sound too thrilling at first, I know, but the game is really, really gorgeous to look at. Everything's so colorful, and the world itself is full of life. The game felt more like a trip to the museum, but I'm totally fine with that personally. You get to see all kinds of animals in the marine ecosystem swimming around peacefully, from smaller fish, to whales, sharks, squids, and even extinct animals. Gameplay wise....Well, you swim, and swim a lot. There are a bunch of collectibles here and there, where you need to explore the ocean a bit more to gather them all.
There's not a single bit of dialogue or specific explanation in the world about what the plot is, but there are paintings and stuff that you can find to figure out. I've heard a few different interpretations on the internet, and that's pretty good in a way, letting people use their imagination at first about what's going on.
The soundtrack itself, like the atmosphere of the game, is really soothing, and this all felt like an awesome movie, in a way.
I would personally recommend it if you like the ocean, or walking simulators, or if you just want a soothing experience.
The only problem I got with this game is that it felt really short. I was trying to enjoy the world without exploring too much, and I was able to finish it in 2 hours or so. The rest of my playtime? Well, collecting stuff, watching animals swimming around, and a couple of extra runs through the game.

The F.E.A.R. series is an oxymoronic franchise of both action-horror and old-school FPS elements. It's derivative from both genres, yet it maintains its uniqueness with its subversions.
It’s generic environments, modern-FPS gunplay, odd design decisions for exposition and limited variety of enemies overshadows the greatness of the subtly of its writing, the high-intense atmosphere, the complex AI and the paranormal elements that make F.E.A.R. distinct. Even when it comes to the gameplay, the series has been torn between the disempowering nature of fear as well as the catharsis of the tension from its high-risk/high-reward combat.
In 2016, the horror elements have not withstood the test of time; the gunplay and difficulty surpasses many games made today that it will baffle you how we are behind the times for AI. In many ways, like other FPS classics such as DOOM or Quake, F.E.A.R is a milestone for the genre that has yet to be understood by the creators/publishers themselves for why it is such a classic.
If any game could warrant from a name-change, F.E.A.R. is the highest on my list. The paranormal elements of enemies, hallucinations, the Alma encounters, the scientific rationale for tampering with psychiatric forces beyond their control all warrant the name it is given. (In many ways, the generic abbreviation fits the game’s confusing mix-mash of ideas.) The horror elements are the focus of the game as well as its story, and none of this is to say that on first playthroughs the experience is not intimidating to your senses.
However, the game’s sense of building tension far outweighs any horror it can instill in you no matter how much you are FPS-Bullet-time-Jesus. From the ambush encounters of invisible enemies, squads that will flank you or employ tactics to get around your defenses, and the paranormal appearances with the atmospheric music all keep your nerves on edge. F.E.A.R. excels in this manner because the core gameplay–the combat–emphasizes that the tension is what will get you killed, not the scares.
The combat itself uses acceptable, if somewhat barebones, gunplay compared to the customizable, experience grind you will find in modern FPS (even old-school inspired ones). Resource management, of ammo, of guns (which you can hold three), of grenades and of medkits harken back to the design philosophy of DOOM-like games where resource management and mastering level-design are the key skills you must master. F.E.A.R., however, doesn’t stop there with this idea as its most marketed, iconic gameplay mechanic is perhaps one more resource to manage as your arsenal, bullet-time mode.
Bullet-time mode is not unique to F.E.A.R.; it’s how it is used that makes it more effective than a mere gimmick found in other games. Until I had played the game recently, I always wondered why bullet-time mode was such an integral part to the experience. In many franchises, bullet-time is a gimmick staple in FPSs that is only there because it’s a cliché.  F.E.A.R., however, offers another reason for its inclusion that adheres to the similar idea of old-school FPSs: Resource management.
In many ways, playing the game without the reflex boost makes the game more difficult than the game was ever meant to be. That’s because bullet-time is another resource meter that offers an illusion of difficulty similar to games like Max Payne. Bullet-time is not just an offensive tool for combat efficiency but a defensive requirement as well; you use it to evade attacks, take out enemies in numbers beyond your normal means of control—and it’s a convenient way to offer the illusion of overcoming difficulty for both console and PC gamers with more time to react and aim your shots while reenacting your favorite John Woo fantasy.
This system would feel shallow and worthless had not the AI nor the high damage output warrant its inclusion. Enemies, rather than being class-specific, change their tactics based on the situation—a normal soldier could flank you while you are distracted, another could become a grenadier or they will fall back to regroup with a greater opposition. The banter, reactions and complexities of their AI system rivals most games made within the last decade since its release. The AI emphasizes that you play more smartly with your godlike abilities while the frailty of your character exercises caution. Use your bullet-time unwisely and you’ll quickly find yourself dead; use it efficiently and you can explode a grenade mid-flight to take out a squad. The added melee and momentum options for attacks/dodges combines all these individually excellent elements of F.E.A.R.’s combat system into one of the most entertaining FPSs you will find.
Now when it comes to the storytelling of F.E.A.R., I find the experience as respectful of your intelligence as much as the combat demands from you being strategic. This isn’t to say that the storyline is original, memorable, or flawless but that the execution goes a long way to respect the player who wants to enjoy the greatest aspects of the game, the gameplay, and then realize all the connections upon each new playthrough.
Most of the exposition is hidden away in conversations, flashbacks/paranormal experiences, as well as seemingly irrelevant details tucked into voice-mails or laptops. (These laptops with super confidential data of immoral practices from corporations are lying around for anyone to discover at the facilities.) While the presentation of this important information is subpar to other games that use the same ideas, it’s the gradual coming all together of details, characters and motives that really establishes the darkest of themes touched on in this game and in future sequels.
It wouldn’t be until F.E.A.R. 2 that the squad would get some semblance of personality and add details about the corporation of Armacham; F.E.A.R. 3 would try, and fail, at establishing some personal motivation and character for Pointman (yes, that is his name as far as you know). The expansions for F.E.A.R., amusingly, foreshadow an understanding too late for the franchise now that the F.E.A.R “trilogy” should have died with the end of Extraction Point where the REAL ending of the series ends as far as the horror elements are concerned.
Looking back at the “trilogy” and the official trilogy, Perseus Mandate exemplifies all the future blunders that would sink the franchise down into the abyss of F.E.A.R. Online. PM retells the same story about Alma, choosing to focus on the horror elements rather than the elements that made the gameplay tense; PM highlights the same revelations of Project Origin with rarely anything new added; and it is a franchise that lives only by its successful marketing and profits are concerned until it all comes down to be ruptured into ashes. (PM is not bad as Timegate knows their stuff for making good FPSs, but it displays everything that befell the series from here on out as cheap cash-grabs.)
Even as I write this review, F.E.A.R. is something I would hope warrants a reboot for the franchise where Monolith can return the series to the aspects that made the gameplay great, not the cheap-scares that were marketable. It is a game I can easily recommend, and if you have any interest in the franchise you should play the first game’s “trilogy” as well as the second game (I personally liked it but I can understand why people think it falls short of the original.)
In the end, F.E.A.R. exemplifies all that seems to be lost to modern games, especially in single-player games, where the gameplay is perfectly paced, interesting and the game knows where to end. The only thing that seems to be forgotten is knowing when something should end, stay dead, and something new should be made, not grave-robbing from the same corpse for sequels.

Deus Ex, despite being released in the summer of 2000, is still one of the greatest role-playing shooter hybrids available on PC. If you're a fan of futuristic settings or the cyberpunk science fiction genre as I am, Deus Ex's storyline and environments should be right up your alley.
Set in 2052, you take on the role of JC Denton (JC supposedly refers to Jesus Christ) a rookie to an anti-terrorist organization called UNATCO. But things quickly get out of control and you are soon involved in a huge conspiracy involving various factions - including the Illuminati and the Hong Kong Triads, as you travel over the world to unravel this conspiracy.
The game allows a great deal of freedom and various choices - you will also have a few multiple endings to achieve. Deus Ex is a branching game, meaning there are always multiple paths to choose from, you could even choose to not kill anyone at all through the entire game - which is a lot more complicated to do than it sounds, trust me!

Zeno clash a first person shooter game set in a crazy some what cave man style world full of mystery and oddity. Sit back and gaze a pone this beautiful word while trying to not die by suicidal squirrels with bombs strapped to them.
Game Play: 8
The game play over all is a typical shooter for the most part. You get guns that you aim and shoot while running around. However this game adds in a nice elemental of first person melee combat. While this game is mostly about shooting than melee, The melee does add a nice touch to it but it also has it's own problems. While trying to melee it tends to feel off and a little clunky. However if you can get the melee down it's pretty fun. Some of the weapons you have are duel Pistols, a rifle, a crossbow, skull grenades, and more. Each has an alt fire that can be used. Pretty much like most other shooters it's mainly point and shoot not much else.
There isn't many bosses to fight in game. However this game has one of my most favorite boss fights of all time. You'll find yourself fighting a blind bounty hunter who sits on top of a dinosaur's head that is at least fifty feet above you. Who gives you a rift to make it far for you to fight him. He sits up there shooting down at you. While tossing down squirrels with bombs strapped to them to chase you around and blow up that you have to kick around and avoid. Yes... you did read that right... mother ♥♥♥♥ing squirrels with mother ♥♥♥♥ing bombs strapped to there mother ♥♥♥♥ing backs! How can you NOT like this boss fight! It is so odd but yet so much fun!
Story: 7
The story takes place in a fictional fantasy world called Zenozoik, and begins in a town called Halstedom. You play as ghat the protagonist of the game, You are running away from your home village after being hunted by everyone from there. You found out father-mother biggest darkest secret and now in fear of your life. With your girlfriend Deadra you both leave the village to trivial to the end of the world to find answers.
The story has a great build up. It makes you want to know whats going to happen, why you are being hunted, and what is this BIG secret that ghat know. However when it's finally revealed what it is, you kinda feel disappointed. You have this great build up of a story to be let down at the end.
Graphics: 9
The graphics really sets the mood. Each level you go to has it's over style and feel to it. The last level you where just in doesn't look like the one your current in. Each level feels different and fresh while keeping to the primal cave man feel of the game. The graphics are all over the place from bright looking to dark. Some how it all works out nicely. You get a real sense of this world.
To be honest, the world to me feels like Alice in wonderland but cave man style. You have such a massive world with crazy looking characters from humans, to animals, to each scene. The graphics really sets this game up nicely. I can not express how much I love the graphics for this game and just how it all comes together to make this world. It's a pretty unique experience. To me this what really makes game shine the most.
Music: 8
The music does a good job keeping pace with whats going on. It helps to make the world to come alive with the background ambiance. The music does a great job to set each level up and keep it feeling unique as much as possible.
Final Though:
Even though the game play is like a lot of other shooters with some added melee. This game just shines when it comes to presentation of the world. You will find your self lost in this crazy mystical world. Wanting to see more of what this world has to offer. I was so immersed in the world alone just because how it looked and felt and with all the crazy characters you end up meeting just really pulls it together to make it feel so unique. I compare this world of alice in wonder land, though not as amazing as alice but it has the great mystical feel to it that keep you wanting more.
However like I said before it kinda of falls off the story with a great build up with a disappointing ending. However the ending is better than some other games out there.
I find this game a good game to play for any one who like first person shooters. However this game IS weird and odd. If you can't get behind outlandish things you may find your self not liking this game.
I sat down and beat this game in one sitting. Took me roughly 6 hours to beat it. So over all I would recommend this most to most people.
Also...mother ♥♥♥♥ing Squirrels with mother ♥♥♥♥ing bombs strapped to there mother ♥♥♥♥ing backs!
Final Score: 8

Sigh...you know, I bought this game on a steam sale and didn't play it until months later.  The hell was I thinking?!  This game, and by extension DYA, their studio, is an excellent arcade machine.  This is a nice Wild guns style game where you are moving and shooting things on a single screen.  Kill enemies until the boss appears, then destroy them.  Rinse repeat.  The game is fast paced and when you die, which you will, it restarts instantly, never having you fall into a lull with no action.  You have plenty of weapons and chances to use them and it's engrossing in short spurts.
That's the key.  This is an arcade game and in short spurts, it's excellent, fun, and has a surprisingly fun story.  DYA goes all in with all its games with voice acting and storytelling which, love it or not, is pretty impressive.  This is a fun 30 minute to an hour game that you play, put down, then play again later for a rush.  It's not long, but it is fun and defines, for me, retro done well.
If you want immersive, beautiful storytelling and design, go for Supergiant.  If you want charming narrative with a dark, witty world, go to Failbetter.  If you want a spectacular arcade game, go to DYA.

I really tried to like this game, but it failed again, again and again.
I am a biased player. Positively biased, being one of the first supporters of UnEpic.
I remember how Fran spent few hours mailing with me and drafting debug tool over and over just trying to nail the bug that was encountered by 3 players out of his playerbase.
That dedication to quality of product I worshipped and brought this example in conversations with other people dabbling in gamedev on numerous ocasions.
However, no dedication to the game itself nor quality I see in Ghost 1.0.
Now lets break it down, shall we?
1) Gameplay is boring and easy
I completed the bloody thing on hard difficulty and I found it to get more and more easy the further I went.
Abosolute lack of skill was required even at the final battle - all I had to do is spam healing and jump around like a madman while holding down the left mouse button.
You are dishing so ridicilous ammounts of damage and such wide arc, that aiming is no longer required - you always hit at least 5 enemies as long as you hold down the fire button.
2) Secrets are nightmare
This is just ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. In order to get access to secret in a room (which are souls, that just kinds start floating around if you trigger them - and which is also never explained) - you need, as mentioned above, trigger their appearance by doing something very specific. And this little something can vary between "stand over there" to "control that bot and kill those enemies in that specific order". Or open your main menu. Or de-equip your powerups. Or crouch for some time without moving. Or whatever you can possibly think of.
Are there *any* clues to which action is required? Nope - just keep doing random ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t until it is triggered.
That is not a puzzle, that is just simon says without actual toy.
3) Skills.
First of all, their description explains jack♥♥♥♥♥♥ The one and only game who does skill description worse is Overwatch, describing Genji's ultimate ability as "unleashes a deadly weapon".
Second of all, a decent chunk of those skills are utterly useless.
And keep in mind impossobility to respec your skills, while you are able to aquire only ~35% of tech tree. Also knowing nothing of what they actually do. Have fun.
4) Game gets veeeery undercooked near the end.
I suspect that Fran was running our either out of time or money. Possibly both.
There are *glaring* problems with end-game content.
My favorite example being is
.
There is absolute blackness for four minutes with some dialogue. Absolute. Bloody. Darkness.
No visual aid at all. Previously game was kind enough to give us a loop of 4 frames for something like that, in that case it is just utter darkness.
Also, lyp sinc is gone. Plot is obvious, ending is rushed and dull.
5) Platforming is frustrating
Especially part in
. I felt like I was playing unfair mario - dying over and over again on the same jump just because I was few pixels short. When that did not happen - horrible controls came in play, which brings us to the next point.
6) Controls are horrible and humane rebinding is non existant
While in combat all is required is just to jump and shoot - it is not *that* relevant since, well, it is not a whole lot of buttons you need to use at the same time. However, if precise platforming is required - and by precise I mean that you will need to be a bloody jeweler with microscope by hand, you will note those flaws very, very easily - most annoying being unable to rebind duck-n-roll to sensible and comfy shift button. Instead, you are forced either to fiddle with movement controls manually, which is not an option when precision and speed is required, to bash any letter on the keyboard *while* you are required to keep hands on WASD and mouse, or stretch your left pinkie all the way to Ctrl. I went with last one and my pinkie was literally achign when I was done with that madness of duck-n-rolling.
Summing it up -
I did have fun with it for first few hours.
Then it all went just straight to hell.
I fail to recognise work of a developer I respected as creator of quality content.

Eugen System's spiritual sucessor to (the woefully underrated) Act of War fell short with its lackluster solo campaign and confusing pace. With three vastly different factions to play in skirmish and multiplayer, the poor unit readability and fussy tech tree made the learning curve needlessly steep and will bounce off both RTS newcomers and veterans alike
Most of these issues are thankfully alleviated with the streamlined Reboot Edition. The story was amazingly well done.  Through the grind (not necessarily necessary -- get to it in a later point), the story was a very strong driving force to finish each and every boss battle.  Finishing each boss battle required amazing consistency on hardcore mode and the payoffs were enough to justify each hour long attempt; each failure after failure.  The bosses are well put together with specific movesets and each requires a certain strategy.  Hardcore mode requires extreme consistency as a successful boss battle may take ten minutes without ever grinding for levels.  Fidget is just about the best companion character that anyone could ask for and compliments Dust very well.  The twos' relationship arc feels very natural and the air of mystery surrounding Dust's identity really immerses you in the experience, seeing the world through Dust's eyes.  Fidget's sassy but timid personality provides nice moments of both emotion and comic relief.  This game is something you need to play to understand and the story makes that all worth it.  Even a play on casual would be interesting -- although the game loses depth on casual as the game auto heals, lacks any real danger, and doesn't allow selection of character upgrades.  Just play on normal if you're only in the game for the story.  The fighting is amazingly crisp and the combos and dashes allow for a skilled player to shine versus a regular button-masher.  The learning curve is very low along with a high skill ceiling and a medium-low skill floor.  The currency in the game is provided at enough of a rate to just barely scrape you by and still have a lot of intensity between strung out save-points.
My only few gripes with this game come from the icicles, bubble sprouts, and enemy 'spams' in combination with those (I say spams in apostrophes because they are tactically placed, however, practical).  Although the combat is crisp, the icicles and bubble sprouts
destroy you for a long time on hardcore mode.  They are essentially random.  Also, a word of advice:  Don't destroy all the cannons like an idiot.  I did that because I thought it was necessary and it turned out to just be tedious.  You'll know the part I'm talking about when you get there.
About the grind:  I chose to not grind levels and only continue with the main storyline.  I also skipped killing most of the enemies through an exploit mentioned below.  The game on hardcore mode took me around 16 hours to finish doing no side missions at all.  My boss battles consisted of me taking away 200 to the rare 600 hit points per combo out of a pool of 40000 to 240000 health.  If one were to actually complete the side missions I assume that these battles would be much easier/less time consuming.  Also, almost all of the enemies in the game one-hit you on hardcore; you were warned.
The use of foreshadowing and subtle hints in order to remind the user of saving and various bits of the story verging on breaking the fourth wall and are absolutely fantastic.  Throughout the story, the player will most likely develop an attachment to the characters in the story through their believable personalities and excellently fitting voice acting.  The use of several motifs perfectly placed throughout the story add to the immersion and magnificence of the story.
I have a couple nit-picky things to say:  Dust's main dialogue stance (with his hand out and pointing) is unfitting and awkward at times.  Additionally, (light spoiler)
.
This is very specific, however, if you down+jump (go down a platform) on the floor with many enemies and moving platforms in Blackmoor Mountains right after your first elevator between screens you fall through the floor, becoming softlocked.
Overall,
is an amazing, well thought-out masterpiece of a visual novel and game that you should most certainly consider playing.  The 96% positive reviews are well-earned and well-deserved.  This game really captures the magic of what rpgs should be and brings the point home through its amazing story and masterful controls.

I have to recognize that I have some bias towards this game.  The creators first game (Unepic) was really enjoyed with hours and hours of time, and this game was watched and followed.  A friend saw my interest and picked me up a copy the first day it was out, and I've been enjoying the game immensely.  While I'm only into the second zone, game play has been both experienced and watched.
I like the game.  This has been an enjoyable experience of slowly gaining power to defeat the enemies.  This game is definitely worth the price, and looks great.
Combat:  Combat is fun and precise.  I use a mouse and keyboard and enjoy the feel of running, jumping, shooting, and rolling presented in the game.
Upgrades:  Experiencing 7 guns, 5 items, 4 geek secrets, 10 upgrades, and 5 skill points I've enjoyed the leveling scale.  Items and upgrades feel appropriate with easy gains giving small benefits (example, collecting all souls in a room may provide +10 max health).  Expensive upgrades like guns definitely feel worth the price.  The skills provide a good choice variety where the people I've seen play pick different options then myself.
Platforming:  Depending on your preference, this may be considered a weak point.  Enjoyed the platforming, but many are placed at an interval so that you need to be precise in your jumps.  The game does offer a double jump for a skill point that greatly mitigates this challenge.
Bosses:  Uniquely challenging, bosses have good variety and change patterns at specific health levels.  Adds a fun learning curve to the game.
Story:  While interesting, the story takes a passenger role to the game.  In some games, I've wanted to go farther to accomplish a goal.  In this game, searching and defeating enemies to get stronger is far more of an objective.  For me, I only remembered the story when it reminded me.  It wasn't jarring or unwelcome, just I enjoyed the game play so much that my goals played less of a reason for me to play/continue.
Visuals:  Main visuals are on par with expectation, but there is a lot of secondary visuals that make nice touches.  Reflection on glass in background, glowing trails, interesting backgrounds.  It shows a lot of time went into the game.
Secrets:  Unepic style... Even though you can choose a guide to help you know what rooms secrets are in, finding them is still a challenge and sometimes seems unfair.  If you enjoyed how Unepic employed secrets, expect no change.
Things I wish I'd have known earlier.
So.... at the risk of ruining some discovery, I feel it would be an advantage to know some of the following points.  I feel these are important points that I was actually annoyed at the game for not better explaining.
1)  Health is rare, and you do not regenerate at save points.
Work on learning how you will get health, it’s a precious commodity.  Note there are repair shops.
2)  Items are reusable, even health kits.
You will find various items in the game that you can use.  Once used, they don't go away.  You can recharge all items via specific shops.  The more items needing recharged, the more expensive it is to recharge them.
3)  Cubes degrade over time.
Easily discovered, enemies and crates drop a currency called cubes.  Every few seconds, these degrade in value.  At the beginning of the game, they drop with a 10 value, and degrade to 1 if you wait too long to pick them up.  A good way to prevent sniping in the game since you want to kill enemies at a closer range to get your money's worth.
4) You loose your cubes upon death
So... you don't get your money's worth if you die though....  This adds great incentive to be careful.
5) You can pickup souls in "ghost" form.
Everyone, go back to the first boss room and pick up the souls you missed.... You'll thank me for it.
6) When using mouse, scroll wheel will switch weapons.
Not sure how embarrassed I should be here, this took until first boss to figure out.
7) Breakable walls take damage.
You can tell if a wall is breakable if it takes damage when you shoot it.  It will usually take more then one shot to break.  Watch carefully when checking for secrets.
Good luck everyone and enjoy the game!!!

Oh man, where do I start? First, I'm a FF7 fanboy, and in all honesty I remember thinking [at 11, mind you] that the story got kind of weird somewhere from the middle to the end, but I'm so glad I've replayed it. I honestly think they took a dynamic from FF7 [I can't say which without TOO much of a spoiler] that people showed they wanted more of, and they basically made this game the epitome of that. It can get a little over cheesy sometimes, but it does help get their point across. I cried a total of two times during this game [Don't hate], one being the ending cinematic. Frankly, that is the hallmark of a great game, to illicit such emotions from the player. It does kill me, hoping that the video camera's battery would last a bit longer, just to show a bit more of our heroes, and i was sad for it to end. I also think that this Final Fantasy had the best start of any that I've played [And trust me, I've played almost all excluding the ones past 12]. For me, personally, FF8 will now be remembered as one of the best stories in a Final Fantasy. I honestly thought I never felt these emotions with any modern game as a result of my long list of experience in RPGs, but no, it's just none of them give you the feels like these "retro" ones.
TLDR : Sound 7/10 [ Yes it's Midi, but for Midi, they made some awesome scores, but -3 for it's dated feel]
Story 9/10 [It gets kind of akward in some places, but you can't help but be drawn in by it's personalities]
Replayability 7/10 [Lengthy game to replay, but so much extra stuff to do if you want that perfect game; I'd replay for story though]
Visuals : 5/10 [FF8 went for more of a realistic look, which at the time was interesting, but if you play on full screen you can count the pixels. There are many mods that change this, but the vanilla game looks pretty bad. With mods, I made mine a 7/10 ]
Characters 10/10 [They really bring these personalities to life, and you can see the rite of passage as time goes on]
Overall 9/10 [Great game with a couple quirks, perhaps even some dialogue that could make you roll your eyes, but as i said before, the characters are easy to fall in love with. One of the best Final Fantasies of the series. If Story and character dynamics are important to you, this game will come through.

It's a good game, every bit as fun as I remember, but I wanted to offer one criticism of the experience through Steam so that prospective buyers are aware:
Controller support is terrible (though there are a few mods out there that make it bearable).  If this game is ever re-optimized for PC, I hope that modern controller layouts are a priority.  Without mods, buttons are referred to as B1 - B10, so you'll have to experiment and find a scheme that works for you.  I know it's an old title, but Steam warns that this game should be controlled by a keyboard as a default.
-On a separate but relevant point, I can't get my Xbox360 controller to work AT ALL through my SteamLink for this game (works fine for other titles).
One big PRO of this re-release on Steam is the Magic Booster you can use in the game's startup menu.  It grants you 100 of many lower level magics, which saves new players a lot of early game grinding for spells and junctions.
Community mod support is robust, though as with all modded games there is potential for trouble.  I've had a few battle backgrounds that don't exist so it looks like I'm fighting in black space, but other mods do well to give the game that much needed graphical boost.
If you're a fan of the series or a nostalgic gamer, I still recommend FFVIII, but be wary of controller support if that's your preferred play style.

It feels like Metroidvania games have had a small resurgence on Steam lately, with games like Rabi-Ribi bringing back feelings of Metroid and Castlevania, despite the original franchises not being treated well by their owners. Luckily, the creator of UnEpic has brought a great little game that understands the strengths of the genre. Now only are there secrets left, right, and pretty much everywhere, but it's fun to explore the environment and to watch the small details that the developer put into the environment. Combat is chaotic, as the randomness of enemies and level design puts you behind the 8 ball at times, as you dodge the reasonable amounts of bullets and threats that the game throw at you. It's the variety that may be the strongest here: and that hits all elements: level, enemy, and boss. Bosses are a spotlight: they are what they should be in this genre: tests of your skills up to that point. And the developer is very responsive: In fact, this review got delayed a day after one of my large negative complains about the game (which I didn't communicate by the way) was fixed. The only real major negative that I have about the game is simple: it crashes a bunch. There seems to be a memory leak if the game is left on for a period of time. But regardless, this is a greatly constructed and well crafted story on top of some great gameplay, and it definitely earns its price of admission.

-A.I that is still pretty much the best seen in a fps game, with enemies that react to your avtions, flank, communicate and scale well with difficulty.

FF VIII is a title I missed out on as a kid, so I bought it now to finally experience this story.
It will definitely offer much content for the player to go through. As with all FF titles there are plenty
of mini-games and side-quests, which all grants valuable and powerful items, so there will be many hours invested in this game. One of the new elements, is that FF VIII do not follow the casual road of the series and is very different in some areas.
There are no level system as we are used to, instead every character always need 1000 exp in order to level up, where in previous titles, the required exp would gradually increase per level. The level system in this title is used to determine which level the monsters are, and what SeeD missions you can undertake (one of the side-quests).
Players will instead rely on a new system called Junctioning. A system where character equips and buffs themselves with magic, summons and moves.
Magic is not learned, but 'Drawn' from monsters, which makes it possible to stock up on 100 Triple + 100 Curaga. Stocked magic is then used as usual, with the character using the chosen magic move.
Summons plays a big role in this title and has it's own system, where you have to spam X to increase it's % damage output.
Also there is only about 2-3 chests in the game...
PROS:
FF VIII offers almost infinite amount of gameplay. You will be busy getting the best gear, solve all mysteries while you adventure together with a friendly crew. The graphics are alright and I had no issues what so ever with how it looked. I liked it. Battles are always a challenge, unless you prepare yourself properly. So you will never get bored of killing bosses too fast. I ran into trouble with both Bahamut and Griever, even though I thought I was well equipped.
You will experience a new, more modern take on the Knight & Sorcerer tale, which is interesting and kept me asking questions throughout the game. The characters had GREAT dialogue and the bonds that happens between them is a joy to watch and follow. I was really fond of Zell and Selphie, who is two great characters that really adds to the game.
You of course not be cheated of the chance to capture a chocobo, which has is its own little (big) mini-game. Get busy and train that chocobo, so you can get some delicious items. I really enjoyed the chocobo part, even though it got tedious sometimes, but I can't have a game with no chocobo training.
At a point, when you have more time and the tools to explore, you will have a lot of things to do and stuff to get.
Again endless amounts of things to keep you busy.
This is purely my opinion and you should only read this when you have finished the game yourself. It is worthy buying, despite these cons.
CONS:
I personally did not find the cast of characters too interesting. They had great personalities and dialogue, so this is based purely on how they look. Boring. I hated Zell's stupid tattoo, but I really enjoyed his personality and he got to be one of my favourite characters. Yet when I play a FF title, I really look forward to their appearances. Sadly few characters stood out, and most had little fantasy elements and more a stale citizen look.
I absolutely got to hate the GF system. Every single time I had chosen and equipped my fav team, I had to change characters out and re-arrange everything. In all FF titles you will most likely loose a teammember for a certain amount of time, but in FF VIII it just happens ALL the time. Some will certainly love this system, as it grants them much control of how exactly to buff their characters, yet I did not enjoy this.
I really missed the chests in the game.
SPOILER ALERT!
For the FF Nerds only:
I really liked the story and found it very interesting, yet I really found it rushed and some points in the game made zero sense to me at all. For example when the Sorcerer kills the president in front of all those people and they just cheer at her. I know it is her mindcontrol and such, but I really think the plot was rushed and had holes in it. FF VII or FF IX had just as good stories, but they were told and experinced much better, and I felt I knew exactly what was going on and it all made sense. Like the bond between Squall and Rinoa happens extremely fast. Like in the beginning she is not that visible, and suddenly she is extremely important and so on.
All in all: Buy the game!

Was totally excited for this game when it came out.  I had played table top games like Eclipse and although I love table tops very much, the setup time and waiting for everyone to take their turn can add up fast.  I was pleased to find out this game operates in real time.  No mess to clean up afterwards either!  The graphics are nice, the music is neat and the game runs incredibly smooth.
However, the problem started when after I conlized a few planets and took a ton of turns, I realized the game is very bland and empty.  There doesn't seem to be much to do, and the upgrade paths aren't really paths as much as they are things you have to get in a fashion you can't choose.   It doesn't feel the same way as other strategy games, where you can focus on upgrading certain paths for units and tech.  It's more like, "Hey, these are the next three things you can research, and you can't research anything else until you do these".
The game is also vast and has tons of planets and moons which you can collect resources from and sometimes colonize, but even colinization is quite lacking as it's upgrading tiles and building a ship port.  I was under the impression there was more to it.
Maybe this game will improve greatly in the next coming months, who knows?  I'd love to fall in love with this game the same way I did with table top space games.
