FEAR is a weird time capsule. It's simultaneously both a Half-Life school, story driven immersive FPS with outstanding tech for the time and an old school revival, balls out action game in the vein of Painkiller and Serious Sam. Throw in John Woo/Matrix fetishism, Tom Clancy tacticool special ops and horror influence from Hellraiser to The Ring and you have the very mid 00's hodgepodge that is First Encounter Assault Recon.
Despite this weird stew of disparate, often clashing, elements, FEAR manages to stick the landing on the one thing that matters most in an FPS: FEEL. FEAR has just the right weight, just the right impact, just the right sound, to make the combat feel incredible. This is in large part due to the the signiture slow-mo mechanic that allows you to bring time around you to a crawl and pull off some of the baddest♥♥♥♥♥♥ever commited to video games. ♥♥♥♥ing throwing a grenade, slide kicking a guy onto the ground, shooting the grenade in the face of three other dudes as you tear someone behind you in half with your shotgun. THE SHOTGUN. Perhaps the most satisfying weapon since the BFG 9000. Not just that, though. The dual pistols, the auto rifle that fires giant stakes that pin people to walls, the weird lighting sniper weapon that skeletonizes dudes. Even unarmed you are a beast with flying drop and slide kicks to knock people to their death.
But this isn't just a cakewalk power fantasy. On normal and higher difficulties you have to plan and you all your resources effectively. FEAR's AI was revolutionary for its time and is still some of the most active and clever out there. Enemies will respond to your flashlight. Suppress and flank you. Retreat and ambush you. Beyond the basic soldiers are spidery assassins that stalk you and heavily armored robots that are genuine threat. While not quite at Silent Hill levels, ammo is relatively limited. You are encouraged to get to know all the weapons out there, as well as get up close and ultilize your melee capabilities.  Scenarios are varied and the level design has a verticality to it, forcing you to examine the environment to find the best route to get around enemy forces and unleash your bullet time death wave.
Outside the combat is where the game suffers unfortunately. Between combat scenarios are stretches of linear exploration interspersed with exposition via audio logs and radio calls, creepy anomalies and jump scares. Despite the excellent high contrast lighting which still looks very good today, the environments are very bland and repetitive. Mostly offices and industrial areas without any character or real sense of being lived in. The game is definitely at its worst when it tries to get spooky. Again, despite its technical strength, the atmosphere is just lacking. And then they try to get you with the eiree ghost girl popping out of nowhere as you go around a corner, but it really isn't effective because of how cheap it feels and how often they do it. The horror elements just feel out of place in a game whose strength is the exhilaration of the dynamic combat. The narrative tries to tie two halves of the game together with a plot about a shady corporation whose crazy experiment to create super soldiers and psychic super commanders went all Event Horizon, but it ends up just being an excuse and an afterthought.
Despite this, the core action gameplay is still some of the best of any fast paced shooter, rivaling DOOM (both 1993 and 2016).

This game feels like playing a cyberified Thief: The Dark Project (which is the best video game ever, in case you didn't know).
It has similarly expansive levels, where you can choose your own routes and there are plenty of neat things to discover.
It has the same open-ended gameplay: you can sneak around and take moments to take down a guard unnoticed, or you can go in guns blazing when your careful plan of infiltration gets foiled.
Yes, it also has the same stupid AI and ugly graphics, but the creative level design and the sheer 'immersiveness' of the game makes you forget about them in a few hours.
There are some rpg elements thrown into the mix as well (like dialogue trees, different skills to learn or customisable cyberware), which are always fun to play around with.
So what are you waiting for? PUT ON A TRENCHCOAT AND FIGHT SOME CONSPIRACIES.

So, this game is probably not for everyone, but I'm really enjoying it.

You build a galactic empire, starting from a single planet. You encounter other races, you can "uplift" some, or infiltrate some technologically inferior ones to take over, etc. There are so many options, so many ways to grow, that there are many different decisions you can make.
However, the game can bog down once you get fairly in and have completely mapped your area. At that point, you might have to start conquering whatever you can around you to keep expanding. That can get difficult and boring, but it's Paradox, so if you like EU or CK, you're probably used to that by now.  (And, in my experience, this is worse the bigger the map.  Try with the smaller maps first!)

I will always love this game, even though it's my third favorite in the Final Fantasy line, (FFVI, FFIX). I will always come back to it. I find it funny that I have a bunch of new releases on my Steam I've been meaning to play, yet I always end up playing FFVII instead, a twenty year old game that I've beaten twice already.
The greatest thing about FFVII that's unique to other FF games is the sheer madness that you can invoke with materias. Combining certain materia combinations will create ridiculously powerful results and make your party members into damage dealing gods. The materia system is definitely one of the best systems in a Final Fantasy game because of the vast amount of possibilities it presents.
For myself, getting to the end of the game is just the beginning, my favorite part of the game is mastering all the materias, breeding and racing Chocobos, defeating the weapons, maxing your character stats to 255 with stat farming, and making your party members insanely powerful.
I would definitely reccomend Final Fantasy VII to anybody who likes JRPG or FF games. Keep in mind, the game's polygon graphics are quite outdated (think Mario 64 with pre rendered backgrounds). But the true strength of this game comes from it's stellar gameplay, masterful storytelling, memorabe characters, and neverending replay value. Speaking of the story, FFVII is has one of the most involved plots I've ever seen in a game, the game has a ton of symbolism, and representations of many dfferent cultures. If you're going to play this, don't rush through, take your time, and enjoy everything it has to offer. And if you are an "Rpg fan," then you definitely owe it to yourself to play this at least once.

The Binding of Isaac is one of the most entertaining, engrossing, and enjoyable videogame experiences I have had in quite some time. At first glance, it looks like a simplistic clone of The Legend of Zelda, but the real meat is hidden by the mashed potatos. Once you start it up and really start playing, you'll find first that the game is fairly challenging, and then you'll find that it is crazy  FUN.
BoI is a game w/ a nearly infinite replay value. Each time you play you choose one of six characters that start off w/ different stats (shot power, speed, shot speed, shot range), and one or two different items. Each floor/level is randomly generated, as are the items you find along the way. And I can't strees this enough, but the items you find along the way forces you to drastically alter the strategy you use, as you can't approach enemies the same if you are shooting tears or firing off bombs from your mouth. And therein lays the glory of this game, it truly is different each time you play, and due to the difficulty, completing a run through is a rewarding experience.
There really isn't much like this game out there right now, and I really urge anyone that enjoys videogames to give this game a chance(or, even better, Rebirth which is a total remake of BoI and it's xpac, w/ some new additions, and is due out first week of Nov). Don't be put off by the low price, pixelated art style, or flash engine, it is a unique experience that will give you hours upon hours of fun.

WARNING! These are initial impressions. Opinion subject to change (though at this point I highly doubt it).
This game is a bullet hell through and through, merciless at every turn. While enemies in the levels are static, their attacks are absolutely not. Everything is aiming at you. Figuring out how to avoid their attacks is an absolute necessity in this game. From time to time in each level a robot will fly around; you can shoot it to get your weapon powerups and one of your four hearts back. These are not only key to your success, their timely distribution is a large part of what makes this game challenging and fun to play- they come in at set intervals, give you set powerups, and if you're not paying attention you'll burn right through their usefulness without doing anything. The biggest thing to note about this game is that you are constricted to a 2D axis of movement (left and right), but your aiming can lock on, allowing for a much greater complexity of attack.
Which brings me to my biggest (and pretty much only) complaint I have with the game. The lock on feature is a very awkward beast to get a hold of- it may not always lock onto the enemy you want, though it is generally fairly predictable given you take the time to position yourself correctly. Locking on is confined to a single button, and you cannot select what it will lock on to, only influnence that by moving closer to/more directly in front of the enemy you wish to target. It's does automatically start targeting the next enemy, though enemies will often bunch up in levels to make themselves harder to hit. As you can imagine this makes chaining lock-ons just a bit awkward. Locking on (like almost everything else in this game) is not instant and so in general by the time you've reacquired your enemy you've likely lost some health. It's not impossible to mitigate, just quite frustrating in parts.
That being said, the rest of the game's mechanics are designed in an extremely intelligent fashion. You generally have three options outside of normal movement to avoid projecties- you can slash at them when they're in range of your saber, you can press up against the barricade (provided enemies haven't destroyed it), or you can roll out of the way (invulnerable to attacks during it). All of these have weight and consequence. The same goes for switching weapons- each enemy has a different resistance to each type of weapon, though a few well-aimed shots from your default weapon will generally make paste of whatever you aim it at, unless it's big and bulky or a boss enemy. None of the powerups works well against all enemies, and your default gun can only ever hit one thing at time, so switching your powerups are essential to finishing the level. It all forces split-second decisions and hairpin timing- this game has a ridiculously high difficulty curve until you learn the levels and enemy patterns.
Lock-on system issues aside, this is absolutely a solid game and I couldn't recommend it enough to fans of shmups and bullet hells.

I think this is one of the better Call of Duty games. Probably my favourite next to Call of Duty 4: Modern Warfare. Sucks that this game doesn't go on sale often, but I definitely got my money's worth when I bought it at around $50 CAD. (~450 hours in multiplayer and ~110 in campaign/zombies, all DLC owned.)
First the campaign mode. I think it's a really unique campaign set in a really interesting time period. Like most of the Call of Duty games, the gameplay is very linear and repetitive, and ramping up the difficulty only results in a mindless, unfair ♥♥♥♥♥how of trying to stay alive. Putting the gameplay aside however, I found the story to be really good. There were some great cinematic moments in the campaign, a really neat plot twist, some great locations and overall solid story.
The zombies mode is pretty fun. Even though I mostly played it to get the achievements, it was still fun to play the maps on solo. I do find the two-hit-to-down system kind of unfair though; it really♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥me off in a lot of moments when i didn't have Juggernaut, or a zombie just performs a double hit. But overall, the maps the base game come with are fun.
The multiplayer is great. Fantastic maps, actual dedicated servers (meaning, community servers with a server list), great weapon balance and variety (though shotgun and sniper selection is pretty meagre) and mod tools. Occasionally, there are performance issues, but most of these were at launch and have been dealt with. It was the first Call of Duty to include customization of it's kind (with emblems, face paint etc.) and theatre mode which is awesome. There is still a very active and healthy population too.
Overall, I'd give this game a flat 8.0/10. It's a great package; solid campaign, fantastic multiplayer and fun zombies mode. In terms of DLC, I guess I would recommend buying them if you are really into zombies and multiplayer as all of the DLC maps for multiplayer were really well done, and the same goes for the zombies maps. They are pricey, so I would get them on sale. I'd probably give each a 7.0/10.

Incredibly solid metroidvania style game with a unique, satisfying, and at time challenging combat system. Moving between different enemies and racking up your combo is great, all while using moves to evade attacks and magic attacks to clear the screen and keep your combo going. Every level is unique while still feeling like a part of the setting the game creates, each having great background art and complimented by the, for the most part, great animation of the characters on screen. Obviously, more detail was put into the player character's movements, while enemies and NPCs sometimes move a bit stiffly. The actual fully animated cutscenes are actually very good looking, especially considering the kind of project this game was
My greatest critique of the game would have to be in your partner, Fidget. She is essentially Navi from Ocarina of Time, except every line she delivers is incredibly grating and unfunny, even if her character design is cute. In fact, most of the humor in this game feels like a mid-2000s furry webcomic, but thankfully the actual story itself reveals itself to be a lot more compelling and dramatic, even if the voice acting can be somewhat iffy.
A very well made metroidvania that manages to overcome bad writing and annoying characters to turn out to be a worthwhile experience for any fan of the genre

You have to compare Ghost to Unepic, the other game from @unepic_fran.  But I won't.  I'm a rebel like that.  It's just one of the many benefits of being a washed up fifty year old full of heart disease and gin.  I just don't give a ♥♥♥♥.
Anyway.  Ghost is a pretty sweet game.  A comparison I will make is to Symphony of the Night.  That was, for all of you youngsters, one of the best games ever made.  Wikipedia has it listed as being on thirty “best game ever lists”, and if there's one thing we know, its that being on a lot of lists is important.
Why!  Why would I compare this to such an amazing classic!  Oh, the wailing and gnashing of teeth!  Calm down you!  Comparison is simply “the act of looking at things to see how they are similar or different”!  I'm not placing Ghost on the level of such a timeless classic.  Or am I?  Suspense!  Carry on, dear reader!
You know, when I was a child, I was much younger.  That's irrelevant.  So why did I even write that?  We may never know.  What we do know, however, is that Ghost is a worthy entry into the metroidvania genre, giving us so many of the things that made SotN such a great game.  I haven't gotten far enough into Ghost to know if the castle flips upside down, but here is what I do know.
1:  The level design consists of rooms, and your map reflects the areas you have explored.
2:  Many rooms have replay value because you can complete them at an “alert level”, but do them again at a higher alert level for more challenge and currency.  Many rooms also have a secret in the “hidden souls” which give you various boosts and cosmetic upgrades.
3:  Aren't llamas weird?  What's with all that spitting?
4:  Interesting cutscenes intersperse the gameplay, making things lighthearted and joyous.
5:  RPG elements that you can choose improvements to your character, and in fact, to the dungeon itself.
6:  Many other things that I can't be bothered to write about, or haven't even seen yet.
So there you go.  I like this game a lot, but sadly, spend a good deal of my time at home in a state that leaves me unfit for games that require any amount of dexterity.  I still suggest this game though, provided you are not an avid consumer of Bombay Sapphire gin or equivalent, and also that you are ready to relive some old-school SotN action.  Four blurry thumbs up.

This game is really good. Like unEpic it has a certain challenge to it. Dodging traps, killing a lot of enemies, planning ways to try and not get killed. I have to say since I bought this game yesterday I have really enjoyed it. Especially for the 10 dollars it was selling for at the time of release.
What this game does really well is it keeps you on your toes in combat, Different enemy types shoot bullets differently so you find yourself jumping around a lot dodging this or dodging that to complete achievements. The combat feels really fast as you never find yourself standing there for very long.
The boss fights so far and keep in mind I am only just past the second boss. I do have to say these bosses are much more difficult than the first two bosses of unEpic. When I first started unEpic I was able to kill the first couple bosses without a problem, but in this game I have died several times to these bosses because making even the slightest mistake can get you in a perdicament since you are unable to reliably self heal like you could in unEpic with spells and potions. In this game you pretty much do not get healing which I really like, it forces you to be a better player.
Some of the differences between this game and unEpic are in my opinion not too big of a deal considering one was an imaginairy castle and this game takes place with robots on a space station.
Some of the differences are.
No leveling up which kind of bummed me out, I liked putting stats into different categories so that certain weapons performed better than others.
Ranged combat.
Less traps.
No multiplayer which bums me out but then again I never really had anyone to play unEpic with either so this doesnt really bother me much.
and a lot more places to save your game, In unEpic if memory servers me right you had one place to save your game. In Ghost 1.0 you have multiple places per floor to save.
So if you like a challenge and something that will keep you entertained for hours. I very much reccomend buying Ghost 1.0 It will feel like unEpic but more spacey.

The gameplay is top quality metroidvania fare, with a multitude of power-ups, new skills and over-the-top weapons, tons of hidden secrets to find, interesting boss encounters and areas, several difficulty levels (of which the hardest is challenging without being unfair) and two gameplay modes - standard metroidvania and a "roguelite" setting in which you mostly lose stuff if you die (unless you can loot your corpse). While a little twitchy, the movement and shooting is very smoothly handled, and feels great on mouse and keyboard.
Sound effects and music are well-done, although I've found the music a little limited, and it repeats often. The voice overs however are absolutely top-notch; I am really impressed with the performances these people have brought to the table. Lines are delivered with passion, and the characters are brought to life. As much as I generally don't like caricatures or silly humour (it's usually delivered poorly), these guys have done things justice in Ghost, with just the right amount of seriousness mixed into the inanity. Great casting work.
The graphics nail the feel of the futuristic space setting aptly, and the animated cutscenes are well drawn.
I'm only 10 hours in, but wow, am I enjoying this. Ghost 1.0 is incredibly polished, and made by people who clearly love gaming and pop culture history. Amazing work for such a small studio, well worth your money and your time.

Perfection.
That is the one word that I would use to describe this game.
ABZU isn't a game, it's an interactive experience. There is no way to die, and only a few times where you actually have to put effort into doing stuff. But that is okay, because the game takes on a different approach. Instead of frustrating you with puzzles and time based challenges, it lets you sit back and relax.
The game begins with you controlling a diver and exploring a vibrant ocean. There is no context why you are in this ocean, but it teaches you the controls and soon you are in the next area of the sea. The controls are bad at the beggining. I don't know if there is a way to remap in the system files, but in the menu, you can only invert stuff. Basically, A and D to turn, W to go down or up depending on if you invert it, and S to go up or down. The mouse looks and right click swims and left click is boost. I didn't play ABZU on a controller, so I'm not familiar with those controls, but I think I would have enjoyed it more with one.
How about the story? Well I'm not giving away any spoilers, just FYI. There is no text in the entire game except for the credits, and the story is mainly for you to figure out from paintings and stuff. There is a reacurring theme which helps you to understand it though.
Art. The art is great. It really is amazing. As you swim through jetstreams with fish circling around you. Or as you ride on the back of an orca and do flips over the ocean's surface, everything looks colorful and consistent.
Okay, great, so what are the cons?
Well, I would say the controls on keyboard are a tiny, tiny con, but that's why the steam page recomends a controller. Also, keep in mind the playtime is 2-3 hours, unless you are trying for a perfect achievement game. Other than, that I would say that it is an amazing game, deffinately one of my top five of all time.
So, if you are considering ABZU, I guess the big takeaway from this review is that you should buy it.
The End.

I remember playing this game in the early 2000s I think I played it the most out of all the Final Fantasies. I was searching YouTube one day and I came across some game theories so to get a better understanding of it I decided to get it on a whim. The game is as great and enjoyable as I remember it even though I played it all the time I always feel like it is a brand new experience. I grew up with it and have always loved it and my appreciation for it only grows as I get older anyway enough gushing you clicked this for a review so here we go.
Graphics: The game does look good it always looked good however sad to say upscale pre-rendered graphics do not hold up well the art though really well done does show its age as they can be blurred and through the sharpened quality you can see errors in the textures a lot easier. Character models however are very well done the pre rendered cut scenes are well made and are well shot and the in game sprits are smoothed out almost flawlessly (blocky Rhinoa legs anyone). Despite these gripes it in no way takes away from the full game. This is my first review so please give me your feed back so i can give you all better ones in the future.
Music: It's final fantasy nuff said the music is excellent and fits the game perfectly. There are scores that strike my nostalgia cords as well as my feels and never fail to get me invested.
Characters: Again it is final fantasy the characters are genuinely likable and compliment the story well except you Irvine stay away from Selphie you fiend she's mine!
Story: It is a well done story however around the second story arc it gets confusing but again what final fantasy doesn’t the story takes you on a journey that will have you locked in place until the very end though some of the story aspects seem clichéd by today’s standards they are however clichéd because they work.
Challenge: The enemies in this game scale up with you so as you grow stronger they will become more dangerous this is a welcome change or a really hated change from previous Final Fantasies depending on who you are. It takes a very good understanding of the Junction system to keep up with the difficulty curve you will undoubtedly find yourself getting smacked around with if you do not prepare well. SAVE OFTEN I can't stress this enough because sometimes this game can be downright frustrating and brutal at times but the payout is rarely not worth it.
Overall: This game was an excellent piece of work in 1999 and the port is an excellent piece of work almost 17 years later it holds up well and is very enjoyable to play with it has a romantic story and plentiful side quests as well as super bosses and hiddend summons that come with their own abilities that you can learn you will not regret playing this I give this game a solid 8/10 despite the clichés the brilliant twists, the musical score, the likable cast and a solid world to explore at your leisure make up for it. The game has flaws just like any other but it is well worth its asking price.

2/10 bad game is bad.
On the longer version, the quality of a Final Fantasy can be measured around 2 major things:
1°) Quality of story
2°) Quality of gameplay
I won't be talking a lot about the story, it is what it is, as far as I am in the game, i'm still not really impressed, but I wasn't that much impressed with the VII, so...
On the gameplay part though, the game is just plain bad. The whole system revolves around Geforces and associations. Which in parts is not bad, the general idea is good but in practice, it doesn't make for a good system.
First, there are no real limits on the casting of Geforces, so you could just spam invoke them to win fights (you can!), and they will take damages for you, so it's a win/win.
Second, the association system implies having specific spells in quantity in your inventory, so in theory, you shouldn't use them at all, otherwise you're just weakening your characters. If you do, you just have to draw the spells over and over again, which is a little tiresome.
The limit system also is kind of a letdown, the system to acquire them is ok, but to cast them you need to be low on HP, which... Well, why would you want to? Worst part is, the system is not even very clear on what is "low HP", sometimes, the health bar is yellow but you can't actually cast the limit.
There are a lot of those ideas that could make the game good in theory but just fail to achieve anything in the game.
You would better consider practically any other FF game, VII, IX and X...

Was totally excited for this game when it came out.  I had played table top games like Eclipse and although I love table tops very much, the setup time and waiting for everyone to take their turn can add up fast.  I was pleased to find out this game operates in real time.  No mess to clean up afterwards either!  The graphics are nice, the music is neat and the game runs incredibly smooth.
However, the problem started when after I conlized a few planets and took a ton of turns, I realized the game is very bland and empty.  There doesn't seem to be much to do, and the upgrade paths aren't really paths as much as they are things you have to get in a fashion you can't choose.   It doesn't feel the same way as other strategy games, where you can focus on upgrading certain paths for units and tech.  It's more like, "Hey, these are the next three things you can research, and you can't research anything else until you do these".
The game is also vast and has tons of planets and moons which you can collect resources from and sometimes colonize, but even colinization is quite lacking as it's upgrading tiles and building a ship port.  I was under the impression there was more to it.
Maybe this game will improve greatly in the next coming months, who knows?  I'd love to fall in love with this game the same way I did with table top space games.

Are you ready to play as a little boy who shoots tears at enemies while he tries to avoid/kill his crazy homicidal mother?
Well boy do I have a game for you!
The Binding of Isaac presents itself as a Biblical Reference and a killer rogue-like game all at once, and I must say the results are amazing. Now admittedly, this was actually my first rogue-like game after seeing so many other people play it. I figured “Oh it can’t be that hard, I could get through this in a few days tops.” But ohhhh no, this game offers so much more and if you think you’re good, you’re far from it.
The game is about a boy named Isaac, whose mother has the quintessential “Call From God” that tells her to kill her boy. Being the devout (albeit crazy) woman she is, she decides to follow through and in a desperate attempt to escape, our hero jumps into…the basement. What ensues next defies all logic and seems to challenge the player as to whether or not disfigured bodies and fetuses are cute or not.
The game focuses on simple mechanics, WASD to move and Arrow keys to shoot, Space for Active items and Shift for bombs! Simple formula, plus some badass enemies that may or may not be nightmarefuel is a winning combo in my books!
When you start off, Isaac (the player) wakes up in the basement of his house. Turns out, his parents somehow built their house on top of the Paris Catacombs or something because you just keep on going deeper and deeper. Each floor is compromised of a randomly generated map whose layout is different every time, the deeper you get, the bigger and more complex it becomes. The goal is make it to the boss room, defeat the (horrifying) boss and descend deeper. Because you know, that how little kids escape from their delusional parents nowadays.
Along the way Isaac will discover items spread across each floor that give him bonus abilities like shooting bombs or friendly familiars and even the ability to wear a Pope hat! Each item also transforms Isaac in some way, whether its good or bad is determined by the item itself, but I’ll be blunt and say that most of them are strikingly horrifying mutations that would definitely make growing up difficult for a young boy like Isaac.
Sadly though, when you die (and trust me, you will die) you lost all of your items and are forced to start from the beginning. Don’t let this discourage you though because I find this the main draw to Isaac. Now I’m not gonna go off and say that we’re all sadists and like to see a poor naked child suffer and die, I’m just saying that the game has so much draw in its simplicity that you have that gut feeling that the next time you play you’ll get better and better.
Design wise I feel the game is neither here nor there. It’s fairly simple and cartoonish but then again this is made by the guy who made Super Meat Boy so you assume it’s gonna be like that despite the tremendous amount of death. Since it’s rogue-like, don’t expect much map differentiation, thematically things change and sure the layout of each room changes, just don’t expect anything too widely varied. A pit here, a pit there, rocks forming a barrier etc etc. that’s about it. Enemy and character design is adorably twisted. Sometimes you think something is adorable one second and then terrifying the next, and other times (most of the time) you wonder what deprived monster thought up this creature your shooting with tears.
But on the music side I actually think its very fitting. I’m not much of a in-game music connoisseur myself, but i sometimes find myself bobbing my head to the somewhat metal, somewhat alternative tunes of the music.
If you’re one that gets easily frustrated and not much into randomly generated stuff, I highly suggest you turn the game down. But if you’re looking for a challenge and want to burn a few hours trying to get Isaac away from his mother, by all means buy the game!

Buy this game!
That is the first thing i need to tell you about this gem.
I bought this game in a bundle a while back and never really touched, forgot it and eventually found it again.
And in my despair of having too many games to know what to play, i gave it a shot.
And GOD DAMN that was one of the best decisions in my life, and you can be sure they are pretty rare actually.
The story is really decent. Nothing too new but nothing too old either. It is told very nice and i really felt the need to proceed and find out what happens next.
The characters are simply amazing. They fluently go from serious to hilariously funny without it ever seeming off. They are just authentic and lovable characters. I liked every single person i met throughout this whole game and wanted to help every quest giver as soon as they said half a sentence. Each of these persons was a unique character and none felt out of place. Whoever designed those deserves every penny you pay for this game.
The biggest problem i saw was the combat system. It is a classic side-scrolling Hack and Slash game and combat was fluid. The only problem is, that even though there were enough different types of magic, the game didn't force you to use them. So if you let it happen, the combat could get repetetive pretty fast. I never had that problem myself and enjoyed every second of slashing through mobs, that were designed so well i almost felt bad for them.
The game also presented a variety of levels of difficulty. The highest could get challenging without ever frustrating you as Dark Souls does, and the easier ones would be perfect to play with kids.
Now even though the game seems childish on the first look, i really loved it as 15 years ols teenager, and still do it as a 16 years old one. So i can only recommend this game and must ask you play it and spread the love, because this game and the developers definitely deserve more attention than they currently get. And yes i am aware they get already more than many others. It is still not enough.

I'm four or five hours in at the moment. I haven't finished, but I cannot put this game down. It is addictive as hell. It calls back all the best parts of Metroid Fusion, the GBA title, but adds in enough new gameplay twists and turns to be something totally unique. And the story and aesthetic of the game are very charming and original, I think.
The first half-hour of the game is frequently interrupted by cutscenes in typical tutorial fashion, but after that it flows quite smooth, only interrupting at well-placed stopping points and never for too long. That, and every cutscene is skippable without leaving you totally in the dark about what to next, in case pure gameplay is your bag.
My only real complaint is that the music is pretty samey and unoriginal; but it fits the tone and is in no way annoying. I only mention it because it's the only part of this game that isn't excellent.
Highly recommended to pretty much anyone, unless you hate combat platformers or metroidvanias.

NOT-SO-COOLS

Semi-open world, quasi-sandbox game about making profit from the land cultivation. No bloodshed, no thrills except of running out of money, questionable challenges... Yet, surprisingly, it's working as the game! Gripping with it's charming simplicity of the peaceful farm life and basic routine to make the day!
After trying Agricultural Simulator: Historical Farming recently, I was expecting everything bad from this game. Surprisingly, I was wrong. In fact, Farming Sim 2013 is really decent enough farming simulator - making you an operator of various farmers tools, starting from tractor with plough or fertilizer attached, going with mowers, harvesters, and even a trailer truck to get your stuff to the buyer.
You're not get your hands dirty there, there is no actual manual labor (except of picking up eggs, maybe). All that you're supposed to do is to dig up the ground, sow it, fertilize, harvest and prepare the new planting. All by using different vehicles and attachments. And you're not even have to do all those works yourself! There are always convinient farmhand to dig some earth for you. Also there are some passive income sources: bee nests, greenhouses and solar panels - in the end, Farming Sim 2013 can be quite a good idling game. Just plant some stuff here and there, leave it be, and after some days passed, voila! - you're a millionaire! And that's not even a joke.
As of downsides, the simulation is far from well-being and from reality in many aspects, starting from engine and physics, going with visuals, stupid gameplay challenges, unhelpful tutorials and so on. It is working - sure, but there is a big question, if you're gonna like it or not.
If you're not minding just riding the tractor across countryside, performing some basic tasks here and there - that's good point. If you were ever wandering, what all those variety of tractors and combines are made for - you'll get a proficient picture.
If you, however, play the games for thrills and hard challenges - that's not the right title. If you're gonna make yourself a farmer - you're not gonna find much useful info there, as well, as it's all not even covering the basics of the real farmwork.
Still, again, as a simulator of farming life - it's working nice enough. Peaceful game, with achievements to unlock and fields to harvest. My mark is 6.5/10.
PS: can't vouch for DLCs - they're pretty much the same, except of landscape

My religious missionaries discovered a planet populated by truly alien beings...they didn't even have exoskeletons!  They were so primative that they still were not united under a world government, let alone guided by the one true faith.  Our scientist-monks suggested we may learn from close but covert study of the natives, but once you've prodded one fleshy being, you've prodded them all.  Instead, I would send in the missionaries with heavilly modified bodies to infiltrate their governments and bring them into the fold "willingly".
After years of work (and one missionary deciding to "go native" and run away with a hoo-man), we finally welcomed the people of Sol into our benevolent family.  All was well, but there were some whom the light did not wholly illuminate.  I felt that the desire to bask in the light of community and follow the calling of One would bring them into line, but while I was concerned with distant battles with a breakaway sect, sentient crystal beings, and space chickens, the hoo-mans were organizing mass rallies and eventually the riots became open rebellion.  Our peace guard barred the doors of the Temple of Glorious One on Sol, and an expedition was rapidly raised, a huge army of Penitant Troops and an equally massive force of armed spacecraft.  We set out to right this wrong.
Once we reached Sol system, we received a last transmission from the Temple as the rioters penetrated its defences and destroyed it.  With heavy hearts I ordered the Penitant Troops to land and bring order to the lawless.  Upon reaching high orbit, the transports learned to their horror that the hoo-mans had built their own fleet in secret...nearly as large as ours...and taken command of the defensive station rotating around the planet.  Every transport blew or burned up, landing on the planet as scattered ashes, soon after followed by our great fleet.  Three corvettes and our War of Peace leader were the only survivors.
We had sought to bring the people of Sol into Unity, to teach them about our faith and higher technology.  In return, they doomed our own empire.  Now something...large...is coming our way.  It stretches across space and every star it passes goes dark.  We pray to the One, may She guide us...

At 54 hours in, I feel like I can properly review this.
I don't generally buy full-price games as I tend to sale-shop and find classics that I have missed, but I purchased this at full price primarily due to the commitment and work done on Cities: Skylines and the work allowed by *a publisher* (Paradox Interactive) to do the right thing.  I do distinguish between developers/publishers yet feel that I will give games a bit more runway when Paradox is involved.
I will say that thus far, they are performing exactly as I anticipated.  The praise for Stellaris is justified and the praise of the development team being committed is as well.  Paradox continues to allow resources to flow much more steadily toward continued development of a released game instead of simply abandoning the current product for a cash grab on "Stellaris II" or being completely focused on paid DLC.
With each update the game feels like the team has not only taken feedback but reviewed logs and gameplay stats to tweak the playthrough.  As of the Asimov patch, the mid-game has become more interesting, dynamic and engaging.  I would hazard a guess that we will see some more "events" occur to shake up the game with some bit of randomness as things move forward.
I will admit, I was tempted to go the new Master of Orion route initially just because I continue to have fond memories of MOO II.  That IP truly defined a genre and the work on the new release is tempting.  But this came down to recognizing that modern gaming is not just about getting it right at release.  It is about sticking around to make the game better even after you've taken your customer's money.  And in the end, that is where I chose Stellaris/Paradox.
Game is interesting enough AS IS and playable enough to keep me monkeying with things through several playthroughs.  Updates and potential for additional content just "appearing" like in Cities: Skylines (who turned out the lights?  When did it start snowing in here?) due to this being published through Paradox Interactive means I will give it some additional runway.
Right now, it is plenty intuitive (although the sector management took me a bit), enjoyable and interesting.  I haven't even started down the road toward some of the other races and philosophies yet.  I also haven't really made to the "end game" yet due to earlier missteps/restarts.  However, now with the latest patch I'm engaged more and the combination of game improvements and me simply learning the strategies better is leading this to be a much more enjoyable experience.
But don't get too cocky dev team.  I still feel like you could drop in some larger universe-effecting events.  Things that might require a large alliance or research treaties to overcome sooner than your opposition to gain an advantage.  And/or some broader effects of leaders dying or ships being lost to make it more "personal" via certain events (e.g. spouse of Captain Smith from Destroyer Devereoux lost at the battle of Apox has gained a following).
And don't think I won't pay for some DLC somewhere along the way, but really, just keep going.

First off. This game is a mix of two games, CK2/EU IV and Sins of a solar Empire. This isn't a RTS but also is. It is more of a kingdom management game with strategy elements.
Some things you need to know about the game before playing or purchasing -
-
. There is a research function in this game which unlock modules/parts for ships, open up building options for planets and many other bonuses which help you advance through the galaxy.
-
. Runs in a system close to EU and CK2, you have very little control and you rely on planning ahead to win fights. Like knowing what your enemy uses weapon wise or what their fleets consist of. You have 3 types of weapons to chose from and each have a special bonus to them, Lasers penetrate armor, Ballistics bust shields faster and have pen chance  and missiles NEVER miss where the other two can. Each of these 3 groups of weapons have subgroups with special abilities or rates of fire so there is a nice selection for ship building. You also have armies which you use in a siege system on enemy worlds. This is more to just occupy the enemy planets for warscore more than out right taking over a planet for your self.
-
. This game uses a system for war which uses goals you set before you go to war. You can chose from a list of goals which up the amount of win% you need to win the battle. To explain, if i want to just show my might, i can go to war for nothing, and end this war when i want but still do damage to the said person by destroying their ships and buildings, but i gain nothing from this unless i am a war loving faction. Or i can chose to make them my vassal, which will cost me a rating of 70-90% win score to gain that goal or force it on the enemy. Warscore works by winning or losing battles and damage inflicted on the enemy faction, so just win your battles and it will go up! Simple!
-
. This can go from simple to complex. Don't be afraid of this feature, many are but it can work out even for lazy people! And it is very simple and explains how it works to you in the building menu. You have a set power limit on parts and you have to try manage that power with parts that give power depending on the ships size slots. If you want to be lazy you can just pick the guns you want and then hit AUTO-FILL and it will pick out what you need and what it also thinks you can add to help out. Then you just name your ship what you want! Fun! Easy! And once you feel comfortable with it you will be making alternate ships to pad your stats for battle and make something which looks like it would lose, win a battle without a sweat (Like running a 1000 power army into a 4000 and winning because you have special parts which regen your health or shoot missiles out of the sky/space).
-
. You make allies and can even form them into a federation which lets you become a massive blob monster which will rule the galaxy, much fun and also very crazy managing involved to keep everyone happy!! This was a feature also in EU and CK2 so if you are a vet of this, just remember how empire forming worked and you know what it is like but on a little bit simpler scale.
-
. You can't take everything you see, which adds to the management side of things. You can't take every planet and inhabit them, which makes sense. You have to extend your influence on space and then build or just protect that space. Create sub-empires and oversee them while they pay you for letting them exist. This is something you WILL have to learn and look a lot into, it can be tricky but don't let that scare you from the game because it is so worth it once you get good at it.
-
. When and if you get the game, and you see no tutorial don't fret. The game comes with an inbuilt one which will activate and ask you if you want it on every match you start. So for new comers do turn it on and listen to some of what the AI has to say, some things will help you from screwing up hard early on, and of course this game does work off trial and error really in a way of management. YOU WILL FAIL MANY TIMES UNLESS YOU AREN'T NEW TO THIS TYPE OF GAME! So just sit back and enjoy your defeats, and learn off them.
-
. Chose from lots of weird alien types from bird creatures to slugs, boy there is a lot of choice here. For the furries there are lots of animal types like foxes and cats. Then you can name your federation name and race name. Pick the traits you want(little limited personally but i can see how they can expand it). Pick the type of government you want, be a god among your people, or a democracy, there are so many other types i couldn't even remember of course but they all have their benefits and problems! Also a flag maker, which is limited but the selection isn't too small, more colors would be nice but modders can fix that.

Stellaris serves two masters, in that it is both an introduction to 4X and grand strategy games, and a game from Paradox, known for the insane depth of games like Crusader Kings. This means that it isn't especially pleasing to either party; some of the late-game strategizing isn't as good as it should be, with clunky mechanics making it difficult to manage large empires, but not in terms of gameplay, only in terms of interface. Some of the early game strategizing is difficult to parse, with some obscure mechanics in warfare and economic mangement. Some things are tedious for no apparent reason, and the pool of possible anomalies is depressingly small compared to the possible scale of the galaxy. Combat is shallow, but initially confusing, which seems to be the theme in this game; there's enormous potential (and some great music), and I simply can't tell you to buy it at the moment. Perhaps someday.

Final Fantasy 7 is a very average rpg by today’s standards. I can see why people thought this was amazing back when it came out but still claiming that it’s one of the best rpg’s ever made I just disagree with. I think it’s mostly just nostalgia talking, this was my first time playing this game, I have played and beat Final Fantasy 4 and 6 before this and I do think that this game is slightly better than those, I thought those were very average as well. I find it very difficult to get invested and care about sprites on a screen or in this games case very low quality looking characters that can’t emote especially after playing recent rpg’s like The Witcher or Dragon Age. The poor writing/translation doesn’t help either. But there has been games like Chrono Trigger where I did like the characters and the story so I don’t know, maybe I just didn’t find the characters compelling in these games. I didn’t care in the slightest when a character died. In this game in particular I was so bored at the amount of time they spend on these drawn out backstories of Cloud, Tifa, Barret etc. These games do tell decent stories but I wouldn’t call them good, the journey these characters go on always devolves into having the stop the big mean bad guy which is ok because there is so many different ways you can tell that same story it’s just nothing too riveting. I also don’t like the pacing because of the amount of diversions the characters get thrown in, it feels like it’s done just to extend the length of the game it doesn’t feel like it has a purpose. I do like how each game tries to change up the world it’s set in though it keeps the games from feeling too similar to each other and I did like the setting in this game. The music was also pretty good the final boss theme in particular sticks out and it’s just epic. Moving on to the gameplay I’m not a fan of turn based combat, I think it’s very slow paced, boring and a chore especially when you have to grind to level up. I do like the turn based combat in FF7 more than I did in the 2d games but it still felt like a chore, I had to put music or videos in the background to keep myself playing during dungeons or when I was grinding. There are some sections in the game that were just very boring to get through like the gold saucer for example where you have to run around for quite a bit to find and where you have to go and what you have to do to progress. The mini games are so clunky and awful I wish they just didn’t bother. I don’t think this game is still worth playing today, if you are curious about it then I would say give it a try but if you are looking for a genuinely good RPG to play then no because by today’s standards I don’t think this game is good. I can’t see myself recommending this game to any of my friends, I have a few that tried it and couldn’t get into it and I checked my steam friends who own the game to see how many hours they put into it and the most I’ve seen is 3 hours. I think there are multiple rpg’s released every year that are more fun and better than Final Fantasy 7. I hope the later games in the franchise that I plan on playing get me invested.

Honestly, this is the only game I've ever played that I've been motivated to play more of solely because I wanted to find out what happens to the characters next, and that makes it a unique, interesting experience that I really enjoy.
Also, people will tell you FF6 is better, and I just don't get it. That's another game you play for the story, and while the dialogue is well done, the plot is split across 14 characters. Where in FF7 you take a close look at Cloud and his background, you don't take nearly as much time on any of the characters in 6. It's just spread too thin across all these characters, which end up not feeling fleshed out or engaging.

So... Dust: An Elysian Tail.
Well if I wrote this review at the end of chapter 4, I'd probably have a pretty glowing review.  It's a glorious looking game, that's well paced, has a lot of action, good variety, good leveling, and interesting story.
But then chapter 5 happens.  Dear god, I've never seen a final chapter like this.  Wait no, I've probably seen it too much, but so often it's in a crap game.  Instead Dust: An Elysian Tail does this in a good game.
Essentially Chapter 5 is a gauntlet.  Not off bosses (though that's a crap tactic too) not of the hardest enemies in the game, but just incredibly frustrating enemies.  The problem though is it's a VERY VERY VERY long series of levels, and the game seems to delight in just having this "big action scene" but instead of being in the background the player has to go through these fights, and they're annoying, so annoying I dropped the difficulty to casual, not necessarily because they were hard, but they were just so grindy and dull I wanted them over with.  Anything higher and you're going to get hit a few times.
Seriously, WTF developers? Why is chapter 5 drop everything great about the game and just get incredibly annoying.
Then you get to the final boss, now up to this point every boss is quite normal fight a single battle with a single life bar and you win.  The final boss?  You fight him across five life bars, four of them full life bars!   WHAT THE HELL?   and it's almost the same fight, almost the same location, just one or two more annoying moves.  The battle felt really good at the end of the first life bar, the second life bar was annoying.  The third was completely unnecessary, and the fourth felt like where the game should have ended, just with out the other three life bars.
Guys, you don't have to annoy the hell out of your games, I played 10 hours of this game.  I liked the game,  I want to rave about this game, why do you feel that you have to push me away at these final moments dude?
And then the game ends, the story ends and you get the credits.  But god there's a foul taste in your mouth.  You're done.  It's kind of like a girlfriend who doesn't want to break up with you because she's moving away so she becomes a royal pain so you'll push her away and won't feel bad.  Except that's the worst thing you can do.  Instead let us enjoy your story's conclusion bring us a great moment and end on a high note.  Literally this game is near perfect (though can get a touch too hard because of distance between save points in a few locations) up to this point but god, it's just such a bitter sweet ending.   Yeah I finished it, but what have I done to my appreciation of the game.
But all in all, I recommend it.  I recommend it in spite of the ending, and I shouldn't have to say that.
If you want a beautiful game, gorgeous art, excellent story (except for an annoying sidekick), brilliant music, wonderful animation.  This game has it all.  This is an exceptional piece of gaming..... until the end.   It doesn't ruin it's greatness before that point, but it could have ended so much better.

Tight controls, a wealth of abilities and an interesting narrative. Ghost is a great game that clearly inherits a lot of sensibility from Unepic-- but it has evolved in nearly every way.
Ghost's difficulty settings include traditional easy, medium and hard settings, but also include 2 modes of play- a traditional Metroidvania approuch (ala Symphant of the Night) and a roguelike setting that strips most of your powerups from you after you die, with a chance to recover some of them from your grave.
I've been wholly impressed with the balancing of the Hard difficulty: it challenges me without trying to prove some sort of 'I Wanna be the Guy' point. The Roguelike setting has proven interesting- creating a system of esclating risk and reward that is woven into the gameplay seemlessly.

Only at the first boss fight right now, but the game itself seems like a solid sci-fy spin on UnEpic. Its a fun metroidvania game with seemingly a lot to offer, although it does reuse a ton of UnEpic sounds.

FINAL FANTASY VIII plays very much like an interactive novel. While it is technically an open world game, this world is pretty much empty aside from the storyline. If you know that something like that will bother you, there is no reason to read on.
You will only like this game, if you like its story:
At the beginning of the game you are a young elite mercenary, who is just about to finish his final tests to become a full fledged member. This guy is antisozial, lacks understanding of his own emotions and has trust issues. The story is pretty much a coming of age story, with topics like taking on responsibility, friendship, first love, etc.. I would say the story is mostly aimed at 12 - 15 year olds. While it is certainly not an award-winning story it is not too bad either and it is always hard to treat those topics without getting too cheesy.

. And you will absolutley want this volume control after a few hours X).

I’ll start by saying Unepic was a game I enjoyed a hell of a lot of on GoG so when I heard about Ghost 1.0 to say I was excited is an understatement but it also meant I had very high expectations. How this game managed to go above and beyond will never be something I understand but I am eternally grateful. I think it’s safe to say i’m a bit of a fanboy for the Unepic dev team so bear that in mind going forward.
If you’ve read my other reviews you’ll know a good story combined with great dialogue makes me very happy and Ghost 1.0 really does have both of these. You play as Ghost, a strange ghostlike being who controls a robot chassis. Set in the future where robots are common, you have been hired by a large corporation (or so you think) to engage in a top secret mission where you find yourself sneaking into a space station to retrieve blueprints and data in regards to the latest most distributed android. Utilizing stealth and combat you’ll find yourself exploring, puzzling and fighting your way through the massive Nakamura space station. The story is very well written and the dialogue is witty and I find myself chuckling often without ever feeling it’s cheesy which is a very fine line in games.
If you’ve played Unepic then a lot of Ghost 1.0 will feel familiar to you, and if you haven’t (seriously, why haven’t you? Go and play it now.) then you won’t have to worry, everything is explained to you in a detailed manner and it should come to you very easily after that. You can play using either a controller or kb&m though I've found the controller doesn’t work as smoothly as some things just won’t work for me e.g rolling. You control Ghost, a spectral being in a robot body and must utilize your weapons and survival skills to overcome the various challenges you’ll face. Like other Metroidvania games you'll navigate from room to room clearing out the enemies or solving the puzzles, sometimes both at once.
Ghost has various abilities and weapons at her disposal along with various upgrades and powerups that can be found and bought through the game. There is also a large skill tree which you can level up as you please allowing you to mould the game to your playstyle. Weapons are Ghosts main form of attack and you can buy various different ones for energy cubes in the shops located around the levels equipping up to four at any one time. Along with your weapons you can also have 4 items bound to you hotkeys. Items will offer you small one time perks like regening a small amount of health or recharging your ammo immediately and they run off of charges which can be refilled at most shops. Lastly Ghost can find and buy upgrades which are passives which are automatically activated and cannot be turned off. These are things such as damage boosts or starting with extra energy cubes and can make you very strong as you collect more and more over time because not only do they stack, you can have an unlimited amount. Ghosts second main feature, and a personal favourite of mine, is the ability to posses other androids. This comes in handy for those buttons & platforms you might not be able to reach, but also is rather effective at clearing out rooms of enemies without taking any damage to her own exoskeleton.
Though there is no difficulty setting as such, there are two modes, Classic and Survival, which both differ in difficulty. Survival is more punishing and meant for those who prefer a bit more of a challenge whereas classic focuses on comfortable accessible gameplay.
The graphics in Ghost 1.0 are fantastic, and everything looks clean and smooth. I love the artwork overall but find myself really, really enjoying the cutscenes. The art in those scenes is very comic book-esque and it’s absolutely brilliant. In fact if the writer and artist got together i’m sure they could make an awesome little webcomic with ease.
The sound is fitting though I haven’t noticed too much of a soundtrack so far, not that I've felt myself missing it.
--- Engaging well written story
--- Great voice acting
--- Large variety of weapons, items, upgrades and powerups
--- Perk(s) if you own Unepic on Steam
--- Very witty/amusing dialogue
--- Probably the best Metroidvania style game I've ever played
--- AWESOME collectables aka Geekies for superficial ingame changes

The only other thing that could possibly be tweaked in my eyes is the amount of healing you find. Not every shop allows you to heal and healing is not easy to come by otherwise meaning you die alot. Since you lose your energy cubes when you die it can become a vicious circle of dying and not being strong enough to advance without buying but not having enough cubes to buy but not surviving long enough to get the cubes etc. Honestly, those are the only issues I can point out right now. I really am loving playing Ghost 1.0 that much so far.
Ghost 1.0 is amazing, it truly is and I can’t recommend this game highly enough. I’ve only put in a few hours so far but since it’s release it’s been the only game I've played. $10 is an unbelieveable price and it’s well worth every single cent so don’t even bother waiting for a sale. .
First, the port is very poorly made, there is no real attention to detail. Some examples include:
* The game minimizes itself when it starts and you have to re-focus the window.
* The game blocks you from using a gamepad right away and requires you to press a key in the beginning to proceed, bad UX.
* The battle transitions look terrible compared to the PS1 version.
* The game uses midi files for music when it is easily modded to play high quality OGG music. They were just lazy with this and it really takes a toll on the game's atmosphere if you don't use a mod for it.
* There is a constant distracting message "achievements synchronized with server" every time you draw magic from enemies, just because there's an achievement for it, but you can't turn this message off.
* When you have to do button prompts (there's a few quicktime events), the gamepad buttons appear as B1/B2/B3/B4 rather than icons, which can get confusing visually, if the event requires swift response.
* After you finish the game, you get a black screen, the devs made no effort to reset the game data and return you back to title screen, you have to manually exit the game via Alt+F4. It shows that they were not willing to do changes for better UX on the target platform.
The environments look great for its time, but the game suffers from a "short area" syndrome. There are many times that you'll enter a specific area that an interesting background/area caters only for plot and gives you no chance to explore. It is first apparent when you enter shops, you are greeted with the shop menu rather than an extra screen, so you can admire the aesthetics, which older games did, and this seems rather lazy.
There's also the opposite happening sometimes, like with the few sidequests, the game will start describing the area/scene with plain text instead of providing some more interesting visuals.
The
, with very little screens in them, often repeated and the game justifies it that it's a "maze" (Tomb of the Unknown King / Sewers) but feel rather linear. In one of them, you battle enemies every single step you make, and the dungeon screens repeat, making it extremely tedious & feeling like padding. There's no real sense of progress or reward.
The World Map looks interesting at first glance, but you'd have explored the 1st half by Disc 1, on Disc 2 you'd be running around past locations and a few new small ones. And by Disc 3 you'd finally reach the other Continent only to be disappointed that the place is nothing but a seemingly huge city with nothing interesting to do in it, and a few tiny dungeons that serve just for plot and an item.
One huge downside is that once you enter Disc 4,
. It tries to justify it with plot (and probably PS1 CD limitations back in the day to fit those large cutscenes), but that really takes out of the close-endgame aspect. In previous Final Fantasy titles, you are free to revisit past locations, find new secrets in them, do sidequests and other interesting things (battle challenges, play minigames, chocobo breeding etc.).
As such,
to be done. Forget field treasure chests with valuable items like in the previous games. There is only around 5-6 Items to be found, instead there are some Draw Points here and there that you can mine magic in set intervals, but nothing that feels truly rewarding.
Side quests are very few, you have your extra GF sidequest, a treasure hunt, a "find the UFO" quest, and a cute but tedious tamagochi-like Chocobo minigame. Most of them are really not interesting and feel forced so that "the game could have sidequests".
The game has
. Enemies now level up along with you which is an interesting concept, but not executed very well and often nullifies any grinding done to improve your characters' stats as the enemy level will always stay higher. On the flip side it is very easy to break the game by stocking up magic and junctioning them to your characters for big stat boosts.
Another issue is that the game does not guide you well through gameplay, a hint of this is that the very first shops in the game already offer you items that you won't need for a good while, like the item "Soft" that cures petrification status, which doesn't happen until much later in the game. A worse, more apparent problem is that
to try and explain its mechanics rather than putting the player under tests.
A major battle system change, which I am personally not a big fan of, was that now Magic are expendable and act like one-use Items (they do not require MP to use). As such, there is a lot of grinding to steal Magic from enemies that you end up junctioning to your characters and don't really want to expend. However it is now entirely possible to just spam GF (The game's Summons) and win every battle as there's no need for MP for them either. This change was unnecessary and
as the player feels like he has infinite amount of resources for a battle, as long as they just grind for Magic.
Money is not earned through battles. You can sell item drops/steals from monsters, but they don't sell for much til you reach Disc 3 portion of the game. The game relies on a Salary system which is based on your party's rank (how many battles you do, story choices, written tests), which leads the player not caring about buying any items from shops much having to wait all this time to get paid.
There is also a nice distraction minigame in the form of a Card game, named Triple Triad, which I have nothing bad to say about the game itself, but it is very easy to accidentally spread the "Random" rule around regions, which makes your cards in your hand random & kinda omits the fun factor, making the minigame frustrating.
As for the story, it's a
, even for Final Fantasy standards it appears to look rather bland, and really a shame as the previous 2 titles had rather complex & interesting ones.
The game's story starts off really slow, then picks up a little, then by Disc 2, it nosedives into boredom. Then it tries to do a twist which is really predictable and doesn't really do much to keep your interest. The villain's motive for being evil is also generic and without real purpose/context other than "I am evil by nature, so I must kill you all". By Disc 4, the game stops trying and it is just "lets just kill the bad guy and go home".
The protagonist is totally non-relatable and one-dimensional. The romance, which the main story revolves around, between him and his interest also seems rather forced at times. The other characters often do some dumb stuff/decisions throughout the story, which you wish the game gave you the option of choice being an RPG and all.
The protagonist's adversary also has no real-or-just closure, which seems lazy and all that time in the beginning spent to establish his character feels like a total waste of time.
When the game first came out, it was hailed as an eyecandy & tech miracle. And for its time, it was. Great detailed graphics, great soundtrack. But the game really suffers from too much experimentation. There were some gameplay/storytelling formulas the previous game, FFVII, established that should not have been changed.
Fortunately, the next iteration of the Final Fantasy series, FFIX, reverted all these poor design choices for the better.
I sadly, cannot recommend this port to anyone looking to either start with Final Fantasy or looking to play the next classic Final Fantasy.
Get this game only if you want it on your collection or for nostalgia reasons, otherwise there are much better JRPGs/FFs on Steam.

I would like to call myself a veteran within the Final Fantasy (FF) franchise now. Granted I am probably overstating myself, I figured it is about time I wrote a review of Final Fantasy VIII. From here on I'll refrain from using Roman numerals just to make this review easier to follow. I played FF8 near to the time it first came out on the PS1. I did not complete it, nor did I have any idea of what was going on - I was a mere child at the time dazzled by the beautiful colours, yet puzzled by the battle system and depressed by Squall’s sadness. Years later, I've returned to FF8 and I can say I have finished the game with a good idea of the actual story… But still depressed by Squall’s sadness. I confess from now that I understand why people would NOT have a liking for this game. There are a number of reasons I can and will point out which would detach the ordinary gamer from any will to finish the game, but I love this game and it is, along with FF6, my favourite JRPG of all time.
*No spoilers*

FF8 arguably has one of the most convoluted story's of any game I have ever played. The numerous fan theories surrounding the game seem to make more sense than the actual game! I do not take that to be a criticism of the game however - as strange as it sounds. The story is not bad in and of itself as it is very easy to follow. It is one of those games where the longer you think about whether the story actually makes sense, the less it does... So don't read into it too much is what I would say.
With that aside, the story takes place in a confused futuristic world. I say confused purely due to the array of varied environments and settings, from educational institutions which feel a lot like mercenary camps, to castles and to outer space. The story itself is a good balance between being engaging and interesting enough to make the player want to be able to find out how the story concludes, whilst still being complex enough to inspire countless fan theories; some of them keep me up at night to this day!
The world of FF8 has remnants of the post-apocalyptic FF7 world, whilst not being nearly as futuristic as Final Fantasy 13. The ending is extremely satisfying to the player and does not leave a feeling of emptiness.
To my mind, there are two main categories of Final Fantasy main characters. There is the quirky and easy-going kind (Tidus and Zidane for example), and the more aloof, lonely and emotionally confused kind (Lightning and Cloud). The main character of 8, Squall, fits in the latter category. If Cloud and Lightning had a child (which would make for an amazing game by the way), Squall would be that child. He initially comes across as blunt, cold-hearted, distant and anti-social, but over time there is a gradual change in his character as the game develops. He becomes a nicer, blunt, cold-hearted, distant and anti-social character. Despite being a character of very few words, every sentence he speaks always manages to be funnier than the last. His lack of character ultimately defines his character.
The secondary characters (particularly Rinoa) provide an excellent contrast to Squall’s personality. None of the characters feel rushed or uninspired, with Zell, Selphie and Seifer standing out as my favourites (Quistis and Irvine are great too).
DO NOT listen to any of the music in this game without having played it first. I say this because the OST is among the greatest I have heard in any game and explains why Nobuo Uematsu will be my favourite video game composer of all time. The music is best experienced in-game first. Whilst I do admit that there are a couple of pieces which are slightly overused, all of the pieces are memorable and unique with a persistent motif running through the whole game. Liberi Fatali, Maybe I’m a Lion, Find Your Way, Man with the Machine Gun, Eyes on Me, Fisherman’s Horizon and all of the battle themes stand out as my favourites. Eyes on Me in particular is played during one of my favourite scenes in any video game –the piece suits the scene perfectly.
I must confess that the first time I played the game, I did not have a clue what junctioning is. I spent the entire game spamming summons until I realised using summons just wasn’t enough. To put it simply, junctioning is the system in FF8 used to upgrade a character’s stats and use magic. It is one of those mechanics which are best learnt while playing the game as it is easier learnt than explained. Nevertheless in contrast to other games in the series, characters do not permanently hold magic. Instead magic is collected by each individual character. That magic can then be ‘junctioned’ to a stat. For example, if you wanted high HP, you could collection the spell ‘Full-life’ a hundred times and junction it to a character’s HP stat. This functions alongside the usual summons you would expect to see in a Final Fantasy game. The system is slightly tricky to get your head around when you first begin playing, but with a little practice it becomes easy. It is a system which could put a player off the game, but the story, the characters and everything is worth the struggle.
Triple Triad: This is easily the most overpowered mechanic I have ever experienced in a video game. It is a fairly simple card game which can be used to collect items which can then be used to buy weapons for example. I personally loved it and would love to see a similar game (albeit less powerful) in Final Fantasy 15.
Final Fantasy 8 is easily one of my favourite games of all time, however I told one of my friends not to play this game. The reason why is that although I love it, I understand that there are many reasons (such as the battle system) why a person would dislike or even hate this game, particularly if you aren’t a fan of JRPGs in general. If you are a fan of JRPGs (particularly the older classics) I definitely do recommend trying this one out. Whilst there are many reasons to hate the game there are so many more reasons to love it. I can guarantee that you are in for the best card game in a game you’ll every play.

"Act of Aggression is a tough sell.  It’s trying to be a game that ushers in the return of the golden age of RTS, but lacks nearly all of the features that made that golden age golden to begin with.  Lackluster factions, convoluted gameplay mechanics, and severe pacing issues hold back Act of Aggression from being one of the greats.  In fact, it’s not even one of the “alrights” either.  While there’s a lot of potential, I feel Eugen Systems squandered most of it, and ultimately, failed to stake a claim in the growing (but still very small) RTS community we have left.   I wouldn’t recommend this title to the average gamer unless it was on sale for more than 50% off.  In fact, if you MUST play a game just like it, I urge you to check out Act of War: Direct Action, the game’s spiritual predecessor.  It’s older and less polished, but the plot is fairly well done and the pacing is much more tolerable.  As for Act of Aggression, sorry guys, but this one’s going to the eastern front."

If you liked the original Command and Conquer Generals game as much as I did, you will love the AoA reboot edition!  This game is my favorite RTS, and is a wonderful throwback to the "golden age" of modern warfare RTS games.  It plays almost identically to CnC Generals and CnC Generals Zero Hour, but is significantly more advanced (the 2016 graphics are a huge plus, and there are tons of amazing hotkeys and unit task assignment shortcuts that allow a level of gameplay above that offered by CnC).
The single resource economy vastly simplifies the financial side of gameplay over the original Act of Aggression, leaving more time to focus on actual attack and defense strategies.  I find games like Starcraft to be a bit too fast-paced and muscle-memory multitasking oriented, so AoA RE seems to fit me perfectly--I have enough time to think things through, but the pace is still fast enough to keep me challenged and interested.
My only beef about this game is that not enough people play it--it's often hard to find a RE online game unless I'm playing with friends.  Eugen needs to dedicate more attention to updating and promoting AoA RE in order to build up the online multiplayer community.  This game has an amazing amount of potential, and I'm sure that I'll be playing it for years to come.
