First off, I'm going to write about the game, not the price tag.  Personally I don't have a problem with them charging extra for it, but that doesn't affect my review.
So here's where I'm coming from:  I've played Natural Selection since the release of the original mod for Half-Life, Combat for Natural Selection, and NS2, but not the Combat Mod for NS2.  I'll be comparing this to both NS1:Combat and NS2.
Main Differences from NS2 and/or NS1:Combat:
Good:
1) No commanders.  Also in NS1:Combat, this is one of the main draws of the gametype.  You don't have to rely on anyone to get the weapons and upgrades you want.  You don't instantly lose because a first time commander is in the chair.  It sets up a more casual game that focuses on kills instead of a big strategic plan of attack.
2) Buildings.  Yes, you can build stuff, unlike NS1:Combat.  A huge change.  Phase gates and Gorge tunnels help you control the map like you're playing a vanilla style NS2 game.  I like it.
Bad:
1) XP Gain.  Another huge change from NS1:Combat is how hard it is to gain XP.  Leveling is much slower and gone is the "area xp" where everyone gets XP in the vicinity of the kill.  You get XP from kills, assists, and captures.  Also making XP gain difficult is that with such a small player base, 90% of the players are already very skilled NS2 players.  If you've never played NS, you will die alot and you will never get XP.
One of the things I really liked about NS1:Combat is it's more casual gameplay style.  Level gains were quick, if you fell behind, you'd get XP anyway.  Here, if you fall behind, you're done.  You can't really compete when you're low level against a bunch of people with armor, and the game doesn't help you out any.
I've read the upgrade progression is very limiting as well, but I haven't been able to level up enough to run into that problem.
It's hard to recommend this game to anyone.  If you already have NS2, it's pretty much the same game.  If you don't have NS2, you're going to die a lot, get stuck at the bottom of the scoreboard, and never given any upgrades to help you compete.  A new player would actually have an easier time in standard NS2, as personal performance doesn't matter as much.

I’m a NS2 Modder and member of the
who spent up to this day over 1,5k hours modding NS2 and allready 50 h doing the same with NS2:Combat ( i won’t use the term NS2:C because for me that’s the NS2 mod NS2:Classic).
So my following review might be from a total different point of view than most other ppl have!
To honor the fact that ns2:combat is a stand-alone i’m trying to forget as much about ns2 first as possible.
NS2:Combat is a Moba-FPS where two asymmetrically teams fight each other in currently two gamemode.
The two available teams are marines and aliens. Aliens are mostly focused on melee fight while marine are classically focused on ranged combat.
While playing a round you get so experience points (exp) by killing enemies or assisting your teammates in some ways ( assist a kill, heal them etc. ).
Every x exp you level up with which you get a skill point you can use to unlock one of certain “skills”.
Those are either upgrades (more damage, more health etc. ) or as marines new weapons and equipment (e.g. jetpacks or exosuits) or as alien you can evolve into another lifeform or unlock certain lifeform abilities.
The default game mode is basically known from other moba games: Both team have a main base building which each team has to destroy to win the game. Only the ai creeds and towers are missing.
But hey both teams have engineer abilities / lifeform which can build up towers if needed to defend a line.
The second gamemode is a capture points gamemode where each teams has to earn currently 500 tickets to win the round by holding certain points on the map.
I would totally answer yes it is if you overall like MOBAs and fast paced action shooters. The "extra spice" ns2:combat has are certainly the two asymmetrically teams.
But with those we are already at the first issue this game like the parent game (ns2) has:
The learning curve.
While new players manage to handle marines just fine (trained by most other FPS-games out there), they do struggle a lot with aliens. This leads towards that currently marines win a lot more rounds unless there is some ns2 veteran carrying the alien team (who knows how to handle his lifeform because of the 1k hours spent in ns2).
So combat would really need a good tutorial specially for aliens (beside the tutorial videos which are there already but i guess no new player ever watches) so those new players are aware how to handle aliens correctly ( e.g. never run directly towards a marine because yeah you are melee and he has a rifle or some other nasty gun with which he kills you before you can even reach him)
Beside that NS2:Combat is certainly a lot fun once you get used to all those things.
What i have to note here is that NS2:Combat suffers from the same performance issues as the parent game NS2:
This means long loading time at first load which they kind of cover up with playing a basic tutorial video at the first start and ofc fps hitches ( both FLG and the NS2 CDT are working at improving this all the time).
So those (including all the smaller not so critical bugs ) should disappear after a while.
Looking at other reviews other steam users often bring up the point that this game is too similar to the parent game and therefore too expensive.
I can’t deny that NS2:Combat is pretty similar to NS2 looking at everything beside the gameplay (excluding how the weapons and alien lifeforms get handled) but neither does FLG.
They even named this game Natural Selection 2:Combat and not just Combat. I guess not because of the franchise but because they wanted to make clear from where they are coming.
FLG is a new gaming studio made by ns2 modders just like me. They decided to try to live from their work. And yeah i can totally see that they did a lot in that one year looking at the code (which is btw basically open for everyone who owes the game). So let me state here that another awesome fact is that the game is 100% moddable.
So why $15? I guess because FLG wants to get something out of it. Everyone familiar with publishing games via steam knows that game devs don’t make anything out of games with prizes lower than $10. And having that in mind the price is totally fair.
NS2:Combat is a small but decent game for all players who enjoy to play FPS- and MOBA-games. I would recommend it to anyone who is willing to try something new beside the standard framework of those two genres.
Yes NS2 and NS2:Combat are not totally revolutionary but they do mix up the given genres in a really good way (in case of NS2 FPS and RTS) and in case of NS2:Combat FPS and MOBA adding a “extra spice” by the asymmetrically teams of aliens and marines.
So overall if that sounds good for you go for it and buy NS2:Combat :D

As a noob I really was struggling with the different aspects of the game at first, but the more I played, I was riding the learning curve. That curve is something I really love about games like this. It’s everything but casual, yet I think it is still accessible to new players that are not familiar with the franchise at all. Still, my head got ripped off pretty often and only near the end of my last play I managed to level up fast enough to keep up with the experienced players on the server.
The game is very, very fast and requires good aiming skills. But not only that, you also need to think about what class you are playing and act accordingly. Sounds obvious, but once you played that little starter Alien and get blasted pretty much instantly, you’ll know what I am talking about. You need to think ahead, use different ways like wall-running and going through air ducts, to kill your better armoured and better equipped opponent. Same goes for the marine, that really needs distance between his guts and the “thing” that tries to rip them out.
You will realize very fast that teamplay is key. Otherwise forward base won’t last long and your base will get overrun. The game has, as many titles nowadays, built in VOIP, that worked very well with a good quality. Use it, communicate, team up and win!
I had a lot of fun and many “omg I died again so quickly” moments, but it never felt unfair or unbalanced. So if you like a new challenge, go ahead and play this game! Bit one tip: maybe really watch the tutorial videos before jumping into the first game… I should have… ;-)

I certainly do not regret buying this game (yeah, I know 200 hours, I have lots of spare time)
Atlantic Fleet is a unique time-killing game. It's a turn-based WWII naval battle sim (sort-of).
There are four gamemodes where you play either as the Royal Navy or the Kriegsmarine: Battle of the Atlantic, Campaign, Historical Missions, and Sandbox
Battle of the Atlantic is the biggest and best part of the game. You control your ships from a tactical map, positioning them where you can either protect your merchant vessels (Royal Navy), or where you can sink them (Kriegsmarine). You sink enemy ships to earn renown, which is used to build up your own fleet. On each turn, your ships may encounter enemies, which then brings you to the combat mode (See further down). Any ships lost, yours or the enemies, are not coming back (unless you change that in the settings, for the enemy, of course), so you have to be careful how you handle your ships.
Of course, you don't have to do all that. This mode is very replayable, and allows you to try out different strategies and tactics, to either try to beat the mode faster, sink more enemy ships, or do the dumbest things imaginable (Kriegsmarine, put one ship in every tile)
The campaign mode is more a secondary part of the game.
Each nation has 50 missions of increasing difficulty, where the player may only use 3 ships. Sunken ships may be brought back in this mode.
Overall, not particularly good, but not bad either.
The historical missions are a nice touch.
There are 30 historical missions that represent actual historical encounters, both well known (Battle of the River Plate) and not (Convoy HX-106).
You can either re-live history, or change it.
The sandbox mode is great for just messing around. You can select up to 10 ships for both nations, and just do whatever you want with them. Maybe test out different tactics or ship combinations, or simply screw around for a bit (10 submarines vs. 10 submarines where they can only fire their deck guns)
Combat: The way it works is each side gets to move all of their ships and fire once per turn. Simple enough.
To move, you simply select how fast you want to go, select your rudder shift, and go. Simple enough.
To fire, you select your target on the combat tactical map, use your ships rangefinders to get the rough range, adjust elevation, and fire. Still simple enough.
Rinse and repeat. Simple.
This is great, because it's nice and slow-paced, and easy to handle.
But it also creates a problem. A battleship effectively has the same reload speed as a destroyer, and moves just as fast. Combat can become one-sided when one side has a single battleship and the other, a couple cruisers and destroyers. The aiming system is too simple, allowing you to fire one or two ranging salvoes, and the next will be a guaranteed hit. Why? Because the shell drop is constant. Each shell fires in a perfect arc, only affected by wind (If you select wind in the options).
It is unlikely this game will every be touched again by its devs, but that's fine by me. Despite the flaws in the combat system, I still found myself enjoying slugging it out with my Bismarck and Tirpitz against HMS Rodney and her sister ship, HMS Nelson
The game has its flaws.
It's a very good mobile game on steroids, and its graphics are pretty good, but they will not hold up to any games nowadays (this doesn't bother me)
Submarines are a little too good for the AI to handle (their only real way of sinking u-boats is with aerial dropped depth charges). If you know what you are doing, you will almost always come out of submarine battles completely victorious.
The campaign just doesn't stand out enough. There's nothing too fun about it. It's just there. It's just a bunch of battles where the only way the AI can beat you is by adding more battleships to their lineup. Oh well.
I've talked about the combat system already.
Despite this, Atlantic Fleet is still a fun game. It has very few, if any, peers. It's relatively cheap. It can be played offline. It's easy to get into, and easy to get good at (good for scrubs like me, who can't handle faster-paced games).
And who knows? Maybe it will get you into naval combat, like it did for me.

Zeno Clash is one of those games that I only played for a little bit, but I was glad for it. It's also a game that I might not fully understand, but I'm happy for its mere existence. It's so different and unusual in approach and design, yet it works rather well. Stuff like this proves that games don't all need to be high fantasy or military shooters to work.
The combat is simply awesome and sublime. Few games really give me that impression of walloping a mob in the face, but this game definitely delivers. I can feel that satisfying recoil with every hard crack of Ghat's fist, and kneeing a baddie in the face is a treat. Fighting is by no means easy, and some enemies are clever and know how to dodge and counter some of the moves. Others are armored, skillful or just plain weird, and you have to determine the correct approach to damage them effectively. This makes for a very tactical game where you have to be able to plan and improvise your attacks, as well as manage your health and stamina.
Weapons are provided, but just don't give that same amount of gratification. Luckily they are only needed for a couple key sections of the main game, and are completely optional at all other times. Most enemies can be beaten with bare knuckles.
My only gripe is really the length of the main campaign. It's a bit shorter than I would have preferred, considering the potential depth of the game's mechanics, not to mention the sheer alien beauty of the game's world. If nothing else I wanted to know more and more about the world, its bizarre creatures and history. Maybe this is expanded upon in the sequel.
There is, however, an interesting "challenge" mode, which consists of a series of matches that get progressively harder, with the player facing various squads of enemies based on characters faced in the main game. Because of it's own length and the difficulties that can be reached, I get the impression that this tower mode is the "real" game, and the campaign is more of a lengthy tutorial.
This title isn't for everyone. This game requires some good tactical instincts and the combat can be a bit slower-paced that some would prefer, but if you like the tribal-punk setting and enjoy first-person brawling, then you'll get your fix here.

Zeno Clash is a wierd game that tries to, and succeeds at, doing something that no other FPS has done.  The story is strange, the characters are mysterious, and the player is left continuously wondering what will happen next.  Unfortunately, the story is also not interesting. The game just throws disparate scenario after scenario at you presented as a series of events that happened before the beginning of the game, and it leaves it largely up to you to connect these events.  The characters are not expanded upon, the enemies are only briefly expounded on, and the main characters motivations are left entirely unclear.  I believe this was a choice made deliberately to add mystery to the story, but for me it only left me wanting for a clear reason to continue to my goal.
None of this would be a problem if the game was fun.  I don't need a reason to complete the game if I enjoy playing it.  Zeno Clash is unique in that it tries to blend melee and ranged combat in an FPS in a way I've never seen before.  The melee portion includes blocking, counter attacks, dodging, grabs, and other staples of good melee combat.  The mechanics of the game is what brings it down in this respect.  It would take a long time to describe exactly how frustrating it is to control the combat, but I frequently ended up performing the wrong defensive move which would result in my taking damage.  Furthermore, the counterattacks don't work.  Almost every time I tried to counter an enemy they would block or dodge my counterattack.
The ranged combat has similar problems.  Guns are not meant to be used exclusively.  You are supposed to pick up a weapon and shoot an enemy as many times as you can until they get close to you.  This part feels good.  Watching an enemy running towards you, it feels great to score those two big hits that send them flying on their back then pelting them with more shots until they start towards you again.  When they start getting closer though is when the frustration begins.  When an enemy gets close, you are meant to lock on to put away your weapon and begin melee.  However, running away from an enemy breaks your lock, so if you are trying to get away, the gun comes back out.  If you are hit with the gun out, it drops to the ground with whatever ammo it had, where enemies can pick it up and use it against you.  In short, again, the mechanincs of this game make it very frustrating to do what you want to do, and to fight multiple enemies.
In conclusion, I wanted to like this game.  I like wierd games, I like difficult games, and I like story-driven games.  I HATE frustrating games, however, and this falls squarely into that last category.  The mechanincs of combat don't work, the story was not holding my interest, and I felt no reason to complete the game.  In addition, I found a Zeno Clash process running in the background of my PC even though I hadn't played the game in days and the game itself was not running, so my hours played are inflated.  I should note I did not finish this game.

Interestingly, rarely do you have the chance to use weapons with projectiles; emphasis is on melee combat and you do have the chance to use some clubs or other heavy weapons beside your fists. Combat is simple but very smooth - the game is very linear and as it is an independent game you can already guess it is quite short.
Story-wise the game is rather silly - it puts you in the shoes of Ghat who is banished from his home after an attempt to kill Father-Mother. Yes, this creature is his father and mother as it seems the entire population of Ghat's settlement was raised by this hermaphroditic creature. Although banished, Ghat wishes to uncover the truth as to what really happened and what secret lies with the family.
Anyways, combat is quite good and the game has a challenge option with levels of a tower to compete against a series of enemies. This is getting difficult gradually - a nice way to pass time once the story mode is finished.
Zeno Clash is somewhat mediocre, but I believe the result of an original idea. If it is on sale this is a highly recommended game.

Gotta keep that Overwhelmingly Positive rating, so here I go.
Dust is an amazing game made by a single person. It's a side-scrolling hack'n'slash brawling Metroid-vania...thing.
Beautiful hand drawn environments and animations. One of the few games that look better while playing than in cut-scenes. Particle effects really make parrying feel like an unexpected comeback, and combining Dust's blade mastery with Fidget's elemental attacks, well... "Don't be near him. The screen just goes vwooshzhzoozhoozh!".
The characters are supposed to look like some older cartoons. ERR Just a friendly warning, but all characters ended up looking like furries, so, yeah, if you have a problem with that, keep it in mind.
Not the most original thing ever, but It's handled very well. The writing, the characters. the flavour text, the way the game handles important story points... it's all just perfect. All the dialogue feels natural, the characters react to what you do and what happens in the story.
I dunno, I guess hearing Fidget react to stupid ideas the same way I did kinda impressed me.
Great combat, maybe a bit button-mashy, but with satisfying combos, parries, elemental attacks and DUST Storm (hint:it's not just throwing dust around, Dust is the name of the main character...The skill implies a lot of blades and slicing). The combat it's incredibly rewarding and responsive.
The whole Metroid-vania thing means that you're gonna find impassable hazards in the world, and you'll have to return there after you learn skills that let you pass.
You can save characters from other indie games and party with them at the "Sanctuary". (The Kid from Bastion, Super Meat Boy, Bandage Girl, Gomez from FEZ, this kind of All-Star team).
12-20 hour campaign. Nuff said.

Final Fantasy really is a series that you either love or hate. It's stories have moments of complete brilliance that tug at you heartstrings unlike anything other mediums are capable of. But they're also these cryptic, jumbled messes, with a million plotpoints happening all at once. The gameplay is unlike anything I've played, and rewards the player for using the open world to its fullest potential, but it always tries to railroad you back to the story and locks you out of content later in the game. Final Fantasy VII waqs my first exposure to JRPG's in any real capacity, and I didn't start playing it until last year. (yes, I really did play 530 hours of this game in one year)
This ended up being a good beginners JRPG, but definitely set me up with the expectation that the series is gonna be just as easy. There aren't a lot of points in VII where the game challenges you, aside from a few bosses that can surprise an unprepared party. The game is also rather linear and straight forward; you can easily beat the game with equipment you get from shops and around the world map. Some of your best materia options are rather inexpensive, or can be picked up rather easily from the world map. No different from any other Final Fantasy game, sure, but I didn't even bother with a lot of the side content in this game until my most recent playthrough. Chocobo breeding simply isn't worth the trouble, as the only worthwhile ability you gain from it is Quadra Magic imo.
I'd say this is one of my least favorite parties in any Final Fantasy game, as they either don't have enough characterization, not enough backstory, or both. Red XIII and Cait Sith are just kind of there after disc 1. Yuffie is just a total ♥♥♥♥♥ to everyone, and Vincent, while plot relevant, doesn't do a whole lot or get many interesting lines. The only characters that grow as people are Cloud, Tifa, Barret, and Cid. The dynamic that the party members have with each other is non-existent outside of cutscenes. The women seem to get along well enough, Yuffie and Red XIII have a human/pet dynamic sometimes which is charming, and that's about it. They give you items in the last dungeon if you split them up well enough, so cooooooooooool?
I'm not one to harp on graphics, as it's usually just an added bonus if the game looks pretty to me, but the model quality in this one is either great or block hands. I know that one of the hugest criticisms this game gets is because of the field models, so I'm just gonna call attention to it and leave it at that. Part of me hopes that the remake makes a joke DLC skin mod for the character where they get their PS1 skins back, for the lolz.
The music in this game however, is just enchanting. There are no adequate words to describe just how much this soundtrack resonates with me. The use of leitmotif is stellar, and adds a layer to the emotions of each character that would have been missing in the hands of a less capable composer. Nobuo Uematsu is often heralded as one of the reasons that each Final Fantasy is unique and memorable, as he has a way of manipulating the wanted emotions out of the player with his scores, nad this soundtrack is one of the many reasons why I love him so. This isn't mky favorite soundtrack in the series, but it's definitely in my top 3.
Do I recomend this game? Yes. To newcomers of the Final Fantasy series? No. Go play Final Fantasy IV first. If you like that, then play VII.

I don't know if it was the pressure of early adult life or the demands of college, but I began to experiment with huge ships in my late teens. I began by looking at huge ship magazines in the basement when my parents weren't around. Then one day, my mom came home early and unexpectedly caught me in the act. Both of my parents were furious. They asked me where I go the magazine from and I said I found it and that I thought it only contained articles on small watercraft. As a result, I started to sneak out at night, telling my parents that I was headed to a friend's house to watch Full House, but in reality, I was in the library, reading up on huge ships. As my career developed, I found an apartment that I could afford and I moved out of my parents’ house. My interest in huge ships only grew. My apartment became a center for trafficking huge ship paraphernalia: model huge ships, pictures, of huge ships; life preserves – you name it. Eventually some neighbors complained and the owner of the apartment building had me evicted. By that time, I was so far gone that I didn’t care and I moved into a hostel. It was the perfect place to continue my pursuit of huge ships. The rent was cheap, drifters came and went, everyone minded their own business, and once in a while a new person would come along with scale models of huge ships in Turkey. We had a lot of wild nights and I was having trouble holding down my job. Eventually got fired. One day it dawned on me that if I don't get away from huge ships, I'll end up dead. By pure luck, I ran into a fellow who went through the same thing and he recommend Trimmer's book. Between the book and my support group, I made progress and got back on my feet again. Last night I almost turned left out of the parking lot instead turning right, as I've done routinely for the last 6 months. Turning left would have meant that I was heading to the Port of Baltimore where huge ships are present everywhere: horns blowing, sailors lashing gear to decks, and merchants teasingly gesturing to the gangplanks as they ask passersby if they want to go for a voyage on a great, big, huge ship. I started to imagine the wakes in the bay and the frolicking of tugs as they pull and push these huge ships in and out of the port. There was a burning desire inside of me: my mouth started to salivate; my hands were trembling; and my eyes darted left and right as they searched for an answer. I thought that maybe I could just go to the port and find one or two huge ships and it wouldn't be that big of a deal. Call it a voice in my head, an angel on my shoulder, or Trimmer's book in my glove box, but I turned right and headed home instead. My support group had a meeting last night and I told them about my near stumble. It felt good to tell everyone that I did not fall victim to weakness. I have my beloved support group and my dearest John W. Trimmer to thank for 6 months - huge ship free.

Preview negative review:
Ok, I played until the 4th level, mainly because I love platformers.
The good:
- It's a platformer.
- It has a kind of interesting story.
- The music sets a good atmosphere (for a while)
The bad:
- You can't skip dialogs or "cut-scenes" (extremely frustrating if you are repeating a level because you died)
- There are some platforms that are unnecessarily slow, and if you fall you have to wait a lot to get back in.
- The buy mechanic is interesting game-wise, but at the same time it feels lazy, because who are you buying the things from. At the beginning it just says: Press S to buy. The gems have also no story.
- The names are way too generic and not very well thought out. Demon King. Charlie. Also *SPOILER AHEAD* not very much emotion when you find your kid.
- Too much backtracking when you light on a switch.
- Hit box of the bats is annoying.
- Nothing new towards the course of the first 4 levels.
- The ghosts are very annoying to deal with, they are too fast and out of nowhere sometimes.
- I got to the 4th level, died, run out of green gems, tried it again, couldn't skip dialogs, died again, quit. Not because I quit games (I got almost of the achievements in super meat boy and dark souls 1), but because it wasn't much fun.
- Enemies can damage you even if you kill them before the visually touch you.
- There's a glitch where you just slide.
- The world is unnecessarily dark and sometimes you can't distinguish enemies or things that hurt.
- Dialogs are not very well written, grammar wise.
I would love to play a polished version of this game. Don't recommend it right now for that price.
Updated Review:
I have changed my review from negative to positive because the dev has been making good updates and decided not to abandon the game.
Collision problems are mostly solved, dialog scenes are now skippable, movement feels smother, soundtracks are good, story is kind of interesting once you beat the game, achievementes are now attainable and not frustrating impossible levels (Death race).
Overall a nice little platformer that has a new mechanic (buying bullets and extra lifes in game).

So far I have only delved maybe 3 and a half hours into the game, plus a good hour many years ago at a friend's house. Back then I didn't quite appreciate the combat mechanics enough to get the game myself and play it. Now that I'm not an idiot, I have to say I really like the combat. These days, games bore me quickly. Same shooter mechanics, same plotlines of rich people being the villains that cause all the drama, and the same quick cash-grab features that we eat up for some reason. Who could have guessed that a Steam Sale of a game made back in 2005 would have shaken me violently out of that rut?
The enemy AI is refreshing compared to the standard. I'm forced to think about how to fight the enemy. The combat itself is dangerous; you can't just go out to shoot people, taking a few hits in the process, and then let your health regenerate like nothing happened. I'm forced to be economical about my decisions, my bullets, and my health kits. The game is also quite deceptive with their slow-mo mechanic that lets you think you can be Rambo or John Woo.
As for the horror aspect of the game, lots of instances I feel underwhelmed as I usually do in video games. However, there are a few that just make me p00p myself--at the very least, I feel VERY uneasy. While I haven't yet finished the game, I just wanted to let people know that it is definitely a nice take on a shooter that I wish I got into years ago. I look forward to finishing this game and playing the other ones that I also got in the sale.

Onto the review:
It’s actually to Zeno Clash’s benefit that it doesn’t really explain itself outside of the basic gameplay mechanics, which are simplistic but nevertheless require a bit of finesse if you’re playing on any of the higher difficulties. To elaborate, combat is your typical mouse-bound primary-light-attack, secondary-heavy-attack affair, utilizing the spacebar for blocking and evading. Uncoordinated lout that I am, this was interpreted as “spam the secondary/primary and run around like a chicken sans head”. This "style" of gameplay actually worked for me, thanks to the normal-level difficulty setting I was playing on, in addition to smartly-placed health items in each area.
Unfortunately, this is also the likely cause of the game’s growing tediousness later on, as, outside of a few close calls and even some deaths, I was just smashing through opponents in area after area. To offset this, there is some variety in the stages; for example, a brawling sequence being followed by a shooting gallery level, or some other contrivance (like using a magic torch to light up pyres and moving statues alike). And the guns, oh the guns.
Indeed, the weapons in Zeno Clash most succinctly sum up the game’s overall art aesthetic; the closest comparison in décor is that of “The Flintstones”, with its brightly-colored yet naturalistic designs. Hell, there’s even dinosaurs (or at least large reptiles resembling them) in a level or two. The guns themselves specifically piqued my interest, as the idea of a primeval-era slugthrower is just surreally fantastic. For example, the pistols, which basically appear to be carved shells with a bunch of nails and rocks stuffed into them, are just fun to look at and use in all of their pea-shootery goodness (which may also explain why I keep running into the same named characters again after I so thoroughly obliterate their asses).
Besides the art design, this sense of backwards absurdity is ingrained in the plot and characters; outside of the aftermentioned blurb, the game leaves it up to the progression of the narrative itself to explain what the hell is going on, eking out small bits of info through dialogue and actions. It's a refreshing break from grandiose blocks of text that describe a game's lore in exacting detail, but I fear the world of Zeno Clash might still be too alien to experience without detailed explanation for some players. At the same time however, it's that same feeling of unknowingness that may spur other players (myself included) to push on and immerse themselves in the absolute weirdness that is this game.
Final words: Zeno Clash is so aesthetically "out there" that it may dissuade players from digging into it, but the fairly-conventional combat system, in addition to a relatable (if somewhat vague) storyline, signifies that this 5ish-hour-long brawler is still worth playing for a couple of bucks.

I grew up with Final Fantasy; and FF VIII is one of the games in the series that I love most.  That said, what Square Enix made available here on Steam dissapoints me.  Literally, I'm having more fun playing Chocobo World (a mini game you can play right away) than actually playing the game.
What I would like to see change:
- Allow the game to adjust to your screen and video card settings, and not get stuck in low resolution.
- Offered like some other games on steam, being able to get the game's soundtrack as DLC.
- Use something other than general MIDI for the music - this was a huge opportunity to bring the music to life (and if the game originally used MIDI on the Playstation, I seem to recall the music sounding better there than on my computer).
- In configuration menus, allow for more than one slider for tweaking sound:  some sound effects in-game are really hard on the ears, and even though the music instruments don't sound great, I'd like at least the option to adjust SFX and BMG separately, not 'all game sounds' from 0-100%.  Along the same token, being able to adjust cinematics volume would be nice, too.
- Provide options limiting the intrusiveness of new achievements!  I'd like to go into a menu page or just to my Steam account to look at achievements.  Getting updates every time I draw something or defeat an enemy is too much and I can't seem to change it.
- FFS (Final Fantasy's Sake), don't require all of us to register for Square Enix accounts to play a game we bought on Steam!  If it weren't Final Fantasy, I probably would have asked Steam to refund my purchase once I learned upon launching the game that I had to register for an SE account to play.  I could understand it if FF VIII were an MMO, or I was using some custom developer tools to make mods or something else.
I will see how well FF VI survived; at least for that game I have the OST to compare in-game music to the soundtrack; so I won't be relying on my fond memories of playing these games on console.  I'm omitting my criticisms along the lines of the game not aging well in general, but as listed above, most of my criticism is how SE has handled making this game available to steam.  If I weren't playing Chocobo World in the background, I'd probably just FF VIII at this point.

I played these games heavily as a child and have fond memories of many of the events of JK and the Mysteries of the Sith. Upon revisting JK, I was filled with joy to find that it hadn't aged quite as poorly as I'd expected. The run and gun mechanics still work, the levels are well-designed and expansive, and even the puzzles can at least be reasoned out. I feel the bland story and characters are buoyed by the fun, campy FMV cutscenes, giving the game a B-movie feel. The lightsaber battles are a little janky and un-fun at this point, but few games are perfect.
In playing Mysteries of the Sith, I found all of the levels I rememberly fondly; however, the feeling with this expansion is completely different. Practically everything in this game feels an order of magnitude more frustrating. The story falls flat, meandering around a bunch of unrelated events until it fizzles out at the end. The characters are worse, Mara being painted as reckless, illogical, and sometimes downright distasteful. Kyle, for whatever your opinion of him was before this game, was at worst a bland, uninspired character. Suddenly, this game turns him into a paper-thin, boring villain for no reason other than need of a climax.
The puzzles have suddenly become several times more obtuse. If you thought Dark Forces was hard to figure out, buckle up. The level design feels like an afterthought. These feel like throw-away levels from JK, possibly explaining why the story feels like an afterthought. The worst part of their design is the constant hiding of the way forward behind grating in the dark corner of a hallway halfway to a dead end. All of this is pretty bad, but the last two levels take the cake. The game spends thirteen levels with scarcely a single use for the lightsaber other than a glorified wire cutter before immediately removing use of all weapons other than it. Two needlessly long levels filled with non-stop ambushes by enemies that can kill you in two hits on easy? Surely, this was top-shelf game design in its day. I merely squeaked through these levels by slowly spamming saber-throw for a lack of a better way to defeat most of the cheaper enemies.
I can understand that JK hasn't aged greatly, and my nostalgia for it certainly elevates my opinion of it. However, it stands as a solid, if forgettable, FPS game set in the Star Wars universe. Mysteries of the Sith is more akin to a steaming mess that reeks of horrific, likely rushed design choices resulting from a desire to cash in on the success of JK.

The game has a lot of repetition and a few annoying flaws, but considering the lack of better titles in the genre and the fair pricing, i think it is good enough.
The better part are the historic battle scenarios. They work well, are fun to play and there are about 20-ish or so.
The battle interface works decently. There is however a distinct lack of beginner support and information. It's the first game i have played in 10 or so years, to not have any kind of mouse-over, tooltip or the like for the main interface elements (there is however a decently detailed manual up for downloading).
There are also no previews for the actions - you pretty much have to guess, how far the ship will move or turn. The airstrike minigame is outright silly guesswork.
Gunnery and ballistics mechanics, which are the main focus of the game anyway, do work rather well.
The dynamic campaign on the other hand is more of a crapshoot.
The strategic map is very clunky, information difficult to impossible to find and intel gathering or recon are straight up not inplemented.
If you happen to (blindly, because of lacking recon) stumble over an enemy ship - the player has no option to intiate combat, only AI can do that. So even when completely surrounded on the strategic map, the AI ships somehow mange to avoid engagements, disapper for a couple of turns and then conviniently (for them) pop up in a completely different area of the map.
The AI is also constantly sinking huge amounts of "allied merchant shipping" in areas, where according to the strategic map, no allied shipping exists.
If i optimistically put aside the notion, that the AI is just straight out cheating, the only other explanation is, that there is no actual strategic layer. Instead the game just makes AI ships spawn in random locations and do random actions.

I don't normally play side-scrolling games, or button-crunching games of any variety, but this is an excellent story-driven RPG with beautiful animation and plenty of action. Most imporantly, Fidget is hilarious!
+ The combat system is engaging and easy to learn, even for an adventure gamer like me. It does get a bit repetitive toward the end, but this is mitigated by a variety of new opponents requiring new strategies to defeat.
+ The visuals are good, but where the animation really excels is in the Anime-style character designs which create very attractive and memorable characters.
+ There is also a fair amount of platform-style puzzle solving and Easter egg hunting.
- Some of the side quests have interesting story hooks, but the majority are busy work: "Collect X number of item Y".
- If you're a sandbox fanatic, you may be disappointed that this game is driven by pre-determined plot.
- I can't actually think of anything else negative to say. Great game!

It took me and my friend about 2 and a half hours to capture a bigfoot. We traveled around and fooled about for probs 1 hours of the playthrough just to check how big the map truly was. We weren't disappointed! The game is terrifying if you play it by yourself in a dark room, it was even scary for the first hour of our coop gameplay, due to us being two crybabies.
Pros:
-Graphics are really sweet, with a decent level design to support it.
-Camera system, traps and being able to hide traps with branches.
-Good progression, it takes a while to kill bigfoot but you can also find 4 lost tourists for exploration sake.
Cons:
- Sound quality is really bad, with everything from desyncronized footsteps to the bigfoot's roar being awful. I also heard a lot of sounds my buddy didnt.
- It seems that the night time is about 2-3 times longer than daytime, making it essential to use ur day to place cameras,
and really hinders you for the exploration for the huge map.
- Game is a bit buggy, biggest con would be how my buddy crashed and we had to find a new gun for him. The wildlife (or should I say, deer?), is also very buggy, my buddy saw deer I couldn't and vice versa. This made us think that the deer had no gameplay significance at all, which we still believe.
- Bigfoot has a very simple pattern, and ends up attacking your van every single night. We had a night with 3 attacks at the exact same location (window next to camera setup.
Overall:
This game has huge potential in being scary, unpredictable, and very DLC-able. I personally can't wait for more updates and maybe some harder difficulties (make him more unpredictable with new animations and ''what the Fk'' moments. I was expecting a moment where he'd come ambush from underwater in the swamp or something like that. I am stoked for the snow map with hopefully a scarier version of the bigfoot (yeti?). Great potential, great first time experience. I give this Early Access game a solid 6/10. And do I recommend for the price? Yes. It's cheap, and should give a blind playthrough AT LEAST 2-3 hours.

Stellaris is a game with a lot of potential. The late-game crises, even with a lack of variety, are particularly amazing. It's a 4X geared for atmosphere rather than competitive balance.
What's lacking is a lot of mid-game content and flavour. Wars after the early game are pretty boring because it's inevitably one huge battle where if you win it's slowly bombarding and invading planets one by one. There is no meaningful diplomacy or espionage and no real relationships between the AI other than alliance blocs.
The tech tree is neat but after 1 playthrough you'll have seen almost everything which is a real shame given the breadth of SCI-FI available. It doesn't just feel like you're choosing a tech path. The laser/kinetic/missile balance also still needs work.
That said there's a very strong modding community and Paradox will continue to pump out partially free DLC. I'd buy it if you can justify having 1 or 2 playthroughs and coming back in 6 months when a couple of patches are out or if you're willing to heavily mod it/

Impressive. First word that comes to mind when I think of this game. The reason that made me write this review is that I've played quite a few games that are like this or at least in its general ball park and the one thing that I have always had an issue with is difficulty. It usually is to hard or to easy and I have always had to handicap myself to have a solid challenge. I have create 2 races and gave them what I would consider to be a moderate advantage (better research and army strength bonues).
With both of these races I got to the point in the game where I was established had more money then I really needed as well as energy and had a very sizeable army. At this point I decided it was time to take over the galaxy. This is when the game actually surprised me. With my first race I started looking at other races and found it saying they had the same army strength as me...which I laughed at. After my first race was destroyed cause of my arrogance I thought it was a fluke. This prompted me to make my second race with a bigger research bonus and army strength.
This time I planned, formulated, and devised my plans for attack, made friends, and waited for the right time to attack. When that came I launched everything I had at my enemies. It was so easy to kill everything. I was sacking planets, killing orbiting platforms, and picking off science vessals and the like. I though victory was secured...that was into an enemy fleet jumped in that was twice my size...I had been wondering why I hand't fought any army yet...and to my horror I realized they had been building up in order to actually take me out. By the time I realized this it was to late and my second race was already on the path to destruction.
Just this makes me recommend this game and that isnt even mentioning the other wonderful aspects of this game. Though I would get a few mods to increase like flag choices and some other cosmetic issues. Also I would like to note that my races didn't fail cause the game was to hard or to easy but because i underestimated its potential and underestimated my enemy. Any game that can allow that kind of event to happen will always get my recommendation.

Final Fantasy 7 is the very first game I ever played when i was young kid (2007 and I was 9) and I replayed it multiple times, now this time I bought it here at steam and even though its been a while since I last played it well I still love it so here is my review.
Pros:
1. Characters - Probably my most beloved group of characters in any game ever from Cloud's spiky hair to Tifa's two large weapons, from their personalities and flaws, their backstories and character development - Cloud, Tifa, Aerith :(, Valentine, Barret, Yuffie, Red, Cid - and I love every single one of them. (The crossdressing Cloud is a classic)
2. World - One of the best in any game. Midgar is probably my favorite in the world of FF7 mostly because of its dystopian feel while Cosmo Canyon is a close 2nd and its theme is so mesmerizing when i first heard it even to this day but in my opinion every place in this world feels unique and always has its own stories to tell which tells a lot of how much work was put into this classic game.
3. Soundtrack - My favorite video game soundtrack ever with One Winged Angel and Aerith's theme being my favorite but every single theme fits well with every character or moments happening in the game or even to a single place like cosmo canyon.
4. Limit Break - While the gameplay of FF7 is almost the same as their predecessor, the limit break is a welcome change to the desperation attack of FF6 in my opinion because unlike the desperation attack of FF6 which you rarely see and use, limit breaks fill up when you take damage which increases the amount of times you can use it and it doesn't dissapear the next battle making it a good preparation for an upcoming boss battle.
5. Story - I don't need get in depth with this because almost everyone knows the story of this game so I will only say this.
Complicated, Tragic but Amazing.
6. FMV - This was visually impressive at the time and when I was kid my mind was blown in my first time seeing it.
7. Side Quests - Fun, Interesting and Rewarding at times.
Cons:
1. Graphics and Character Model - I dont really care about the graphics but I'll address it anyway. It certainly didnt stand the test of time and it can turn off some people who haven't played this game yet but want to try it.

My favourite childhood PS1 classic on PC!
Wow, what an experience! One of the most memorable videogames of all time at such a low price - just buy it if you haven't already.Although there is probably a great deal of nostalgia in play with my experience, there is a great story to be discovered here by newcomers who can overlook the dated graphics.
The story is incredibly rich, and is personally my favourite out of all the games I've played. Each character is integral to the plot and has a deep backstory just waiting to be explored throughout the game's main and side quests. The writing is excellent and the plot will have you aching for more, which you will get by completing all the side quests and talking to as many people as you can. You play as Cloud, a cold mercenary that learns the value of friendship through overcoming his incredibly troubled past with the help of his team - an excellent protagonist whose character develops well throughout.
You will be thrown into a huge open world (after the first 30 minutes or so) in which you have to hunt down the antagonist, Sephiroth, and unravel all the mysteries that follow. Each location is distinctly different and has plenty to see and discover by talking with the folk.
My favourite part of this game is the music, being a composer myself. It is without doubt one of the best game soundtracks of all time. Each character has their own theme song, and the way they are used in certain situations will make you burst into tears (those who have played will know what I mean). The music itself is so well written with great contrast! From the Main theme (world map 1), which is incredibly epic and powerful, to the Sephiroth theme, which invokes fear and anger. Let's not forget the Aeris theme - a beautiful piece. If you like the music in this game, check out any symphonic orchestra versions on CD/youtube and you will appreciate it so much more. The problem with the game is that the music is recorded in MIDI (computer instruments) - but the writing is still great.
The combat is pretty RPG standard turn based, which is OK for some like myself - if it ain't broke etc...
This PC port is EXCELLENT and arguably better than the original, since I can launch the game from my old laptop in less than 20 seconds! Loading times are cut and you can get right in without the irritating black screens.
Personally, I don't have any gripes with this game as I don't particularly care much for graphics - but some newcomers will be put off by this. Remember that the game is 20 years old now! And don't let this put you off experiencing one of the best stories of all time :)

The world of Zenozoik is strange, dirty, and down right alien at times. The character and terrain designs oscillate between beautifully surreal and head-scratchingly mismatched. Everything you see is a wonder to behold and, however improbable, feels as if it belongs there, feels alive. Following Ghat around as he tells his tale and very slowly reveals what he knows was thrilling. No matter how many times he refused to say more, I didn't feel like I was being stalled because it was clear how deeply the secret affected him. His character was fully formed and relatable. But the ending itself felt rushed and not quite as climactic as it seemed to think it was. The big reveal was satisfying, it was the lack of answers pertaining to the newer character that the conclusion centered around that made it somewhat hollow.  If said character was not introduced and the plot remained focused on the conflict between Ghat and Father-mother, I would have no complaints about the storyline. The combat, however, has some issues. Combat is the bulk of game and it never feels quite right. The sights and sounds seem right, when a blow connects there's good feedback, but I never could tell what was and was not going to hit me. The enemies will become invincible at times, during charge up attacks and after being knocked down, which doesn't go along with how the combat itself is presented. There's also not a whole lot to the combat which is a blessing at first, but causes it all to become repetitive later on. In the end, none of that is going to stop me from playing the sequel when the mood hits me, but I'm not exactly rushing into either.

Wickedly good game that still holds up. The AI is surprisingly smart and knows how to flank, there's multiple approaches to levels, the weapons feel great but don't feel overpowering, even melee combat is well executed.
One thing that stands out is that there's the ability to lean behind cover, which as odd as it sounds, makes this game less of a cover shooter. Staying stationary generally won't work.
This game isn't so much a horror game as it is an action game with horror elements (which is probably obvious), but it does do a really good job of making you uneasy at various parts. Some parts legitimately scared me, and not in a cheap way like with a half-baked jumpscare. It's not in-your-face with the horror elements, which makes them that much more gripping when they do appear.
It's also an excellent example of how limitations of the time were used to invent new mechanics (especially in implementing 'horror' aspects). I can't really go into details without spoiling some great moments.
Definitely a must-play. It's cheap, it's wildly fun, and it's way better than the sequels.

F.E.A.R. (First Encounter Assault Recon) is a horror-themed FPS from 2006. I got it for free from a friend a few weeks ago as a gift because they had an extra copy from some bundle or another.
It's an interesting game and for one that is ten years old it's held up remarkably well, I'll cover some things below in detail but first, if you're looking for a *horror game* this may or may not be what you're looking for.
FEAR (I ain't typing the dots every time, sorry) isn't like many more recent games that seek to either hit you with jump scares repeatedly or ratchet up the existential terror (something like, say, SOMA). FEAR is an FPS first and foremost, the vast majority of things in this game can be shot, wapped on the head with a gun, or given a flying judo kick (note: this is somewhere between awesome and hilarious, depending on the kind of person you are you'll either judo kick everything or avoid using it at all). And being able to defeat most of the things that present that scary factor does suck some of the terror out of them, but, there are also what I'll broadly term 'hallucinatory' entities that you can't defeat, and even that aside, the game does a *remarkably* good job of keeping tension high even when you know this.
Still, FEAR is an FPS and lives and dies on its gunplay, which is remarkably solid. It's a little different than what you're probably used to if you haven't played something more than ~5 years old in a while, but it's fairly easy to get a handle on. The game doesn't have ironsights as such but there's a "zoom" button you can use to much the same effect. You can also get through most of the game's encounters by shooting from the hip just fine providing your aim's decent. The game's core mechanic is a sort of bullet time button. It's not a unique feature, but it's used to decent effect here and I must say, hearing the deep-voiced replica soldiers' voices slow down as they yell "♥♥♥♥" and you shotgun them in the face is
It does a lot to keep the atmosphere from becoming *too* oppressive. Other than that it's pretty standard 2000s FPS fare. You can carry three weapons but there's only about (without looking it up) 8 or so in the game so you can make almost any combination work, it's not the most challenging game in the world and anyone with experience in, say, Halo, should be able to tackle it easily, but to me at least challenge has never really been the point of a game like this.
Lastly there's a lot to love about the environmental design. It's a *little* repetitive but this is to an extent justified by the setting (most of the game takes place in an office high-rise). You'll be seeing, basically, four types of areas: run-down abandoned buildings (mostly in the beginning and end of the game), office buildings (which make up the vast majority), maintenance areas within said office buildings, and rooftops. But it's well-constructed enough that it works and the local audio logs (messages left on phones) are nice. The dialog is vulgar, often to the point of exaggeration, and you can kinda tell it was aiming to be "mature" in a very 2006 sort of way, but it's not bad and I often found myself amused by the constant back and forthing between various evil corporation bigwigs trying to pass blame off onto other evil corporation bigwigs (which makes up many of the phone messages). There are a few NPCs but they're mostly not worth mentioning just because the same criticisms and praises apply.
I'd recommend FEAR if "a good mid-2000s shooter" is something on your shopping list, or if you're just looking to try something you missed out on when it was new.

It's a fantastic game. If you're a horror fan, it's a must play.
Not only is it a very strong horror game, it's a damn good first person shooter. It shows a very strong polish that allows it to defy age. The environment's hitboxes were particularly strong. They all seemed very accurate, and I was able to use the thin gaps in the environment to my advantage. Not once was I hit by a bullet and questioned that it shouldn't have been able to hit me, nor the contrary.
The graphics hold up well. I wasn't distracted by the graphics like I was in, say, the Elder Scrolls: Oblivion. Genres play a role in that, of course.
The story is interesting, but lacks a grip. What I mean is, I was eager to reach the end, but I wasn't interested in the journey. For the first half of the game, the notes and buildup to the story are rather dull. It picks up the closer you get. It took me a couple weeks to play through the first 6 hours, but then I completed the next 5 all in the same day. The first part wasn't bad, but I usually found myself playing other games because I wanted to play them more than F.E.A.R.
The gameplay is, simply put, fun. I enjoy first person shooters, and this is better than many in that regard. The combat was challenging at times, but not rage-inducing. The AI is excellent. What I love is that they're not given benefits to make it more challenging. If you're quiet and sneaking, they don't know you're there until you open up on them. Once they know where you are, they strategize and move, focusing on taking you out. Once enough time passes without any indication you're still there, they'll take note of that and expand their focus and try to locate you. It's the best AI I've played with in a considerable amount of time. The environment usually allows for creativity in the situation. As in, it's not always linear. The character gets unnerved. Getting hit with bullets severely impacts your aim (which sways ever so slightly). This is what I mean by polish; everything had its fair share of attention.
I usually hear F.E.A.R. regarded as one of the best horror games, and it deserves the spot. While the story takes too long to get moving, the rest of the game excels from start to finish.

This game is essentially a much more polished version of the Natural Selection 1 and 2 'Combat mod', created by the same authors now under the name Faultline Games. It utilizes the engine, core gameplay elements and graphical elements of Natural Selection 2 but is not directly affiliated with Unknown Worlds. Essentially, this is a mod being sold as a standalone game at a 15$ price point. This isn't by itself a deal-breaker as long as ample content and quality is provided..
The combat is fun, the leveling up elements seem well thought-out, the music is great, and the map design(albeit limited number of maps) seems to be excellent. This mod seems to 'fix' a lot of core elements of Natural Selection 2 which may have driven away more casual players. Since there's no Commander or resource metagame you're more free to play aggressively in more of an arena FPS environment. Teamplay gameplay is still rewarded but you're not entirely reliant on your team to have an enjoyable experience. I'm actually getting a lot of fun out of this fresh take on NS2 and while it does play exactly as advertised, it still feels like a mod of an existing game which I already own. With only 5 maps and the game's clearly reduced complexity compared to NS2 I am curious to see what player numbers look like in a month, or two months out.  Continual 'officially released content' will be very vital to sustaining any kind of player population.  Since this
, the developers should not be relying on the modding community to provide for them.
Faultline Games integrated a 'ranked' system for a lite form of skill-based matchmaking. You can still manually select servers but players have a skill value assigned based on their in-game performance. This is great. It allows for more intelligent team balance, if it were implemented. What's isn't great is the fact that rather than allow and enforce non-modded dedicated servers, server admins and gaming communities will be forced to rent ranked servers from a pre-selected list of server providers. No running your own (ranked) dedicated server on your own equipment. In my opinion this goes against the very roots of what makes PC gaming great.
Had this been offered as a 5$ DLC to NS2, it would have made perfect sense. A price point of 10$ might have made more sense.  The game really is stuck between a rock and a hard place; by selling it for too little they risk not making any profit, but also since it is a stand alone game Faultline ends up alienating the existing NS2 customer base by 'making us buy NS2 again'.  Even a basic integration between the two games such as a launcher which has a server browser list that shows servers from both 'editions' would go a long way to stop this product from being such a dividing force in the NS2 community.  I know there's grand plans to continue to expand on NS2:Combat's features, effectively making it the CS:GO or 'CoD' of NS2, but currently it just isn't there yet. It would be entirely possible to put 95% of this game's content into the original NS2 as a mod.
As it stands, with
and at a price point more expensive than you can find the full NS2 game, I can't honestly recommend it.
1) There is NOT a commander or resource gathering metagame. There are no RTS components from NS2.
2) There IS fast paced Human vs Alien combat set in a game with already well established abilities and technology.

Dust is a medium sized, hack'n'slash/platformer/RPG with big bucks behind (similar to what got the famous 2012 game, journey).

The story is good enough for me. The sound (including voices) and the music (final fantasy-ish) are on the same high level. But I still wonder how they managed to draw such an ugly world map.
The gameplay is relatively easy assuming you are patient enough to be grinding XP for levels. The gameplay will be boring/repetitive, because some stages are a bit too long, and many times, suffer from a lack of "density of action". That knowing you will have to re-run many stages several times with different abilities in order to acheive 100% completion... also there, you will be grinding XP for levels in order to make the game clearable.
There is a common default in RPGs: either you miss levels and the game is super hard, either you did a lot of boring XP grinding and the game is super easy because you are way over-leveled. So the stages are calibrated to be reasonably clearable at a specific level: if you are below, it's unreasonable, if you are above, it's too easy. This balance issue should be addressed in all RPGs, here it's not the case then you are free to torture yourself like a masochist or get bored at over-leveling your Dust and then slice throught the game like a hot knife in butter.
Technically, I got a few bugs (exceptions), and the controls felt slooooow/unresponsive in fight. It does run on linux based OSes with a recent mesa3D.
On the overall, I do recommend this game.

Dust: An Elysian Tail is a beautiful game. The art style is so entrancing that it's worth noting how easy it is to get drawn into this world before discussing anything else. Yes, it has anthropomorphic protagonists, but that really shouldn't keep you from giving this game a chance. The combat is tight and fast paced, providing some challenge without ever feeling overwhelming. I was able to get through most of the game without too much trouble fighting enemies, all of which match each location well and build a world you want to explore. I came much closer to 100%-ing the game than I ever planned to, because I had so much fun using the game's many platforming mechanics to explore every inch of each level. There are plenty of collectibles for people who enjoy that kind of thing, but if you'd rather plow through each level and just complete the story, you'll still have a great time. I do want to give the writing some credit here. While I can't say I was particularly surprised by where it led, the game does a great job fleshing out the characters and getting the player invested in uncovering the secrets that hide what really happened in our hero's past (yes, it's an amnesia story. Yes, it goes exactly where you think it will. No, that doesn't hurt your enjoyment of this game). The variety of movement options to explore the map are all fun and rewarding when you pull off each combo just right. I'm still amazed all of this was created by a solo developer. It truly raises the bar for a personal project like this.
If I had to give a criticism, I'd say the ending is a pretty harsh difficulty spike. The final boss has multiple steps to it, and the final level is WAY more difficult that anything you've played to that point. It's not brutal, per se, but it does feel like a more gradual curve could have helped brace the player for enemies who know how to block your combos effectively. However, this is the most minor of nitpicks.
I loved this game, and if you enjoy story-based adventure/platformers, you'll likely love this too. I couldn't recommend it more highly.

Paradox has done it again with an excellent Grand Strategy game.  As usual I have a video review here:
This game has just about everything you could want; exploration, diplomacy, war, trade; and all in SPACE!

Overall this is an absolutely amazing game and I recommend it to all that are interested in the strategy genre.  In fact it is probably the best game to get into Paradox's Grand Strategy games as the exploration and expansion ease you into the diplomacy and war.

This game is an old, classic masterpiece of an RPG.
You are JC Denton, a nano-augmented human, who is working for UNACTO, fighting against terrorists. Of course, nothing is what it seems and it turns into a huge cluster-molest of a conspiracy.
The Story is super well done, having loads of text to read which either connects to history or situations in the world. Loads of characters for you to interact with and areas to visit. The story is quite lengthy as well.
The gameplay is what really excells here. This game is famous for letting you, the player, complete missions/areas the way you want to finish it. This means you could either go in guns blazing, avoid everyone, hack security systems and more. Though, guns blazing isn't really the best way to go in the beginning of the game as you will be very inaccurate with fire arms.
There are, however, some aspects of this game that cannot be overlooked.
The graphics are bad. This is an old game, so that can be excused. However, I can understand how it can be a turn off when you never played the game and are used to "shiny graphics".
The voice acting is memorable due to it being so bad, that it's good.
Also, I have noticed some small bugs, where you have to use cheats to continue the game, due to NPC's not appearing or talking to you. (This only happened 2 two times, once per playthrough, different characters.)
However, the bad aspects are overshadowed by the wonderful story and the amazing gameplay.
This game is one of those games that you have to play at least once in your life. Additionally, somewhere on the internet you can download a texture pack for somewhat better graphics. But graphics is not everything and there aren't a lot of games with such a well made story and gameplay combination.

Atlantic Fleet is a turn-based naval strategy game that takes place during World War II. Originally designed as a mobile game (the sequel to Pacific Fleet, a mobile-only title), AF has made the transition to PC remarkably well.
PROS:
+ Turn-based (which I imagine would be a positive if you're looking at purchasing a turn-based strategy title).
+ Nice graphics. The ships could use a bit more AA, but you can easily fix that in your video card's control panel.
+ Detailed ship models. Individual components can take damage and affect the ship's performance. Fire can also cause explosions which by themselves can practically destroy a vessel.
+ Impressive physics. If you order your ship to stop, it doesn't suddenly halt, it takes time to stop (like a real ship would due to inertia) and your shots are affected by the wind (if this option is turned on; it's off by default). Even smoke, from fires or done purposefully to obscure ships, will blow differently depending on the wind, which could be used to your advantage or become a detriment.
+ Lots of options available to tailor your experience.
+ There's two different campaign modes and a single mission mode, the latter of which contains both historical missions and user-created missions.
+ Hotseat (1 vs 1 on the same machine) is available in the single mission mode.
+ A large selection of military and civilian ships of differing classes available, the majority being from the Royal Navy and the Kriegsmarine. There are also a few ships from the United States Navy, but AF focuses on naval battles between the British and Germans.
NEUTRAL:
+/- As an American who lives in Canada, I would've liked to have seen more ships from the United States Navy and at least a few ships from the Royal Canadian Navy as well. As noted above in the "Pros" section, I fully understand what the focus of this game was, but even so, it would've been nice to see.
CONS:
- Single missions have no land masses at all, it's entirely open ocean. That's fine sometimes, but the lack of land sometimes seems odd, especially when you can have aircraft fly in (from airbases on land) that seemingly come from nowhere.
- You can't fire individual turrets independently of one another. You either fire ALL of them or NONE of them.
- I can't find a single good reason (beyond role-playing purposes) to use a ship's secondary armament as these turrets have shorter range, less firepower, and are more easily damaged than the main turrets.
- Lack of knowledge revolving around WWII-era naval combat can hinder you, such as not understanding the significance of a ship's "belt" or when to use AP vs HE ammunition.
- It's sometimes too easy to locate and destroy submarines using destroyers or aircraft.
- Torpedoes seem unusually easy to dodge (although this might be a byproduct of using a turn-based system).
- How and when a ship explodes feels almost arbitrary when it comes to fires. Sometimes a fire can blaze for the entire battle (or go out) with little-to-no consequences, but at other times, a small fire could cause a huge explosion and sink the entire ship. I know there are real-life reasons for this, but without the capability to allocate repairs, it feels unfair that one moment the ship could look fine (no systems damaged) and then explode and sink.
- No Steam Cloud
VERDICT: As a big fan of naval warfare and turn-based strategy titles, I love Atlantic Fleet. It's one of my favorite games on Steam.
That said, if you're looking for a fast-paced game, Atlantic Fleet might not be your thing. AF requires you to plan and think your actions through, so reaction time is of very little importance. I think that's a good thing, but I know some people would feel otherwise, so it's important you know what you're getting into before you buy it (and then get stuck with a game you either don't want or are forced to do a refund).
To sum it all up, yes, I absolutely recommend Atlantic Fleet, provided you're in the market for a turn-based strategy naval warfare game that takes place in WWII.

Quite a fun little game, lots of playability here.  Generally a good game to relax with, but it really is hindered by some unfair game designs and good ol' RNG ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t.
The game is pretty simple in practice.  Maneuver your fleet to get good positions, aim your guns and try to sink the other guys.  There are a really large amount of different ships, from the most gigantic battleships armed with 9 16 inch guns, to tiny 1 gun corvettes and submarines.  Damage is fairly realistic (as far as I can tell) with the ability to try to target specific areas on the ship.  My personal favorite strategy is to target the main guns of the enemy ship, and after a few good hits you can effectively cut down their ability to deal lots of damage.
However the game isn't perfect, and there's 3 things that really irk me, and have caused a few rage quits.
1. Spawns and initiative.  So when you do a mission, you have to spawn in, and one side gets to move first depending on if they're the attacker.  This means they generally have the initial advantage, because they get to maneuver and fire first.  Regarding spawns, sometimes one side can get royally boned just because they spawned in a terrible formation and area.  I've had missions where I've spawned in a cluster, with 2 enemy submarines on either side of me.  That basically lost me the mission before I could even fight back, because each sub launched 4 torpedoes in a spread and I couldn't maneuver away from one without hitting the other.
2. RNG and fire directors.  Much like real warships, the guns are controlled by fire directors.  These basically get a range number from radar and spotters and whatnot, and then tell the gunners what elevation they need on the guns in order to hit the target.  Just like real life, in-game fire predictions get more and more accurate the more you fire at a target.  You should expect to miss long and miss short before actually hitting the target (if you follow the fire directors, more on that later) reliably.  However the fire directors seem to be completely broken.  I've had games where the fire director gives me first salvo accuracy, and I've had games where the fire director is directing me to miss by hundreds of yards after having been hitting salvos for several turns.  It seems the AI for this game is so inconsistant when it comes to aiming.  It gets so bad that I can't really feel like I can trust the fire directors, because for every one salvo I fire that hits perfectly, there are 3 that miss for no reason.
This leads on to part 2 of the whole fire direction stuff.  The computer controlled opponents have a mixture of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t good fire directors, and terrible fire directors.  So earlier I mentioned that you can expect to miss several salvos before you hit any shots, but with AI opponents that's not true.  I usually can expect about half of the AI ships to hit their first salvo perfectly, and pretty much all of them to be hitting their second salvo.  This is really infuriating, because if the enemy battleship hits their first salvo against yours, you are pretty much screwed from the start.
3. Mission balance.  Some of this could come down to "difficulty curve" or something like that, but some of the missions are incredibly unfair.  The main issue is the difference in numbers.  You can have a maximum (maximum) of 3 ships in your fleet.  Meanwhile the other side can have 5, 6, maybe more.  This means that you have a very finite amount of guns to hit the enemy with, and they can pretty much do whatever they want.  No matter how good your ships are, no matter how well you maneuver, you're still getting surrounded and outgunned, which coupled with the fire director issue, can lead to aggravation
However, these 3 issues aside, it's a pretty fun game.  I especially like the historical missions, where you can alter historical outcomes

OK... where to begin... Let's dive straight in, shall we?
PROS:
- It's cheap! Given there's a newer version out, this is a bargain. (Of course, why you'd even CONSIDER buying a new version is beyond me, once is truly, SURELY enough...)
- It provides a very clear insight into the riveting, high octane world of farming!
- lots of vehicles, accessories, things to load, unload, fill, plough etc (if that's your bag...)
CONS:
- I wanted to die while I played this...
- It's a simulator about farming - and yep, you guessed it, it's 'somewhat' realistic. That means it's so frightfully boring and dull you'll have trouble stopping your brain from exploding.
- There are in excess of 3000 people who own this game who gave it the thumbs up... Why is that a CON? Well... let's put it this way, the type of people who'd most likely give this a thumbs up probably like watching grass grow, and can't get enough of farming so they turn to a simulator to continue the experience into the evening. I'm shocked. Seriously I am.
SUMMARY: It's not that the game is terrible. In fact, you could very reasonably argue that in playing a farming simulator, you need to set your expectations lower than a crack ho' turning tricks with Jack the Ripper. But here's the thing - even knowing it's a farming simulator, it still was so awfully dull, so painfully boring that I can't believe I played as long as I did.
I mowed some grass at a golf course, I drove a tractor with a trailor perfectly lined up next to a harvester to catch wheat, then dumped said wheat in a grain silo, I took a load of peanuts to a place so they could attract a runaway elephant back (yep, you heard me right), i sold a tractor, I ploughed a field. Then I realised I was SPENDING MINUTES OF MY LIFE, JUST WASTING AWAY DOING THIS!!!!
The tutorial was mildly amusing for 5 minutes, then the game just continues the awful, mind-sapping exercise. Oh man, how this game will sap your very soul!
