I must admit, after watching my father play this game on the PS1 when I was young, and then when I was older getting to play it myself on the same console, my nostalgia glasses for this game area pretttty thick. But, I'm going to give this a good review anyways, and try to be as unbiased as possible.
Pros:
-An interesting "Junction System" that allows customization of characters stats through their "Guardian Force" (who in the previous games were merely summonable monsters).
-While the graphics aren't great by today's standards, they're definitely a step up from the PS1 version! There's new resolutions to choose from (and you can play in widescreen! Woot!) and the character models are significantly less pixelated than before!
-A Fantastic story, like seriously. Even though I haven't beat it yet, this is really a cool story that I'm really enjoying.
-Good characters that I've remembered throughout my entire life of gaming. Squall is just so great, and wow his gunblade is so cool!
-The combat is really fun! Honestly one of my favorite things to do in this game is just waddle around on the map and fight monsters. There's just such a good variety, with such good design, plus I'm partial to turn-based combat.
Cons:
-The music. Okay, the music in this game is amazing, but the quality is not. Square used the original "midi" files from the old PC release rather than the good files from the PS1 release, however, there is a community mod out there that replaces the files and makes it all better!
So there! I tried to look through my nostalgia glasses and give you a good review of a really cool, really memorable Final Fantasy game. I hope you enjoy it as much as I have!

TL;DR: A good tactical shooter, still holds up well today.
So as a note, I am not an expert on FPS's, nor the particular history of the FEAR franchise or how it affected other shooters. I am merely writing this review in regard to the game as it stands today, not historically.
FEAR (I'm not putting those periods in every time I write it) is ostensibly a tactical shooter with horror elements. Fairly old now, after playing it I feel it still holds up well. It is a fun game to play through, and the visuals hold up well enough, given when it was released. The gameplay itself holds up amazingly well, and it is a very engaging game.
The gameplay itself is mostly in the tactical shooter genre, in that you by yourself (No squadmates), confront large squads of fairly intelligent AI enemies. While not a cover based shooter, it is important to use cover to your advantage, as the enemies definitely will, and you can get minced fairly quick just acting as a turret. The enemies themselves will call out to each other, use cover, suppressing fire, and the like in order to try and take you down. How the AI compares to more modern shooters I am not sure, but it felt smart enough that I wasn't gunning them down in droves easily. The environments are varied enough that you are adjusting to each level's style to look for proper cover and where enemies might be hiding. There is a bit where it feels like you are in offices forever, and it starts to drag a bit. Finding your way through the game is pretty much going from A to B, only a few choices in routes that diverge very shortly. There are some items to find and story elements to listen to, but nothing that stops you from plowing on through. Movement has almost no execution challenges, which was a big plus for me as I am currently rather tired of FPS's that try to be platformers.
Tool-wise, you are given the pretty standard FPS variety to choose from, rifle, shotgun, pistol/dual pistol, SMG, along with some fancier guns with more limited ammo (Rail gun, particle gun, multi-rocket launcher, assault cannon). You can only hold 3, so I went with my two main stays (The shotgun which took out enemies fairly quickly if aimed right and close enough, not using up too much ammo), the rifle (ran out of ammo quicker than I got it, but good for precise shooting), and a fancy gun depending on the stage. You also get 3 different 'grenade' types, the standard sort that also explode on contact, mines, and remote detonated sticky bombs. I mostly used the first two, as the last required you to put away your gun, and I felt that the set up required wasn't worth the boom. In addition to weapons, other pickups include health (you can hold up to 10 health kits, I was usually maxed or close), armor, and items that permanently increase your maximum health and reflex. The pickups were valuable enough that I was scouring stages for ammo/health/armor/power ups, with the added bonus that it also lets you find the story elements as well, but I never felt I had to scour every inch of the stage.
The reflex was probably the selling point for the game along with the smart enemies, as it puts you into a slo-mo mode that allows you to take more careful aim and dodge better. It recharges pretty quickly, so you can use it every other encounter or so if they are coming at you rapid-paced. Mostly it felt it most useful for taking very careful aim (it let you adjust for recoil very well), or for nailing groups with the shotgun more readily. The slowed sound and effects definitely make it feel awesome.
The story is one of the horror genre, though it mostly gets that through the hallucinations and pop-up moments from the resident spooky girl. I wasn't too freaked out by it, as you pretty quickly identify which illusions can hurt you (hint, lots of fire, humanoid things rushing you), and the rest just serve to be spooky. The story is decent, there have been far better since it came out to fit into the horror genre, and the fact that if you can't shoot it, it can't hurt you causes things to stop being spooky/scary.
The only part that probably doesn't hold up nowadays is the graphics. The textures are flat, shots of the city in the distance are decidedly not cinematic, and faces are really blegh. I'm sure someone who keeps up with the most recent FPS's would scoff, but I found it didn't detract from the experience at all. It doesn't affect gameplay, so I didn't care.
Overall, FEAR still holds up as a fun gameplay experience. It is no longer top of the line, but the shooting elements hold up well, and it is good for an evening or two of fun getting through it.

What could I say about Zeno Clash? It's a first person brawler with some gunplay, in a unique and bizarre world with weird characters, weapons and a similarly strange story. The game itself is quite short, but it's the appropriate length. It's fun. I loved every single minute of it and the tower and the pit bonus adds a little more challenge to the overall moderately difficult game. I recommend it full-heartedly.

Easily one of the most original experiences I've ever seen in a PC game. Making a beat-em-up in a first-person situation was about as clunky as you could imagine, but it came out much better than you'd think. Still, it felt unfair and needlessly frustrating at times. It has a very 80s feel with the design looking like it came out of The Labyrinth and Dark Crystal with the tone of Mad Max and Water World. Zeno Clash is beautifully rendered too with the scenery and chaacter models ooking like they could actually have been made out of clay. The combat, which is the core gameplay, was solid and satisfying despite it's short comings. Never thought I could use the mouse and it feel like I'm really punching somebody! The voice acting is very flat and the story is very shallow, but the story didn't need to be very deep and the awkward voice acting added to the surreal and abstract feel of the whole thing. The music fit the atmosphere and the mood perfectly, similar to Abe's Odysee. I felt like that's probably the sounds you would hear in that universe. Zeno Clash is an easy recommendation for anyone looking for a fresh first person experience with some unique challenge.

Everything about this game except for the gameplay itself was either mediocre or just bad.
The combat is solid and simple enough. The platforming was okay, though there are moments where it's difficult to tell where a platform starts and ends, not to mention spike hitboxes. The inventory system was great actually, particularly the way the game lets you 'catalogue' materials so you only really need to find them once, after which you can buy materials to craft the items you need.
The quests didn't really have much to offer except story and money, but they were fun and simple enough to do.
The game is actually quite short, which is probably a good thing because if it took any longer I don't think I would have bothered to finish it.
Unfortunately, the game tries hard to have a solid story but it just ends up being extremely cliche and overly edgy. The voice acting doesn't help, especially when the main character sounds like a teenager trying to be cool, and the sidekick is extremely annoying at every moment.
Most of the characters in Dust are furries, some which inexplicably have Australian accents. Along with the art style the game has, you really have to be into crudely drawn furries to enjoy the characters. Otherwise none of them seem to be very likable.
The music wasn't bad but it wasn't very memorable.
Overall, I can't recommend the game unless you're a huge furry that likes incredibly cliche stories with amnesic protagonists and tragic backstories.

I must admit, after watching my father play this game on the PS1 when I was young, and then when I was older getting to play it myself on the same console, my nostalgia glasses for this game area pretttty thick. But, I'm going to give this a good review anyways, and try to be as unbiased as possible.
Pros:
-An interesting "Junction System" that allows customization of characters stats through their "Guardian Force" (who in the previous games were merely summonable monsters).
-While the graphics aren't great by today's standards, they're definitely a step up from the PS1 version! There's new resolutions to choose from (and you can play in widescreen! Woot!) and the character models are significantly less pixelated than before!
-A Fantastic story, like seriously. Even though I haven't beat it yet, this is really a cool story that I'm really enjoying.
-Good characters that I've remembered throughout my entire life of gaming. Squall is just so great, and wow his gunblade is so cool!
-The combat is really fun! Honestly one of my favorite things to do in this game is just waddle around on the map and fight monsters. There's just such a good variety, with such good design, plus I'm partial to turn-based combat.
Cons:
-The music. Okay, the music in this game is amazing, but the quality is not. Square used the original "midi" files from the old PC release rather than the good files from the PS1 release, however, there is a community mod out there that replaces the files and makes it all better!
So there! I tried to look through my nostalgia glasses and give you a good review of a really cool, really memorable Final Fantasy game. I hope you enjoy it as much as I have!

The mandatory account sign-up rubs me the wrong way. If we could use a star system here on Steam that would certainly cost this purchase a star. It doesn't take away from the game itself, though. I had no technical issues with the installation, account sign-up, or the game itself.
FF8 is an underrated title in the series. I see a lot of people saying it was the beginning of quality downturn for the series, and I mostly disagree. The "draw" system for acquiring spells is a bit monotonous at times, but that's the only flaw that could have been thought out better. I may not like every feature of the game, but I chalk all of my other issues up to simple taste preference. You can't please everyone.
Where this game fares well is storytelling, and that's really what these games are known for. Relatable characters on journeys that pull you into the game, and almost make you feel as though you have a personal stake in defeating the antagonist(s). The length of the cut scenes may seem a little excessive at times, but I enjoyed the vast majority of them.
The mini-game is card-based, for those concerned with making this game last as long as possible. It isn't as repeatable long-term as Chocobos from FF7, but on the plus side you can start playing cards a lot sooner in the game, and most rare cards are attainable even if you choose to skip the task (or miss it) originally. Like I said, it's not as fun as breeding and racing Chocobo from 7, but they were never going to top that for my enjoyment anyway.
Overall it was well worth the purchase. I have the original discs for PS, so I waited until I saw a nice sale on it.. but for those who are looking to play for the first time, or play again and no longer have it on Playstation, I think it's worth the full price.

You don't self-heal and you can have more than two weapons but something DEFINITELY does not feel right.  There is basically ONE enemy and they pass this off in the story as the soldiers all being clones.  Combine this with lackluster weapons and barren indoor levels and you have some VERY boring and repetitive combat that NO amount of "bullet time" can spice up.  Throw in the embarrassing "scary" creepy kid and poltergeist moments and you have something that is scary but not in the right way.  Watching the making of video is pretty embarrassing as well and just shows you the over-produced bloat and ego that went into this game.

This game is superb. If you are looking for a great indie 2D action platformer, this is a game to get. The game mixes level-by-level gameplay of older side scrolling games with secret hunting and exploration of a metroidvania.  Fuse that with a combo system that actively rewards the player with bonus XP for playing skillfully and you have one amazingly fun action-platform-metroidvania-brawler-whatever-it-is-but-who-cares-it's-great. The first thing that will hit you is the amazing hand-drawn art and animations. This is an absolutely beautiful game to behold. The voice acting is a bit spotty at times but overall, well executed. The bomb sprout puzzles are a bit tedious but so satisfying when you solve them, bosses were way too easy but still fun none the less, some of the diolague can be excized as it outright tells you a puzzle solution, but it doesn't handhold so often that it becomes patronizing, and the ester eggs are just adorable. I haven't found half of the secrets this game holds, so there's still a lot of stuff left for me to do. But, I did complete the story; I will not spoil the ending but I will say it is an ending that leaves lots of mixed emotions, but in a good way.
TL;DR the game isn't perfect, but no game is. This is the most fun I had in a 2D game since Castlevania: Symphony of the Night. Some nitpicks here and there but those could be attributed to the fact that the development team was one person, and a multi-man team could have made more mistakes than fixed them.
Overall, this game is a 9/10, one of my favorites, and it definately deserves the overwhelmingly positive reception it gets.
Still the best RPG ever made.

Excellent software for people who like to create characters and have them fight in epic battles, but are too lazy to actually play those battles. I wouldn't say it's a "game", because the most "gameplay" you can do is drop a land mine or start an event. Otherwise, the characters play it for you and deliver a neverending stream of silly updates.
It's a glorified character editor. You get the most fun out of creating characters, sharing them through the Workshop, and passing around screenshots of update texts. It is easy to create characters, write update files and draw maps. This is a double edged sword as it means the Workshop has a lot content, but Sturgeon's Law hits hard and a lot of it is low effort trash.
All in all, it's a fun time waster and cheap enough to not regret the purchase, especially on sale.
What could be improved:
The weird 'windowed' mode. There is a full screen option, but editing characters is not available in it. The borderless window can't be dragged or resized. Both display options are neither here nor there.
The map editor is a hilarious simplified MS Paint that has nothing but a handful of "surface materials" (water, sand, grass, mountain 1, 2, 3) and "add trees". That's it. Except for "water", the surfaces make zero difference either.
The game does crash quite a bit, though I mostly experience it when closing it and therefore don't lose any data. Still, annoying.
The Workshop could really use some categories, at least the basic tabs for Character, Map, Update File, Event. As it is, it's a mess and I can see why some people don't bother wading through piles of trash to find what they are looking for.

-Addicting space strategy opera-
This seems like the Galatic Civilisation 2-successor I wanted except it's real-time with pause.
For the new player: Stellaris plays much like civilization in space including the dreaded "just-one-more-turn-phenomenon".
Features:
Exploration, expansion, extermination (optional) or cultural/diplomatic win.
Different ethics highly change your playstyle e.g. with xenophobe you only get mean first contact hails to select. In democracies the boss is selected among your leaders which mixes your staff around and so on.
Context sensitive random event and crisis system, large scale galactic threat events.
You can add planets to sectors under AI control so you don't have to micromanage your large empire. Indeed you have a cap for solitary planets.
Game is highly modable.
Space looks nice.
No performance problems or crashes for me.
-minor bad things-
There's an extensive tutorial but many conccepts are still cloudy (on the other hand there's also a wiki built-in)
Some UI bugs and fighting with the controls and finding infos. Try to uplift a species for example. Pause is your friend here.
If you play a lot events become repetative but more will be added later I guess.
It could be even weirder but then I'm also reading Rhodan so take that with a grain of salt.
-mixed feelings-
Games really depend on your neighbors and where you start as you're never far ahead in the tech/power race in this game even in "normal".
If you want achievements you'll have to play ironman (only one autosave slot).
Death and ruin can come quickly in space. You will take losses of beloved admirals and beautiful worlds. I personally rage quit after an "ally" snatched a key planet away with a colony ship only 3 seconds ahead of my own colony ship.
My best admiral started taking drugs then died ahead of her time.
TLDR; you can buy that, it's good.

There are few series I love more than the Jedi Knight series, but Mysteries of the Sith was always the one I put on the backburner, saved for a rainy day. So while I heaped praises upon Dark Forces II, I had no idea just how much better its expansion was.
Mysteries of the Sith is a great game in ever respect, even removed from the context of its series, or even of the Star Wars series as a whole. I had always viewed Dark Forces II as the bridge between Quake and Half-Life in terms of its structure and design, but really that honor is more suited to Mysteries of the Sith. It presents a world that feels believable and lived in (not an easy task in 1998), and conveys much of its narrative through visuals and gameplay with an elegance that few if any of its contemporaries can claim to match.
Like I said, this is a great game if ever there was one. It's a shooter that ranks high among others of its era, and it's certainly one of the best Star Wars games ever made.

is a clicker title and it starts off decent with a puppet show style...but after a while, you discover that you've probably made a mistake.
basically starts you off with a hero who you can power up and provide support as his "god".  If this warrior dies, it's curtains...literally!  You'll lose some gold and restarts at the same wave.  You'll later unlock new powers, perks, and heroes to help you out.

games.  So, props to the dev there!
The balancing, however, is quite unforgivable...especially for a clicker title.  It starts out simply enough, but soon ramps up the difficulty, especially at bosses and most notably at the dragons (marked at "100" milestone stages).  You can keep powering your heroes up or assisting them as their "god", but even your godly powers have limits...adding boosts have cooldowns and sometimes aren't even enough to help your heroes survive boss fights.  You'll find yourself clicking your heroes to heal rather than clicking enemies to provide additional damage often.  You can click with all your might, but often times, you will either tire yourself out or just end up having your heroes perish!   At that point, I'd just suggest investing in an autoclicker and being done with it.  (Tip:  Healing is a better idea than attacking)
That said, no...I don't recommend

The game has nice art, and I like the level design and where the developer is trying to go with this game.  It does feel like this developer is trying to do something good and make a fun game, however at its early access release right now, it sadly isn't a game I can recommend for purchase at it's $7.99 USD price tag.
Main problems with this game are:
1) Right now, there is no graphic settings available in the options at all.  No resolution settings, and not even a full screen off/on setting.  This means that I'm looking at a window about half the size of my default 1920x1080 resolution and I would have to change my computer video settings to match the game just to have it full screen!  Ugh.
2) Another complaint I have is that using the keyboard in this game, while it can be done, just isn't a satisfactory option.  A controller is almost a MUST to really be able to play this game effectively, at least in my opinion anyhow because the keyboard controls just feel awkward and out of place.
3) My biggest complaint with the game itself is that your avatar feels like a weightless paper doll just moving over a background and this makes fighting and hitting a monster unsatisfying.  The floaty movement and feel of your avatar and the monsters as well also takes away a lot from what I feel like could be good gameplay.
All in all, right now in early access, as much as I want to like this game, I just cannot recommend it until more updates and work has been done to this game, and well... that's what early access is for.  My recommendation is to wait on this one and see what it looks like mid summer 2016 to fall of 2016 and if progress has been made and the game at least has a fullscreen option, then perhaps it will be worth it's price tag at that point.

This is the sort of game that I wouldn't play normally. After it came to my attention (rather sideways), I saw it looked better than the average Early Access game.
This is a point in it's favor, much as it shouldn't have to be. Early Access should have lots of quality games like this one, rathder than the usual crud that seems to collect there (and in Greenlight) these days. As a reviewer, I haven't done a lot of these games, but after a good look at it, I simply had to ry it and try and find a way to tear it apart.
I failed. Not in playing it, which I did rather nicely-- in tearing it apart. There have been a few things in the Discussions that people have complained about, and I didn't run into any of it. There's a tiny amount of controller lag, but not enough to create problems even for people that don't like platform-y action hacky-slashy games.
The only real gripe I have with the game is the controller information image that's displayed on one of the loading screens-- it would be nice to have that available to people using controllers from the escape menu or someplace else where they can refer to it rather than a quick peek and gone to who-knows-where forever.
The game is good at tutorializing in an unobtrustive, easy to ignore fashion, but after awhile it goes away and if you've put it down for awhile and come back, it might be a tad difficult to pick up again. The progression elements are quite nice, and all of the pickups are easily identified and have functions with the exception of a gold-colored pickup that I never found out the purpose of.
This was the second game we covered in the stream, and for my money it was an excellent buy. It's one of the rare games I want to play more after the review. It was easy and intuitive to pick up and play, and the difficulty curve wasn't steep enough to frustrate, but it did provide a challenge as I got further into the game. Never enough to make me want to uininstall it, but enough that I didn't feel all-powerful.
Some people will find the first couple of levels incredibly easy, especially if they have a lot of experience with this sort of game. I don't, so your mileage may very. The main character is yet another draw-- not in the way she's dressed, but in the history of the character that the game is based on, and the bits of lore that surround the Tyrfing Cycle (which is a proper Norse legend).
Grab your favorite control method and some popcorn, fire the game up and enjoy. For even the full price of $8.00 US, the combination of solid gameplay and pretty 2D graphics that evoke the culture from which they were derived is worth that and more. The dev is repsonsive, and is trying very hard to get reported issues dealt with in short order.

Blamdown Udder Fury
Top-down Twin-stick Shooter
Guru Games
Guru Games
is a top-down twin-stick shooter developed and published by Guru Games.
You play as a cow who goes on a rampage to try and find her kidnapped partner. You will join the resistance and battle Donal Drump. Yeah, this is the story.
Nothing too special and not all that funny, and it really doesn't even matter: it is just a premise to have a cow with a machine gun and bazooka destroy buildings.
Powered by the Unity engine, the game doesn't look too good. The performance is pretty weak, staying at 30fps during most of the playthrough, and the physics are all over the place, with some ragdolls and buildings just collapsing while others fly into the air. The cartoonish look is unpolished but not unpleasing to look at. Thankfully, there are no game-breaking bugs, and the experience wasn't worsened by it.
The gameplay is very simple: you have unlimited ammo for your SMG and bazooka, and in each level there are some objectives to complete that usually require the destruction of something. The more buildings you destroy, the higher the Chaos meter raises, causing the arrival of more and stronger enemies.
In Survival Mode, you replay story levels and you try to survive as long as possible. An interesting mechanic is that every once in a while you are forced to upgrade both yourself and your enemies, making you choose the lesser evil
Other than being too simple for its own good, I had a problem with the health drop: when I had full health dead enemies dropped HP items like flies, but when I had close to 0 HP I got jack! This lead to forced restarts and some frustration.
The more time you spend in a level, the more enemies appear that will try and kill you. "Thanks" to the lack of health items in the moment of need, your goals become unachievable, so you start rushing every single level instead of trying to blow everything up. There are also 2 boss fights in the game that are insultingly easy to beat, especially compared to all the trouble that you go through just to get to them.
The game's soundtrack is joyful but nothing special, and the sound effects are decent even if a little too loud when there are many enemies on screen.
After you have finished the 2-hour campaign, you can play Survival Mode and you can try to unlock the 63 achievements that require a lot of time spent in Survival Mode.
Overall, this is a short, simple twin-stick shooter that earns its cheap price of 5$. Highly recommended when on sale.

similar to Company of Heroes , but very complex , you can control groups and squads , or you can control single units , even control acuratly with mouse aiming and arrow key movements.
for example say you have 1 tank unit , and 2 infantry soldiers , you can have the 2 infantry soldiers fight as a group or fight as single units(1soldier). you can use cover and environment to hide during combat.
say an enemy tank arrives facing your own tank unit , you can either let the tank engage automaticaly or you can take control of it, then use mouse for accurate aiming , each vehicle parts with different resistance or weakness.
you may decide to only destroy the vehicle tracks , or turret , to disable it depending on the situation , without completely destroying the vehicle , wich you can later repair and use for your own soldiers.
use the arrow key to control tank movements all while controlling the camera and turret targetting. or simply left click for move orders and let the AI control itself.
each single soldier or vehicle have its own inventory and can rearm from dead bodies or pickup helmets from fallen soldiers , after a long battle you can find alot of weapons ,helmets and grenades that might be better then your current equipment. items are found on fallen bodies or may be dropped on the ground.
the environment is destroyable so you can drive a tank into objects or fire explosive rounds to clear a path for your infantry , for example as a defending team you may want to shell the area you will be shooting at so that the invading enemies do not have any cover to protect themselfs.
you can also create very customised squads with machineguns , antitank weapons , grenades, by changing the inventory of each individual soldiers live on the battlefield.
the game does not give you a tutorial but simply information messages poping up as you play. it is hard to learn . but you learn from your mistakes , you click and read everything , and it becomes much easier after a few missions.
you can also control game speed , with 6 different speeds , slow down when you need to think or control large number of units in a short time.
you can also scavange for ammo and weapons on dead bodies and rearm your veterans so they can continue fighting. each individual unit has its own inventory and grenades , ammo , etc...
i personaly enjoy this more then company of heroes (not that company of heroes was bad , i did post a positive review for both game. lol) , Men Of War is more difficult, more advanced, and much more fun for people looking for a tactical strategy game.

Who is this Game For?
==================
F.E.A.R. is a secret force that deals with paranormal phenomena. In this first-person shooter, you become the new point man (what else?) who’s tasked with stopping a military experiment that’s gone bad. Fans FPS who doesn’t mind a little horror will find this game very enjoyable. The game’s graphics has aged a little, but the game play, AI and controls still hold up to this day as some of the best in FPS history.
Is it good?
=================
The scarier parts of the game are portrayed effectively, and some players will certainly react to the game’s eerie atmosphere. The in-game weaponry is rather basic, and includes a pistol, a submachine gun, a shotgun, and a rocket launcher. The most appealing gun is Nail gun, which fires high-velocity nails into enemies and can even pin them to walls. You can also kick enemies, as well as punch them or hit them with your rifle butt. You can only carry three weapons at a time, which forces you to choose the best ones for you. Another feature that can help you in the game is called Slowmo, which is similar to Max Payne’s infamous bullet time feature.
Does it have any problems?
========================
Being an older game with an old engine, some people might have problems. While had no problem, anyone else should be able to fix anything by check the PC Gamer Wiki:
.
Final Thoughts!
====================
The enemy A.I. in F.E.A.R. is great and, along with the excellent graphics engine and wonderful sound, you can play through many intensely enjoyable combat scenes. Most of the scenery explodes around you when impacted by bullets (like shattering wood, breaking windows, and parts of walls splatter all over), and the sound is certainly complementary to the general feeling of the battle scenes.

Stellaris is at first glance a decent game. Up to 1000 star systems to conquer. You may think the possibilities are endless. After a few games i had to realize, that the game lacks content. The game depends on the unique races u can create and this makes a lot of fun, but start is always the same. Your first planet has always the same size. One starsystem close to your home has always no ressources. As soon as you build your first mining station outside your home system pirates will show up. Always. After an interesting starting phase, the game becomes more and more boring. Diplomacy doesn't really work. The AI is not willing to cooperate with the player, even if the relations are great. Warfare is pretty boring. Build up a decent fleet with the right configuration, than wipe your enemy out. Build up an army an simply conquer world by world. The sectors, which help you govern the galaxy are a nice idea, but the system is flawed. The player can only control a few worlds her-/himself. In the beginning 5-7, later a few more. In a 1000 star galaxy this is not much. On these worlds you have to build your fleet and armies. The sectors govern themselves, that is nice, but they don't really help you in wars. They don't build fleets and defense only if they are told to do so. Most events are triggerd by your science ships while discovering the galaxy. After a while you realize, that there are not many diffrent events and they repeat and repeat. Soon it is so boring, that you stop playing. Multiplayer might be fun, but players from around the world play on one server. The results are laggs, disconnects and no fun. To keep the game running, the speed has to be turned down. This way games take days to finish.
Update: The first patch is out, but the game is still bad. Many things were changed and it was fun until I had to realize that the peace system is now broken. Found myself in a 1vs2 and won againt the odds, but i could not demand anything, only a white peace. So, there is a lot to be fixed. Wait until christmas!

The main part of the game, the majority of what this game is about, is the tactical solution though, and considered that, the shortcomings of the strategic don't bother that much. What the strategic part of the game allows for is overall victory and managing your total fleet, wich it handles good enough, but it is a bit simple in its strategy layout and is sort of counter-intuitive.
All in all, the core of this game is the tactical simulation, and as such it's the best turn-based game like this that I've played since Fighting Steel. Strongly recommended for those interested in the tactics and fighting of the atlantic war.

After a few major patches, and a lot more hors into it, I changed my views on it.
While it's still not perfect, and the tutorial is still lacking for completely new players, they reworked and fixed a lot of the problems the game had, making it a real contender for good 4X games, especially the space ones.
Still, I need to warn people that are not used to 4X games, because this one seems to want to take an extra step towards the even more complex genre of Grand Strategy (Europa Universalis or Crusader King from the same publisher for example), so you will have to contend with a fairly significant amount of layers, rather than more vague and global things loke global happiness.
Like most 4X, the AI will sometimes feel a bit nonsensical in how they approach you or other AI, because they lack subtlety, and tend to utterly dislike any empire that doesn't agree with them (on ethics and policies).
That said, if you can stay for long enough to learn a bit about the various systems, the game has quite a lot to offer, and if you take into account the fairly good dlc and the mods, there is quite a lot on the table.

NOTE: This game was given to me by the developer for review purposes. This did not influence my review in any way.
Note: Blamdown Udder Fury is currently in Early Access. The version reviewed was the latest as of the date of the review (20160609).
Blamdown Udder Fury is a rather silly twin-stick shooter in which you control a cow intent on causing destruction with your bazooka. It doesn't make a lot of sense, but that's fine; it's not supposed to.
The game starts with a quick and simple tutorial-like introduction. You're given control of a cow, you jump a few fences in search of another cow, and you discover that the farmer has taken her and left the farm. Vowing to destroy the farmer and get her back, you pick up some weapons that someone carelessly left behind and you start shooting everything in sight.
Graphics - Graphics are bright and colourful, with cartoon-like models and simple textures. There's no zooming in or out of the view, and no way to rotate it either, often leading to frustration when your character or the enemies shooting at you are hidden by level geometry.
There are a number of detail level options that I didn't play around with; running at maximum for everything caused no problems to my old gaming laptop, so any new semi-decent graphics chipset should be able to handle the game easily enough. But even on maximum settings Blamdown won't win any awards for best graphics. They're suitable for the casual style of this game, though.
Sound - The game's music track is a bit frantic and I found it a bit grating within the first hour of play. It's reasonably well produced, though. Sound effects, too, are effective and do their job solidly.
Gameplay - Control of the game's bovine hero is via controller or mouse and keyboard. The default control layouts for both work well, but after getting a bit frustrated with the controller I reverted to mouse and keyboard, as it seems to be a bit more accurate. Either way, you can move and aim independently, like any twin-stick shooter, and you have a primary and secondary weapon. You can also do a quick dash to evade enemies (most of which are faster than you), or jump to dodge, shoot flying enemies, or reach above-ground areas.
Each large level of Blamdown Udder Fury gives you a number of goals to complete before either being picked up by your seedy-looking friend-cow in a helicopter, or confronting one of the bosses, depending on the level in question. These goals are almost always related to causing chaos by blowing up buildings, people, and vehicles with your bazooka.
As you raise the chaos level, however, the game throws more powerful enemies at you in greater numbers. It's not too long before you have cow catchers, machine gunners, cartoon tanks, and jet-pack-powered heavy weapons guys hot on your hoofs, causing a fair swathe of destruction around them.
Unfortunately, dodging enemy bullets while simultaneously dishing out destruction of your own is not as easy as it could be, as each structure or vehicle that you destroy breaks up into a number of indestructible jagged pieces, each of which can block your movement as well as your bullets. It's a weird design choice and it makes the game more frustrating than it should be.
Blamdown is more of a casual game than a die-hard twin-stick shooter, but it doesn't try to hide that fact. It lacks the vast equipment or upgrade trees that tend to be common to the genre, essentially leaving each level to stand on its own, with no real progression. It's fun, but limited.
Bear in bind that Blamdown is still in Early Access, too; there's a chance that some of this will change.
Pros:
+ An original story with some humour
+ Colourful cartoon-like graphics
Cons:
- Exploded objects often get in the way of movement and gunplay, causing more frustration than is necessary
- The lack of progressive achievements, such as character improvements, weapon upgrades, and even Steam achievements, makes the game feel a bit pointless
- Level geometry sometimes hides the action
- Poor grammar in some of the in-game text
Blamdown Udder Fury is a competent casual-style twin-stick shooter. If you're after something that's a bit of fun, without too much thought required, give it a shot.

Blamdown: Udder Fury is a twin-stick shooter. It’s has story mode and a survival mode in which all you do is cause chaos. Think Just Cause 2 but with a cow instead of Rico and top down instead of third person. Game is very fun if you want to just sit back and relax as it doesn’t take itself too seriously.
Blamdown: Udder Fury’s graphics are decent. They’re nothing too special but sort of pleasing to the eyes. It has those blocky type textures and from a top down view they look pretty neat. The environment is fully destructible and the maps are pretty big for a top down shooter. In addition to that you get these comic book type words like “Blam”, “Kaboom” and other such words, these look very good as well. There were no problems in FPS and the game played very smoothly. There were a few graphical glitches but then again the game is in Early Access, so hopefully those will be sorted out eventually.
There are only two soundtracks available at this time. They both sound pretty nice and have cheery music. Though a bit more variety wouldn’t hurt. The sound of guns and the enemy tanks etc. are also okay. Sound can be improved by adding more soundtracks.
In the story mode you’re Moonalisa and you’re out to take revenge from the evil farmer who has killed and made burgers out of your lover, Rosa. The Campaign has you go to different states. Missions involve mostly shoot stuff, pressing buttons to activate stuff, hacking doors, killing enemies and cause chaos etc. There are boss battles too e.g. the first boss battle is a guy in wheel chair in a hamburger factory and there’s meat grinders everywhere.
You have a main weapon which is a gun (a laser in ball shooter? In the ‘LastVulture’ map) and a bazooka both of which have unlimited ammo. Other than reloading you can keep firing forever. The bazooka has a cool down meter which you can see around the cow. You can shoot buildings, lamp posts, traffic lights, innocent people, cars etc. Every object you destroy nets you points. Basically you can shoot everything in a map and destroy it to earn points which also raises your chaos level. You can also jump and double jump in this game. Jumping can be used to climb on top of buildings or shoot down soldiers with jetpacks. In addition to that you also have a dash ability which you can use frequently, just like the bazooka it also has a cool-down so you can’t just spam dash all the time.
Survival mode has you play Moonalisa and you get to cause chaos until you die. With each increment of chaos level, new and more aggressive enemies start spawning. The early level enemies are guys in vans trying to catch you with nets but as you progress, tanks, jetpack soldiers with bazookas, soldiers with guns etc. start to chase you around the map.
The first time you gain a chaos level you get an upgrade such as no reloading, health regeneration over time, faster bazooka cool downs etc. The second time you level up you must choose an upgrade for the enemy side, they include upgrades such as jetpack soldiers, harder tanks, laser gun soldiers etc. The process repeats itself like this for every level.

Sadly one of the weaker men of war games I've ever played. I found a lot of bugs and issues with this one which ended up making the experience  of playing...painful. The biggest problems were:
1. Helicopters - Pretty much any map where there is helicopters, as these machines of death are painful to kill and will likely destroy your forces with you having nothing to fight back with. Any map with you using one becomes a game of random hope as the helicopter will sometimes crash on it's own or fly off the map making it useless.
2. Too much bush - A lot of time you can't figure out where the enemy is or where your forces are due to the thick bush. Sadly a lot of times you will have to just remember where enemies are coming from with trial and error.
3. Units getting stuck - A lot of times I found my units getting stuck on the map. A few times they glitched themselves into the water which either instant kill them or have them stuck there forever. Other times I had my units wander off the map to the point where I can't reach them.
4. Unbalance - The bigger issue is balancing, you have some missions where your completely overwhelmed with no way of getting more units (not like previous men of war games where you get waves of reinforcements or the ability to call in units). Other  times you get tanks or apcs that completely destroy the other team as they have nothing to fight back with.
Overall I felt this game was the weaker of the bunch. It was a good attempt but sadly it was one of the worst experience I had with a men of war game.

(no spoiler review) Final Fantasy VIII:  A pretty good RPG with some really interesting mechanics. It is now the highest number FF game I've beat, so you can tell I'm behind in the series. Even though I only just beat it, I actually owned and played FF VIII the year it came out, but got so addicted to Triple Triad that I never progressed the main story more than a few hours; so it felt really good to go back and finally beat it.
A lot of the game systems threw me off at first.  Understanding Junctioning and GFs took me a really long time to figure out. Once I got used to the system, I really liked it. It was addicting to level up by GFs to get new abilities and stats on them, especially when it meant I could open up a stat to junction magic onto, which made the characters much more powerful.
However, as the game progressed, the attaching gfs and abilities to each character became probably my biggest complaint about the game. The reason for this is that every friggin' 10 minutes your party either splits off, or certain characters become unavailable, or you switch between parties, and every single time you have to switch junctions, abilities and magic to your new group (and if it affects their hp then you have to waste cure magic to bring their hp up). This drove me crazy and really disrupted the flow of the game.
I highly enjoyed the Steam version of FFVIII. I read a bunch of complaints about the Steam version, but the only one that I thought was valid was that all the music was in midi format, which made it all sound horrible. Luckily, someone created a mod that replaced all the midi music files with non-midi ones, so once I installed that, I got all the regular music back again. Another bonus of the Steam version is that the game comes with a lot of cheats. They have some pretty heavy ones, like always have full health, or always do 9999 damage. The only "cheat" I indulged in was the amazing high-speed mode. By pressing F1, you could activate high-speed mode which sped everything up by a factor of five. I found this to be a great QoL feature that I used mainly during the game's ridiculously long summon sequences, grinding regular battles, and parts that I had to repeat due to me dying and reloading a save. This feature, along with the Half-Encounter/No-Encounter abilities one of my GFs learned, made it so I could cut through overly long segments and random encounters if I didn't want to deal with them.
As for the story and characters, overall I thought they were good. The story got really complicated and weird towards the end, but I liked it. I had to research some stuff during the game and afterward, because the game didn't explain many things that the characters would talk about and reference, which was frustrating. I know a lot of people found Squall too moody, and he was very moody, but I really enjoyed the arc of his character. I think my two favorite characters were Quistis and Zell. I also really enjoyed Laguna, Ward and Kiros.

This game achieves what it sets out to do; Intimidate and terminate as you'll spend a fair amount of time tactically gunning your way through a plethora of relentless killing machines blocking your path. The horror in this game is done very well despite being old. However, there are cheap jumpscares that are used HOWEVER they are very small in quantity and aren't really that spooky but that isn't the most defining feature of the horror elements; it's the atmosphere that creeps you out the most. The environment contributes a massive part to the horror as well as even with visuals that are older than a decade it can still get you shivering and squirming to the point where you might need to call it a night and continue off the next day.
The gunplay is astonishing and the mechanics employed keep the game fresh and interesting as there is a sense of progression as bigger & better weapons are found later in the game as well as scarily strong enemies that enforce strategy and resource management, (e.g. use the 1-clip rocket launcher on a group of guys or save it for the colossal mechanical beast later on). The A.I in this game is truly mesmorising as groups of soldiers can work together efficiently and the lesser units will tend to protect the heavy of the group, resulting in a somewhat challenging firefight. However, these are fairly rare and once you understand how the units operate you can always predict what they'll do and more often than not you'll actually be right.
The bullet time is a great tool and the ability to further extend your joyful takeovers with 'Reflex Boosters' is a great addition to the game, the same can be said for 'Health Boosters'. Despite the usefulness of such tools it wont make you Rambo as the enemies can easily kill you just you can easily kill them.
But there is one major issue I have with the game grouped with smaller issues and this is the fact that the difficulties aren't challenging enough even when on 'Masochist Difficulty'. Another issue I had is where weapons had disappeared once I had dropped them, at first I thought this was a simple bug and restarted but the issue persisted.
Nevertheless, F.E.A.R is a great FPS and offers an experience you wont forget with a brilliant story, some interesting characters (not all of them are that great to be fair) and top-notch gunplay.
Highly recommended.

Astheticly pleasing. Its a clicker game and it knows it. It quickly gets to the point where you need an autoclicker healing your hero to be able to even progress past any boss.  Unlike other clicker games the stat level system dosnt scale like other games. This leaves the impression that you need more time idling to be allowed to level up much at all. If you have this impression you would be right, It more or less requires you to sit there idle (auto clicker or any clicking of any time optional) And wait till you collect enough money to level up a decent amount of times which is required to make any form of impact. The bosses of the first hundred levels are recycles for every hundred levels. Speaking of farming coin for leveling up the coin counter visable caps at 999999. This is an odd decision to me as to reach the past a stat level of 240 or so its going to take you about a tenth of The counters max to obtain ONE level. Dont worry (Those that will leave this for hours on end.) The game keeps count of all your money even if there is no visual representation. If i had to ask for them to add something its to Increase the visual cap. This would be nice as there is an achievment to obtain 5000 total levels and half of the stats level off between 80 and 120 (or so). Speaking of these level caps on half of the skills. These are the critical strike chance and the speed/ Potency stats. These cap at a third or a forth of a second per action. Considering how long this game takes to complete and brick wall difficulty of any bosses I have to recommend that the Developers remove the hard caps and add soft caps  (add heavy deminishing returns ). Even requiering 10 levels to speed up by a 0.01 of a second would be more worth it in the long run and allow a bit of east when trying to obtain the end goal of 5000 levels.
A note on the final enemy kill total achievment (One million), Even if you have a monster you can instantly kill you only get about 2-3 kills per second. This means the game will need to idle for quite a long time.  If you avarage 2,5 kills it will take you around 112 hours or so of idling.
Remember its a clicker game. Would i recommend it. Sure why not if you want easy achievments to rack up your count just dont expect to get any past the few hour mark till you get to the 120+ hour mark.

Stellaris is at first glance a decent game. Up to 1000 star systems to conquer. You may think the possibilities are endless. After a few games i had to realize, that the game lacks content. The game depends on the unique races u can create and this makes a lot of fun, but start is always the same. Your first planet has always the same size. One starsystem close to your home has always no ressources. As soon as you build your first mining station outside your home system pirates will show up. Always. After an interesting starting phase, the game becomes more and more boring. Diplomacy doesn't really work. The AI is not willing to cooperate with the player, even if the relations are great. Warfare is pretty boring. Build up a decent fleet with the right configuration, than wipe your enemy out. Build up an army an simply conquer world by world. The sectors, which help you govern the galaxy are a nice idea, but the system is flawed. The player can only control a few worlds her-/himself. In the beginning 5-7, later a few more. In a 1000 star galaxy this is not much. On these worlds you have to build your fleet and armies. The sectors govern themselves, that is nice, but they don't really help you in wars. They don't build fleets and defense only if they are told to do so. Most events are triggerd by your science ships while discovering the galaxy. After a while you realize, that there are not many diffrent events and they repeat and repeat. Soon it is so boring, that you stop playing. Multiplayer might be fun, but players from around the world play on one server. The results are laggs, disconnects and no fun. To keep the game running, the speed has to be turned down. This way games take days to finish.
Update: The first patch is out, but the game is still bad. Many things were changed and it was fun until I had to realize that the peace system is now broken. Found myself in a 1vs2 and won againt the odds, but i could not demand anything, only a white peace. So, there is a lot to be fixed. Wait until christmas!

That said, if you can stay for long enough to learn a bit about the various systems, the game has quite a lot to offer, and if you take into account the fairly good dlc and the mods, there is quite a lot on the table.

Found this game by chance in a store, and immedeately became kinda curious, since warships are pretty much my fetish
, but didn't really expected much from it, so, despite the low price, I waited for sale and only then picked it up. And when I launched it, I was immideately sucked in, because this game is a real gem not only for those who likes boats. And here's why.
This is a turn-based strategy, where you manually control a fleet of several warships, manually managing each ship's movement and weapons. Since the game got "Atlantic" in its title, you can play either with Royal Navy or Kriegsmarine ships. Both sides have a lot of historically accurate ships (with a couple of prototypes that weren't build or excessively used during the WWII) and slight advantages in certain areas (Britain has a lot of BB and can use CV, while Gemany completely dominates in terms of SS).
As you should expect from a TBS, you switch turns with your enemy, manually setting speed and angle of movement of each ship and (here's the main catch of this game) manually setting the angle and direction of guns. That's very different from standard "% to hit" and requires player to actually estimate the needed angle by the eye, judging by the previous shots and a couple of very inaccurate hints from the game. How hard is it? Well, around 0,3-0,5 degree usually determine if you hit or miss. And even if you have a perfect eye, the wind can come into play as well. Want to sink someone with torpedoes? It's easier, you need only to set the direction of each torpedo, keeping in mind the direction and speed of the enemy, however, any ship will try to dodge this, so the only real option is shooting in barrages. 4-8 torpedoes are pretty hard to dodge, but use all of them for one sure kill or save some for other ships? That's the question. Also you can gain access to land-based or carrier-based aviation. Again, bombs/torpedoes/rockets are aimed manually, by controlling one plane per turn. After setting the angle, you need to wait for a right moment to dive and then the right moment to attack, while there's a chance to be hit by AA guns. Sometimes this can be trickier than shelling, but the result of a well-aimed attack can be absolutely devastating.
Needless to say, you need to learn to become good here. Skipping training is not an option at all, and even after that you will have to play a lot before you can hit your target in first couple of shots. However, I find this much more interesting than looking at random misses with 90% in CQC
and the feeling of landing a perfect shot from just the first estimation by your bare eye is priceless.
Aside from training, there are several modes you can play.
1) Campaign
Doesn't really feel like one, but it's a great playground to test different ships and learn how to use them. There are 50 missions, completing them give you points, which are used to buy new ships. Ships gain levels (up to five stars), which gives them small passive buffs like AA defence. Late missions are pretty much a challenge, since require you to encounter pretty strong and non-standard fleets (like BB+SS), while you can't take more than 3 ships with you,
2) War in the Atlantic (dynamic campaign)
Guess this is the main mode. You gain access to the huge map, each turn you can move your fleets up to 10 ships from one area to another, main goal here is to sink a very huge amount of transport ships of your enemy. As time goes, some historic events occur, like occupation of France, giving Germany access to more naval shipyards. Also random air attacks happen from time to time, damaging ships not far from land and docks, increasing repair times. Not all ships are available from start, for example you can't build Bismarck and Tirpitz until the date at which they were operational in real life. Another nice touch - permadeath for any ship. Every destroyed ship (except SS or DD) is a huge loss and can have a huge impact. Personally I can remember how I lost Admiral Hipper to HMS Queen Elizabeth in a hour-long battle, and only thing that felt comforting was knowing that she's not coming back either after eating 20+ shells and several torpedoes.
Bad thing about this though is that you need to sink every transport ship manually, unless they come without escort. It's fine at first, but after 10+ encounters it becomes boring as hell. Especially with submarines, since they have pretty limited amount of torpedoes, and only one weak gun. Also playing on map can be confusing at first, as tutorial doesn't really explain all the things, like where you should hunt the transports and stuff.
3) Single missions.
Some battle that took place during WWII, several ships that took part in it, with damage they had at the start of it. You can take each side and try to repeat or revert the outcome of a battle. Simple as that, but can be pretty challenging.
Personally I completed dynamic campaign one time and almost finished campaign two times, which took me 60+ hours, so the amount of gameplay is pretty huge.
For a game that originally came from mobile devices it looks pretty decent, since developers say they overhauled it a lot.  Water looks nice, and models, while having not-so-high resolution textures, make up for it by being nicely detailed and historically accurate. Fire and explosions? Yeah, probably not the best looking, but at least the explosions are huge and colorful. Overall - nicely looking game, but don't expect anything stunning here.
Not an expert on how the ship should sound, but the sound of main guns firing is pretty powerful, Explosions have a pretty satisfying bang and sounds of AA guns firing will haunt me in nightmares. So I guess the sounds are at the very least OK.
A must have for anyone interested in naval warfare, or enjoying TBS and looking for something original. For such a small price (around 8 times cheaper than AAA-title in my region), you get a very interesting game with a high skill cap and potential to suck you in for tons of hours. And if it's on sale (and it's on sale at the time when I wrote this) - don't even think about hesitating. You won't regret it.

Let's start by facing the facts. Yes, it's old. Yes, the levels look kind of bland. Yes, the character design leaves a lot to be desired. However, you're still going to be hard pressed to find an action-RPG that actually uses that title and means it. You are dropped into the shiny black boots of JC Denton, a UNATCO secret agent who looks every bit like he escaped from the Matrix, as he goes forth to try and figure out just what's going on. However, that's the charm of the game. A lot of games claim to have open ended missions, but which really boil down to 'you have three ways to get into the objective building.' Deus Ex reads 'open ended missions' as "You can choose to be an ace cyborg hacker, a sneaky melee expert, a walking collection of guns and explosives, or anything in between, and still have a way to make it to the objective." In theory you can play through Deus Ex once in a week and reach an ending, but really, are you going to let all that unexplored opportunity go to waste?

By far the Playstation version is better than the Steam version:
[PROS]
-Steam achievements
-Smoothed graphics or original Playstation 1 graphic settings available
-Great soundtrack*
-Attacking can be hands-on (Example: using Squall’s gunblade or Zell’s Limit Break)
-Magic Booster available via the launch menu
-Cheats are available via the Function keys
-Cheats do not affect Steam achievements
-Tons of creative monster/landscape designs
-Triple Triad card game
-Chocobo World included
[CONS]
-In order to play Final Fantasy VIII an account must be created with Square Enix
-Save files CAN BE LOST due to the Steam's cloud syncing, so be sure to turn off cloud syncing before playing (Library>Games>Right click on Final Fantasy VIII>Properties>Update>Uncheck 'Enable Steam Cloud Synchronization for Final Fantasy VIII')
-*Great soundtrack but… the sound is awful on the Steam version due to MIDI; however, this can be fixed
-Guardian Force (GF) summoning time can be too long such as for Eden
-If you’re hardcore into grammar the typos (mostly in the beginning of the game) may drive you insane
-Rinoa.  (She has always driven me insane since the first time I played this game, and the few times where you have to save her in the game I never wanted to save her)
Then there's the PocketStation game Chocobo World available via the launch menu to Final Fantasy VIII.  This mini-game can be muted via your computer's sound settings (Windows 7>Speaker/Volume Control>Mixer) and run in the background taking care of itself.  Personally, I find Chocobo World boring; however, Boko the Chicobo can find items (ranked A through D), which can be useful to your saved game once you finish your first Chocobo Forest (Final Fantasy VIII 'Disc 2').  Also, leveling up Boko to certain levels and meeting certain event requirements in Chocobo World can allow Boko to use powerful attacks in FF8's main story with Gysahl Green.
Keep in mind that the Steam version of Final Fantasy VIII is far from a remake; therefore, the graphics, sound, and game play are still on par with the Playstation version released in 1999.

Dust: An Elysian Tail is a fast paced 2D side scroller action game, you play as the mysterious warrior, Dust, Immerse himself into a beautiful world on a mission to search for his true identity. With a Blade of Ahrah, capable of withstanding an entire army of feral monsters and trained warriors alike. The story starts simple yet engaging along with the stun visual graphic, a very detailed of nature and climate change animations from starts to the end. You can explore such a fantastic world and wonder how it can affects your feeling/emotions in such various way, a beautiful, gruesome and sorrow atmosphere alike. Let along ingenious composed background musics building up atmosphere. Every single location in this game has its own charm. Literally, every things were made and perfectly placed in the right direction.
The characters are given well written script, and executed flawlessly with skilled voice actors, they managed to bring the most of characters and gave an ingenious expressions that match every comedy and serious situations alike. The relationship between Dust and other were explained in beautiful way, funny and serious, every moments you can feel they are a real person.
Despite a game made entirely by a bunch of adorable furries cartoonly, the story is surprisingly dark, a clever way of satirizing, parody of our own world were presented in this game. The war, the hate, and at the same time with a feeling of love and hope, good will of people who desire peace. The astounding in depth perception in story is what make a game truly amazing. It's surprised that it was written by one person, it's not surprised that a story might seems short when you compare to other game but Dust: An Elysian Tail's tale managed to make you admire them, and they stay in your heart for a long time.
A game can be easy, the combat mechanics are not that complex but they were executed in a very clever way, enough to engage people to keep playing with it, you can chain your combo to beyond 1000+ hits if you're good enough. The game has story quests just like all other RPG like game, and a bunch of side quests for sake of learning about lore and people. The playthrough gives you a lot of satisfied, as you slash countless number of enemy after another, show-off your skill against an enemy of nature. A boss can be simple battle but it was built with such a hyped climax battle as if it's an all for nothing, you feel so engaged by a duel to dead between two characters that swing blades against each other for sake of their unshakable ideals. You will feel inspired and it will stays for a long time enough for you to replay another playthough, not just for sake of completing everything but to experience every single pieces of this masterpiece once more.
However, despite easy/simple combat mechanics, there's hardcore mode that offers challenge, playing in hardcore mode is basically a no damage run for a most part. You can just grit your way to the top or decide to dedicatedly grind your character so he can withstands anything, it's up to you how you will play a game, you're seeking for actual challenge or it's just mere name just to show off on save data file.
An outstandings in every detailed like this indie game with only one drawback of being short story which acceptable, cannot be found elsewhere. Dust: An Elysian Tail stands as an one of the most unique indie game worth attention by all means.

Really amazing game.  I wanted to point out a few things in my review.  I was a little bit worried when I got this game because of some posts I read.  Those posts claimed that, among other things,
1) the AI was too aggressive (always warring)
2) limited in terms of the decisions that you can make
3) governors were useless
4) There were no combat tactics (hah!)
5) There were no supply routes
6) There are no politics
7) There are no 'guerilla tactics'
8) more stuff about how there isn't enough content...
I thought this was all wrong actually.  I found that the AI was very logical.  If it weren't for the fact that I hadn't strategically established embassies, stabbed certain allies in the back, waged societal warfare to breakup some of the enemy empires, and etc, I probably would have been invaded and utterly destroyed, since actually the AI (and the governors) are really good at making decisions with regards to how to distribute supplies properly.  There are absolutely military tactics, I've used divide and conquer, pincer maneuvers, and I have used smaller faster ships to rapidly erode away at enemy mineral/energy/etc planets to destroy their resources before I blitz their capitals with my main fleets.  Moreover, the game designers keep everything interesting by adding anomolies, and if they happen to read this, when they go to update the game in the future they should totally add new anomolies to keep players interested (I really like them, they add a mass effecty type of feel to the game).
To make a long story short, I found that:
1) There are intricate politics that are actually very interesting to observe and manipulate.
2) There are plenty of battle tactics, you just have to slow the game down and get creative...which is how it should be anyway.
3) The AI was very logical in its rivalries and alliances, and in order to keep your empire going you have to keep track of what all the other empires are up to and when might be the best time to stab your ally >:) in the back and take their planets.
4) There are absolutely guerilla tactics, in fact I've had to put down lots of rebellions and its really difficult.  I've also waged societal warfare on enemy empires.
5) The game is very different based on what type of race you play as.  For example if you are some types of alien species, the other aliens in the game just dont like you cuz of how you look haha.
6) The game has interesting lore and anomolies.
In my opinion the main thing the game is lacking is more intricate land warfare.  Its basically just land your troops and see if your ticker goes down faster or slower than their tickers.  Then again, the game is already fairly complicated enough.
All in all I'd give it a 9/10

Stellaris – It’s a pretty fun 4x game.
My first and current play through has been going really well. I started with my awesome cat people of the ‘Fevarian Imperium’ who have the ‘Fanatic Xenophobic’ and ‘Militaristic’ traits. Unfortunately due to an oversight they have a preference for colonizing tundra worlds, of which are few and far in-between.
Anyway, I’ve managed to expand out and colonize my twelfth world of which had a copper age civilisation already inhabiting it. This is fine I thought, I’ll just establish a colony and bring them into the Fevarian Imperium, heck when I get the ability to ‘uplift’ them, they can be given an entire system to themselves (Found a system with 3 continental words just perfect for them but not me). I even began theorising a way of relocating them early so I can fully colonise their world.
Apparently my catfolk populations disagree. Two factions developed, one wants to enact an extermination policy and wipe out the natives, the other wants to enslave and prohibit the natives from breeding – essentially letting them die out. My first attempt to nullify the factions, failed and triggered a civil war. The Extermination faction controls the planet in question + 5 others, while the Extermination through slavery faction controls the rest.
Hence I’m watching my formally fanatically united society ravage itself in what has been a crippling civil war, all because they couldn’t agree on a method of extermination.
10/10 – Would Underestimate how Fanatically Xenophobic societies work.
PS - Non Vanilla review, used mod that changed how factions work.

Mysteries of the Sith is an expansion pack to the second entry in the Dark Forces Saga, Jedi Knight. In some ways it improves upon its predecessor, and in some ways its a few steps back.
The game gives you a good, if false, first impression in the opening level. While Kyle Katarn is training his new apprentice (smuggler-turned-Jedi and future wife of Luke Skywalker, Mara Jade), the Republic base they're at is attacked by the Imperial Remnant, using space stations disguised as asteroids to ambush their enemy. You spend this section playing as Kyle, and its a breath of fresh air from Dark Forces II with a sprawling, semilinear level and two or three new varieties of Stormtrooper to fight.
However, this level was either designed to catch your attention so you'd be strung along with the rest of the game, or was indicative of the original vision that ultimately didn't pan out, as once you move on from the Republic base things quickly deteriorate into largely linear run-and-guns punctuated with both the unintuitively specific progression of Jedi Knight and at times the baffling moon logic of the original Dark Forces. The impressive scope of Jedi Knight is also lost, leaning more towards the relatively cramped and linear confines of the later Jedi Outcast. One notable exception to this is the final level in the Sith Catacombs, which involve a series of puzzles spread along the perimeter of a massive central chamber that gives your efforts a sense of continuity and scope.
Finally, the story is the absolute thinnest of the series, which given the flat characters and often thin establishment of Jedi Knight, says a lot. While I never was at a loss as to what I was doing at any given location and why, there is no overarching story to the game whatsover. After the initial attack by the Imperial Remnant, Kyle leaves Mara Jade behind to look into an unrelated matter, and the Imperials never come up again, apart from a minor occupying force on a later planet that never factors into the plot at all other than as someone else to shoot. Mara is left to run errands for the Republic in the meantime, first by gaining the assistance of a crimelord for supplies, then by guarding and then recovering a Jedi Holocron when it inevitably gets stolen by pirates. Absolutely none of these things relate in any way to each other or the final act, other than Mara's hand in all of them.
Mara Jade is a more interesting person than pre-Jedi Outcast Kyle Katarn (being little more than a gun-for-hire in Dark Forces and a bland grizzled action hero in Jedi Knight), but she is without question the most horrible person I've ever played in a Star Wars game who wasn't a Dark Sider trying to make their puppy-kicking quota. When sent to negotiate with the crimelord I mentioned earlier, the doorman speaks highly of her former smuggling career but says his boss is uninterested in seeing her due to distrust of the straight-laced Jedi she seems to have become. Her response? Kick down the back door, murder about 80% of the crimelord's employees, and then force him into negotiations at gunpoint. He relents in return for a favor, but the fact that we're supposed to be rooting for Mara here kind of disturbs me.
Once that's dealt with (an affair that mostly involves a chase through a city, being captured, killing a rancor, and then fighting your way out of your target's base), the crimelord agrees to a business relationship with the Republic, but not before Mara Jade decides to blackmail him one more time, just for kicks. This plotline never comes up again, as we next see Mara overseeing the transport of a Jedi Holocron, when her ship is attacked by pirates and she's forced to smuggle herself onto their ship, fight her way through their docking facility, then to the base of the collector it's been sold to in order to retrieve it. This plotline has nothing to do with anything else either.
Finally, Mara decides to go looking for Kyle as she hasn't heard from him since he took off on his private investigation. At this point the game largely plummets into Xen Syndrome, as you wander through a swamp with nonsensical puzzles (you can't pass unless you use Force Persuasion on the statue? What?), overpowered enemies that will kill you in two hits (and in the case of the trash-squid things, can't be killed at all for some reason despite Kyle gunning down a dozen or so of them in Dark Forces), and the complete inability to use any weapon except your lightsaber for the rest of the game. Oh, and there's Sith Zombies for some reason, because I guess that's a thing now.
It turns out that the strong Dark Side aura of the ruins on this planet sent Kyle, who has been established as a borderline-neutral individual throughout the games, off the deep end into crazy Sith hermit. Exactly what happened to twist him that way is probably a more interesting story than the actual game, where after a few ignored attempts to get you to either♥♥♥♥♥♥off or join him, he decides to finally try and kill you dead, at which point your only option is to turn off your lightsaber to convince him that he's not far gone enough to start offing his friends. At which point you leave, the credits roll, and two massive plot points that occured between this and Jedi Outcast (Kyle switching from a yellow to a blue lightsaber and eventually giving up his Force powers) are left entirely unadressed.
In summation, this game is roughly on par with Jedi Knight in quality, with every improvement balanced by a downgrade.  And much like Jedi Knight, I ultimately can't recommend the experience. Basically nothing happens over the course of these two games couldn't be guessed at based on offhand comments in Jedi Outcast, and quite a few things that ARE mentioned in Jedi Outcast are never actually addressed in these games. Not needed for the story, and the gameplay isn't up to snuff with Dark Forces or Jedi Outcast, so just play those and skip these lesser installments.
