I loved playing Coredumping's Software, Inc. and Greenheart's Game Dev Tycoon, so when I saw this, I had to have this game.
Unfortunately, Startup Company doesn't seem to deliver in the gameplay department as it does on graphics - just the opposite of both games I've mentioned.
First, there is no tutorial. I understand this is still an early access game, but it really could do with a tutorial. I didn't struggle per se, but the importance of certain mechanics such as hiring specific types of employees didn't register to me early enough. Also, I never could figure out how to construct modules, which were necessary for certain contracts.
Second, it needs better UI organization. I wish I could move around windows that block essential information underneath. I also wish there were shortcuts to essential buttons that determine what kind of work my employees are assigned, instead of clicking on their names above their avatar's heads and then clicking on the work they need to complete every single time (unless you hire a manager, which unlocks later on), which is about every thirty seconds. If this doesn't sound bad, the buttons for their names and the furniture they're using are so closely positioned that I end up misclicking about half the time. Also, the game could do with a better time management system. The regular play speed is way too fast for me and would have liked a slower speed in order to prevent wasting time between micromanaging employees.
Third, better balancing. Unlocking things to program/design costs $1000 per employee, and that is just ridiculous. This means it takes ~$1500 to recruit and hire a programmer, $4500-5500 base salary for that employee, and $6000 to unlock all beginner skills for that programmer alone, all while managing a mandatory $40k loan. It just doesn't make sense to me. Also, you need to hire an HR manager, which doesn't unlock until later on, to control what hours the employee works. Huh??? This means an employee can come to work whenever he or she damn well pleases... like at 10 while another comes in at 8. I really don't understand.
Overall, this game feels like it needs a lot, I mean, a lot of polishing. Everything feels tedious and doesn't feel fun at all. This could be because I haven't gotten very far but even then, I don't see very much entertainment value in taking a mandatory loan, having very little control what happens in the office overall, and clicking a bunch of buttons that are in very awkward places. It sometimes feels like a mobile clicker game like Adventure Tycoon, just with buttons that take several clicks to get to, and in that sense this game completely lacks depth compared to other similar games.
So far I'd have to say I'm really quite disappointed in this game and would not recommend it at this stage, especially at $10. Let's hope that devs can improve it before it's released. Meanwhile, I'd love to get a refund.

TL;DR Version: Great game, great AI, great story and great gunplay. A must buy for FPS fans and even tactical shooter fans. 10/10
One of the best FPS games I know of. Great AI, interesting story and fantastic John Woo-esque and tactical gunplay. The game has a unique combat system which I wish today's developers would take a note or two of, the game puts you up against squads of 5 soldiers which communicate with each other and co-ordinate to try to take you down, which in higher difficulties can make the game genuinely difficult because the AI are extremely intelligent. As an example of such, during my playthrough I had to resort to taking cover in a room with open windows in which my enemies could see me through, instead of charging me head first like most modern FPS games AI would do, they actually had 3 of the 5 soldiers laying down suppressing fire and trying to flush me out with grenades, while the other 2 were trying to flank me, at the end of the gun fight I was flanked and killed due to the fact that I had no idea that the enemy were flanking my position. As a result of that gun fight I laughed my♥♥♥♥♥off because I hadn't been outsmarted in sooo long by AI and it was such a enjoyable experience. In my books F.E.A.R has the best AI I know of and still holds it's own even after 11 years, F.E.A.R is truly a masterpiece and I wish there were more games like it. The story of F.E.A.R is quite interesting but it is true that at times it can feel very drawn out but the visceral gun fights and atmospheric horror keeps you drawn in. It's a game that doesn't rely on jumpscares and forced perspective views to scare the player and I will admit that in my first playthrough I had some heart pumping moments which I won't spoil. All in all F.E.A.R is a great game to grab and for $9.99 USD it is a great deal, even for people that aren't fans of horror, I believe this is a game that every gamer should experience and it will forever be one of my top 5 FPS games and I also inspire to take what F.E.A.R has done right with it's combat and atmosphere and down the line create a homage of what F.E.A.R was in a game I hope to create in the far future. 10/10

Garry's Mod is a game that you can't technically call a game. It's more like a community-made collection of many games with a built-in level editor. If you can imagine it, chances are it's been made by someone, and if it hasn't, you can make it yourself. I've seen a lot of things since a friend gave me this game, and most of them have been pretty good. Of course, with every light, there is a dark. The Workshop is expansive and unrestricted, so oftentimes you'll find a poorly-made save or dupe that steals from someone else's creation instead of what you're actually looking for. Thankfully, if you don't get easily triggered by this, you can just keep scrolling through, even if it takes a while. There are glitches, of course, and not all of them are fun. However, I have yet to encounter many game-breakers in my time with GMod. I only have one major complaint, and that's the fact that some of the achievements are next to impossible, namely the 'secret phrase' and 'play with Garry' ones. Then again, I'm no completionist, so I can overlook that.

The atmosphere, the graphics, the idea behind the game are wonderful.  As are many of the characters, even the character you play is quite amazing himself. It's an immerssive game that captures the player and throws lots of enemies at you and lots of very neat little details. This game, based on the books definately does feel like an RPG. The gameplay is relatively satisfying, with visuals probably outdoing the gameplay itself but they create a very uniqe atmosphere which I prefer to other RPGs.
In this game the choices actually do matter, there's quite a few and it's not just black or white (morally speaking). What is also unbelivably suprising about TW2 is that, despite the game coming out in 2011. This game on Ultra looks still up to date as ever, it looks astonishing truely.
While this game succeeds in delivering a good RPG experience, there are some issues which don't make it a 10..
- The saving game system is far from perfect, not allowing you to save over games or choose the name of your saves instead every time you save it creates a new save. Doing this can make a huge cluster of saves which freeze your game every time you click load. So you must periodically clean old saves.
- 3 big skill trees to pick from but very few skill points make it quite difficult to build the ultimate Witcher.
- The game is actually quite short, especially if you don't do the side quests. Of course, after this there is the Witcher 3 which only continues the best kind of fun. The amount of hours I have are not correct, as I tried to play this game before but never completed it so it's more hours than needs be.
- The facial animations are subpar, not really great at showing off emotions of the characters.
- The combat is unforgiving at the begining, defiantely needs getting used to and remember Space is your friend.

This is one of those games that I would really like to love and it's still good game. Negatives come down to game being extremely frustrating and slow for no good reason.
Main issue are the controls. If this was mobile game on device with no physical buttons, I guess this would make more sense. You are controlling girl who is following slowly little green ball which follows your cursor. So it's this conga line just to move the character and even if you are doing interactivity with either green or purple balls, you can't just click/tap something, you have to actually drag them there - slowly and unaccurately as camera will also always move. The character moves really slowly and they can fall over edges if your cursor and thus green ball happens to be couple pixels too much to some direction. Everything just makes everything slow and all mistakes feel most of the time not justified and when they do, it just adds in to frustration because you know you have to do everything slowly again.
Second problem is the way you learn games mechanics and puzzles - guesswork. I love puzzle games a lot, but usually those give me tools and make worlds rules clear. In here, some situations did feel silly afterwards, but I still bumped into a lot of those, where I simply couldn't clearly notice what it was I was supposed to be doing. This was highighted in first chapters boss, I had trouble figuring out that the boss was coming after me because it's all same audio level mono sound and only indication was that green ball moved to other edge of the screen automatically. Another big thing was that I was unaware that you could still make input even if the boss manages to catch you. This wouldn't be that bad if the game wasn't so slow to control.
Technically it could be better but at least it's serviceable. Understandably assets are low quality and resolution only goes up to 1920x1080 and 30 FPS, OS cursor is used so inputs don't feel as sluggish. However bigger issue is that there's some really noticeable scaling artifacting in many places, especially with shadows. Not too much to distract too much but still there. As it was made for Vita, there's not much that you could ask without them redoing the whole thing.
If you can get past all that, there's soul to this game and things that can keep you interested to see it trough, but I couldn't get past them.

The Witcher 2 is the second game in The Witcher trilogy based on the books of the same name. Compared to the first game, TW2 improves on every single aspect. The graphics are amazing, probably one of the best in recent years. The music is great. The combat feels a lot better compared to the first game. The voice acting is also better. You can feel emotions behind the voice. The facial animation in TW2 feels real compared to the stiff faces in the first game (Zoltan's crazy eyes). The story this time takes on a larger scale which involves different sides that you can choose, meaning the choices you make in this game matter a lot.
Overall, The Witcher 2 does an amazing job serving as a sequel for the first game and as the second game in the Witcher trilogy.
If you're interested in the books. I suggest reading the books first before playing the games. The games take place after the books so there are a lot of dialogues and references that spoil the events in the books. Besides, there's a satisfying feeling when you meet the characters from the books again in the games.
The books order: The Last Wish -> Sword of Destiny -> Blood of Elves -> Time of Contemp -> Baptism of Fire -> The Swallow's Tower -> Lady of the Lake

A good game with bad moments
For a game of its budget, there are some good cinematics, the characters are interesting, and its enough to keep you engaged, particularly now that the title is much cheaper.
Now for the bad news. There are a few issues with the capacity to enrage you either into perservering or throwing your keyboard or controller across the room. I list them in no particular order below. It will sound like a negative review below. Actually it's not true, I just want people to be forewarned.
Irritating mini-games
There a series of sort of mini-games where you need to mash buttons in a particular way or get punished for it repeatedly until through a sort of classical conditioning (like Pavlovs dogs) you get your food pellet of progress at the end. Examples of this are the bare knuckle boxing where a button will flash on the screen suddenly. The arm wrestle is another one of these where you have to struggle to keep your icon inside a bar using the mouse (in my case).
A predilection for♥♥♥♥♥♥and bums.
Okay I'm a guy and don't mind my hit of fantasy soft porn, but even I had to roll my eyes after practically every chick has gravity defying boobs and is either an angel or a ♥♥♥♥♥ (often literally).
Alchemy - a pointless skill tree.
I focused on swordfighting, why would you create slightly better potions that time out when you can consistently do more damage? Many games have these game balance issues but I found Witcher 2 didn't handle it as well. Crafting doesn't keep up with stuff that you simply find or get rewarded, a problem I've found in other titles also.
An annoying badly lit maze.
At one point of the game is a dwarven mine that is a type of basic maze. However its badly lit and you need to use Cat which gives you cat vision. The cat wears out. I thought about it and the main issue with getting lost was simple HUI (Human user interaction issues) like having sunlight sneak through under the bottom of the exit door, so the player takes a hint that that is the exit.
More Classical Conditioning type puzzles.
There are two in chapter 2 - completing a witch ritual to break a curse, you need to keep clicking things in a certain order, or you get forced to restart. It gets old quickly.
The 2nd is seeing through the eyes of a dead assassin, you have to walk behind the other assassin step by step, I would do this and the sequence would restart and I would have to redo it. Now I wasn't doing anything blatantly dim, I would literally be behind the other guy and the sequence would restart. This is very frustrating and I'm now stuck.
Overall, my 5 cents is that it has an inside group feel to the design, where the development team didn't bother to test some of their ideas, and realise 'hey' this part of the game is actually kind of crap.
It's polished, but with dollops of developer bird poo on the dash 3.5/5.

What the devs say: "A crazy puzzle game unlike any other".
What the devs mean: "Yet another platform puzzler that looks and plays like it was farted out in the 1990s with a pirated copy of Klik n' Play. Touch key to unlock door, then go through door. Collect coins for points. Avoid enemies. If you die, you leave a weird box on the ground that looks like a glitched out door sprite of some sort (seriously, wtf is this even supposed to be), which can then be used as a platform. If you die in a narrow corridor, your path is now blocked forever, reset level and try again. Sometimes the sounds glitch out. If you try to use the "freeze time" powerup when you don't actually have one in your inventory, you're treated to the clangorous sounds of a Merzbow demo. Hit detection is ridiculously finicky, and your hitbox actually changes based on whether you're facing right or left. If you so much as look at an enemy, you instantly die. The finicky twitchy controls make this very, very likely. Every time you launch the game you get to watch the thirty second unskippable introduction which is sort of like a Pac-Man intermission or the intro to SMB3, except since it's unskippable it cannot be skipped, due to being unskippable. Please give us $6.99 for this experience."
What they should have said: "A sh­itty puzzle game like many, many others".
The game loads and plays and only occasionally glitches out, so I mean it COULD theoretically be worse, but there's still no reason whatsoever to play this game, and even less reason to pay money to do so.

Stellaris is a game of exploration.  When I was playing through the first few hours of this game I got a real sense of exploration and that I was out there expanding my empire and building my civilization.  It almost borded documentary and sim game, its that detailed... at least for me.
The game has similarities to Master of Orion in it, but cleaned up for how it would be played today.  I can spend hours and hours on it and i would just feel like I only scratched the surface, and the map I play right now is only considered Medium sized Galaxy... its has a few hundred star systems in it...  That's how big it is.
Graphically, this game is really impressive, down to the planetary rings and astriod belts and solar flares that the systems star create.  They've even paid very close attention to the movie Interstellar as the Black Hole looks just like that!  Amazing to see the detail that went into this.
Ship battles are pretty cool when you have an armada of ships fighting space creatures or enemy ships and you can zoom in on it for close up action.  When you know you're about to get the snot beat out of you, there's a quick emergency jump to another system.  The retreat system is pretty good as you can cut your losses and run, down side is that since its an emergency jump out, you don't know where you've jumped to right away.  I guess it's more of a consequence of what happens when you run, not bad, but not great.
The research tech tree is not bad as your scientists that are specialized in certain fields will make research for that tech faster.  Same goes with the Generals of your fleet, some might have traits that give you bonuses to the stats your fleet already has.  Politicians are the same in how they govern the civilization.  This is a pretty good thing to have as you now have to think about who you want to hire for the different roles.  Downside is in spending Influence on these people, which I get into next, resource management.
There are 3 main resources that you need to get, Energy Credits, Minerals, and Influence.  Now Energy and Minerals are normal to come by and you gather them by exploring from system to system, cool.  Influence, that's another beast altogether.  It's as if you have to antagonise the other races to gain influence, like it forces you to poke a stick at your neighbour and see if he/she hits back... What if you're a Pacifist and you're not for wars but you want to make a Federation and have your culture be the envy of all others, how do you gain Influence?  As far as I've been able to get into the game, only now have I built structures that generate Influence slowly or there are election quests that are about the equivalent to "Daily Quests" in MMOs, every election the government asks you to build research stations.  If you don't have anymore stations, disband it and build again... that's not a good way of building influence in a game as far as I can see, so I hope the developer notes this and creates a bit more balance in terms of resource gathering for Influence.  A good example of a way to obtain influence that meshes well with the game atmosphere would be if you have had successful trades over a certain amount of time, your diplomats can gain resources of Influence over time, especially if you have Embassies in every alien home planet.  I just find getting Influence either too slow or not clear cut and at times can prevent you from advancing, ie. if you run out of influence, you can't hire any new scientists or generals if they die of old age (yes they age in the game and have a lifespan).  So spend wisely.
All this being said, I've let you know the good and bad.  This game will definately satisfy the explorer in you if that is what you enjoy, it will not dissapoint.  I've spent over 20hrs in-game and I feel like I barely scratched the surface.  So if you had your choice of space 4X games out there and wondered if Stellaris is worth getting, ABOLUTELY YES!  I'm hoping that the developers iron some of the balance on resource management a bit better.  If they can iron out that part, I'd have to say your looking at the best 4X space sim since Master of Orion 2 of the good old days, only better.
That's my view of Stellaris.  Now go out there and explore, conquer or make some alliances, the choice is yours.

Excellent game, worth every cent spent. I didn't expect much out of it when i bought it, as it is far from all those AAA games sold at 50-60€.
Time is flying when you are playing this game.
PROS:
- Historical accuracy: you will build and use ships that were actually used during the battle of the atlantic in WW2.
- Ballistic realism: once you get used to the physics and mechanics of aiming, it produces realistic battles.
- Beautiful, yet not resources consuming: i'm pretty sure this game will run on most, if not all PCs/laptops/tablets
- Huge replayability: i haven't touched the "campaign" mode, and i'm currently playing my second "Battle of the Atlantic" mode (which is a campaign from septembrer 1939 through 1945, where both factions pursue different agendas, and is closer to what i would call a campaign than the former mode). Lots of options to customize your battles.
CONS:
- A few bugs here and there, random crashes during campaign battles (but no harm caused: the game auto saves progress between turns played, so you at most have to replay one turn of the campaign, yet it can be frustrating at times)
- Can be a bit tricky to learn, you better be ready to get your geometry classes underhand (or even easier, use a real life rule to measure ballistic trajectories on your screen)
- The game, being very low budget, lacks cinematics, briefings, and other things that bring immersion and / or context. If you are unfamiliar with WW2 history, and don't know what happened back then, the game won't provide you with background.

Well, hearing it from a person obsessed with the FF series, it may not be as convincing to get this game.
Let me just start with this: This game just so happened to be the first game I ever played. Back when it was on the PSone, I literally started with this, then moved to Mario, and so on. Crazy right? You'd figure that Mario would have been the first. Either way, when I first played this game, I don't even remeber what my innital take on the game was. I thought 'Why did I play this? What made me want to play it? How did it even play?" Well, I found the answer to that after finding it a second time on the PSone.
The game is set up pretty well. You start off with just a base idea of the game, and don't even really grasp how it works in the beginning. However, as you progress through the game, things become much more understandable. You become so over powered that you feel like you're invincible. Still even with the game being a little confusing, it has both its up and downs.
First, the good stuff. The main attraction; GF (if i remember correctly, that's for Guardian Force). These are the main mechanic in the game. Without them, all you can do is attack....... literally(more on this in the cons). Even so, they can become insanely powerful if you level them up, and they can learn new abilities that you can then use both inside and out of combat. Some are for making battles easier, some for making battles non-existant, some for making items like potions and elixirs; the list goes on and on. The GF's become the driving force behind this game, and it's really a neat mechanic to get behind.
Next comes magic. Now this is both a negative and a positive, as the magic isn't really special. What magic can do, depending on your GF's, is be used like and equipment to increase your player's stats. Meaning, if you have the right magic for your character, their stats become so powerful that even boss fights feel like a walk in the park. All in all, it isn't really that bad.
Now, the cons. First off, those GF's. As I mentioned before, without them, all you can do is attack. I mean it. You can't use items. You can use magics. You can't use anything accept for the weapon in your hands. It can really hurt in a lot of battles you aren't prepared for, especially a boss fight. And if you forget to equip the GF's to your character; it just makes the feeling even worse compared to when you do it on purpose. Yes, you have to remember to take care and equip all of your GF's before you go into battle, otherwise, suffer defeat. And speaking of care.... you remember those GF abilities i mentioned earlier? In order to get them, you have to grind for a while to get enough "AP" just to unlock these abilities. Don't get me wrong, that's the concept behind a lot of games, and it's completely acceptable. However, the issue is how many abilities these GF's have and how many you are able to use. Great! You've unlocked the most powerful ability in this GF. In order to equip it, you have to unequip the only ability saving your life in combat right now..... Even when you unlock the special GF ability that allows for four abilities to be used, most of the time, the abilities are so similar, that it becomes a personal fight with yourself on how you want to optimize this one character. What's worse is that, say you don't have that character in your party. Well, you need the GF equiped to them, so you unequip it from them. Unfortunately(if i remember correctly), you have to go through the trouble of optimizing that same character all over again. It becomes a hastle, makes you not want to unequip GF's for the sake of making it easy, then you end up in a situation where you are fighting a boss and needed the abilities of one of the GF's you can't use right now because it's equiped to another character somewhere else. Major pain, and I still love this game. Makes you wonder how.
Next on the list of cons is magic. Like I said before, it's both a pos and neg when it comes to this. Firstly, magic isn't infinite. You don't have a mana pool to draw from in order to cast these spells. Instead, you use a system known as "draw" to take the magic from your enemies in the middle of a fight. Personally, I like this system because of the randomness you get from each enemy, meaning you can base your fight off of just the magic you can draw from them. However, the issue is how many time you can use it as well as getting rid of useless stuff you don't need or can't use(by "can't use", I mean it's pointless to use it to begin with. Like using a level 1 spell on a level 100 monster..... pointless). Being as you draw magic from your enemies, there is a limit to how much you would be able to use it. Understandable, it's just frustrating to have to suck it out of your enemy for and hour just to get enough to be able to really use it for your characters stats. Thing is though, that you get much better magic down the road(obviously). You only have 8 pages of magic with 4 slots in each, meaning you can only have a total of 32 different spells at once. Say you've filled up your slots. Finally! You've found the one spell in the game that will max out your characters stats..... But you have no room for it. Well, unfortunately, you can't just delete your magic. That would be too easy. You can give it to other characters though...... oh right! You made all of the other characters max out the exact same spells so that their stats would be awesome too. Well, there you go. You have two options. Either fight and use nothing but the spell you want to "delete",which you most likely have 100 copies of(yeah. you can have a total of 100 of those 32 spells), or ignore it and move on with your life. It really does hurt when I run into this situation. It sucks, plain and simple.
Really, these little issues are that big of a deal. Yes, it's a pain to respec your character every time you want to use it. Yes, it sucks when you can't draw the magic you want. However, these are such obvious obsticles the we, as gamers, can easily overcome them in a heart-beat.... no; even faster than a heart-beat. These obsticles are nothing. Really, they just add to the experience of a well made(yet not really well told) story. And that's always the selling point for me in games. I don't care for your phanshy grafiks or your smooth lighting.... I want a story that will grab me by the neck, shake really hard, and then ask me if I'm okay. All in all, a rating for me on this game; it well deserves an 8/10 for me, though it would be 9/10 if I could, you know, use my items without the help of and almighty being.

htoL#NiQ (or Hotaru no Nikki) is a puzzle-platformer with indirect character control. The character in question is a little girl named Mion, and your goal is to guide her unharmed through the ruins of abandoned industrial plant. To guide Mion, you need something to get her attention. That's where fireflies come in - you have two of them. One is called Lumen, and it radiates bright light, which attracts Mion and helps her fight darkness. Other is called Umbra, and it resides in Mion's shadow most of the time, but can travel through unlit areas, operate mechanisms and distract monsters. You can control Lumen and Umbra either via mouse or analog sticks on your gamepad.
You can also use Lumen to stop Mion at her tracks or to make her pull a lever
It should be noted, that the reason you can't control Mion directly is not just a gameplay gimmick, it also plays part in game's storytelling.
Let's talk about the story then. It's different from what you'd expect from a Nippon Ichi game, as its tone is dark and dramatic, and there is (almost) no comedy whatsover. The
game takes place in a year 9999, many years in the aftermath of a global catastrophe. Naturally, everything is revealed through Mion's perspective. Once, she wakes up to find herself alone in some room. The room appears to be in the middle of ruins of some strange old industrial plant. All around Mion is the darkness, with strange creatures lurking inside. Not the greatest place for a little girl to be, right? Luckily, Lumen finds Mion, and then tries to help her get out. Soon after, Umbra joins in too.
This game doesn't have neither text nor voice narration, the story is conveyed visually, some times directly, but for the most part - through memories of events from the past. These are collectibles which you find in various hidden places and hard to reach spots throughout the level.
Visual storytelling allows for multiple interpretations of what you see, but it's a double-edged sword, as it can either get you more involved or become the obstacle to understanding the situation. But if you like games which make you want to stop and think about what's actually happening, to connect the dots and to recreate the big picture - you'll definitely like the story of htoL#NiQ. The game won't chew the story out for you, but it won't abandon you either - you can always rewatch memories you've already collected from the main menu.
htoL#NiQ has a storybook-like art style, which accompanies its storytelling model. The palette of greens, browns, greys and blacks delivers the atmosphere of ruins properly. Developers dedicated a lot of attention to light and shadow in this game, and it creates a rather unique presentation - for example, in the shadows you can often see something you can't see in the light, and so on. Memories of the past, on the other hand, have different style completely - they use isometric pixel art.
The music is (for the most part) a very peaceful calming ambient. It matches the gameplay well: htoL#NiQ isn't a fast paced game at all, you'll spend most of the time thinking about solving your next puzzle, so having a relaxing and non-intrusive soundtrack is very important.
Speaking of puzzles, it has a fair variety - every new level the game introduces some new puzzle elements and mechanics. Puzzle difficulty isn't very high, but htoL#NiQ can make you think for a while. Still, that's what you come to the puzzle game for in the first place, right? The overall difficulty curve won't cause much discomfort, there are only so many places which demand a certain level of precision or timing from player in the latter part of the game.
Overall, htoL#NiQ is a great puzzle game that has an excellent visual presentation, light paced gameplay and a great story with unusual way of storytelling. According to SteamSpy, at the time of this review it has sold around 11k copies, which makes me sad, as there are not too many good games in this genre, and htoL#NiQ is a good one.

Pretty hollow and overhyped game (heading towards Spore levels in difference of promised versus delivered content). To make another comparison, this game and what was stated it would be like is much how Civ: Beyond Earth is compared to Alpha Centari (aka SMAC). Sure, it's not really a bad game, but it's also not really a good game, either. That said, I'm sure once you buy all the DLCs that are likely to eventually appear, it will be a very good game. If CK2 is any guide, though, you'll end up paying a ton for it. If you want to play a good 4x space game, I'd recommend looking to the likes of MoO or even Galactic Civs over this (I find they actually have greater depth and fun).
Things that the game is missing: AI with any tactical sense (larger enemy fleets will "dance" between targeting my two smaller fleets in their territory), diplomacy with some depth, spying, trading, variation in buildings. Research is one of the few things that is done in an interesting way, but really it's more novel than anything. On the other end, the warscore system needs a rehaul. That you can vasalize an enemy's ally that is larger than you when that enemy (who's actually smaller than you by a large amount) declares war on you by just taking out mining bases and other harasment is silly at best; the flip side is that if you have conservative demands, your enemy gets 10 years to rebuild their forces with impunity (and get in the way of your expansion) after you steam-rolled them with your now larger fleets, even though they declared war on you initially.
I'll probably never come back to this game now that I have my head buried under books.

One of the worst RPGs I've ever played (and I've played a lot of Japanese budget titles).
The story, sound, music, and visuals are all great. Nobody can deny that.
Where this game fails, is the gameplay - and I mean all of it.
For some reason, every single action has a significant delay to it - even in the menus.
Have fun navigating your items and equipment when there's half a second of delay between every single action.
Want to move down the menu? Half a second between every single entry.
Want to press up to go from the top straight to the bottom? Not in this game. You take the long road.
For some reason, nobody at CDPR seems to have played a single console RPG (which this is) in their entire life before they made this game.
A dedicated map button? Doesn't flipping exist, even though the back/select button on the controller isn't bound to anything at all. You'll have to open up the regular menu and select "Map", again, with that disgusting delay between every single input. Press too early and the game will simply ignore it. You'd think they would have noticed this during testing, but I assume they just didn't care.
When you're done being annoyed by the menus, the game likes to give you quests without providing quest markers. Have fun clearing all the Nekker caves without consulting an FAQ, because the game sure as hell won't tell you where they are. Other locations in other quests are marked, but these aren't. God knows why.
Oh, and if you manage to actually complete those sidequests, all you get is a lousy 75 exp reward that equates to 7.5% of your current level. Remember when sidequests in Witcher 1 would give you four times that? I sure as hell do. CDPR doesn't.
But you know what? That's stuff I can deal with.
What's inexcusable is the sheer incompetence when it comes to the game's combat system.
Transitioning from Witcher 1 to Witcher 2, Geralt suddenly has a weak spot on his back, making him take double damage whenever an enemy attacks him from behind (even at an angle). This will happen all the time, because the game just loves to swarm you with at least half a dozen enemies on a regular basis. Get close to anyone, and the other guys will immediately surround you (and murder you). Wanna use a trap? Doesn't matter. Geralt's trapping skills are so bad, it will take him a full two seconds to set and prime said trap - more than enough time for your enemies to get in a hit or a backstab.
Using signs is worthless as well.
Not only are they much weaker than in the first game, they now cost single units of Vigor (of which you have two).
Spending one vigor cuts all your damage by 25% (because for some reason, Geralt is now "fatigued" when casting spells), and using up both points of vigor reduces it to 50%. In short, don't use signs. That's another excellent lesson they teach you in CDPR's school of incompetent game design. Instead of complementing your kit in fun ways, you are being punished for daring to use the tools you have been provided with. If you love me, why do you keep hurting me, daddy?
On the defensive side, you can dodge, parry, and counter.
Dodging is by far the best of the bunch, because it sometimes causes you to not get hit.
I say "sometimes", because the game likes to register hits, even if you're already several steps away.
Whatever the game does, it certainly does not communicate its invincibility frames properly, providing players with the feeling of being treated unfairly.
Parrying is a terrible idea in general, because, for some reason (yes, again), you are still taking damage. Enemies seem to hit your sword so hard that it does physical damage to Geralt. Did I mention how much of a weakling he has become since the first game? As if remaining stationary in a game where backstabs can outright kill you in one or two hits wasn't punishing enough, they still had to punish you for daring to parry.
Counters are fairly nice, but on top of putting you in danger of taking a full hit, they also consume vigor (because of course they do). You're also not going to counter a whole lot, not because of the vigor cost, but because you simply can't afford to stand still and wait for an opponent to attack you, while you are being swarmed by the rest of the lot trying to backstab you. Apparently, combat must be restrictive and punishing, not fun and exciting.
There's also a distinct lack of AoE effects in this game, which means you're not properly kitted for most of the combat situations the game throws at you. Have fun taking out one enemy at a time whilst trying to dodge those deadly backstabs and with no healing in case you get hit (and you will get hit).
Geralt also has to sit down and meditate whenever he wants to drink a potion.
Because the mighty Witcher can throw bombs and lay out traps during combat, but using a flipping potion is too complicated for our great hero. You have to drink them in advance, which means you have to either know, or guess, if there's going to be an encounter or not. Good job, CDPR. If you happen to suck, at least you do it with flying colors.
Even during the Kayran fight, you refuse to pull out the camera to allow players to actually see what's going on while they're fighting an enemy the size of a small house.
In a nutshell, this is a game of hitting "Attack" and "Dodge" a lot.
Some people will tell you to get good at the game, but this is not about player skill.
This is about design, meaning "you just suck" is not an argument, but rather an indicator of your inability to even understand my criticism (and yes, I have played and beaten Dark Souls, because Dark Souls has GOOD combat).
I loved Witcher 1 (which was already pretty flawed, but still good) and was really looking forward to this game, but it ended up being a massive disappointment.
With terrible, unresponsive menus, broken and unreliable combat, and tedious and unrewarding sidequests, I don't understand how anyone can rate this a 5 or more. It's a terrible game that isn't worth playing under any circumstances.

This game is easily one of the top games in my ever-growing Steam library. The gameplay is a bit of a button-masher IMO, but you can play it with precision and execute some VERY cool, fast-paced combat moves (and generally rain death on Dust's enemies). (There are some puzzles and like segments that require more thought and precision, and those are fun too.) The story is interesting and peppered with plenty of humor (I swear, Fidget is a fountain of memes, and breaks the fourth wall into ... well, dust), drama, and both heartwarming and tear-jerking moments.
Plus, the voice acting is top-notch, the music is amazing, the visuals are very pretty, the level design feels great and navigating the world doesn't grate on my nerves like in some games with Metroidvania elements. The game runs very smoothly on my seven-year-old machine running Debian testing (there's a little stuttering on my laptop, a Thinkpad X201, but not enough to frustrate me, honestly it's great that it runs that well).
I will advise playing this game with a controller of some sort (I have an Xbox 360 for Windows (ha!) controller). I haven't tried playing with the keyboard, but if you aren't used to using a keyboard for combat-heavy 2D games, you'll probably struggle here without a gamepad. To the game's credit, it makes good use of the 360 controller's button layout, and playing on it feels natural after you become familiar with the button mappings.
Most games, I try to plow through so I can move on to the next game (I blame my huge backlog), but this game is so fun that I'm starting to take my time to just explore and knock out some of the side quests.
Put simply: give this one a go. I think you won't regret it.

A very competent game, but flawed in nearly everything it tries to do. It has the Metroidvania map, but it's actually a linear game with little side pockets for secrets. It has loot & RPG stats, but there are no interesting choices to be made in character development. Dust is mostly an action combat game though, and this is where its shortcomings are least forgiveable.
See, combat in Dust is a sloppy, wanton thing. Tons of enemies, all overlapping (this is a 2D game remember), many barely telegraphing their attacks or behavior states. Over this, the player is zipping around the screen, belting out attacks, all with accompanying splashes of flamboyant visual effects. The problem is that the developer seems to have thought he was creating a super precise, mastery focused combat system. That's how he tuned the game on higher difficulties, anyway. You're a glass cannon, with single attacks instantly reducing you to near death. This is a real problem when you can barely tell what's happening on the screen.
The game is also very pretty, and if that's what you want out of it, I doubt you'll be disappointed. Otherwise, there are probably better options out there. Guacamelee, maybe. I didn't love it, but it does Dust's style of combat right.

This is finally a game of the old school-variety, the kind of game i have been missing. It is deep but to-the-point, has lots of researched detail (the amount of ships is amazing) and a very nice manual. It also offers plenty of content, including battle scenarios and a lengthy campaign.
All this for a reasonable price. For a WW2 buff, the detail level is impressive and the general feel of the game is that old style of being reasonably easy to handle, but very deep if you scratch the surface. It reminds me a bit of the old days of Silent Hunter, in that it is a slow paced game of positioning, looking at the map and pondering how to get in range for a salvo without getting in a direct line of fire yourself.
Everything is there, from different ammo types to wind, quality of spotting information affecting estimations, submarines, air forces and to top it off there is a very detailed damage system, where ships will take damage to different compartments depending on hit location, ammo type etc. which in turn affects how it floods and eventually sinks. Subsystems can be individually damaged.
Played many hours on ipad-version, and i will likely play a lot more on the PC port.
If you want to get a bit of nostalgia for how a well packaged and developed, quality game, used to look like, get this.

The 'Battle Of The Atlantic' mode, is where this game really shines. It is immersive, intense, and challenging. If you're the British, you really have to juggle your ships around to protect the convoys sailing from America to supply Great Britain. Attacks by the Germans seem to occur wherever the Royal Navy is spread too thin, or not at all. If you can hold out until America enters the war, you've got a much better chance to win. So up until the end of 1941, the Brits are holding on by their fingernails. If you decide to play as the Germans, be prepared to sink an inordinate amount of tonnage of convoys in order to win. You'll have to sink a considerably high number of Royal Navy ships as well, so you can remain focused on merchant shipping, without losing too many Kriegsmarine ships and subs. Would love to see this game engine made into a Pacific campaign as well.

Buy this game if you (a) enjoy having to make clicks all the time (i.e., you're the only worker here, so you're not going to have time to sit back and enjoy watching the business machine you craft); (b) enjoy a workspace that does not permit you to arrange the interface for easier clicks (i.e., there's only one open panel allowed and it sits slaps bang mid-screen); (c) enjoy being forced to make decisions without having the decision support info/criteria available (i.e., when accepting a contract, you cannot review how long a single component takes to build, so you cannot then calculate the total minimum project time you could complete it in, nor can you move the panel to find out how employees are presently resourced); (d) enjoy not having to make strategic decisions (i.e., you'll need to decide how many/what type of employees you're going to need without having sight of a business plan); (e) think that startup companies are exclusively tech-related businesses (i.e., if you would like to start a delivery company or a pizza company, forget it). Obviously this is early release, so I might expect (b) and (c) to get fixed by the time it's fully released, but that's not going to obviate (a), (d) and (e). Lastly, there's really weird maths everywhere (e.g., on the level progress bar: at 170,100 out of the 200,000 to qualify for level 11, the game says I'm 72% of the way there (85.05% actually). Thus, for me, the developer has demonstrated convincingly just what a tough business this IT lark is - and just in case I didn't get that, he sent me two emails thanking me for spending my time on his product. He sounds nice and I wish him the best, but this is not for me: this game wants me to work, and I want to run the company, not work for it!

Black Ops is proof that CoD can be a fun series... When it's handled by Treyarch. Overall an improvement over Modern Warfare 2, while also serving as well written and well performed sequel to World at War. The combat is smoother, it (the game) looks slicker and is more colorful, and the singleplayer is probably the tightest in the franchise up to this point. The multiplayer also remains a highlight, being a huge improvement over the previous titles, and I'd argue better than any of the later titles. It's the single-most solid CoD entry, apart from the original and Modern Warfare.
The few cons, though, primarily rest in the multiplayer. Although it may be the best laid out version of the famous game mode, there are some balancing issues in terms of some weapons; namely the FAMAS. Now, for the most part, if a weapon is over-powered, then use it. The issue with it is the whole leveling up system, which means that newer players either rely on luck, the also powerful MP5K, or try to find maps where there aren't too many FAMAS players.
In addition, the CoD Points system is a great idea, but could have been better implemented. For example, what's the point of obtaining points when all of the weapons are still locked by level requirements? You might earn a  lot of CoD Points, but they're useless if you want a weapon you need several more levels to unlock with. EIther leveleing should open up more than one thing to buy, thus giving you more options to spend your money on at a time in the early and later games (Note that mid game more things do become unlocked at a stime, but this usually centers around different logo layers or reticules, all of which are cosmetic features). Note that when you do buy a weapon, you have all of the attachements unlocked. You just need to spend CoD Points on them. That makes sense, but why only the attachments? This mode could have worked better, but still does some things right. Overall, the redundancy of parts of the point system can still be overlooked.
Ultimately, we're still looking at one of CoD's more solid modern gen entries, and I'd suggest picking it up. Good servers can be difficult to find (There's a ton of so-called "Tactical Crouch Servers," and other servers ban game elements outright), but with or without, the singleplayer and the Co-Op Zombies mode are also very fun to play.
(NOTES: Aside from the PC, I've also played this game far more extensively on the PS3 and Nintendo Wii, totalling more than a hundred or more hours)

First off I got this game due to getting a 50% off from crafing badges, I normally dont go for these kinda games but I have to admit that personally I like it!
For this review I would like to remind everyone that this game is still in the early stages of development so ofcourse there are things that can be improved on. Just keep an open mind about its potential!
I loved the idea as soon as I pressed 'play' and got to see it. At the moment its very simply layed out so its easy to figure out, prety much everything is customisable, and you can delete the default content (characters, maps, events, updates) as you please, unlike most games it doesnt stop you from completely removing content you dont like. Further more it prety much encourages customisation! Currently I'm already working on a whole theme pack for this game with fully ballanced characters, maps, events, and status updates! its actually quite fun watching the outcomes when you understand the stats.
Ok so onto what I think can be improved apon.
1) needs to be a bit more stable, when exiting character edit the game crashes, fortunately it saves all ive done and its very quick to load back up.
2) More variety in terrane features for map creation please, things like abandoned buildings, broken machines and vehicles ect, could make the maps a little more interesting.
3) more types of outcomes during events, I know deaths are quite straightforeward, but it would be interesting to see effects like characters becoming confused and attacking their own team, or something that adds a flair of unpredictability.
4) on the new game setup It would be nice to have quick functions for setting up groups prior to the start of the game, for a simple example being able to pit red team against yellow and green against blue... hell that gives me a great idea... tournaments!!! like gladiatoral tournaments, so one game mode you can have your free for alls, and another is team V team in a progression to find out which team is the best!
5) stat modifiers, I know characters can find and craft items whilst they wonder the battlefield, but things like spears or bows, do they just guarantee instant kills or do they modify stats. it feels like they just grant instant kills with a chance of failing, but I think it would be better if they were stat modifiers, for me that would make it much more interesting.
6) in terms of balancing, its really up to how the developers want to see this game progress. but I would like to be able to set a max or min total of points for characters to be allowed into that map. when I create my characters I personally allocate 30 points to each character, however, I make sure each character's exact allocation is unique that way when I see a character with 1str killing a character with 10str I start to see how the other stats are relating to each battle scenario.
Basically all that isnt a criticism but rather its an affirmation that I believe in the potential of this game! People who get bored by this simply arent looking at the grand design, yes its initially silly, but if you are a perfectionist like me, its absolutely fantastic! I love being able to customise everything! On that note, if we do get stat modifying items (items should be its own category like updates and events) I would very much like to edit them too! also at match set up it would be nice to be able to give characters specific equipment, like some kind of godly quartermaster, the way we can currently give food and water.
7) this brings me to my last note... about insanity, its cool and all, and I get it its a means to an ends in certain situations, but I would like it either to be optional, or alternatively there should be a way to characters to counter it by minor increments... I like to see my characters battle it out till the end, I dont mind accidents but constant suicides gets a bit boring... especially when the character who has the most kills decides to just off themselves, leaving the 'pacifist' character as the winner... although that is interesting from a certain perspective, personally I want to control their motivation to survive too!
I hope my suggestions help! but also I hope more people try it out and fully explore all the features! try making your own custom content before you make a judgement, I really reccomend going with a theme, you could do anything from robots to zombies, hell you could make battleships, it fuctions the same, just make sure you reword the updates (just create your own from scratch its so easy!) you'll find that if you are a creative person you will enjoy it! Also I recomend setting a limit to how many points you allocate each character... its no fun when you allready know which one is going to win from the get go! This is probably the longest review I've ever written... for such a cheap game too... who would have thought it!!! :)
Oh dang I nearly forgot... point #8!!! on the workshop please add more categories, have a look at space engineers workshop if you want a perfect template, they have all the categories so its easy for people to search for characters or maps or events or just updates... I completely love that you have allowed each of these items to be uploadable to the workshop, its just dificult to work out if someone else has attempted to make what im making by sifting through each page one by one, Id also like to be able to put each category of item into one single pack for ease of search and for others to download. I'm personally happy to be an active contributer for this 10/10 for a unique idea and execution please keep it up :D

One of the worst RPGs I've ever played (and I've played a lot of Japanese budget titles).
The story, sound, music, and visuals are all great. Nobody can deny that.
Where this game fails, is the gameplay - and I mean all of it.
For some reason, every single action has a significant delay to it - even in the menus.
Have fun navigating your items and equipment when there's half a second of delay between every single action.
Want to move down the menu? Half a second between every single entry.
Want to press up to go from the top straight to the bottom? Not in this game. You take the long road.
For some reason, nobody at CDPR seems to have played a single console RPG (which this is) in their entire life before they made this game.
A dedicated map button? Doesn't flipping exist, even though the back/select button on the controller isn't bound to anything at all. You'll have to open up the regular menu and select "Map", again, with that disgusting delay between every single input. Press too early and the game will simply ignore it. You'd think they would have noticed this during testing, but I assume they just didn't care.
When you're done being annoyed by the menus, the game likes to give you quests without providing quest markers. Have fun clearing all the Nekker caves without consulting an FAQ, because the game sure as hell won't tell you where they are. Other locations in other quests are marked, but these aren't. God knows why.
Oh, and if you manage to actually complete those sidequests, all you get is a lousy 75 exp reward that equates to 7.5% of your current level. Remember when sidequests in Witcher 1 would give you four times that? I sure as hell do. CDPR doesn't.
But you know what? That's stuff I can deal with.
What's inexcusable is the sheer incompetence when it comes to the game's combat system.
Transitioning from Witcher 1 to Witcher 2, Geralt suddenly has a weak spot on his back, making him take double damage whenever an enemy attacks him from behind (even at an angle). This will happen all the time, because the game just loves to swarm you with at least half a dozen enemies on a regular basis. Get close to anyone, and the other guys will immediately surround you (and murder you). Wanna use a trap? Doesn't matter. Geralt's trapping skills are so bad, it will take him a full two seconds to set and prime said trap - more than enough time for your enemies to get in a hit or a backstab.
Using signs is worthless as well.
Not only are they much weaker than in the first game, they now cost single units of Vigor (of which you have two).
Spending one vigor cuts all your damage by 25% (because for some reason, Geralt is now "fatigued" when casting spells), and using up both points of vigor reduces it to 50%. In short, don't use signs. That's another excellent lesson they teach you in CDPR's school of incompetent game design. Instead of complementing your kit in fun ways, you are being punished for daring to use the tools you have been provided with. If you love me, why do you keep hurting me, daddy?
On the defensive side, you can dodge, parry, and counter.
Dodging is by far the best of the bunch, because it sometimes causes you to not get hit.
I say "sometimes", because the game likes to register hits, even if you're already several steps away.
Whatever the game does, it certainly does not communicate its invincibility frames properly, providing players with the feeling of being treated unfairly.
Parrying is a terrible idea in general, because, for some reason (yes, again), you are still taking damage. Enemies seem to hit your sword so hard that it does physical damage to Geralt. Did I mention how much of a weakling he has become since the first game? As if remaining stationary in a game where backstabs can outright kill you in one or two hits wasn't punishing enough, they still had to punish you for daring to parry.
Counters are fairly nice, but on top of putting you in danger of taking a full hit, they also consume vigor (because of course they do). You're also not going to counter a whole lot, not because of the vigor cost, but because you simply can't afford to stand still and wait for an opponent to attack you, while you are being swarmed by the rest of the lot trying to backstab you. Apparently, combat must be restrictive and punishing, not fun and exciting.
There's also a distinct lack of AoE effects in this game, which means you're not properly kitted for most of the combat situations the game throws at you. Have fun taking out one enemy at a time whilst trying to dodge those deadly backstabs and with no healing in case you get hit (and you will get hit).
Geralt also has to sit down and meditate whenever he wants to drink a potion.
Because the mighty Witcher can throw bombs and lay out traps during combat, but using a flipping potion is too complicated for our great hero. You have to drink them in advance, which means you have to either know, or guess, if there's going to be an encounter or not. Good job, CDPR. If you happen to suck, at least you do it with flying colors.
Even during the Kayran fight, you refuse to pull out the camera to allow players to actually see what's going on while they're fighting an enemy the size of a small house.
In a nutshell, this is a game of hitting "Attack" and "Dodge" a lot.
Some people will tell you to get good at the game, but this is not about player skill.

htoL#NiQ: The Firefly Diary is overall, a pretty good game. I'll break it up into pros/cons, as I usually find those easier to digest when scanning reviews.
Pros:
-Great artwork
-Good audio design
-Great overall atmosphere
-Interesting story
Cons:
-Obtuse, vague story that requires extra commitment to understand(notes on this below)
-Tries to be like a platform game, but really just a puzzle game
-Clunky controls make the "platforming" element frustrating
So overall, I recommend this game if you find the artwork and atmosphere compelling. This is where the game really shines. However, if you are the type of gamer who prefers really solid gameplay and controls, then I'd look elsewhere.
Additionally, the story is tough to understand without extra digging. I actually enjoy games that make you work to understand them, but this one goes a little beyond the norm. You may need a guide to find the "True" ending. (But it's not impossible to find on your own, so if you want to give it a shot, go for it!) However, the last element will not be found in game... you may be able to infer some of this from the atmosphere and setting, but if you want all the details, there are a series of 3 promotional videos that explain some aspects of the world. The videos were not released in English, but can be found subtitled on Youtube with some digging.

Stellaris is a game of exploration.  When I was playing through the first few hours of this game I got a real sense of exploration and that I was out there expanding my empire and building my civilization.  It almost borded documentary and sim game, its that detailed... at least for me.
The game has similarities to Master of Orion in it, but cleaned up for how it would be played today.  I can spend hours and hours on it and i would just feel like I only scratched the surface, and the map I play right now is only considered Medium sized Galaxy... its has a few hundred star systems in it...  That's how big it is.
Graphically, this game is really impressive, down to the planetary rings and astriod belts and solar flares that the systems star create.  They've even paid very close attention to the movie Interstellar as the Black Hole looks just like that!  Amazing to see the detail that went into this.
Ship battles are pretty cool when you have an armada of ships fighting space creatures or enemy ships and you can zoom in on it for close up action.  When you know you're about to get the snot beat out of you, there's a quick emergency jump to another system.  The retreat system is pretty good as you can cut your losses and run, down side is that since its an emergency jump out, you don't know where you've jumped to right away.  I guess it's more of a consequence of what happens when you run, not bad, but not great.
The research tech tree is not bad as your scientists that are specialized in certain fields will make research for that tech faster.  Same goes with the Generals of your fleet, some might have traits that give you bonuses to the stats your fleet already has.  Politicians are the same in how they govern the civilization.  This is a pretty good thing to have as you now have to think about who you want to hire for the different roles.  Downside is in spending Influence on these people, which I get into next, resource management.
There are 3 main resources that you need to get, Energy Credits, Minerals, and Influence.  Now Energy and Minerals are normal to come by and you gather them by exploring from system to system, cool.  Influence, that's another beast altogether.  It's as if you have to antagonise the other races to gain influence, like it forces you to poke a stick at your neighbour and see if he/she hits back... What if you're a Pacifist and you're not for wars but you want to make a Federation and have your culture be the envy of all others, how do you gain Influence?  As far as I've been able to get into the game, only now have I built structures that generate Influence slowly or there are election quests that are about the equivalent to "Daily Quests" in MMOs, every election the government asks you to build research stations.  If you don't have anymore stations, disband it and build again... that's not a good way of building influence in a game as far as I can see, so I hope the developer notes this and creates a bit more balance in terms of resource gathering for Influence.  A good example of a way to obtain influence that meshes well with the game atmosphere would be if you have had successful trades over a certain amount of time, your diplomats can gain resources of Influence over time, especially if you have Embassies in every alien home planet.  I just find getting Influence either too slow or not clear cut and at times can prevent you from advancing, ie. if you run out of influence, you can't hire any new scientists or generals if they die of old age (yes they age in the game and have a lifespan).  So spend wisely.
All this being said, I've let you know the good and bad.  This game will definately satisfy the explorer in you if that is what you enjoy, it will not dissapoint.  I've spent over 20hrs in-game and I feel like I barely scratched the surface.  So if you had your choice of space 4X games out there and wondered if Stellaris is worth getting, ABOLUTELY YES!  I'm hoping that the developers iron some of the balance on resource management a bit better.  If they can iron out that part, I'd have to say your looking at the best 4X space sim since Master of Orion 2 of the good old days, only better.
That's my view of Stellaris.  Now go out there and explore, conquer or make some alliances, the choice is yours.

It took me a little time to get into this game, but it was worth it, and I'm still learning stuff.  Yes, the game has a long learning curve. I suggest, at least for your first few attempts at playing, to run it with the tutorial-level advice turned on. That won't tell you everything, so it's good to bookmark the wiki page, and to ask questions in the Steam forums (people there have been very helpful, even though I felt like I was acting like a total newb).
In short, this game is a 4X on steroids.  Things starts very slow and you'll have lots of choices to make, especially if you choose to design your own race. There's a lot of levels to the game, but you really don't have to understand everything at the start.  I suggest starting out like I did, following the 'missions' in the tutorial.
Eventually, your empire will get bigger, and then you'll be forced to split everything up into sectors.  Sectors are the games way of dealing with micromanagement.
Also, you'll need to choose leaders based on their cost and traits.  You'll need to pick 3 main research leaders/scientists in each of the 3 main tech trees.  You'll need to pick at least one military guy to run your battle fleet or fleets, and you'll need to assign scientists to science vessels. If you have an army, you'll have to assign a general for that as well.
You'll find any number of different anomalies while your science vessels search the stars around your home planet, and you'll be given decisions to make, the simplest one being, do you commit that ship to analyzing a dangerous anomaly (because there's often a chance of your leader dying). You may have a chance to analyze some some ruins or recover information from a recent combat, or dig up an ancient spacecraft, or initiate a much longer 'mission' to collect biological samples across the galaxy.
Also, depending on your form of government, you may have to deal with elections, and that opens up whole other side of the game: Politics.  With the race I'm playing now, I only have to replace my Empire's leader when the previous one dies, and because I'm in a kind of 'scientocracy' (that's not the name, just that I can't recall what its called), he's selected from my current scientists, and each one has an agenda. You can push for a specific candidate by spending influence, or you can just not do anything, and let things happen as they will.  Each leader has a specific agenda, and will give you different advantages for the duration of his term.
Anyway, that's the game in a nutshell.  In my current game, there are 1000 systems (I hesitate to call them star systems, because a few have black holes or quasars or pulsars at their center), and each system can have any number of planets and asteroids.
If I were forced to compare it to other science fiction 4X games, I'd say that "Sword of the Stars" comes the closest, especially with the different choices of travel mechanisms, and random events, and so on. I'd say if you like SotS, yoiu'll probably like Stellaris as well.

Where to begin...
I first heard of this game a number of years ago when the lads from the YouTube channel "Hat Films" played it and gave a brief review in one of their videos. The video was only about 15 minutes long, but something about it struck me as being really interesting. Over time, I kinda forgot about it, but then, fast-forward to the 2016 Winter Sale, and I suddenly had a vague memory of the game. I bought it on a bit of a whim during the sale, and started playing.
I can honestly say that I have never gotten so engrossed in a game before, or been so determined to complete it to see how it ended. It's that good.
The game itself isn't that long, with only a handful of locations to discover and explore, but what makes it great is the backtracking that you can do as you find new and better items and abilities in order to get things that you were unable to reach during your initial playthrough.
The mechanics are pretty basic, but MAN can you mix and match different moves and attacks to pull off some pretty sweet combos. The feeling that you get when you FINALLY manage to pull off a 1000+ hit combo is incredible.
The characters are generally pretty fun, with Dust and his little group of friends having a great dynamic with each other. The side characters and quest-givers, while not the focus, still feel like solid characters, making the game that much more enjoyable.
The boss battles are, for the most part, pretty straightforward. Unfortunately, even if you are unfamiliar with the controls and what is most effective in different scenarios, the boss battles can be completed very quickly by simply mashing the basic attck button and not letting them fight back.
The story is basic, but interesting, with several plot twists thrown in here and there to keep you thinking. No complaints there.
As for replay value, HOLY CRAP. I would gladly play through the entire game multiple times. Other than for the purpose of achievement hunting, the game is fun enough that it would present a nice challenge to start again from scratch, with no upgrades or bonuses. The fact that there are multiple levels of difficulty helps, too.
On a side note, the entirety of the game, with the exceptions of publishing, soundtrack, and voice acting, was made by ONE GUY.
TL;DR
Awesome game, great story, fun characters, solid mechanics, and a metric crap-ton of replay value.

Like many people who purchased Stellaris I've been a fan of the 4x genre of games for quite some time. After reading both positive and negative reviews from multiple sites (including Steam) I decided to pick it up and see for myself.
On my first go around I created a custom race and started playing on a small galaxy with the hope of just getting my feet wet. My impression of the game was mediocre ... but as I played on I realized that the game itself was quite fun but the interface was getting in the way. Once I got the hang of where things were and how to navigate the galaxy efficiently I had a blast! Well, until mid game where I started to get bored growing my Collectivist, Pacifist empire.
- Customization is king.
- Great content at the start of each game.
- Multiple playstyles work well with the game. It's not just a weapons fest, or a political sim.
- It's obviously a great foundation for future DLC
- Developers are responsive on their forums and seem to be taking feedback seriously.
- Mid game is still a problem. There is stuff to do, but it's much less engaging that the start of the game.
- It's obviously built as a foundation for future DLC.
- The interface takes a while to really grok. I find I constantly reset the camera so it's top down as to see where stars REALLY are.
- There are only 2 victories, both of which are very aggressive.
- Space combat is way to simple.
There is work to do to make this good game great. I think Paradox will take the time through patches (and probably DLC) to get us there. And like other Paradox games I'm sure fun DLC will be available down the road to keep the game fresh.

For many of us, we seek to relive the nostalgia that FF8 would offer to us through steam. This review will be a juxtaposition of the PS1 version and the Steam version.
I guess I'll start with a few pros:
+You can simultaneously play Chocobo World while playing FF8. Chocobo World was not offered on the console version of FF8, so I thought this was a nice addition to the game.
+There are much faster loading screens. I think this was one of the most notable things seeing as how I would spend 50% of my time on the console version just staring at a black loading screen between transitions.
+Cloud Saving - No, not referring to FF7, but this is a nice way to save your progress without having to deal with memory cards. You will always have your non-corrupt Squall wherever you go.
Now, for some cons:
-MIDI files are messed up. If you're a big FF fan, you will know that the music plays a big role in the series. The fact that the MIDI files sound like garbage just tells us that Square Enix did not give a **** about the PC port. Thankfully, there is a mod/fix for this, so it's not that big of a deal.
-If the Square Enix servers are down, then you're not able to play your offline single player game. I'm not sure if this is primarily because of the cloud server, but it's annoying.
-You need a Square Enix account to play. This can be problematic because.. well, a lot of people experience all sorts of problems. Some have problems navigating the site, while others are still waiting for their email confirmation.
-This is the PC version, but that doesn't mean that the keyboard controls will be great. If you want to fully enjoy the PC experience, I would recommend a controller for your PC. I bought one for about 20$.
I actually did not swap out the music, did not have (too) many problems with accessing my account and still managed to almost get 200 hours into the game.
All in all, despite a handful of annoying flaws, I like the PC port. Am I adamant on strongly recommending this game? No. In fact, I would ONLY recommend buying this if you have played a previous version of FF8 and/or if it's on sale.
If you are new to the Final Fantasy series, I would not recommend this as you will probably be dismayed by the frustrating flaws of the steam version. This could potentially just leave a bad taste on your tongue overall for FF8, too.
TL;DR - Buy if you're a veteran and/or if it's on sale; skip if you're new to the game.

Fear is one of those games its better to buy on sale instead of full price. Not in the sense thats its a bad game but because its the first and there are a few issues i'd like to address that would determine wether or not you buy this game. First of all the amount of time it takes to beat this game on normal is around i'd say 5 hours if youre truly speed running and not exploring the levels or dying. The main reason why I disliked this game and preferred fear 2 is it feels like a movie thats dragging on for too long and your bored (Batman vs Superman am I right?) This is a game you should play off and on when you feel like to full immerse yourself into the atmosphere of the dark corridors and paranormal encounters. Secondly  the gameplay is fairly decent and the enemy AI is pretty smart and they've got some humorous voice chatter; Though there are times you will die from a bunch of enemys swarming  you and the limited amount of supplies you're given (this brings another issue) The main problem with fear is the gameplay mechanics are annoying and somewhat limited: There are some melee moves and cool kicks you can do, but it felt like there should have been more punching moves or silent finishers instead just knocking someone in the back of the head with your gun. Another problem is the annoying armor system in this game and how it barley protects you and also the limited amount they give you in some chapters. This can all be changed though with slow motion, because of its ability to help you get to cover and do other cool things such as upgrading the duration. The flashlight is horrindously bad because of the really short lifespan, now ill give it credit because of the horror aspect but it doesnt really do anything because of the not so scary jump scares, there were only two that got me mostly due to good placement and the atmospheric music putting me on edge(the not so scary jumpscares are fault because of the dated graphics, if I played this in 2005 maybe it would have surprised me but in 2016 it doesn't do anything.) The weapons are decent by far and are the only thing that breathes life into killing the same enemies over and over again but once you findthem all it gets boring.
