F.E.A.R. is a standard first-person shooter that uses bullet time—that’s honestly all it is—which came as quite a surprise to me after reading the widespread reviews lauding it as one of the greatest shooters of all time. The plot is the typical what-has-science-done, with an Evil Corporation (as if there were any other kind in video games) in pursuit of engineering super soldiers. So a psychic military commander sends his puppet soldiers to take over Armacham Technology Corporation (ATC) headquarters, a warehouse emporium of weaponry, medikits, and indestructible office equipment. Enter the nameless, mute protagonist, as part of a special army unit designed to face paranormal threats, and his squad mates, who are consistently separated, injured, and subject to all manner of contrived reasons to keep them from interrupting the solo FPS design. “You’re just going to send him in alone???” the radio crackled for the umpteenth time.
The gunplay was praised again and again as being spectacular, but it’s just a typical FPS experience. F.E.A.R.’s own iteration of the arsenal with which any FPS fan is familiar functions exactly as expected, with one exception; kicking people is far more damaging than multiple machine gun rounds piercing through their torsos. The only distinguishing feature of the gameplay is its infinitely accessible bullet time mode, which trivializes every encounter throughout the entire game, even on the hardest difficulty. Shifting in and out of bullet time mid combat is pretty, but nothing near the level of mind-blowing so universally spouted from critics. It is by no means bad; it’s decent, but only that.
Enemy AI was next on the list of sheer adulation, and was claimed to be “some of the best AI in shooter history.” Imagine my surprise when armored soldiers, who make up 80 percent of the game’s enemies, loudly proclaimed through their megaphone helmets that they were throwing a grenade at me, which then detonated two feet in front of them. I don’t remember if any of them ever did manage to hit me with a grenade, but I do know they were constantly informing me of what they were going to do, or how many of them I had killed. And for some reason, whether I was hiding behind a box, retreating, or charging head on, they would constantly shout at me, “HE’S TRYING TO FLANK US!” It’s not their fault, I suppose; someone built their armor with megaphones in the helmets… but weren’t they supposed to be psychically coordinated soldiers?
I did begin to feel a certain attachment to these armored soldiers, for all their loud, bumbling ineptness. There were many times they could’ve had the drop on me, if only they had not shouted, ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥!!” or something like that when they spotted me. At one point, an armored truck full of them tried to run me over, but when I moved out of the way, they just kept driving, right off a building. Sometimes one of them would shout to the other, “TAKE COVER!!!” to which the other, surrounded by hallways, doors, tables, and walls, would scream, “I DON’T KNOW WHERE TO GO!!!” I even started to let them have all the time they needed to awkwardly wiggle underneath fences or clamber over walls in plain sight of me before I gunned them down.
Of course, no review of F.E.A.R. would be complete without mentioning the horror, something which critics across the board have deemed bowel-voidingly scary. But it just wasn’t. Throughout the game, several hallucinations occur that are supposed to be unsettling, but 99 percent of them can’t actually hurt you. With no real effect upon the player, and no way to interact with them, the visions take on a haunted house ride kind of feel—spooky happenings just outside the safety of a cart on tracks. I found myself startled once or twice upon turning around to see a little girl just behind me, but when I discovered that I could move toward and back away from her indefinitely to raise and lower the volume of the scary violins, I couldn’t help but laugh.
The ever popular mechanism of discovered audio tapes takes the form of voicemails, but the majority of them are poor voice actors reading aloud passive aggressive corporate squabbles. They failed to flesh out the story to any further degree than what-has-science-done; the game as a whole never delivers on its narrative. Ambiguity is a useful tool in crafting horror, but F.E.A.R.’s story remains largely undeveloped by the end of the game. I think some developers wanted to make a standard action shooter but were also into Japanese horror films, so the result was a standard action shooter with Japanese horror elements that might as well have been delivered from a TV screen.
I will close with some of the non spoiler questions this game has left me to consider on my sleepless nights. Firstly, why do dead bodies sometimes randomly fly through windows, and why are there so many in the ceilings? ATC headquarters was taken over by psychically controlled soldiers, right? How did they even get the bodies up there in the first place? Or was it the little girl? Was she just stuffing them up through the tiles so they could conveniently fall down as I passed? And why does the protagonist spontaneously combust when he falls into pits? I did it several times out of disbelief, but sure enough, just before the screen went black, orange flames engulfed my entire body. What exactly are those shinless, tan men who float into me and pop like a fleet of suicidal balloons? And why do the armored soldiers sometimes blast off like rockets when I shoot them in bullet time mode? Machine gun fire shouldn’t send an armored body rocketing across a room, bouncing off walls and screaming.

Firstly, this is my first Paradox game so I cannot compare to previous games from the developer.
However, the 40 or so hours I've spent on the game so far has been in one game. I started as the "Solarian Star Republic" which was a militaristic, xenophilic human government with a personal mandate to have the most powerful fleet in the galaxy. After a few pre-emptive strikes on a former ally (I swear they were going to attack me!), they'd been absorbed and I sat as the 10th largest in terms of volume of space, while my military was 3rd in the galaxy. Not only that but I'd formed a Federation which was the most powerful alliance of star nations in the galaxy. Following that, there was a bit of friction with a fallen empire and I, again, pre-emtpively struck them with a force three times more powerful than anything they had (plust the allies who decided to help out). After absorbing the fallen empire after the shortest war in the history of the galaxy, I looked over my new domain of space and began aggressive colonisation of my newly found paradise. Finally having a chance to breathe, I looked over the Solarian League (I renamed it) and realised that, although I'd acted in terms of non-expansionist policy (I'd aimed to destroy my threat, not expand my territory), not ONCE had I been on the defencive. Now, my empire was the 2nd largest by volume and, by far, the most powerful military and, I'm guessing, the most powerful economy (thank you Fallen Empire).
If you couldn't be bothered to read all that, I'll summarise my point quickly. This game lets you play how you want, at whatever speed you want, for as long as you want. There aren't many games that do THAT right.

After playing this game for almost 600 hours, I can say that it is the ground work for a great game, but even now it's a good game.  Even better, like most Paradox games, they will be making many updates and improvements over time.  Hopefully that won't cost a small fortune in DLC though.
Pros:
Good graphics
Various exploration and galactic events
Diverse government and race types
Multiple races in an empire are actually handled properly
Designing ships and stations is pretty easy
Research is not all one type, but instead is split into physics, society, and engineering (about time someone realized that not all scientists are experts in all fields and can just bounce between them with no regard for their specialty)
Stations can be used to increase your amount of resources and expand your borders, not just build defenses
Research costs scale with empire population size, so you can't just blob out and expect to out tech everyone instantly
Updated balance and techs
Cons:
Controlling/Upgrading/Building Armies is a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥(why can't they act like, you know, garrisoned transports, so you can control group them, and send them to a location)
Defending your empire is still fairly difficult due to space combat encouraging doom stacks with only one or two minor fleets to go around killing enemy stations
Interface is functional but could still use some work in terms of being able to quickly and easily manage your empire when it gets bigger
Some notifications pop up way too much, while others don't pop up enough (why no combat warning when my stations are in combat)
Ship design needs to have more impact on what type of ship you're trying to make, either a heavy slow armored ship, or a light heavy weapon ship (they could add in more diverse ship sections, and cause armor to slow the ship down, maybe include different types of engines, not just linear upgrades)
No control of ships during combat, and no way to give formations or any type of orders beforehand
Most ship graphics are overly blocky and don't look like actual ships.  For reference on how to make ships look awesome while allowing multiple sections, look at SotS2.
Overall, it's a good game, but with more work on the interface and the combat balance, the game could be epic.  So while, I recommend it, I still think it needs more work to be a truly great game.

The Witcher 2 is a continuation and a tremendously improved game released by CDPR 3 years after the first Witcher game. The game has everything improved from the Witcher 1. To see all the improvement, from the gameplay to the storytelling, I would recommend playing the Witcher 1 first. This is gonna be another TL;DR review from me:
1/ Story: The story continues after the final battle in Witcher 1, Geralt now lives with Triss, still suffering from amnesia. The Witcher 2 continues using the amnesia plot to reinvigorate the story, which creates amazing plot twists and storytelling method. The quest's story, if I am not mistaken from the Witcher 1, continued to be narrated by Dandelion. The story in Witcher 2 has two paths: Iorverth's, the commander of the Elves rebel Scoia'tael and Vernon Roche's, the commander of the Blue Stripes and loyal soldier to King Foltest. Geral will travel with either of the two to find the Kingslayer, Letho to clear Geralt's name and discovers a bigger plot twist. However, for me, the story could have been made a little longer :( The game was so great that I wanted more.
Choices DO MATTER A LOT IN THIS GAME. If you have played Witcher 1, you will see some of your choices impact in the Witcher 2, though not that much.
The World in The Witcher 2 has a lot of things you can do, which is great, from barber shop, bookshop, inns, swordsmiths, armor shop, potion ingredient shops, a lot :3 you can definitely spend hours in the world without getting bored! But!!!! As with any Witcher game, Money is a huge problem =_= .
2/ Weapons and Armors: The Witcher 2 delivers a massive improvement from the Witcher 1, with new and improved crafting items for weapons and armors. A huge lot of new armors that have different cool look on Geralt of Rivia :3 This is one of the best things I loved to see after Witcher 1. New blade oils, new runes to add to your weapons, and also new enchantments for the armors. Definitely a massive improvement!
3/ Combat: A huge difference from the Witcher 1, the combat has beeen improved by CDPR to be more realistic and more dynamic and active. The players can now dodge, swing the swords in light or heavy attacks whenever they want to, making it less.... awkward in the Witcher 1. The new daggers and bombs, together with the critical effect from the weapons and the Signs, do create a perfect combat stimulation for the players.
4/ Leveling up and Meditation: The game offers 3 different branch of playstyles: Mutant - Alchemist, Combat, Magic and 1 basic obligatory initial branch, although the players can actually get all 3 different playstyles in one playthrough ! Each skill can be upgraded twice, having new effects and improvement, creating a variety of playstyle for each player.
Meditation system can now be done in most places, a great improvement from the campfire meditation system in The Witcher 1. The game still keeps the traditional Alchemy - Resting - Character leveling up options in Meditation, however, if I am not mistaken, The Witcher 1 allowed the player to drink the potions whenever they want to, but the Witcher 2 only allows that during meditation.
5/ Game saves: The game can import the saves from The Witcher 1, which includes your Armor and your best weapons $_$ Which is a major boosting start for the Witcher 2. I really like the fact that they do import your choices in the first game as well. Some characters from the previous game will recognize you on the way.
However, the Witcher 2 suffers from the problem of having too many saves (auto-saves from quests) and unable to delete them easily. Which is a problem, since the players will have to delete them manually, one by one. This is a problem continuing from the Witcher 1.
6/ Mini-games: The Witcher 2 re-introduced Dice Poker - still the same from the Witcher 1, though brutally harder and more difficult, as if the opponents are geniuses with huge luck in poker game - always get the upper hands of probability; Bare hand Fighting - now a quick timing game; and Arm-Wresting - a super hard game that will make you reload every time just to win it, especially in the final Numa arm wrestling match, you gotta try to win it first try, without accusing him of anything to get 15% damage perk, this is something not many people know.
But, in overall, the Witcher 2 is a major success and a great game, a must-have in any Witcher fan's collection. Having played this game really hyped me up for the Witcher 3 game, I hope to see what impact my choices in The Witcher 2 will have on The Witcher 3 so much.
The OVERALL SCORE , to me, is 9.5/10 (-0.5 because of the money problem and also because of the mini games and the saves). However, I gave that -0.5 because those problems are trivial and still can be handled , though not with ease.
And also for one IMPORTANT THING: THERE IS NO NEW GAME + IN THIS GAME, which you won't get to taste much of your two sweet swords in the end game..... #sad

I'd give this game a 10/10 for sure. Highly recommended, worth the money.
The sound track alone is amazing, Hyper Duck Soundworks did an amazing job in making the sound track, it gives each part atmosphere and makes the game what it truly is. I'm not one to generally finish games, but this one just kept on making me come back day after day. I finished the story on normal and I basically got 100% (I didn't 4 start all the trials).
The story wasn't really anything amazing, there were some good moments to it but it felt rather...bland...I guess. It wasn't bad by any means, it just wasn't anything special. There's 21 side quests, all of which are easily completably, there really isn't much difficulty to the game. Boss fights were ok, they ended quickly but I also may have been over leveled because I went for everything I could get my hands on.
Combat in general was good, you feel like a god when you mow through 10 or so enemies one after the next. I do wish it was quicker to switch between swinging left and swinging right, some enemies got a few cheap shots on me due to the fact I was attacking one to the right and I couldn't switch directions quick enough. I also only found myself using the lightning projectile attack as opposed to the other two you receive as they didn't feel very helpful.
My biggest complaints have to be with parring system and the terrain damaging system. There's a certain enemy that has to be stunned inorder to do any sort of damage to it but it can be very difficult to tell when to stike and parry it's attack. I found myself getting hit 4 to 5 times before I actually was able to succesfully parry and kill the enemy. Also as a side note, if you buy the game, don't ignore leveling up figet; there is an enemy that can only be killed via projectile, keep figet up there or else you're going to have a bad time, take it from me...
The terrain damanging system was probably the worst part for me. There were 3 type of terrain damage, with reskins of one of them. The first, and the worst of the bunch, are spikes. Obviously if you touch the spikes, you take damage. This being a 2D platforming adventure game, required you to do some parkore around said spikes. It would be fine if you only took damage, but to make programming the game easier, the developers made it so that every time the player took damage, they also were knocked back a significant amount and were stunned. Plenty of times I had to jump in between two spikes and I hit one of the and was knocked back onto another bed of spikes and had to try to jump back before my invincibility frames ran out and alot of the time I hit the same patch again, or I'll be climbing a wall and hit spikes and fall all the way back to the bottom again. Also, I don't know if this is a bug, but even when you increase your defense skill, damage taken by the spikes doesn't decrease; you still take about 100 health of damage, but yet all other terrain damage seems to go down as the defense skill goes up. The second type of terrain damage are these AOE pieces of sh**. Every time the character gets close, the shoot out liquid stuff that hits the character and stuns them and knocks them back, it also does significant damage at first. To make matters worse, they usually group them up so when you get hit by one, you get knocked back by another one which goes off right as the invincibility wears off and it becomes a never ending cycle of damage. Best advice is to run as soon as possible. It also sucks because if you try standing around and mowing down enemies, may times these things will go off and knock you down in the middle of an attack. The third type is reskinned several times, the first time it's seen is when it's fire, the second time is when it's rocks, the third is when it's snow. Both times it's frustrating because when your hit by the fire or rocks, you're knocked back. Combine this with platforming and now you've got timing puzzles that, when screwed up, usually mean that your getting sent back to the beginning.
Now on to some things that I love about the game. The first is that it wasn't a grindy game, enemies didn't scale with you,  they were dependant upon the area, so if you were in a late game area, you gained more money and experience. There are 60 possible levels and in 20 hours, I made it to around level 40. The second thing I loved was the merchant system. You use materials that are dropped by enemies to craft things and it's much cheaper to craft than it is to buy the it's straight off the bat, but the way it works is that if you sell the shop keeper one of a certain material, that material will slowly start to turn up in that shop over time which means you don't have to grind around for that item. I found myself using this machanic alot through out the game. I do like the regen machanic as well, I ended the game with all the healing items because I would regen health faster than I'd lose it. The only issue I have with it is that the first regen item doesn't show up for quite awhile so by time you actually aquire it, you probably already have a surplus of other healing items available and enough money to buy plenty more. I also enjoyed how certain items would scale up power buy 1.x times it's power, I felt like this game the item long term use.
Overall this is just an amazing game despite the few issues I had with certain mechanics. The jumping was ehh, especially when on a wall. The sound track was amazing, absolutly superb. I can't praise it enough, I never got sick of hearing any of the tracks. I'm hoping for a sequel some time soon, hopefully they have Hyperduck Soundworks do the track again. The atomosphere of the game is quite good, even though the story is something out of WWII. Everything works well together and I enjoyed the voice acting.
Buy this game and go into it with an open mind. The story may not be the best but trust me, it's worth 14.99.

When I was much, much younger, I went to a CofE primary school, and we sung hymns every morning. At the time, I hated it, but looking back, it was very good for me. One of my favourite hymns was "Here I am, Lord" by Dan Schutte.
Now, F.E.A.R. is one of those games that pretends to be horror. Now and again the spoops come out, the hallway spins, ghosts and cute little girls whisper at you. Blood fills the screen. Fires. Screaming. Then it goes back to normal. The normal of F.E.A.R. is frankly fantastic gunplay, with a wide variety of weapons that each feel distinct and powerful. The single pistol can be used for sniping. The shotgun feels ♥♥♥♥♥♥ic. The HV Penetrator nails people to walls with 20mm pieces of rebar. The weird, scifi guns are a bit of a waste of time as you don't get too much ammo for them, but are nonetheless fun.
The foes you fight are mostly five-to -seven man squads of highly competent soldiers. They try to flank you, communicate, supress you with fire, flush you out with grenades, and generally behave as soldiers hunting a highly armed and dangerous psyop would. It's a pleasure to fight against them as they actually pose a threat. Sure, they're easy to kill, but they put up a hell of a fight.  They communicate through shouting to each other, telegraphing movements, grenades thrown, whether *you've* thrown a grenade, and most importantly where you are. They even tell each other to retreat.
Now, that snippet about hymns is relevant as one of the things they shout is WHERE SHOULD I GO!!? This is usually just before you kick them in the face so hard their head spins some 1240 degrees. And to that I answered, I HAVE HEARD YOU CALLING IN THE NIGHT- screaming, gunfire, robotic groaning- COVER FIRE- grenades- I WILL GO LORD, IF YOU NEED ME- crates falling-I WILL HOLD YOUR PEOPLE IN MY HEART.

After some thorough thinking I can't recommend this game for reasons stated below, but it is a thin line between me reaching this conclusion and recommending it.
For starters I am disappointed in the lack of interaction between Lumen and Umbra, Lumen is a movable light-source that causes objects in the game to cast shadows, but this is just a visual effect as nowhere in the game is this capitalised on, the shadows that Umbra can move around in are always the same size, at best the shadows are parallaxed slighty depending on Lumen's position and there are no puzzles that require you to place Lumen next to an object to cast a bridge of shadow for Umbra to cross over, nor is it used to shield Mion from the Shadows by making them unable to reach her own shadow. I feel this is an aspect that could've been used to great extent for more creative puzzles.
Speaking of puzzles, a lot of them are extremely frustrating past the first chapter which makes the game into a trial and error simulator where you watch Mion die again and again due to a slight oversight or mistake, except for the multiple cases where Mion dies due to something you couldn't possibly have predicted.
Did I mention the game being extremely frustrating? I haven't brought up the practically impossible stage 4 boss yet, I honestly don't know what the developer was thinking with this one. The mechanics for the boss are very simple, it has 24 waves and it randomly picks 1 out of 2 different variations of memory, for the first one a picture flies across the screen and you need to spot the details of this picture and pick the matching one out of 4 choices. The other one shows you a card and shuffles it with 2 others before promting you to select the correct one.
Sound difficult? Each time you fail or succeed the boss speeds up, unlike the rest of the game you actually get 3 extra lives so to say before the boss kills you. But the difficulty lies in the fact that roughly around the halfway point the boss speeds up so fast it's practically impossible to guess this correctly without the use of a 3rd party video recording program to review each of the waves in slow-motion to even catch a glimpse of what's going on. This is just awful game design which could be fixed by making the boss slower. To add insult to injury clearing this boss without retrying and getting all 24 steps correctly awards you with the achievement "You're Just Naturally Lucky?" No, I just have the ability to record my gameplay.
The things about this game that I really liked however is the cute art style and the soundtrack which leads to a nice ambience throughout the game's different stages.
The story is not told through narration and requires hard work (and patience) from the player to reveal fully, and even then it is up to the player to try to piece it together and guess what's actually going on.
In conclusion, it's a great game, but it's flawed in its execution and the stage 4 boss is ultimately the biggest nail in the coffin that prevents me from recommending this title.
I do hope the publisher and developer has plans to localize its sister-title "Rose to Tasogare no Kojō" for Steam however.

About a decade from now, a battalion of cloned supersoldiers and their commander, named Paxton Fettel, tear through a company called Armacham Technology Corporation for unknown reasons, butchering anyone in their way. You've recently been assigned as the Point Man of a group called F.E.A.R., a special forces team focused on combating the paranormal. Your main mission is to kill Fettel. Once dead, his army of soldiers will shut down. Additionally, you are forced to try and unravel the mystery of a paranormal presence in the form of a little girl.
This original title scared the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of me. Absolutely scared the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of me. From the atmosphere, to hallucination sequences, to the girl herself. Could hardly take it. However, as scary as this game is, it's still labeled as a horror/shooter game, and you'll be doing a ton of shooting and walking around.
Visuals/Atmosphere: This game is 12 years old this year, and it still holds up pretty well. While lacking in a vibrant color palette, the lighting and blood from the enemies gives it a pretty good look. It also does a really good job creating tension and suspense. Quiet voices, scurrying footsteps of a little girl, people peeking around corners and fading out of sight will definitely make your skin crawl. On top of that, whenever you are in a hallucination, its something you should be afraid of, and something that is also relevant to the story completely if you piece everything together.
Story: This is where the game is a bit hit-or-miss. While very compelling and having a great mystery, the end result is a little bit meh and doesn't make a ton of sense. It is an interesting twist, and definitely makes you think about it a lot, and I love that in a game.
Gameplay/Pacing: These enemies are pretty awesome. Arguably the best AI in gaming history, Replicas will definitely give you a run for your money if you are playing on a high difficulty. Accurate, vocal, human, and deadly, these guys always fight in a squad. Not really that wave idea where numberless hordes of enemies spawn in one way, these guys use their environment to their advantage: They'll take cover, issue comands to their allies, flush you out with grenades, the whole deal. The squads of enemies are strong and formidable, but you are given a special trait to give you and edge in combat; slow-mo. For a set amount of time you can slow time and greatly improve your shooting ability, and dodging grenades or rockets. On the flip side, while the idea of squads is awesome and a nice change, it causes some problems with the way the game is paced out. While there are a total of about 5 levels in the game, the last level is the most varied and definitely the longest. However, the office section in the middle... good god. An endless number of cubicles and vending machines and its horrible.

Hotaru No Nikki, stylized as htoL#NiQ, is a 2014 dark and atmospheric puzzle game for the PS Vita and later ported to the PC in 2016. The premise initiates with Mion, our small protagonist, waking up to a dilapidated, shadowy world with her memories missing. Mion has to navigate this world with the guidance and light of her two firefly companions, Lumen and Umbra. Danger lurks at every step and corner with monstrous machinery, deadly plants, and shadowy creatures all providing sudden and rapid death to Mion should she make any small misstep during her journey.
The core mechanic of Hotaru No Nikki is to drag your fireflies around to move Mion and interact with objects. The game throws a twist in this mechanic by introducing a Shadow world that can be interacted with by your second firefly. In this shadow world, hidden objects and triggers are displayed that are necessary to solve puzzles or occasionally are traps themselves. Mion herself is a defenseless loli that can only run away and cower, so it is strictly up to the discretion and resourcefulness of the player to guide her through to safety.
Hotaru No Nikki is a lukewarm puzzle game that doesn't ever truly shine with its atmosphere, puzzles, or story. It has many unpolished aspects and oversights within its gameplay, has an insane difficult spike in certain places, and does not fully commit to its tone and atmosphere. However the games amazing and cute visuals go a significant distance to redeem it.
Before I talk about the puzzle designs, I will talk about the movements and design. The level design is such that there are consistently vast and wide areas to be traversed and some puzzles will utilize this space to the fullest extent. That’s unproblematic by itself, but when Mion’s movement is atrociously slow or certain puzzles require 5 minutes + just to go through with the most difficult sections at the very end that will kill you and reset the puzzle, it becomes primarily a waiting game. The level design itself is not polished either with the designer creating certain save points next to teleportation areas that take 20 seconds to teleport, only to come out into a quick-reflex event that’ll kill the player if he’s not quick enough. Then thus failing, the player has to wait another 20 seconds to teleport before attempting the quick-reflex event again. This could’ve been easily, entirely avoided if the developer just simply placed the player after the teleportation. This is one variant among the many where the designer’s lack of polish creates a bunch of needless waiting time on the player’s part.
Hotaru No Nikki is not committed to its tone and atmosphere. I say this because the game demonstrates that it’s not afraid to be graphic for the sake its tone,
However it doesn’t go the full way in utilizing graphicness to create a dark tone. There are literally no death animations. Mion just falls back when she’s hit by a box or enemy with some blood splats on the screen and the game resets. Falling off from a high location, the game just quietly turns black and resets itself. Falling into water Mion doesn’t struggle at all to show that she’s drowning/can’t swim before the game resets itself to the last checkpoint. Because of this, all the other attempts to create a grim atmosphere fail because our Loli protagonist is visually invulnerable to the world around her. To contrast, a game like Limbo does this excellently with adaptive gruesome death animations for practically every encounter. But Hotaru No Nikki doesn’t do that, the dangers feel disconnected from Mion and the tone just doesn’t work.
Now for Mion herself and the fireflies: we never get to know Mion’s personality beyond the fact that she’s a timid Loli. This is even after acquiring every memory fragment in the game. She doesn’t say anything and doesn’t express any other emotion besides fear
. The only personalizing dynamic at all is the family scenes during the memory fragments.
The game is ruthless and unreasonable for difficulty spikes to be found at intervals. There are two categories of puzzles in the game: observation oriented and strict timing. The observation puzzles are usually fine, but the timing puzzles are consistently brutal. One segment of the game Mion has to get to and descend down a ladder that is being shot at by a plant. The idea is to quickly get to and descend down during the spaces between each shot by the plant. The opening to actually do this is nigh frame perfect and hence quite difficult. Also, you do not get a save point near the ladder. Rather, you start off at the very beginning of the level and have to walk another minute to get to this section each time you die. There is a completely different mechanic of difficulty introduced at certain parts in the game, where you have to navigate Lumen the white firefly through narrow mazes with death on all sides. There is a moment in these maze puzzles where a super compact and precise maze takes place with electrical rods running up and down during the meanwhile. After finishing this brutal maze, the player is immediately smacked in the face with a super tricky timing puzzle where the solution is not easily evident and failing to act upon it within 4 seconds results in Mion’s death. Of course, you don’t get a save for completing the brutal maze puzzle and have to do it all again before getting another opportunity at the timing puzzle.
For the puzzles of observation, none of them are particularly clever or engaging. This coming from a chess player and avid consumer of puzzle games of all types, the puzzle designs don’t seem to be created by a designer who understood the underlying principles of each mechanic well. Rather it comes off as an experimental creation by someone who doesn’t play puzzle games and is poking his first time into the genre. There is no super creative engagement of the mechanics within the puzzles, there is no well consisted or well organized structuring for the puzzles as a whole either. The puzzles of observation come in fairly disorganized form that engage in seemingly irregular types of game mechanic and solutions without overarching cohesion.
The story itself, or the memory fragments, provides an interesting amount of intrigue and suspense as the game plays out and it develops quite well. The ending both regular game and post game does not provide any answers, closure, or meaningful information but rather throws an entirely unheard of and unrelated plot point completely absent and irrelevant to the plot until that very last moment. But I’m not going to hold this against the designers too much for they are game designers, not writers. Their sustaining the intrigue and suspense of the plot itself was a good accomplishment and is probably the most solid aspect about the game aside from the art. The music on the other hand is simply lackluster all around.
I can’t recommend this game to the general person because of all the problems I’ve outlined. A general person would have a difficult time to immerse and engage himself with the good aspects about this game since he’ll keep running into all of its other problems. The game fails as a creative or engaging puzzle game, fails at maintaining a dark atmosphere by not being committed to it, has lots of unpolished nuances that result in frustrating waiting segments on the players behalf, has stupid difficult spikes that are completely unjustifiably, has one-dimensional characters but an intriguing story, and has good art but crappy music. But I still enjoy the game a lot purely due to it's visuals and would recommend it to anyone who has patience and can appreciate the artstyle.

This game is widely known to be a great entry in the series, one that has great pre-rendered cutscenes (both for the time and still today), fantastic music, an intriguing plot filled with action and drama, and a heartfelt love story that starts with two unlikely people and builds over the course of the game.
I personally love this game and believe it lives up to its standing - but the Steam / PC port is simply not the version to get thanks to the ridiculous and ugly Square Enix DRM popup that shows up every time you run the game, as well as the soundtrack sounding like trash since they used MIDIs instead of MP3s.
There are many ways you can enjoy this game. Go out and seek an alternative.

But even with such a mammoth complaint filed away, htoL#NiQ is still a shuffling collection of rage quits and tantrums. Some of this is down to Mion’s atrocious speed and the way she shuffles after her firefly helper on her little, unsteadily legs. On one hand, it does promote a huge aura of vulnerability and inspires a certain measure of protectiveness from the gamer. On the other, waiting for her to get from point to point can be excruciating. For the most part, the game itself keeps in sync with the laborious pace; little shadow monsters try to chase down the little heroine at set intervals but never dial their pace up from an uncomfortable creep as Mion casually strolls away. Other pitfalls are less forgiving and demand a series of prompt and precise commands the interface is often not up to. To this end, you will often easily figure out what you need to do to bypass a puzzle or a deathtrap; you’ll just find yourself eating countless deaths while you try to unsuccessfully pull it all together.

Final Fantasy 8 tells the story of teenagers who are taught to be a special forces for hire called SeeD, based out of their respected regions schools called Gardens. Using the best in weapon training, Magic and Guardian Forces (Summoned beasts that devastate opposition), they are hired as security, front line combatants, support and all around imposing presence.
The story follows several of these students as they stumble away from being mercenaries, to being in the middle of a plot of a powerful Sorceress bent on ending reality.
With all the talk about how good Final Fantasy 7 is, its easy to overlook the next in the series. Final Fantasy 8 was the third Final Fantasy game I played. Final Fantasy 3 was the first one I played off a second hand copy that Blockbuster got their hands on some 20+ years ago. By the time I got to Final Fantasy 8, I had played though FF 7 and enjoyed it. I was hoping to find another fun RPG to play, and I was not disappointed.
FF 8 was the first one to make me feel for the characters. I transitioned from a story, that was for the most part ok, but very little else, to a story that had me feel. For that, this game ranks above FF 7.
The game gives you tough boss battles that are very risk vs reward heavy. With the way you gain your Limit Breaks, you can go down several options with each boss; Full health, Full health and use Aura, or keep your characters at critical hp levels and burn down the boss fast. It may seem like these are fairly simple, but that's what makes it so solid. Its not complex, its not jumbled up, but it still requires you to think for a few seconds about healing your character, or hoping they survive to let lose their Limit Break.
As far as the Final Fantasy games go, I give this a solid 9/10.
Its not perfect, no game is, but its a damn good one.

It took me a little time to get into this game, but it was worth it, and I'm still learning stuff.  Yes, the game has a long learning curve. I suggest, at least for your first few attempts at playing, to run it with the tutorial-level advice turned on. That won't tell you everything, so it's good to bookmark the wiki page, and to ask questions in the Steam forums (people there have been very helpful, even though I felt like I was acting like a total newb).
In short, this game is a 4X on steroids.  Things starts very slow and you'll have lots of choices to make, especially if you choose to design your own race. There's a lot of levels to the game, but you really don't have to understand everything at the start.  I suggest starting out like I did, following the 'missions' in the tutorial.
Eventually, your empire will get bigger, and then you'll be forced to split everything up into sectors.  Sectors are the games way of dealing with micromanagement.
Also, you'll need to choose leaders based on their cost and traits.  You'll need to pick 3 main research leaders/scientists in each of the 3 main tech trees.  You'll need to pick at least one military guy to run your battle fleet or fleets, and you'll need to assign scientists to science vessels. If you have an army, you'll have to assign a general for that as well.
You'll find any number of different anomalies while your science vessels search the stars around your home planet, and you'll be given decisions to make, the simplest one being, do you commit that ship to analyzing a dangerous anomaly (because there's often a chance of your leader dying). You may have a chance to analyze some some ruins or recover information from a recent combat, or dig up an ancient spacecraft, or initiate a much longer 'mission' to collect biological samples across the galaxy.
Also, depending on your form of government, you may have to deal with elections, and that opens up whole other side of the game: Politics.  With the race I'm playing now, I only have to replace my Empire's leader when the previous one dies, and because I'm in a kind of 'scientocracy' (that's not the name, just that I can't recall what its called), he's selected from my current scientists, and each one has an agenda. You can push for a specific candidate by spending influence, or you can just not do anything, and let things happen as they will.  Each leader has a specific agenda, and will give you different advantages for the duration of his term.
Anyway, that's the game in a nutshell.  In my current game, there are 1000 systems (I hesitate to call them star systems, because a few have black holes or quasars or pulsars at their center), and each system can have any number of planets and asteroids.
If I were forced to compare it to other science fiction 4X games, I'd say that "Sword of the Stars" comes the closest, especially with the different choices of travel mechanisms, and random events, and so on. I'd say if you like SotS, yoiu'll probably like Stellaris as well.

For most clicker games, you start out fast, then slowly start making less and less progress as time goes on. Keep in mind that most clicker games (not this one) use a scientific notation system to continue using infinitely-ish high numbers. This game does not.
Instead, 99999 is the biggest number you will see in this game. Once an upgrade costs this amount, you can purchase the next level for 99999 gold. And another without the cost increasing. Infinitely.
This makes the late-game super broken. I got my warrior's attack so high that I was one-shotting monsters in level 200+. The gold gained allowed me to purchase more attack, and I could move up a few levels and continue one-shotting. Because late game progress is so quick, I experienced a bug in the game. My "5000 level ups" upgraded had not activated, even when I had 20,000+ level ups. I contacted the developers and they provided me with a solution (thank you again!).
This game is worth playing, but there's no real incentive to continue playing past all achievements. There is no "ascension" in this game (similar to Plantera, another game made by VaragtP). This is a huge flaw, and will reduce a lot of playtime for most users.
$2.99 is steep for this game. VaragtP, if you make another clicker-type game, please give it more depth. Allow replay-ability with an ascension sort of idea implemented. This game is short and sweet. I wouldn't call it a waste of time, but I felt like there was a lot missing.

Like many people who purchased Stellaris I've been a fan of the 4x genre of games for quite some time. After reading both positive and negative reviews from multiple sites (including Steam) I decided to pick it up and see for myself.
On my first go around I created a custom race and started playing on a small galaxy with the hope of just getting my feet wet. My impression of the game was mediocre ... but as I played on I realized that the game itself was quite fun but the interface was getting in the way. Once I got the hang of where things were and how to navigate the galaxy efficiently I had a blast! Well, until mid game where I started to get bored growing my Collectivist, Pacifist empire.
- Customization is king.
- Great content at the start of each game.
- Multiple playstyles work well with the game. It's not just a weapons fest, or a political sim.
- It's obviously a great foundation for future DLC
- Developers are responsive on their forums and seem to be taking feedback seriously.
- Mid game is still a problem. There is stuff to do, but it's much less engaging that the start of the game.
- It's obviously built as a foundation for future DLC.
- The interface takes a while to really grok. I find I constantly reset the camera so it's top down as to see where stars REALLY are.
- There are only 2 victories, both of which are very aggressive.
- Space combat is way to simple.
There is work to do to make this good game great. I think Paradox will take the time through patches (and probably DLC) to get us there. And like other Paradox games I'm sure fun DLC will be available down the road to keep the game fresh.

Atlantic Fleet seems awesome at first, but then you realize it's the same thing over and over. As the Germans, I'm controlling subs which are grossly OP . So at the beginning of the battle, I randomly spawn right next to a couple of enemy ships and sink them before they can even react. Then I sink the escorts, because there's no reason to run away from an oncoming destroyer unless you're out of torpedoes. After that I run down the merchantmen and sink all of those. And apparently I need to repeat this about 200 times to win the game (haven't done so yet) since wiping out an entire convoy doesn't mean much in the big scheme of things.
Surface battles, it's really a question of who finds the range first and which shot(s) get lucky. You don't get to utilize your range advantage with big ships because you spawn within gun range of enemy destroyers. You also can't fire your primary and secondary weapons at the same time, so battleships are kinda lame actually. I've never tried it but I suspect 3 destroyers or MTB's could take out a lone battleship.
Aircraft are incorporated as sort of an arcady mini-game. A mini-game that is absolutely terrible.
That said, the graphics are excellent, the ship damage model is perfect, and the gameplay is smooth. Atlantic Fleet is a lot of fun within its limitations, and this game is worth it if you get it on sale.
IMO if they set this game in the late 1800's before subs and aircraft, and concentrated on surface to surface warfare, it would be a lot better. Maybe a WWI game would work.

: 7/10. Mostly because issues involving the port itself to Steam. If you never had the experience of this game, it's a must to buy in a special sale. BUT, if you have a Playstation 4, get the game there.
For the rest of the critique, I'm one of the thousands of players that (re-)discovered the Final Fantasy franchise with this game in 1997, yet I'm not going to be condescending with it. I like the game, but it has been impacted by the passage of time and is not my favorite one of the franchise.
A weak point for this port. You can get the old (and very bad aged) graphics or modify the aspect ratio to fit modern resolutions (not a good idea as the original rendered backgrounds were untouched) or that the characters are with modern resolutions. Which is good, although makes more evident the limitations of Square's team at that time with the 3D. The spells special effects are a little meh for now, but the summons special’s skills are nice.
The people of Square were experts for making 2d sprites for the SNES. Yet, for their switch to the 3D age with the Playstation, they were simple rookies at that time. The “Chibi” style is not bad by itself, however, the fact that they were unable to design skirts properly (they are like 60’s pantaloons) the poorly proportion used for Barret’s hands, or the way that the helicopters were made (or the fact was impossible to distinguish a character from the helicopter when those were in the background) are proof that Square didn’t have enough time to learn the new tricks. This is even more appreciated if you compare FF VIII or FF IX against this game’s graphics.
At the moment, this port was released seems there was an outrage with the quality of the music. But, I played this year, and the music was OK. Actually, in this aspect, the game aged very well. The music is still superb.
This is one point where the port plays badly against the game. This is a port of a previously port. So, its support for moderns controllers (such as Xbox ONE) is not that good. I had to make a manual configuration of the buttons, and even worse, it was not possible to use the D-pad on the Xbox ONE. Only the left stick of the controller. As a result, in more than one occasion I ended selecting the wrong option in combat due to the high sensitivity of the stick.
Also, because this game was released before the DualShock was released, you need to press constantly one button for forcing Cloud to run. This is where the PS4 port is better, as the default is to run instead of walking (plus, the correct configuration for the buttons).
Many of the mini games of this game were bad at their time, but now I felt them even worse because you need to remember which button is [CANCEL] or [MENU] instead of being able to see colors of the original game. To be honest, I hated all the mini games on this occasion.
They are still enjoyable if you have the patient for farming the materias. You don't need to reach level 99 for beating the game's super bosses. In the way that you play with your materias will make the things funny. Though in general, the materias make that your characters  become empty shells to add the materias (a different feeling to FF VI or FF IX).
If it's cliche now, it's because Square made it cliche at that time. The quality of the history is good. The development of many of the main characters is OK. I can’t say the same for the optional characters, but they have some progress.
Personally, I found the quality of this history to be behind of FF VI, but better than the one of FF X.
This porting, doesn't include anything new for the American players, except new potentially deadly bugs such as the glitch with the Beta spells which can force you to reset the game. By other hand, many of the beneficial bugs are still present (Except probably the one related to the GNRC).
Maybe the most iconic problem with the bugs is with the Enemy Skill Materia, as you can still miss some spells due the original glitches YET,  mastering this materia is part of one of the achievements.
By other hand, you don’t find an issues related to changes to the history, or designs for fitting better in the new expanded universe, something that probably will happen in the new remake.

I played this for a short time and watched a "Let's play" for an hour or so, and while it has potential, "Startup Company" feels like a clicker game at the current state. It is very text-heavy, most of the time you look at menue screens and tables. This is okay for a economy-sim, but I am missing one vital thing: the office does not feel alive, because nobody moves around. Just watch the trailer: it shows off a lot of the different interfaces and menues, but the office is rarely shown, because nothing is happening there.
Example: you buy a coffee maker and this adds a few % on the productivity of your developers or something. Fine. Eco-sim, numbers, effects. BUT: I want to see the staff actively USE the new appliance I got them! -> They don't. -> I am disappoint.
Conclusion: If I can't see my actions affect my peons workday (other than in numbers), it does not feel real.
At the moment, the game is not "alive" enough and thus not for me. I will give it another try if and when more visual feedback is added, though. I would love to see people scurry about in my office. And I can see how this could be fun, because the basic gameplay seems solid - it just lacks flavor.

This game is a combination of elements from multiple genres and they fit together like a puzzle - seemingly disparate pieces fitting together to make a wonderful work of art. Dust: An Elysian Tail has fun combat, incredibly cheesy dialogue, and a story that seems to be rote but actually has a few gratifying twists. I loved every second of playing, and I think anyone who likes metroidvania type games will too.
GAMEPLAY - Excellent
the melee combat and magic system are fun. The craft system actually produces items that are useful instead meaningless like most games. The side quests are fun to go on too - not just for completionists. The combat can get tiring at times... lots of using the same combo unless the enemy is specifically different to force you to switch it up.
All in all through incredibly awesome.
VISUALS - Exceptional
The creator is a trained artist first. All the characters and backgrounds are bright and vibrant, and they all move together creating a beautiful scene to play in.
STORYLINE - Excellent
The story is funny, the characters are endearing. The writing is incredibly INCREDIBLY cheesy, but it fits in with the rest of the story. It makes overwrought work.
MUSIC/SOUND - Exceptional
Hyperduck is freaking awesome. I love the soundtrack.
SOCIABILITY - N/A
It’s a single player game - no social portion at all.

Here's a game you should definitely try! It's both great and well... incredibly average, but it's satisfying from start to finish.
This is a short game, you can easily complete it in about 3 hours. It's a kinda sloppy melee first-person brawler.  Its combat system isn't bad, but it gets clunky at times, specially in group fights. However, punching enemies into a 5 meter flight makes you feel like a badass. And the ragdoll physics on the corpses are a nice touch as well.
I haven't played Zeno Clash 2 yet, but I will soon enough, and I assume the combat system has been polished since 2009, although I've heard it focus too much on team fights, which is where the clumsiness comes in... But I digress.
The game shines in its world and characters, which are all really weird, but at the same time, charming. They present neat ideas that feel like they should have been much more explored and fleshed out, but everything seems experimental here, hence its length.
For example: "The Corwids are not slaves of reality, so they can be insane. Oxameter walks in a straight line without letting letting anything change his path... and that's what Oxameter does." There are other Corwids with interesting... "features", so I'd definitely recommend picking this up if you're interested in them alone.
Now, another problem I have, in regards to the exploration of the world, is that, since the game goes from one arena to the others, you barely have any time to explore the areas and take the time to appreciate the world they've created. While you're in combat, you'll be busy to look around, and the scenes end as soon and you beat everyone up. This still leaves you with an idea of what it is, but too vague for my liking. Again, I hope Zeno Clash II solves this "issue".
Voice acting is pretty bad, but it's bearable, and didn't ruin the overall experience for me. The cutscenes follow the same route, with some cheesy animations, but again, that wasn't my reason to be playing the game, so it didn't really make much of a difference.
So, for the conclusion. If you're interesting in world, creature and character design, this is definitely a must-buy. They've done a great job there, I thoroughly enjoyed it!  If you're coming for the combat system, or a grand scale story... well, you'll not find it here, not quite. Still, I'd encourage you to pick it up on a sale, since it's a very interesting game to play.
Well, I'm off to play Zeno Clash II now, I'm definitely interested in what comes next. Cheers!

I wanna make one thing clear: I love Final Fantasy (and RPGs in general). I have played the heck out of FFs 1, 4, 5, 6, 7, 9, 10, and 14, and loved every one. I really, REALLY want to like 8. Square decided they wanted to do something different. That's not necessarily a bad thing, but it came crashing down in this instance.
Side note: Credit where it's due, this game has a great soundtrack. The boss theme and Man With the Machine Gun are just two tracks I enjoy having stuck in my head. Nobuo Uematsu has
disappointed.
Anyway. Lets go down the list of reasons this game doesn't want me to like it.
-
: Lets be fair; I was prepared to tolerate the draw system. Magic is a limited resource in all RPGs, and frankly, this seemed considerably less limiting. In itself, I don't mind the system of "draw magic, cast it later". It's everything attached to the system I don't like.
-
: FF8 is the only FF game to implement enemies with levels themselves. Your characters can level up as you adventure -- that's just standard for an RPG -- but unique to FF8, the enemies you encounter have their levels set to roughly match yours. Long story short, this means that leveling up is actually detrimental, because the enemies level up too. Oblivion is another game that does this (and it's one of the few flaws with an otherwise dang-near-perfect game), which causes players to just never level up because doing so would be stupid. Leveling up is a key component of any FF game, but it's butchered in FF8.
-
: Good God, talk about complex character customization. I won't go into all the details, but this is one of the main reasons I just can't enjoy this game. You can boost a character's stats by "junctioning" magic to that stat. This boosts it by a value that's unique per spell, per stat, multiplied by the number of casts you have of that magic. You can stock up to 100 of each spell. Here's where my big problem comes in; you stock this magic up by "drawing" it from enemies. It's a combat action on its own that does nothing to the enemy, and gives you an average of 5.5 casts of the spell you drew. That means when you find a new spell to draw, you need to draw about 18 times to get a full stock of 100. PER CHARACTER. Of which there are six. I probably spent over an hour just drawing up a full stock of about six different spells for about four different characters. Just...no. That's just ridiculous. To the PC version's credit, it comes with a "magic booster" that lets you get a full stock of a whole bunch of spells for all characters any time you want, but that feels like cheating. It's giving you a bunch of spells much earlier than you could otherwise access them. I just can't feel right by cheating in such a way.
There are several different ways they could have made this system suck less. Capping at 10 instead of 100, for example. That still doesn't change the fact that the junction system as a whole is easily the most convoluted RPG system that exists.
-
: FF7 had this issue too; your characters' combat abilities are defined primarily by the way you've set up their junction system (or materia in 7). You can set up Squall as a bruiser and Rinoa as a mage, then swap their junction setups and have them both perform the other role just fine. This limits the personality that the characters show -- and the issue is only compounded by the immense amount of time you'll spend in combat just spamming draw. This sounds nitpicky, but other FFs reinforce their characters through their combat options. In FF6, Edgar
like the machinist because he was the only one that could use an autocrossbow. Sabin
like the brawler because he was the only one that could suplex a freaking train. Shadow
like the ninja because he was the only one that could hurl a shuriken. All those varying combat options reinforced their character.
-
: My last little nitpick that makes the game an absolute joke. Squall's limit break lets him smack an enemy upwards of five times, each for standard attack damage, and the only requirement to use it is to be low on HP. Theoretically, you could make mincemeat out of the entire game just by keeping Squall's HP low and spamming his limit break on anything that moves. Honestly, Square, what was wrong with FF7's limit break system? That worked just fine, and would have easily suited Squall's insane limit break.
So yeah. I really, really wanted to like this game. I gave it several chances. I just...can't. On the other hand, FF7 is available on Steam, go grab that! And/Or the remake coming soon!

htol#NIQ, or Hotaru no Nikki (if you want a clearer pronounciation), reminds me a lot of various indie puzzle platformers such as Limbo, and Braid. It is also a dark and twisted puzzle platformer game.
You control a firefly that controls a young girl and that firefly acts as her guide. You also control a firefly within her shadows that can manoeuvre its way through other shadows and use it to do things like activate switches, cut roots, stun shadow monsters, and more.
The controls are very simple and all you need is just your mouse to play. You can play the game with a controller, sure, but as it was originally a Vita title where you used the touchscreen to control the firefly, the mouse is a natural with this game.
However, even if the controls are simple, you'll learn that it's not easy playing this game. You'll face trial and error when you learn that Mion dies in one hit. This means that you have to be extremely careful on guiding her. On top of that, this is a puzzle platformer. You have to solve a lot of puzzles using both fireflies. Each level presents itself with various new puzzles to take on, from levers, to parasol/mushroom floating, and even lumen mazes that remind you of some science experiments where you're not allowed to touch the edge. Bosses make big use of the environment around you making it so that you will have to do certain things to beat that particular boss while still providing a means of trying to kill Mion. I like the variety in these puzzles, however, as with most puzzle games, they aren't easy. In fact, this is a trial and error game, where one mistake might be the end of Mion. At least however, it provides the right amount of frustration where you can overcome all the trials purely on skill (it's not luck that wins, other puzzle games). Want an extra challenge? Each level, including boss levels, has special achievements ranging from finishing a certain portion of a level in a certain amount of time and in few things (door openings, lever pullings), to discovering a hidden moon, and more.
Perhaps the big thing about this little game is the backstory. Scattered in each level (except boss levels), are memory fragments. Touch them and you'll be taken to this isometric pixel game where you'll learn so much of the game's backstory... who Mion is, and the secret behind her parents. Behind this game lies some of the darkest secrets towards the game's story. Be on the lookout for these memory fragments, because you may be in for a shock. And to make it clear, it may feel like a horror game, but it isn't entirely horror.
The bottom line, this is a fun puzzle platformer game that harkens the good days of indie puzzle platformers. It was a big shock to me when I learned a lot about this game's story, but it also made me think critically on puzzle solving, while still getting frustrated by all those deaths (Fun note: dying does give you some achievements). Also another part of why it reminds me of indie platformers is the art style, which is magnificent. In an age where most people play mostly uninspiring puzzle games on mobile, this is the puzzle game that I need to help break the trend. You should give this game a go, especially if you have a tablet PC or a Vita.

I have a strange relationship with this game.
The junction system is amazing; its QTE scenes drive me up a wall. I fell in love with the characters, when they weren't being bland obnoxious plot devices. Its story is grand and beautiful; the romance can choke a horse. It is the game that sparked my passion for storytelling; it is a game that rouses my passion for critique.
This was the first Final Fantasy I played (I would later find it difficult to get into its predecessor). While VII's opening scene was mysterious and atmospheric, you could feel here in VIII how personal the story set out to be, even though you knew nothing about these two men or what their beef with one another was about. At the moment, it didn't matter--- you felt immersed in characters who each wanted something badly enough to entertain the hell out of us to get it.
The graphics in the cut scenes and environments were cutting edge, barely manageable on the original Playstation console (for those unaware, the original copy of the game was laid out on four beautifully covered compact discs). They were employed conservatively, providing emotion through character's facial expressions at the right moments, even though no voice acting was ever used. This brought the characters to life in a way I hadn't seen before. And being a dumb kid (I was eleven), these kinds of visuals helped my imagination stir. Manipulative? If you think so, I won't get you started on the music, another element applied with deadly precision to suck me deeper into this world.
The story centered around people young enough to be in school but old enough for me to look up to. It opens gently and welcoming with a local, homey sort of feel. You're on a small island with your school on one side and a cozy little town on the other. Some forest, a little cave with fiery monsters but you don't have to go there yet, a beach and the loveliest music from the streets of Balamb to the halls of Balamb Garden. Even the world map's score injects the mystery of exploration into the experience.
Pages of gameplay exposition nobody wants to read and everybody skips is clumsily slapped on in globs at several points when it should have been woven into the exploration that the atmosphere demanded. Setting the first quest on a timer was also uncharacteristically uninviting (especially for a younger kid--- I always hated timers, no matter how forgiving, which to be fair, this really was).
The story kicks off with a battle that's sort of explained but not really. All you know is that you're being dropped into a city-state that's fighting occupation from the neighboring empire.
This is where my main criticism of the game begins.
One can argue that a younger guy (the protagonist is 17) is not going to be well-versed in politics or little skirmishes waging on the other side of the world. But Squall doesn't seem to know a thing about the world he's studying to protect. It's like he beamed in right before the start of the game. I think a lot of my confusion could have been assuaged had my main character some intellectual binding to the world in which he grew up. He's always expressing himself to the audience in thought, which was a good way of developing his outlook on things from one situation to the next--- subtle hints on his opinions concerning the expansive Galbadian Empire would have provided some desperately-needed grounding. It's not a very big world--- two superpowers and three sparsely-populated independent continents which exist mostly for the side quests. A few cities. Maybe this was the game's way of highlighting the story's elements, but it seemed that all the key global events could be processed by the equivalent of a high school senior.
While it could be said that Squall knew all of these things, but didn't care enough to ruminate on them, some of the technical exposition leading up to the event could have been chopped down and garnished with the overall state of things. But then again, much of that would have been obvious to the people of this world. If it was only the opening mission that did this, maybe I could have blamed myself for not keeping up with the database, if there was such a thing pertaining to Galbadia's occupation of Dollet, but the story gets very complex very fast, and could have been tied up better (who the hell is Rinoa supposed to be again?)
Having said that, once you get a grip on things--- the complicated politics, different cultures, the relationships and histories of nations, the inception of Garden, the threat of the sorceress--- the world was fascinating and remarkably well constructed. If you play through several times, you will see how consistent and sensible everything is. It's like the writers had a brilliant tome detailing everything about this world and pulled only pieces from it to write the game. This is not inherently a bad thing, but in this case there needed to be more.
If such a tome exists, and I believe it does, it needs to be found. Because of all the entries in this franchise, it is the eighth installment which will benefit the most from not only a remake, but a reimagining.
That is why I love this game as much as I do: I see it for what it could have been. My imagination stole from it so much more than what was given.
The characters were so different from one another, their interactions felt alive (of course, this has almost always been the case with Final Fantasy). They were funny, they were annoying, they were scary, they were sympathetic or any combination of these. They had desires, likes and dislikes, dreams, ambitions, opinions (I would have liked some more gray in the moral compass though). There were some characters who needed work, and I think their overarching development of friendship could have been done better than filling in the empty spaces with that ham-fisted "it turns out we all grew up together" subplot. Individual scenes were fleshed out well and the imagination is taken by the hand to do a lot of the work on its own, which can be a bad thing just as often as a good thing (both, in this story). Looking back, there are many things I thought I remembered about these people that simply were not there. It goes back to my initial thought that important content was removed from the game in the final cut (considering the four discs as it was, it wouldn't surprise me).
Scenes that should have been more detailed to capture the weight of the situation were squeezed into these incessant, contrived QTE sequences that are a disservice to the narrative and the gameplay. It was really bad. And the game just kept throwing them at me. And playing this game with a keyboard made them exponentially worse. Now I'm forced to stop and think about how cheap they are instead of glossing over them with a controller.
I think Final Fantasy VIII was robbed by its own ambition. In the wake of Final Fntasy VII, the developers set out to push a new world into beautiful complexity with a story that flowed smoothly around every corner of it. But they also wanted to push the boundaries of CGI, binding the audience to the characters, making us feel what this grand world was putting these young people through in the first game featuring anatomically-accurate characters. I strongly believe there is a lot to this game that we have never seen, and perhaps this could have been the biggest, most powerful game of the generation and of the series had it been made a few years later. All of the potential for this I saw in dark seems of this brilliant world.
It may never have that remake for a number of reasons... not the least of which being Square Enix. But I can't blame them. I am in the extreme minority, calling VIII the Final Fantasy I loved the most (though IX came very close). There may not be a strong enough market for a Leviathan developer to put the time and creativity into rebuilding an old, faintly-praised project from the ground up. Anything can happen. There needs to be more VNs like this. The descriptiveness of the scenery and events I would say hold up to actual literature, a feat rare for VNs, even heavily lauded ones you see being praised in the western VN fandom. I have no knowledge of how the original text was, but this translation gives me the impression that the writers have experience with writing for an audience other than those who would read VNs.
Gerberias, Matricarias, a scaly thrush, various types of antique furniture, the types of boats, a bulbul... The writers have a clear love for nature and the world and it pays off in making the world of seabed feel fully realized. These little details are by no means necessary for the plot, and yet it sells the characters and the world they live in. Which is very important for this work in particular because a large part of the plot heavily focuses on these characters, their worlds, and their identities.
It's a hell of a beautiful if bittersweet romance story with a cast of characters you can't help but feel for. The only thing I disliked about it was that it ended exactly as I feared it would. But the journey is, as always said, just as important as the destination, and there are no shortage of twists and turns to keep you captivated as you take a peek into the lives of our heroines and how the struggles they face unravel as they try to make sense of the strange events in their lives.
One unique thing this VN has that I've noticed is the plethora of sound effects used to accompany scenes. In most VNs you have sound effects of things, but I can't help but suspect this VN is somewhat inspired by Higurashi and the idea of "sound novels".  The sound effects in this game are oddly quite varied. You'll hear even oddly specific sound effects like washing dishes, the crunching sounds of eating candy, and so on. The sound effects don't seem to be specifically made for the game, but the amount of work to find these sounds to accompany the scenes in the game is really impressive. This in a way also complements a message the game occasionally delves into in regards to memories and the sensations associated with them, so I would say these were done with careful deliberateness, and should be noted as a good point for the game, as little import as it is I would figure for most VN fans.
I also can't help but point out that though the game has a description of being yuri themed, and while there are a few scenes that one can construe as fanservice-y, the relationship between the two heroines is not just a means to shovel fanservice. It's a romance story/drama that has the maturity you would expect from one. I definitely think this is something VN fans should give a shot, especially those who are looking for something a bit different from the usual VN fare of action battle epics, fantasy/sci fi stories and the likes.

I'm slightly disappointed with this title, having played the original witcher game. It is way too short and lacks a good epilogue. There are only 3 chapters in this one and each takes roughly 5 hours to complete, whereas the original had 5 chapters and a much better epilogue that did not feel rushed. Now, the stronger aspects of the game are its graphics. There is a massive improvement in the visuals, a much bigger leap from the original than from Assassins of Kings to Wild Hunt. The combat is also an improvement, however I actually prefer the combat in the original since it involves less rolling. You no longer have different fighting styles. Geralt performs the same attacks on both humans and monsters, and this is where the combat of the witcher 2 lacks variety for me. On the other hand, its easier to get the hang of it. Its closer to popular AAA titles like Assassins Creed, with counter attacks, and you no longer have to be pointing at the enemy in order for Geralt to swing his sword.  It feels more fluid and makes the fights a lot faster. All in all, a descent continuation of the story, however the game is a lot shorter than the first one and does lack a good ending.

Firstly, this is my first Paradox game so I cannot compare to previous games from the developer.
However, the 40 or so hours I've spent on the game so far has been in one game. I started as the "Solarian Star Republic" which was a militaristic, xenophilic human government with a personal mandate to have the most powerful fleet in the galaxy. After a few pre-emptive strikes on a former ally (I swear they were going to attack me!), they'd been absorbed and I sat as the 10th largest in terms of volume of space, while my military was 3rd in the galaxy. Not only that but I'd formed a Federation which was the most powerful alliance of star nations in the galaxy. Following that, there was a bit of friction with a fallen empire and I, again, pre-emtpively struck them with a force three times more powerful than anything they had (plust the allies who decided to help out). After absorbing the fallen empire after the shortest war in the history of the galaxy, I looked over my new domain of space and began aggressive colonisation of my newly found paradise. Finally having a chance to breathe, I looked over the Solarian League (I renamed it) and realised that, although I'd acted in terms of non-expansionist policy (I'd aimed to destroy my threat, not expand my territory), not ONCE had I been on the defencive. Now, my empire was the 2nd largest by volume and, by far, the most powerful military and, I'm guessing, the most powerful economy (thank you Fallen Empire).
If you couldn't be bothered to read all that, I'll summarise my point quickly. This game lets you play how you want, at whatever speed you want, for as long as you want. There aren't many games that do THAT right.
