ABZU is all about great visuals above all else. It's not about underwater exploration as many would think as its experience is quite railroaded (to the point you can't even look where you like at times). Fine, I can live with that. But the problem is the story can't really carry this game by itself which is a problem in such linear games. The puzzles are interesting at first but it gets old pretty soon and somehow, everything else just feels like it was made just for the sake of showing the graphics. Engine demo if you will.
By the way - the controls of this game are really abysmal (I tried both keyboard and gamepad). The worst, it can't be even configured at all. To swim, you actually have to hold the trigger (or RMB) and that is very tiring for your fingers after a while. It took me a lot of time to get used to it and it still annoyed the hell out of me by the time I was finishing the game.
While the game can by nice to look at, artistically, its story is actually very shallow and forgettable and its non-inventive gameplay doesn't help either. Everything was over before it really started (in some 2-3 hours or so). I came in expecting some greatness of Journey - as many people had suggested this game is similiar - but in the end I came out very disappointed. Abzu can't even compare to mysticism and overreaching motives or the message Journey had. Well, Austin Wintory did the soundtrack at least, and it isn't quit bad I guess. But the visuals alone are not enough to make a fun game.
I wonder where all the praise to this game cames from. The lack of other similiar titles on PC, maybe? Well, for me I don't really recommend this one.

An expansion to Star Wars Dark Forces 2 Jedi Knight, this time, we follow Mara Jade, another Force “User” who has a two way learning relationship with Kyle Katarn. While you will be demolishing the poor cronies of the Empire with Kyle for the first two missions, you will be getting to know Mara for the remainder of the story. The live action cutscenes are no more however, (which I must say is a HUGE disappointment) and are replaced with in-game cutscenes which in my opinion are a step down in quality. There are some graphical improvements to the game as once again, you are led across the galaxy to new set locations, new enemies and people to meet and new weapons and force powers. Priced less than $2 during the sales (Pro Tip: Look for coins in the couch or change in soda dispensers), you can not go wrong in finding out the conclusion to the Dark Forces series. This is not the end for Kyle Katarn, the Chuck Norris of the Star Wars universe however…
*The game requires DosBox however, with the Steam download, everything will be set up for you to enjoy as soon as the game is downloaded.
Story/Characters:
Mara Jade, a mercenary who works for Talon Karrde (In this game, works with Kyle and the New Republic) is the main character. There are many different locations you will be going to, many of which is in the Expanded Universe books and such. Also, many of the cutscenes or scenarios in the game harkens back to the Original Series (think Dagobah) which was a nice touch in my opinion. The last several missions are one of the spookiest and well, excellently crafted atmospherically set pieces I feel in the whole series.
Gameplay:
Mostly the same from my previous Dark Forces 2 review as this is an expansion for said game. There are not as many mini bosses in this one, and in my experience, the difficulty really ramps up exponentially at the end which gave me several frustrated moments because of the lightsaber still being random and inelegant (Obi-Wan you lied to me!) but still, solid stuff.
Graphics:
Once again, same sentiments from my Dark Forces 2 review. The 3D technology is still not “there” yet but you get the gist of what you’re whacking away at with your lightsaber.
Sound/Music:
Sound and music is still excellent. The voice acting in the cutscenes was a bit more on the “meh” side but that did not impact the overall game too much for me.
Controls:
The game allows you to use a joystick or the standard keyboard and mouse. You may also customize hotkeys from everything from moving to weapons to force powers.
Replay value:
Little to none as there is no Light or Dark Side paths you may take.
Online:
This expansion adds new maps and play modes but I feel you’ll be up a crap creek without a paddle (Note: That is not good) if you want to play.
---

Whether or not you consider it a true rogue-like, Isaac is best judged by their mantra: both luck and skill are significant factors. Luck determines what kind of layout you get each floor, the number of items present and their nature. Skill determines how you manage those random factors and balance risk and reward. With a simple control scheme, several unlockable characters, and plenty of items to discover the game's replay value is fairly high, more so if you're an achivement hunter. That's not my thing, but the difficulty and variety of achivements should satisfy those with that particular itch.
Let's make this clear: if you want a purely skill-based game, Isaac isn't it. Death will come often. Most times it will be your fault, but not 100% of the time. As it was written in flash, the game can and does lag if too many projectiles, enemies, or both are on screen... Or at times for no clear reason. It's not a constant issue, but frequent enough that most players will notice its sporadic and unwelcome appearance.
Despite those issues with the engine, Isaac is a thoroughly enjoyable game for those who can stand its artistic and gameplay eccentricities. A remake is on the way an indefinite time down the line, that promises to eliminate the engine issues and go for a more pixellated art style, among other changes. It looks to be the superior version: wait for it if you can. If you can't, there's plenty of fun and/or death to be had with the original.

I was given a Review Key for this game and my original review can be found on Geek Pride -
Over the past year or so, there has been a veritable panoply of “Idle” games released.  In this exceedingly crowded Idle Game market, it is rare to find a game that stands out for its simplicity and its addictiveness.  Tap Heroes, however, is one such game.
Tap Heroes, like many such Idle games revolves around you, the player, clicking on enemies in order to progress.  Or, you can leave your “Heroes” to battle the enemies themselves.
What is interesting about Tap Heroes is that there is a “Healing” system in place.  Unlike many other games of this type, your Hero takes damage from the monsters he battles.  Taking too much damage can quickly see you in some serious trouble.  You have the option of clicking frantically on your hero to heal him, or, hiring a Mage to automatically heal your Hero.
As the game progresses the enemies become even harder and do more damage to your heroes.  Luckily, defeating an enemy gets you loot.  You get to spend this loot on upgrading your heroes to deal more damage or take more damage, or on upgrading your own clicking power to also deal more damage or heal damage inflicted upon your Hero.
Tap Heroes has a beautiful, retro, 8-bit graphical style for the characters and is a real pleasure to watch.  The animations flow smoothly, and seeing the monsters wince in pain when they are hit is a real joy.
There are more than 70 different monsters and bosses in the game, spread across 10 distinct regions.  This, combined with a veritable plethora of achievements and Trading Cards unlockable exclusively on Steam make Tap Heroes a potentially limitless game.
In all, if you enjoy “Idle” type games, I would heartily recommend Tap Heroes.  It is simple, fun, good to look at and a nice way to pass the time whilst waiting for your guild to log on to steam so you can all go on your next raid.

I cannot believe I waited as long as I did to pick up Dust: An Elysian Tail. For the past three years, I saw the Dust:AET as some cheesy, furry fan-fiction RPG with no substance. That is, until I decided to pick the game up after noticing it being on sale for only 3 dollars. Not only did Dust:AET manage to amaze me with it’s story and characters and how good they turned out to be, but it’s also an addictively fun action-RPG with one of the best soundtracks I’ve ever heard in any video game, let alone an XBLA indie title.
The first thing that you will notice about Dust:AET is the fantastic visual style. The color palette is bright and full of life while the animation of all of the characters, especially for Dust, looks phenomenal. Very few characters in games look as good as Dust does as he dodges and flies through the air during combat. The game’s environments are nothing to scoff at either. The different areas that you control Dust through have their own atmosphere and tone to them, and the backgrounds in each of them are detailed and varied. Each zone looks better than the last and every character you meet along the way is memorable and three dimensional. Thanks to the beautiful visuals, Dust:AET feels like an animated movie all the way through, and no corners are cut with the visual representation or the animations of any of the characters.
To make the characters feel even more alive, the writing for each of them is amazing. I cannot think of a single time where I wish I could just stop talking to whoever was in front of me. Every character is likeable, dynamic, and unique. Even Fidget, a high-pitched voiced nimbat who serves as your sidekick throughout the journey, manages to get me to like her because of how well written she was. I really could have believed that these characters were real people with real struggles (If you can ignore the fact that most of them are furry and anthropomorphic). By the time I had reached the end of my journey, I had truly felt like I had made some friends with these characters. To add onto the great writing and storytelling, all of the voice actors are great. Not a single line made me groan and every delivery was perfect and was done with emotion, which is more than what can be said for most indie games with this amount of voice acting.
Last but not least, Dust:AET has one of the most memorable, catchy, mesmerizing, emotional, and straight-up GOOD soundtracks that has come from a video game in a long time. Just listening to the main menu theme is enough to give me chills. Every area has it’s own new song to go along with it and it’s always a delight to listen to. Whether it’s heavy, solemn, or sad, Dust:AET’s soundtrack is sure to impress. Every single element within Dust:AET’s presentation works so well together that anyone who plays for even a short amount of time will surely be astonished.
After all of that amazing art and story, Dust: An Elysian Tail is also a very fun and satisfying Hack and Slash - RPG hybrid. Dust:AET follows a classic Metroidvania style of gameplay and rewards the player for high hit combos and exploration of the different dungeons you visit. Every second you explore you find more treasure or keys to use to continue upgrading Dust, which serves as an excellent way of encouraging the player to explore every nook and cranny of the world. In true Metroidvania fashion, more areas become accessible as you unlock more abilities as well.
Dust:AET’s combat system also is varied and satisfying enough to stay enjoyable throughout the entire experience. Combos are satisfying to pull off and it has one of the best leveling systems I’ve seen in a game of this type. Together with Fidget, Dust is a very powerful force; Fidget’s magic combined with Dust’s windstorm ability creates a flurry of attack across the screen which allows you rack up absurd combos and is very satisfying to pull off. Dust also has parries and dodges and air attacks that he can string together with regular sword strikes to really string together some amazing combos in a show of amazing animation and particle effects, turning every battle a moving painting. The only problem present with the combat is the boss battles. I won’t spoil any of them here, but all of them can be taken down with the same combo spammed over and over again while they don’t really put up much of a fight, and there didn’t feel like there was enough of them either. Otherwise, the combat system of Dust is perfect.
I cannot say enough good things about Dust:An Elysian Tail. The visuals, atmosphere, and music are all perfect, and the characters and story is memorable and entertaining. The combat is visceral and fast, but manages to pace itself with the gameplay and stay fun throughout the entire ~12 hour game. It’s a game I would recommend to anyone who has ever had fun with a video game story, and it isn’t an experience anyone should miss.

Elegy for a dead World removes the narrative element, one that I consider to be the most important in a game, and mostly puts it in the hands of the player. I say mostly as, the beautiful art, sound and music of this game greatly enhances your ability to build this narrative and somewhat guides you. There are actual guides as well, as the writing prompts often have suggestions of subjects for the page you are to write. Don't be scared to venture away from these, as the environment the game puts you into provides you with a vast amount of emotions that propulse your writing.
You don't really have to have an interest in writing or even be good at it. The lack of interface and introduction "menu" does great at putting you within the atmosphere of the world. Obviously, if you  hate writing, you aren't going to be pleased by pretty skies and noises. If you are open to try however, I have a hard time believing that this game will fall short of producing enjoyment.
Overall, the experience given by Elegy for a Dead World is really meant for anyone who has interest in exploring their creative mind. It's not a large expense and it breaks most game design conventions, but it does provide a fulfilling experience and a similar feeling of achievement that traditional gameplay elements would.

This was the first title by the 'Choice of Games' that I have played, and I was pleasantly surprised to rediscover the 'choose-your-own-adventure' genre in digital form, having only encountered it previously in childrens' literature. 'Ratings War' is, however, far more comprehensively realised than most examples of it's kind on your bookshelf. The story itself is engaging, reasonably original and has a good sense of narritive cohesion, though now on my second run-through I'm unsure whether the choices I made had any real impact on the story itself, rather affecting other more superficial (but equally important) features. It's difficult to give a specific example without spoilers, but romantic implications, for instance, may arise that affect your gameplay.
I picked it up at £1.34 in a sale but at it's normal £2.00 price 'Ratings War'  more than reasonable for an evening's entertainment. With a playtime of around 3 hours and some deal of replayability it's definitely worth a look. The free demo contains the first chapter, which I think is enough to decide for sure if this is the game for you!
To conclude, in case you haven't realised this by now, I would thoroughly recommend this game to any fan of crime fiction.

From developer Novel Tea Games, and publisher Lost Fables, comes Runeous: Part One. Released in 2016, this is a casual indie simulation game with a few small achievements.
Runeous is a two part story and within part one, we are introduced to the main plot line and the main characters of the story. Taking roughly 20 minutes of game play, Runeous: Part One follows the story of a small group of heroes in a world that has been ruined by the wars of history.
Rune stones possess magical qualities in the world of Ceir’a, and they fuel the world; however, their secrets have long been lost. Humans research them to try and rediscover what they hold. However, Ceir’a is under a new threat, an evil empire beginning to rise, and Leif must work with a Jacawi - Eme, to thwart the rising. However, not all is as it should be when the fabric of nature itself begins to fall apart.
When I first entered Runeous: Part One, I wasn’t expecting much at all. Maybe a small, short graphic novel, and based on the art work, that was exactly what I was getting. I had no idea what this game was about before I first opened it, so finding out it was a fantasy game was rather a pleasant surprise.
The first thing that caught me eye was the art work. I didn’t think the art work was as good as it could have been,; the character designed has worked hard, and that’s easy to see but in my own personal opinion, it just didn’t seem right.
The story line itself was really interesting and I found myself really pulled in. The ending was absolutely spectacular and I cannot wait for the second part of this. I’m really disappointed I couldn’t find it on the Steam Store already.
There are some little things about this game, however, that were rather annoying. For instance, taking so long to go through each speech; as the narrators told us the story, there was a long lapse between each line of speech and that could have been sped up a little bit – it was extremely annoying. Spamming space, clicking frantically, etc, would not speed it up. You cannot skip the spaces between dialogue which is something that made me frown quite a bit. The longer it takes to continue the story, the quicker and easier it is for someone to lose interest – as someone with attention disorders, I’m really lucky I managed to keep myself entertained with the story.
At the end of the day, this is a solid 3 out of 5 stars, a few different things could be changed, but Runeous is a good game that holds its own. It does well, and the cliffhanger is absolutely wonderful. I had goosebumps on my skin and anxiety in my stomach, and other than a few technical things, there is literally nothing I can fault about this game.
A definite recommendation from me.

ABZU is all about great visuals above all else. It's not about underwater exploration as many would think as its experience is quite railroaded (to the point you can't even look where you like at times). Fine, I can live with that. But the problem is the story can't really carry this game by itself which is a problem in such linear games. The puzzles are interesting at first but it gets old pretty soon and somehow, everything else just feels like it was made just for the sake of showing the graphics. Engine demo if you will.
By the way - the controls of this game are really abysmal (I tried both keyboard and gamepad). The worst, it can't be even configured at all. To swim, you actually have to hold the trigger (or RMB) and that is very tiring for your fingers after a while. It took me a lot of time to get used to it and it still annoyed the hell out of me by the time I was finishing the game.
While the game can by nice to look at, artistically, its story is actually very shallow and forgettable and its non-inventive gameplay doesn't help either. Everything was over before it really started (in some 2-3 hours or so). I came in expecting some greatness of Journey - as many people had suggested this game is similiar - but in the end I came out very disappointed. Abzu can't even compare to mysticism and overreaching motives or the message Journey had. Well, Austin Wintory did the soundtrack at least, and it isn't quit bad I guess. But the visuals alone are not enough to make a fun game.
I wonder where all the praise to this game cames from. The lack of other similiar titles on PC, maybe? Well, for me I don't really recommend this one.

I like Stellaris a lot. But like most games, it has some flaws. I will briefly talk about a few aspects which might help potential buyers decide.
Compared with other real-time strategy games (the most complex game i have played before is the anno series), Stellaris is quite complicated. The tutorial text boxes do a good job of getting you into the game quickly without having to read too much explanation at a time. Some mechanics, however, are never explained at all and you might only find out about them after many hours of play. That did not keep me from having fun during those hours of ignorance though.
Every game i have played so far was vastly different. There are countless different strategies you can use and all of those can lead you to victory if you play right. But the semi-random science progression, the quests and events, the ethics drift of your population and the AI-Empires will make sure you are facing different challenges, even if you try a similar playstyle twice. When i was trying to focus my empire on synthetics (robot populations with artificial intelligence) i expanded right into a fallen empire which did not like AI-related research at all. This forced me to go a different route, lest i be crushed by their ridiculously advanced military.
Considering everything you can do, and all the information you might want to view in this game, the interface is alright. it is, however, far from perfect or even good. There is always a way to find what you are looking for, but it gets quite tedious at times. Say you want to start a nice slave colony on that jungle world you just discoverd. Good look finding those tropical-preference-fanatic-collectivist-mushroom-folk which migrated over from the empire next door a decade ago.
Don't expect tactical combat. The game has depth when it comes to customizing your ships, composing your fleets, chosing commanders. These decisions can make the difference between a devastating loss and an easy win, without spending more on your army. However, once a battle starts, all you do is watch.
Multiplayer with friends works great. Public games are more problematic. There are not too many people playing public games online, so it takes quite some time to fill up a game. Since a full game of Stellaris takes many hours, lots of players will leave for one reason or the other.
The main part of the stories emerging in this game takes place in your head. The game itself mostly presents you statistics, descriptive texts, still images and maybe a space battle here and there. For me personally these stories are still more compelling than the narrative of most triple A games, because they are mine and they are always unpredictable.

Pros:
- Very nice to look at
- Soundtrack is quite enjoyable and calming
- Game has different combinations you can burn to unlock the next catalog and earn "stamps." These combinations help immensely with keeping a player interested.
- The story and the originality of this game really managed to draw me in from the beginning.
- The plot holds a pretty interesting metaphor.
- Almost all of the items burn in some special way or do something interesting when they are burned, which also makes the game that much more entertaining.
Cons:
- Gameplay is definitely quite repetitive after a while; All you do is burn things. The combinations DO help to make this more entertaining, but really only up to a point.
- Without giving too much away, I found the ending to be a little unsatisfying. I don't regret playing it to the end, however, I was just expecting a little more.
- Very little replay value. I finished 52 out of the 99 combinations before I completed the story, and I might eventually go back and do the rest of the combinations for the fun of it, but beyond that I don't expect to ever to this game again.
- The "wait times" for some of the objects feel just a little unnecessary; I didn't mind the 30 second or 1 minute timers, but some of them took nearly 3 minutes. At that point it felt almost like the developers were just trying to extend the gameplay time but it ended up making for some dull moments.
Overall, I found Little Inferno to be quite relaxing and, for the most part, entertaining. The gameplay was eventually quite repetitive, but not to the point of me losing interest. The short story was quite pleasant and although I personally didn't find the ending as satisfying as it could've been, I did enjoy the overall message the game conveys (which is left up to the player to figure out and interpret). I do plan on going back and finishing the different combos just for the sake of being a completionist, but after that I don't expect to play this game again.
I would not recommend buying this game at full price, but if you can catch it on sale (like it is now), I would definitely recommend it.

While ABZU has a lot of positives, I absolutely can't recommend it as long as it installs intrusive thrid-party malware like Denuvo onto your system. There's no reason for this, and it makes having to clean up after an installation a huge pain. I also fault Steam for not making this clear ahead of time, as it would've certainly resulted in me not purchasing.
The game itself is a somewhat boring exploration game. It does not have a story or dialogue, but it is a calm atmospheric journey for a couple hours. If you just want to move through the water and look at some fish then it's worth the time.
There are some truly majestic and awe-inspiring moments, but sadly they're not that common. And you'll have to deal with some incredibly clunky controls to move from one to the next. It's also annoying that you can't tell where loading zones are going to happen ahead of time, so you can accidentally move forward and be unable to go back. That's a real problem for a game that's fundamentally about exploration.
ABZU has a great soundtrack and pretty visuals. It's somewhat entertaining over its short timespan. But it contains serious flaws, and unlike most games the developers put the problems there on purpose.

I get as trong feeling this game was developed to one up Endless Space 2 before it comes out.
But to the actual reveiw:
Pros:
-Lots of modules and customizations for ships
-The game style is different from anything I've seen or played before, and I love it.
-Beautiful visuals while still not being too RAM/GPU intensive
-A sci-fi 4X that isn't Endless Space for Mac
-CUSTOMIZATION! Nothing in your empire has a set in stone name.
-3 tech trees (Tree may not be the proper description)
-You can uplift aliens and have them join your society.
-Planet management is realistic, you need to employ governers and map out sectors to make contolling more than 5 planets efficient, and the sectors usually are better at managing themselves than you are.
-Decisions and certain researches have reprecusssions (AI can cause robot uprisings a la Terminator)
-Leaders, admirals and scientists actually die after enough time passes (Take that 6000 year old Napoleon from Civ!)
-Did I mention this is a breath of fresh air to a somewhat stale genre? Because it is.
Cons:
-Until over 300 years passed, the AI never declared a single war.
-Strategic and luxury resources are limited for how necessary they are.
-Sepratist parties don't gain any support and just die off in 10-20 years
-UI is confusing, even after 20 hrs of play time.
-Sectors build stupid things somtimes, and never build military.
-Ground forces feel uneeded and stupid, until you are invaded and realize it adds to the already large load of things you need to manage.
-Your people hate everything you do, especially allowing aliens to be in positions of power, eveb if said people are xenophiles!
-Influence system is very annoying early game
Conclusion:
If you like endless space or strategy games in general, buy it. It's a great game made by a great studio, and it brings a new prespective to the strategy genre.

Really cool use of shadows and lighting add to the horror. When the bullets start flying the game looks awesome, especially with slo-mo on, with sparks and dust flying all over the place.
The singleplayer section is around 6-7 hours in length, with there being a few bonus missions available after finishing the main campaign. There was multiplayer available, though unfortunatley the servers have been shutdown (The game is around 9 years old.) From what I played of it back in the day, I found it pretty fun to play. Standard deathmatch and CTF modes were included.
Overall, Perseus Mandate is worth your time and money in my opinion. If your a fan of the original and the sequels, you'll like this. Fans of horror and First person shooters will like it too.

My Bite Sized Review - F.E.A.R.
The Good:
+Shooting gameplay shows it's age but is still satisfying
+Slow-Mo mechanic works really well
+A good variety of guns to use
+Game blends action and horror well
+Levels are dark and sometimes legitimately spooky
+Story gets more interesting near the end of the game and finishes with a cool finale
The Bad:
-You are fighting a clone army, enemies are all the same (except near the very end of the game)
-Levels are mainly bland - offices, sewers, warhouses, science labs - gray walls and explosive barrels pretty much sums it up
-There are 3 - 4 times were you as the character get up or exit a car with smooth first person animation, it is not used enough though
-The story is pretty boiler plate until the end of the game
-Other characters are not used enough and should have had more to do with the story
-Multiplayer is officially dead unless you use 3rd party software
-Oddly large disk space ???? 17GB for a game this old?
The Verdict:
I actually really enjoyed my time with this game. As a fan of the original half life and games after it, this game blends horror, matrix style slow motion, and first person level puzzles really well. I also really like the last hour of the game where the story picks up and stuff starts flying off the rails. My biggest knock against the game has to be that for 6 - 8 hours you kill clone soldiers, which can get pretty boring if you are expecting new enemies and tactics like those found in other games.
To tell you all the truth though, if this game was 4 - 6 GB, I would keep it installed and maybe play it once a year, I thought it was really that good and it has that charm. But for some reason, this game with it's sub par graphics and only 8 hour campaign is damn near 18 GB (the same size as a 60 hour RPG or MMO), and as soon as I noticed that I knew I needed to uninstall it to make room for other games. I recommend it though.

One of the best FPS singeplayer experiences I've had. F.E.A.R.'s like the wierd lovechild of a John Woo action movie and a J-Horror ghost story, it's a combination that shouldn't work but it does.
So first thing's first: you can slow down time for an edge in combat. This is awesome as the game also allows for diving sideways through the air with a pistol in each hand like a bonafide badman and delivering mid-air roundhouse kicks to your enemies' faces. Very, very satisfying.
However this feeling of empowerment is offset by the fact that this is a tough game because of:
The second thing: the enemy AI in F.E.A.R is incredible, it puts more recent shooters' whack-a-mole bots to shame, these guys work together as squads to bring you down, flank, use grenades and do the unexpected. Other enemies like cloaked assassins, mechs and ghouls add some variety but the real stars of the show are the replica soldiers, seemingly generic grunts elevated to memorable bad guys by the excellent squad tactics they employ.
Third thing: F.E.A.R has decent sci-fi/horror story and some good characters you'll be itching to kill but what it has in spades is atmosphere, action and spookiness aren't typically good bed-fellows but F.E.A.R does a damn good job of sowing an atmosphere of dread between its shoot-outs. It's not going to make die-hard horror fans crap themselves but it'll definitely set you on edge.
Visually it's dated overall but seeing bullets ripple through the air and debris and viscera bloom into slow-mo clouds of carnage still looks really cool and brings a feeling of heft to every shot you fire. The lighting's very well done and the sound design (incl. music) is great.
To sum up: Monolith had a very different, esoteric vision for this game and their execution of it is brilliant, it needs to be experienced. The combat is spectacular, the bullet time, the AI and the weightiness of every shot come together to make absolutely brilliant gameplay.

A walking simulator with science fiction writing prompts.
The three landscapes are in a visual style that I personally find very pleasing. Plus, there's enough visual detail for many possible interpretations and focal points to draw out several stories from these three planets. I wish there were more planets to explore and write about.
The jetpack is the only way to get around. Walking is way too slow. I also encountered a bug in the Three Ruler's world when I left a building I couldn't use my jetpack anymore and each time I pressed TAB, the game sent me back to the first writing prompt location. I had to shut down the game to set it back to normal.
The writing prompts are interesting. The prompts give you different perspectives from which to write that ought to influence the story to have another outcome. It's clear that the person who wrote the prompts had students in mind, and as a teacher, I appreciate the effort. Creating a cohesive history between the three planets with the writing prompts is a fun challenge as well... though that was a self-imposed challenge on myself.
I really enjoyed playing this game. I love writing and I love science fiction. However, I'd have a hard time recommending this game to most gamers, especially for three levels at 15 euros.
I would recommend this, but only to select individuals, and would further recommend grabbing it on sale for yourself or someone who you think could appreciate this game.

The world ACE Team has created is really unique, and you'll always feel that there's much more to see... and to fight. Because Zeno Clash is above all, a brawling game, and it excels on it. The extraordinary plot backs an addictive and satisfying combat system, and luckyly the game includes modes beyond the main history which will sate your thirst for beating throwing you right into the action, in the increasingly harder stages of a tower which progressive destruction will delight you by its smart use of physics.
Zeno Clash is an indispensable, which will remind you why some games deserve to be considered art; exalted visuals, surprising lore and relentless fights await you. Welcome to Zenozoik, brother.

Ever wanted to take charge of a story? Or wanted to write fanfiction, but can't find the inspiration to write? Elegy for a Dead World gives you the space to write. No matter if you are a writer or not.
Elegy for the Dead World has three worlds, each having ten prompts you can choose from. From correcting some grammar for practice to telling a speech to your fellow citizens, each prompt takes you on an adventure. Before entering a world, you choose between the prompts, which has the structure of a Mad Libs book. Each varying in input, whether it calls from it in the prompt or you wish to put in more input. "They covered their planet with ____ and created ____" can range in input of entering a few words or adding in more and more till it's a paragraph or more. It's structured in a way that you can put as much input you want, and the story will still go on.
Each prompt, you travel through the world, sightseeing as you find the feathers indicating you can write; if you are doing freeform writing you can pick anywhere. Once you wrote in each section, you go to the edge of the world where you can publish, edit, or exit. This is where you see your story on the page, as you don't travel through the world like you did when you wrote it. Instead each page has the backdrop of where you were with the text. It may have been more interesting if you actually traveled into the planet, with the words fading in as you walk towards them.
The achievements may be the worst thing about Elegy for a Dead World as it goes against what it's about. Being a reader of fanfiction, I always appreciate the writer as they are not doing it for money but to put something out there. This seems to be the case as well, but focusing on trying to get nonwriters to write. Having achievements to get 1000 upvotes (or commendations) is not only impossible, due to the lack of a playerbase, but can set a wrong impression. Why play Elegy for a Dead World if you can't possibly get 1000 upvotes? Maybe if the achievements were more towards publishing stories it would be fine.
The art in Elegy for a Dead World is amazing. Each world has a different look and color pallet, along with a varying number of enterances you can go into. Each having their own breathtaking areas and backgrounds as you walk through each writing. Your character standing out as you walk or fly through. The area where you choose a world also has a unique color pallete, varying in pink with a bright white light outlining the area. I only wish there were more worlds to explore than three, as there is not much to motivate the player to do more prompts as you see the whole world in one prompt. The scenery doesn't change with a different prompt, having the player motivate themselves to write rather than exploring and writing.
Most of the sound is varily well done as it gives each area it's own personality. Each having a main sound, which can follow by sounds of rain or hums from objects. Even the area where you choose a world has it's own sounds as it has hushed voices talking over one another. The only gripes I have with it is that sometimes the sound isn't cancelled when you exit out and the sound where you can teleport to a feather is a little too loud.
Elegy for a Dead World runs really well, having little to no lag. The only problems was the loading speed of both the prompts popping up before you select it and the stories. As you can find yourself waiting for the next pages to load or the pictures of where it was written to load.
+ Gorgeous art
+ Provides an area for people to write
+ Interesting prompts
+/- Some sounds are too loud
- Limited
- Achievements could have been handled better
- Not much of a player base
Elegy for a Dead World is great for those who like to write, or want to write. If you want a muse to write about, this has three world you can take inspiration from. I would wait for a sale, however, as a $15 price tag may be too steep for what it provides.

On the downside, the editor is bit janky: the cursor disappears sporadically, the text editor seems to randomly go into select-all, and the squintworthy font makes spellchecking a bit tricky. Also, the explorable areas are quite small: I hoped there would be a much larger world to explore. Finally, the user interface is not well designed resulting in navigation not as easy as it could be.
These are minor faults luckily. Overall, the game does what it sets out to do well. It is very pretty and the sound is evocative. Plenty to stimulate the imagination.

Final Fantasy VIII in my opinion is one of the most overlooked in the series. It had a intriguing story and cast of characters that was unlike others before it. It also has the distinction of having one of the most interesting and perhaps outlandish weapons ever created, the gunblade.
Final Fantasy VIII on steam shows its age but the gameplay mechanics still remain compelling. As with other traditional FF games, the game features a turn based battle system. A few notable differences however is the junction and draw systems. By junctioning a GF (Guardian Force) You can summon a powerful entity like Ifrit, or Shiva or cast magic. The draw system allows you to 'draw' magic from enemies, etc. to store on a character.
You play as Squall a cadet of the Balamb Garden military academy. During the course of the story you will meet a varied cast of characters as you experience the growing conflict between Balamb and Galbadia. The PC version of FFVIII is largely the same as the PS1 classic. However it does have a few little bells and whistles. FFVIII on Steam has some graphical updates which cleaned some things up. The downside is that the touchup makes some flaws more apparent. In the skyboxes, and the world map you can see noticeable seams or grid lines. Its not a game breaking issue but serves as a perfect example that making a older game look pretty is not as straightforward as one might think.
If you haven't played this game or are looking to revisit it; the Steam version is a great way of doing just that.

I like Stellaris a lot. But like most games, it has some flaws. I will briefly talk about a few aspects which might help potential buyers decide.
Compared with other real-time strategy games (the most complex game i have played before is the anno series), Stellaris is quite complicated. The tutorial text boxes do a good job of getting you into the game quickly without having to read too much explanation at a time. Some mechanics, however, are never explained at all and you might only find out about them after many hours of play. That did not keep me from having fun during those hours of ignorance though.
Every game i have played so far was vastly different. There are countless different strategies you can use and all of those can lead you to victory if you play right. But the semi-random science progression, the quests and events, the ethics drift of your population and the AI-Empires will make sure you are facing different challenges, even if you try a similar playstyle twice. When i was trying to focus my empire on synthetics (robot populations with artificial intelligence) i expanded right into a fallen empire which did not like AI-related research at all. This forced me to go a different route, lest i be crushed by their ridiculously advanced military.
Considering everything you can do, and all the information you might want to view in this game, the interface is alright. it is, however, far from perfect or even good. There is always a way to find what you are looking for, but it gets quite tedious at times. Say you want to start a nice slave colony on that jungle world you just discoverd. Good look finding those tropical-preference-fanatic-collectivist-mushroom-folk which migrated over from the empire next door a decade ago.
Don't expect tactical combat. The game has depth when it comes to customizing your ships, composing your fleets, chosing commanders. These decisions can make the difference between a devastating loss and an easy win, without spending more on your army. However, once a battle starts, all you do is watch.
Multiplayer with friends works great. Public games are more problematic. There are not too many people playing public games online, so it takes quite some time to fill up a game. Since a full game of Stellaris takes many hours, lots of players will leave for one reason or the other.
The main part of the stories emerging in this game takes place in your head. The game itself mostly presents you statistics, descriptive texts, still images and maybe a space battle here and there. For me personally these stories are still more compelling than the narrative of most triple A games, because they are mine and they are always unpredictable.

A great game, with stellar voice acting from the amazing late Rik Mayall. I grew up playing this game on the Playstation in my early teens, and have fond memories of completing the game with a squad of Hero pigs. Countless Death Bowl matches with the father also abusing madness gas. That being said, this PC version is extremely bug-ridden. The AI pigs do not move, and mostly spend their time launching bazookas and grenades as far as they can, or in the case of the Spy/Sniper etc. using hide if nothing is in range which can be abused with the right strategy.

That being said, you can still play though the game relatively well. The controls are relatively easy to use and the native resolution isn't too bad for such an old game. I'm not sure if an upscaling patch or fix is avaliable for those with larger screen resolutions.

Game boils down to being basically word association puzzles. You get a given a clue and then find the items you think combine to make that clue.  For instance the clue "Barbeque" might expect you to burn some charcoal and a burger at the same time to solve that puzzle.
It is all wrapped up in cute graphics/story and a slow drip currency/income that you buy items with to burn (so you cant just brute force burn everything at once to check every combination).
The reason I don't recommend this game is that after the first few levels the clues become too "meta" i.e. if you dont know your indie game history then then clues are impossible to solve without looking online.  For instance many of the clues reference obscure things in previous games the developer has made.

Honestly this game has a lot of potential and I have enjoyed my time thus far with it. It's a fairly simple Battle Royale simulation (like Hunger games). I really don't feel like I need to go over the basics of the game it's pretty self explanatory but I will below.
Essentially you pick who you want to fight against each other (you can creates custom characters, use workshop characters, or use the base characters) and then they go at it on a randomly generated (or created) map of your choosing. You can create "event" circles that essentially are there to harm competitors. You can create landmines to hinder competitors and call in airdrops to give competitors supplies. Last person standing wins.
WARNING! Wall of text below.
Will update as game is updated.
-Easy character creator.
-Good range of base characters.
-Easy to use map creator.
-Easy to use event creator.
-Fairly simple UI (at first you might be a little confused but after 1 game it's fairly simple to navigate and understand).
-Character interaction/item interaction (people will team-up/have an invisible inventory so it adds an extra layer of watching who gets to airdrops and such).
-Time speed up (so you're not waiting around forever in the final 5 or so).
-Pretty decent variety of maps.
-Easy to upload content to workshop.
-Workshop in general adds an extra layer to the game.
-Harambe.
-A lot of bugs that need to be fixed and QoL improvements (creating group with same name as another un-checks all in that group, unable to edit "catchphrase", etc.).
-Some crashes here and there.
-Lack of animation, mainly for preset events (although it's somewhat understood due to custom events).
-Ways people are killed are repeated multiple times over and over.
-Doesn't tell you what stats do exactly. It's fairly simple to infer what they are but overall it's a bit hard to understand what they mean from the get-go.
-Crashing after deciding not to pick a character portrait for a custom character.
-Lack of settings option (more resolutions mainly).
-A controls menu (mouse scroll to make events small/bigger and stuff like that).
-There's another game on steam called Ultimate Arena.
-Make a separate box for kills/unique interactions. I want to be able to read both but especially at the start of the game it's very difficult. (Be able to toggle them on and off).
-Possible view of characters inventories.
-Give the player some better interaction with contestants. Like give them the ability to heal contestants and stuff like that. It's in a great general direction currently but could be improved upon.
-Different shaped events (like a straight line for an bombing run or something like that).
-More unique events (like feasts, airdrops that take a while to hit the ground and other stuff like that).
-Tired meter? I know it's based on stats but it would be nice knowing when people would fall asleep.
-More variety in loot (I see a lot of bricks and spears) - could also tie in with inventory system and kill lines.
I've really enjoyed commentating Battle Royale's since my friends can't see my screen and overall completely enjoyed by experience for $3(USD). I personally created the Dota 2 character/Map and based their stats somewhat off stats from the actual game.
Like every game it's a unique experience for everyone but I personally tried to highlight what I enjoyed. For $3 in my opinion you cannot go wrong.

I get as trong feeling this game was developed to one up Endless Space 2 before it comes out.
But to the actual reveiw:
Pros:
-Lots of modules and customizations for ships
-The game style is different from anything I've seen or played before, and I love it.
-Beautiful visuals while still not being too RAM/GPU intensive
-A sci-fi 4X that isn't Endless Space for Mac
-CUSTOMIZATION! Nothing in your empire has a set in stone name.
-3 tech trees (Tree may not be the proper description)
-You can uplift aliens and have them join your society.
-Planet management is realistic, you need to employ governers and map out sectors to make contolling more than 5 planets efficient, and the sectors usually are better at managing themselves than you are.
-Decisions and certain researches have reprecusssions (AI can cause robot uprisings a la Terminator)
-Leaders, admirals and scientists actually die after enough time passes (Take that 6000 year old Napoleon from Civ!)
-Did I mention this is a breath of fresh air to a somewhat stale genre? Because it is.
Cons:
-Until over 300 years passed, the AI never declared a single war.
-Strategic and luxury resources are limited for how necessary they are.
-Sepratist parties don't gain any support and just die off in 10-20 years
-UI is confusing, even after 20 hrs of play time.
-Sectors build stupid things somtimes, and never build military.
-Ground forces feel uneeded and stupid, until you are invaded and realize it adds to the already large load of things you need to manage.
-Your people hate everything you do, especially allowing aliens to be in positions of power, eveb if said people are xenophiles!
-Influence system is very annoying early game
Conclusion:
If you like endless space or strategy games in general, buy it. It's a great game made by a great studio, and it brings a new prespective to the strategy genre.

I enjoy Sims like this, and this is a fun game. Good time waster.
Though at the moment it doesn't waste all that much time. As only a few hours into it and you've pretty much gotten everything you need. However as said in game, this is a game made by a single person, so I would like to commend you on your efforts and think you've done a wonderful job. The game needs more, that goes without saying (although it has been said with the 'Early Access' tag, and people would do well to remember that).
Some things I think should be worked on or added however;
Selecting each employee can be a little difficult at times because it seems the camera pan option takes priority, so you may not be able to click on the employees if you move the mouse ever so slighty as you click. Also, having to click on the Sales Execs to search, accept, and complete each contract is some what tedious and a better system for this would be appreciated.
It would appear as though the research team loses their functionality real fast, I researched everything and then did away with all of them as I didn't have a need for them and they were soaking up money without having to do anything (best job ever though).
Completing contracts seems as though it is clearly the way to go with the amount per job ramping up at a reasonable pace, whereas the income for hosting your own product is very slow. I believe changing the system in which it's bases on to show highs and lows in user gain and loss would be better than a straight #user per minute based on hype %. I feel it would make it a little more exciting, kinda like hitting a 10 10 10 in game dev tycoon, not saying it needs to be the same, but hopefully my thought is conveyed.
More options for specialisations would be nice, such as tending towards tv or web multimedia, or focusing on social media and so on.
Larger workspaces in order to create better set out work spaces, rather than cramming your employees in to maximise space and filling what little is left to simply boost them. Plus of course more stuff to put in there (not a big concern in my opinion)
Giving Managers the ability to command their team to create exactly what is needed for the current contracts automatically. Then perhaps making them either harder to get or just more expensive to have. Not that the game has to be fully automated, but of course not every CEO goes around telling each individual employee to do one specific task in order to complete a contract.
Also the game seems to become some what resource heavy in the later part of the game, noticed some freezing and what not.
Other than that, good job, as said. Keep it up!

Having played it on the Xbox 360 for a large amount of time (1000+ hours overall), I would recommend this game to fans of the series as well as someone who is inexperienced with FPS games. Like most games in the CoD series, the game is fairly self explanatory on how to play. The depth however that arises in the balancing of weapons is far greater than most players would think however. Quick Scoping is viable but difficult to perform in comparison to other games, and the assault rifles are fairly balanced for their ranges. While some guns are obviously better than others, it's entirely possible to have fun with every one of them due to the variety in attachments and class system that Black Ops provides.
The zombies mode in this game is definitely the best one out of the CoD series since 2015. The sheer amount of content that Treyarch puts into these zombie maps should be a good enough reason to buy them. I remember spending hours and hours doing the easter eggs in order to uncover the plot and bonuses that each zombie map had. Learning the strategies for surviving based on the amount of players you have is also a great experience. The DLC maps provide new zombie maps (as well as some multiplayer maps) that contain new perks, guns/gadgets, easter eggs, and value from the time you will spend playing them.

Elegy for a Dead World is different. To be completely honest, it is so specific and niche that in some way it may just appeal to a very broad audience. I know that this sounds like a misleading plotpoint about contradictions, but this describes it perfectly.
Elegy for a Dead World tells its own story to you, and then you become the narrator for those around you. You choose things to leave out, add a line that never happened here and there and end up creating a story of your own based on another. This feels, at least for me, very much like what we, as a people, do throughout our whole lifes. We adjust, manipulate and forget, just so that our own story fits to what we desire it to be. Be it darker, lighter or along the same route. But not only does this game let you tell a story to someone else in a different manner, that they may have experienced it - Funnily enough it helps along your writing skills and in a way, which I find nothing else did before.
I may have only played a short bit on this account, but trust me, it is a worthwhile experience and I'm glad it exists.

I struggled for a long while to figure out how to describe this game, and I think "the video game equivalent of the Disney movie Fantasia" is a good place to start.
Full disclosure: I have wanted a game that emulated scuba-diving for a dog's year, so I was sold on ABZU from the premise alone. ABZU is undeniably gorgeous, and I would be willing to bet that even the best systems will struggle to render all the fish at times -- but even my older system could manage to run this with minor hangups, it's more than playable. I think focusing more on the environments and the world instead of the technical details of diving served this concept well, and swimming through the world ABZU has to offer, discovering its secrets, and struggling to hit the screenshot key yet again because everything in this game is beautiful -- it's a joy to play and a treat for the eyes overall.
The world of ABZU is its biggest draw, and it's rich and vibrant with life and teeming with literal thousands of fish at every turn. There's a lot of variety, too -- some of the areas you visit are gorgeous reef-strewn vistas, others are spooky pelagic wastelands, and some are... unexpectedly hellish, but overall the beauty of the game really shines even in its darkest moments -- and it even managed to wring a few emotions out of me, too, on top of everything else.
But as for what you do, well... has anyone here ever played Ecco the Dolphin? No? Just me? Well anyway, you swim about and solve some puzzles to progress; progression is it's own reward in ABZU, as you unlock more areas and more of the... loosely-termed story unfolds. The only words in this game you will find are in the opening minutes of how to control the game -- ABZU is more of a silent film than a storybook, but that's just fine, because the visuals and music carry it well -- and really, you're underwater. Words would be an odd fit, wouldn't they?
But at the end of the day... ABZU is a strange game to classify. It's an adventure game in some sense, as you explore and solve puzzles -- but there is no combat, and none of the puzzles are particularly troublesome. In some ways it's a bit like a walking sim -- gorgeous atmopsheres to explore for the sake of exploring them and discovering the story of the place in which you find yourself -- but it has more gameplay than the majority of them, so it's not quite that, either. ABZU sits in its own pretty little box.
And I think that's just fine. This is a good game, if system-resource-intensive, and it's a great way to kill a few hours for sure.  I'll definitely replay it just to swim around and finish achievement-hunting -- diving out of the water on the back of a shark has not gotten old yet.
I can definitely recommend ABZU for anyone who likes exploration and unique experiences -- or someone like me, who just wants to go diving. I'd still recommend picking it up on sale if you're on the fence, but -- it's got enough love and work put into it that I personally find the asking price reasonable.
Thank you for reading.

Part of why I think this game gets so much hate, even from me, is that it came on the heels of one of Final Fantasy 7, of of the best selling and most well loved RPGs of all time. Final Fantasy 7 had a brilliant and customizable battle system, an engaging story with interesting characters and an awesome soundtrack. Final Fantasy 8 has... an awesome soundtrack, at least. To be fair, the story is pretty interesting all the way through the end of disc 1, but then things get so weird and hard to follow and major plot points are added and removed on a whim, as though the game has ADD and can't decide on what kind of story it wants to tell you. But the battle system is...oh god it's a total trainwreck.
So one of the many flaws of this game's battle system is its "junction" system. In FF8, magic spells are treated as a consumable item. Kind of a weird choice, but I don't have a problem with that necessarily. What I DO have a problem with is that spells are a consumable item AND the game allows you to "junction" them to your character to improve their stats. The better the spell, the more the stat increase. If you follow this chain of logic, you'll realize that if you have a high level spell junctioned to your character and you cast that spell, your character's stats will actually decrease. So then what's the point of casting magic? There is none in a normal playthrough, especially when you consider that your summon monsters, called GFs in this game, can be called upon to essentially cast any magic spells you'd want anyway, provided you don't mind watching a 45 second cutscene of the GF appearing EVERY FREAKIN' TIME. There's lots of odd decisions like this that slow the battles down in FF8 and make them tedious. Even the way you get magic is a chore. You can "draw" spells from an enemy, but depending on a few factors the game doesn't really explain, you'll only typically get around 3-6 spells per draw. Which means you have to sit in a battle and farm draw for quite a long time if you want to get up to the maximum of 100. But really the most broken thing about this game is when you discover you can manipulate limit breaks. Your character's chance of limit breaks are actually random in this game, another odd choice. The less health you have, the higher the chance of the limit break. But if you cycle your turn order, you can keep re-rolling the calculation that determines your limit break, essentially letting you limit break whenever you want. Totally. Broken.
Now that I'm done ranting about the battle system, on to the story (mild spoilers in this paragraph). It really does seem like it's gonna go somewhere for the first, maybe quarter or third of the game. But then we hit a point after disc 1 where the narrative has an identity crisis and starts grasping at different ideas and concepts and inserts them randomly into the story which results in a totally insane mish-mash of disconnected themes and gaping plot holes. I know Final Fantasy is a universe where characters get shot, sliced and burned in every battle, but the first huge narrative red flag is when one of the main characters is freakin' impaled through the heart with a giant icicle during a cutscene... and then is totally okay in the next scene. Like the game barely even acknowledges that it took place. Come on Final Fantasy 8! If you're not gonna take your story seriously then I can't either.
The artwork and music are the huge redeeming factors of this game. FF8 features some of the most gorgeous hand-drawn backdrops in any RPG I've seen. And this might be controversial, but I think FF8 is Uematsu's best work. At the very least it's my favorite of his work. The relaxing "Breezy", the entrancing "Find Your Way", the mysterious "Under Her Control" and the nostalgic "Fisherman's Horizon" highlight the soundtrack. And of course "Man With the Machine Gun" does its best to keep the mindlessly tedious and broken battles from being too much of a nuisance.
Summary
This is far from the best Final Fantasy, and misses the mark on battle system design and storytelling. At best it's an average-ish RPG with a trippy story, some awesome music and inspiring artwork. Still there is something sort of intangibly alluring about playing this game. I must admit I've replayed this trainwreck at least 3 times now.

Unfortunately, Stellaris is at once deeply flawed and obviously incomplete. Drawing lines between the two is not so simple a task.
The centerpiece of its mechanical and conceptual failings is its Sector AI system. In the broadest of terms, this is a "friendly" AI component that, in any reasonably-successful playthrough, you must use, on pain of crippling penalties to your empire's efficacy. And it is terrible.
The ability of the human player to give it instructions is severely limited, and, even within those limitations, the Sector AI is belligerent and stupid. But let me be clear: those limitations themselves are crippling and unreasonable, and speak to deep conceptual flaws with the game. Sectors are created by linking multiple star systems together, and those star systems must be "next to" each other according to the game. Thus, Sectors are a geographical organizational method. The trouble is, virtually nothing else about internal empire management is about geography. One system might contain two planets that the player will want to specialize in very different ways - and, indeed, might be encouraged to specialize in different ways by the presence of planet-specific bonuses or penalties (e.g., lower food output, higher mineral output, more research, less happy population.) But a Sector can only be told to focus on one broad area of development. So, even if your Sector is comprised of a single system, it still could be wholly incapable of coming even remotely close to doing what any middling player would know to do... and all of this is assuming it could even follow limited instructions properly. But it can't. It cannot develop new planets even close to ideally. It cannot construct (or refrain from constructing) spaceports ideally. It cannot manage population units on planets' tile-squares effectively. While I'm sure it does many things right, it does so many immediately-obvious things wrong so often that the well is thoroughly poisoned. No partial credit for building a car that goes really fast but explodes and kills all its passengers.
Other game systems suffer similar deep conceptual issues, but nothing quite so severe as the Sector fiasco. Sadly, the Sector fiasco has tentacles that go everywhere. But still: ship design isn't well-thought-out, even after a balance pass in 1.1. Weapon balance is not up to snuff, which includes the balancing of various defenses. The method by which wars' successes/failures are tallied and weighted is horribly flawed. Diplomacy is, much like the whole game, both flawed and incomplete. Espionage does not exist.
As many other reviews have stated, Stellaris's unique flavor - fueled by "events" that trigger occasionally on their own, or are more often discovered via scanning new planets in new systems - is loaded up into the early game, leaving the middle-game and the endgame incredibly barren. When a player gets to mid-game, all at once they are confronted by an omnipresent "friendly" AI that is behaving inexcusably badly, and a lack of anything else to do except to pick a war to fight, grab more territory, and slowly crawl their way to a hollow galactic domination that barely feels earned, let alone alive.
I cannot in good conscience recommend this game. On its own terms, it is a failure that feels rushed, incomplete, and poorly-conceived in many areas all the way back to the drawing board phase. If I were to raise the bar and judge it on my terms, it would fare even worse.

Tap Heroes is a typical clicker game.
You oversee a group of up to three heroes (plus one familiar) as they fight a never-ending horde of ever-more-powerful creatures, one after the other. As you progress through the game your heroes become much more powerful, but so do their enemies.
The graphics have a unique puppet-theatre sort of style that I really like, but which may not appeal to everyone. The game is played out on a stage (complete with curtain and set in the background) and the monsters and heroes are paper puppet cut outs with extremely simple animations. It works well and sets Tap Heroes apart from other clicker games.
The game can be played windowed or full screen, and that's about the only graphics option. The interface includes lots of nice big icons and you'll quickly be able to navigate your way around it.
Sound is fairly basic. It's okay, but nothing special, although I find the attack sounds a bit annoying. I usually get my clicker fix with the sound turned down for this reason.
If you've played any other clicker game you'll be familiar with the basic gameplay, although Tap Heroes does do a couple of things a bit differently to many of the other clickers. The first is that your party has only one hero -- your warrior -- who faces each monster directly, and as he attacks the monster he is, in turn, attacked back. The other heroes support the warrior by healing him and poisoning the monsters, although you can also buy a familiar for the mage that does do ranged damage directly as well.
The other new feature is that you can either click on a monster or click on your warrior to heal him, and you can improve your attack and heal powers individually.
But other than these new additions, the game plays like a fairly limited clone of any other clicker out there. You can't increase your party beyond the three heroes and familiar and you can only buy a very small number of special abilities to use (and these don't charge unless you're playing).
Pros:
+ Great graphic style
+ A couple of new ideas for the genre
+ A lot of achievements
+ Trading cards
Cons:
- It's not free, and it's not as good as other free clickers
- Attack sounds are annoying enough to turn the sound off
- 'End game' is REALLY boring, even for a clicker game -- so much so that you'll most likely not bother with the later achievements
Tap Heroes is a nice entry into the clicker game genre, with a great graphical style and some novel elements.
However, it's not free, and when you compare it against some of the free clicker games out there, Tap Heroes falls short in many aspects. Given these free (and better!) alternatives I don't recommend picking up Tap Heroes unless you're a clicker game fanatic. Instead, I'd suggest you try Clicker Heroes for arguably the best clicker game on Steam, or Sakura Clicker if you're into a more 'mature' anime theme, albeit without achievements.

This isn't the worst game ever. But it certainly isn't one of the better games I've played. I went into F.E.A.R. with high expectations, because almost everyone was saying that this game was amazing. But, and I'm NOT sorry to say, I was rather disappointed with this game.
The gameplay isn't anything special. The gunplay is actually pretty bad. There are games much older than this, such as the Half-Life games, with much better gunplay, and the slow-motion just gets repetitive after a while. Put simply, walking through corridors and shooting the same soldiers in slow-mo every few minutes gets old pretty fast.
The level design is some of the laziest I've ever seen. Nothing but dimly-lit grey corridors. And that's your lot!
Then, there's the story... Or lack thereof. Throughout the game, I had no freaking clue what was going on or what I was fighting for. The game makes no clear explanation as to what you're doing, or why. You're just placed in these random places and shoot♥♥♥♥♥♥ with the occasional paranormal... thingie that comes out of nowhere. There is ZERO narrative!
None of the characters were even remotely memorable. Most of them only make appearances that last mere minutes. I only remember one name, Norton Mapes. As for the main character, he was just some generic mute. Nothing more, nothing less.
Also, this game is pretty short! I managed to beat it in less than ten hours. And this was a full-priced game at launch? Inexcusable.
The one thing I give this game credit for though is the enemy AI. For a game from 2005, the enemy AI is top tier. The soldiers react almost instantly to your presence, even at small things like your flashlight, and their accuracy is pixel-perfect. They don't miss a single shot at all! But that's just about the only thing this game has going for it, really.
Overall, I think this game is seriously overrated. It's gameplay wasn't anything special, the story was crap, and it was ridiculously short. But I have played worse. It isn't horrible, but it certainly hasn't aged well and I wouldn't play it again.

Crypt of the Necrodancer is a dungeon-crawling roguelike with the unique gimmick of having to move on every beat of the music. I have to refrain from gushing about this game, so I'll try and keep it professional.
I have about 300 hours in NecroDancer, and probably around 40-50 in the mobile version. It's simply a fantastic game: a fair, challenging, straightforward dungeon crawler with a very puzzle-like texture to it. There's a diverse item pool with a multitude of equip slots (head, armor, weapon, held item, etc) that has just enough variety to keep the game fresh every time you play. The enemies are predictable but come en masse: you'll be fighting skeletons and slimes, when a Minotaur (with lute strings strung between his horns) bursts through the wall and forces you to move aside. Every situation is beatable: at no point do I die in NecroDancer and feel it's unfair.
The best way to describe the game is with the Deep Blues boss: a chess set that moves its pieces across the grid to attack you, with the goal of eventually defeating the King, all to a mellow jazz soundtrack. Navigating around each piece on every beat, planning your next movement, and thinking three steps ahead are all fairly necessary in the fight, and in the game in general. A common complaint about NecroDancer is its difficulty curve, but it's really not too hard to get the hang of: switch to Bard (the character who can move independently of the beat, as fast or slow as the player likes) and toy around in each Zone, fighting each enemy in the training area, and getting a feel for each weapon.
The AMPLIFIED DLC is worth it at 6 dollars and a steal at half the price. It introduces another zone, Zone 5 (20 percent more zone!), multiple new characters, an awesome boss voiced by nerdcore rapper Mega Ran, and a slew of new items and game balances (whyyy, Ryan Clark, does my Ring of Courage not give me a damage boost now?) . It's the way of supporting the devs' continuing work on the game. Buy the soundtracks if you like, but most of them are on Spotify and all of them are on Youtube if you can't.
Conclusion: Buy it. You will not be disappointed.

Part of why I think this game gets so much hate, even from me, is that it came on the heels of one of Final Fantasy 7, of of the best selling and most well loved RPGs of all time. Final Fantasy 7 had a brilliant and customizable battle system, an engaging story with interesting characters and an awesome soundtrack. Final Fantasy 8 has... an awesome soundtrack, at least. To be fair, the story is pretty interesting all the way through the end of disc 1, but then things get so weird and hard to follow and major plot points are added and removed on a whim, as though the game has ADD and can't decide on what kind of story it wants to tell you. But the battle system is...oh god it's a total trainwreck.
So one of the many flaws of this game's battle system is its "junction" system. In FF8, magic spells are treated as a consumable item. Kind of a weird choice, but I don't have a problem with that necessarily. What I DO have a problem with is that spells are a consumable item AND the game allows you to "junction" them to your character to improve their stats. The better the spell, the more the stat increase. If you follow this chain of logic, you'll realize that if you have a high level spell junctioned to your character and you cast that spell, your character's stats will actually decrease. So then what's the point of casting magic? There is none in a normal playthrough, especially when you consider that your summon monsters, called GFs in this game, can be called upon to essentially cast any magic spells you'd want anyway, provided you don't mind watching a 45 second cutscene of the GF appearing EVERY FREAKIN' TIME. There's lots of odd decisions like this that slow the battles down in FF8 and make them tedious. Even the way you get magic is a chore. You can "draw" spells from an enemy, but depending on a few factors the game doesn't really explain, you'll only typically get around 3-6 spells per draw. Which means you have to sit in a battle and farm draw for quite a long time if you want to get up to the maximum of 100. But really the most broken thing about this game is when you discover you can manipulate limit breaks. Your character's chance of limit breaks are actually random in this game, another odd choice. The less health you have, the higher the chance of the limit break. But if you cycle your turn order, you can keep re-rolling the calculation that determines your limit break, essentially letting you limit break whenever you want. Totally. Broken.
Now that I'm done ranting about the battle system, on to the story (mild spoilers in this paragraph). It really does seem like it's gonna go somewhere for the first, maybe quarter or third of the game. But then we hit a point after disc 1 where the narrative has an identity crisis and starts grasping at different ideas and concepts and inserts them randomly into the story which results in a totally insane mish-mash of disconnected themes and gaping plot holes. I know Final Fantasy is a universe where characters get shot, sliced and burned in every battle, but the first huge narrative red flag is when one of the main characters is freakin' impaled through the heart with a giant icicle during a cutscene... and then is totally okay in the next scene. Like the game barely even acknowledges that it took place. Come on Final Fantasy 8! If you're not gonna take your story seriously then I can't either.
The artwork and music are the huge redeeming factors of this game. FF8 features some of the most gorgeous hand-drawn backdrops in any RPG I've seen. And this might be controversial, but I think FF8 is Uematsu's best work. At the very least it's my favorite of his work. The relaxing "Breezy", the entrancing "Find Your Way", the mysterious "Under Her Control" and the nostalgic "Fisherman's Horizon" highlight the soundtrack. And of course "Man With the Machine Gun" does its best to keep the mindlessly tedious and broken battles from being too much of a nuisance.
Summary
This is far from the best Final Fantasy, and misses the mark on battle system design and storytelling. At best it's an average-ish RPG with a trippy story, some awesome music and inspiring artwork. Still there is something sort of intangibly alluring about playing this game. I must admit I've replayed this trainwreck at least 3 times now.

The biggest plus from this game is the art, both quality and quantity wise. The main cast has a wide range of poses which is quite impressive considering the detail of each sprite, and even the less important characters who weren't even named got a sprite while they would be corporeal voices in other VN. Some tips for new people never playing this:
-DO NOT grind levels. Wait until disk 3 when you get cactuar because you can junction +Hp bonus, +Str bonus, +Vit bonus, and +Spr bonus on *level up*. If you wait you can get 255 all stats (max).
-Coming from above, do not level until disk 3!! Use guides to find the best magic to junction. For example, stick the spell life or full-life until health to hit 9999.
-Do not sell anything. Abilities from GF's can break items down into magic. You get payed anyay from walking around.
- Stuck? Enter a boss battle with yellow health on squall or zell and their limit break is the best in the game. With squall's lion heart you can almost anything.
-You can't rush this game. Just sit back and enjoy the show!
