I used to absolutely love this game. The game is fun, and is much like
(only at the time, there were no 3D
games which made this unique at the time), only with pigs and some hysterical yet hilariously crude voice acting from Rik Mayall (RIP). I've had it for both PS1 and PC before, and it is a childhood favourite.
So why don't I recommend the game? To look at, the PC one is much nicer than the PS1 version, with the graphics being smoother and, unlike the PS1 version, where multiple of the heavy weapons (bazooka, mortar etc) had the same white, cannon-like model, all of the weapons have their own unique model that matches their menu icon. Despite this, the PC version has multiple quite drastic flaws which sadly make the game unplayable on PC.
-The AI is as thick as pig♥♥♥♥♥♥ On the PS1 version, they would move to tactical points and make intelligent decisions, especially in later levels. However, on the PC one, unless they jetpack to a weapon crate, they rarely move, if they do at all. I've been able to trick the AI into killing via friendly fire before by standing parallel to two of them. He tried to shoot me with a sniper rifle and killed his team mate instead.
-From what I remember, the music is bugged. Memories of playing this on the PS1 remind me of how good the soundtrack actually is for this game, but from what I remember of playing it on my PC many moons ago, the music often didn't play when it should do, and at times, the wrong music would play. Whilst this might not be the biggest issue, it is still very annoying.
-Most importantly of all, if you have Windows 8 or higher, the game is unplayable, full stop. From what I have read, this is down to the development team no longer having the source code for the game, and thus would have to remake the game from scratch to make it playable for Windows 8 onwards. Seeing as most computers that are used for games now have Windows 8 or higher, this is a major issue.
Don't get me wrong.
is a fantasic game, but only on the PS1. If you are able to get a copy of the old PS1 version and still have a PS1 or a PS2 to play it on, I highly recommend it. As far as buying the PC version through Steam though? I wouldn't bother, which is a true shame, as I absolutely adore this game.

Tap Heroes is a clicker based as the name implies. As per usual you start of quite weak, lacking buffs/powers and have to invest coins into becoming "Stronger". I think that this game would feel quite at home on a touch screen device or mobile phone as something to kill time on a bus or at lunch.
You can improve your own clicking abilities or choose to improve your heroes. This gives the game light RPG elements where you can improve the heroes Attack, HP, Speed, Crit. Otherwise your own clicker attack,healing and crit can be improved which is all typical for a clicker game. The game has "stages" and bosses on the 10th stages (10,20,30 etc). You could compare this system to Sakura Clicker in terms of how the enemies and bosses appear.
As you progress you will encounter a new currency "Gems". These are blue currecy which can be used to purachse new types of heroes (mage who heals automatically, rogue who ranges and poisions mobs). These new heroes can also be upgraded simialr to your main hero. You can improve your heroes with Gems by 25% in different stats depending on the hero which is very cruicial to maximise damage. Gems can be used to buy temporary buffs which include attack increase and drop increase and many others.
Dying means you lose all your held coins so making sure you are AFKing mobs that do not kill you is cruial. This means that not clicking slows down the coin process by A VERY LARGE AMOUNT. In 4 hours of afking this game I only managed to get to the boss on stage 40 which is I believe still quite early in the game. Music wise and sound wise I instictivly muted them as my experience with clickers most of the sounds are way too repetitive.
The pixel style looks nice but on large pc monitors in fullscreen it can be quite an eyesore. Definately worth running in windowed mode so you can afk this while doing homework or playing another game stopping to buff your heroes sometimes. I prefer the medieval and RPG theme in this game over the cutesy Plantera.
Overall for a game that does not have any hidden DLC (as most mobile games have) for $2.99 you get a lite RPG experience with fairly nice pixel graphics. As far as clicker games go you'll be stuck in this one for quite ahwile before you get to the "end game" I feel. If you enjoy clicker style mobile games this should tickle your itch for them 7/10.

The Binding of Isaac is a satisfying, simple rogue-like game with a Legend of Zelda dungeon feel to it. You explore a map room-by-room fighting off the various creatures that you find within to progress onwards towards a boss, usually collecting an item or two along the way to upgrade Isaac or to use in combat, and then after defeating said boss make your way to the next floor. This sounds a bit droll, but that's because that's only the core of the gameplay in a broad stroke.
The game itself has a story that I won't go into (mostly because it's so simple you'll only feel like worrying about it during cut-scenes) and an overall feel to it that's somewhere between hilarious and horrific (in a hilarious way.) The enemy design is like something out of a child's nightmare (monsters that have bloated heads and cough up evil flies, headless bodies that stumble around spouting blood, floating babies that screech and shoot stuff at you) and the items are either common household objects with a dark humor to their use (EPECAC makes you 'vomit' an explosive ball, Mom's Pad is an activatable item that makes all enemies back away for a short period of time) or items which would come off as 'horrific' in reality but are somewhat hilarious (Max's Head is a severed dog's head that makes Isaac's eyes grow larger and the tears he shoots as a weapon be larger and hit harder) when rertieved. The bosses are interesting and grow in challenge as you go, and the game has a variety of extra rooms and secrets to keep you exploring dungeons even when you may want to make a b-line to the end.
The game's replay value is massive; unlockable items, characters, floors and endings makes you want to repeatedly go through the experience no matter how often you may die, and while it sometimes all revolves around how lucky you are with your items it has enough skill-base in the play to keep you trying harder and harder.
Overall I'd say that Binding of Isaac is the best rogue-like indie game I've ever played. I've spent hours on it and haven't beaten the final level still, but I pick it up every so often once more and see how far I can dig in. Definitely worth having in your library.

FInished the game 5 minutes ago, tears still on my face, 10/10
In all seriousness, this is the most beautiful game I've ever played, the fact that it was for the most part made by one person just makes it better as well. knowing that the world you play in was drawn by the same person who coded the game just sets it apart form anything I've ever played, most games have so many people working on them and thus the original idea for the game is for the most part lost, but Dust: An Elysian Tail is the product of just one person's imagniation, and a very talented person at that. Getting it for $3 felt like stealing if I'm going to be honest.
World:
The game has a variety of Different enviroments and areas to play in, all carefully painted and seamlessly put into a playable game world. Each area has a different atmosphere, the forests feel beautiful and peaceful, mountains feel like a winter wonderland, and the lava area feels like the end of the world. while areas can be repetitive, they don't make you feel any less immersed in the world. I actually felt like I was in an endless pit when I was exploring the caverns below the village, and felt like I was in a deserted infected wasteland when I was in the sorrowing meadow. sometimes I just have to stop and look around at the drawn world around me and take in the beauty and effort that went into it.
9/10
Characters:
All the characters are perfectly designed, you won't find two similar characters in this game. You have Dust, a, initially clueless warrior who must rediscover his past. Fidget, a cheerful and happy companion who has very cute voice lines and comments. and you have Ahrah, a talking sword who guides Dust and Fidget through their journey. these are the main characters, and they fit together perfectly in the story. There are many other characters with their own personalities like Ginger, who has a gloomy feeling through the game (you'll have to play to find out why). none of the characters feel repetitive and boring, and if there is a character you don't like, you're probably intended to not like them. all in all, each character feels unique and thought out. The game shows emotion in it's characters so much that I cried twice during the story, and I've never cried over a movie or video game before. not afraid to admit it either. There's also some amazing art of the world and characters that fans have drawn. just turn on google safe search, wouldn't want to get yiff'd, would you?
10/10
Combat:
(I was playing on tough difficulty)
Combat in the game is awesome, (though a bit easy to be honest). you feel like a badass flying through the sky pulling off 500 or 998 hit combos (I only needed 2 more ; __ ;) and trying to keep every enemy stunlocked while in the air feels rewarding. I'm more experienced in third and first person shooters, so I don't have much to say about the game's combat. While it did feel easy, the consequences of getting hit (when you actually do) are huge, having half your health for the next 5 or 6 fights with no health items can put you on the edge.The only thing I'd change about the fighting would be to put more health regen and making every fight start with full health, but in turn make every fight much much harder. it seemed to me that I was still felling the effects of getting hit once or twice a few fights back, even as I progressed forwards and I often felt "screwed' in a sense. 1 health, 0 comsumables and still a ways to go (this does make me feel genuine adrenaline whien I'm surrouded with that one health, a huge plus). The combat felt very good even when a ton was happening on the screen, enemies stunned in the air, fidget projectiles everywhere, dust flying through the air and the game still ran smoothly.
8/10
Muisc / sound / voice acting:
I booted up the game and had no info on the characters, story, world or any aspect of the game, and the main menu music still had me feeling moody already. I was interested in the game's characters and story before it even started. the world music is also amazing, they really set the stage for the game extremenly well. the one thing I hate about some games is how the music tries to force emotion, but in this game the music goes with it instead. the gorgeous art and the stuning sound went perfectly together and created a world anyone can be immersed in, the soundtrack is probably the only music from any game I'd listen to outside that game, and the emotions I felt while playing the game are already associated with the music in my mind, making the tracks sound that much better. whenever something sad happened in the game, the piano always made me want to tear up, and I did twice. The sound effects are amazing as well, my sword felt heavy while swinging it through the air, deep whoosh sounds and high pitched wind sounds went together perfectly, and pulling off 200 hits in a few seconds also sounded amazing and satisfying. the deep bass sweeps when hitting an explosive wall or parrying an attack also sounded great on my subwoofers, and it added a bit of unique sound needed amongst the mess of sword strikes and explosions. The voice acting was also amazing, a bit exaggerated at times but where emotion was needed, it was delivered. little to none of the voice acting felt fake or pushed, and each character sounded different, adding to their personality. my favorite voice had to be dust's, he was able to sound relaxed, serious, and devastated at different times through the story. amazing work here
10/10
Story:
The story is fairly simple, a warrior dressed in cyan wakes up in the middle of a forest with no memory of who he is and travels with a foxy companion to discover his past and save the world (TwoKinds anyone?). The story was good, but the characters are really where the game stands out. That's not to say the game's story is bad, but the other aspects of the game hold it to such a high standard that I'll probably remember the world and the characters more than the storyline itself. though the story does take an interesting twist later on. not much here, don't want to spoil
8/10
Animation:
Diolouge Animation -
The talking animation takes a style I have't seen in too many games before, the characters in dialougue scenes look like images being subtly scaled up and down, It's not a bad thing but It is very simple.
8/10
Combat Animation -
The combat animation was awesome to me, I play my games at 60 fps but I had no problem in combat where the animations for dust only play at 24 or so fps. The reason being each frame in the animation is a drawing, a piece of art that I can look at. every once in a while when the combat gets easy I start focusing on Dust and I notice amazingly drawn frames of him, even in the heat of battle.
9/10
Cutscene animation:
No spoilers, but there are two Anime style cutscenes in the game, and they blew my mind. they took the focus away from the combat for a moment and focused on the art of the characters, and the story of the game, and they could not have been placed in at better times. I won't spoil anything but they take place at perhaps the two most cruical parts of the story. I know it probably won't happen, but an anime of this game would be amazing, if it were done in the style of the cutscenes already in the game. one of my favorite parts of the game here
10/10
Glitches:
My game only crashed once. Other than that the game ran perfectly even in the heat of battle with many projectiles and things flying everywhere. The closest thing to a glitch I could find was animation cancelling duck attacks and being able to chain them together as fast as you could click, but it left your back open and wasn't viable in higher level combat. There was also a glitch which made fidget 5 times her size, which was hilarious, but it reverted when I went to a new area.
9/10, nothing problematic here.
Overall 10/10, amazing game that I would reccomend to anyone, even if the furry art style is a turn off for you

After playing this game for a good amount of time and pursuing to beat it on Hard, I've noticed this game isn't the failure that most people deem it to be. In order to play this game, there must be a basic understanding of proper guerilla warfare, and knowing this is VERY useful. This game is not for everyone however. This game is a test of skill for those who are familiar with the Men of War series and its mechanics.
A few thoughts after in-depth play (Post Scriptum Edition):
First of all, if you can earn every achievement without cheating, kudos to you. It is not an easy task to earn all of these achievements, because the final US Mission can be quite intimidating on Hard difficulty.
Second, a quick reading of Sun Tzu's Art of War would be useful. You'll know what part I'm referring to if you do read it.
Third, the game is not broken. I've played it with no issue, so it seems the problem is originating from the user. Sorry, but that's the case. It certainly is not your average Men of War game, so I can understand why people would say this. Compared to Men of War: Condemned Heroes, which is coined as being another 'impossibly difficult' entry in the series, this game is flawless. I think the struggle players encountered with this game is symbolic. The United States certainly did struggle in Vietnam. Everything was about winning through attrition... the player has to win a mission of attrition as well because of how long a single mission can take without losing a single squad member. This was probably not intentional on the developer's part, but still an interesting characteristic.
Men of War: Vietnam offers a unique experience that is not for everyone. If you are new to the series, please take care to avoid this game. This was my first game I bought in the Men of War series, and it was a bitter mistake at first, because most of my time was spent figuring out how to play the game. Definitely don't want to do that here.

Is it scary? No. Is it creepy? Kinda. Is the shooting fun?
I don't know what it is about the shooting, but it just feels so visceral. Especially during bullet-time, every shot has weight. The guns are loud and impactful- something I feel is missing from lot of games these days. The enemies flinch and react to your shooting, and they don't just slump over dead- they die screaming, exploding, firing off a last gasp of bullets in their death-throes. It's not a wacky-fun ride like Bulletstorm tries to be, but the shooting has enough of an impact to keep the game fun.
The level design deserves a special mention. It's nothing beautiful, but it's very open ended. There are multiple paths and hidden secrets filled with goodies for the scavenging. It rewards exploration. This allows allows enemies to be very, very smart.
I don't know why, but the AI in this game feels fantastic. They actually work together as a team, having some units flush you out with grenades while others wait for you to react, or have a single individual rush your position, forcing you to move. They often try to flank you by going around the non-linear paths, and have a good bit of variety to them.
If you want a horror game, don't buy this one. It's not horror. It's a shooter that sometimes puts on a haloween mask and goes "boo." If you want an unapologetic shooter filled with violence and hard, satisfying guns, pick this one up.
(Also there's a generic framerate issue you can fix by disabling all HID-compliant devices in your device manager. It's an issue with logitech.)

For the record, this is my first time playing/sitting through a story game like this. I do enjoy a wide variety of game types, and have far more hours of game time in general than I'll ever admit to my wife (most of it pre-dating Steam). So, since I cannot review this game against its genre, I'll review it for the experience overall.
The long and the short, I'd give it a 3/5, considering that it is a first release and a trial run for the developer.
I won't lay out any spoilers about the story itself, but I will talk a bit about the game content. If you want to be fully surprised by what's to come in this story, stop reading now, go play first, then come back.
- 3/5
The story itself was interesting. There was nothing very original in the concepts laid out, but it was still a fun read. In this Part One, as the developer already told us in the release video, we only get a taste for what is to come. It could have used an editor with strong written English skills to fix the punctuation and grammar in several places, but there is nothing so broken as to be unreadable or not understood.
- 5/5
The character and background artwork are both wonderfully done. I'm not sure what more I can say about that, I really enjoyed them!
- 4/5
I think there were three tracks throughout the whole: a common background, a battle track, and a suspenseful track for the cliffhanger. For the length of the overall story I thought this played out nicely. The only thing I didn't care for was the transition between. It was fairly jarring to me moving from the common track to either of the others. The suspenseful track could have been a bit longer. I read at the pace of the text cursor for the most part, and the track had just turned its first loop as I was finishing up reading the last bit of text. If it lasted five to ten seconds longer it would have lined up with the text. A small thing, but it did jump out at me.
- 2/5
The mechanics are very limited. Having only played through once I honestly don't know what function they served. I will play through at least once more choosing different options to see how it changes the story, if at all. Since the developer said this is only a taste of what's to come I'm currently chalking this up to "future use", where the choices you make now will impact the story later down the road (thinking Chrono Trigger trial). Also, having the effect of the choice listed right there on the choice seems odd. Again though I'm new to this genre, maybe that's a norm? The only thing I can compare to is the same mechanic employed in some D&D RPGs, where the choice affects your alignment and NPC response, and part of the game is figuring out which choices to make when. Anyway, starting to ramble... In summary, I found the single limited mechanic to be unnecessary.
- 2/5
Very little in the way of configuration. All forms and dialogs had default icons, and dialogs felt "out of the box", not skinned/incorporated. Very rough/alpha feel, but again I think that's what this was intended to be in the developer's grand scheme. First release, feeling out their future a bit. Would still be nice to see some cleanup in a patch. For a story game I would expect immersion is key from start to finish, so incorporating all of the small elements is mundane, but would make a significant difference. Also, should go for a widescreen aspect ratio, not square. I say this again for the same of immersion. If I can't fill up my screen I'm being distracted by what else is going on.
I hope that was useful to you. I think this was my first review on Steam as well, so if you've time/inclination please give me feedback on the review.

TLDR:
This is an OK game/visual novel about a group of individuals with some goal (it isn\'t too clear) after a war that happened 600 or so years prior. It involves runes and stuff of the sort. To my knowledge, it has some choice but I don\'t think it has much of an outcome on the story as of now. It\'s free and doesn\'t take long to read, so it isn\'t like you are wasting several hours on a half-decent story. The art design is pretty good and the music is repetitive. No settings can be changed. Overal score: 6.5/10
Pros:
+Free
+Only takes ~30 to 40 minutes to read (I dunno, I was writing this review while reading it.)
+Great art style
+Pokes fun at itself (i.e. explains a character even though he was called an \"insignificant bookworm\". The game then says that it\'s just \"setting up the stage\". Two of the characters are narrators, so they have an excuse to break the fourth wall.)
+Fairly detailed
+Credits actually look kinda cool
Neutral:
=Some choice- however it is obvious which one is the better because it either has not effect, a +1, or a -1 right next to the option.
=Mediocre soundtrack- its just the same few chords being looped.
=Some terms may be difficult for younger audiences to understand.
=The story is okay, but it doesn\'t really resonate.
=The story explains circumstances at awkward times.
=There are times when it seems like a choice should be made but no option appears. However, in other times a choice can be made that doesn\'t really need to be there.
=Convenient changes in plot are convenient. Characters conviently claim nothing is wrong while others conveniently say that something is wrong. The story conveniently ends on a plot twist.
Cons:
-No way to change settings- so you are locked in a window with music that you can\'t really adjust. However, the window can be changed size by dragging the corners, but if not done correctly, the images will be stretched awkwardly.
-People have rectangular monitors. Don\'t use square images and a square window when making a game.
-Dialog is iffy- it isn\'t the most believable but I guess it sort of fits the \"time frame\" or \"style\" that the developers were going for.
-Displays the actions for the characters as -(action)-. For example, it would appear as -Clears his throat-. It may get meshed together with what they are saying and it may become confusing.
-If you missed some text, it is impossible to go back to it if you did not save beforehand.
-Once you start skipping text, stopping it is a bit buggy. I misclicked it in the settings menu and ended up missing out potential key parts of the story.

I'm horrible at writing reviews but here we go..
Short Version: That online hunger games simulator site on crack. It's like insane how much better this is but it goes around the same concept with many more characters, a steam workshop built in, and its just really great. I'd recommend. Hopefully more updates come out to add even more.
Longerish:
Ultimate Arena (Written as of 2.0) is a game where you can create or download (From the workshop) a bunch of characters, and watch them fight to the death Hunger-Games style. What sets this apart from the Hunger-Games simulator site is the extended roster (As far as I can know theres no limit to how many characters you can have in storage) and the extended amount of fighters fighting (250 is currently the limit.)*, as well as all the easy customization in Map and Events. Events being much easier to make in this, but slightly less customizable as of writing this.
Interactive Gameplay:
Slightly interactable to make it even better, where you can set off events in a size you want, and can place care packages and mines... You can also move characters, cause them to spontaneously die, feed them to cheat that one character, and degroup them.
Other Gameplay:
So aside from that the fighters go on their own, you can slow down the speed to read all the updates of what happens (but note that as of writing this you can't make custom updates unfortunately), and you can watch in amazement as they fight and blow up from mines constantly. That is it. While it may sound boring, its actually really amazing and can even be hilarious if you add characters you have an attachment to, such as characters from shows, animes, or real life. Plus they make little teams and its fun to see Hitler team up with Trump or Hillary. Or all 3.
Customization:
As I've stated, the customizable parts are the Maps, events, and characters. The character creator gives you a (Slightly bugged: i.e the tags crash you instantly) cool customizer for characters that lets you put different stats for them, a colour icon, and etc. For the map editor you can.. Make maps. Not much to go into detail there, my one thought on it is the brush isn't as good as it needs to be, but that isnt really much of an issue. The event editor lets you create simple events, but is very limited. That aside it really does put customization into what happens during the matches.
Overall:
I'd recommend this for people that like the Hunger-Games simulator, or just like some ultimate brawl arena type thing where they can watch a bunch of people fight. While it's one of my favorite finds on steam so far I do think that one of the best things that could happen to this game is some extra updates for customization. Other than that though I'd definitely say this is a step up from the Hunger-Games simulator, so I recommend this to people that would like that sort of thing.
TLDR;
Harambe killed trump in this game for me once.
*In my original review I wrote 100 is the limit... At the time, it was 100. This was updated about 3-4 hours after I wrote the review to 250. Great timing there. Much better limit.

Little Inferno is a game developed and published by Tomorrow Corporation, the same people behind 2D BOY who created World of Goo
Little Inferno is a very strange game. Upon startup, the game immediately presents nothing but a fireplace, and tasks players with simply burning the few letters they have with them. Immediately afterward, a catalog is sent, and the rest of the game is spent purchasing items and setting them aflame, watching the strange animations each item has
The humorous thing about this game, though, is that it WANTS you to feel that way. In fact, it encourages it by making you wait long, painful periods of time for your new kindling to arrive. And yet, for whatever reason, I found myself enjoying the experience
It was strangely appealing, setting things ablaze, and I wanted to see what would come of my neighbor, who continuously sent me letters
In the end, the game throws a massive twist on you. This isn't a criticism to Little Inferno; rather, this is the highest praise the game could achieve, because it is exactly what the developers sought to accomplish
Little Inferno is a remarkable work of satire, I truly believe this game will be remembered for all time as one of the most humorously self-aware experiences this medium has ever created!

Review for Stellaris, Update 1.1 "Clarke", Single-Player only, 160hrs, 4 games played
[TL; DR;] In it's current state, I sadly cannot recommend it.
[Full opinion]
This should have been an early access game. It was apparently rushed and suffers for it during mid- and especially late-game.
The early game is wonderful. It's fun, the UI feels great and you get that wonderful sense of discovery. There is something new around every corner. The multi-tiered events are a great idea and are a lot of fun.
Unfortunately all of this breaks apart during mid-game. At that point you have probably outsourced a lot of your planets into sectors. But you still have to micro-manage some of the game's aspects, like terraforming and colonization.
The game, however, does not give you enough information. There is no list of ALL planets (just those you colonized) so if you want to colonize a new planet you start searching the galaxy map manually! It's atrocious.
There is no list of bases around planets, you have to zoom-in to the system and look for yourself. This is fine if you only have like 3 star systems. But once you expand your territory you will start to hate the UI.
Why can't I change settings on an Observation Post inside a sector? The sector AI does nothing with it but if you want to change your policy you have to remove the system (which costs you Influence, a rare and precious resource), change the setting and then reassign the system again. Why?? Did nobody play-test this? This is stupid as hell and so unnecessary!
There are not enough options to filter the messages you are getting, so you get flooded in stuff you have no interest in. The important bits don't stick out and you click them away by mistake. Of course there is no list of previous messages. So it's gone forever. A new planet got terraformed? Well, good look searching the galaxy map for this one planet.
And while we are at the topic of messages: why do they zoom in to the star system?? They should open the planet/station window since 95% of the time this is where you want to go. But no, it zooms you in, you click on the planet, manage it, zoom out. And you do this for every message. Zoom-in, zoom-out, zoom-in, zoom-out, zoom-in, zoom-out.... :(
Instead they should open the planet window which would greatly improve the flow of the game. And if you really have to zoom in, there is a button on the planet page just for that.
Put in summary: the UI is designed to work in the early game but is woefully underdeveloped later in the game. You have no overview what's happening and no efficient way to manage a sprawling emipre.
Add to this several bugs and performance problems and the game literally falls apart in mid-game.
This game needs a lot of love from the developers still. And I hope it will receive it.
Right now the game feels incomplete and unpolished. It feels rushed and released prematurely.
Which is a shame because I can see huge potential here.
Paradox, keep working at it. Gamers, wait for those problems to be fixed.
Oh, and what the hell is this policy that I cannot even LOOK at the support forums if I am not registered and logged in? This is painfully anti-consumer and quite unacceptable. So people are having problems with your product and you make them register just so they can inform themselves about the state of potential patches?? D*ck move... :(

When I saw Tap Heroes being offered for sale, I was swept up in the clicker-game craze that the Summer Sale 2015 brought to Steam. Adventure Capitalist and Clicker Heroes were games that I played daily, so I decided that spending a small amount of money (I think I paid $.99) for another clicker title would be alright.
So what is it?
--------------
Tap Heroes is a clicker game where you click on a monster to damage it, kill it, and get loot from it. You then use this money to upgrade yourself or your party of 3 adventurers so you can click on a monster to damage it, kill it, and get more loot from it more efficiently. Rinse and repeat ad nauseum.
The game is pretty colorful, the characters are nicely drawn, there's a decent amount of enemies to kill, and there are a ton of levels to go through with one stipulation: Once you beat level 100, the game starts over at level 101 and there's nothing new other than an increased difficulty. If you play past this point, the only thing left is to chase achievements.
Is there anything good about this game?
------------------------------------------
Yep. It's a pretty decent time waster that you can open daily do a few things, and close again without worrying too much about it. Your characters will continue to earn gold even when the game is off. You can also have the game idle in the background while you play something else if you're wanting to burn through a couple of levels in the game.
As stated before, the graphics are nice, the interface is easy to use, and because the game comes with an upfront purchase price, there's no in-game microtransaction store begging you to purchase real-money currency to help you speed through the game. Tap Heroes knows what it is, and it does it pretty well.
Is there anything bad about this game?
-----------------------------------------
Yep. Once you make it past the initial first 100 levels, you've seen everything the game has to offer other than an increase in difficulty. Once you push past level 300, there're no more achievements for getting any higher unless you set a personal goal for yourself.
The music is alright to begin with, but it quickly gets old after a few levels because it's the only music track in the game.
The game is also very minimalistic compared to other clicker titles. There are no special gimmicks, no hard resets that boost your powers, just pumping money into making your heroes stronger over and over and over. It's a game that's easy to get bored with.
Let's talk about the achievements.
--------------------------------------------------
The game comes with 50 of them, and you'll earn most of them over the course of just playing the game. There are a few, however, that will require a substantial amount of effort to attain, one of which I'm still working on after pumping over 200 hours into it (Kill a million monsters). To 100% this game in any reasonable amount of time, you're going to have to simply leave the game running in the background night and day for weeks. You'll also probably want to get a free auto-clicker program at some point. Another achievement, Click 250,000 times, is going to kill your mouse, your wrist, or both.
Despite a couple of ridiculous achievements, getting most of the achievements will give you a sense of "Hey, I've completed this game and squeezed every bit of substance I can out of it", which is what any set of achievements should set out to do.
So, overall, do I recommend Tap Heroes?
-------------------------------------------
For the most part, I'd say yes, but only if you're going to pick it up when it's discounted. It's fun for a time, and I've definitely gotten more out of it than the initial dollar I spent on it, but it'll quickly wear on you if you try to play it for extended periods of time. It's simple and minimalistic, and that's probably a good thing for some, but I know myself and others who have had experience with other clicker titles were left wanting a little more variety and options. At this point, I'm only playing the game to 100% it and then I'll probably never open the application again.
I wish I could choose something in-between the yes and no recommendations, because that's where the game falls. It's not great, but it's not terrible either.

This is a game about being an IT development company. It isn't about making games, it's about making the components used to power the internet. And it is a GOOD one. It is extremely accurate, well designed, expertly executed, and far from boring. I have at this writing over 20 hours offline playing. It is a clickfest BUT you need to hire the entire spectrum of employees as your company grows. Designed by one person it is amazing and intense. HUGE fun if you are a simulation geek like I am. And if you came from the industry, you'll find the game to be an accurate representation of what your life was like making digital components for the biggest, cheapest companies in the world.

Review (22-Dec-2015):
This is a clicker, but not a normal F2P clicker like all the others on Steam. This one costs EUR 2.99/USD 2.99 (luckily I got it in a bundle). On top of that, it has some basic achievements that are easy to get and level 300 is pretty easy to get to. After that starts the boring grind to finish the worst achievement grind ever. Ofcourse the insults to any gamer with a basic sense of real life: the dumb "MASTER TAPPER", 1 handed applause please for clicking 250.000 times. Then there's "KNIGHT" (defeat 100000 enemies), "MASTER" (level up 5000 times) and "TAP HERO" (defeat a staggering 1000000 enemies). Now these last 3 would be ok, if the off-line grinding would be at the same rate as the on-line grinding but alas. There is hardly if at all any off-line grinding. So to gather any gold to get the MASTER achievement you need to run the game long enough to level up 5000 times in total, and to defeat 1.000.000 enemies (to get both KNIGHT and TAP HERO, you better be prepared to keep that power bill, oops, PC running for a few nights so your final 3 achievements will net you a clean 100%. Well done, dev.
Update to review (25-Dec-2015 @ 21:22): I've now been running my PC 24 hours constantly and this game for 2 days straight and it's gone from hitting the 100.000 enemies mark at 24 Dec @ 16:35 to roughly 246k enemies killed. At this rate I expect to keep my PC running for a rough estimate of another 6 days. This game should be called PSU killer.
Final update to review (31-Dec-2015): I just checked, I hit TAP HERO, the 1.000.000 enemies, also known as the ultimate noob achievement at the 30th of December 2015 at 22:53 after having ran my PC continually on this game. Yes, that's right 24hours/6 days straight for a single achievement. I have the bloody troll of all troll achievements.

Picture this, the weekend spent in your parents basement, donning a cape made out of old teeshirts, wearing a hat made of tinfoil, and holding in your hand a 8 inch stick you found in the back yard..  huddled around a table with 5 of your closest friends.  Teenage angst in your eyes as you reach forward to grab a set of dice and hope that you roll high enough to stop the least liked kid in your group... Jimbo.. dressed up in his high priced ogre costume.  You let the dice fly and.... ahh fiddle sticks.. he got the best of you this time..
I can still remember my days playing Dungeons and Dragons, my many days picking up rpg's of days gone past, the Final Fantasies, the Breath of Fires... Dragon Warriors.. well this game is nothing like them, in fact the only thing it has in common with those games or a fun game are the main characters..  Warrior, mage and Thief..
What can be said about Tap Heroes... well the first thing that comes to mind is this game can be found elsewhere for free.  The idea behind the game has been done to death lately, the only difference between this game and those games are.. this game will cost you 3 dollars, while the other games like Clickr Heroes are absolutely free to play.
So surely for paying money you get a more well thought out and polished game?  To answer that question is NO!  Tap Heroes manages to offer less content than you'd get in one for the F2P idling games on steam.  While the other game gives numerous heroes or characters to buy, this game offers you a very generic three characters..  The Warrior, The Mage and the Thief, sure they are the cornerstone of any RPG, this game isn't an RPG it's an Idle game.
Everything about this game seems to pale in comparison to the free alternates out there... This game in a nutshell is this... buy upgrades, click on enemies for the first 10 levels, then never click again as your weak clicks don't even make the enemies break a sweat and the warrior is already doing 10 times your click damage by level 5.  This game lacks any bells and whistles, no skills for your characters..  you get 6 major spells which you the player can cast,, they are your run of the mill fair, more clicks per second, more gold, wash away an enemy, etc etc etc...  nothing special..
So with all this negative surely a game you pay for has some positives to it?  Well yes, Tap Heroes is set up like an old fashion puppet show you'd put on by cutting out some paper characters, pasting them to a Popsicle stick and set inside a cardboard box.  That alone is pretty unique, also the enemies aren't really as repetitive as the other clicker/idle games, I was surprised to see how many unique enemies the game actually had..  Last but certainly not least is the inclusion of trading cards..  All of which are unlocked for the low price of 3 dollars, unlike the 10 or more you'd need to spend on those other clicker/idle games for cards.
Is this game worth the money..  the honest answer is no, other free games do what this game does... only better.. The only way and I do mean only way I'd recommend this game is if you could get it for under .50 cent, this way you can sell the cards and the game will be free, like it should have been in the first place..

Creative writing is a pretty daunting activity to get into at first, since as the overused saying goes, the possibilities are endless. To see a game revolve around this is unique, but the execution is rather dull.
Walking simulators get a lot of flak for lacking gameplay, but I enjoy them because often a story is there in place of the interactabilty. This however lacks both: gameplay wise you are stuck holding D to your next destination, Tab to start writing and thats it. The story is as good as you can make it and that's where my gripe lies; the foundations given are so bland.
I only wrote one story, but checked out another story stucture to see what they are like and they are extremely generic. "There was once a world created by ___. It was ___. Suddenly, ___ happened. In the end the world was ___."
The concept of a game to enable people to start writing creatively through visual and auditory aids, offering a platform to compare and rate other peoples stories and have them do the same to yours is fantastic, but when the gameplay is so slow and the foundations are so boring it gives you little to no reason to not simply load up word and write freely.
I will add that visually the game looks great. The game uses shadows and colour really well to emphasise the tone of the world your on (however this does work against it since you're meant to be setting the tone...). The sound is also a strong point, but again, it seems to dictate the tone it wants you to write in.
Overall, I appreicate the effort but I don't see a reason to buy this at full price when you could just as easily submit your writings to forums and discuss them there.

I would like to give a positive review to this game, but I cannot. I got really frustrated playing it and gave up. Here is why:
1. The aim is done using an inclination angle. Yet, since ~1800 that people know how to convert an angle to a distance. I don't want to do that calculation on my own, and the game does not do this calculation for me (it recommends a crappy angle that anyone can do better after 1h of gameplay). Therefore, you have no way of mapping shoot inclnation to distance from target, which makes no sense.
2. The ships start too damm close from each other in the beginning. A Battleship e.g. can start at torpedo range from a destroyer, and puff, no longer a battleship on turn 0. This makes no sense. In the dynamic camping, a Battleship can also start a battle with a destroyer, and sink it because the destroyer is not able to flee (destroyers are supposed to sail ~2x faster than a BShip... except in this game where 2 destroyers accept engaging a battleship)
3. The bearing of previous shoots is not saved in the list of previous shoots (which is required for the lead when the wind affects shoots).
4. The bearing of the previous shoot is not "saved" in the gun for the next turn. Conclusion: you need to actually write it somewhere (for every ship in your fleet) in case you want to keep a constant lead on the target.
5. The map does not allow to measure distances (e.g. a compass?) I was actually using paper grid on the monitor to try to infer what was my previous distance from target, the new one, and see if other shoots were already made at this distance (because, from 1, you cannot convert distances to angles, you only have the previous shoots angles, nothing else). Nonsense.
6. The torpedos are extremely overpowered. Here, u-boats eat destroyers for breakfast, and destroyers sink u-boats with torpedos, not deepcharges. I has never able to use deepcharges because u-boat sinks the destroyer while I move torwards them. Often, in the same turn the torpedo is shoot, the torpedo reaches the destroyer (torpedos are 100% accurate). Historically torpedos require a minimal distance to avoid exploding on the u-boat immediately after launched, and that is a reason destroyers approached u-boats as fast as possible.
In summary, the developers made a huge effort to add very nice models of the ships, make the game pleasant to see, but neglected an important part of the game, the shooting. I got frustrated and uninstalled the game. :/

neat addictive, so far not too deep simulated, still not too abstract little WW2 naval action game.
It has enough simulation aspects and accurate details to satisfy history freaks. At the same time your degree of interacting is limited enough to keep it simple.
Combined with turn based gameplay, you get sucked in to enjoy that "one more turn" desire.
Basically you do 2 things. First move your vessel some distance, by adjusting rudder and speed settings. Thereafter you use the firepower by selecting a group of guns or torpedoes, adjust barrel elevation and/or direction to shoot, fire!
If you are interested in naval warfare, especially of WW2, if you are familiar with all the famous ships and classes of that time, you can enjoy pretty accurate and beautiful models of these in this game and even create customized matches.
There is also some fun with using aircraft carriers, aircraft attacks, Uboats, anti-sub-warfare and a few German Hilfskreuzer.
The simulation aspect is somewhat limited, still it is lots of fun even for simulation enthusiasts (which I also claim to be). So to be fair, I again have to say that mostly everything is heavily simplified. Yet the potential for further enhancement is visible all over the game.
The developers are very communicative and accessible in the steam forums. Currently they are getting shelled by tons of ideas and suggestions of the increasing player community.
The devs already hinted that they totally intent to enhance the gameplay (probably not with this game though, due to limitations in the coding) and if you read how they reply to many discussions in the forum, they are obviously not new to naval stuff therefore my hopes are high that they might produce some decent naval simulation sometime in the future.
The built in "Battle of the Atlantic" campaign mode offers a map of the Atlantic on which you can strategically put your available vessels on patrol. This reminds the veteran naval wargamer of the now vintage GNB series.
So this game could be the first step of a project leading to a modern GNB clone with all its former strategic gameplay aspects of managing a navy in WW2, adding tactical battles feauturing beautiful visualized ships.
This game is clearly worth a lot more than the 10 bucks I payed for it. Considering the little price tag, chances are high you won't regret a purchase, even if you are not that much into the genre.

First off, alittle about me is I love RTS games in general. Been playing them since I was about 6 years of age or less and they still have countless hours of my life dedicated to them. The company behind Stellaris has already a fantastic lineup of amazing games they have released over the years which are full proof amazing RTS's you cannot go without.
That being said, Stellaris is no exception. Most of the reviews on here seem bland as they talk about the lack of updates or things to do mid game, but with how many options there are in the game already people need to use their minds and just create their own events. Maybe enlighten a hostile proto race, get two people to go to war, create new races and different socioeconomic sectors etc etc. Just because the game doesn't have literal events later on does not mean it's not worth it. Name one RTS that literally has events the entire time that are unique and randomly generated that aren't super short games.
They even pledged to keep releasing updates to it over time for free instead of making people purchase for DLC and other stupid things that I think people are just too relaxed with. They are a godsend and this game has already taken a huge part of my day away from me each day and I don't regret it.
Specifically I like how this game is not just a Overcome and swallow game but more of a diplomacy and exploration/Overcome/Swallow game. It's all how someone plays it. Have not found too many scifi RTS games that focus on the bigger picture rather than just the combat aspect of space empires etc etc.

Review for Stellaris, Update 1.1 "Clarke", Single-Player only, 160hrs, 4 games played
[TL; DR;] In it's current state, I sadly cannot recommend it.
[Full opinion]
This should have been an early access game. It was apparently rushed and suffers for it during mid- and especially late-game.
The early game is wonderful. It's fun, the UI feels great and you get that wonderful sense of discovery. There is something new around every corner. The multi-tiered events are a great idea and are a lot of fun.
Unfortunately all of this breaks apart during mid-game. At that point you have probably outsourced a lot of your planets into sectors. But you still have to micro-manage some of the game's aspects, like terraforming and colonization.
The game, however, does not give you enough information. There is no list of ALL planets (just those you colonized) so if you want to colonize a new planet you start searching the galaxy map manually! It's atrocious.
There is no list of bases around planets, you have to zoom-in to the system and look for yourself. This is fine if you only have like 3 star systems. But once you expand your territory you will start to hate the UI.
Why can't I change settings on an Observation Post inside a sector? The sector AI does nothing with it but if you want to change your policy you have to remove the system (which costs you Influence, a rare and precious resource), change the setting and then reassign the system again. Why?? Did nobody play-test this? This is stupid as hell and so unnecessary!
There are not enough options to filter the messages you are getting, so you get flooded in stuff you have no interest in. The important bits don't stick out and you click them away by mistake. Of course there is no list of previous messages. So it's gone forever. A new planet got terraformed? Well, good look searching the galaxy map for this one planet.
And while we are at the topic of messages: why do they zoom in to the star system?? They should open the planet/station window since 95% of the time this is where you want to go. But no, it zooms you in, you click on the planet, manage it, zoom out. And you do this for every message. Zoom-in, zoom-out, zoom-in, zoom-out, zoom-in, zoom-out.... :(
Instead they should open the planet window which would greatly improve the flow of the game. And if you really have to zoom in, there is a button on the planet page just for that.
Put in summary: the UI is designed to work in the early game but is woefully underdeveloped later in the game. You have no overview what's happening and no efficient way to manage a sprawling emipre.
Add to this several bugs and performance problems and the game literally falls apart in mid-game.
This game needs a lot of love from the developers still. And I hope it will receive it.
Right now the game feels incomplete and unpolished. It feels rushed and released prematurely.
Which is a shame because I can see huge potential here.
Paradox, keep working at it. Gamers, wait for those problems to be fixed.
Oh, and what the hell is this policy that I cannot even LOOK at the support forums if I am not registered and logged in? This is painfully anti-consumer and quite unacceptable. So people are having problems with your product and you make them register just so they can inform themselves about the state of potential patches?? D*ck move... :(

The 1000 character word limit for each section of the prompt is a little limiting, but is also a good exercise in not being too verbose, and the ability to read and "commend" other user's work is a wonderful feedback tool (although there is no proofreading function whatsoever, aside from the aforementioned grammar workshop which I admit I did not use, so I don't know if that has an actual checker or not).   All in all it's a good tool to practice writing with.  Whether or not you think it's worth $15 is up to you, but I do urge you to not get it for less than $10 if/when it goes on sale.

This is the best WWII naval battle game so far: my path of great naval games has gone Dreadnoughts (on Amiga), Task Force 1942, Fighting Steel, and now Atlantic Fleet.  The ship models are realistic, though lacking individual differences between class members and rebuilds, eg all county class cruisers are Berwick style with cut down aft deck and large deck house rear superstructure, London included; all QE class are as QE, Warspite has no faceted bows and Malaya and Barham have been modernised, similarly Repulse looks like Renown, etc.  This would be nice to see, like the different placements of mainmast between Scharnhorst and Gneisenau.  But that is beside the point - this game is a delight!  It plays convincingly and really delivers some of the best battles I've played - looks splendid too.
What could be added - well, the extra models as I suggest, I would love a "ship editor" so I could "make or modify my own" - similarly a scenario editor.
I have tried to get merchantmen to ram subs, but perhaps this isn't allowed?
I would like more "bridge info" - compass heading, the bearings at the top of screen are always relative to the ship.
I would like to choose the order in which my ships move and act.
Perhaps the armour penetration values need tweaking to make sinkings more difficult (more realistic) - in real world, most naval engagements were lengthy and far fewer ships were sunk (or even hit) - but in Atlantic Fleet some heavy armour is penetrated too easily - I guess it is a balance to find between realism and gameplay needs.  Currently there are two difficulty settings - perhaps more settings for "easy" (lots of sinkings), "harder", "difficult". and "realistic" (for die-hard naval enthusiasts like me!) could be given?
How about a Jutland WWI game with this engine? - I would certainly buy it.  Armoured cruisers, protected cruisers, pre-dreadnoughts, battlecruisers (which really did blow up after a single salvo hit - at least British ones did), the emergeance of light cruiser and heavy, larger destroyers and the great dreadnought battlewagons
So how about French ships, Italian ships, Russian ships - this engine is worth it (we have Washington in the Atlantic, we should have New York too, and some US destroyers - Mediterranean campaign for both world wars (including Black Sea and Dardanelles?), and yes, integrate the Pacific in with it.
This calls out for a lot of expansion - because it is brilliant.  Buy it, play it, enjoy it - this is the game I have been waiting for at least 10 years - splendidly executed - well done.

If I could title this review I'd probably call it "Fish are Friends, not Food".
I'm just gonna come out and say it. Abzu (i can't type that umlaut thing it takes forever to grab the character and paste it in so forgive the bad formatting of the name please) is just Journey but underwater for 90% of the game. It even has some of the exact same (though obviously visually different) set-pieces. The game plays out almost the same themes as well.
This is in no way a bad thing though ,as Journey was an absolute masterpiece. This game is in the same way just as beautiful and breathtaking and pretty to look at. Maybe not quite as emotionally resonant for me, but I still adored all of the game.
It took me perhaps somewhat less than (or somewhat more) than two hours to complete it, but I didn't find all the secrets and hidden things obviously (pools to release creatures, meditation statues, and nautilus shells) despite my cursory but not undedicated efforts.
It's full of beautiful breathtaking little moments, it's a very chilled and relaxing game, its soundtrack is...a little on the dischordant side but still very beautiful, and the graphics are stunning.
I have some issues in that I couldn't seem to alter the controls at all and the right stick of my pad refused to stop being inverted, wheras my controls for the left stick (actually moving around) were uninverted, so it became something of a nightmare trying to angle the camera in the right direction, or swim in the right direction sometimes as the disconnect between the two control sticks orientation caused many mistakes. The options menu in game just didn't seem to work at all, possibly a glitch ,not sure what caused it.
It lacks any multiplayer functionality like Journey had, so you won't find other divers wandering around, but you aren't totally alone. The various sea creatures swimming about are interactable with in various ways. At one point a pod of dolphins was merrily swimming about an area, and I decided to see if I could leap out of the water with swimming and do like, a somersalt mid air before splashing down again. Turns out you can! ... also turns out the dolphins really like this and start to join in and swim with you and also do tricks like leap out of the water when you do as well.
Which, I mean, I dunno about you but I was absolutely overjoyed with!
The climax of the game is beautiful and a lot of fun and a great payoff after the previous level, and the game, like Journey, is an excellent example of Environmental Storytelling. You have no words or explainations, you must piece together events and the story from the murals you find dotted about between levels (which you seamlessly traverse between. Cutscenes are organically placed within the game and largely are very short and don't take away control for too long.
One of the later segments does have you walking about on dry land for brief periods, but it's quick to get you straight back into the water where you can have the most fun, whilst giving you an interesting quick look around the world outside of the water.
All of this combines into a short, but beautiful and wonderful game that you absolutely should play.

Little Inferno is a game about you burning things to stay warm in a frozen city. Everytime you burn something, you get coins. These coins allow you to buy things from the catalog. More things equals more burning which makes you more coin. There are seven catalogs to collect, which unlocks more things to burn. The catch is, you must unlock them by combining certain objects together. As you burn things, you get some nice letters from others around you, which you can burn as well. Some letters contains items. Some letters require you to give an item. This is all part of progressing the story.
This game is beautiful. The flames and how they move on objects are truly beautiful. Even some items can change the color and texture of the flames. Each item does a certain thing and each combination is amazing. Some are easy to understand and others make you think. I honestly love this game for the visuals and the humor it gives off. Not to mention it's functions.
Overall, this game is amazing and I recommend this to anyone who wants to waste time and/or is seeking a great story from a game.

"F.E.A.R."
A review by Richard Valkinsenn.
"What's the first thing you remember?"
F.E.A.R. is, hands-down, one of the best single-player action experiences out there. While the game's visuals have dated horrendously, it's overall gameplay has aged incredibly well.
There's a unique blend of action and horror on display in the game's narrative, balancing and often mixing both effectively and memorably. The game's action is brutal and relentless, though its frenetic, lengthy, and heavily stylized firefights are broken up by short breather sections in-between, so the action never feels tiring. It also strangely never becomes repetitive, even though you'll be seeing a lot of the same environments throughout the game.
Fear is the name of the game, both literally and figuratively, and the game features high amounts of genuine creepiness before, after, and even during it's insane action sequences. In fact, the game seems to pay homage to Japanese horror with it's atmosphere and it's chief antagonist resembling Samara from "The Ring." And thankfully, the game's creepiness relies more on the building of atmosphere instead of cheap "jump" scares, though, admittedly, whatever of these scares there are in the game are very well-timed.
Overall, F.E.A.R. boasts a unique blend of action and horror that combines seamlessly and effortlessly into one unique and memorable package that still delivers.
Final Verdict:
I (still) love it.

absurdism is difficult. that which is otherworldly, that which is abstract understanding, can only stem from relations of relations of corrupted understandings. people gravitate toward things far removed from understanding. people talk and caw about games having disparate worlds, but zeno clash is true. zeno clash features a world so far removed from anything in fiction or in living. its an absolute triumph of visual direction. zeno clash is a textbook on the deranged. with all of my praise though, it does remind one distinctly of oddworld. however, zeno clash’s world is much more lively - less barren to say - and there are many humans. though there are many other creatures as well.
whatever zeno clash ended up looking like, the base idea is something I would sell myself off for. I am incredibly glad this game exists. beat ‘em ups are eternal for me. what rings incredibly true for zeno clash is how traditional it is. you fight with two kinds of punches, light and heavy. a light punch can strike up to three times and can be comboed into a strong. strong punches are kind of like a wind up punch; space yourself away from your target and dash in with your fist. both are incredibly satisfying thanks to impeccable animation and hit detection. if an enemy becomes dazed, they can be thrown. and that’s basically it. the basic tendency calls back the roots of the beat ‘em up genre, a very comfortable thing for me, and a very different trace of influence for a modern game. especially considering the direction beat ‘em ups have taken with devil may cry, ninja gaiden, and god of war - although those are fantastic titles - it’s nice to see a game toning things back. except, I’d probably enjoy a hyper-complex combat system more, in all honesty.
if zeno clashed revolved around limited arena battles punching the trash out of fugly foes, and in saying that it does anyway, then it’d be a fantastic game that anyone looking for new ideas in their vidcons should play. it wouldn’t raise any intellectual hell, but exist as something more primal than serious sam, with an even goofier atmosphere. the boxing arenas are still totally worth it. but what was a successful formula gets bogged down by forced variance. ace team wasn’t content with the gold they struck - or maybe the gold was struck from altering their original first person shooter formula? either way, there are guns in the game. shoehorned guns. guns that are not fun to shoot or use. if they were options to use in the battle royals then they would be tarnishing, but forgivable. they are not. the gunplay is forced numerous times. thankfully they are not long, yet the damage is still felt. it’s not like anything is broken with the guns - it’s just they’re incredibly mediocre compared to your fists. the endworld is an exception to that with interesting and fun ranged combat. though pacing of using a magic wand leaves some to be desired and the enemies you fight are nothing more than zombies, it’s still darkly enchanting.
ranged weapons present one problem and melee weapons present another. melee weapons have a light swing and a heavy swing, much like your hands. once again, they function like they always have in the genre. they’re usually satisfying to use and offer a break from cracking skulls with your knuckles all day. the problem isn’t in the melee weapons, but when you’re given them. not too often can you use them against normal facepunchers. heavyweight enemies can only be damaged and toppled by heavy weapons and only the charge attack really does any damage. this leads to very mediocre and unsatisfying fights. there are no gambits allowed, no subcombos to pull off, no variety to speak of. you distance yourself, wind up attack, strafe, bash, retreat, repeat. and zeno clash will just throw these fatties at you as the game progresses. they’ll be one with small guys, one coming right after another, and at one point in the game two at a time. the two at a time encounter is pretty damn cool honestly. still, they are static and unfun encounters, and drag down what should be the pinnacle of the game.
if zeno clash had a more organic presentation it would be legendary. if you traversed large and odd levels, fisting waves of enemies, it would have ascended. even if it had rather linear levels with stop and fight sequences, it still would have delivered a wholly amazing game. instead you’re more often that not pitted in smallish arenas to fight your rounds. there are more traditional fps orientated levels to be found, but in those you do not punch, which is all the more confusing. levels are relegated to being plot excerpts filled with gameplay, instead of having the plot compliment the gameplay. its pacing is haphazard and disappointing. it wants to have this grand adventure and yet its levels are arcade in nature. not like double dragon arcade, but dig-dug. they’re just rounds. that feeling is even more horribly accented in the second half when you repeat most of the places you already walked through on your return trip home, just with harder enemies.
sheer repetition is zeno clash’s greatest flaw. guns are no different from eachother besides how many bullets sit in the chamber. melee weapons offer no variation aside from different looking skins. both guns and weapons have wonderful models, but that’s not the kind of variation I’m vying for. there are many different and awesome looking enemies. those many different awesome looking enemies will be fought two to even three times each. their names are the same, I guess they are the same people, but when you fight the same enemies in the same level as a few hours before it feels really freaking lazy. with the two bounty hunter confrontations, both very great despite relying on poor gunplay, it’s more than obvious that ace team really wanted variation in their game. so the design choices in the meat of their game sit in ugly defiance to their vision. a real frustrating execution overall.
writing is stilted. purposefully, the characters need to assume their roles as midsavages. there is a mighty depth and conviction to the script. made up words and made up accents. though, the voice acting does not match the quality of writing, and is rather poor. the story itself, framed as a mystery, compliments the game’s piecemeal length. when it’s all said and done though the plot is a bit flat. it’s not really about what ghat did so much as ghat dealing with why he did it. with the characters being in a generally unrelatable state of mind, the implications aren’t so interesting to learn about. what’s great about the script is the weird things, the corwids, father-mother’s society, the endworld, golem’s crypticness. these things really draw you in. it succeds in vision and skill of writing even if it does not have the running time to tell a deep story.
zeno clash is an addled burst of fraught strangeness smoothed with brand new gameplay. its short length makes it very easy to recommend, but it also is its greatest limiter with unrealized ideas all over the place. zeno clash is a small game and isn’t content with it. because of that, I’m not exactly content with it either.

It's a clicker game and it introduces a few new things. Each of the three heroes (that you need to unlock) has a different set of attributes and can vary your 'tactic' (I use the term in quotes because in the end it boils down to one factor to progress) by investing in certain attributes. The graphics have a nice cardboard/pixel look and the music is nice.
Is the game worth three bucks then? Not really. The initial variety stops pretty fast and you run out of new things to unlock (which is the whole point of a clicker game) quickly. There's also only one real factor to winning boss fights and that eliminates the possible different approaches to play the game. There are so many clicker games around and they bring a lot more to the table for free(...mium).
If you really like the graphics and don't mind a rather limited game experience (even for a clicker), wait for a sale or for it to show up in a bundle.

As a little boy whose parents and grandparents farmed, I grew up in the 1980s pushing little diecast Ertl tractors around on the carpet and making my own tractor sounds, pretending to be a farmer and working my own imaginary fields. Now that I'm an adult, I have enjoyed hours and hours of challenging farming satisfaction thanks to Farming Simulator 2013.
The Titanium add-ons have added literally hundreds of hours of fun trying out new equipment, and the Westbridge Hills map was a terrific purchase because it more closely resembles the area where my family farmed in Michigan.
I'm currently downloading FS 2015, and while doing so I thought I would put in a good word for FS 2013. Some people might not understand the appeal of a farm sim, but once you begin you're almost immediately hooked. I became bored with Facebook-based games like Farmville within minutes, but I was blown away by how engaging and realistic FS 2013 is, and having seen gameplay footage of FS 2015 I realize it was just the next step in the evolution of farming sims. You plant crops, care for animals and slowly amass a fortune as you build a business in a very realistic manner. I told my parents I started a game and had three tractors, $50,000 in the bank and $150,000 in debt and they said, "Well, that sounds like real farming!" The mowing missions give you a quick boost financially, for example you can earn $11,000 for mowing a patch of grass at the golf course. That's slightly unrealistic, but considering my mowing rig costs about $70,000 it's realistic in that you have to buy the equipment and then do the work until the gear "pays for itself."
Farming Simulator 2013 is seriously challening on the Hard difficulty level. Your crops are worth very little and money is much more difficult to come by. Even on easy mode where the cash flows a little more freely, I've wasted entire days trying to reach a certain dollar amount. There's always something to do, there's always something to buy. Every thing you want to do - i.e. raise cattle to sell milk daily -- requires specific equipment and the know-how to use it, sometimes trial and error -- and while the game cannot be absolutely true-to-life, I think it does a terrific job conveying the experience of trying to make a living as a farmer. You can even buy a few wind turbines and let the cash roll in as you amass a collection of classic tractors like a lot of the old-timers around here have been doing for the past several years. Likewise, you can invest in more land, more gear and more employees like a lot of the bigger family operations around here and turn yourself into a business-savvy Ag baron.
BOTTOM LINE: It's a big -- no gigantic -- sandbox full of almost every real life piece of gear you could hope to purchase from many notable brands -- except for John Deere, of course, which publishes its own game that I haven't played because it costs $80. Since I've begun playing FS 2013 I've noticed real farmers in my area using the same gear that I've purchased in the game and I admire the detail the designers put into each round baler and Case IH harvester. I get to play along without having the financial responsiblity of purchasing a $500,000 Grimme self-propelled sugar beet harvester. If you were a farm kid like me who went to college and found a career in the city, this game lets you experience what might have been had you chosen to try to turn the family farm into an Ag empire.
Highly, highly recommended. I have spent nearly 450 hours playing this game -- which is a little shocking -- and honestly, I still haven't planted every single field the game has to offer. Some gamers complain about minor imperfections, but I grew up playing an Atari 2600 and the original NES. This game is sweet!

The concept of Elegy For A Dead World is fantastic, but the execution leaves a bit to be desired. I found the writing prompts to be limiting and more akin to ad-libbing than truly creating my own stories. I highly commend the developers for their effort, though, as this serves as a sort of introduction to creative writing for many gamers who would otherwise not try their hand at writing fiction; it encourages players to use their imagination and share their work. The amount of content is lacking for a $15 game, though on sale or as part of a bundle, it's worth it for the unique experience, combining cosmic visuals and a great atmospheric ambient soundtrack with a focus on writing prose fiction.
My recommendation is a mixed one, as many will not like this - gamers may find it boring and too non-gamelike while writers may be disappointed in the manner in which it delivers prompts, only allowing you to fill in the blanks in set phrases instead of composing your own prose from scratch. Regardless, Elegy For A Dead World is interesting and inspired, breaking the mold of what's expected of videogames and encouraging creativity above all else.

Stay away from this game! It's not worth your money or your time.
.The main plot is a cheap copy of Naruto's but it lacks all the charm and makes no sense. It starts of as a variation of Masashi Kishimoto's first mangas (involving main events from the Chūnin Exams and the Sound Four) after what it devolves introducing a made up religious cult mixed up with Akatsuki's plans... Bottom line: the whole thing is a 10 chapter mess.
.The dialogues are so bad, full of clichés and swears, that you won't even want to read them. And what little you do read, is poorly written and you notice several mistakes.
.The combat system is terrible, there's no option to remember your last action and it feels clunky. Among other things, there's no way of knowing whose turn it is (you need to be aware of each members AGI but enemy turns are not displayed so you can't know who is going to attack when). Also enemy attack animations take forever (when there's no way of skipping them) which prolong the fights' length unnecessarily and you can easily skip your turns by mistake.
.Enemies are ALWAYS stronger than you and more numerous. Their defences are sky high and they deal a lot more damage and negative effects than you, so the only way to progress is using items in combat (which I hate).
To make things worse, the game forces you to play with different characters all the time (which you honestly don't care about) so you can't just focus on some of them because you'll have to fight with pretty much every character later on. This, in turn, forces you to invest more money in their gear and spend more time trying to beat the most bothersome parts of the game (specially chapter 8). And to top it all off, enemies will spawn at random (appart from the ones you can see and avoid) and the Flee option rarely succeeds so you are constantly saving your game to maintain your progress at the same time you try to figure out how to solve the puzzles so you can finally finish all those parts (you end up ignoring treasure chests entirely since most of them just contain more dreadful enemy encounters anyway).
There are two particular encounters that deserve a special consideration. In both of them you fight with the Beast mode active and all your attacks will deal exactly 1 point of damage to your enemies. The only way to beat the first of these encounters is causing the Burn state to your foe and pray not to receive too much damage so that you can heal yourself using items. The second ecounter is even better: the whole fight comes down to sheer luck. Your personal skill in both these fights won't have any impact and the only thing you can do is keep replaying them until you finally emerge victorious (fortunately the game allows you to repeat your latest encounter, otherwise it would be even worse).
.The character progression is awful. Enemies have auto-level and the skills you learn (when you level up) don't usually help because they barely cause any damage to your foes. As a result you end up using just a couple of spells and skills from each character. For example, from the 15+ skills Kitt can learn I ended up using only three or four, and the same happened with J.C., Maddie and Spark only it's worse in their case because you have both spells and skills. Alas, I only used two or three spells with each character and one or two skills because I could deal with enemies faster and using less energy that way. This comes to show most of your characters' skills are wasted which is yet another prove of the horrible gaming design of this release.
.The game`s optional content consists on premade fights (which you face with just one character what generally makes winning them an impossible mission), trades that allow you to get a bit more money or experience with J.C. (that you end up getting anyway through normal progression) and the ocasional quizz. But there's no crafting system, despite the fact that you can get several crafting materials.
Overall: 1/10
