Early Access Watcher Final Review: Ultimate Arena
Update Version: Full Release
Disclosure: This game copy was bought by the reviewer.
I am probably the last person that should review a game based like this based on the subject matter, but thankfully my entire premise for these reviews deals with the amount of value the gameplay has in reference to the asking price. The game has evolved very little since my initial review, which is not surprising given the simplicity. A map editor was provided as well as a event editor. Steam Workshop support was also added to allow the importation of community made "characters." Achievements also made there way in.
The original review still applies and reflects how meager the offerings/changes are to the final product. I am giving this a general pass due to a lack of content in relation to the asking price. I will even justify the decision using patch 1.7: "This update is extremely, EXTREMELY extensive. The patch notes are below - Added Harambe." Harambe is not in the character list.
- This game manages to survive on the idea of showing a "what-if" prediction of who would overcome in a last man standing battle. The look of the game cannot be any simpler: it is a bunch of white figures on a crude map background. The menus register clicks, the matches play out fluidly and the image uploader didn't cause any issues. The game manages to almost work perfectly, but considering how little is here it should be.
The game is comprised of two phases: selecting candidates and watching the outcome of the arena match. You can use images to create new candidates which adds to the total count. While watching the match, you can lay down mines, care packages, or start a event which can make life harder for the remaining contenders. Play by play commentary is displayed on the right side of the screen showing who killed who, if someone drank or ate, and if someone is losing sanity. Once the final contender is left, they are displayed as the winner in quick match or the game resets and starts again if it is an endless match. This is the entire game, watching little people run around a screen until one is left.
This is a tough candidate to rate. The task the developer has set out to achieve is complete in this game, but it barely qualifies as an interactive medium. I cannot in good faith recommend this game, especially at the price. If this program has any use, it might be for picking potential winners of the Super Bowl. You could just as easily put names in a hat to fulfill this assignment though. -
Pros
- It mostly works
Cons
- No real gameplay
- No content
- No Harambe included

Tomorrow Corporation is selling gadgets world wide. Somehow a freak snowstorm smothers Earth. So they ship out “Little Inferno” and suggest people burn their stuff to stay warm. They do and then they run out of stuff. So Tomorrow Corp finds a way to let them burn things they order Tomorrow Corp and help them make money. In turn they buy more and then burn more, etc. etc.
I like this game, but it’s one of the most exceedingly weird games I’ve ever played. While it is a puzzle based game it does have its fair share of uselessness for a sandbox game. It falls along the lines of The Incredible Machine, but you set it all on fire. Regardless it doesn’t have much of a story. It seems like its going for a anti-consumerist and anti-pollution statement, but it is rather bland due to there not being enough backstory, or even a story to promote said message. You can watch the trailer and pretty much surmise that’s what they’re talking about.
You get a few characters who pop in from time to time. Who give some back story, but are mostly useless. Like one lady who turns out to be your neighbor, Sugar Plumps, but she doesn’t say much more then Hello and then asks for items. She eventually gets weirder as the story goes on, but its nothing unusual if you’ve already accepted the dreary world. Then there’s the Weatherman who is virtually useless. He gives the forecast for the weather for the next few days, but since you never go outside I don’t see the point of him at all. Sure his character could be hinting at the anti-consumerist and anti-pollution statement in the game, as mentioned before, but I’m not interested in politics when I play a game unless they are vital to the story like Metal Gear Solid.
Many of the puzzles are damn simple. It combines almost a match the objects and a reverse pictionary game, where its words instead of pictures, and you have to guess the combination of things to burn. Like in the first book in order to solve one puzzle you have to find two things to burn simultaneously that match the theme. In a way its like poetry for pyromaniacs. They’re fun, but they aren’t required in order to play the game. In all honesty the game isn’t possible to fail. So you can play it as much as you want or as little and avoid the puzzles all together. The thing that distracts from the puzzle is the disturbing nature of some of the puzzles. Some when combined you can hear whatever it is scream as its set ablaze. Or the explosion will be so bright it will wash out the screen for a bit.
The graphics and art style are probably the most notable things about the game. They are consistently dark and mulled. The crudeness of the figures are almost reminiscent of those ‘troubled kids’ you see in all horror movies. You know they draw ugly frightening bears and they come to life or something. Some would even say it’s reminiscent of Tim Burton’s art style, but his has a round features to it while this has a crude grease pencil look followed by someone’s tormented 5th grade scrap booking project. Sometimes the creatures are too damn dark and it seems that the artist forgot to use his white crayon to highlight details on the item. Other times it gives you a odd cozy feeling while still feeling mildly disturbing. Now since the things you buy to burn come to life and scream in pain while you’re burning them it just makes it that much more creepy. Its like the items want to be burned. It sounds evil in a way, but its funny/odd to observe.
I can’t recommend this to everyone, because it’s a weird puzzle game. I like these kinds of things, but it has maybe 4 hours worth of play time total. So if you can stand a mild morose atmosphere and teddy bears crying as you burn them alive then this is at least worth a try. If you can find it for $5 I’d say it’s worth it. There isn’t any replay value, but it is a fun and very creepy experience. I wish I could give it a higher rating because it is really a fun game, but it doesn’t have enough story for me to warrant it.

The Witcher 2 is not for everyone. Of course, the same could apply to just about any game, but this is more complicated. Since the game is based on Andrzei Sapkowsky's novels and short stories, it will appeal to people who are familiar with the history, politics and lore of his universe. Everyone else will probably feel alienated. Sapkowsky's world is vast and detailed, and this game does a very poor job of introducing characters, locations and historical events.
The Witcher 1 had a coherent and self-contained story, but the literary lore was still there for those who wanted to peek behind the curtains and find out more about the inner workings of the world. The Witcher 2 gets tangled in byzantine political schemes, so much so that most of the time it feels lika a history lesson rather than a fantasy game. Important craracters appear with no introduction, faction and location names get thrown around a lot, and even if a newcomer to the series will eventually figure out the difference between Temeria and Redania from the codex entries, they probably won't care.
The other problem is that you can practically feel the budget trickling away as the game goes on. It looks gorgeous, dialogue is exciting, animations are impressive and the art direction left me gawking at every character costume I came across. The first half of the game sets up the story and world nicely, builds up a lot of intrigue and provides ample room for questing and exploration. But halfway through you start seeing less and less cutscenes, and by the end everything just gets resolved in a few confusing exposition dumps. It's a relatively short game as well – my playtime here represents a full playthrough with most of the sidequests done and some retries in places with ridiculous difficulty spikes (Yes, there are quite a few of those). Apparently, there are 16 different endings, but the game is nowhere near as enjoyable to warrant another playthrough – not when Youtube is around.
Frankly, I wish less budget had gone into all those flashy graphics and alternate endings that most people will never see, and more into polishing the dodgy combat mechanics, messy narrative and characterization.
This game is good for people who have read Sapkowsky's novels and like to see the world nicely illustrated, so I guess that's technically a "recommend". For those who liked The Witcher 3, this is not necessarily a must. For those who just want a good standalone story-driven RPG, well... Maybe get it at a discount.

If you see this game as 'Total War: WW2 Navy' you will get its concept immediately - the strategy map is there to move around units, repair and refuel etc, and the main fun is in the battles - although they are turn based not real time, although some aspects like animations and ships sinking are done in real time - its a bit weird but it works! And the battles are remarkable with plenty of deep gameplay - I especially love the torpedo plane runs and try to ram the subs which is more difficult than it sounds.
The custom game on its own is worth the money - had loads of fun pitting a Flower Class Corvette against a U-Boat like in the film the Cruel Sea. And if you want to see what HMS Nelson against the Graf Spee would be like you can do that as well along with practically every type of other ship.
But the main fun is in the dynamic campaign - kudos to the devs for putting that in! Its really addictive. Yes the missions are great but the dynamic campaign is where the game shines - you never know what you are going to meet - U-boats or battleships or cruisers etc and you get differing weather and time of day. The weather moves in a realistic manner. The game features ballistics, damage control, smoke, torpedoes, Swordfish, hedgehogs, squid - you name it its all in here.
As yet it never gets overwhelming - managing a sub and firing a spread of torpedoes is really easy, flying a low level torpedo plane attack is dramatic, takes skill but its also scary, but not complicated. Learning to get the range of that distant battleship before it gets yours is similarly nervewracking and exciting - its easy to get to grips with the mechanics but actually doing it takes experience.
Best buy I have made for years. Its a simple game with loads of depth, loads of accuracy and surprisingly deep mechanics, and the dynamic campaign means it will stay fresh for a long time. And for £6 its a steal, it should be at least £20.

Dust is a masterpiece! Everything in Dust: An Elysian Tail is drawn and animated by hand, and it is stunning. A great deal of meticulous thought and planning went into designing each and every location, every enemy, every little detail. The animation is SO good that more than once I found myself distracted by how beautiful the layers of parallax-scrolling background looked, only to moments later watch as the gorgeous ‘Retry’ menu phased into existence due to my untimely demise.
Positives:
- Stunningly Beautiful World
- Simple but Powerful Story
- Fluid and Natural Gameplay
- Atmospheric Soundtrack
- Pitch Perfect Voice Acting
- Secrets! Lots of Secrets!
- The Tutorial
Negatives (The last two are nitpicks):
- Bosses
- No ‘Retry’ Option Against Bosses
- Leveling Up is Too Easy
Like the artwork, every detail of the gameplay is refined and near perfect. Using Dust Storm to draw in Fidget Projectiles, amplify them, and fire off a bullet-hell; this is the defining gameplay mechanic of Dust. It’s a clever idea that builds from two simpler elements to form something spectacular. But the game doesn’t just let you spam this or any other powerful ability; you run out of energy for Fidget Projectiles, continuous use of Dust Storm eventually damages Dust. In both cases there are clear visual elements to indicate when these limits are close to being reached, and they’re integrated excellently into the artwork of the game.
Battles tend to be quick and decisive, with Dust slicing through hordes of enemies at astounding speed. But strategy is also an integral part of the game. Try to quickly slice through every enemy and Dust will be blown away. Literally. Some enemies explode when Dust is in range, some enemies shield themselves from attacks, some fly, some teleport… The variation of enemies and their abilities makes each new encounter a fresh and unique experience. And at its core are battle mechanics that are not only solid, but also very refined.
To be fair, I can’t say that all of the game’s mechanics are perfect (I’m nitpicking). Probably the biggest (near trivial) issue with the gameplay is that there is almost no restriction on gaining experience. Low-level enemies give exactly the same amount of experience points regardless of Dust’s level. As a result, killing low-level enemies while backtracking for secrets can quickly make the game too easy.
Speaking of Secrets, they’re everywhere! Many of them are cleverly hidden or require solid understanding of Dust’s abilities. Some of the secrets are just downright devious (some I’d even categorize as diabolical). But there are always enough hints that finding every secret is not a frustrating task. Treasure chests require keys in order to open them, so sometimes finding a secret is only half the battle. Furthermore, many secrets are blocked by resonance-gem doors or require a special ability in order to access the area. While this makes backtracking a requirement in order to 100% the game, it adds an extra level of depth and interconnectivity to the world.
While not directly secrets, the nods to other videogames are very welcomed. A lot of these nods also poke fun at these games, but in a way that only a true fan can do. And the integration of these elements within An Elysian Tale make the world of Dust feel like one part of a grander design.
The story is both mysterious and emotional. The mystery of Dust’s existence drives the story forward, but the simple yet meaningful experiences allow for growth in both Dust and Fidget. The ending is easily the most emotional part of the game… to the point where one might feel regret for even the main antagonist. Everything comes together perfectly, and ends in a satisfying but bittersweet manner. That said, there’s still a lot we don’t know about
Fidget. Like her favourite color (shiny). There’s a lot we don’t know about the world of Elysium; things that are hinted at but not explored. And there’s a lot we don’t know about Dust; the actions and choices that define his dark ‘past’ – the actions and choices that make him who ‘he’ is.
The music sets the perfect atmosphere for each area of the game, but it also stands on its own as an amazing and emotional work (it’s award-winning for a reason). The sounds, while easily overlooked, also contribute greatly to the immersion and realism of the world. And the voice acting, oh my god is it pitch perfect! Every single line of dialogue in the game is voiced. But surprisingly, there isn’t a bad delivery to be found. And the characters are so alive because of it.
Have you ever played a phenomenal game brought down by an atrocious tutorial? Sadly, I have played games like this. It’s heartbreaking when the dedication and sacrifice of the developers can’t be appreciated because the part of the game that teaches you how to play is poorly implemented. Fortunately, the Tutorial in Dust is not only good, it’s as good as a Tutorial Sequence could possibly be! It explains the controls and gameplay in a simple but clear way, and it integrates much of this explanation into the opening dialogue. Not only does it do this well, it does it in a way that is completely believable and even entertaining. The tutorial goes beyond what is needed, but I personally think that every game should strive to have a tutorial as perfect.
OK, so most of this review is well deserved praise, with the few negative points being more along the lines of ‘meh’ than a serious issue. However Dust does have a serious flaw, and that is its bosses. First, the good points; the bosses look amazing, are well animated, their attacks are interesting and varied, and um… So here’s the issue; the strategy for the first boss is
‘hit it with the big talking stick’. Can you guess what the strategy for the next every other boss in the game is? This works fine for the first boss because you have to fight two giants, two of the same boss, at the same time; you have to attack one giant while keeping an eye on the other and dodging both of their attacks. It’s an intense, but enjoyable battle. And a good introductory boss fight.
And the rest are effectively identical, only instead of two of the same boss, you only fight one… and it just doesn’t work. OK, some of the bosses summon non-boss enemies, and the final boss spans several screens and uses new abilities in each one. But it’s still the same boss fight every time.
I guess you could argue that the boss fight with the spirit actually spans the four haunted mansions since the boss chases Dust through each one. And to be fair, these sequences are amazing! It’s a letdown that the actual boss fights themselves are so lacking, because they really are phenomenal visual designs with some great animation to go with them.
With that said, the bosses only account for maybe 1% of the total game? And to be fair, the bosses do have enough to them to at least provide some level of challenge.
I did mention there is no ‘retry’ option against bosses. In the rare instance that you actually die against one of the bosses, being able to jump right back into the boss fight would be ideal. As is, you have to go through every cutscene leading up to the fight before getting to the fight itself. It’s not really an issue because the bosses are so easy. But if the bosses were a true obstacle (as they should be), this would be a much bigger consideration.
Overall, Dust: An Elysian Tail is near perfect. Recommended. Period.

It's all it's simpleness, it's very enjoyable. There's quite a satisfaction attached to hit an enemy ship with a full broadside or to sneak up with your subs and sink that flag ship. The controls are quite easy to learn and it's not in the same spirit as the Navy sims out there. There are some "mini games" within the game as well when you do torpedo runs with e.g. a Swordfish airplane. It's quite crude in it's implementation but still you can use it to your advantage when you are close enough to your own airsupport.
With that said, there are quite a few problems.
1. The enemy subs seems to be able to exit combat at will. Several times I've had them locked on by up to 4 destroyers and suddenly you just get the message "U-96 exits combat". This has to be fixed. I would understand if the sub was able to evade my fleet, but there's no way for it to escape once the sonars have located one. In real life, yes, but in the game no.
2. Air strikes. The problem with these is that you can't freely put a marker on the map to carry them out. They have to be locked onto a target. And if the target is a sub, well, then you have to click on the actual sub and not on the surface. This is quite an issue since the only ships that can target a sub are the destroyers, it means that it's a hit and miss click fest until you get lucky.
3. Targets are not shared among the rest of you fleet. It seems that the Captains wants to keep enemy ships to themselves. Not very realistic. If one ship spots an enemy, of course they would let the rest of the ships know the bearing and distance.
4. The end game is not clear. Not clear at all. I'm not saying that there should be missions as such since it's a sandbox, kind of, game but some things just doesn't make any sense. Take merchant ships for instance. Frequently you get messages that some Nazi sub has sunk some 30000 tons of loot near Greenland but it has no real impact on your game. It doesn't feel very necessary to protect them besides that it gives you an opportunity to sink some enemy ships. As an enemy sub Captain you don't earn any "money" either for civilian ships, only military. Given that the whole Atlantic navy war was about sinking as much goods as possible, this makes no sense what so ever.
5. I've had several glitches with the aircraft carriers where they suddenly become invisible. Invinsible would be nice sometimes, but the camera bugs out and only shows a grey window. You can still command them, but it's pointless since you can't se what they are doing.
6. Ranging. This is also an issue since you have no tools to range an enemy ship. If you can visually see a target, apparently they have hired a flock of monkeys that sits below deck and gives you a guestimate of the range. Now, I know how it works in real life (the same as for artillery on land) that you shoot-correct-shoot, but they did have crude range finders (optical devices that when converged on a target would give a estimation). Luckily, most of the time, the enemy seems to share the same trained monkeys. It would also make sense if your more exprienced crews would give better rangings than a noob ship. It should pay off to keep a ship alive.
7. AA. There should be a way to fire on incoming aircraft. It seems that it's a pure 50/50 now if your ships will be able to hit them with their AA artillery/guns. Some aircrafts, the ME 110s in particular, never seem to miss either with their torpedoes.
There are probably more stuff that I can't think of at the moment, but these are some issues that leaps to mind.
Overall, yes, it's quite fun and enjoyable. You don't have to be a sim freak to figure it out and once you get to fight with your big Battle ships that fires shells the size of small buses, it's very fun. Beware though, it's more towards arcade so if you are looking for a sim you need to keep that in mind.

This is a fun little RPG to pass the time. Bottom line, it's enjoyable if a bit amateurish in spots and inexplicable in others (why are the forests littered with chests just waiting to be opened?) Yes the dialogue is a bit juvenile and heavily-inspired by Naruto but its not a direct rip-off. No more so than the dozens of Chrono Trigger or Final Fantasy inspired games are rip offs of those series. Instead of knights and kings you have ninjas and kages (and yes, some other very Naruto-like elements).  Some weird mixing of words that sound more like Chinese than Japanese are also in the game like "X-tu". So if you are tired of the standard western knights and dragons in your JRPG then this is a nice change. The gameplay is fun without endless exploration of mazes and excessive doubling back or random foes as seen in some other similar inexpensive RPG maker titles. The story progresses well without too much time in dialogue or too much time in random combat. The difficulty level is fine for a casual JRPG and I would even boost it for a challenge. I did not feel that the generic RPG maker tiles or artwork detracted from the game - they seemed suitable to me, but I have not played others that use these particular graphics. One downside as I see it is that some of the powers the characters develop far too quickly and just out of the blue in the wilderness. I would have preferred to see them develop these skills by training them in the village and practicing with them, than getting a Monte Haul of skills.

Let me ask you a question: Do you like rhythm games? Do you like roguelikes? If you only answered yes to one of these, I'd still recommend picking this up, because the two genres complement each other here REALLY well.
This isn't your typical rhythm game. Rhythm games often require split-second decisions and memorization of several strange inputs in response to subtle inputs. NecroDancer is not quite like that. Every failure is (usually) your own fault, since you're given plenty of time to react to different enemy patterns, and traps are very obviously placed to help in their avoidance.
All you're given is a very simple control scheme: the arrow keys do everything. Need to move? Arrow keys. Want to attack? Run into an enemy with the arrow keys. Wish to use an item? Use a very simple 2-button combo with, you guessed it, the arrow keys. Easy to learn, but hard to master.
The level design is great as well. I mean, one would assume that a randomly generated bunch of zones would be hard to make "good" but it actually does fairly well. Every zone has 3 levels to it, of slightly increasing difficulty, and each zone increases in difficulty slightly, until you finally reach the final zone, and all your skills are put to the test before finally defeating the final boss and winning. It's a good example of level progression.
Of course, a rhythm game has to have good music, and let me just say this game has GREAT music. The original tunes are written by DannyB, composer for songs from Super Meat Boy and other titles. But, if you get tired of that, there are also 5 other remixes (7 in the DLC) that you can easily swap between at any time!
Speaking of DLC, the Amplified DLC is fantastic as well! It adds 4 new characters, 3 new bosses, and an entirely new zone filled with electric wires that implement a new attacking mechanic! I won't go into too much detail here, but let me just say it's REALLY GOOD.
So in essence, if you feel you have a good sense of rhythm and decent pattern recognition, this game is for you! And if you're not good at that, don't worry about it! The community for this game is FANTASTIC and they've really helped me get good at the game. (I won't go so far as to say I'm GREAT but y'know.) This game will bring many hours of fun, and that's just with Cadence, the base character. There are 9 other characters to choose from in the base game with their own gimmicks, which will bring you even more fun times and a lot of challenge to boot. I hope this review helps with your purchasing decision.

The tale of the Raegarian Galactic Republic:
There once was a world that reached to the stars with the objective of creating a vast republic of many worlds. For many years this republic grew and flourished, gaining many friends and uniting them all under a single republic using peaceful means. There was no need for weapons of war, and the sole concern for many decades was ensuring there was enough space for the burgeoning gem of the Republic.
But the good times came to an end, and the dark times came. Some were not content with the path the Republic was taking, one of peace. They beleived that the Raegarian Republic should become an Empire, after all the Raegarians funded most of the other races projects and defense forces, why shouldn't they be in charge of everything? So they rebelled, the core government powerless to stop them as it had to deal with a temporary energy crisis and had little political capitol to spare to divert the disaster.
The rebels quickly took control of vast swaths of the frontier sectors of the Republic, and became increasingly belligerant towards the peaceful inner sectors. So, a decision was made. A new leader elected. A new doctrine adopted.
A grand army of the Republic was created, utilizing the extensive scientific knowledge of the Raegarians no expense was spared as the energy crises ended at last, and every planet was expected to assist in the rapid constrtuction of this army. Soon, the Raegarian Republic that once valued peace above all else had a fleet second to none and a clone army meant to occupy countless worlds. A great war broke out with the rebellious sectors, one that lasted for decades. The people hated the thought of warfare, but the risk of letting their belligerant brethern continue ravaging the borders was too great, so slowly the public attitude became increasingly supportive of ending the war through brutal means.
Finally, a doctrine of total annihilation was adopted, the "liberated" worlds refused to peacefully reintegrate, and entire worlds were glassed to end the threat once and for all for the war began to cost too much in both lives and resources. By the end, the Raegarian republic had become a military dictatorship in order to maintain its efforts, the people disinterested in returning to their peaceful ways, the thought of another unexpected war weighing heavily. The one-time allies began to grow suspicious of the Raegarians, and eventually began abandoning the one-time alliance out of fear the Raegarians had become something dangerous. They were not wrong.
The Raegarian Republic eventually separated itself as its military interests were ignored by its remaining allies, and rechristened itself the "Raegarian Empire" ironically. Fearful of a multiple front war, the Raegarians blitzed several holdings, forcing their membership into the new empire to buffer its frontier. Soon, only a few holdouts remained, backed by the sole remaining Federation of liberty and freedom. But then they came...
From beyond the void, a race of extragalactic creatures invaded the galaxy, striking the Raegarian Empire from behind while the fleets were massing on the border with the Federation. By the time the fleets had responded to contain the threat, many planets had been lost, the Raegarians reeling from the overwhelming numbers. In the first major fleet action, the Raegarians suffered heavy losses and were forced to regroup for the first time since the rebellion wars.
Initially, the Federation breathed a sigh of releif, thinking the new threat was their savior. They ignored the Empires frantic pleas for assistance, even with the offer of freeing many of its border worlds. But after years of far away war, costing the Empire many lives and planets just to direct the bloody path of conquest, the war reached the Federation as well. Then they realized the Empire was fighting a foe they could not beat alone, which meant the Federation certainly could not either.
A treaty was eventually made as the alien slaughter began decimating the Federation worlds, a return to a form of unity and the two governments threw all they had at the invaders. The war lasted years before the tide began to turn in the natives favor, and the Raegarians finally ended the war when they captured the leader of the alien invaders in a daring assault deep into their territory... where their one-time homeworld was located. The end of the war brought a unsteady peace between the factions, but having seen enough war the galaxy returned to a relative peace looking for threats from outwards instead of inwards, vowing never to be caught off guard and mired by squabbles again.

Hogs of War Review
Written by SMK - 28/07/2015
"WELCOME TO BOOT CAMP!" - Major I.P Grimly
Yes, indeed, welcome one and all to this review of my favourite game of all time, Hogs of War.
Now, before you leave because you can clearly see this review will be biased, it will not be. There are a lot of problems with the game at the moment and many of them are unfixable. All problems that I have encountered in this version will be noted.
Small history lesson first, this game was created by Infogrames who developed the original Alone in the Dark series and also published Robot Arena 2 and Roller Coaster Tycoon 3. This game began to be sold in June of 2000 on the PSX and later the PC. The game didn't sell well due it's bad use of advertising on TV. A second game was in the works but was however cancelled due to the takeover of Infogrames by Atari in the mid-2000s and due to a lack of funding for the game.
Anyway-
The game.
There is a small backstory behind this game which kind of develops throughout the game. The initial story is that some pigs have enlisted into the army, Major I.P Grimy (Narrated by Rik Mayall) informs them about the 'Isle of Swill' which they must get to so that they can control the world. To do this, they must take all of 'Saustralisa' which many other nations own. The story develops in each mission before it starts where a written document awaits you by Major Grimly telling you what to do and how it will affect the war. That's about all the story there is until the end when you get a few cut scenes about one of the pigs. (Which I won't spoil.)
The story offers an excellent level of challenge which builds up as you progress. There are a few missions that break this mold however but it feels amazing when you beat them finally.
In the campaign, you control a squad of pigs which you can upgrade as you complete missions. You get one upgrade point for beating a level with a pig dying but you can get two for beating the level without losing any pigs. You can also get more medals later on by doing specific tasks asked by Grimly and that's why it's important to read the mission details before each mission.
A quick section on graphics too... The graphics aren't any good by today's standards as you might expect. However, I believe they've held up rather well and the game is definitely something which shouldn't be shunned at because of it's graphics. Especially in comparison with the PSX version.
The game plays in a very similar style to Worms. It's turned based combat in 3D using weapons to kill off enemy pigs from different nations in a WWI setting. The pigs are based off real life nations during World War 1, for instance, Tommy's Trotters represents the UK, Garlic Grunts represent the French and the Sushi Swines represent Japan. You have a turn timer in which to perform your pigs actions. Your pigs have classes and depending on the class you're controlling depends on what weapons the pig will have. I.E, Engineers have TNT and Mines while Paratroopers have Jetpacks and Machine Guns. The pig's health also depends on which class they are. During the time that you're given, you can walk around, get in a tank or a shelter, find some weapons but as you might imagine, the main objective of your turn is to damage or kill a pig which can be done in an amazing amount of creative ways from as simple as smacking them with your Trotter to throwing some Madness Gas their way to make them go insane and start hopping around.
The gameplay is solid turn based combat, nothing wrong at all. Extremely satisfying to kill pigs from afar using the Mortar or Airburst. Close combat is still fun as long range, especially as it becomes much more tactical. This is enhanced if you play hotseat multiplayer also.
The game is narrated all by the British comedy legend Rik Mayall who is unfortunately no longer with us however his fantastic impressions live on through this game. And this is one of the best parts of the game, hearing Mayall's voice is fantastic. He does brilliant impressions of all nations within the game which will make you laugh every time you hear them. Despite them being stereotypical, they shouldn't be taken the wrong way as everyone gets the same treatment, even the British.
(As a side note, Mayall also played 'Lord Flashheart' in 'Blackadder Goes Forth' which is a World War 1 based comedy mini-series featuring other British comedians such as Rowan Atkinson which he is also God-like in and I highly, highly recommend it.)
Despite all this however, especially in the PC version of the game.
First of all, the AI pigs do not move. This was a bug in the original version of the game and wasn't fixed by Infogrames and therefore cannot be fixed now.
The music is way too loud and cannot be lowered in-game. The kick in the teeth is that you can't lower it by tabbing out either because it will lock your PC up. This isn't a big problem if you lower your sound before you start the game however.
The music constantly plays when it's not suppose to. For instance, when you drop in to a game, you are suppose to hear one small song to start the mission but for some reason, the game plays the extended version of the song and then plays another one on top of it. This also happens when the enemy team is taking its go where it will play 2 songs instead of just one, this can become annoying because it will sometimes overlap into your turn too.
The game has a number of graphical glitches if you use the Steam GUI. For instance, you'll get a skeleton pig when the pig runs away and towards you when it switches screens or the text will freak out and become random lines or text. (As far as I'm aware though this doesn't disrupt gameplay.)
One last thing is that this game can crash. I finished a mission once and it just crashed after the mission so make sure you save your team after every campaign mission.
Just a quick look at some technical stuff too.
Load times are non-existent in this game.
The options are basically useless as changing the resolution will do nothing. The sound options seems to work at times.
Controls are not re-mappable.
There is no controller support.
As you might imagine, there are no dedicated servers. The only way to create a game is either portfowarding or using hamachi which I haven't tried so I cannot tell if it'll work. (I will try this and update this later.) They will not add dedicated servers in the future either.
Game runs like a dream. Locks at 25 FPS in-game and that's how it's meant to be played so...
To conclude, you can make up your own mind if you want this game. But at a price of £3.99, this game is absolute steal, to me, the game is absolutely worth it at this price and despite all it's glitches, it's still playable and is a ton of fun.
I will recommend this game but you have to be good at multie tasking.

As much as the developer made efforts to make choice and consequence matter, as lush as the visuals are, and as detailed as the book-inspired world is, The Witcher 2: Assassins of Kings is a tremendous mess of a game which largely does not deserve its tremendous praise.
From the entirely false premise put forward by the developers that this can serve as an effective introduction to the world (it doesn't, you are constantly wondering why you should care about any of the people, places, or things being discussed by characters you also don't care about, frankly whether you read the journal entires or not), to the mechanically abysmal yet unduly punishing combat (even FCR 2, the developer-made mod to overhaul the combat, is not an improvement), to the thoroughly consolized, supremely inefficiently designed UI and looting systems, the game does not actually add up to a consistenly enjoyable experience in the least for gamers who A) aren't already heavily invested in Geralt de Rivia's world via either the previous game or the books, B) enjoy mechanically sound, bug-free, sensible game design, and C) perhaps most of all, don't like to have their time continually wasted by clunky mechanics, poorly set-up plot elements, uninterestingly characterized NPC's, and even utterly pointless encumberance issues (any RPG player knows to hold on to as many things as they can, which means many trips to your storage container so that you can store crafting materials the overwhelming majority of which you *will not* ever have the opportunity to use). Even currency quickly becomes a non-issue for the careful player, as there simply aren't enough things you could find desirable enough to actually buy during the game's intensely frustrating but ultimately fairly content-light campaign.
In fact, the annoyances and poor design choices one can list hardly stop there. Character progression is some of the most unsatisfying I've ever encountered: having to go through a 'Training' tree to actually begin working on the style you want is as unenjoyable as it is ultimately pointless and thematically absurd for an experienced witcher like Geralt (FCR 2 grants Geralt all six of the Training skills, so at least one of the developers explicitly agrees with this criticism). Once you're finally able to begin work on the path of your choosing, the level 35 cap prevents any reasonable expectation of multiclassing; you are either a very focused mage, swordmaster, or alchemist, or you are probably poorly built. While I suspect the developers wanted the player to 'commit' to a particular path (just as they are clearly encouraging players to play twice), this still doesn't amount to a remotely deep, fun, or interesting build system.
The map system is similarly the poorest implementation I've ever seen in such a widely lauded title. The minimap does not indicate North, which actually means that it indicates very little at all: while in many AAA titles you are consistently staring at the minimap to figure out where you are going (both a curse and an aid), I found myself relatively rarely looking at the Witcher 2's minimap. While it will show you a trail or path, that is roughly the extent of the somewhat-useful information it imparts. Additionally, quest markers are often poorly placed if not outright misleading, as they do not account for elevation and will indicate the physical location of the NPC you need to find even when you aren't inhabiting the same world space as them (in which case the marker should direct you to the door they are behind, but frequently doesn't). These problems are easily the most evident in Vergen, the Iorveth-led second act which places you in what is also perhaps the worst designed town I've ever had the misfortune of bungling around in an RPG, with its multiple elevations, maze-like streets, and pointless interiors and bridges.
All of this isn't to speak of the larger overworld map, which although visually immersive (it looks how a relatively primitive map from the Middle Ages might), tells the player so little useful information that it in some cases might as well not exist (particularly without North on the minimap). Somehow even more of a joke are maps of the entire region: despite the fact that these were clearly included in the game to inform the player as to where the different political territories are located in relation to one another (something that is actually quite important to know since the entire plot is a political intrigue), the map *is not in English*. Yes, really, you can't read it, and as such it tells you literally nothing. It's just colors and shapes.
This all ultimately brings one to a discussion of the one big thing most agree this game does well: plot-significant choice and consequence. Think of it as somewhat the opposite of a Telltale game: rather than your choices having largely to do with how you characterize yourself in addition to a few often minor plot divergences, your choices result in actual plot differences (the content of nearly all of the entire second act hinges on a single decision near the end of act one, though contrary to what some might have you believe, you don't actually inhabit an entirely different world space and will eventually visit at least parts of the other side of the map). This is certainly laudable and is clearly where the chief unique efforts of the development went for the Witcher 2.
Again, however, it would be much more laudable if the game itself had any proper sense of gameflow or consistently interesting, engaging, polished mechanics. I'd care a lot more that two playthroughs are so different if the writing had done more to invest me in the people, places, and things I know so little about (e.g., Geralt's v/o sounds enjoyable enough, but lacks any range or clear emotional finesse much like his facial animations, resulting in a main character who seems as relatively unengaged from what is happening around him as the player ultimately is), and if playing through the game again didn't also mean replaying a largely homogenous initial two chapters (regardless of your choices) to get to the plot divergences you care about.  Note, Telltale critics, that while the games are increasingly criticized for the lack of plot variation present in the choices you can make, the games still frequently tell some of the best stories available in gaming, full of emotional resonance and player engangement, and this is precicely because of the emphasis on characterization.
The Witcher 2 is also a good opportunity to question what kind of choice and consequence is even desirable in gaming; while games like the Witcher and Mass Effect market themselves on choice and consequence, the ultimate product of the many extra hours of development is often just an excuse to play the game a second time. This does not necessarily make the game more interesting, it just gives a reason for the player to go through much of the same content a second time with an often at most 10-20% difference. While the Witcher 2 is better at that percentage than perhaps any other game with these production values, it doesn't change the fact that the game is such a chore to play, that the writing is so unengaging and the characters so often uninteresting, that the question of whether it is worth playing the game a second time becomes a genuine one when it really shouldn't be.
I respect the developer's enthusiasm and good relationship with the source material and fans, but they missed the mark in far too many ways, and I don't think this game has aged well nor will it continue to stand up to the test of time. While I furthermore admire the Witcher's attempt at mature storytelling in gaming (you aren't saving the world, and can't), there are ways to tell these scaled-down stories much more enjoyably while maintaining that humbling perspective, minus the boorish characters and unengaging politics.

The Witcher 2: Assassins of Kings is a decision-driven fantasy RPG released by CD Projekt RED in 2011.  Like all The Witcher games, The Witcher 2 is based on The Witcher series of novels by Andrzej Sapkowski.
The Witcher 2 (W2) takes places in a fantasy world heavy inspired by Slavic mythology and Polish history.  The universe of The Witcher games is steeped in political intrigue and features strange monsters and magical forces that influence people's lives for the better or worse.  In this world, a sect of mutant warriors called "witchers" (or hexers) serve as itinerant monster slayers for hire.  One of these witchers is the famed Geralt of Rivia, also known as the White Wolf.
The game picks up shortly after the ending of The Witcher (W1), which showed Geralt of Rivia defending King Foltest of Temeria from a mysterious assassin.  In the aftermath, King Foltest "orders" Geralt of Rivia to serve as a glorified bodyguard.  However, a sinister plot by a mysterious faction compels Geralt to search for answers, reacquainting him with certain figures from his past.  Still suffering from amnesia prior to the events of W1, Geralt must regain his memories and find out who is killing the Northern Kingdoms' monarchs.
W2 feels fairly shorter in story length than W1.  Nonetheless, the decision-driven storytelling of W2 remains strong, and I found the supporting cast highly memorable.  The game presents almost entirely different story paths which start near the end of Chapter 1 and dramatically change your character's quests and location for the majority of Chapter 2.  The grey morality surrounding monster slaying, philosophical issues, and political matters remains a key aspect of the decision-driven narrative.  The game ends on a bit of a cliffhanger and some plot lines seem unresolved...at least until The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt.  Nonetheless, the narrative remains fairly compelling.
Finally, the import system is not as comprehensive as in games like Mass Effect 1-3, but some decisions (e.g. decisions on Princess Adda, Siegfried [Order] or Yaevinn [Scoi'atel], and a couple other characters) add/change dialogue options and alter certain NPC interactions.
The timed attack clicks of W1 have been replaced with a more "Dark Souls"-esque combat gameplay style (if you want to use that analogy).  Geralt has a basic skill tree alongside three other skill trees for alchemy, swordsmanship, and magic.  I favored a build centered around swordsmanship with some perks in magic, but found most of the alchemy tree useless for this build.  Like in the first game, your character uses two swords: steel for humans, silver for monsters.
Enemies can feel RELENTLESS early on.  You may find yourself underleveled at first, but can become a powerhouse of destruction near the end.  This unbalanced difficulty, however, may deter many players.
The alchemy system of W2 does away with alcohol bases for potions in W1.  Instead, you simply combine ingredients and voila: a masterpiece.  You must have the necessary ingredients and recipes beforehand from looting and finding merchants.  Meditation is now required to consume potions, but is offset by being able to
outside of combat.  In addition, you can utilize bombs, specific sword oils, throwing knives, and traps against your aggressors.
As this is a decision-driven story game, dialogue remains key to discovering info and shaping the outcome of the narrative.  You can utilize persuasion/intimidate/axii abilities to steer a conversation to your benefit provided you have the required level for each.  Be mindful that your decisions can have drastic story consequences.  This game does not hold your hand.  You are free to choose the path you believe is right.
The game offers several side quests, from contracts to arm wrestling, brawling, and dice poker.  There is no fast travel, so you'll be backtracking a lot to complete these.
I played the game in English since that's my primary language.  W2's voiceacting has certainly improved since the last game and features quality vocal talent for many NPCs.
The music is AMAZING.  It is highly atmospheric and more than captures the mood and identity of each area you're in.  Some of the combat music may really get your blood flowing during fights.
The game looks gorgeous, especially if you have the hardware to enjoy the lighting FX.  On high graphics settings, the environments and character models are bristling with detail.

No time to read: Like XCOM! On the sea!  But with Nazis instead of aliens! And ships instead of soldiers! And a much better action camera! And less performance problems! Also, you can be a Nazi! Wait... come to think of it, it's not that much like XCOM, but Atlantic fleet is still a great turn-based tactical naval game with a nice strategic layer as well.
The core of Atlantic fleet is the turn-based ship combat. Each of your ship gets two actions, a move and fire action like XCOM. However, unlike XCOM the accuracy of your fire is based mostly on your input (instead of just the RNG in XCOM). Once in your fire phase, you have to manually set the elevation and traverse of your guns to hit enemy ships, like in the artillery games of old (Worms, or Scorched Earth). If you miss, you need to adjust your artillery settings based on where the shells landed. In the artillery games of old, this sort of trial and error can get frustrating because you don't have any idea what angle you should use at first to get shots anywhere close to your target. Fortunately Atlantic Fleet avoids this by allowing you to 'lock on' to enemy ships and giving you an estimated distance and elevation required to hit your target. You can then work from the estimate and dial in your shots until you consistently hit your target.
Atlantic Fleet succeeds in evoking the same sort of tension you feel when lining up a shot or when you're getting shot at in XCOM. In cruicial shots you end up praying to the RNG gods (or in this case the simulation gods) that your next shot hits the enemy in a crucial location (engine, steering) so you can get your ships away in one piece. And the damage modeling seems to be pretty good too. If the enemy takes out your steering, you can only change your throttle settings and can end up going in circles (like the Bismarck did in real life). If your propulsion is taken you then you become a sitting duck.
The game wraps up the core turn-based naval combat in three game modes: Single battle, Campaign and the dynamic 'Battle of the Atlantic Campaign'. Single battle is just a collection of historical battles, campaign is a sequence of increasingly difficult battles as well as a prestige system that allows you to buy new ships to improve your fleet. The best game mode is the 'Battle of the Atlantic' dynamic campaign, where you can move your fleets around a map of the Atlantic Ocean as you fight your enemy at the strategic level. It's pretty detailed, requiring you to cycle ships from sea to port as they take damage or run out of ammo, and also has the prestige system from the non-dynamic campaign that allows you to buy new ships to replace your losses. It sort of reminds me of the campaigns in the Great Naval Battles series of yore. I've only played this for a few hours but I'm already enjoying preying on British merchant shipping with my submarine wolfpacks, and I can see myself playing this mode for many, many hours.
On the down side, it does show its mobile game roots. Some of the controls clearly work better on mobile (clicking and dragging the elevation in traverse wheels using a mouse can downright make your hand hurt after a few hours, clicking buttons in the UI just don't have the same feedback you'd expect from a PC game). Graphic settings are pretty barebones (yet still better than most mobile ports).
That said, the graphics themselves and the sound design are pretty good, especially considering that this was a mobile game. Like XCOM. its great graphics. sounds design and action camera allows you to 'feel' the battle, not just 'think' it. Just remember if you're on a laptop with both an integrated and dedicated graphics card to make sure the game is set to run using the dedicated card, otherwise it will lag badly trying to run on the integrated card.
The game has a lot more detail and systems that I won't have time to discuss here (smoke, anti-sub weaponry, torpedo spreads, air strikes), but overall it shows a lot of attention to detail and is a lot more 'realistic' than I expected a turn-based naval game to be, especially one that started out on mobile.  All in all it's good, and if you like naval combat at all (especially WW2 naval combat), you should get this game.

First let me say that I really like the game, in particular for its "gunnery and aiming system". It`s a fresh and demanding change compared to "Victory at Sea" and "Battle Fleet 2". In this game, especially in comparison, experience will not make you too powerful, or the game too easy.
Basically you constantly need to update the direction of your batteries and control the angle of the guns and you have different indicators to help you with that.
However, the most reliable source of input is your own experience and the map on which you are able to track where your shots have landed during the past six turns, and how the fleets have moved since then. And after a while of playing you will get a better understanding of how much you need to adjust the range when your fleet is crossing the T, instead of steering head on towards the enemy and therefore drastically reducing the distance.
You have the option to extend the starting distance of the opposing fleets and add a wind modifier to the battles, so the engagements can get quite demanding and sometimes you will need several salvos to score your first hit.
So, you keep comparing your own assessment of the situation to the targeting computer`s calculations and making a better choice based on the map recordings than the value the computer is offering is really satisfying and can make the difference of landing the first hit, or watch some nice magazine explosions on your own ships.
The main and only game mode for me to play (after the "tutorial phase" has been finished) is the dynamic campaign. I want to be suprised by the events and random engagements and build my own fleet which I try to protect throughout the campaign (in the dynamic campaign you have the option to build 30 ships, 10 ships maximum per fleet).
The dynamic campaign in this game tries to be historical correct, so the engagements mainly happen around merchant shipping. The Axis forces try to sink a pre-defined value of supplies and the allied forces will do their best to stop them.
Unfortunately, for me personally, this historic setting is a little bit too repetitive for my taste. I like clashes of big surface vessels, but, since they didn`t happen for real with Germany trying to avoid Her Majesty`s Royal Navy, you won`t find them during this dynamic campaign.
Sure, there are battleships around and you will fight them, but as an escort or rather small fleet. To reach the objective in sinking or protecting the convoys you need to spread your forces and this means you need cheap ships and many of them. ...and this means submarines or destroyers.
And this brings me back to my aforementioned point: Submarines and Destroyers are not my particular favourite class of ships.
...and during the dynamic campaign there`s a lot of Submarine vs. Destroyers. ...I mean... a lot. ... I mean ...a grindy lot.
Probably historically correct, but for me not very thrilling. This also has something to do with the implementation of submarine warfare in this game, which is rather simplistic.
If you create a wolfpack and an engagement is about to start your submarines will be automatically placed around the convoy. This means a few of them are already in a good spot for firing their payload, but others have no chance of keeping the pace of the surface vessels, at least not when they are submerged.
Since the game takes the "workload" off of you to manually have to destroy each and every merchant ship after you have knocked out the escort (which is a huge plus), you actually focus your fighting on the enemy combatants. Should you be able to destroy them, you are able to stop the battle and all merchant ships will count as "sunk".
So, there are 1-3 destroyers and (a little bit historically uncorrect I would say) instead of hunting the merchants, you start to hunt them. How do you hunt a destroyer moving in a torpedo-evading zig-zag line? You fan out your payload... and you do this with all of your subs. With a little bit of luck you will hit them badly, badly as in "there won`t be any opposition left" and you just "collect" the merchants...
Should you not be as successful and one of them is even starting to bully you, no problem, you just dive away and are able to disengage from the battle. Hm...
And as mentioned before, since you try to sink all merchant ships that have ever been built, these kind of engagements will happen a lot.
As a destroyer captain you just have to move over a sonar contact marking and drop your depth charges close to it. Hm, also not so thrilling... at least for me.
But, this is just my personal opinion, maybe the way submarine warfare is implemented in this game is exactly your thing...
For me the game shines in its surface battles. When you encounter an enemy battleship and can say good-bye to the idea of "I even won`t let them scratch the paint job of my battleship!!!"... Then it`s gloves off and a nail-biting shoot-out will commence.
Things I noticed which give the game a little raw look and feel to it are an unintuitive interface with no tool-tips.
Instead of dragging a wheel with pressed mouse button to reach an angle of "16.3" why not just let the player enter a value with the keyboard?
When wanting to buy a new ship during the dynamic campaign you have to switch on the labelling of the map, which makes names and ports visible. Then click on a zone in front of a port to get to it. Then, in the harbour screen, you need to click on the "purchase" button...
Why not just add a purchase button below the map on the main screen?
Submarines have no heading indicator above the surface when they are diving. To check where your sub is going you need to move below sea level with the camera and look for yourself.
All different ammo types are on the same button, which you have to click several times to get to the one you want... and at the end of the battle you will notice... "Oh, I had 3 air strikes available?"
You want to check how many torpedoes are available or have been reloaded? Click the ammo button. You realized that you have none available and want to continue to the next turn? Press the same button again until it shows "Done"... Hm, a dedicated "End Turn" button would be smoother and more user friendly...
It looks like that the sea has always the same swell, unfortunately there`s no difference in visual depiction of rough or calm sea.
I`m also missing some sound effects, like UI/ button sounds or firing of depth charges and torpedoes...
I think the game has a lot of potential and I really like it. It is not my intention, if my criticism sounds a little bit harsh. I merely wanted to explain that some things might feel a little bit rough for potential new or interested customers.
The scenario might not be the perfect one for me (probably a Pacific game will match a little better for my taste), but`s that`s just my personal thing. The same is valid for this completely subjective "review".
The production value of this game is great and the naval warfare experience is unique nowadays, the developer is very active in the forum and, if you are only a little bit interested in turn-based navy engagements I would suggest you give this game a try.
It isn't premarital sex if you have no intention of getting married.

I have a whole collection of blood-soaked, dark, foreboding, violent games because I really enjoy them.  I love first person shooters.  I love steampunk cities, dark mysteries and stealth operations.  But once in a while, it's nice to get away.  Have the game equivalent of a vacation.  Spend some time  reminding yourself that bright colours and magical places still exist.  Welcome to Abzu.
Abzu doesn’t set up the premise with a cutscene.  It doesn’t start with with a Patrick Stewart voice-over that explains everything.  You simply enter the water, and begin to discover your surroundings for yourself.
And what surroundings!  You glide gracefully through schools of fish, long swaying sea weeds, underwater caves, nooks and crannies.  You follow a linear path but along the way are large areas for you to explore.  These large areas contain a variety of sea life from tiny fish up to eals, even sharks and whales.  These larger areas also feature a statue on which you can sit and meditate.  In meditate mode, the camera will lock onto a particular fish and follow it as it goes about it’s business.  You can move from fish to fish.  These meditation spots can be accessed individually at any time.  Putting Abzu on has replaced my screen saver for ever.
Abzu is beautiful.  I have had to try constantly while writing this review, not to use that word in every sentence.  Its not something I can really effectively put across.  You just need to play it.  Screenshots look great but even videos don’t manage to convey how it feels to play. If you are looking for a challenge and some action, Abzu isn’t going to fit the bill.  However, if you want to have a beautiful, graceful and magical relaxing experience, I highly recommend it.

I will be honest. The only reason I am here on Steam is because of Elegy for a Dead World.
I will first describe my motivations behind the said-sole reason a little bit, before I share about my experiences in the game and what I think of it.
As a writer and casual gamer, I was absolutely thrilled to discover this game some months back. A game where one can write?? Who knew that writing and gaming would one day be so elegantly combined?
I wanted it so much that it was at the top of my wishlist from the moment I read about its existence. I waited patiently until I had the right time to do whatever I needed to do to get my hands on the game. Install Steam, even though I never had plans to do so previously. Purchase Elegy for a Dead World, even though I had never purchased any games or in-game purchases. This was the game that would make me change my plans.
And was the plunge worth it? Oh hell yeah.
I loved the gorgeous visuals that greeted me when the game launched. I chose to enter Keats' world, and I was not dissapointed. It was simply breathtaking, so beautiful that I explored so slowly, just to soak in the views, notice all the little details.  The audio crept up on me, mysterious, subtle, haunting, but never too overwhelming, which helps to evoke the atmosphere of the world. All these little things add up to create a richly-inspiring landscape, which is very helpful to writing if you ask me.
But the best bit was, of course, the writing. I was surprised to find that there are several types of prompts to choose from, which would definitely allow me to revisit the same world multiple times, because different sets of prompts would inspire completely different tales in my head. One of the choice of freeform writing is fantastic too. Even though I really appreciated the prompts triggering my imagination and creativity, I like knowing that I do have the choice to use the freedom to write whatever I want in that world.
My first try was to fill in the blanks at Keats' world. Not only did I enjoy the act of writing a tale inspired by such a breathtaking setting, my brain was already coming up with ongoing streams of ideas even before I received each prompt. The prompts were at first surprising, but I went with the challenge to create a tale that was shaped by both the prompts and my own words. I was again delightfully surprised to learn that I could edit the given prompts too, which further spurred my creativity as I played with various ideas and phrases until I was satisfied. This took me approximately one and half hours as I crafted and then refined my story.
Suffice to say, it was a real treat, happiness and satisfaction swelling in me as I finished that first story. I have since went back to Keats' world for a second visit using a different set of prompts. I still have several other ideas to write about that place. My plan is to try all the different prompts, and then attempt the freeform writing, and possibly go back for yet another try if I want to. I will do this slowly, over the weeks and months to come. I have yet to even touch Byron's and Shelley's world. I expect the other two worlds to be no doubt as breathtaking and inspiring as Keats', serving as the springboard to many more tales.
Oh, and gameplay has been quite smooth. No major glitches. As long as I can write without disruptions, I am happy.
One thing I will say about this game is that while it has been an enjoyable ride, I don't think it is for everybody. The reason why I enjoy it so much is because I derive a lot of pleasure from writing. My internal drive to write is why the gorgeous visuals and mysterious audio only added to the richness of the scene before my eyes, amplifying my enjoyment of the writing experience. How could I not enjoy the writing process when I could get inspiration in spades from this game? There are also, of course, some who will greatly benefit from the breathtaking visuals as a starting point and be inspired to write about it. But I doubt that everyone will enjoy the writing process as much.
If you're the type to glance at a scene and want to move on to something different within a short period of time, this might not be the game for you. But if you're the type who could marvel and admire a richly detailed scene for a long time, or if you're the type who could come back to the same scene to discover something new every time, then I would recommend Elegy for a Dead World. And if you like writing or plan to try it, I would also recommend this game.
It has been a rewarding journey so far, and I have just started. I cannot wait to see my future tales unfold in the three amazingly breathtaking worlds. I don't know the final forms of the stories, but I'm damn sure that I will find inspiration every time I visit one of the worlds.

Wow, this game is horrible. World of Goo was incredible, so i decided to try some more by the same guy, but this was just a waste of money. It's got good reviews... idk, maybe there was some artsy element that I missed, but I was just but I was just bored.
So you start off with a tiny stash of cash and a small collection of toys you can order. You order stuff and it appears after a delay, and then you toss it in the fireplace and burn it, which always gives you a few more coins than you spent. Symbolism for the insatiability hunger of human consumerism maybe? Idk, but it got old in a hurry.
Most of the toys react in some novel way as you burn them... the dragon breaths fire, the ear of corn has popcorn pop off of it, the moon changes gravity so things orbit it. I imagine you could make some tiny rube-golberg machines if you were so inclined, but the space is so limited that it's pretty limited so I didn't have much success.
Also there are hidden combos of items. If you burn certain items together, you've completed the combo. Once you've got enough, you unlock new toys to burn. So a big part of the game is looking at the titles of combos and trying to guess which toys are required, which is easy when you've only got access to a dozen items, but once it's closer to 100 it starts to take some trial and error. A message about sitting in the same place, looking at the same thing, and still searching for novelty? Might be a meta commentary about spending too much time on a computer looking for interesting games, but that might be something I'm superimposing on the subject.
There's a thin plot about a relation with the girl next door. You get letters, and exchange toys with her. She's fascinated by a mystery of the inferno. And the environment of the game, the whispers of the world outside the inferno are quite haunting. But, that was the only interesting part of the game that I could see, but there wasn't much of it.
Anyway, eventually you hit on a mystic combination of items and burn the house down, and then you've got to find something else to do. The end.
I usually enjoy artsy games and games with social commentary. World of Goo kept surprising me with understanded but poignant imagery. Little inferno though? No so much.
I unlocked all the items and completed the endgame, in about 3 hour, which was much shorter than I like to see a $10 game take. Maybe there was symbolism I missed, but this was just a waste of time and money as far as I could see.

To get right to the point, get the Crusade expansion for this game. It adds quite a selection of new mechanics to 4X the heck out of your GalCiv3 game. It also has many new features and AI enhancements (and continues to be updated with ever more AI tweaks as loopholes are discovered).
GalCiv3 started out well enough and was was quite playable at launch. However, over time I felt it needed more "shine". It wasn't bad but I just wanted a little bit more. Two years and numerous patches and enhancements later, it has come a long way and, to be honest, it's superior to what it was at launch. But, when Stardock released the Crusade expansion things really started to come together nicely. Yes, it still has some bugs but far, far fewer than two years ago. In short, it plays very well and so does the AI. The AI isn't perfect (no 4X game is) but it will give you a challenge, expecially if you are relatively new to the genre.
All in all, I'd say GalCiv3 (with the Crusade expansion...again, get it ASAP) is a good turn-based 4X that continues to be improved and added on after two years from launch (and more is coming). The road here hasn't always been pretty and the fans have had some heated disagreements with the developers at times, but together they have managed to put together a solid 4X game that should be enjoyed by any turn-based 4X fan.
Remember, GalCiv3: Crusade. Get it. You'll be glad you did.

I'm giving this game a contingent "yes". If you played FS2013, this is disappointing, if this is you're first time, then you'll like it. It's a good game overall but adds almost nothing in the 2 years since FS2013. Sure logging has been added but this is a game about farming, and very little has been done in the actual farming department.
First off, let me say this is definitely FARMING simulator and not USING FARMING VEHICLES simulator. What I mean by that is the concept of farming, what to do and how to do it in terms of growing crops is solid. What's not solid is the actual gameplay of the vehicles. The physics is pretty bad. The vehicles have no weight to them, accelerate and decelerate instantly, and have horrible turning physics (I'm NOT referring to the turning when you are attached to a tool but do not have a counter-weight up front, that is good attention to detail, but turning in general is awful). The cockpits are alright, but nothing lights up, very few instrument gauges work, and nothing is clickable. A few new vehicles have been added, mostly those associated with the new tree logging though.
Furthermore, nothing has been improved when it comes to growing crop. You still have the same options and equipment. You'd think the devs with all this time would add something new like beans or even vinevards or fruit trees, but no, same as FS2013. Same can be said for farm animals. Nothing changed. You also get the same side, repetitive side missions. This is a REAL big disappointment, 2 years and the devs can't even think of a new side mission?
The world still feels so empty and unlived in. There is no sense of "people" living around you. If you go into the one town you might see a one or two people walking but that's about it. There is some traffic but its not convincing at all. There is no AI really and they drive at like 5 mph for some reason. I wish the game gave you a reason to use your lights and turn signals when on the road, but with such unbelieveable traffic there's no option in even pretending to role play.
At this point you might be wondering why I'm recommending this game after saying only negative stuff about it. Well, if you haven't played FS2013, then you won't be so disappointed. The game itself is very fun and makes you think about how to manage your crop and sell it at the biggest profit. The little side missions are fun (considering you haven't played FS2013) for the first few hours and are a nice change for pace from normal farming. The graphics are generally nice and reasonably well-detailed. A nice touch added is that your tractor and farming equipment now get dirty with use and can be cleaned off with a pressure washer (although equipment gets dirty way too quickly). Overall it's a solid game, especially if this is your first time. If you ever see this on sale for $20 or less, I'd say definitely pick it up if you're interested. At full MSRP however, you should checkout some gameplay and really think about if this is the kind of game you'd enjoy. If you're someone who plays a lot of sim games, then the answer will probably be yes. If not, maybe wait for a sale to get the most fun/$ out of it

This was really, really great. Fast paced action with super tight controls, Dust does exactly what you tell him to, it makes it so satisfying to play. My advice to any regular gamers though: don't play it on normal, it's too easy, you'll outscale the enemies pretty heavily by the end of the game. So go for the harder difficulties. Overall, good characters. And holy crap I love Fidget so much. I don't know how many times I'd say something about what a character said, then she would quip the exact some thing I was just thinking. Favorite character EVER. Everyone else is great too. Dust, even Ahra are great, sympathetic characters. Almost all the characters feel like real people, not flat and lifeless like a lot of games have. I'd just like to know more about Gaius' backstory. And Fidget. There's was a bit, but not enough to get a full picture of where they were coming from before the events of the game.
Full voiceacting was great, all the characters were well voiced. They delivered the story believably.
Then there was the story. Pretty simple and straight forward. Yet, also really tight and well thought out. It kept things nice and grounded and showed all of the well paced character development throughout. Absolutely wonderful.1
The choice to go with animal characters was interesting. Largely because it allowed the game to tell a story about
without it being as obvious as it would if they'd gone with a human cast. The one thing I wish it would flesh out more in the story was how the whole war and all got started. Just what
Besides that, a little more explanation of Ahra, Fidget, and the blades of Elysium and all that. Where are all the other Nimbats and how do they fit into the picture of this world anyway?
So basically, I really loved what they did with the story, I just wish the backstory for the different aspects of the world were more fleshed out, to give you a better idea of how it all fits together into the story they tell in the game. Hell, I'd love to see a game with Fidget as the main character, telling the story that lead up to this one. That would be awesome.

Like it's predecessor, The Witcher 2: Assassins of Kings is a rather dark fantasy RPG that places you in the skin of the Witcher named Geralt of Rivia - a professional monster-slayer who, through circumstances beyond his control, always end up having to kill far more humans than monsters as he is dragged into the maelstrom of Byzantine medieval politics.
As usual for the series, The Witcher 2 shines when it comes to storytelling, and more specifically, when its presenting you the consquences of the choices you make. This goes so far that the better part of the game actually exists in two mutually exclusive forms, based on which faction you side with. Many of these decisions will be tough - in some cases, you see what appears to be a good choice and a bad choice, only to understand that the eventual results are the other way round and you should have picked the minor evil instead of insisting on being a naive goody-two-shoes. That the better part of the people with whom you work also has a perchant for screwing you over does not help.
Despite (or because) of its heavy penchant for story-telling, the game does have its drawbacks. The combat system requires some getting used to, the UI has been heavily streamlined to aid the game's launch on consoles, the side quests typically are lackluster and few in numbers, and although the game's maps seem to hint at a kind of open-world gameplay, the variety of places you visit actually is quite limited, as is the potential for open-world exploration. The Witcher 2 generally feels much shorter than its predecessor, even with the strong replayability factor of the mutually exclusive factions.
Despite of these shortcomings, The Witcher 2 still will be a treat for all people that like themselves a fantasy store that is much more mature (and cynical) than the typical 'Hero-in-Shining-Armor' babble of the classical High Fantasy RPG.
