I have a whole collection of blood-soaked, dark, foreboding, violent games because I really enjoy them.  I love first person shooters.  I love steampunk cities, dark mysteries and stealth operations.  But once in a while, it's nice to get away.  Have the game equivalent of a vacation.  Spend some time  reminding yourself that bright colours and magical places still exist.  Welcome to Abzu.
Abzu doesn’t set up the premise with a cutscene.  It doesn’t start with with a Patrick Stewart voice-over that explains everything.  You simply enter the water, and begin to discover your surroundings for yourself.
And what surroundings!  You glide gracefully through schools of fish, long swaying sea weeds, underwater caves, nooks and crannies.  You follow a linear path but along the way are large areas for you to explore.  These large areas contain a variety of sea life from tiny fish up to eals, even sharks and whales.  These larger areas also feature a statue on which you can sit and meditate.  In meditate mode, the camera will lock onto a particular fish and follow it as it goes about it’s business.  You can move from fish to fish.  These meditation spots can be accessed individually at any time.  Putting Abzu on has replaced my screen saver for ever.
Abzu is beautiful.  I have had to try constantly while writing this review, not to use that word in every sentence.  Its not something I can really effectively put across.  You just need to play it.  Screenshots look great but even videos don’t manage to convey how it feels to play. If you are looking for a challenge and some action, Abzu isn’t going to fit the bill.  However, if you want to have a beautiful, graceful and magical relaxing experience, I highly recommend it.

I have been looking for a decent competitive FPS for a while now, and it looks like I have found it in Paladins.  Graphically it is much nicer than Team Fortress 2 (and plays much better), and you can see what is going on (unlike in Lawbreakers).
Movement is smooth, weapons seem to do a decent amount of damage - and you can at least kill a few people without continually dying.
It does look as though cheaters (mainly with aim bots) are starting to purvade the game - which is to be expected with a free game.
There are other annoyances : If you leave a game, and then restart it, if the game is in progress you are dumped into the game again - only this time, the only way to exit it is to ALT+TAB and then kill the process.

This game provides many hours of fun - the main campaign is well over 10 hours, without knowing the exact length; but due to the difficulty of some of the later levels, you might not have the willpower to see it through to the end.
The story is engaging, as every completed mission brings a new development to the plot, and additional dialogue between the characters. It genuinely feels like the quests are there to accommodate the plot, and not the other way around, which is above what most RPGs offer in that area. There are over a dozen characters, six of which are generally your party members, and they each have interesting personalities and side issues, such as rivalries and romance.
There is a nice variety in the types of missions, but they most commonly consist of travelling through a maze of treasure-filled pathways with random encounters, until you reach the area with the main boss. Battles run long, even the less important ones, and you frequently must use multiple items to replenish your stats.
Exploration is limited to wandering the town, visiting shops, and speaking to locals who occasionally have something new to say, or some special item to give you.
There is a huge diversity of items to buy at the shop, and you usually have lots of money to spend. It is likely you'll need a lot of stuff for battles, but unfortunately, it is impossible to predict which items will be useful on your next mission.
The hitch of this game is that some missions are very difficult, and virtually impossible to beat unless you have the right items, and/or equipment. Often in these cases, the only thing to do is to go back to a previous save, lose up to an hour of progress, and buy the items necessary. If you don't have a previous save, you're simply out of luck.
Overall, this is a great game, in terms of both story and combat, but if you are intent on game completion, either remember to save often, or give the game a pass.

I purchased this game because every once in a while, I just want to play a "big dumb shooter" without having to engage in complicated gameplay or storytelling.  The Call of Duty franchise has usually been consistent at providing that simple niche; simple goals with a bunch of baddies in the way.  Sadly though, Black Ops fails to even provide that base experience.
Even by "Big Dumb Shooter" standards, Black Ops fairs poorly.  There is just too much going on to truly enjoy the experience.  I enjoyed the first two Modern Warfares because of the way they moved from skirmish to skirmish within each level and one moves at a consistent but self-provided pace.  In Black Ops, it feels as if I am being dragged along without truly providing any input to the gameplay.  In fact, a great deal of the time, I felt I could simply not do anything and the game would still play itself out.  Though there were a few shining moments (the prison break for one), they are lost within the mire of overstimulation.  The game feels much too hectic and yet at the same time, lifeless and unchallenging.
I did not finish Black Ops and I do not intend to.  Perhaps it gets better in the later levels but I just couldn't continue on with it because the gameplay is lackluster and (unsurprisingly) the story is uncompelling.
It's a good creative writing excercise with some good graphics. Recommended, just don't expect to get achievements from it, if that's your thing.

Fantastic game on par with Final Fantasy VII. The Final Fantasy series has been around since the dawn of the gamer age and many RPGs have been modeled after the success of this series. Final Fantasy VIII is no exception. It is to this day a masterpiece that  captures the imagination and brings one into an epic and unique universe.
Pros:
Great gameplay - The junction system allows for magic and summons to effect the stats your characters have depending on how strong and what type of magic is placed into which stat slot. There is an open world to explore, which can allow access to towns and secret locations. This feature was removed from Final Fantasy X onwards.
Unique Story - When this game was on the Playstation 1 it was 4 discs long. The game starts off with a cut scene followed by putting you straight into the action where you must complete a trial to obtain your third (you gain the first 2 from the computer room) Guardian Force. The game does an excellent job at character development and allows you to literally read what the protagonist, Squall is thinking.
Cons:
Dated graphics: While its true this is an old game, the graphics are still respectable and wont burn your eye lids off looking at.
No voice acting: You have to be ready to read a lot of text because theres no voice acting.
Conclusion:
Overall this game is a GEM and must have for anyone who enjoys Final Fantasy or classic RPG's.

It's also two journeys: first a story all about how Cloud's life got flipped-turned upside down and how he became the ex-SOLDIER of a town called Midgard. Secondly it's most likely gonna be a hallucinatory pub-crawl across Nostalgia Avenue--for you the player. I would lay-down several hundred words of dubious usefulness regarding the technical merits of Final Fantasy VII but, Steam's prescribed word count has spared you. You should thank them. So, instead of the controls, graphics, sounds, setting and the menu-hell--I am going to use this limited space to bounce around some slightly different noise.
or
, they say. Well, my major gripe about Final Fantasy VII is it's brutal apathy for the value of your time.
No no, I'm not talking about the leveling or farming, any of that can be dialed into to anyone's personal preference these days--like most games. What I am talking about is the game's penchant for providing content of limited availability and it's indifference in ever really indicating this to the player. A great example of this is very early in the game the morning after your first reactor raid while departing the slum for your next mission; there is a scene where you can have a short discussion with one of the protagonist's childhood friends, Johnny about him leaving town. However, if you were to walk into Johnny's parents house and speak with them first, you would learn about their troublesome son leaving town but, then when you exited the house Johnny would have departed and since you never talked to Johnny, you have no idea what those folks were ever talking about. It seems small in itself but becomes a thread that is woven into a greater quilt of disconnects between the narrative and the player. The effective experience at times becomes a PJF meme;
.
So, if you want to enjoy Final Fantasy VII properly--that is to say
--you will have to roll back to previous saves hours at a time and invest other countless hours in guides and walk-throughs. I can't be certain whether this opaqueness is something that is simply inherent to a project of this scope (but, editing is a thing--if it don't make sense and you aint got the resources to have it make sense;
) or, is it a vestigial remnant indicative of this game's epoch--a time where shrewd publisher's could sell game guides at twenty bucks a pop and the average consumer didn't grasp the concepts of artificial replayibility and fluff padding, that time when the defacto metric for a good RPG was how many hundreds of hours of "playtime" were contained in between it's many discs.
Ultimately I'll leave you ruminate on those implications and form your own opinions however, what that means for Final Fantasy VII as a game is that the organic experience is the significantly poorer one. The Game exists too gleefully as an enigmatic specimen that demands methodical scrutiny, one that will not forgive your failures of demystification. The best you can hope for are the moments of deliberate, non-consequential whimsy and even then there are things to decrypt. I want to love the game but, it pushes me away. It takes pleasure in torturing it's biggest fans in perceptively calculated impenetrability. To know Final Fantasy VII, you must spend your nights like Neo in the beginning of The Matrix, attempting to hook-up with your homeboy MoPho; trawling obscure and arcane forums, sifting through  the patterns in the static for any relevance there may be, while hoping and praying that you didn't (ohjesuschristourlordandsaviorgivemethestrength!) MISS anything. Final Fantasy VII doesn't care that I have other things to do, it just wants my time--
of it. And in true sado-masochist fashion--I lovingly capitulate like the loyal subordinate I am.
I'm coming back to this game and it's siblings in hopes to better understand the franchise as a whole. I look at XV and I am spellbound... until I hear how it plays and I cross reference that with what I recall from my experience with previous titles and then filter that through years of rose-tinted nostalgia and the sum total is;
The games have clearly changed over the years but, our opinions of what to expect from them really haven't. Maybe it's time. Let us sing our swansong to everything we loved about the past games and then visit the idea of working on some new

. Look, we still got beautiful boys casting even more beautiful magic in a world with the most fabulous hair-dressers and superhuman hair products. Breathtaking vistas, bizarre monsters (new and old favorites) and a lexicon of enough esoteric names that would make even Vin Diesel's DM  pine with envy (perhaps a few strippers too). All topped off with the perfect amount of that Japanese quirkiness we've come to know and love JRPGs for but, without heavy-handing it to the point that you hide the game from your friends. I think now is a good time for all of us to return to the roots of the series in reverence to everything Final Fantasy was in previous generations and to form an appreciation for all the things it will always be--now and in the future. 3. Ship design: it would seem like you can custom design your own ships but here are your choices: (depending on the platform) you can put 1 large weapon, 2 medium weapons, or 4 small weapons. Quite often it won't let you build the design you want without pressing the 'auto-complete' button which changes your ship design.
4. Combat: you have no control over your ships once they engage. You put all long range weapons on your ships, guess what ?, you are going to point blank range for fighting.
5. Game killing mid game slow down: has nothing at all to do with how good your system is according to the developers, even on their beast machines they get ridiculous slow down. Rather than build a new platform that uses multi-threading and optimization, they used an older gaming platform that assumes you are only using a single core with limited ram. By turn 200 you are experiencing a massive performance slow down of the game, by turn 300 (if you can actually make it there) the game is unplayable, a single click on anything in game may take 30 or more seconds before it responds, if at all. Making it to end game is all but impossible. So you play for a bit, then start a new game. Frustrating.
So in short:
1. you can design you own race, poorly.
2. you can design you own ships, poorly.
3. you can engage in combat, poorly.
4. you can play the game to a point, then you have to start a new game
If they fix the game slow down issue, this game will be playable. In its current form we are beta testers

This is one of my favorite shooter titles with a singleplayer campaign.  I can do without the Multiplayer, to be honest.  There's never really been a big shortage of shooters, and I think other multiplayer ones do it way better.
However, the singleplayer action is fun, loud and visceral.  My only big complaint is it doesn't feel like there's enough to kill.  With Reflex Time, which causes you to be able to move much quicker than everyone else, you can decimate and wipe entire squads with only your hands and feet if you choose.
Though the graphics probably aren't impressive at all by today's standards, when this game launched, the lighting system was one of the best.  The story is also told almost entirely through gameplay with only a minimum on scenes you can't control.  Though the story can't be altered (it's not an RPG), you can miss bits of it if you don't explore the levels.  Exploring offices, finding laptops and listening to voicemails are how you piece together various story bits and finding them all really fleshes out the story and brings a little life to the various NPCs involved.
What makes playing through a few times fun is all the various ways you can kill the enemies.  Sometimes stealth is possible, melee attacks are strong, precision pistol shots, making red mist with the shotgun, making pin-up art with the Penetrator, creating skeltons and scattering body parts across rooms with traps.  The game really needs a never-ending survival mode because combat is extremely fun, and is easily the best part of the game.
To me, this game is a classic.

The Binding of Isaac. So much I could possibly say about it. Let me start off by saying I have played this for about a full 2 days time (48 hours) and I have loved almost every second of it. Now that that is out of the way let me state the reasons I like it and a couple of things that I want in Rebirth. By the way I'm also talking about the DLC for this game in the review also so make note of that.
Positives:
The Graphics. The graphics in this game are just great.
The items. The game has so many items, there are still probably a ton I haven't found.
The difficulty. The game is purely skill based. The only time luck is involved is what you will get from rerolling and the slots.
The enemies. Sure you got flies and spiders which aren't that great, but then you delve deeper and find all sorts of horrors.
The creativity. The game just oozes creativity.
The story. I just like the story.
Negatives:
-Lemon Mishap and Wiggle Worm. These are two items I just can't stand. Lemon Mishap spawns are small circle around you which makes you move slightly faster. Wiggle Worm makes your shots move around like the Medusas in Castlevania, usually missing your enemies.
-No save mechanic. I understand that it was made in flash, and that saving will be in Rebirth, but I'm just warning you.
-Sometimes you need a bomb to get a bomb. This is just a little pet peeve but in some rooms a bomb is surrounded by rocks, which means you have to use a bomb to get a bomb. It's just pointless and wastes time. Sometimes it's a double bomb which is fine because you gain, but sometimes it's a single bomb.
That's about it. I would give it a 9/10. It's an extremely creative and fun dungeon crawler. Every game is different and requires skill. I would reccomend you buy it, and if you like it, maybe even Rebirth. By the way if the creator of Rebirth is reading this please don't change the graphics. I've seen what the new ones look like and I just really prefer these ones. I'm still going to get it regardless though.

I passed up on this game a while ago because I wasn't entirely sure about it. Just a while ago, I purchased the game for $5 on Steam and started playing it. This game is extremely fun. There is no reason for anyone who likes games to not get this game. The game costs $5 and I've already played it longer than some $20-$40 games.
STORY:
You play as Isaac, a small child who has been thrown into the basement under his house after his mother supposedly heard a message from god telling her to sacrifice her son. You, as Isaac, must traverse the basement, going deeper and deeper in an effort to survive the horrors in the depths below.
GAMEPLAY:
The game takes place from a Birds-eye viewpoint, and you control Isaac using WASD and his tear shots using the arrow keys or the mouse. His tears can shoot in 4 cardinal directions (NSEW) and are used as Isaacs primary attack. On your way, there are secret rooms to find coins, shops to purchase items, treasure rooms to get new abilities, boss rooms to fight bosses, devil rooms to give up some hearts for a rare and special item, and so forth. The game has enough variety to keep me coming back for more and trying to perfect my "run".
GRAPHICS:
The game uses a sort-of cutesy vector graphics format, which works well in contrast of the dark undertones of the game. Elements and enemies that need to stand out do so, while things that aren't as important don't attract your eyes attention, something very important in games similar to The Binding of Isaac.
BALANCE:
The Binding of Isaac is well balanced, but it is easier to talk about what is not balanced rather than talk about what is. Tears Upgrades tend to be rather useless, as they are outshadowed in usefullness by their bigger brother "The Damage Upgrade", and the knockback produced from tears can go out of control with enough tears upgrades, sending enemies flying in all directions and making it harder to dodge. The game is also based on luck quite a bit, from the upgrades you draw to the rooms that you find, but it also requires a lot of skill, something you earn from playing the game. Additionally, some of the upgrades just plain suck. Other than that, the game is well balanced.
OVERVIEW:
The Binding of Isaac is a Birds-Eye dungeon crawler with a fantastic concept and huge buckets of replayability. This game would be high up on my Top 10 Favorite Games list if I had one.

I really enjoyed playing Dust, it's a bit of a middling experience for me. The backgrounds and controls are great, I could move around feeling very in control, and for an action platformer that's pretty important, and it certainly scratches the fluid gameplay itch. There's hidden items, secrets, trials, and quests, so you can always do more, which is great as well.
I guess I just left it feeling like the sotry and characters were a bit too corny. It sort've reads like an anime fanfiction, without being too contrived or boring. The characters can be cute and funny, but the drama comes off a bit empty. I certainly didn't finish the story with a feeling of perspective or insight, it's pretty simple. The interactions of the three main characters are worthwhile in a saturday morning cartoon way, but I never really got into what Dust was doing or felt there was much at stake (even though there technically is). It has a pretty straightforward anime-like ending too, but in the end I still had fun playing.
The fighting system isn't very complicated, you just boost stats (it kinda forces you to boost all of your stats, because otherwise you can't continue boosting one, meh,) and you don't get many more moves then what you start with. It's not too much or too little, and while playing zooming around with all your crazy moves is pretty fun. I think I played on normal, and it wasn't ridiculous, but it wasn't a cake walk either. You can kill most enemies very easily, but some take a bit of strategy or you're just gonna get killed. Honestly, the fighting isn't all that diverse, and neither are the puzzles (it's 98% finding a bomb and taking it to a breakable wall before its timer runs out).
But in the end it made me laugh, it was fun to play, and I enjoyed exploring all the beautiful environments. If you're like me and just love seemless platformers, you could do way worse. Don't go in expecting a dramatic masterpiece and you'll probably have a lot of fun.

This is a fantastic platformer with a lot of polish. A definite must own for any fans of this genre.
The gameplay is a 2-D platformer with some RPG elements such as building stats and collecting loot, and crafting more powerful armor, rings, etc to buff your character. The controls are tight and responsive, however, quick movements while platforming and attacking can have undesired results in movement.  I played with a 360 controller and the button layout is great and is integrated perfectly with the game.
The animation style is good with 60fps throughout. The character animations during dialog sequences seems to get reduced to 30fps. Probably left over from the Xbox 360 port. The soundtrack is also wonderful and really stands out. The voice acting also needs to be recognized as it’s done really well.
The game is very rewarding in both combat and exploration. You uncover chests and keys required to open those chests by exploring each stage fully. It’s not too difficult as the map shows you if there’s anything missed in a particular screen and your companion Fidget will also prompt you. It’s a great guidance system for completionists.
One neat aspect has to do with the shops. You can sell the items you collect and the shop will save them and continually get more stock of that item. So if a recipe calls for something and you don’t have enough…the shop will most likely have more stock for you to buy to complete the recipe.
The combat, while rewarding, is also limited. You gain new abilities but no new fighting styles or moves. There are combos you can do but eventually you revert to doing what works over and over again.
+60fps (except dialog screen character animations)
+Great animation style
+Very good soundtrack
+Generally tight controls
+Polished
+Some light RPG elements
+Autosave and manual save (only at save points, which are plentiful)
+Rewards exploration
+Combat system can be repetitive

A wonderfully skillful game where every death is your fault and there is always room for improvement. Necrodancer offers a wide range of challenges among its many characters and modes, from Bard and Single Zones as training wheels for new players to Coda low% as a feat so brutal only one person has ever pulled it off (and only pre-DLC).
Although the rhythm gimmick may seem odd at first, it works really well when you realize that Necrodancer is actually a pure Berlin Interpretation Roguelike, just with each turn occurring at a steady pace. And having a fixed pace makes the game amazing for speedrunning and racing. There are lots of tradeoffs to make between survival and speed, you can start off by playing it safe and then pick up the pace as you get the hang of things. The head-to-head racing community is where things really get exciting, as you have to walk the razor's edge between losing because you went too slow or losing because you died.

Seeing there are so few reviews, I decided to share my own impression of this promising yet sadly overlooked game.
As a die-hard RPG person, I felt this game is quite different and refreshing. The story and the lore behind it seem very original and interesting so far, and they synergise well with the world's atmosphere.
The game feels very immersive, I think you can really see with how much love to detail they're creating this world. What I think is also a really nice addition is the idea of "role playing features", like being able to set up camp anywhere, to name just one. As far as I can tell so far, dialogues also give you enough options to allow for some more immersion, and I'm eager to see the choices and consequences they've planned.
The game world in general is very open, the landscape is gorgeous, and I think even just exploring a richly detailed forest can be enjoyable, if you're into that.
That said, there are, of course, rough edges and lots of polishing to be done. Some bugs here and there as well, though nothing game-breaking in my experience. What I'm most disappointed in however, is the (still) very lacking optimization. As pretty as it looks, the game is extremely demanding, so if you're playing on a somewhat older rig, chances are you might not even hit 30 fps on lowest settings, so be warned.
Content-wise, there's already several hours of storyline, but according to the devs an upcoming update would double that.
I really hope the IndieGoGo campaign is going to be a success, as the devs seem dedicated and this game certainly has lots of potential.

However, just like for all the games in the series, you are expected to master everything right from the beginning and you won't get a little bit of help (apart from hints during loading screens). And it is a difficult game. Therefore, I think that only regular players of the series will be able to enjoy it. Other than that, at more than 8 euros, it would be a waste of money in my opinion.

Destiny Warriors is a RPG Maker made game whose whole premise is taken almost verbatim off of the manga Naruto, even titles, characters, and events are basically the same. Storyline is bland and the use of vulgarity takes you back to when you were in middle school and started cursing for the first time. Generic, unoriginal soundtrack with a flood of grammatical errors help to unimmerse you from what would be a terrible game to an unplayable game. Battle system is riddled with tediousness and unbalanced scaling, just plain boring with a lot of glitches (ex: where the tooltip for certain abilities would let you attack multiple enemies and only give you one attack). Everytime I tried to take a screenshot or close the game it crashed by itself.
Battle System:
Enemies do little to no damage and spend half their turns defending and just dragging the battle out, one mob does about 20 damage when it attacks yet when it poisons a character they take 100+ damage a turn. Oh yeah, your characters start out with an absurd amount of health and level up at an insane rate despite killing the exact same weak enemies. Your main character does around 100 damage with his standard attack, the enemies you encounter at the start have about that much health. The kicker? Your characters do not actually have any weapons equipped when you get them, not even a basic rusty sword or anything which is just plain lazy and makes me wonder what in the hell are they infusing when they use weapon enhancement abilities? The majority of the ablities are lazy renamings (your non-clone clone jutsu also has thunder clone, fire clone, etc. variations) and have animations that don't match them at all. Based on the clips provided on the steam page it appears that even later in the game the damage values barely change if at all.
Pros:
+ If you don't know anything about Naruto then you might have some fun
Cons:
- Storyline is a bland blatant rip off of one of the more popular manga's (Naruto)
- Generic Soundtrack straight from RPG Maker
- Battle system is boring and unbalanced
- Dialogue is extremely poor and vulgar and full of grammatical errors that create and unimmersive experience
- Littered with glitches

2/10

Preface: This is a very SHORT "game". It honestly feels like a preview rather than the whole product. It's also certainly not for everyone. It's geared more towards the type of person who writes long headcanons for their villagers in Banished or create elaborate backstories for their Bioware characters. For people who have used programs like Zen Writer, this gets you into the same kind of simplified mindset-- there's nothing but you, the art, the sound, and the words. You won't get the editing and organizational capabilities of programs like Scrivener, but it's extremely useful for allowing you to write without the distraction of fiddly program features. That said, there's a lot to recommend it to gamers and writers alike.
PROS
+ Beautiful artwork. Like absolutely stunning.
+ Great prompts-- just enough to get you thinking if you need them, but without guiding you too much
+ Export option-- love the ability to export your stories, though only as HTML
CONS
- Too short! Needs many more worlds, with more complexity
- No spell check
- Space available for writing is limited to 1000 characters per prompt-- definitely not enough when you're on a roll!
- No ability to export as a simple word or txt document
- Atmospheric sounds are good, but repetitive (and loud!)
What I would dearly love is a game that expands on the worlds available by tenfold, and that gives a more comprehensive writing program with adjustable capabilities.
SUGGESTIONS (just in case the devs ever want to expand or someone wants to make a similar program)
* Add a lot more worlds
* Spell check during edit mode
* Quick access to each prompt area on a world from the end menu, with short previews of each prompt text (so that users don't have to read through each area chronologically to find where they want to edit).
* Include a manual save option so that we can simply press, say, f11 to save without closing the prompt box
* Unlock the word limit for each prompt area
* Allow users to import music from their hard drive into a "writing playlist" (like Zen Writer) to use when they don't want to listen to the in-game music/sounds.
* On-Screen volume control
* Export to text document option

I sat down and played through Byron's World once last night.  I ended up writing a pretty neat story that I was happy with, but I felt pretty worn out afterwards and wasn't sure if I would come back.  However I got home today and felt like pulling it up again... and I played through Byron's World again with different writing prompts, and wrote something just utterly different and also awesome.  I feel like this game is something I'm going to keep coming back to over time... I haven't even started on the other two worlds yet, and I could definitely spend more time on the first.
This game does a great job of providing you lots of creative cues and stimulation without pushing anything specific on you... the result is an incredibly wide variety of pieces generated by yourself and the community, sharing a handful of symbols and themes.  It seems suited to gradeschool classrooms, but it is certainly not juvenile.  I think the concept is an excellent one, and I'd recommend the game to anyone willing to put some creative effort into it.
It does have a lot of downsides, however.  One, the menu system is not great.  Publishing your stories and reading and voting on other people's stories is confusing; it's difficult to search through other people's writing (there's basically no tools for doing so, just one view showing most recent works and one view showing most voted for works); there are bugs and/or just poor behavior (like being shown the same story again and again even after voting on it).  But at the end of the day, once you figure out how it works, it is not too big a deterrant.
Perhaps more frustrating is the disconnect between reading and editing your story; you write and edit your story while walking through a richly illustrated landscape, and then when you are done you can read your story in a sort of picture book format, with images taken from the landscape automatically populated in your book.  However, you can't edit the story from the picturebook view as far as I can tell, and reading the story while walking through the landscape is slow and awkward, since it takes quite a bit of time to get from one place to another.  Looking back on it now, it is fairly easy to switch between book and landscape, but I just get a general feeling of clunkyness and frustration from the post-experience editing.
In conclusion, I think this is an excellent, novel idea, good for adults and children alike, and with beautiful artwork and well chosen, stimulating writing prompts.  It lacks a lot of UX polish, but definitely still worth the time.

Updates bring extra bugs - the current latest being is you cant replace the weekly quest (even though the icon for it is present).
The game can no longer be wholly recommended now unfortunately.  It is losing a lot of its shine.

WARNING: THIS GAME IS EXTREMELY TWISTED AND GROTESQUE!!! DO NOT BUY IF YOU ARE FAINT OF HEART AND/OR OFFENDED RELIGIOUSLY BY THIS GAME'S THEME AND BACKSTORY!!!
This game is really dark and depressing. Everything in this game is warped, deformed, and become/already are abominations, Isaac especially.
Anyway, the story essentially is: Isaac's mother is a deranged Christian that thought she heard God's voice commanding her to sacrifice her son, much like someone in The Bible, whose name slips my mind. Isaac is forced to fight his mother and her army of abominations to protect himself.
Pros:
+ The game is addictive. It's like FTL where it keeps you coming back for that "One last try."
+ The game's theme is really warped and twisted, which actually supports the dark backstory. Sets the mood quite well.
+ No two runs are the same. The game is completely randomized, so you never know what you'll encounter next attempt!
+ Decent character variety with unique special abilites they come with.
Neutrals:
+/- The game is a Rogue-like/Rogue-lite, which means it's really difficult as well as being randomized.
+/- The game has a really evil theme. THIS IS NOT FOR THE FAINT OF HEART NOR THE RELIGIOUSLY-OFFENDED!!!
Negatives:
- The game does not support 1920x1080 (AKA: 1080p) resolution. If you play on a 1920x1080 native-res monitor, be prepared to play this game in either windowed mode or fullscreen with bars at the sides.
- The game is NOT forgiving to newbies. You WILL die over and over and over and over and over and --- well, you get the picture.
- Lack of room variety. There's only a few notable rooms to my knowledge: The Angel Room, The Devil Room, The Boss Room, The Treasure Room, The Arcade Room, and The Glitch Room. While that list may seem like a lot at first, it rapidly becomes clear that you're only likely to find two of them; The Treasure Room and The Boss Room.
This game's worth your $10, overall. You'll definitely get your worth out of it if you play it maybe 10 or 20 hours.

I have never played F.E.A.R. before, but when I saw the game for $2.50 a while back I had to pick it up and put it in my backlog. Now that I've completed the series I'm writing reviews for each game.
Performance/Graphics:
Tons of video/advanced options available and the game is not intensive at all with current hardware. You'll more than likely be able to crank this game to 11 and enjoy it at butter smooth 60fps(or higher) with no drops whatsoever. Of course the graphics are dated at this point, but for a game that is over 10 years old at this point it holds up pretty well.
Extra Content/DLC:
The extra content is "worth it" if you end up liking the game and want more backstory. Technically the extra content isn't "canon" so if you're looking for more canon backstory then don't bother, but if you just want more to play then go for it. I personally did not play the DLC so I can't comment on them performance/combat wise, but I did read the wiki about the plot for them and I'd say they're both great additions.
Combat:
The game itself has very good weapon mechanics and varying weapon choices, also it has armor and health management, so use your medkits wisely and look for armor pickups when needed! You can hold four weapons at once and various grenade types. Fighting is fluid and the slow-mo(bullet time) the game features is a nice touch and it really helps when things start getting hectic, or if you want to see explosions in slow motion.
Atmosphere:
There is a horror atmosphere to the game and plenty of jumpscares/scenes that will make your heart skip a beat and body tense up. Definitely turn off the lights, put on a pair of headphones, and play at night to really make your skin crawl. Or don't and play in the middle of the day like a sissy, your choice not mine.
Story:
The story itself is interesting and definitely makes you wanting more. I'm not posting spoilers, but I can guarantee you this game has a great story behind it and is definitely worth a play.
Price:
Like I said I got this game and it's two DLC's for $2.50 a while back. For $9.99 I'd honestly consider woth picking up, at $4.99 definitelty pick it up, and if you see it for $2.50 you're definitely missing out big time if you don't buy it at this price point.

This is an absolutely fantastic game that is worth 4.99$ any day in my book. Besides The Binding of Isaac's fantastic zelda/roguelike gameplay, it has a surprisingly deep and intricate unlockable loot system, where you're always excited to get a new powerup or upgrade to add to your character that will cause him to look even more deformed and strangely creepy than he already is.  Moreover, this is one of the most replayable games I have ever played in my life, and while the amount of hours that most reviewers have logged on this great game can speak for themselves, I figured I would explain just why the replayability factor in this game is so huge. It's because every dungeon is randomized, with different items and upgrades, different bosses, different enemies, and different secret rooms in hidden locations every time you play. So while the levels themselves may be labeled the same (E.G "The Caves 1), every room you enter is unique to that specific playthrough, and there are absolutely so many unique items and powerups that it would take hours to list them all. Overall, I highly recommend buying this game, whether it's on sale or not, because I can guarantee you that if you give this game a fair shot, it will be one of the best 5 bucks you have ever spent in your life.
Sidenote: This game is also absolutely phenomenal for multitasking, I mean I can literally play this game while watching a movie or TV show like The Office, while talking to someone about deep matters, or while listening to a college lecture and still retaining all of the important information being handed to me. That alone should be a major selling factor for this game, because after you get the hang of it, you can play this game while doing almost anything if you know what I'm saying now.  5/5

This game... I cannot describe the awesomeness that I felt as I played it. First, I wake up in the middle of a forest thinking "Ooh, pretty!"... Then I get to hit stuff and feel like a NINJA. No seriously, the fluidity of the movements... I spent an entire hour going back and forth between two areas of the map just slaying the mindless grunts and feeling like a master swordsman.
Then there's the story. It's mysterious, funny, and a little sad, but thoroughly enjoyable. You play as Dust, the mysterious main character with amnesia, on a quest to find his identity... But fate has a deeper purpose in store for him.
You are accompanied by Fidget, who looks like some kind of flying fox-weasel but is actually a significant part of your offensive capabilities.
Oh yeah, there's also a magical talking sword.

Submarines are significant as they should be in something about the battle of the Atlantic, the game also has destroyers with the various ASW systems to fight them,
It reminds me of the early SSI type naval games that were intended as simulations. Its the only thing that has come close in a long time anyhow.
Hopefully the developers do well enough to develp this further, with multiplayer and a scenario editor, this will be hands down the most authentic modern WW2 naval game current.

I saw the reviews and I still ended up trying the game... ugh. Lots to cover and much to agree on with others.
The game description states an epic 12 hr JRPG and being a lover of RPG, I bought it via a bundle to try. Continued reading the description and yes, the plot is just like a familiar and famous ninja manga. The story plot is essentially large chunks of the ninja manga and that is just unfortunate. I feel the game could have had a much more interesting story than doing a spin-off. Next thing you notice as you start the game, is the english dialogue. This is either aimed towards a much younger crowd where the people either find cursing amusing/to be giggled at (oh my goodness, did that character just say that!) or the developers actually thought people would like such type of dialogues. My opinion: no. De-values the game and detracts from the game as well - too many errors in the dialogue. If you are even remotely a grammar nut, you will cringle throughout the game when the characters 'talk'. Next, the 'travelling' aspect of the game. There truly isn't much space to travel. The storyline is so rigid that you can't possibly deviate it, skip it, or come back to it at all. IE: you don't want to progress in the game, but want to explore the town/buy items/etc. More often than you want, you can't do it, because when you try to enter the store, your character may say 'I don't have time to do this, I have to meet ... blah'. To me, that detracts from RPGs I'm used and maybe someone likes it, but I hated it. I understand the need to progress the storyline and all, but severely limiting what a character can do in-between the plot is just aggravating to the player. Next, 'world map'. No such thing. You can't travel freely 90% of the time. Again, it's all limited depending on your progression in the story plot. Next, battle system! The game teaches you how to initiate, avoid, and fight. It's nice how they did it and through the game, I liked the battle design until a certain point. My gripe with the system is not how the battle system is made, but the balance behind the battles. Your characters learn new skills and techniques (xtu as they are called) as they level up (great stuff right? No need to find skill books or etc), their cost of using each skill or technique goes up. One skill can cost 100 and the next skill learned that is suppose to be the next level of the skill is 200. The amount of damage from the skill costing 200 does less damage than the skill that costs 100. That is ridiculous! Other similar things: 1) A skill says the ultimate skill, does 1 damage to the enemy, but a skill that you started the game with does at least 20 damage (WTF), 2) an enemy is clearly resistant to fire damage, but only to certain fire xtu - fire wall doesn't work well, but fire storm does (WTF), 3) the skill list is not organized for each character, 4) your xtu techniques doesn't get that much stronger as your character's level get stronger/you equip better weapons (IE: fireball deals 100 dmg at the beginning of the game, deals roughly the same when I maxed out the character's level with a much better equip), 5) TP reset - like mana, but they get reset out of each battle, which is aggravating because some skills need 100 TP for activation, but you have to either use an item or wait a round or two to reach 100 TP to even use it, at which point you will realize you will die before you reach 100 TP via a regular way. 6) xtu states randomly attacks 2 enemies, I use it and it ONLY attacks the enemy ONCE - the game is full of glitchs. Even aside from all those points, the most aggravating part of the game that made me stop playing (even though I bared with it all till almost the end of the game) is the balance between the enemies you fight and your character leveling up. Enemies in the game are progressive, meaning as you level up, they level up accordingly. You will notice it as you get stronger in the first part of the game. While this made me think the game is pretty cool to do it, it is broken. Once you reach your level cap - lvl 50, you will realize you are fighting eneies that are 1) higher level AND 2) above your combat statistics' capabilities (because the game was designed to have progressive enemies that will always be higher than you). IE: in a boss fight, there is the boss character and 3 henchmen. The boss character is WEAKER than the henchmen, because the henchmen follows the progressive enemy mechanism more than the boss. While you may think better equips, playing defensively, trying different strategies would work in the end, I assure you, it does not. There are items in the game where you can boost your character's stats. I bought LOADS of them to pump my characters up. The enemies just get stronger based on your stats. At this point, after the carnival part of the story plot, I am facing 4 enemies that are faster than me, deals approx an average of 1K~2K dmg per attack from each enemy, while my characters are max level, has the best equip they can get at that point in the game, exceedingly boosted, and their skills synergizes well with each other. I COULD NOT get past that battle for the longest time. I have died within 3 rounds of battle where the first round I'm attacking and the next two rounds I'm trying to survive, but fail each time. It's near impossible based on the progressive enemy mechanism. After a whole day of trying, I only got past it due to RNG - random number generator - on status afflictions. I got lucky and the enemies were stunned, paralyzed, or frozen. That was the only way I could think of to pass the battle. Which apparently, is the end of the game, because it states 'To B continued'. Yes, the game states B instead of BE.
Other things: the game tries to be funny and nonchalant about breaking the 4th wall in the game. No, that just proves how lacking the game was designed. This game can't even hold up a match to Deadpool's capabilities in breaking the 4th wall. The game also limits your ability to buy certain healing items as the game progress. IE: can't buy a potion that heals 25% of max hp, but you must buy the 50% one now. Minor thing, but not cost-effective in cases where I only want to recover 25%, but I have to use a 75% potion to do it as I can't buy the other one anymore. Gaining money can also be an issue in this game. You can get loaded with gold easily if you choose to get the accessory (lucky coin) and fight/grind in the game when there are monsters to fight. However, getting the money does almost nothing, but for you to buy healing items. Getting better equips can be argued to be a pro, but NOTE, this brings difficulties with the mechanism where enemies get stronger than you consistently as you grind/equip better items. At the carnival stage, there are some awesome armor and weapons to buy, but cost a lot. I was able to afford it, but because the stats on those items are so great, my enemies are THAT much stronger as well.
Overall, I played game for approx 14 hours with 4 hours of it being trying again and again to pass a battle via RNG and status afflictions. There are definitely multiple flaws in this game where I would not recommend others to play it. It's an aggravating game to play with all those flaws and even more so if you can't win a battle, because you are doing so well in the game due to the imbalanced design. If you want to play this game, you have been warned. 2/10 from me.

I'm rating this as negative, but really i want to give it a 5/10.
Some of what's positive about this game can be found in other RPG maker games. Solid combat system, weapon/armor customization, story focus, linear gameplay. There's also a decent amount exploration for optional quests, and chests are plentiful. I can respect the effort to try and make the story themed around ninjas to get away from the generic medieval rpg maker game (though i will explain an issue with this later). It's also interesting to see the author experiment with a skill mechanic with the tp resource as i don't normally see RPG maker games use anything other than mana.
Where this game looses points is in the writing. As an rpg maker game, you're writing is like %50 of the reason why people will pick up your game, so here are some notes about this games writing.
-The game tries very hard to explain things very clearly, which leads to a ton of extra text that doesn't feel like it's doing anything. For example the phrase "speaking in a soft voice" wasn't necessary because the characters dialog already had gaps and stutters in it.
-Thematically you're supposed to be a ninja in training, but the scenery you're in and the people you interact with aren't really themed appropriately. This is of course, an issue with making a game with RPG maker as there is a limited amount of sprites and textures provided to you, but that isn't an excuse for how jarring it is to see a knight is heavy armor in ninja academy.
-The plot itself was alright, until i realized that huge chunks of it were ripped-off of young naruto's story. Finally watching anime pays off!
-I never thought i'd say this, but the grammer bugged me. So many sentences just felt akward; I'm not good at mechanical writing in general so i can't explain why but half the dialog doesn't work out in my head cleanly. Normally weak writing isn't an issue for me, but for RPG's where a huge part of the investment is the story, it sucks and really drains the enjoyment out of what's supposed to be an interesting part of the game.
There is also a major issue with the abilities in the game, they are incredibly unsatisfying to use. Almost none of the mana based abilities do more than you basic attack, so the only reason to use your abilities is to either deal AOE (area of effect) damage, deal a specific elemental damage, or to heal.
Some minor notes: there is achievement for beating the character Zane in training, however you train with the guy twice. When you beat him the first time you don't get the achievement, which made me think the game was broken. Some clarification on that would be nice. Also i would like it if i had a chance to buy equipment with the party members i'm going to use, so i'm not having to guess what equipment they can use.
Ultimately i found myself liking the game, but i suspect that's because i'm a sucker for straighforward RPG games with linear progression, not because the game was especially good. It's not to not need a walkthrough to get through the game for once. If you've played other RPG maker game you know what you're in for, maybe get it for the easy achievements but otherwise i'd avoid it.

I recommend this game for writers, not for gamers. Yes, it is a game. No, it is not a typical game. It is a 2-D side scroller where the objective is to write. It gives many writing prompts to help warm you up to the concept (mostly from romantic poets Byron, Keats, and Shelley in the public domain).
This is not the part I like about the game. I like the freeform writing option. You are not limited to certain spots to write, and you are not confined to a previously written prompt. You can stop wherever you want and write whatever you want.
The art and music are minimalistic yet stimulating. I find myself staying in one area and writing for a bit and then moving to the next area to seek more inspriation. This works, because the music and scenery change as you wander through the areas. Neither are overpowering and act as more of a white noise to help you maintain focus.
I recommend this game to any writer. I would say it isn't necessarilly a $15-quality game, but if you are a writer, and it inspires your writing, then you cannot put a value on that.

Elegy for a Dead World, developed by Dejobaan Games, LLC and Popcannibal, is a unique experience to be had by anyone and everyone who has or had aspirations of becoming a writer. You will take on the task of writing the stories of this Dead World. You can either take on pre-created stories with fill in the blanks, or you can strike out on your own in several different areas and create a masterpiece with only your mind as the guide.
Graphically you are given a soft and colorful world, devoid of any body, minus you. There are several different areas that you will be interacting with, and each piece can be the key to the next part of your story. If you are going the pre-created story route you will notice writing quill symbols appear where the next part of the story will take place. You will also be presented with a side scrolling flow, which is fitting since you need a beginning, middle, and an end. The really nice thing though is that there are different levels in the scenery, so there's a feeling of depth to the worlds that you will be walking through. To guide you along your journey you will be walking a person in a suit through the areas. To be honest weakest piece of this entire experience is the person that you will be controlling, especially when it comes to time to write something into the story, the arm just doesn't seem to act the way it should on the being, but serious that's about it for weakness.
Since you will be penning much if not all of the story there's not going to be any voices to work with, unless of course you want to lend your voice as you type the story out (but of course that will be just for you, there's not option to record voices). There is, however, music, and it is truly haunting. I believe its that way to help add to the atmosphere of where you are, and allow you to think about what the next piece of the story will be.
The controls are quickly explained to you, you are going to be moving from left to right, and you will need to hit tab to enter a writing piece. You will also need to press up in you want to go into structures, or down into different areas.
You might have noticed that I've been shying away from the term game because this, to me, isn't a game, its a tool, and experience, that definitely deserves some attention. This is really a writer's sandbox. Sure there's a couple of boundaries you can't really break out of, the setting, and the overall theme (all though I'm sure if you really put your mind to it you could change the theme to whatever you want it to be). I've written a couple of stories, and to be completely honest every time I finish one I'm ready to write another. The experiences I have within these worlds stirs up my creative juices and I feel like I have to get more words out.
Now that being said if you don't like reading and writing when you don't have to, then this is definitely not for you, but for those who want to see where your creativity can take you, you have to try this out. Seriously, I was a little hesitant when I heard about Elegy for a Dead World, and wondered how well it would allow me to write my own stories, but after going through the pre-created stories, I have to say that I'm not only impressed but blown away. The greatest thing is that it digitally publishes your work to their own little cloud where others can read it and then comment on it. It also gives you a story book form where people don't have to traverse the world to read your story, but do get what you are trying to convey through words and pictures of the area where you wrote pieces of the story.
I truly hope that this takes off and that stories come pouring out of this. I would like to see more worlds to put my stories into, but as it is, this is definitely something that I highly recommend. This EASILY gets a 9.3 out of 10.

Little Inferno is a game about letting go of the past.
Like the writings of Aesop, Little Inferno could be described as an allegorical narrative. From the outset of the game, we learn that nothing matters, except for its capacity to burn. Even the rules of the game are among the first things that are incinerated. From there, nothing is spared from the fire. Photographs, cardboard hearts and letters, everything that could be considered sentimental is burned, destroyed, and forgotten. This is a sentiment that I can personally relate to.
Modern consumerism is also explored, and perhaps, one could argue, taken to its logical conclusion. Meaningless things are bought and burned to make way for more meaningless things. This is a cycle that can continue indefinitely, and unless you choose otherwise, probably will. It is a stark warning, but in this warning is also a kind of comfort.
In conclusion, there is much to discover in the modern computer game Little Inferno. It is a whimsical adventure that hides a serious side, and after extensive exploration I am left with one, final regret. It is a regret that I cannot throw my life onto a fire in the way that is depicted in this game. All I can do is take an overdose of sleeping pills and strike one final match, letting it fall into the strategically placed pools of gasoline spread around the house. This will be my final act. Goodbye.

I've been a long-time fan of Paradox and their game and was eagerly looking forward to their first game set in space.
The early game is fantastic. Early exploration, trying to get the economy going, potentially fighting off (stronger) neighboring empires. And there's nothing like watching your proud fleet being decimated to nothing by a supposedly weaker neighbor, just because you didn't invest in shields against their mighty energy weapons.
Now, there's still some bad. As others have noted, the game bogs down after a few hours. Once you have expanded, sectors are the key to keep micro-management to a minimum.
However, those have got to be tweaked through patches... as there is still plenty of micro-management going on:
- You can't assign ships to these sectors, so you have to hope that they create their own construction ships.
- That means that you need to build up multiple fleets and have to manually patrol them. While you can your fleet to be aggressive and basically attack any enemy station of ship in the same system, it would help if you could also designate a defensive fleet patrolling a sector.
- Collecting debris after battles is a nightmare.
- Assembling fleets is tedious if you want to spread it out across your empire. It would be better if you could design your fleets and then the various space ports in your empire start producing the required ships as needed and sending them to their rendezvous point.
But all of these issues, while annoying, have not kept me from thoroughly enjoying the game. Highly recommended!

Little Inferno is a great casual game with just enough goal-oriented tasks to keep you playing through to obtain every achievement.

F.E.A.R.: I’m not F.E.E.L.ing it…
When F.E.A.R. came out back in 2005 it was considered to be a game changer! Not on the level of Half-Life 2 or anything, but, people loved it! They always talked about how good it was. The horror elements were well done, the enemy AI was fantastic, the shooting was super great, and the graphics were amazing. You had to have a pretty beefy computer to play this game.
Maybe back in 2005. Because, man has this game aged poorly. Like, really poorly.
Not only does the game look... bad. It’s really not that fun either, sorry to say. Now this is probably due to the fact that I have ten years of games between the release of F.E.A.R. and now to compare it to. I can definitely see how, at the time, F.E.A.R. would have blown my thirteen year old mind. But as it stands, in 2015, F.E.A.R. is very underwhelming. It feels like a pretty standard shooter, with some cool bullet time and horror elements thrown in.
I’m sure if I could force myself to play more I would probably get something out of it. But as of four hours into the game all I’ve done is: run through long hallways murdering puppet soldiers in an industrial complex, and an office building, while occasionally being frightened by a little girl. And... she doesn’t show up all that much, sadly.
To be fair, there were moments where I was genuinely enjoying myself. Rolling up on fools with a shotgun and slo-mo sliding into them while tearing them to shreds with buckshot is really cool. Like the first 50 times. Then it just becomes an easy “I win” button. Now, the horror aspects of this game were the main draw for me. And trust me, they can be genuinely disturbing and definitely made me jump more than once. But, as you play through the game you can see the seams at the edges of the experience. After about two hours I could tell when the game was going to go from ‘action’ to ‘horror’ just by level design.
Big well lit area funneling into a small dark hallway? Scare incoming. Better turn on my flashlight!
Eventually I just got bored with the game. There wasn’t enough of the creepy to keep me interested, and the ten year old shooting and level design weren’t doing F.E.A.R. any favors.
I honestly spent a large chunk of my four hours trying to figure out where the hell I was supposed to go. Which is the weird thing, because this game is quite linear. Sadly it’s very easy to get turned around, and everything looks the same… Plus sometimes the level designers expected you to intuit where to go without any indication. I felt like I was playing Duke Nukem, or Doom, considering how many times a seemingly decorative A/C vent was actually the way forward.
I hear this game gets pretty crazy towards the end, but I can’t bring myself to continue any further. I wanted to try and complete every game I reviewed for this project… but, I don’t really want to spend anymore time on this one. Especially considering I have over one hundred more to do.
I think the coolest part of F.E.A.R. is probably the firefights. Although the shooting is rather lackluster compared to today, the effects of your combat are really cool. Glass will break, the walls, floor, and ceiling will have large chunks blown out of them. And large amounts of dust, that actually lingers, will be kicked up. It forces you to move around, and looked really cool. Plus the bloody aftermath was always satisfying...
The dust tech is the most impressive part of this game to me. Seriously.
Honestly, this game reminds me a lot of Psi-Ops, an old game for the PS2. It revolved around a paranormal military task force fighting against another paranormal military group. It had all of the same hyper violence, weird psychic powers, creepy horror segments, and strange meat puppet soldiers. Expect I played it at the time... so I liked it.
It’s not that FEAR is bad… It’s just like an old movie. It was amazing when it came out! It’s just, going back and looking at it compared to ‘modern’ releases, it just doesn’t hold up.
Luckily I picked F.E.A.R. up on sale for like $2.75. If you’ve never played FEAR and always wanted to. Watch a let’s play. Or, if you absolutely have to play it, grab it on super-sale. It’s… really dated.

Let's start with the good -
looks great, controls well, has a passable soundtrack, and the writing can be quite funny at times. I laughed often at the deuteragonist Fidget's lines, and while she was entirely grating at first introduction by the middle of the game I only found her likeable.
Unfortunately, main man Dust himself never improved much. He goes back and forth between being some edgy amnesiac dude to bland to a bleeding heart. He doesn't improve in motivation or reasoning, even after his exposition scenes. The villain meanwhile twirls his mustache at every turn while literally slaughtering men, women, and children alike. Fun.
This game never really marketed itself more than a simple beat-em-up, but the mechanics here are beyond simple. You have essentially four attacks - a ground clear, a ground slam, an air knock-up, and some attack where you spin through the air. Fidget also has the ability to shoot projectiles which are amplified by your spin attack, but there's very little difference between the 3 options and they don't interact with your other attacks in any way besides juggling enemies.
This wouldn't be a problem if the game was varied in other ways... but it's not. Enemies are basically all reskins of each other and the best way to play is button mashing due to the number of mobs that can clutter your screen. The game has a parry mechanic, but outside of it happening randomly the only times you bother to make use of it are for enemies designed to require its use. In fact, none of the attacks in your repertoire feel particularly natural to use - they all seem as effective as one another and there's no combo system to speak of. There is
degree of animation canceling utilized via crouching, but again it's pointless to use given how
requires absolutely zero strategy or mechanics to speak of.
Level design is passable at best and at worst makes you want to tear your hair out. Levels are simply too long for what they offer. Like the gameplay, they're repetitive and on the rare occasion things are mixed up, it's in an annoying fashion. I have absolutely zero idea why anyone would think that hazards that essentially explode randomly would be a good idea, much less to cover entire sections of levels with them. And surround them with spike traps. I certainly love having three hazards explode at once, leaving no opportunity to dodge, only to send me into conveniently placed spikes so that I may die without option. Fun.
Anyway, regardless of all these multiple faults I did, I suppose, have some fun with
. Despite the terrible story, the repetitive gameplay, and the occasionally annoying level design, the game did offer some honestly cool moments. The animations and sprite effects when dealing with a group of enemies can look amazing, and stuff like grabbing a guy with your sword then slamming him into a group of enemies takes a long time to get old.
With that, I'd recommend
to the younger gamer. It's something I would have loved at a young age, where flashy effects and simple gameplay were the bee's knees, but for anyone else I'd probably pass.

Many people believe F.E.A.R. (subsequently just called FEAR) is a horror game, which is not quite right. The term which I find most appropriate to describe FEAR would be "a military themed sci-fi/horror FPS".
FEAR and its two expansions, Extraction Point and Perseus Mandate, stand at the pinnacle of the FPS genre. Admittedly, FEAR lacks some variety in environment and enemy design. You'll spend most of your time shooting at enemy soldiers in offices and warehouses. But what FEAR is weak at is easily overshadowed by what it is good at, because everything else about this game is just
good.
The game takes a serious and realistic approach with a tight atmosphere, and is consistent with it. At one time, it handles like a military shooter where you fight against enemy squads, and at other times you'll be stuck in nightmarishly visions or surrounded by supernatural beings, which is done so well that it never really feels out of place.
All the weapons sound and feel amazing. From the dual pistols, which are a lot stronger than they look, to the futuristic Particle Weapon and Repeating Cannon, there's not a single weapon that is boring or not fun to use. The shotgun is one of the best in history of computer games.
The enemies aren't that rich in variety, but make up for it with their behaviour. For a major part of the game, you'll battle the Replica Soldiers. Even now, 11 years after release, FEAR is heralded as the game with the best artifical intelligence thanks to these guys. They can crouch through tight spots, jump through windows and move furniture to use as cover, not as part of scripted events, but as their natural behaviour. Replay one particular fight, and it will never turn out the same way. These guys are just so much fun to fight. What's more is that you can really see and feel how your attacks affect them. Shooting a soldier will make him stumble and throw off his aim, while nearby explosions will throw enemies off their feet and may knock them down. Replica Soldiers' behaviour, actions and reactions make them incredibly satisfying to fight.
The level design doesn't offer many varied environments either. Yet it's incredibly well done with love to the detail. You will almost always have multiple ways to reach certain places. You can run along a corridor and take enemies head on, or crouch through the vent and ambush them from behind. Despite spending a lot of time in offices and warehouses, you'll still visit some amazing and incredibly atmospheric places, especially in the expansions. A futuristic cloning facility here, a creepy hospital there, these places are memorable and well crafted.
When you're not fighting enemy squads, you're usually in the horror part of the level. Sometimes you'll experience this through some kind of dreams or visions sent to you by Alma, who acts as the main antagonistic force in this game. Other times you have to fend off otherworldly beings that appear through portals. FEAR offers frequent jumpscares as well as drawn out segments with tight and creepy atmosphere.
Both expansions are outstanding. Extraction Point is essentially more of the same, while Perseus Mandate cuts back somewhat on the horror parts while giving you more heated firefights in return.
FEAR and its two expansions represent some of the best the FPS genre has to offer, and easily make it into the top 5 best singleplayer FPS ever made. It is a must-play for anyone interested in the genre.

While I did not like this game as much as the original Witcher, it is still an amazing experience. You can tell the devs had a lot more money this time. The dialogue is a lot better, the voice acting is top notch and the graphics still look great.
The story is a lot more focused on politics à la Game of Thrones. It is more down-to-earth than the first game where you had to basically save the world. It is alright I guess, but I missed the fairy tale atmosphere of the original. This one is more dark and cruel.
The potions and oils in the first game were OP as ♥♥♥♥, so this time they are useless most of the time. You cannot drink during combat, they only last minutes and potions also have negative effects. The alchemy is dumbed down and not as fun.
Dice poker was also dumbed down. Fistfighting turned into a boring QTE. The new arm wrestling is easy as hell too.
What I liked was crafting. You can craft weapons as well as armor, boots, gloves and trousers from the stuff you find or loot from killed monsters. It feels nice and rewarding.
Combat in TW2 is a lot more difficult than in TW1. I started playing on Hard but about halfway through I switched to Normal because it was so frustrating. You do not feel like a god of rage dancing in the middle of a crowd of enemies swinging your sword anymore. Now it is more like: stab, stab, roll, stab, cast sign, stab, roll...
You can tell this game was made for consoles so the UI takes some getting used to. You have to scroll all the time.
The choices you made in the TW1 have very little impact here which I was quite disappointed about.
All in all I enjoyed it. It is still a great RPG.

After playing this game for a couple of days, I'm now ready to write a review.  I read all of the reviews, including those on Metacritic and other professional reviewer sites which said it was exceptionally hard.  So, I hummed and hawed, not sure if I should spend the money or not.  I'm glad I did because this game is not so challenging that it is frustrating and I abandon it.  It's challenging, but in the way that we want it to be so that we don't master it in two days and get bored.
The attention to detail is fantastic as is the sheer number of orders you can command your squad(s) with.  If you want a simple, "no read the manual" kind of game that you have a handle on within 5 minutes, look elsewhere.  But if you're willing to put just a bit more time into it -- not much -- then buy it.
Conclusion . . . If you are into the Vietnam conflict, I give this game an 8.7 out of 10.  If you're just a fan of the genre in general, I give it a solid 7.8 out of 10.  My only advice is to stick with it for more than 5 or 10 minutes.

Cons, or bugs I'm sure will be fixed:
For me, even with a pretty decent rig, I experienced the choppy areas and strange looking rock and water textures that have been reported. I've read that they're working on the FPS performance already, so I'm very much looking forward to the patch.
Combat for me is frustrating and a bit clunky, not sure if it's because of the engine or the performance issues that are being addressed. Some of the controls aren't explained or easy to find, like switching between first and third person (I know it exists, I just can't remember where it was in the demo) and sprinting is caps lock rather than shift. I'm sure these will also be addressed as they receive reviews and bug reports.
I've noticed a bit of dead space between areas with not much to explore between them, but I'm also just tinkering around on novice mode for the view. I'm hoping to eventually run across some more distractions between the back and forth quests. :D
There IS a bit of back and forth so far, if gopher (go-fer/fetch) quests aren't your thing. I gripe about them when I'm playing, but ultimately enjoy the exploration.
Pros:
It's a unique story, one very well thought out with quite a bit of lore behind it. While I'm not typically a fan of playing as a beast race type character, the lore fascinates me, so I don't mind it much. And I'm REALLY looking forward to being able to play as an Icecore. :D The artwork is great, music is great just from what I've heard so far, the voices are pleasant to listen to through all of the dialogue, which can be quite lengthy at times. I list that as a pro because I like story time, some of you might be a little less patient with lengthy dialogues. Though if you're looking to play an RPG, I can't imagine why you'd dislike that, except I suppose to get on with the killing and looting.
Class selection is pretty extensive, giving us old favorites like warrior, rogue, mage, along with different ones I'm eager to try out, like warden. We'll also be able to make our own from scratch--I sense the potential for quite a bit of re-playability there, and I hope there's some different dialogues to go with the different class/RP styles.
The interface, while confusing at the moment, has the potential to be nice and simple once polished and explained a bit more thoroughly, and I know what exactly I've just equipped. Looking forward to relaxing with a nice pipe, once I actually manage to acquire one.
The landscape does have some lovely bits of scenery, and I'm a sucker for firefiles and a pretty night sky. I also enjoy long walks along the beach...
I'm probably leaving out quite a few things, but I don't want to throw out TOO long of a wall of text, and some of what I've encountered so far will be more appropriately reported on their bug tracker forum for fixing. If the story interests you at all and you can spare a few bucks, I do actually recommend purchasing it, even at this point, knowing you're still playing a work in progress. No matter how extensive beta testing was and will be, there will always be issues that come up that a wider audience with wildly different gaming rigs will discover. The best way we can show support and to help the devs out is to report bugs and issues, and provide constructive feedback. I have a good feeling they'll listen. :)

Even for a super cheap RPG maker game, this is pretty bad.  Every enemy is a damage sponge.  They also use defend actions constantly, dodge a lot, and you miss frequently.  Every fight slogs on way longer than it should, and these were just the opening fights in the first zone.  I couldn't stick with it long enough to get to a boss, but based on the evidence, I'd guess that would be even more sluggish.  I've played a lot of rpgs over the years, and I've never had so much trouble just killing slimes.  How do I hit one low level flower, which is for some reason a sentient enemy, with a fireball, a burst of shadow magic, a lightning infused broadsword, and a flurry of blows, and still not reduce it to even half its health?
As for the story and character stuff, I've never played a Naruto game, but I would imagine this is what they are like.  You play a group of graduates of "ninja school".  Just like ninjas in the real world, you are teenagers in brightly colored uniforms, brightly colored headbands, and brightly colored hair, using magic to do battle with forest vermin.  For some reason, even though you all still live with your parents, you have a lot of facial scars, and several of you are suffering from mental disabilities.  I know there are plenty of people who would be excited by the prospect of some sort of Naruto sprite rpg, but for me, it just made me want to throw up a little bit in my mouth.
I didn't play for very long.  I suppose it's possible it gets better eventually, but first of all, I find that extremely unlikely, and secondly, I don't care enough to find out.  I think I paid a total of like a quarter for this game in some rpg bundle during a sale, and I still feel like it was probably not a good deal.

This is a game about walking the ruins of empty, dead worlds and writing about what you see and what you feel. It's a good introduction to writing from a prompt, and the three worlds presented all have somewhat different styles that suggest different storylines. Each also has several prompts, providing structures for your writing from prose to poetry to comedy songs, so even though there are only three worlds there's plenty of replay value in each. You can also read other people's creations based on the same prompts as you, which can be an interesting window into the writing of others and sometimes lets you stumble on a small-scale masterpiece or two.
My only complaints - and they're trivial ones - are that the game does nudge you towards a somewhat melancholy outlook when writing, and if anything the visual cues are
at guiding people in their writing, leading to similarities in the stories written about each world even when using different prompts. But these really are minor issues.
Also, I want more worlds to explore - but that's just me being greedy.
If you're interested in writing, or just unusual games that are a step outside the norm, pick this up. Play once or twice through each world, read what other people have written, and you'll have your money's worth in no time.
