My one piece of grief is the placement of objects. When you setup walls and then try to put a drink machine or a plant next to the wall it never sits against it. The game seems to be setup with a grid but the walls sit on the lines of the grid. So objects you lay out don't line up to the walls. For example your drink machine is probably a couple feet from the wall which looks funny when trying to make your office aesthetic.
Summary, great time wasting game that will kill some hours while laying in bed watching TV. It's not quite involved enough to really dive right into. The price is perfect for what you get though, recommend the game 100% but it's probably something you'll play for a couple weeks and move on.

So I have never felt compelled to leave a review on a game before, however, I started to follow the progress of this game when I came across it here on steam.

My only con at the moment is that the employees feel a little bit lifeless, it feels like they need some animation, walking in, in the morning and back out again at night. Maybe walk to the water machine, or a managers desk. Something I hope is added further down the line.
Another, comment, not really a con, is that when it goes through night mode, it gets a little too dark, this doesn't help if you want to do some admin during these hours, e.g. change tasks, build offices etc.
Overall, great game with stacks of potential, and for this price it is an absolute steal!

Paradox has become my new favorite game developer.  Their Europa Universalis is endless fun; it has the depth of gameplay that other strategy games are lacking.  It keeps delivering more entertainment the more time you put into it.  So I was blown away when I saw that the same developers had made a SciFi strategy game.  So much inventive and thoughtful content went into making this game where most other SciFi game developers seem to put in the least amount of effort possible (or less).  For example, the possible races are weird but numerous and plausible, and the preset lists of names for different races' ships make sense and are clever, e.g., bird fleets can be called "murders."  The look of the galaxy map is great with plenty of detail, but the game won't bog-down your computer needlessly like other SciFi games.  And the politics and ethics systems are realistic as opposed to corny.  Stellaris doesn't have quite the depth of Europa, but there isn't a rich history of space colonisation for Paradox to draw on.  I've never writen one of these reviews before, but I felt compelled to support Paradox in the hope that they continue producing great games.  For Stellaris, I hope more personalization of the ships and perhaps a slightly more detailed planet surface mechanic would be available in future DLCs.  There are also the trade details that Europa does so well that is lacking in Stellaris.

I am a sucker for scuba diving games now since I played Endless Ocean on the Wii. When I saw this, I was taken completely by surprise. Everything, and I mean, everything looks absolutely GORGEOUS. The artstyle has that "Journey/Wind Waker" cell-shaded style which I'm into (less is more).
Unlike my experience with the Endless Ocean series though, there just isn't much length to the game. I completed this in less than 2 hours, and I didn't really try to rush it. It's very linear and there's no challenge whatsoever unless you're trying to look for for the nooks and crannies hidden in the game. The story is very shallow, but it's an art game anyway. It's supposed to be subtle and not a thousand page essay given to you. It's kind of how you want to interpret the story.
The gameplay isn't much, if not awkward at first, since a lot of it is holding the right trigger to swim, press A to boost, press X to interact and use the analog stick in weird ways possible, but you can fix the settings to your liking. But hey, it's an artistic diving simulator, what did you expect?
The way each chapter executes is perfect, from the transitions using jetstreams to the overall color choices and music that times in perfectly. Barely do the chapters really repeat the same exact formula, so if you're going in blind, don't expect the same thing to happen every 15 minutes.
It may not be that perfect of a game. In fact, it's not a game at all. It's an experience to reduce stress and relax in the art genre. I'd recommend it, but like a few other people, wait for a sale, because $20 is a little steep for a 2 hour game, but I will definitely be repeating it whenever I feel like it.

This game is epic!
190 hours for 40 bucks and I forsee 1000+ hours of game play I will get out of this in the end.
Game starts out with a 4x feel that I have never seen before and I have played a ton of 4x games.  The exploration and first contact is perfect.  I can replay this game a million times and play out the early game like no other 4x out there.  The hunting of monsters and exploring of systems and events are awesome and in very good supply.  Im still finding new events I have never seen after many new starts. Tech is handled in the best way I have ever seen.  You basicly get 3 cards to pick from every new tech you research.  This make tech interesting and diverse, it also changes up your tech "deck" based on the different traits/ethois you pick.
The Grandstrat of the game is not on par with EU IV or CK II but its got allot of potential.
The end game could use a bit of love but I have taken an empire 300+ years and had fun the whole time.  Took well over 60+ hours of game play to the finish a map depending on how you handle the speed.  The end game events are cool but could use some balance fixes and AI interaction improvements.
I feel like the majority of development went into the new idea and exploration/graphics of this game knowing that expansions can bring in a ton of the GS content if people really want it.  Had it been a $60 game it likely would have taken another half year or so and would have been what we will have in an expansion or two.  Im happy to play now for $40 and see if I want the expansions (hint: I will)
Mods will also start to come out of the wood work.  This game is really easy to mod.  I have done a simple mod to expand tech costs to slow things down and added more hitpoints to ships and stations so they last longer in combat.  There are also a ton of mods already out there like 40k and more events mods but they are shadows of what they will be in a few months.  A B5 mod and Star Trek Mod are defently being made and will be perfect for this game.
The MP of the game is awesome.  I have 8 friends that play currently and have spent around 100 of the 190 hours of game play in MP games with friends.  We have so far got up to 4 players in one game but are hoping to soon get a 10+ player weekend game going.  Currently its go to MP game for my group of friends.  Hot join is awesome and the ability to play with mods and expansions along as the host has it will insure that even if my friends don't get the expansions we will still play with them in MP.

I think that Zeno Clash is worth playing, especially for the ridiculously low prices for which it can be purchased during sales.
The combat is interesting and varied up until you are required to apply the same mêlée combat techniques to the majority of enemy types. There are more than 10 different fighting moves, without regard for any of the hand-held weapons, but with time you will find certain combinations to be most effective.
During a one-on-one fight you can easily achieve a nice, powerful rhythm - however, when there are many enemies it can be difficult to single one out to focus your efforts.
For less gung-ho players this may result in the tiresome process of wearing multiple enemies down one jab at a time. Drop a grenade amongst foes to speed things up.
From this you may infer that too much of one thing can become dull, so luckily this tedium is broken up by special enemies that require more than fisticuffs.
For example, heavy-set enemies can be overcome by using evasion or timed attacks to bring them to a state of vulnerability. Large, mentally-unstable enemies' weaknesses must be exploited to bring them down to your level so that you may cure their neurosis with, you guessed it, more punching.
This does something to alleviate the familiarity of the dodge-punch-block-kick reptition of fighting, though these types of enemies are, too, used repeatedly.
Sore knuckles and noses is not the only draw card for Zeno Clash, and if you aren't going to play for the combat then please play this game for the fantastic artistic design - for the music, visual art and script.
I found the surreal landscapes and the outlandish flora and fauna to be both beautiful and unsettling. The ramshackle settlements and deformed, (often literally) animalistic citizens had me yearning to see what grotesqueries would arise next and I found this incredibly engaging for the duration of the game. The voices are many and varied, highly emotive and serve to easily differentiate the actors and how they feel towards the protagonist - as well as showing their individual strengths and weaknesses of character.
If you appreciate well-executed gameplay and beautiful art direction then I believe that you will enjoy Zeno Clash as much as I did.
If you have played it already then I urge you to buy it for a friend who has missed out.

Firstly, this is a  review in progress.  Seeing as I've only had a first impression.  It would be unfair of me to give a negative review without having had a full experience.  My revulsion is reactionary based upon what I believe to be mundane expectations of a space 4x game.
Combat-there isn't any.
Galactic Civilizations III is considered one of a couple standard bearers for the 4x genre.  Specifically the 4x genre with a science fiction setting.  As you can imagine it's in many ways a high quality game.  However, I'm nonplussed that any game that claims the genre would abandon tactical combat.  Unlike many younger players, I prefer turn based combat.  I'm talking about a system like Master of Orion 2 which you may purchase at GoG for the price of five candy bars or whatever.  Galactic Civilization III involves many more lower tier combats such as space pirates in order to somewhat satiate that normal 4x desire of seeing your fleets perform.  However, not only does the game allow you to cheat by having a preview of the forthcoming combat results (not even kidding) it gives you a simple procedural combat video that has already auto resolved based upon stats and loadouts.  There were auto battling functions in Master of Orion 2 so it's not as though I'd be averse to auto resolved combats as an option-especially in regards to lower tier combat.  However, you lose something when there's that small ebb and flow created by player error or merit in tactical events.  The strategic layer of war is as well represented as you could; involving fleet placement and logistical concerns like resource exploitation.  I know nobody is looking for logistics simulator 2000 (not a real game) but it was a given that fleet placement matters.  As it ought to be a given for turn based combat-because there is more player interaction from a tactical perspective in gosh darn "Twilight Imperium 3-4," these are board games.  At least the player is inputting rolls in the tactical combat.  It's a saving grace to varying extents based upon your taste as a player, that you still have control on customization.  However, after a few play throughs this surely will be more an element of min-maxing provided that you do not absorb a gaming FAQ first as I'm sure is a feature for this generation of gameplayers, because their lack of outrage is troubling for the future of the genre-it really is.  Part of the exploration aspect of a 4x, especially one set in space is the notion of not knowing whether or not that you had researched and customized a fleet that could stand against the likes of an unknown adversary.
Side note:  This is no fault of the genre particularly, however wouldn't it be interesting for there to be a game mode wherein there are progressively more advanced and ancient aliens based upon how much closer they are to the big bang?  That your civilization would be allowed to compete with other peer civilizations as it attempts to ingratiate itself with the elder civilizations?  That a victory means being accepted as a to quote this game an ascended galactic civilization.  That your own peers could vary in development in regards to whether or not they had survived mass extinctions or weren't subject to one?  The parity of a medieval fantasy 4x denotes that the races developed more or less on the same time scale.  I know that this would be too punishing for most gamers, but it's intriguing isn't it?  Another thing that would be interesting to me in particular are moving galaxies.  For instance it wouldn't change the map you already see.  However, an addition to the map would be random arms of another galaxy for space empires on the edges of the map.  The cultures there maybe interacted with much in the same way as those in your own galaxy except for a limited time.  If you would be so bold as to expand into another galaxy prepare to be cut off from the rest of your empire on the notion that you'll have only the spacecraft you took with you initially.  So you'd have to have the foresight of colonization in order to sustain yourself.

A gentle nudge on the stick gets you good control in fast corners, slightly more pressure gets you through tighter ones, and everything jsut felt good. Come here, I've started this game several times. Every time, I spend about an half an hour trying to tune the controls to get the same nice, responsive feel that the first Shift game had, and every time I fail. How much the car turns compared to how much you push the stick on the controller just doesn't feel right. Transitioning between small and large steering adjustments are way too sudden, making it stupidly hard to tune the controls for both fast and slow curves. The stick goes from feeling completely unresponsive to over-sensitive in a fraction of a second, even with speed steering off and deadzone at zero. I"m going back to the first game.

This is a very solid 4x space sandbox experience.  Given its extensibility and depth of systems, it has infinite potential.  It has all the mechanical bells and whistles of a solid game.  The developer has regularly updated with both base game and dlc related enhancements.  It's a gorgeous game graphically and can produce some insane maps.
Its weaknesses lie in a lack of a tactical ship combat system.  It's frankly as bad as Stellaris in this respect.  There's detailed ship designs, but the strategic layer isn't internal to actual combat (like your ragtag crew can't out-tactic the big bad).  The other weakness of this game is in its lack of immersion.  They have a good basis for lore, but it falls flat in the actual gameplay (even the campaigns are kind of weak).  I guess with its extensible nature, perhaps immersion can be modded in or left to the player's imagination.
All in all it's a pretty good game, and I would reccomend to anyone who isn't looking at a strategy game for narrative (unless you're creating your own.)

I flippin' loved this game.  Do yourself a favor and get it.
I had played Witcher 3 prior to this game so I was expecting it to be not as good, just learning backstory.  I was wrong.  I may even like this game BETTER than 3.
The graphics are of a different style, but that style is stunning.  It's not as open world as some would like, but I find the more you open up a game, the less impact each choice has on the world.  To me, there is little more interesting than determining the fate of kings and nations.
There is a completely different second act and part of a different third act depending on your choices.  This demands a second playthrough.
Each character is so well done and interesting that when the game is over you miss them immediately.  You will have an opinion on every one of them, as opposed to the many games that have gobs of npcs blurring into the background in a fog of forgetability and boredom.
Triss Merigold is the dream girl for most red-blooded males, and the type you actually want to save, but you most choose if you do.
Letho is possibly my favorite antogonist in a game.  He's a regicide, a master of subversion, a witcher that throws the realm into chaos, and yet I never really found myself hating him.  When you finally catch up to him in a wild-westesque showdown, you're as likely to want to have a drink with him (which you do) as kill him.  But again, that's your choice.  You can be the angel of vengence, or you can let your old friend go.  Incidentally, if you do let him go, he shows up in 3.

Excellent shooter with a horrific background. This games mix intense firefights and scary moments. The story is also nice, which is rare for a FPS. Graphics are also nice, and the illumination is really nice with the shadows.
There is also a slow motion "power" you can use a bit like in Max Payne, which is very useful for the hard situations.
Regarding the expansion packs, the first one, Extraction point, is a nice sequel to the regular game. The only thing is maybe it has less "scary moments" since there are few during the campaign, but a lot at the end.
The second expansion, Perseus Mandate, is really great. You follow another group during the events of the first campaign. There are nice features added, a good challenge with more nervous firefights, and nice scary content. I really loved this expansion.
To conclude, I strongly recommend this game, specially because you can have it for a few $/€ during sales.

Abzu creates one of the most relaxing, stress-free underwater experiences I’ve ever played. By emphasizing freedom of movement over survival, it gave me all the time I needed to soak in its gorgeous art direction, marvel at its fluid controls, and listen to its epic orchestral score. During the course of this fascinating three-hour adventure full of deep-sea mysteries and discoveries, its moving melodies ebbed and flowed with my emotions and fueled my curiosity to reach the finale.
Abzu’s intriguing underwater world is presented with little introduction – you’re a mysterious diver who awakens and begins to explore – but it generates enough mystery to propel you through a series of stunning locations. From seaweed swaying in the current to mysterious sunken shrines, each area shows off Abzu’s fantastic art direction, attention to detail, and an impressive sense of scale as you swim through enormous chasms under the sea.

ABZU can only be described as an experience. It's a swimming simulator that takes the player through different, varied, and colourful environments with fantastic orchestral music for different levels. Much like the game Journey, ABZU relies on simple puzzles to finish objectives, and thus requires little in the way of brainpower. It anything, this game is the perfect game to sit back, relax, and chill - to go with the flow of the water and the waves.
The art design and detail is absolutely gorgeous, and there are plenty of different fish and sea creatures to fill the varied levels you swim through. This also includes the lighting, which I thought was absolutely gorgeous, especially when there were large schools of fish swimming about. I also liked that, though the game uses real species of sea creatures, the combinations of the creatures with the environments gave the oceans and otherworldly feel. The game feels a little strange to control and move about (almost sluggish) but I did not feel it to be too much of detriment, except for one section where a bit of precision is needed to avoid traps.
ABZU has no solid story, and what story there is can only be inferred from pictures and ruins that you travel through, as well as some physical interactions that your character performs. It gives a great glimpse into the world, but if you're seeking something more concrete this game won't be up your alley.
ABZU is visually stunning, and I personally liken it to a moving painting as you transition through the levels. Despite this, it is still very short, and while I would like to recommend it for the full price, I think this game is better with a discount. However, if you enjoy games in this kind of niche, and enjoy the experience aspect, definitely pick it up at full price if you're able.

Little Inferno burns briefly and beautifully, deserving praise twice over for both the casual game on the surface and the moving story hidden beneath.
At first glance, Little Inferno is a simple game. Set things on fire, pluck money from the ashes, order more things, wait a while for them to arrive, set the new things on fire, repeat. Repetitive, but the sights and sounds of fires consuming a variety of flammable objects are varied and exciting enough to burn away any tedium. There are also Tomorrow Stamps (which allow instantaneous deliveres) and the game doles such stamps out generously through either chance or by igniting initially-unknown combinations of items together. Little Inferno includes a check-list of these combinations to fill out, giving you another activity of investigation via incineration.
But there is more, beneath the plentiful ashes and behind the humorous satirizations of casual gaming. As you kindle and scorch, you'll find yourself introduced to a small cast of characters through combustible correspondence, sharing stories of themselves and the world outside. Little by Little Inferno, this game fuels a fiery tale, building up to an explosively satisfying finale.
Overall, this is a game I can easily recommend. Whether you buy it yourself or for an unsuspecting friend, Little Inferno is one hot way to burn a few hours and warm your spirits.

This one is difficult to review.
On one hand for the price of the game you get quite a lot of new features andcontent that you may not have experienced before in a space 4x. It may keep you playing, but just barely.
All the new features aside, it lacks a lot of the great stuff other space 4x games have used in the past, and some features are down right bare bones.
-espionage - does not exist
-diplomacy - barely useful and bare bones
-space combat - is (except for the retreat buton) a completely un-interactive, is a visual auto-resolve
-ship customization - poor and not very meaningful
-game performance - mid to late game there is a horrendous amount of lag and stutter
-ground combat - poor but as a defence, few if any space 4x have done this part any good except for Star Wars Empires at War.
-planets -Steallaris makes these a more interactive and fun and does it better of most 4x space games. But they are still not meaningful or strategic. Other 4x have done a much better job.
Overall, for the price of the game, if you are really hungry for a space 4x game, then buy this. You will still get some satisfaction.
If you're good and are somewhat interested in this in passing. Then don't buy it, wait for more patching and DLC. It may still yet get better.

-Good graphics

Cons:
-No up-to-date game manual or in game encyclopedia.  You will have to hit up the message boards or the GCIII wiki online to answer a lot of your questions.

Bottom line: This game is a fun 4x space game.  If it's on sale with the Crusade expansion, get it.  You definitely need the Crusade expansion.

If you are into grand strategy this game will be up your alley. I could go on about it but I will just mention one single thing that I and all who enjoy this type of game must and will want to know. There are a LOT of buildings you cannot destroy.
In a game where one of the ways of winning and my prefered way, is taking over territory (planets, in this case) planets with limited useable areas, someone had the idea of adding the Indistructable trait to MANY buildings, some of which are next to useless, buildings that you aquire early on, so you tend to want to use them, knowing or thinking that you will replace them later on, only to come find out that you can't because they are indestructible. On top of that, when you take over a planet, you come to find out the stupid Ai built many of these buildings on said planet, basicly making the planet next to useless. (Found me a decent size planet in the front lines, only to come find out the Ai built, cities, tech buildings, and other useless buildings all mixed in said planet, making it useless as a front line planet and/or as a specific resource planet)
Others may find this makes the game more of a challenge, as for myself, I see it as handcuffs. Especially in a game where no such restrictions should be implemented. I do hope they change this, for at this moment, this kills the game for me. I could go more into detail but I just left the game and not in the best of moods.
11-24-17
Well, after some help from a dev, and a lot of searching, found a way to change this issue. The game files can be changed, changed in a huge way, to the extent that you can actually change a lot of the game to your liking, and especially these indestructable buildings. Was truly suprised and glad to find that, since now I can truly enjoy this game as much as I did GalCiv 2. The issue above still remains until you change it yourself but, the point is that you can, thanks to the devs for that.
As for the game itself, it is truly a fun game, if you are into grand strategy you will enjoy this game, from designing your own race to your own ships. Watching my ships trading fire with the Ai is truly enjoyable. The Ai is still a bit slow, even at high difficulty but still able to suprise you at times. I do recommend it since it is so much fun, and there is a lot you can do and see in it, inspite the whole indestructable building issue. Glad also to see that the devs are still committed to the game; that, is something you don't see as often as you/we would like.

Should YOU buy Startup Company? I have made a short video to help you decide that:
PROS:
- Probably the most polished, bug-free and complete feeling early access game I have ever gotten my hands on
- The price is hard to beat for this genre even though it’s not complete yet
- The developer is extremely active and communicative with players, being very open to feedback and transparent with his ideas
- Already has plans for big updates on improving the product experience, making it more exciting and addictive, expanding offices to allow for more employees and bigger spaces, and then asking the community what they want after all that is done
- Very easy to learn but quite in-depth the further you get into it
- Has great pacing with all of the level-ups and unlocks, making sure to not overwhelm you with the features
- Steam achievements and mod support!!!
CONS:
- My biggest gripe is that there isn’t really any personality in the game. The employees are just mindless drones that do your bidding and don’t create drama. Sure, it’s simpler, but drama makes things interesting!
- Only one music track at this time
- Currently there are just 3 office sizes which feels a little constricting but there are plans to change this
- There’s not a huge selection of in-game cosmetics for your office but I imagine there will be lots of things on the workshop
Overall, Startup Company is a great little game that already has hours of fun for the simulation aficionado. In its current state the game already surpasses the value of its price, and if you’re a person who enjoys business simulators and want to show your support for future development, you can’t go wrong in buying this game.

I played this game ages ago on the console and it was never really one of my favorites - as much as I love the Final Fantasy games, this one was only slightly higher on my list than FFX. It's just the game overall that sort of drives me insane on this one, with the card game, obnoxious characters, and the incredibly stupid battle mechanics.
That being said, it's more than playable still. It's a time killer for me, more than anything, but this is still faithful to the game, at least as far as I've seen so far. The graphics are decent enough, pretty much on par with what I remember from the Playstation and not on par with more recent games, but still good. I believe there's a skip feature on this for cutscenes, but it's convoluted to access, so I just kind of twiddle my thumbs through them if I have to watch one more than once. But the controls are easy enough to reconfigure and use quickly.
Really the only faults here for me are ones that already had existed in the game to begin with.
That card game that is nothing but a massive waste of time. It's pretty much impossible to win any games at the start anyway after you're given your first few cards, because they are useless and everyone around you has much better ones. So it's not even worth playing against anyone until a bit later in the game when you've had a chance to gather some new cards. And even then, it's really not worth it unless you just like to drag your game out for no real reason.
Drawing magic is tedious and annoying, and while it's more convenient than an MP gauge that runs low constantly, draw points are often unpredictable and not always the best plan. Luckily, the game comes with a cheat you can access upon start-up of the game that rids you of this problem by maxing out your magic, but if you don't like to play with cheats on, it wears on you after a while. Waste battle moves to gather magic from enemies, or hope you find a few draw points for what you're looking for while you're out wandering around the map; it was a neat idea, but not terribly practical for the long haul.
Then there's the GF system, which requires you to attach a summon to a character to have any battle options other than 'attack'. Again, it's an interesting idea, to an extent, but then simply giving you the option to assign summons to certain characters and leave it at that would have been fine. The way this is done, you literally HAVE TO assign one to a character or they can't even use items during battle, and that is just ridiculous. It forces you to constantly re-adjust your set-up any time a character joins or leaves the party, which while that tends to happen anyone in one of these games, this entire system makes it beyond ridiculous.
Granted, there is an upside - every character has the potential to summon during battle, and for boss fights, or just higher level creatures you probably should have run away from but don't want to, this can make things go quickly when you have three characters just constantly summoning their GF for their turns. There's also the benefit of being able to swap magic around between characters for the optimal set-ups, which, while I do hate this system overall, they did at least do it effectively.
And as for the story, well... It's Final Fantasy, what do you want? It's big, wartime-related, and that's about all there ever is to them. Obviously there's other little elements, but at the end of the day, it's what every Final Fantasy game boils down to in the storyline.
So all of that being said, the game is still *good*, it just depends heavily on your taste in Final Fantasy games. VII, VIII, and IX were all relatively different in set-up as they gave some new things a try, and that's good. It's helped sort out what does and does not work for the current games. This one is never going to be my favorite, and I certainly wouldn't even really count it in the top 3 for the franchise, but it's worth playing if you enjoy the games as a whole. Just prepare for some frustration with some of the mechanics.

If you've never played a Final Fantasy game in your life, then here's a great place to start.
The Final Fantasy games have suffered from their ups and downs over the years, and VIII is no exception. If you take the time to search for opinions on the internet, you'll find a myriad of opinions ranging from one extreme to the other.
At it's heart though, I've found the game enjoyable, replayable - and the few aspects I do not like are swept under the rug.
As with most FF games, it relies on turn-based combat, but don't let that fool you. It is possible (and quite easy when you get the hang of it) to finish the game without levelling any of your characters at all. There are side quests aplenty, including the Triple Triad card game, which is fun for the most part, and the chocobo forest mini game.
The story is quite in-depth, so while I don't recommend it for the very young, based on this, it is still age and gender friendly - there is romance, comedy, plot twists, and a story and world so rich you might just not want to leave it.
The art style might take some getting used to, but the menu, and how magic and summons integrate with characters, may be the biggest hurdle for new players. Simply put - I didn't use magic. Summons are "junctioned" to characters to grant them abilities, not the least of which is the ability to link collected magicks to your stats, giving them a significant boost. This is the primary method of getting stronger. As you level, so too do the enemies, meaning you can't outlevel them. It is a unique system among FF games, but somehow it works, and works well with practice.
If you're already familiar with FF games, you might have already decided whether or not to get this game, but if you haven't, it's definitely worth a look-see.

I feel like I've played enough time on every individual (current) champion to write a review at this point.   Please note that I have played every Hi-Rez game to date (I am an oldschool Tribes fan, and used to love their reboot), and have purchased the founders pack on this game.  I have also played it's counterpart made by Blizzard (and still do, on occassion).
That being said, I like this game a lot more than the expensive alternative.  Let me quantify that though; I like it a lot more for CASUAL gameplay.  Because Hirez knows about as much as balancing champions as koalas know about swimming.  The new champ they just put out (Jhin) does just as much damage, and attacks just as fast in melee and in range.  Certain team comps constisting of entirely hitscan champs do way too much damage to overcome.  And last, but certainly not least; my favorite champion (Barik) gets his♥♥♥♥♥kicked because his ult is garbage.  He is the only one on the game that has an instant cast ult that has a random startup phase.  There's no reason for it.  His ult is basically Makoa's Q, plus a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ avoidable turret in the middle for no reason.  And if you cast it while you actually need it, you'll die before it finishes.  Which restarts the cooldown.
That being said;  I like this game a lot more than the 60 dollar alternative.  Unfortunatley, if you're playing competively, or even really casually, you better get a premade team together.  Because 9 times out of 10 you're going to get match made with people that don't even seem to have their monitor on.  Because that's how FTP games work.  You get ♥♥♥♥♥♥ players every, single, solitary, time...
AND!  It's still barely half way through public beta.  So there's plenty of time for improvement.  If they treat it more like Smite than Tribes, there's plenty of opportunity.  If they treat it like Tribes... well then I've just put a bunch of money in another game for no reason.  Time will tell.

Abzu creates one of the most relaxing, stress-free underwater experiences I’ve ever played. By emphasizing freedom of movement over survival, it gave me all the time I needed to soak in its gorgeous art direction, marvel at its fluid controls, and listen to its epic orchestral score. During the course of this fascinating three-hour adventure full of deep-sea mysteries and discoveries, its moving melodies ebbed and flowed with my emotions and fueled my curiosity to reach the finale.
Abzu’s intriguing underwater world is presented with little introduction – you’re a mysterious diver who awakens and begins to explore – but it generates enough mystery to propel you through a series of stunning locations. From seaweed swaying in the current to mysterious sunken shrines, each area shows off Abzu’s fantastic art direction, attention to detail, and an impressive sense of scale as you swim through enormous chasms under the sea.

F.E.A.R. is one of the best games I have ever played.
First Encounter Assault Recon has got to be one of the most iconic horror games ever made and creates its feel from atmosphere and an incredible story. This game mixes a fast-moving FPS with a grudging horror so perfectly that the two ganres seem like they were meant to be. The characters, the main Villan especially, are likeable and, in Paxton Fettel's case, downright perfect.
Now, yes, this game is old, but I am an avid believer that graphics don't matter. How good a game is should depend entirely on the gameplay and story, not how pretty it is. It's like finding your soul-mate. What they look like or wear isn't what you fall in love with. It's who they are and F.E.A.R. is just this kind of beautiful that doesn't come around anymore (speaking metaphorically.) It's the Marilyn Monroe of horror: Old, Iconic, and beloved.
Is this the perfect game? No. Of course not. Even Marilyn Monroe had stretch marks and meat on her bones, but that didn't make her any less beautiful. F.E.A.R. is the same way. There ARE a number of glitches in the game, some that make it hard to continue, but those are so rare that you'd need to reload the game one-million times to actually get it to happen once. It also has some slow moments that get a little boring and some map areas that will have you walking in circles for hours, but that's just part of it's charm. The game is INSANELY scary, too. The little bug that this game creates under your skin will crawl through your flesh and eat your bones. It's not just scary, either. It's exciting with its wonderful gun-play and it's sad with its heartbreaking plot. You'll feel for the villan as much as you want to kill him.

What is different in the Steam Version?
*Cloud saving
*Support for modern resolutions
*Aali's driver is no longer necessary to play on new computers.
*Slight graphics improvement (optional)
*Works out of the box with Xbox360 controller (but some commands still require using the keyboard, which is ridiculous).
*Videos are heavily compressed and look worse than the original PC release.
*The music is poor quality, ruining the game's great soundtrack.
*Steam achievements
*Magic Booster.  Gives a selected save file a bunch of magic for free.
*Using the F# keys, you can use a number of built-in cheats.
Many of the issues can be resolved through mods.  There are high resolution FMV mods that fix the movies,  "Roses and Wine" replaces the game's music with OGG versions that sounds much, much better.
Other mods, based on the "Tonberry" mod, enhance the graphics and menus even further, but these mods are not compatible with the Steam overlay.
Now the game itself:
When I first played this, I was excited from finishing FF7 and eager to see the followup.  I saw the opening movie, and it was about the most cinematic gaming experience I had had at the time, and I felt I was watching the evolution of an artform.  The cinematics are still astounding to me.
But as I played the actual game, I felt a little underwhelmed.  Not because this is a bad game by any stretch.  It's an excellent game.  But coming from FF7, which had a story I felt very involved in, to this story, I felt it was messy and directionless at times, and it was a letdown.  It's just not very engaging after you've gotten past the beginning, and then it starts time hopping with an entirely different cast of characters, taking you out of the main plot.
My biggest problem, and it is a divisive one, is the junction system.  Many people have argued in favor of it because they like the link between magic and abilities.  I feel it discourages the use of magic, cheapens the summons and the draw mechanic is stupid and tedious.  You would spend ages on a single battle just doing the same command (draw/stock) over and over and not actually fighting, not even grinding.  Then when you drew enough magic to junction, you would avoid casting it because it would drop your stats down too much.  This is a Final Fantasy game that is heavily focused on magic, which discourages you from ever actually using magic.
The summons of FF7 have been replaced with GFs, who can be summoned freely.  The GFs still function as summons, but with no limitations.  It's encouraged for you to just keep using the summons instead of your other abilities, because the more you summon, the stronger your affinity, which makes your summons more powerful.  That said, it is still less that w-summon KotR/mime/mime over and over to be the Weapons in FF7.
Finally, there is Triple Triad, which is a card game within the game.  It is sometimes enjoyable and sometimes too time consuming and out of place.  It seems awkward in a serious situation to stop to play cards with a stranger.  Sometimes I actually enjoy this game, but it becomes a chore.

Playing FEAR in 2015, this game feels like a funny mix of old and new. The level design and environmental puzzles come straight out of Half-Life, but the over-the-top shooting and meathead soldier enemies resemble Crysis or the new Wolfenstein games. Ten years on, FEAR seems like it's having an identity crisis. Of course, in 2005, it probably didn't seem so strange to mix these elements together, and thankfully, in this case, it works.
It's also supposedly a "horror" game, though it mostly fails on this front. The plot involves secret cloning experience and it features occasional jumpscares, but the actual gameplay is all 100% classic shooter. Ever the famous "ladder moment" didn't make much of an impression on me; I actually don't even remember encountering it in the game.
What really makes FEAR shine is the AI. Most of the battles are against enemy troopers, and the way they try to flank you and out-maneuver you is really second to none in shooter games. This is one game where the soldiers won't just run at you spraying wildly. Their hunting and survival instincts are advanced, but the player has a balancing weapon in the form of the bullet time mechanic. It's great that they decided to add that, as I think it's probably what prevents the game from getting needlessly frustrating like Far Cry 1.

If the handful of Vietnam War movies I've seen have taught me anything about the war, it was a bloody, brutal affair where neither side was necessarily in the right, and everything was backed by totally sweet hard rock. I imagine that simulating the humid, dense Vietnamese jungles and their effects on combat is no simple task, but it's what Russian developer, publisher and even retailer 1C has attempted with Men of War: Vietnam.

ABZU can only be described as an experience. It's a swimming simulator that takes the player through different, varied, and colourful environments with fantastic orchestral music for different levels. Much like the game Journey, ABZU relies on simple puzzles to finish objectives, and thus requires little in the way of brainpower. It anything, this game is the perfect game to sit back, relax, and chill - to go with the flow of the water and the waves.
The art design and detail is absolutely gorgeous, and there are plenty of different fish and sea creatures to fill the varied levels you swim through. This also includes the lighting, which I thought was absolutely gorgeous, especially when there were large schools of fish swimming about. I also liked that, though the game uses real species of sea creatures, the combinations of the creatures with the environments gave the oceans and otherworldly feel. The game feels a little strange to control and move about (almost sluggish) but I did not feel it to be too much of detriment, except for one section where a bit of precision is needed to avoid traps.
ABZU has no solid story, and what story there is can only be inferred from pictures and ruins that you travel through, as well as some physical interactions that your character performs. It gives a great glimpse into the world, but if you're seeking something more concrete this game won't be up your alley.
ABZU is visually stunning, and I personally liken it to a moving painting as you transition through the levels. Despite this, it is still very short, and while I would like to recommend it for the full price, I think this game is better with a discount. However, if you enjoy games in this kind of niche, and enjoy the experience aspect, definitely pick it up at full price if you're able.

I am a fan of Paradox games. I consider EU4 and CK2 to be one of my favourite games and I also enjoyed Cities: Skyline. I was pretty hyped when I heard about Stellaris and I hoped that it would be something like EU4 but in space. I was wrong.
I know that it took lot's of time to make EU4 into the game it is today and I cant really compare the two games but seriously. It feels like the developer team didnt play Stellaris themselves before release. There are so many obvious things to improve and fix. From my point of view the developers seem lazy and uninterested to make a proper game. Yeah sure they are releasing patches to fix most of the problems but there are still alot of things missing from the game.
I feel like the developers thought that mods are going to fill the empty game and they are right. Modders are creating different events and expansions but I feel like its not their job. In other games most mods are made to customize the game but right now modders are FIXING the game. Improved sectors? planetary rally points? Auto improving buildings? Better politics? Building ringworlds? How is it that the developers though: "Yea no we are not gonna bother with that. If the people want more than 20 boring colors for their flags they are gonna make a mod for it." For me It shows that the people who made the game werent very interested in it.
Lots of people like Stellaris and I see why. I can dominate the galaxy but all that good potential gameplay is weighed down by the bugs, micro-managing and general you-cant-do-that-its-not-in-the-game-ness. Mods are very fun. But the game should have some content on its own.
Also, when researching new technologies is very important and thus you spend alot of time on it then it should be more fun than "Let me click on this and wait for 50 in-game months.
5/10- Has potential but right now its as empty as space itself.

For a few weeks now I have been looking for an rpg that I could lose myself in on this 2007 macbook pro that only has 256 mb of vram on an old video card and 3 gigabyte's of ram. The search has been long and hard.... then yesterday I during the Steam Autumn Sale I picked up Dust...
Oh my god! Dust is such an awesome game, and I don't know why I have completely ignored this game in three years since it's release. I am a gamer who got into gaming with games such as Legend of Zelda, Secret of Mana, Castlevania, and Metroid. This game has elements of all those, and it stokes that nostalgia nerve so hard that I just want to experience more of this game.
On top of that the story is great and has tough emotional moments that will make you think twice about your actions. The music is so pretty and it always fits the mood of what's going on. In fact, there are many times when the music stops cold, leaving a feeling of either dread or just calmness, depending on the situation.
The art style and character design is kind of unusual, where every single character you meet is some kind of animal person, but that is cool, again it's a throw back to some of the quirkier games in the 16 and 32 bit era.
The combat is also a lot of fun. It is fast, you'll be using your mouse to kick up a wind storm, put a little magic from your helper in the mix to create a wide variety of effects.
There is a wide range of difficulty levels that will suit every gamers needs, so you can go for hard mode and have a real challenging experience that really requires you to respond to things and be on your toes, or you can go on casual difficulty and just enjoy the story and the exploration side of the game.
Overall, if you've grown up on games from the 16 and 32 bit era, if zelda, metroid, and castlevania are some of your favorite retro games, you will love this game.
For someone looking for another 80s/90s syle exploration rpg, I highly recommend this game.

A really well made 4x strategy game set in space with great visuals.
Pros:
>Great empire builder allowing you to edit every factor of your nation from cosmetics to governing policies and ideologies, from a big selection allowing for varied nations in every game.
>Strong and entertaining early-game, with interesting anomoly popups and early diplomacy with other factions.
>Indepth ship builder allowing you to create your own classes of ships using a range of weapons, shields etc that you researched ingame.
>Downright FANTASTIC visuals. Planets and solar systems are beautifully rendered, and the 2D alien avatars in diplomacy and pop windows are drawn beautifully.
>Satisfying fleet battles, especially between two 10k+ stacks. Lasers shooting around, rockets exploding, bombers and fighter jets shooting lasers. It's pretty epic.
>Engaging user-friendly planet modification, in which planets are divided into seperate tiles, each with different resources. Each tile allows you to build one building that boosts that tile's production or contributes to the planet's overall resource output. You can also manage your population much more easily.
>Massive research trees divided into three categories give you a wide range of new things to see, unlock and create.
>Epic science-fiction themed soundtrack that never gets tiring to listen to.
>A ground forces system where you have to recruit armies on your own planets and ferry them to enemy planets to occupy. It's okay, but generally gets bogged down in the furious scrolling and clicking during a war.
>Mod support, giving you access to a ton of incredible gameplay and graphics enhancements that ultimately improve your gameplay experience.
Cons:
>Very weak mid/late-game. After you finish exploring the galaxy there are no more interesting pop ups and random events like in Europa Universalis IV. You just tend to build ships in between wars and watch your empire slowly grow.
>Terrible AI team mechanics. If you're in an alliance and you go to war with another empire, your ally's fleets will follow yours around resulting in a giant death stack. You're unable to set up planets for them to occupy or blockade like you can with ally troops in EUIV. Generally your occupied planets will be taken back because your ally is too stupid to leave forces behind.
>Shallow diplomacy mechanics, limiting you to trade deals, war declaration and vassalisation demands. If you're in a war where the AI is the warleader, you may find yourself ripping your hair out because the warleader is too stubborn to peace out.  The Nation comparison box needs to show percentages, not "Superior, overwhelming, inferior." I often end up wrecking 'superior' nations just because they have a couple of corvettes more than I do and have a "level 3 power plant" research that I don't have.
>Lacking rebel faction interactions makes it very difficult to deal with rebel uprisings if your influence income is low. There needs to be better ways of pleasing rebels and easing revolt rather than bribing leaders and suppressing media.
>More indepth sector management. The game at start caps you to being able to rule over 5 planets. After that you need to create sectors in order to have more planets in your empire. Sectors are essentially micro thriving sub-nations within your empire that will focus on building specific buildings that you can set in the empire screen. However they restrict you in your ability to manage the population especially when there's divergence leading to a rebellion. This causes problems.
>Various bugs and glitches with the AI here and there. Examples include: An enemy 12k fleet had gotten stuck in the edge of a solar system trying to evade my allied death stack and ended up getting destroyed rather than warping away. Another example is that my ally had two planets right on the border of a Fallen Empire. Everytime their truce was up the Empire would declare war, kick my ally's♥♥♥♥♥and force my ally to abandon the two planets. As soon as the war ended my ally would recolonise the planets and the cycle repeated itself. It was irritating to say the least.
Despite its flaws Stellaris has huge potential to improve. Knowing Paradox, i expect alot of DLC packs to come out soon. If you like EUIV and Victoria 2 and are a fan of science fiction, this is the game for you.

-The one and only Arena Event of the simulation unfolds, and from 9 options... the Ugly Barnacle is randomized.
-Everyone immediately dies within 20 minutes of each other.
-Winner is declared: Nagito Komaeda, Ultimate Lucky Student.
So, to clarify:
> Out of the five remaining on Day 3, Nagito was the only male student. He won.
> At the end of the game, he was the least sane, surpassing even Chiaki. He won.
> There was a 1/9 chance for 'The Ugly Barnacle' event to be randomized. It was.
> From there, he had a 1/5 chance of being the last person to die to the Ugly Barnacle. He was.
> He also had a 1/31 chance of ultimately winning the game at the start. He won.
> So in total, for this to happen to someone, they would've had a 1/1395 chance. It happened to Nagito.
Why?
Because he's the Ultimate Lucky Student.

I'll do my review doing a comparison between Shift 1 and Shift 2 Unleashed
Pros:
- Better AI.
- Night time.
- Improvement on the car interiors, a lot of details. Really good shadows and reflections.
- Nice effects like dirt on the windshield or vibrations on the hood.
- Helmet view, great addition but it can make you dizzy.
- More variety of cars.
- More variety of tracks.
- More customization.
- Feels more like a simulation, still kind of arcade.
- Drag races.
- Better UI.
- It's fun.
Cons:
- Easy even on hard difficulty. The real challenge is learning how to handle the cars and getting the best times on the track.
- Bad optimization on some tracks like Miami, frame drops on certain spots.
- Bad graphics on the outside of some vehicles. There's not an improvement over Shift 1.
- Can't change the sensitivity of the triggers in game like the first game.
- Some bugs like the hands not moving with the steering wheel or the high settings appearing as "_LOW_"
Tecnical stuff:
- No crashes atleast for me (Using Windows 7 Ultimate 64 bits).
- No input lag atleast for me (Using a Xbox 360 Controller).
- Can't choose a language. This is the first time that i see something like this on Steam, there's no language tab on the game properties of Steam or in game. The language is choosen by the language on your computer. I'm mexican so the default language was in Spanish but i really want it to play in English.
Even when there are some improvements from the Shift 1, i'm still not sure if i would recommend to buy this game because there are more options on the market. Maybe if you buy the EA Racing Pack on sale you should try it yourself.
If it works on your computer and you like racing games, it's worth your time.
EDIT: I highly recommend this game, just make sure it works on your computer. If you really like racing games, buy the EA Racing Pack on sale if you can.

This is one of the most complex, in-depth dungeon crawlers that I've played in years. The character variety and the differences between them, as well as the procedurally generated levels, give the game many hours of replayability. The gameplay itself is very fast paced, due to it's rhythm-based nature, leading to a game that creates an almost real-time dungeon crawling experiance. The music, also different between almost every character, is all fast paced and fun to listen to on it's own. The spritework all has a unique level of charm to it, with the way each one moves in reguards to the music, in addition to the amazing amount of detail worked into each sprite that makes them almost come alive. The absolute best part of the game, however, has to be the bosses. Each boss is based off of a different kind of music, from blues, to metal, to even a giant rapping mole in the DLC. The songs of the bosses are each works of art, even moreso than the rest of the game, and every single battle, and it's mechanics, are each unique and memorable. This game is a masterpiece.
The only things I have to complain about are that the two-player mode is not very well implemented, and could use some work, and that the controller support is awkward and using any controller makes the game almost unplayable.

At first glance, the game appears to be prettier than Stellaris, but upon taking a closer look, it falls short of the mark. The ship customization is much more involved, as you can build your own ship from the ground up. The problem is that the game seems very confused as to what I'm trying to do when attaching ship parts. Often making the pieces refuse to lock into place, or attach in a completely different location from what I wanted.
You also can't play multiplayer with people who don't have the same DLC as you. Unfortunately, nobody told me that before I bought the bundle edition with all the DLC included! I haven't been able to join any multiplayer games yet, because I can't find anybody who has all the DLC packs that I do.
Making custom empires is also lackluster compared to Stellaris, as the selection of diplomatic portraits is very slim. As in, there's like 1 or 2 at most for the core races, and then only 1 each for a bunch of custom races. This wouldn't be too terrible if it wasn't for the fact that they didn't even bother to add in citizen portraits for the custom races. Meaning that while you may look like a new type of alien in the diplomacy screen, all of your citizens are going to look like the core races, which really breaks the immersive feel.
I can't bring myself to create a custom empire, because I can't bring myself to view it as a custom empire. In my mind, they will always been humans, or Drengin, or Snathi, or Slyne, or whatever. These racial portraits already have templates, names, cultures and backstories that I automatically associate them with. As opposed to Stellaris, where the races were mostly blank slates that you could build off of.
Finally, the game has multiple bug issues that makes it impossible to advance the game. I've had one instance where the NPC's never ended their turn, and another instance where the game didn't acknowledge that I had defeated the enemy teams. Even after several reloads, in which I was fairly certain all other factions were dead and I ruled the map, I was forced to restart the entire mission because the game didn't recognize the enemies as having been defeated.

This is the ultimate love/hate game for me. I'll begin with the negatives. The junction system can be a chore to set up since you have to draw magic from enemies and casting it by the amount you have drawn instead of having the traditional MP (mana) system.  The story is pretty shallow and some characters just seem unnecessary. The soundtrack is pretty hit or miss. Lastly, the game can be pretty easily beaten by spamming Aura+GF combos from a certain point onward.
Now with the good. Despite the rather shallow story, Squall and Rinoa's character development is pretty neat to watch unfold. Once your junctions are set up, the battle system can be pretty fun at times. There's plenty of fun sidequests and of course, there's the well known card game: Triple Triad. The game does have a certain charm to it and big part of it are the cohesive and well-timed cutscenes. The cutscenes were ahead of their time when this game was released and graphically still hold up very well. The final boss fight also rivals that of Kefka (FFVI) and Sephiroth (FFVII) in terms of epicness and challenge.
To keep it short, this game is worth playing as long as you can accept it being very different from the traditional Final Fantasy game. Don't try to play through it as if you're playing VII or IX. Learn the junction system and use it properly. I've seen so many others try to play the game and end up not enjoying it because they didn't ever learn the junction system and played by just pressing 'Attack.' It's
worth getting if you're looking for a story that'll keep you wanting more. IV, VI, VII, IX, and X will provide much better stories than this installment. If you can accept its flaws, it can prove to be a good game with a certain whimsical charm to it and will provide you with plenty hours of playtime.

Pros: - You can enjoy it for months. At this price, there's not much to complain.
- CG is not so bad. Compared the new games, of course, there's a lot to be desired, but really it isn't so bad.
- The story keeps you moving. It's not repetitive.

- Limit breaks of each characters vary greatly and are all interesting.

Cons:
- It can be so corny and cheesy at times. The romance between Squall and Rinoa takes up so much time and is just lame. I almost puked when Rinoa jumped to his lap and the sappy romantic song started to play. Seriously! All in all, you can't go wrong with Final Fantasy. Despite all the cons, it's still way better than most other RPGs out there. I turn the sound off and just hit the button randomly while reading a book or looking at my phone to get through all the cheesy love scenes.

There are already thousands of reviews for this game that discuss the pros and cons of this game in great detail. I'd instead like to highlight some of the more glaring flaws of this re-release.
Nothing has been changed. It looks, sounds and plays just like the original PC release. Considering the lack of work that has gone into this re-release, it's not worth the price if you already own a previous version. A character booster has been added, which I doubt very few people would bother with.
Some achievements have also been added; they're shallow attempts at artificially lengthening the game. The most time-consuming of these achievements is "10,000 kills" - as the title suggests, one must kill at least 10,000 enemies. In a game where killing too many enemies can be detrimental, this is a silly achievement. I finished the game with only a couple of hundred kills, as do most players. Anyone who sets out to achieve 10,000 kills will likely use some king of key-pressing software. I would have preferred some achievements that require the player to use skill, perhaps more like the "Contrived Finish" achievement (wherein one must finish the game without the protagonist leveling up), as these kinds of achievements at least encourage the player to play the game differently.
Anyway, it's Final Fantasy VIII. I recommend it so long as you pick it up when it's on sale.

It wasn't ready for launch.  It runs well for me with obvious end game slow downs but it has broken quest lines, broken diplomacy, broken trade and broken alliance mechanics.  It'll be alright after months of patching but that's not good enough.  The framework for a good game is certainly there but the mid to late game boredom and lack of content is a legitimate complaint.
Paradox has convinced many of its fans that it's okay to backfill a game with DLC.  It is not.  A game is to be polished, robust and content rich at release.  Add ons are simply for making a great game better, not playable and somewhat interesting.  This trend is to be punished.
I'll wait for the 3 initial patches to roll out before trying again.  There's no point in going into detail as so much has yet to be fixed.  I look forward to a polished base game eventually.  There's also no point in buying it in its present state and with the flood of DLC to come you may as well wait a couple years for the complete game.  Why bother with the death by a thousand cuts routine.  Disappointing as I really hoped this would bridge us over until Endless Space 2.

It's not like a fantasy game where something illogical happens and someone says "a wizard did it" but it comes up with the idea that an unkown ancient being(s) that came billions of years before man, created and developed a power to enable then to travel around star sytems and create an empire.
The reason it is so replayable, much like Civilization, is because at any given moment anything can happen. For example, my playthrough showed that even if you have the strongest empire in the whole galaxy, there will be some force out there that  can destroy you in an instant.
What I would really love to see with this game, is not from the developers, but from the small content creaters and modders. I think this game is the ideal canvas for a Mass Effect mod. I have been looking through the workshop and over the depths of the internet and have encountered many different people trying to accomplish this. If just one of them was to pull it off like the mods of Sins of a Solar Empire, then this game would be perfect for me and anyone else who is fan of the Mass effect trilogy and a fan of strategy games. Plus you can go for the same story as Mass Effect, but change it a bit so that the story of Mass Effect ends how you would want it to.
Over all this game is amazing, it has a long way to go, and hopefully the developers will work their arses off for this project. It's already an amazing game and I want to see how good it can get.

I feel like I've played enough time on every individual (current) champion to write a review at this point.   Please note that I have played every Hi-Rez game to date (I am an oldschool Tribes fan, and used to love their reboot), and have purchased the founders pack on this game.  I have also played it's counterpart made by Blizzard (and still do, on occassion).
That being said, I like this game a lot more than the expensive alternative.  Let me quantify that though; I like it a lot more for CASUAL gameplay.  Because Hirez knows about as much as balancing champions as koalas know about swimming.  The new champ they just put out (Jhin) does just as much damage, and attacks just as fast in melee and in range.  Certain team comps constisting of entirely hitscan champs do way too much damage to overcome.  And last, but certainly not least; my favorite champion (Barik) gets his♥♥♥♥♥kicked because his ult is garbage.  He is the only one on the game that has an instant cast ult that has a random startup phase.  There's no reason for it.  His ult is basically Makoa's Q, plus a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ avoidable turret in the middle for no reason.  And if you cast it while you actually need it, you'll die before it finishes.  Which restarts the cooldown.
That being said;  I like this game a lot more than the 60 dollar alternative.  Unfortunatley, if you're playing competively, or even really casually, you better get a premade team together.  Because 9 times out of 10 you're going to get match made with people that don't even seem to have their monitor on.  Because that's how FTP games work.  You get ♥♥♥♥♥♥ players every, single, solitary, time...
AND!  It's still barely half way through public beta.  So there's plenty of time for improvement.  If they treat it more like Smite than Tribes, there's plenty of opportunity.  If they treat it like Tribes... well then I've just put a bunch of money in another game for no reason.  Time will tell.

Wow.. I dont even know where to start with this game... Ok, here's a start: DONT BUY THIS GAME. DONT PLAY THIS GAME.
Wanna know why? Keep reading:
The story is "ok" - at best. And the dialogues are a bit funny, I'll give you that, but lets begin on the CONS:
Balancing is stupid. Enemies will always be above your level and strength and can 1-2hit kill you easily. There's a level 50 cap but it doesnt matter if you're grinding and reach max level, cos enemies are STILL GONNA HAVE MORE LEVELS, STRENGTH AND HP OVER YOU AND CAN STILL 1-2HIT KILL YOU.
And the design on this game.. GOD, the design! Get this:
This game is about Crowd Control abuse. CC them and you can keep hitting them for 20 turns until they die (this is bound to happen a lot). If YOU become target of a CC chain, you lose. Simple as that. And that's pretty much how every boss in this game works. Believe, it's not fun to watch them hit you 5 turns in a row and you cant do anything but watch and die.
The spells are all messed up: Spells learned on lvl 20 that cost 100 mana ARE STRONGER THAN SPELLS LEARNED ON LEVEL 45 AND COST 350 MANA. Spells supposed to be of the same element, won't work the same way on an enemy. Example: 3 fire element spells on the SAME enemy can cause: 1 to hit for super effective, 1 to hit for normal damage and 1 will cause enemy to resist it.
Oh, and game will force you to play with a set party that it formed on its own. Like throw 4 fire magicians in a dungeon with only fire resistant enemies. The struggle is real, and it happens often on the story line.
Whoever made this game should go back to school. SOOOO many typos, bad grammar, lack of proper punctuation, etc. Its trully awful to read it.
Game is flooded with items that are very much alike when it comes to its effects. There are potions, ramen, lunch, ninja food, etc. They all heal for %hp or mp and SEVERAL HEAL FOR THE SAME % AS ALL OF THEM. It's just unnecessary to have so many items alike.
Loot is totally useless. They are super rare to drop and cant be used for crafting or anything other than sold on the stores, for like 5 bucks.
Some items have the same sprite AND description, but are different items!
Super easy to break the game: buy a gold boost item, play for a while, get rich and buy everything you'll need for the rest of the game.
Bottom line: dont put yourself through this suffering. Dont support this poorly made game. Dont buy it.

At no point does Zeno Clash attempt to make excuses for it's insane universe, no explanation is given for anything that does not fit within the games context, things simply are.
Some will love this and some will hate it but either way you can't help but admire the writers for making such an uncompromising world that gives you one WTF? moment after the other with barely a second to catch your breath.

Very challenging, but oh so satisfying! This game is a true test of skill, one that I absolutely recommend purchasing. Starting off nice and slow, you are offered a diverse array of weaponry and items to enhance your experience as you break skulls to the beat. It is immensely tile based, almost strategic, but instead of having the luxury to take your time and plan out the best methods, you are forced to think on your feet.
There IS a mode that lets you pause and think as you play; The Bard. There is also an item called the Pacemaker that briefly lets you move at your own pace like the bard, but I tend to avoid both of those. The joy I find in this game is the rapid thinking, the bitter defeats, and -- to make up for those bitter defeats -- the amazing victories.
This game is definitely not easy, but it's so so worth the try. Not to mention the soundtrack and it's remixes are incredible, and despite playing this game ever since it was in Alpha oh so long ago, I still find myself going back to the soundtracks and listening to them.

The Witcher 2: Assassins of Kings.
Originally, I wasn't planning on buying this game. Then I heard the Save File from Assassins of Kings would influence Wild Hunt's, and I though, eh, why not? I don't regret it.
I have never truly played a Witcher Game. I only knew some of the characters (Such as Geralt), but it was such a famous franchise, that I wanted to play it, to try it out. So here it goes:
I had never quite played a Witcher game, I was gonna play Wild Hunt until I saw the news of the game save, but I manage to pass the game in Hard. Personally, I believe the game is pretty friendly to new people who come to Witcher, the game isn't TOO complicated, and the story you can understand it without playing the first game.
It may be because I hadn;t played the first game, but the story line failed me on this one. I didn't feel quite excited to know what would happen next, nor did I care for it. It didn't ruin the game, but it also didn't do it any favors.
Since Assassins of Kings isn't really an open world game, exploration isn't a big part of it. But you can wander off and fight some monsters, even find some cool things like locked chests you can find keys to open, and the side quests are even a bigger part of the game. Completing Assassins of Kings without doing them would be too quick.
The fighting on this game is great, it does not allow you to enter every battle and utilize the same strategy you've used throughout the entire game. You are given 6 spells and must utilize them to your advantage, as well as heavy and slow blows and a LOT of dodging. The fighting is fun, if you have the patience to learn how a monster is to be killed.
The controls in this game are standard. WASD for movement, looking around with mouse, and fighting with both right and left clicks. I won't go into detail with the rest, because I'm not here to give a lesson on controls, but most definitely very easy controls to learn.

In my opinion, the game was not tough at all after a while of understanding the monsters. I passed it on Hard, and some fights you are allowed to avoid, which are the harder ones. Although that comes from personal opinion of not playing in Insane mode.
The game is really fun, the fighting is great, characters are loveable. What didn't succeed on my part is the story, it was weak, and I personally adore story. I'd recommend the game for anyone who loves fighting with strategy, and wants to play Wild Hunt with their save file.

There are already thousands of reviews for this game that discuss the pros and cons of this game in great detail. I'd instead like to highlight some of the more glaring flaws of this re-release.
Nothing has been changed. It looks, sounds and plays just like the original PC release. Considering the lack of work that has gone into this re-release, it's not worth the price if you already own a previous version. A character booster has been added, which I doubt very few people would bother with.
Some achievements have also been added; they're shallow attempts at artificially lengthening the game. The most time-consuming of these achievements is "10,000 kills" - as the title suggests, one must kill at least 10,000 enemies. In a game where killing too many enemies can be detrimental, this is a silly achievement. I finished the game with only a couple of hundred kills, as do most players. Anyone who sets out to achieve 10,000 kills will likely use some king of key-pressing software. I would have preferred some achievements that require the player to use skill, perhaps more like the "Contrived Finish" achievement (wherein one must finish the game without the protagonist leveling up), as these kinds of achievements at least encourage the player to play the game differently.
Anyway, it's Final Fantasy VIII. I recommend it so long as you pick it up when it's on sale.

Quest Hunter is a fun Iso-RPG mixed with a "Zelda-type" of adventure game with what I consider to be a pretty refreshing art style, as I am getting burned out of seeing pixels in every indie game.
QH has been somewhat hard for me so far, as I have died probably about a dozen times. Being armed with only a shovel to start out with (no Shovel Knight here), I'd say I'm not doing too bad...It's a slow pace at first, then gets much faster as you progress.
I haven't tried the co-op yet, but it's something I will surely check out soon. QH has a lot of potential, I'm not blown away by it, but I like it. Right off the bat I'd like to see more skills as you level up and more enemy variety. Gameplay-wise and the look and feel of QH kinda reminds me of games like Wanderlust Adventures, Magicka (minus the spell system), and DeathSpank.
Don't let the Isometric view and the RPG tag fool you If you're looking for a Diablo clone. This has puzzles and adventure style of gameplay mixed in and is no way comparable to Diablo, which is not a bad thing at all, just wanted to get that out of the way for anyone that was possibly wondering what the actual gameplay consisted of. QH seemed a bit "kiddie" to me at first but only before I died a dozen times and also before I started to feel the old-school/Zelda-type of gameplay it delivers.
My only con atm is that dying is pointless in it's current state. Part of the reason I've died so much is that I'm not afraid to. I would like to see QH updated with some sort of penalty for dying besides being warped back to a checkpoint, which always seems to be very close by.
I recommend Quest Hunter to those seeking a simplistic Iso-ARPG/Adventure game. I'm addicted to it atm and I'm looking forward to grinding my way to the top and then showing off my "OP-ness" with the online co-op. Over an hour in and I just got my first real weapon and a hat so I'm stoked. I'm looking forward to more updates to this game, and I feel the game will be something beyond great with more content.

This is, hands down, one of the best shooters ever to cross a computer screen. Despite its age, its aged well. The story, implementation and mechanics of this game should stand as an shining example to modern day companies.
You play as an unspecified (so you can project yourself as the character) special forces operative, recruited by F.E.A.R. the First Encounter Assualt Reconnaissance. Your main mission is to hunt down an AWOL commander in charge of an entire battalion of mindless commandos. However as you get closer and closer the mission becomes less about one of Capture-or-kill, more Prevent-the-apocalypse.
The graphics are better than minecraft and the soundtrack really secures the ambience of the game. Despite its age there are virtually no problems with the game. The only one I did find was a sudden, seemingly random, drop in FPS which I later found to be a problem with my mouse. Not my mouse specifically; there is some problem with the game not properly supporting a Logitech wireless mouse. Using a Microsoft wired one I didn't experience the problem again.

With the vanilla game, however, it has its limitations. Aside from 'make money', there are no goals and no directions. There are missions, but those could be considered 'side jobs', eg mow the lawn or forklift this box over there. This offers a great amount of freedom into the game, but it can also be overwhelming for new players.
Overall, this is a great farming simulator, but it falls short for anyone expecting it to be more than just a farming simulator.
