10 Year Retrospective Review- Does F.E.A.R. Still Hold Up?
Short answer: Yes.
When I first sat down to begin my pre-review playthrough, the first thing that stood out to me about Monolith's seminal FPS was just how astoundingly well it has aged. Much like Half-Life 2 before it, F.E.A.R.'s atmospherics, story, and most importantly gameplay are still respectible and even outstanding by today's standards.
Story:
You assume the role of an elite special forces operative known only as the "Point Man." Your mission- stop a rogue psychic commader leading a battalion of cloned supersoldiers. Along the way you'll encounter many different faces, enemies, and settings in your pursuit of your target. The closer you come to apprehending your mark, the more you realize that there are far more parties involved in this incident. A multi-million dollar corporation, a handful of researchers and scientist, and most importantly- a little girl in a red dress. F.E.A.R. is disturbing, convoluted, creative, and dark, and as the story twists and winds like a spider's web you will find yourself drawn in and immersed.
Gameplay:
Where F.E.A.R. truly excels in more than any other aspect is in it's perfectly executed combat. F.E.A.R. enjoys being caught between the old-fashioned shooters of yesteryear and the more modern flare seen nowadays. For example, you can only carry 3 weapons, but each weapon you'll find is fun to use and different. Or how you need to track down health packs although your health will self-regenerate up to a certain point (dependant on difficulty). Every bit of F.E.A.R.'s gameplay feels polished. The weapons are nice and vaired, combat is tight and responsive, melee combat is surprisingly viable and fun throughout. Crucial to all of this is F.E.A.R.'s revolutionary enemy AI. Replica soldiers are smart, reactive, deadly, and always find ways to surprise you. Just the other day during my 6th or so playthrough of this game I witnessed interesting new tactics deployed by the enemies that I hadn't seen before.
Presentation:
At 2005, F.E.A.R. was arguably the prettiest looking FPS since 2004's Half-Life 2. Showcasing many advanced lighting and particle effect techniques, F.E.A.R. was an absolutely gorgeous game in it's prime. 10 years removed, it has begun to showcase a few cracks in the paint. Character models are still good looking, and the particle effects still look excellent, but certain items, enemies, and locations are looking a bit dated. None of this is a dealbreaker, though, and where F.E.A.R. truly shines is in it's brilliant atmospherics. Every location you explore has it's own interesing themes, visual design, and flow. Shows dart about menacingly, sounds goad you into checking over your shoulder, apparitions follow you about, and all of it is perfectly scored to an oppressive, disturbing, brilliant soundtrack.
Package:
Unfortunately, the game's weakest aspect is most certainly in it's replayability. A lack of other gamemodes, multiplayer, or unlockables will surely mean you'll only play through this game for it's single player campaign. The campaign is long enough, and depending on your personal skill will take bewteen 9-18 hours. Fortunately for those who find one lone campaign to not be enough, this version comes with both of F.E.A.R.'s excellent expansion packs. Each comes with a compelling single-player storyline that builds on top of F.E.A.R.'s twisted mythos that will last you anywhere between 6-12 hours. Perseus Mandate in particular is worth replaying for adding several new enemy types, weapons, and a slew of bonus "instant-action" missions.
If this wasn't enough to win you over, keep in mind that even 10 year's later, I still enjoyed it every bit as much as the first time. That's gotta count for something.
Recommended.
Pros:
-Engaging story
-Precise, fun, refined gameplay
-Loads of weapons, each as fun to use as the next
-Atmospherics rivaled only by the best of survival horror games
-Responsive, challenging enemies who've yet to be matched by any other FPS
-Comes packaged in with both of Vivendi's expansions, easily doubling the playtime
Cons:
-Lack of replay value
-Neither of Vivendi's expansions are considered canon to F.E.A.R.'s official sequels (sadly)
-Some environments can look uninteresting compared to others
Do you know the true meaning of F.E.A.R.?

I wanted to like this game, I really did. Many of the screen shots I saw and descriptions I read showcased interesting sci-fi scenarios and appeared to paint a vibrant and interesting universe. Unfortunately upon closer examination that turned out not to be the case. Each solar system is basically a randomized version of the previous. Same goes for the other civilizations.
The core Paradox gameplay is there and works well. Things like leaders, advisers, technologies, ect are detailed and well fleshed out just as they are in the EU series, for example. Unfortunately, while this is a strong skeleton on which to build a game, it is not enough to provide a fun experience in and of itself.
This game is essentially a random procedurally generated universe built upon a well developed Paradox core. Without the specific rich historical context provided by EU or HoI it ends up being all breadth and no no depth. It doesn't help that due to the setting the map isn't really fun to look at or visually appealing.
It's a great idea for a game. The music is good, the concept artwork is beautiful. But the gameplay itself is shallow. You can't hit EUIV with a sci-fi stick and expect good results from the resulting mess.

: Developed by Giant Squid and published by 505 games, ABZU is truly a remarkable adventure game showcasing just how far we've come with graphics and level design. So much so that this quaint little thing ends up being more of an art form.
"ABZU" is from some of the oldest mythologies; AB, meaning water, and ZU, meaning to know. ABZU is the ocean of wisdom and takes you on a deep underwater journey discovering new worlds in the heart of this ocean. With each area showcasing the different types of species that reside in it, it's a game that could be suitable for any age to play and enjoy.
You collect hidden shells, little probes to help you on your journey through to new areas and bring the ecosystem back to it's former glory by releasing fish from all of the hidden pools. Showing off its beautiful before and after life transformations.
: Absolutely superb. As you're swimming around, the detail put into all of the environment and things like depth perception is amazing. The transformation between areas are immaculate and upon freeing all creatures to that area, the before and afters have you wowing constantly.
: Honestly throughout the entire game it has you in such a peaceful kind of trance. You can waste hours just floating around with Killer whales or whale sharks. Even leaving the game running in the background as a screensaver on meditation scenes, the serene soundtrack will help you relax around the house, or while doing paper work and the like.
: Nice array of graphic changes to make it playable on lower ended PC's as well as detailed  and crisp for those higher ended PC's as well. Inverted and normal control settings are also a really nice addition.
: I personally don't like the use of controllers and stubbornly used my keyboard and mouse to play, which did make it a little clunky at first but slowly ironed that out as time went on and I became smoother with it.
I did make an effort to use it with a controller as well, since it was intend to be played with such but personally, I still didn't like how jerky it was.
: Even in game form, ABZU managed to capture how majestic creatures of the deep truly are and it felt so humbling to be swimming alongside them even in game form. To have those indescribable feelings from a game, you know it's doing something right!
This game is absolutely worth it as an experience and something to chill out to after a stressful day, or just to zone out to while the aesthetics keep you in a serene state of mind.
I think it could even be used as an educational tool for young ones. An absolutely beautiful art piece taking you deep into the unknown.
Despite what time of gamer you are and a lot of people not considering this an actual ''game'', I challenge even you to play through this experience and find something you dislike about it, I guarantee  you'll have a hard time because it is such a gorgeous adventure.

Obviously this game is popular for its artwork, but the combat is also fun and simple. Visually the appeal lasts throughout the entire game, it is simplistic but impressive. The combat is easy to get a handle on and you have a few choices as to whether you want gamepad, keyboard, or keyboard and mouse combo. You have dodge left/right, 2 buttons to perform all your attacks and combos with, a magic attack and a few other skills you pick up over time. Fighting chains together very nicely to a hack and slash feel with the need to dodge on harder stuff. Certain mobs have certain ways they must be taken out or require countering so it isn't too simple, you always have to consider what you are fighting. There are also environmental things that come out throughout. A good portion of this is platforming so your jumping skills need to be on par to get through.
There are a few sidequests to go about, not too much in exploration aside from finding all the chests. You will need to rely heavily on food to survive and constantly crafting or buying equipment upgrades. Your best stat investments are simply Attack/Def as much as possible then a 2:1 health:magic ratio. It is pretty easy to get the money and drops and even on the 2nd hardest difficulty, the game wasn't exactly challenging really. If you get 2 rings with 3x item drop, this would be why as you get a huge amount of food drops.
The story in itself is decent, but it does play the amnesia character card which I think is a bit lazy. There is some humor in the dialogue so it is reasonably amusing. One thing to consider though - all characters are animals in here. So this would be a paradise for furries but it might also be the main turn off for some.
Overall it is worth whatever sale price it is on for, it is pretty fun and nice to look at. Would have liked to see it go on longer.
Personal experience score: 8.5/10
Story: 7/10 - Nothing complicated but decent, it builds off the typical main character with amnesia and has some twists to the story
Sound: 7/10 - Decent, but could have had better music. Also the voices in the few cutscenes are 2x louder than the game itself
Graphics: 10/10 - The highlight of the game and what it is well known far, the art style is very nice to look at
Controls: 9/10 - Very easy to use, my only complaint is facing the direction you want to attack seems to be a bit problematic at times
Game Length: 6/10 - Coming in at around 13 hours for a full playthrough on the 2nd hardest difficulty with having explored 100% and collected around 75% of the treasure, add a few more hours if you plan to explore

It wasn't ready for launch.  It runs well for me with obvious end game slow downs but it has broken quest lines, broken diplomacy, broken trade and broken alliance mechanics.  It'll be alright after months of patching but that's not good enough.  The framework for a good game is certainly there but the mid to late game boredom and lack of content is a legitimate complaint.
Paradox has convinced many of its fans that it's okay to backfill a game with DLC.  It is not.  A game is to be polished, robust and content rich at release.  Add ons are simply for making a great game better, not playable and somewhat interesting.  This trend is to be punished.
I'll wait for the 3 initial patches to roll out before trying again.  There's no point in going into detail as so much has yet to be fixed.  I look forward to a polished base game eventually.  There's also no point in buying it in its present state and with the flood of DLC to come you may as well wait a couple years for the complete game.  Why bother with the death by a thousand cuts routine.  Disappointing as I really hoped this would bridge us over until Endless Space 2.

I was sceptical upon purchasing the game, watching small clips of gameplay from various youtubers. However I can comfortably say that even though this game is pretty expensive considering some alternative stragegy games are cheaper, that I am happy that I spent the money because not only does it have great gameplay and an amazing "make your own" desicion style to it. But the replay Factor is absolutely unreal.
The fact that the game developers have gone out of their way and put an intense amount of detail in it, from the name of almost every planet known to man, to the actual science behind some of the missions. It's not like a fantasy game where something illogical happens and someone says "a wizard did it" but it comes up with the idea that an unkown ancient being(s) that came billions of years before man, created and developed a power to enable then to travel around star sytems and create an empire.
The reason it is so replayable, much like Civilization, is because at any given moment anything can happen. For example, my playthrough showed that even if you have the strongest empire in the whole galaxy, there will be some force out there that  can destroy you in an instant.
What I would really love to see with this game, is not from the developers, but from the small content creaters and modders. I think this game is the ideal canvas for a Mass Effect mod. I have been looking through the workshop and over the depths of the internet and have encountered many different people trying to accomplish this. If just one of them was to pull it off like the mods of Sins of a Solar Empire, then this game would be perfect for me and anyone else who is fan of the Mass effect trilogy and a fan of strategy games. Plus you can go for the same story as Mass Effect, but change it a bit so that the story of Mass Effect ends how you would want it to.
Over all this game is amazing, it has a long way to go, and hopefully the developers will work their arses off for this project. It's already an amazing game and I want to see how good it can get.

Weird game.  Weird art style, weird characters, off the wall gameplay.  Think Final Fight or Streets of Rage in 3D from the first person.  Every level is basically a boss fight, and you get to use your hands to beat the crap out of everybody.
Every level is fight, fight, fight, run, dodge.  Little else, and your companion character is totally useless.  (What NPC tagalong isn't?)
As frustrating and repetitive as Zeno Clash is, it sure gets the blood pumping, and there is just enough story to keep things interesting.  The world is shows us is fascinating and bizarre, and it has the audacity not to explain anything.  I got that rare feeling there is a consistent story hidden under the surface, and that made me want to see it through to the end.
The revelation at the end is more than enough to make the game epic as hell.  I was disappointed the game is so short, but the sequel makes up for that.  The story that is only implied in this game is revealed in all its detailed glory in Zeno Clash 2.  This of this game as a prologue to its sequel.
Both games are overlooked gems.  They deserve more attention.

Normally I'm not into these type of old Turn Based JRPGS. I've tried Fire Emblem and Bravely Default, but they never really clicked with me. Now a friend paypaled me money to purchase the game and now that I have finished the game after 40ish hours, I can safely say I'm glad I got this game and it's probably the best b-day gift I have ever gotten. After playing FFXV and Crisis Core, I was pretty motivated to play this game. And based on what I've played in FFVII, I can see myself playing through the older Final Fantasy games for most of this year.
The story has been and still is amazing and the simple yet satisfying gameplay is pretty nice. Idk why, but for this game, I feel a lot more motivated to grind in general regarding turn base JRPGs compared to before and the cast itself is likable with each one contributing an interesting personality. Even with the old visual styles, I found myself very immersed with the story because of how good it is and the characters that help bring it to life. I can't believe this game was released the same year I was born, so I never had the chance to play this game at all. The Soundtrack, obviously it's amazing whether you're fighting or roaming around the land. Very memorable and during certain scenes, very appropriate as well.
The DRM regarding the square enix account, idk if that has been a huge issue prior, but I was watching my friend stream it and he had no issues with it and I haven't had any issues either. Ignore the negative reviews that mention the DRM cuz that doesn't hold it back. Sure you may need an internet connection, but honestly we're in an age where we need an internet connection.
Overall, I honestly couldn't really find any flaws with the game that are very notable that could ruin the experience. I am aware that there are some glitches that can ruin the game, but thankfully I haven't ran into any of them. Outside of them, the game is perfect and definitely one of the best video games I have played of all time. I'm really glad I got to start on this game now because I almost avoided the game just to wait for the remake, which is still a few years away from being released. Now here I am just satisfied with FFVII and now even more excited for the remake to come out as well as having a huge urge to play through as many old Final Fantasy Games as I can. And I'm still not even done with FFVII because of a lot of post game content I definitely plan on doing, which will take up a lot of my time still. If you want to play an old game to get yourself into the FF series, definitely start with VII. You can't go wrong with this.
Oh and as to note this game is just a little over $10 right now and I don't see why they would raise the price on this game, so for just that price, you get at least 40ish hours of immersive gameplay, and it's amazing how much an old game can really give you an amazing experience.

Galactic Civilizations III is a very complex game and sadly doesnt give you sufficient tutorials. I bought it together with the Crusade expansion. So i started the game with the tutorials and the Crusade campaign, which is basically instructions on how to build on your planet and how to move ships. Sadly this franchise is far more difficult than building random things and moving ships (and sadly the tutorial and the main game (current patched version) work very differently).
Gameplay:
It´s basically an turn-based 4X game.
You are given tons of stats and management screens and ofc you can guess what they are maybe used for but it takes  a lot of time to fully understand the mechanics behind this (at least for me who is not used to 4X games). After around 10 full hours I found out that its basically producing gross income (like research points/construction points per turn) and asigning them to things you want to do. For example construction costs for a building are -200 which means you need to produce "construction points" every turn until you hit that goal. So lets say you produce 50 "construction points" per turn you will need 4 turns to finish this building. Same for Research. But basically you dont intuitively know what everything does and have to try out a lot of things before you finally understand. Even after 40 hours I cannot claim that I know everything this game has to offer.
Graphics:
Decent, but not overwhelming. A great positive thing is that all major civilizations have animated models and unique backgrounds. There are also nice sequences for game-end-events.
Campaign/Customizability:
Well i dont have all dem DLCs, but as I read there are small faction-based campaigns that tell abit about that faction. The main focus of this game is undoubtedly the customizability: Create own Factions, design own ships, define the game parameters as you see fit.
Conclusion:
There are very much things to discover, research branches to explore and unique faction abilities to find out about.
Sadly it doesnt come beginner-friendly. As a 4X-Veteran or owner of the previous titles of the franchise it should be fine nontheless. For me (as a beginner) it became a nicer game the more I found out about it, but ofc you also need the time to do so.

Can't wait to see what they do about politics in the next expansion !

The Witcher 2: Assassins of Kings.
Originally, I wasn't planning on buying this game. Then I heard the Save File from Assassins of Kings would influence Wild Hunt's, and I though, eh, why not? I don't regret it.
I have never truly played a Witcher Game. I only knew some of the characters (Such as Geralt), but it was such a famous franchise, that I wanted to play it, to try it out. So here it goes:
I had never quite played a Witcher game, I was gonna play Wild Hunt until I saw the news of the game save, but I manage to pass the game in Hard. Personally, I believe the game is pretty friendly to new people who come to Witcher, the game isn't TOO complicated, and the story you can understand it without playing the first game.
It may be because I hadn;t played the first game, but the story line failed me on this one. I didn't feel quite excited to know what would happen next, nor did I care for it. It didn't ruin the game, but it also didn't do it any favors.
Since Assassins of Kings isn't really an open world game, exploration isn't a big part of it. But you can wander off and fight some monsters, even find some cool things like locked chests you can find keys to open, and the side quests are even a bigger part of the game. Completing Assassins of Kings without doing them would be too quick.
The fighting on this game is great, it does not allow you to enter every battle and utilize the same strategy you've used throughout the entire game. You are given 6 spells and must utilize them to your advantage, as well as heavy and slow blows and a LOT of dodging. The fighting is fun, if you have the patience to learn how a monster is to be killed.
The controls in this game are standard. WASD for movement, looking around with mouse, and fighting with both right and left clicks. I won't go into detail with the rest, because I'm not here to give a lesson on controls, but most definitely very easy controls to learn.

In my opinion, the game was not tough at all after a while of understanding the monsters. I passed it on Hard, and some fights you are allowed to avoid, which are the harder ones. Although that comes from personal opinion of not playing in Insane mode.
The game is really fun, the fighting is great, characters are loveable. What didn't succeed on my part is the story, it was weak, and I personally adore story. I'd recommend the game for anyone who loves fighting with strategy, and wants to play Wild Hunt with their save file.

2015-04-25 - Someone has wisely chosen to split the campaign game review from criticism of the multi-player game.  They are certainly two completely different games.
There is a potentially interesting story here if the decision was made to focus on scripted drama instead of video gameplay, where choice and free-will are the implied drivers of the narrative.  Instead, we are spoonfed gameplay on rails where if you do not follow the lead of the puppeteer, you are, more-or-less, destined to failure and repeating the same scene over and over until you "get it right".  This, of course, shatters the immersion and turns an entertaining romp killing "bad guys" into a chore as you try to figure out the appropriate stimulus required for the response to move forward.
If you are expected to follow a script and did not receive it before the curtains were drawn...well, that is not a recipe for success.
The older I get, the more precious my time is.  I have not stopped playing a game for any other reason than lack of focus before I came upon this game.  To be fair, this realization was a cumulative understanding of the series, but the fact remains: this is the first game I uninstalled from my computer with no intention of ever completing that also actually incentivized me from uninstalling the sequel without even playing it.  Tar and feather me if I ever play another Call of Duty game again.
If you enjoy the growing trend in single player action gaming where player reaction is defined more by responses and key presses irrelevant to the normal mechanics of the game, then you will be at home with Call of Duty: Black Ops.  Otherwise, I would recommend you avoid the game as any interesting narrative is likely to be lost behind the repetition of getting the dance steps right.

Greatest simulator I have ever played. I love to do alot farming however it's just not possible in real life within my area cause my area is so poor that we only have very few farming equipment and is old as our ancesters so for that reason I play farming simulator.
Pros:
-The engine only loads up so much of the surrounding area as a radius as much as it will allow so that the performance won't bogg down so much if it were to be unlimited.
-Allows you to add custom made mods and a very large amount of them, as many as you want.
-The missions can help bring you up from debts however it is much too easy to gain a few thousand dollars in just one mowing job or transport goods using a frontloader from some place to another.
-Very large amount of farming equipment from the base game plus with the free DLC in the titanium edition.
-Love how you're able to reset you're equipment or vehicles back to the farm in case it gets stuck somewhere and can't get it back.
-One map from the base game gives you small fields while the other map gives you large sized fields.
-The PDA system is a huge help and the layout is just right.
-The controls on witch keys do what is also a helpping hand.
Cons:
-The base of the game only gives two maps? Thank goodness the game allows mods or there would only be two boring maps.
-The missions make getting out of debt too easy. You can make an easy million dollars just by doing the missions and have the setting set to ask every 2 minutes.
-The game is one giant chunk of mods. Without mods, the game is extremely lame and not fun.
-Is transporting goods and mowing yards the only two missions? There isn't even very many transporting goods or mowing jobs.
-Cars never should have been added, there more a hassle than fun to look at.
-The base only offers a total of 6 fruits. Again, thank goodness there's mods.
-Base only gives 3 different animals. Once again, thank goodness for the modding.
-Can't test anything out before buying so if you want to check somethin out you purchase then check it out and do a reload of the game.
-Not every tool (like the pull behind amazone sprayer) will attach to any of the newer tractor's but will with the older ones.
-Greenhouses require manure AND water.. Plants will grow just fine with manure alone. Why not ask for liquid manure instead, it's the same thing.
As you can see I used "mods" quite often. The game is total s*** without them so that's why I said it's one giant chunk of mods. Great simulator and worth the on sale price but the DLC's made by the dev's aren't worth a buck. I would get all the custom made mods rather than to spend $30 on DLC's that will only give me a few new vehicles and tools each.

This game is a great port. Escellent in fact, but nothing is without flaws. Thank fully this game doesn't have too many of them. First lets look at some purchase perks. The game comes with baked in cheats, mods, acheivements, and chocobo world. To thouse who've played the original Chocobo World on it's own should be enough to want to purchase this remake as previously the only way to play it, and take advantage of the unique to the game items, were through cheats/hacks, or having a playstation pocket, and a playstation that could read it, so for this content alone you might be getting your money's worth. Next square enix has included acheivements. I don't have to tell you how achievements (or trophies if you think with a playstation mindset) didn't became mainstream until around 2005, so they are new and it gives you something to do along the way while playing, although there is plenty to do without them. The mods, are great. most importantly, the speed mod is great. If you've ever been pressed for time and not a lot of time for sitting through un-skippable cutscenes, or watching about 3-4 mins of traversing a map it definately comes in handy. Lastly the cheats. The game comes with some cheats built in such as the 100 spell cheat where you can draw a spell, and either press the cheat button, or save the game and run the cheat and you will have 100 of that spell. I haven't actually used any of the cheats, because I don't want to deprive myself of the bits of grinding here and there, but It's there if you need it.
Lots to love here. This game gives you options. No you will not have a different ending, but you have options to give yourself a different playthrough. The game levels itself up as you do, so you can play it a stratight shoot, or you can withold your level and work on crafting and farming items. You can grab the first magic that comes to mind, or you can be selective to carry the best magics. A lot of people will drill that the stat's suffer from using your stronger spells, but it's perception. I think of it as it expends energy to use the stronger spells making you weaker with use. With no GF challenges, or other self made playing challenges you can replay the game and have a whole different experience.
You've heard the positives now here are a few sour spots. The music. As you may have heard plenty beofre the musing isn't the best. It's heavily synthesized and sounds like a fan did all the music in their favorite mid player. It's the same as it was in the original game but with the concerts put out, most have grown acusomed to the higher level of music. It's a minor setback, one that could have been corrected by square enix much like the visual updates. The magic system. It is unique, and has a lot of give and take, but just as much as I applaud the using mgic drains your stats idea, the magic just isn't that strong. There aren't that many powerful spells, and because of it you're likely not to try creating any mages, or see your characters have much in differentiating stats. The controls for this port are bad, you can change your controls, but I haven't found out how to succesfully setup a controller, even with an xbox controller and support for them in the game. Even worse you can't turn off (or I haven't found out how to) controller controls and as you use your keyboard. In any dialogue that involves the controls the control controls display until you press, and/or hold down your keyboard keys. it's very frustrating.
As the title imples the game is defeinately a great buy due to the many perks, and how they way outweigh the cons.  If you want a very engrosing story, amazing cutscenes, music you will catch yourself humming to, Interesting gamign mechanics that offer plenty of replayability and hours upon hours of standard gameplay. Plenty of secrets, so much that you may need a guide or two to find them all. Lastly, the mini games chocobo world, and triple triad are good enough to be spinoffs of their own, and are beneficial, albeit optional, to the game. If you've been on the fence about it, or you have wanted to try it previously but haven't yet pick this one up or regret it.

inb4 fanboys mark this review as unhelpful because I didn't give it a 10/10.
Bear in mind that I am reviewing this game from the 2015 point of view, having not played it back in its day, and I have zero nostalgia for it.
Giving a review for this game is extremely difficult. It has a lot of interesting systems that make it one of the most interesting Final Fantasy games in the series. On the other hand, everything that is good and interesting about the game is opposed by a nearly equal ammount of convoluted or just plain terrible design decisions that will frustrate a modern player to no end. Some of this stuff may have been able to fly on the PS1 back in 1999, but in 2015, this stuff can grate your nerves. So let me try to point out the good and bad.
DRAW SYSTEM - THE GOOD: The draw system refers to the fact that characters don't have personal magic on them at all times. Instead, magic is reduced to consummable items (e.g. to cast Blizzaga, you will need to use 1 blizzaga item). To get more spell items, you have to "draw" them (i.e. steal them) from enemies. The number you get is random. Sometimes you get zero or one, but a lot of times you'll get 5 or 6 at once. Each enemy has a menu of spells you can steal from. More useful and powerful spells can only be stolen from mini-bosses, bosses, and rare enemies. Once you've stolen the spell items, you can use them in combat or you can fuse them to specific stats to boost a character's parameters, like boosting fire def, or adding fire to their attack, or increasing HP or vitality, etc. You have the option to either steal the enemy's spell (add it to your inventory) which just gives you the item and ends your turn, or you can cast the enemy's own spell at the enemy party immediately.
DRAW SYSTEM - THE BAD: As much as all of the above is interesting, you may find it frustrating that spells are essentially just items. You may also find it frustrating that, in order to stock up on specific spells (especially more rare ones), you just waste a lot of turns usings your characters to steal, steal, steal, etc etc 100 times. Stealing the spells is primarily useful for boosting parameters. The guardians (who we'll discuss in a moment) are so powerful that actually using the spells in combat is only sometimes---but rarely---useful.
GUARDIAN SYSTEM - THE GOOD: The game calls them "guardian forces" for some reason, but let's call them what they really are: summons. So this game decides to make summons front and center. You collect new summons as you go through the game, which can be assigned to any character. Every summon has its one powerful spell it can cast, but if you grow each summon (like a pokemon!) it can become more powerful, boost the parameters of the ally using it, give the user more skills/abilities, or allow the user to summon it into battle more quickly. The summons are powerful, and you will want to use them a lot.
GUARDIAN SYSTEM - THE BAD: The summons are so powerful that you will want to use them almost exclusively. Physical attacks and magic attacks are, on average, so pathetic compared to summoning that you will only end up using physical/magic attacks "just for fun", or in the rare circumstances when you need to beat some enemy's gimmick. (basic attacks get better over time, but do you really want to wait 60 hours for them to get better?) What about elemental weaknesses? Yeah, enemies have them, but if its a choice between casting firaga or summoning Ifrit on them, what are you going to do? You'll spam Ifrit. Managing the guardian forces is also laborious. It's about as exciting as meticulously shifting all of your materia gems around in FF7, only it involves an even more convoluted system of sub-screens, and sub-sub-screens, and even sub-sub-sub-screens. If I were new to RPGs, I would have quit this game out of frustration just on account of its dogpiled menus. Also, even though the game has TONS of summons to find, you will absolutely miss the vast majority of them unless someone tells you in advance that most of them can only be stolen from bosses (via the "draw" command) or under special circumstances. You essentially need a strategy guide opened up as you play, if you don't wanna miss a ton of them. Also, the summon animations are sooo long. They are painfully long. And since they are the focus of the game, you have to sit dumbly and watch them a lot. This is slightly improved when they level up enough to learn "boost", which allows you to play a button tapping mini-game to pass the time during the animation and raise the attack power of the summon, but 1) you'll have to check a strategy guide to learn how boost works, because the game can't be arsed to explain it; 2) they are sooo long though.
CHARACTERS - GOOD: In-game character models look much better than the dopey FF7 ones, although their faces do look kinda pinched and weird. Squall always looks cross-eyed, but I accept that because it amuses me. The characters and story get more attention and are overall more appealing than FF7 in my opinion.
CHARACTERS - BAD: A lot of cliche (but that's typical of JRPGs). Squall is a stereotypical angsty and brooding I-hate-everything-and-have-a-bad-attitude-leave-me-alone-and-get-out-of-my-room emo teenage boy type. At least at first. As a teenage boy I would have thought he was the coolest. As a grown man, I find him immature and irritating. He gets better. Oh, and as much as other FF8 fans have told me they like the segments, you also will have your game and story progress continually interrupted by a "Biggs and Wedge" sequence, where you have to play through a complete dungeon and story sequence as some characters you don't know. After you play a lot of them, they will start to tie into the main story more and make more sense, but for a long time they are complete non-sequiturs. Who are these people? Why do I care? Can this just be over so I can go back to Squall and friends? What is the point of this? Maybe you'll dig it, but these felt like disruptions (or interruptions) to me, so I didn't care for them.
OTHER - BAD: Convoluted menus. Fails to explain some game features completely or gives very poor explanations of other features (there is a tutorial/guide available, but its helpfulness varies). While the draw/guardian (aka steal/summon) systems are interesting in a lot of out-of-combat ways, they also make the inside-combat part of the game feel lopsided and weird. Plus they require an inordinate amount of fiddling in menus---as bad as fiddling with materia gems or worse (but, hey, some people love all of that fiddling, so if that's you, have fun). The game also some very bad dungeons in it, such as one dungeon consisting of 15 copy-pasted floors of the exact same doughnut-shaped room you have to run completely around (i.e. poor design trick used to make you trip more random encounters while not caring enough to make the dungeon any more interesting). The game is also a completely clutz when it comes to save points. Don't be surprised if you are made to sit through 30-minutes of unskippable story sequences and then ambushed with a boss fight you had no way of knowing was coming. No saves. If you die or forget to steal the guardian force, prepare to do that entire 30-minute boring story sequence again. This doesn't just happen once. It is a repeat problem. The game tends to suck at save point placement in general.
Steam only allows thumbs up or thumbs down, when what I'd like is a pair of shrugging shoulders that says "mixed feelings". You might like it! But for me personally, in 2015, the number of tiny annoyances, deliberate inconveniences, and questionable or convoluted design choices just adds up to me banging my head against the wall a little bit too often. Like the world's cutest dog that also won't stop sh***ing on the floor, it is a thing I feel compelled to love with all my heart but equally as often feel compelled to drop off on the side of the road.

I was sceptical upon purchasing the game, watching small clips of gameplay from various youtubers. However I can comfortably say that even though this game is pretty expensive considering some alternative stragegy games are cheaper, that I am happy that I spent the money because not only does it have great gameplay and an amazing "make your own" desicion style to it. But the replay Factor is absolutely unreal.
The fact that the game developers have gone out of their way and put an intense amount of detail in it, from the name of almost every planet known to man, to the actual science behind some of the missions. It's not like a fantasy game where something illogical happens and someone says "a wizard did it" but it comes up with the idea that an unkown ancient being(s) that came billions of years before man, created and developed a power to enable then to travel around star sytems and create an empire.
The reason it is so replayable, much like Civilization, is because at any given moment anything can happen. For example, my playthrough showed that even if you have the strongest empire in the whole galaxy, there will be some force out there that  can destroy you in an instant.
What I would really love to see with this game, is not from the developers, but from the small content creaters and modders. I think this game is the ideal canvas for a Mass Effect mod. I have been looking through the workshop and over the depths of the internet and have encountered many different people trying to accomplish this. If just one of them was to pull it off like the mods of Sins of a Solar Empire, then this game would be perfect for me and anyone else who is fan of the Mass effect trilogy and a fan of strategy games. Plus you can go for the same story as Mass Effect, but change it a bit so that the story of Mass Effect ends how you would want it to.
Over all this game is amazing, it has a long way to go, and hopefully the developers will work their arses off for this project. It's already an amazing game and I want to see how good it can get.

2015-04-25 - Someone has wisely chosen to split the campaign game review from criticism of the multi-player game.  They are certainly two completely different games.
There is a potentially interesting story here if the decision was made to focus on scripted drama instead of video gameplay, where choice and free-will are the implied drivers of the narrative.  Instead, we are spoonfed gameplay on rails where if you do not follow the lead of the puppeteer, you are, more-or-less, destined to failure and repeating the same scene over and over until you "get it right".  This, of course, shatters the immersion and turns an entertaining romp killing "bad guys" into a chore as you try to figure out the appropriate stimulus required for the response to move forward.
If you are expected to follow a script and did not receive it before the curtains were drawn...well, that is not a recipe for success.
The older I get, the more precious my time is.  I have not stopped playing a game for any other reason than lack of focus before I came upon this game.  To be fair, this realization was a cumulative understanding of the series, but the fact remains: this is the first game I uninstalled from my computer with no intention of ever completing that also actually incentivized me from uninstalling the sequel without even playing it.  Tar and feather me if I ever play another Call of Duty game again.
If you enjoy the growing trend in single player action gaming where player reaction is defined more by responses and key presses irrelevant to the normal mechanics of the game, then you will be at home with Call of Duty: Black Ops.  Otherwise, I would recommend you avoid the game as any interesting narrative is likely to be lost behind the repetition of getting the dance steps right.

FF7 is a challenging, engaging, and relevant story told through the seemingly innocent lies of video game tropes and fiction. When I played FF7 for the first time as an older teenager in the late '90s, I didn't just play it, I lived it. I'm not sure if it's the best video game ever or not, but no other game has influenced who I am as a person as much as FF7 did.﻿
I'm not a Final Fantasy fan in general – too many cliché, campy JRPG game tropes and poor, shallow, and often recycled story telling themes intentionally obscured by contrived and otherwise pointless ambiguity as an artificial substitute for genuine intrigue and a compelling narrative. No, I just like FF7 for what it has to offer beyond what all the other FF games do. In a word, substance.﻿ The realization of FF7 was a bold, groundbreaking, original, and risky endeavor that resulted in a phenomenal triumph, the likes of which the industry has been too talentless, cowardly, and greedy to replicate since.
This reissue has some silly account marketing crap to navigate through on initial setup, but is still very much worth getting for the FF7 content in all of its classic goodness.
This game is a definitive masterpiece and a necessity for any connoisseur or collector of this art medium.
Bask in the glory that is FF7 and enjoy!

Plays pretty much just like the first NFS SHIFT. More newer cars, less levels but more exp required to level, more car modding, same amount of customization. Drag race mode is fun but the controls are weird as all hell. My layout for shifting gears is right thumbstick up = downshift, right thumbstick down = upshift similar to a sequential gearbox (the very reason my layout is like that is because its based off of sequential gearboxes). In drag racing/standing mile it gets inverted, and its just gets all weird. No way to customize it either from what I've seen in the settings.
I haven't gotten very far in in terms of career or levels (Level 15/20 at the moment) but I'm not earning much money (none in most cases) out of quick races either. This could be either due to my career progress or my level, or the simple fact that I'm not racing against anyone and just cruising around tracks testing cars.
Minor flaw but when you works convert a car, you can sell the car, but you don't get all the money back. What I mean is, back in SHIFT, lets say you spent 500k on upgrades, you spend another 150k to works convert the car. Total spent is 650k right? Now when you sell the car. You get 650k back. Not in SHIFT as far as I'm aware. I maxed out my R32 Skyline and Works converted it, decided to flip it for other cars. Noticed I don't have as much money all of a sudden. You can however own multiple versions of the same car. Unlike SHIFT where once you own say the Corvette C6 Z06, you can't buy it again.
Speaking of my beloved Corvette C6Z, its not purchasable in this game. You have to unlock it
and once unlocked, thats it. You can't buy a stock C6Z so if you Works convert it, it stays Works converted. You don't HAVE to works convert it because you can buy the Z06GT3 (looks virtually the same as the Works converted C6Z but I'll have to look at it more closely to determine that) and the C6.R GT2 car but its just...I want to own a Works converted and "stock" C6Z.
If I'm correct you also have unlimited garage space unlike SHIFT where you unlock more garage space as you level up. This is also due to the fact that you can own multiple copies of a car. What I like about that is being able to own a Works converted and a non-converted race car. Granted I don't plan to own any Works cars but I can if I choose to and still have a non-converted car.
The coolest thing is being able to build a drag car or horsepower monster with the Drag Build category in the upgrades, downside is you are limited to either the Standing Mile or 1/4 mile events. Kind of a bummer if you ask me because, the things you're upgrading are the clutch, engine, turbo, and fuel system and nothing else. But to be fair, it does say DRAG SPEC so I guess taking them to a road course wouldn't be great since its drag spec parts on the car. I seriously wish you could take the Speedhunter's R32 GTR out onto a track instead of a standing or 1/4 mile event.
Speaking of upgrades, on a stock car that allows for upgrades you can see how much horsepower, torque, and weight HOWEVER, you need to be in the upgrades section with a part selected in order to see these stats. You can't go to your garage like SHIFT and select a car and switch it to numerical stats. This means, if you unlock a car through completing events like say the Standing Mile events or the 1/4 mile events and you unlock the monstrous Twin-Turbo 97' Viper or the WORLD racing Pro-FWD Reaper Scion t/C drag car, you CAN'T see the stats like horsepower, torque, and how much it weighs. You can see the top speed, acceleration, handling, braking, the drivetrain layout/powertrain, what class the car is, what performance rating it is BUT you can't see the power, torque, or weight of the car.

FF8 is a good game. For those new to FF this would be an odd start. Each FF has a little gimmick within their gameplay. FF8 introduces a "junction" system which can be confusing at first. In actuality it's pretty lame, but a cool concept. In previous FFs magic would drain MP, but in FF8 magic is drawn(upto100) from various points in game, and from monsters. All while requiring a GF(gaurdian force) to be "junctioned" to that character. In order to actually buff your characters, junctioning magic is required. Unlike in other FFs leveling hardly boosts stats. It is required to draw a lot of one spell just to buff a character efficiently. What makes plain leveling useless is the fact that enemies are level'd according to the party's average level. People have beaten the game low level'd with proper junctions alone.
Also... you can find yourself mashing GF summons early on... which means watching a cutscene, damaging enemy, and continuing fight. Not only is combat a bit dull compared to other installments, there doesn't seem to be much enemy variety. The final area's random encounters are monsters that you fight throughout the game. Although the little summon cutscenes are pretty great for 1999.
Other than the combat the game plays like a novel. A very nice story, and smooth character developement. Even with a story that is all over the place, literally, it is shown beautifully. Oh, there is also extra things like "Triple Triad". It's a card game played with cards collected while progressing. There's a whole bunch of other things involving the cards, but no need to mention it. Just more things to do rather than blowing through the story. Never bothered playing any card matches(or using cards) in my playthrough.
Like I said in the first sentence... FF8 IS a good game. IMO not the best FF, but definitely better than some of the  recent releases.

Stellaris - Review // UPDATE 1.1
Stellaris strikes me as a very refreshing, yet pleasantly familiar space 4X at the same time and reminds me the most of a very ancient DOS-based 4X called Ascendancy.
It just so happens that Ascendancy was also the very first 4X I have ever played in my life, and it also happens that very few other space 4X's after that managed to keep my attention as long as that one in nearly twenty years.
But with Stellaris, the whole thing is back. Forget GalCiv 3, forget MoO. Stellaris does it all, does it right, and probably has the most reliable and supreme patch support after release of all three. DLC? No - major updates for free, and you will only pay for actual new content and only if you really want to - not because the deeper game mechanics actually force you to. Paradox approaches games the way they should be approached: as a living product that is never truly perfect. Evidenced by not only their own patch and aftersale support history, but also by enabled Mod Support from day one.
The base game Stellaris is a feature-rich and feature-complete 4X that offers, starting with update 1.1 "Clarke", some of the most interesting AI/diplomacy strategies, and a micro-to-macro style of gameplay that is perfectly in sync with the way your stellar empire grows in size (over time, the game allows you to move micro managing to 'Sectors' that are auto-governed and puts a soft cap on the number of planets you have direct control of).
All of the above still leaves one of the most enticing and cool bits of this game behind: the absolutely brilliant writing. Literally every trigger, every event and every action is meaningful, well narrated and invites you to immerse yourself in your space empire. Combined with the absolute freedom in your rise to power, this gives the otherwise 100% random generated universe great body and context.
If I were to name one drawback of the game, it's that you can't press 'One more turn'... You just end up looking at the clock at some point, which is usually a bunch of hours later than you really intended to.

So, here we have Destiny Warriors RPG, "heavily influenced by Chrono Trigger, Final Fantasy and the Dragon Quest series". Those are some big names. So how heavy is this game influenced be the aforementioned titles? Not much. I - being a lover especially of Chrono Trigger - didn't even see a hint about it except that both games are basically in a classic RPG-Style.
What did I like?
-The beginning wasn't exceptional but ok.
-The game itself works - most of the time.
-I really did want to see how the story progresses and it all ends. But it seems I can't drag myself through the end. It's just too painful.
-I liked the idea of implementing quizzes regarding the games setting for getting some additional items and one part of the storyline.
-Some thought and work has been invested into it.
What did I dislike? Oh boy, actually a ton...
-All the assets are as far as I can tell stock assets, which does not need to be a huge downside. But be warned: you might've seen these faces and animations in a lot of games, you've heard the songs thousands of times, the sounds are old friends (which might be a plus if you're very into it)...
-At the beginning, it plays pretty smooth, your characters learn new abilities, they progress through levels and get stronger. However, soon leveling is almost obsolete. Enemies will then always take lower damage and dish out more than your characters can. The only attacks which work good are so Chi-expensive you need to carry ludicrous amounts of Chi-pills with you; and healing kits or "tents" (which revive all of your crew). "Elemental attacks" aren't really that powerful even against the correct "contra-element". Gear does more for winning a battle than leveling. Luck DECIDES MOST OF YOUR BATTLES. Even if your "gang" has the highest possible levels (it is 50 for some chars, less for others) you'll get your♥♥♥♥♥handed to you in later battles.  Even with the most pricey armour and weaponry. Tactical options are limited to finding the attacks which work best; and still you have to press Enter all the way through battle for a long time. Your only chance of taking some influence on the battles is using gear which might give extra protection against certain "elemental" enemies or... trying to escape. Which most often will not work near the end, even if your chars are maxxed. I don't know if it is even possible to win this game without cheating. I guess by poor chance it might be possible.
I've played lots of RPG-Maker games and underdogs (I like to give many games a chance), but seldomly have I met something so frustrating. It is a frustration that sets in too late for you to notice to pull the plug. I know how many games require a good deal of grinding but here you do it just to see that IT DOESN'T HELP AT ALL. After you've done it.
-The storyline. I don't want to put too many spoilers in here, but a good deal of it is pretty blunt. There's things never hinted or talked about by any (N)PC, it's just "BOOM - THERE IT IS - IT ALWAYS WAS LIKE THAT - TAKE THAT, SHUT UP, DO YOUR MISSION". It is extremely linear (well, many (RPG-Maker) games are to a certain degree, but here you are accompanied with this feeling right from the start. Minor Spoiler for one example: You get a world map at a certain point in the game which allows you to travel around. But you can only visit places you've already been to. Yes, sometimes there are little changes, but nothing too much.
-Sidequests. They are not really quests. You can - yes, spoiler - trade in some (sometimes extremely rare) loot items for cash or experience. One by one. Always going through the same dialogue. Or you can fight some monsters which most likely will "rip you a new one" for some experience. Wow.
-The Battles (again): Everything is drawn out, tons of battles are there to slow you down. Regardless of your difficulty setting you'll lose hours of your life just trying to escape or fight through the sheer number of encounters you will face. You'll spent much time restarting the game completely if you try to avoid some seemingly unnecessary fights by just reloading your game. Why? You can't flee many battles because the enemies are faster/better skilled than you. You can't just quickly restart the game with F12 because this crashes it in most instances.
-Loot. How can loot be bad? Well because there often is none, instead you get additional fights which draw out the game even longer. You might have to fight even the hardest baddies to just get an empty chest or another soul-rending encounter. And often you get mediocre stuff you'd already have discarded because you need better gear to even get to the area where this stuff is located. Only money seems to help a bit.
-Crashes when trying to restart with F12 (which might be a compatibility problem with Steam, I can't tell for sure), Crashes when you're trying to use some in-game items (like the great series of the "Kitt"-Books)
-This is a minor complaint, but the writing and grammar... well there are noticeable errors all throughout the game.
-Somebody charged money for this.
I didn't even finish it yet which I wanted to accomplish before writing this review - sometimes a good ending may make up for a lot of trouble - but it is just getting slower, sluggish even, unfair to non-working, more boring and repetitive towards the end. I guess sometime I might get to it but as for now... no. Just no.
There might be more to say but I feel like I've already invested too much time into this game altogether. If you ask me this is not a recommendable game. Even if you get it heavily discounted.
As it is with reviews, this conclusiion might contain some subjective impressions.

At first I loved this game. I was definitely a Naruto rip off, but there were quirks and commentary that made it humorous. (Spark will forever be known as Dude Elf to me thanks to looking like an elf, and the first dialogue coming out of him including "dude") The different types of skills and weapons made for an interesting game play, and it was relatively easy to level up. I was confused when Max suddenly capped, but figured he was the Sasuke character and would be lost eventually. Overall though, not that bad.
Then the ninja tournament came. Suddenly the battle system became a joke. The status effects and speed of the opponents was so ridiculous that I had to redo the first battle at least 20 times. Things only went downhill from there. The enemies, especially boss fights, were ridiculous. Enemy defense was so high that attacks that used to do hundreds or even thousands of damage were now doing 1. When the beast modes finally showed up...wow that was a let down. Rather than power up during beast modes, character skills were limited and the bosses in particular seemed to be exceptionally strong and fast.
I will give an example: in the first temple, you are forced to fight clones of your current party plus the phantom summoning them. Round one was pretty balanced. They had my attacks, I had theirs, so just working out how to attack them so that I came out on top was both easy and straight forward. Then round 2 happened. The characters are forced into beast mode while more clones pop up. Suddenly my characters were down to less techniques than I could count on a hand. That's nice and all, except they are dishing out attacks that both freeze and take out half the hp of the characters (keep in mind my characters are both capped, wearing their strongest armors, and have items equipped to add to their power and defense.). What happens when I dish out the same technique which my character happened to keep? 1hp damage. Compared to thousands on their part. I'm sorry, but what? Add on the fact that these guys have status effects, are insanely fast, and have both a healer and a phantom which can resummon clones in a turn, and it was something worth rage quitting over.
Now I am at the second temple, and already there are lizardmen who are showing the same ridiculous effect spam and healing techniques. Let's also include here that they are pretty high in level, which would put them on par with the main guy on the team, but the game has forcefully pair him up with his ten levels lower father (which the game says can equip armor and a weapon...which he cannot), and a character who is lvl literally 28 levels lower.
I haven't even finished the game yet, but this is one that I'm seriously considering just letting sit unfinished.

For years I've avoided this game, mainly going by the kind of reviews that currently plague this Steam page.  But, I decided to take a leap of faith, and guess what?  The game is awesome, and highly recommended if you've been playing the PSX version through an emulator to get slightly better graphics, and especially to those that have been rocking the older PC version, which was buggy and contaned inferior music tracks.  Let's check off the list of improvements, eh?
- Overall smoother looking graphics AND backgrounds
- Same music as the original PlayStation game
- "Easy" mode that boosts all of your stats so you just enjoy the story (requires Cloud save and to be online)
- Can be modded if you want (though outside of Steam)
To be clear, you DO have to create a Square Enix account, but I've only had to login once and never again.  Try that with your Origin or UbiPlay games.  And to all those people complaining about have to be online, this is what happens if you want Cloud saving and are online with Steam.  If you don't want this, turn off Cloud saving and you can take Steam offline.  You lose the ability to use your save between computers, but you can also be offline all the time.
Now, things aren't perfect, but this is more indicative to it being based on the PC game.  While I am primarily a PC gamer, FFVII just feels unnatural on the keyboard.  I'm sure that if I played a few hours I wouldn't care, but right now thinking about juggling all that materia whilst using the keyboard gives me the cold sweats.  Luckily, it does have partial controller support.  You know the drill for Steam; get a compatible controller or an app that can get you own working.
So, to recap:  This game rocks!  You have to create a SQ account, but since you only login once, I don't see what is the big deal.  I mean, you have to login into Steam to get this far, don't you?  Plus, you get to cheat right out of the box (no mods required).  So, if you've always wanted to get a better looking version of FFVII, or haven't played the game but was curious as to why it is lauded so, go ahead and pick this game up.

This review is from the perspective of a new player to the series. Yes I have “played” the first witcher but dropped it after realizing how broken the game play is.
The points:
+ Controller support
+ Combat
+ Dialog
+ Characters
+ Art/Level Design
+ Solo
+ One Ring to Rule Them all/ Lesbomancy
~ Animation
~ Story (my bad)
~ Menus
- The world
- Short
- Triss’s BS
8/10
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Okay let's start off with the middle ground issues, the ones that were annoying but didn’t break it for me. The animation at times was great the problem is the other 50% of the time they look like ventriloquist dummies, which is worse than the Mass effect stare. The story is very hard to follow and get into the swing of understanding it however after about 3 hours in I could fully understand what was going on. The menus leave much to be desired but it’s a huge step up from witcher 1, it took about an hour to get used to after that didn’t have much issue.
Now the negative, the world makes no sense I don’t understand how 8 tiny countries smaller than rhode island can pump out more then the huge southern nation. I’m sorry but these nations are conquered. The story is short like COD level game short for a RPG. And Lastly Triss’s ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, this is not a damsel in distress issue. The issue with Triss is it’s obvious by the 80% mark of the main story that ALL this time she has been lying and manipulating you, BUT NOTHING COMES OF IT. no dialog, no nothing, I’ll be starting Wild Hunt sometime today if this is not brought up I will mark that game down as well for this.
Now for the good, I glad this game has controller support because rolling around using a keyboard would have been a massive pain. And it’s done very well, I have some issues with inventory but besides that everything was handled well. The combat is actually combat in this game I can sense hints of Dark Souls, which isn’t bad because this game has a better combat system then Dark Souls (no one likes a game that ques your button presses). The dialog is not Mass Effect level crap of good, funny, and mad. It’s actually a bunch of options that may lead you to what you need. The Dialog system shines best with the Golem in the mission The Secrets of Loc Muinne. The characters are properly developed and have depth to back them except for Triss(her whole character is “she wants your D” -.- not joking). The world is beautiful and the levels are large enough for the time spent in each area to make it worth it. And lastly the solo experience, this is Geralt’s story not “Geralt and his friends” story. At first I thought I would hate this, but as time went on it made you feel more awesome. Do to the fact you were doing everything on your own.

I never had a chance to play this game when it came out, so I'm reviewing this without Nostalgia blinding me.
That being said, however, I can see the magic behind this game and why so many people love it. I know people like Pros and cons lists so..
PROS:
-Amazing Combat System
-Wonderful Story (Although there are a few RPG cliches here and there, but for it's time, it was semi-original)
-Supports Controllers, so you don't have to stare at your keyboard thinking wtf is the OK button.
-So... SO many hours of gameplay. Seriously, I have 63 hours and I haven't 100%ed the game, even with a walkthrough. So if you go blind, you're in for a hell of a ride (I'll get to why I used a guide in a sec)
-A ton of extra content besides the main game, including bosses and sidequests.
-The game holds up beautifully by today's standards. The backgrounds are appealing to the eye, and for it's time, it really looked nice.
CONS:
-There is no new game+ unless you use something like a save editor, which I don't recommend.
-There are a few cliches in the story. Nothing major.
- The reason I ended up using a guide for this game was due to there being missable content. I recommend searching up a guide just for this. Try not to read ahead however. I personally recommend bover_87's FAQ/Walkthrough on Gamefaqs, as that is the one I personally used. Just beware if you go in blind it is highly possible you will miss items.
-Some of the sidequests are annoying (*cough* Fort Condor *cough*)
-Apparently you need internet Connection to play the game, which is a drawback
-There is a glitch that happened to me that causes the game to crash whenever I exit the save menu (I don't know how to fix it, however you can still save, you just need to relaunch FF7 afterwards, this happened late in the game for me)
All in all, the game is definitely worth getting. It's one of the best games I've played in a long time. You will NOT be disappointed. HOWEVER, I've heard the PS4 version is a lot more stable and has more features (speeding up the game, disabling encounters, etc.), I have not tried the PS4 version. Also, I'd look up more about the character booster, as it seems to level up stats, and disables XP gain. So for those who own a PS4, consider that as well.
Also, for those who are waiting for the remake, it is most likely going to have different mechanics, including the combat system, and I recommend experiencing the legendary tale for what it is.
For games like this one I recommend:
-Wild Arms 1, 2 and/or 3.
-Final Fantasy 8(I have not played FF8)
-Chrono Trigger/Cross(Also not experienced)
For games possibly like the upcoming remake(subject to change):
-Kingdom Hearts 1 and 2
-Final Fantasy XV

1) You DO NOT NEED TO BE ONLINE 24/7 TO PLAY. You just need to have internet while you make a square account. Then once you're logged in, go to 'FF7 Launcher Settings' and disable 'Cloud Saving'. There you go. FF7 will never need to be connected to the internet again.
I point this out because I keep reading reviews that say you need to be online 24/7 DRM blah blah... and its completely untrue. It put me off of buying the game for awhile. Screw that. Now you know.
2) They updated the character models and enemies and they did a good job. Its a perfect mix of old and new, slanted towards old. The models are improved, not changed. And if for some reason you hate it, in the launcher theres a toggle. You can have the exact Ps1 graphics if you want. But once you switch you'll want to go back to the updated version, trust me on that.
3) Check out all the different mods for the steam version of FF7. Depending on how far you want to go, you can mod this games graphics pretty hard.
TLDR: If you played FF7 as a kid and loved it then get this. 6 bucks is a steal.
TLDR#2: You don't need to be online 24/7 to play. That's a myth. So don't worry.

This game is everything that the original Shift wanted to be. If you enjoyed Shift, then this is a no-brainer - get this game. Yes, the racing is very arcade-y, but what do you expect? It IS Need for Speed!
The AI makes a decent job of looking like each car has individual intelligence, but it's 50/50 between being impressed by the AI behaviour and being vexed & frustrated when they ignore the fact that you are on their line and take you off the road.
Some of the noises and handling of the cars can be a little weird, but at least you can iron out the handling with tuning. As with almost every other car game of its ilk, by the time you've beaten the 'rival' and won his car, you don't actually need the car - this feature is useful if you intend to replay events, but for me it was 'I don't need your car now, plus I've just beaten it anyway!'
The (now) free Speedhunters dlc came in useful and, overall, it was a fairly decent, enjoyable game (one of my best memories of a race game will be a 20 lap endurance race on Mount Panorama in a Gallardo. Until the engine blew, in lap 18, it was one of the most fun times I've ever had in a racing game!) and, for me personally, the feel of progression lacked a little something - it didn't really feel like I WAS advancing, just doing a seemingly endless grind of different tracks and faster cars. The addition of the drag and drift was mixed for me. I can see where some people would love (and hate) these events, but in my playthrough, they were just 'there' and so I did them. I actually preferred the drifting in Shift!
A slightly mixed sounding review, but all I can say is that if you like serious racing sims, steer well clear and if, like me, you also enjoy something a little lighter now and again, then this is well worth your time.

After waiting for more than two years to have this game become playable on my PC (some people even can't play it until this very day, check the internet for various troubleshooting threads), I finally managed to get this game going. Was it worth it?
Positive aspects:
- lots of tuning possiblities for the cars (which you don't need at all, at least some candy for car nerds :) )
- full and realistic car sounds
- variety of race modes, e.g. timed laps, drag race etc.
Neutrals:
- the amount of cars represented is rather mediocre by today's genre standards
- nice leveling system, but the rewards are a bit unbalanced (500$ for a race win, 10.000 for a low level up)
Negative aspects:
- this game is dark at night races! I had to put up my monitor's, my graphics card's and my windows' brightness levels to somewhat near maximum to tell the game i have an own sun running right in my pc. and still, I can only see 50 meters ahead of the track.
- the controls feel soapy. you get used to it, but better use a controller or a wheel. using a keyboard you will have a hard time, especially in late-game races as gt1 and super cars are naturally iffy
- career mode feels a bit plastic with a campaign representing rather unknown race drivers (at least for europeans who know Schumacher, Loeb, Rossi etc.). Basically, you're going through races without further ado, win a car here and there and that's it. they could have put more effort into that
Below the line, I would recommend the game after all. It's all about arcadish racing, and there are certainly better and more recent games out there, but as a fan of the NFS franchise, you don't do anything wrong buying it. But make sure to check if it runs on your machine right after!

overwhelming emotional issues after this game... I love it!
*edit* Now that i have time to write the full review.
The game is amazing, the art style is simple and very beautiful.
The combat is old school side scroller perfected in my eyes,
and the story is very perfect once you unravel it all.
So lets start there at the story,
You play as Dust, an Fox-morph anthro character. who cannot remember a thing. you wield a sword who is sentient. Cant really remember it's name as its been a while. Then you have Fidget who is a support/Navi type character. Now hold on before you walk away.
Fidget is not annoying! Shes hilarious. She breaks the fourth wall like mad and is very adorable.
Dust is very cliche hero type who lost memory yet fights the 'bad' guys to learn about himself. yet it really works out with how the story plays.
Youll fight through and meet a series of other characters from a blacksmith squirrel, who has the crazy hots for Dust, to a mysteriously cliche loner female who looks like she could be related to Dust.
The combat;
Now heres the fun part, combat is very fast paced once you get mid to late game. EArly game its semi slow semi fast. Youll have a few magical attacks but its mostly combo skills youll be working with, each help and there is some fun to juggle lifeless corpses endlessly....
Visuals;
Artisticly beautiful, the art matches the game. It really captures alot of details for a cartoony sorta look but the areas youll see will really make you feel sorta awed.
Emotional factor!
Now here is the big kicker, i originally got the game cause i don't see many 'furry' styled games. I find them really unique and interesting (hey grew up on some old furstyled games, don't judge)
after playing and beating... i was emotionally hurt, There is a sad level factor to it that i won't spoil.
but after this game i couldn't help but search for more and more emotional like games to make me have all the feels.
So honestly in the end i give this game a 9/10
The reason i give it a 9, is because there is no sequel yet... it needs a sequel!

Everything wrong with this game can be summarised in one sentence:
It's not obvious in the beginning, but once you level up to 20-something, the absolute r3tardedness of it all becomes clear.
Some examples of what I mean:
1) At level 27, ceteris paribus (i.e. all conditions being equal), your normal attack is 61, versus your enemy's normal attack of 519. This is with the best available gear and maximum power-ups in the form of various item purchases.
2) The elemental attacks are frigging meaningless - e.g. you would think a "flaming rat" would be immune to fire right? And yes, for
fire attacks they get very little damage. But for a few fire attacks, they receive the same damage as others, and can also suffer from the "+burn" status effect - even though the graphics clearly depict them as being already on fire (and their element is fire)! Where's the logic?!
3) At the ninja tournament, you are suddenly made to use characters you
. (The game always forcefully assigns characters to you to fight with throughout.) As a result, because these characters were not prepped or appropriately levelled up for the challenge, it is nigh impossible to win the battle using them. You have to be popping +HP pills all the time, and even then it's a huge challenge (you just have to betting on the fact that your opponent won't kill you using one of their specials, which have the potential to wipe you out at one go, since your opponents are several levels higher than you are, and equipped with the best possible gear!!!). Where's the fun in that???
4) Normal attacks, which consume no MP and TP, deal WAY more damage than magic/skill attacks. I'm talking figures like 448 (using normal attack) as opposed to 92 (using MP/TP attack). Get lost!!!!!!
5) You never ever get a chance to remove status effects like +poison, +blind, +burn, etc because some of your enemies are so fast that their turn keeps coming before you even get a chance to move. This in particular happens during the ninja tournament. So, just wait to die. Kthx.
I suspect most of the these problems have to do with the fact that, after you reach a certain level, the game just suddenly starts assigning you enemies that are at least 2-3 levels higher than you. So when you're at level 27 for instance, you could be facing 6 enemies at levels 28, 27, 29, 29, 25, 28 respectively. And yes, it's YOU (one person), versus 6 of them. What the hell.
It's a pity because I kind of enjoyed the game in the earlier stages, before it started going completely insane with the battle system. many of them during battle. Shan't elaborate because my consternation at this game is growing with every word I type.)

to proceed without some extreme hair-tearing and head-banging (against the wall or table) due to the anger and frustration that this game's battle system will induce in you.
I should also mention that the English is beyond atrocious. E.g. "insensitive" used instead of "incentive"; "peak" used instead of "pique", and so on. And you get spellings like "rouge" (instead of "rogue" - and the wrongly-spelled version appears for the WHOLE game!!!), "paralized" (instead of "paralysed"), etc etc. Very often, the words are spelled like
, instead of what they actually are. He could probably write his own dictionary with the sheer number of words he's re-spelled.

One of the more genuinely strange games I've ever played--made all the more strange by the fact that it doesn't seem to be cribbing from any familiar sources (at least that I am aware of) to construct its game world. You play a guy who is cast out of his tribe after murdering your hermaphroditic Father/Mother under mysterious circumstances. As the game progresses you piece together the events leading up to the murder all while evading your siblings who are out for vengeance.
Oh yeah, and it's also a first person beat em up. Despite being such a potentially disastrous genre hybrid (FPS fighting games have rarely worked) the fighting mechanics and controls are actually implemented fairly well. Likewise, the art direction is top notch. Ultimately the central game mechanics are a bit limited, but the game is smart enough to be brief, ending just before you start to get bored with things. I probably prefer "Rock of Ages" (by the same team), but this is a worthy first game from them.
