This game actually becomes soon unplayable. It's bug ridden. I encountered several bugs, the worst and lastly gamebreaking bug is a bug that I encountered during the "Tournament". I have savegames and the fights went well, till the second day. I had reduced the opponent to zero hitpoints, normally knocking her out, but somehow the NPC kept kicking and lastly I ran out of health - Epic fights? Indeed I felt reminded of Le Morte d'Artus and the epics fights where the knights fought for days on, without any sign of weakness and fatigue - sadly in the game also unrealistic and utterly frustrating. Lastly the game closed with a bug, and needed to be shut down by either task manager or... closing the window externally... This actually is a sign of unresolved function calls, that can cause the RPG Maker machine to get quirky.

This game suffers from being the sequel to an amazing game. GalCiv 3 is like Jacob Dylan, pretty good, but mediocre when compared to it's predecessor. I got this game for 5 bucks as an upgrade for owning GalCiv 2, except it's not really an upgrade. In fact, I started piling on  DLC, trying to get something close to the Twilight of the Arnor experience...to no avail.
This game needs at least the Crusades DLC to be even remotely interesting, and even then, the new features are either forgettable, or better implimented elsewhere. Sure the graphics are improved, but GalCiv is still basically a top-down 2D experience that revolves around gameplay, not graphics. The combat looks pretty, but since it's hands off, it's just a collection of good looking cutscenes. Gamers in 2017 are expecting more.
The ship builder is still awesome, and  to it's credit, the game seems like a robust platform for modders. However, when one of the selling points of the DLC is bringing back races and ship sets from GalCiv 2, you start to wonder about the point.
A victim of the curse of high expectations. 6/10 < (GalCiv 2 ToA 8/10)

Not recommended as an RA game; but I do recommend it, with reservations, for less diehard RA fans, and for those looking for a more casual RTS experience. RA3 is a huge departure from RA2/RA2MD for both good and bad.
Don't be fooled by my playtime on Steam; I played the retail disc over and over.
Pro:
- Three distinct factions with distinct playstyles. Each faction receives their own campaign, which are satisfying enough.
- Naval combat is greatly expanded compared to the older RA games. Most buildings are amphibious.
- Gorgeous visual effects, especially for anything that happens over water. Modern hardware handles all the realtime lighting and reflections with aplomb and the result is a feast for the eyes.
- Very, very beautiful water indeed.
- Co-op campaign gameplay. Sometimes the players fight side-by-side while other times they perform completely different duties.
- Each and every unit now comes with a secondary function. These functions either give the units another attack or trasnforms them into something else entirely.
- Unit countering is heavily based on the use of secondary functions, for better or for worse.
- Blatantly overpowered RA2 units return with heavy, if sometimes too heavy, nerfs.
Con:
- Absolutely HUGE amounts of campiness. I've always thought that the campiness in RA was a side effect of its political satire (President "Dugan" = President Reagan); EA has proven me so, so wrong.
- Very, VERY overly and unnecessarily sexualized women. Blatant sexual innuendo all over the place. Tanya in RA2 was hot, but a badass kind of hot. Not so in RA3. They're pin-up models. They practically squeeze their cleavage in your face.
- Factions are characters are heavily stereotypical and borderline offensive. The Soviets are pictures as inept baffoons drunk on "World Communism", the Allied are muscleheads screaming "freedom", "justice" and "MURICA", while the Empire of the Rising Sun (Japanese) are a collage of how Anime and other Japanese/Asian culture are perceived by the mainstream West, with giant walking mechas, transforming machines and soldiers wearing cone hats.
- Generally poor unit balancing. The Soviets dominate the ground, the Allies dominate the skies while the Empire dominates the sea. This does force players to use combined arms and those secondary functions more often.
- Cartoonish colour theme. All colours are bright and highly saturated. Unit and structure design is again cartoonish and stereotypical.
- VERY bad AI pathing. See my review of Tiberium Wars.

I was one of those people who actively hated Final Fantasy 7 back in the day thinking that it was just all unnecessary hype (I'm more of an FF6 kind of guy). Having played it now, though, I can see the source of praise. This is a great FF to start with, but it has some problems that make it feel rather dated even more so than the GBA ports of the first handful of games.
The story is great and the characters are all well-rounded and interesting and you actually feel for them. Kind of hard to do seeing as the dialog is very dated in terms of translation, but they're just that well-written, I think. And I think that's it's primary selling point -- the story. It's a fun time capsule for what it's worth and it stands up to the going version of FF6 at the time in terms of character and story and it might even be a bit better in some respects given that it has fewer characters, meaning more time to bond with each of them instead of having only one feature per character to go through an arc with like it's done in FF6.
That said, I think that the controls and balancing are VERY dated. Command inputs are rather clunky when compared to other FF of the era (glad they fixed this with FF9). Accidentally targeting your ally with an offensive spell just because they walked up to an enemy or healing an enemy because they walked up to an ally is annoying and I wish that Sqaure hadn't experimented with the targeting system the way they did. The menu overlay in-battle as well as navigating through the Materia menu may take a bit of getting used to especially if you forget there's a [SWITCH] command on the button layout.
Graphics, while great for their time, are rather dated seeing them in HD. The HD character polygons don't blend as well against pre-rendered low resolution backgrounds and it breaks the immersion a bit and makes things look more dated than they should. I think I'll give the graphics settings a few more tries to get it to emulate the old CRT-TV graphics on the PS1 as close as possible.

I am writing this now because I do not think that I will be able to finish this game. As usual, it’s hard to decide whether to recommend or not when I know others will not be as bothered by certain things as I am, but it is my review after all so here are my issues with FEAR:
1.	It did not age well. The sky looks terribly flat and the level design consists mostly of gray corridors.
2.	The game clearly has 2 gimmicks which it wants you to see as soon as possible: the slow-motion effect and flashy gun particle effects.  That is its thing, its selling point and it’s not enough to make a whole game. The game becomes boring after a while.
3.	The girl from The Ring. The story of FEAR is actually not that bad but the antagonist is clearly the little girl from The Ring horror film and, again, it feels too on the nose.
4.	The gameplay is the ultimate example of a classic PC first-person shooter where you have a health bar that goes down as enemies hit you, and the enemies WILL hit you the very moment they see you from a mile away, which feels unnatural. In a shooter like this, the game becomes about the health bar management and I hate that gamy feel.
The good stuff: well, some of the jump scares are quite creative and overall the graphics are not the worst I guess.
The AI, despite the annoying super-accuracy and reflexes, is quite smart. Enemies will throw grenades at your last known position and jump over obstacles (smarter than some of the modern AI in games).
IN CONCLUSION, I bet it was cool in its day but I am getting incredibly tired of this game. And to prove that this is not just about this being an old game, I am also playing Doom 3 that was released a year earlier and it is a way more interesting game despite having many similar problems.
Update: I uninstalled the game and feel sooo much better now. I was forcing myself to give another try because it is a well-known game, but holy moly, am I happy I don't have to play that grey goo anymore.

Need for Speed all who grew up with that franchise know what that means. Fast cars, nice roads/tracks and lots and lots of action. Even the cops need a rest and so the Shift2 train leaves for arcade and simulation city...  but is it a real simulation then? Back in the day and compared to Race07, GTR2 and other real racing sims of that time Shift2 is no hardcore sim neither is it today.
Compared to Project CARS, Shift2 is more arcade sim racer than hardcore sim. So if you want a real racing sim you better switch to Assetto Corsa or Project CARS. For me Shift is a very good game if you can get used to the sim/arcade controls with that touch of simulation We have  static weather (mid-day, dusk and night) and for today´s standard kinda rusty graphics.
Driving through the night however is still impressive as your and your opponents headlights the only light source on the track so when you drive in the middle field you can see nice lighting effects on the cars infront of you and see the packs headlights in the rearview mirror. The sound is superb imho.  The ricer Turbo sounds amazing when it kicks in, exhaust backfire sounds are awesome! For car lovers yeah that´s the kinda sound we wanna hear.
The Career mode has lots of different races which will be unlocked when you level up your driver level. The higher your driver level the more upgrades, vinyls and stuff will be available to turn your standard car in a roaring racing car.
AI  behavior seems legit to me but you have to upgrade your car otherwise you´re not leading the pack!
Shift2 also includes official GT3 and GT1 races which were the reason I bought it. These races will put all your skills to the test. Multiplayer is still available but you should have friends around to fill the mostly empty lobby.
If you like racing games this is definitely worth a buy.

I've come to the conclusion that F.E.A.R is almost my favorite shooter. It's almost the perfect shooter really if it wasn't for interval 11 and the tedium of shooting the waves of paranormal crossing over during your escape. Despite the shortcomings which are few, this is the best gameplay in a first person shooter I've played.  It all just feels so great and really does make you feel like "a god among men" as Harlan Wade put it to Pointman. All of the guns feel powerful the way they impact the enemies and the enviroment which coupled with the amazing sound design of them leads to firefights that leave you feeling like a complete bad♥♥♥♥♥looking over the carnage you just inflicted. The game gets a lot of praise for its ai and rightfully so as the enemies reactions are always impressive as long as you give them time to react before killing them. I especially like how they might be taking cover from you and one shouts out that he's in cover then another replicant will tell him to shut the ♥♥♥♥ up. Also really like how F.E.A.R. has an explanation for why there are so many bad guys to kill. I know it's just a video game but it always bugs me anyway when a game prided on its narrative just throws random bad guys at you (Uncharted). It's especially cool in this game considering the replicant forces context. Speaking of the narrative I think F.E.A.R. has a very interesting one and all it's just a little weird that your team was formed to combat the paranormal and supernatural and yet every time Fettel's signal disapears nobody knows whats up or the Armacham problem is written off at first as a "gas leak" not expected paranormal activity but when you find delta force teams flayed corpses nobody bats an eye. Still the story is properly spooky and keeps the ball rolling. Again shortcomings aside this is one of my favorite shooters. Probably my favorite shooter of the last generation and some might argue the best. I cant recommend it enough.

Review date: 18/02/2015
Just finished a 90% completion game, so heres my report:
The game is a solid port of the PSX version. There is no new content, no big difference and no significant bugs. It is the good old FF8, except for a few bugs that I've found:
Cons:
1. Selphie sprite on the world map has a weird square shadow below her.
2. Same thing happens to Ragnarok when landed in a inclined surface.
3. In Galbadia, most of the civilian character sprites are ♥♥♥♥ed up beyond all recognition. Really low resolution pixelated stuff, but you can still recognized they are supposed to be human beings.
4. If during a battle you pause, when you unpause the battle theme song will restart. This also happened once when I walked around the world map, entered Ragnarok and landed immediatly.
5. The music is different, although some of them I can't be sure if it's worse or just different (i.e. the Battle and boss theme). But Ultimecia's Castle ST is horrible, it begins as pure ear♥♥♥♥♥♥if compared to the fine piece of art it was in the PSX version.
6. Some animations causes terrible framerate drop and sound desync during the move execution. Community speculated it was whenever motion blur appeared. The only animations where I've noticed this happening: Gilgamesh appearing, summoning Eden, Rinoa's Wishing Star limit, the Death of the final boss, the first few seconds of the Terra Break attack from Omega Weapon.
7. Controls are clunky, and the game refers to the buttons as B1, B2, B3, B4, etc... Independantly if you are using a gamepad or keyboard.
Neutral:
1. Siren does not need to be level 100 to refine Curse Spikes into Dark Matter.
Pros:
1. You can use hardware graphics and use anti aliasing, so surfaces are smoother and some times you will have the impression that graphics are better.
2. It comes with Chocobo World! Well, this is a pro if you never came to the realization of how ♥♥♥♥ing creepy a 2 meter tall yellow chicken is. Seriously, Chocobos scare the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of my body.
3. It has Steam achievements, which will make you feel less of a waste of a human being when you beat 10 000 enemies, reach the gil limit or get Boco to level 100.
Final conclusions: Most of the cons are not really a big deal. The only two I consider that can actually affect your experience (if compared to the PSX) are the numbers 6 and 7. For con 7, you can just plug in a gamepad and waste five seconds memorizing the button mapping, problem solved. For con 6, not only it pisses you off, but it actually makes Eden Boost unusable, so it really sucks. But if you play the game properly, by the time you get Eden you won't even be summoning GF anymore. Game is great, it is a good experiece. If you miss FFVIII or if you've played every Final Fantasy but never had the opportunity to play this one (just like me), go ahead and buy it! If you've never played any Final Fantasy before, get FF7 first. It is the same price and a better introduction to the series. Or buy both! The series are awesome.
Oh yeah, and just one more thing:

Surprisingly, I'm finding myself QUITE disappointed with this title.  As someone who was once part of multiple teams working on an independent followup to Airport Tycoon/Airport Inc., I was more than excited to see Airport CEO come along.  It seemed to have everything I always wanted in an airport simulation.  However, once the actual gameplay begins, when your airport is up and running and it's time to start dealing with airline contracts .. disappointment set it very fast!  PLEASE tell me the current airline contract system is NOT how flights are going to be handled in the final version!  Having to DAILY look through contracts and plug flights into your schedule (reminiscent of ad hoc flight scheduling in Airline Tycoon) is more like a puzzle game than airport simulation.  If this is how airlines are going to be modeled and how flight scheduling handled .. I will be asking for a refund.  Daily airport operations should be more focused on logistics, on dealing with incidents that cause gate changes and allocation of resources and staff.  Airlines do alter their schedules but not DAILY.  This is not realistic at all .. and realism is KEY whenever you're talking about a simulation style game.  For that reason, at present, I must give a, "Not Reccomended" to Airport CEO, hard as it is for me to admit that.  My two cents.

Dust: An Elysian Tail is a truly unique game with a fabulous Story, fabulous grahpics, AND fabulous gameplay.  I will start with Gameplay.

Dust:AET is a Hack-N-Slash Metrodivanian side-scroller type, without the 8-bit graphics. (more on graphics later) That being said, this type of game needs a fine control.  And Dust:AET delivers that. Upon finishing the game, I did research and found that this game almost was done in 8-bit. A horrific thought. I kid you not when I say I have taken screenshots of the game and used them as my desktop. (Wait, is that illegal? I don't care, Figit is adorable!) Really, I cannot say enough about the art.  Oh. Airport CEO and SimAirport have the interesting distinction of being two games which are essentially the same - and each one has their flaws.
Of the two, Airport CEO probably has a slightly higher learning curve as the game feels more like you are running an airport. Setting up a roadway pattern and the need for a gate to allow vehicles to access the tarmac is a nice touch.
However, the attention to detail (including general aviation, another nice touch) doesn't necessarily make Airport CEO the better game. There's more micro-management with the contracts, where you have airlines come in and set up daily flights for a week, or you have to slot in a certain number of flights over a week period. The airports the planes take off for is also incredibly random, with almost every plane destined for a non-commercial airport, detracting from the realism somewhat. And both games suffer from the fact once you've built one airport, that's the challenge. I run sandbox mode on both games now just out of lack of patience, and knowing there'll be a point where you hit "the limit".
Is Airport CEO fun? Mostly, when you're not in the throes of some odd baggage carousel bug. Would I recommend it? Do you want to run an airport? Do you mind micro-managing contracts? If yes to the first two, then go for it, it's a great piece of work. If yes to the first, you may want to try SimAirport first if you're on a budget. Ambivalent on airports? Then it's not quite a good enough game for me to recommend - yet.

Stellaris is a masterpiece.
This game really has everything I could ever want in a sci-fi grand strategy game. To list a few of the things that make it stand out for me...
> Race Builder: This thing is really robust. You start with picking a race arch-type (mammal, insectoid, mollusk, etc), then go on to pick a sub-type via a picture. Then you forge everything from scratch, such as your race's description, your home planet, your traits, your ideals, your government, among other things. You really feel like you've created something that's your own. And when you're done you can add them to the pool of races that the AI can use if you desire.
> Exploration: You use science ships to survey star systems, fleets to expand your sight range, and diplomacy to see others star maps and sensor links to name a few ways for you to expand your sight of the galaxy. Along the way you run into random events, procedurally generated solar systems, quests, and the occasional run in with galaxy spanning races of world devourers. Between the sights, events, and racial interactions, you really feel like you're part of a living breathing galaxy that you have an influence on.
> Customization: As already touched on in the race builder portion of this review, you have a great amount of options when forming your initial race, but the customization doesn't stop there. You have a very open research system that allows you to research 3 different fields at a time. When researching a field, you are presented 3+ different choices to choose to start researching. As you've researched things, you are presented more random choices, but are also presented with choices that add to what you've researched in the past. This really gives you a sense of adding onto your research along a path that you've decided on, while also giving you the chance to divert, or start researching some of the  choices you've neglected in the past. Besides research you are free to build planets in any way you see fit with the planetary tile system. On each tile you can build a number of base buildings that are unlocked at the start of the game, and a number of ones that are unlocked via research. These buildings can either add to your resource income, or add additional effects on the planet. Outside of the tile system, you also have star-ports that are attached to your planet (once you've built them). These start ports have their own tile/upgrade system that lets you further customize each of your planets/star-ports. There's also a ship builder that allows you to build ships in a modular fashion while also equipping them with weapons and plenty of utility items. It's a lot of fun researching parts and making a fleet that reflects your play-style.
> Diplomacy: When you can see an AI do something, and work out in your head why they've done what they did strategically, you know you've found something worth while. In Stellaris, I mainly play the diplomat. Forging alliances, making trade deals, keeping the peace, and slowly expand my influence in a peaceful manner. Stellaris allows you to do this and makes it interesting along the way by really showing you what these other empires are like behind the curtain. The first time I had an empire I had been friends with for centuries leave a federation I formed I was actually emotionally impacted! I believe that speaks for itself.
> Combat: I have to admit that I'm not really well versed in combat due to my peaceful play style, but I have battled a few times and keep up on a very large fleet that rivals the largest warmonger in the galaxy. The game has the options there for very in depth space battles. Sure, you could just blob everything together and hope for the best, or you could use the ctrl-group feature found in many RTS games and control your fleets in such a way that allows flanking, strategic positioning of weapon groups, and baiting scenarios. And with the pause feature it doesn't matter if you're not a seventeen year old Korean playing Star Craft 2, you'll still be able to play at your own pace in a very strategic manner.
> Moddability: The workshop is full of awesome mods and the game has only been out a month. There are even full theme mods that allow you to play with a WH40k theme. Give this game a year or two and I'm sure there will be some for the major IPs that everyone loves such as Star Trek, Star Wars, etc.
> Updates: I'm new to Paradox games, but so far they've shown me that they really care about their product.  They've issued an update that has taken player feedback into consideration along with balancing systems out that players have shown them need fixing. They've mentioned that there will be more free updates on the way, with future DLC content if the game does well. I personally feel like the future will bring great things for a game that's already amazing.
> Multiplayer: Who doesn't want to explore the galaxy with your friends? It's there, it's stable, and it works great.
...I think I'll leave it at that for now. Stellaris is quickly becoming one of the top games I've ever played. I can't help but come back to it time and time again to see what's in store for my civilization of space faring humans. It has presented me the opportunity to do the things that I wish humanity was doing right now.

I am changing my review to a thumbs down, and that is because the game is, currently, completely and utterly broken. It is unplayable.
In GC3, the economy works like this: production = raw production (multipliers).
Raw production = population (multipliers).
Basically, population is EVERYTHING. A bunch of factories on your planet might boost production by 50%. Base population is 3, so 3 x 1.5 = 4.5
However, a city will add 3 population, so adding just one city will allow you to have a population of 6 on the planet, which will make 6 production without any factories at all. Growing one's population is extremely important in this game. The civ with the highest population wins.
And here is the problem. The developers created a new system where one needs to build farms to create food, and then build cities to grow the population cap. The problem is that the AI does not know how to do this. I and several other people have tested this out and it is true. The AI cannot grow its population (with one rare exception). Because of this, the AI can never be an economic competitor.
Imagine playing a game of Civilzation where the AI cities never grew past population 1. It would be a laughable waste of time, the AI, even on the highest difficulty, would be a joke. And that is the state of GC3. It has been this way for months now and they haven't fixed it. Bad, bad, bad. I paid good money for a broken game, I expect them to fix it ASAP. If and when they do fix it I will change my review back to a thumbs up, provided they do it in a reasonable amount of time (soon).

I bought GC3 in the latest Humble Bundle after following a friend's recommendation. Having played galactic 4X games since the C64 days, the PC classic "Master of Orion" still defines the genre. And GC3 still does not deviate much from this formula, except in unfortunate ways.
GC3 choses to have an open 2D map, where suns, planets, resources, black holes, nebulae are spread out. Distance is measured in squares. Players can colonize planets and build starbases to expand their territory and spread their influence and claim vital resources and ancestor artifacts and build shipyards to expand their military arsenal.
The first big problem with the game it is far from self-explanatory, not even the tutorial is. There seems to be no in-game encyclopedia, and while some things can be found out through hovering the mouse over the right item, many options and things in the game lack a proper explanation.
The second big problem is the "ship designer," a huge timesink for no other reason to make your ships looks pretty. Setting GC3 apart from similar games, it's mostly a waste of time. You can imitate a lot of designs and people did just that, but when it comes to actual function, it's neither documented nor intuitive. What you REALLY want to do is modify a design to carry a different assortment of components. Good luck with that. Thankfully modifying designs is in the end unnecessary because the database is so big. Time would have been spent better elsewhere.
The game did not crash on me but is slow to load and a resource hog. It has many small interface bugs where a click might not do what you intended - like being interpreted as having been done in a different menu or square. The "Arnor spice" bug is neither well documented nor explained online - but once you go through all the hoops of acquiring this key resource it keeps on vanishing before you can use it. You need it for endgame construction, and I had to harvest it by the truckload until it stopped disappearing.
Unless you fiddle with the resource settings in galaxy creation, good luck with finding sufficient key resources later in the game. Two planets had the super fertilizer "Monsantium" (haha...ha) in the whole galaxy - and all farming upgrades depend on it plus the path that gets you "Arnor Spice." Figuring out these connections is... trial and error. Some later buildings have strange preconditions, too. "Arnor spice makes everything twice as nice." is pretty much the info you get. Great.
Automation is also limited and a bit buggy. I had a conquered planet modify its own queue while being under my "Direct Control". Conquered planets show the AI is hopeless about arranging buildings to maximize boni. The limited space per planet will make you actually tear down buildings to rebuild them in more effective patterns. The whole "building A gets bonus near X, Y, and Z" is a nonsensical mini puzzle game, anyway, because you later often find out that some structures cannot be torn down - and not really in all cases clear why. I ended up having "once per player" structures multiple times on the same planet when conquered. Buggy AI ignoring rules...
The best strategy of planet development seems to be "Pump all into the core world." Made a one planet civilization the 2nd on the leader board and surpass my 10 planet civ in research. (Until I squashed them.)
The animated battles have horrible camera controls and aren't all that interesting. Again, this was not worth the time put into it - just to show off the ship designs. Compare "Star Wars: Empire at War" - there every battle looks interesting.
Some techs are so badly explained, I don't even know yet what they do. Like apparently you get interceptors at some point.
Conclusion: Some old-fashioned MOO2 still does mostly everything better.

Review date: 18/02/2015
Just finished a 90% completion game, so heres my report:
The game is a solid port of the PSX version. There is no new content, no big difference and no significant bugs. It is the good old FF8, except for a few bugs that I've found:
Cons:
1. Selphie sprite on the world map has a weird square shadow below her.
2. Same thing happens to Ragnarok when landed in a inclined surface.
3. In Galbadia, most of the civilian character sprites are ♥♥♥♥ed up beyond all recognition. Really low resolution pixelated stuff, but you can still recognized they are supposed to be human beings.
4. If during a battle you pause, when you unpause the battle theme song will restart. This also happened once when I walked around the world map, entered Ragnarok and landed immediatly.
5. The music is different, although some of them I can't be sure if it's worse or just different (i.e. the Battle and boss theme). But Ultimecia's Castle ST is horrible, it begins as pure ear♥♥♥♥♥♥if compared to the fine piece of art it was in the PSX version.
6. Some animations causes terrible framerate drop and sound desync during the move execution. Community speculated it was whenever motion blur appeared. The only animations where I've noticed this happening: Gilgamesh appearing, summoning Eden, Rinoa's Wishing Star limit, the Death of the final boss, the first few seconds of the Terra Break attack from Omega Weapon.
7. Controls are clunky, and the game refers to the buttons as B1, B2, B3, B4, etc... Independantly if you are using a gamepad or keyboard.
Neutral:
1. Siren does not need to be level 100 to refine Curse Spikes into Dark Matter.
Pros:
1. You can use hardware graphics and use anti aliasing, so surfaces are smoother and some times you will have the impression that graphics are better.
2. It comes with Chocobo World! Well, this is a pro if you never came to the realization of how ♥♥♥♥ing creepy a 2 meter tall yellow chicken is. Seriously, Chocobos scare the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of my body.
3. It has Steam achievements, which will make you feel less of a waste of a human being when you beat 10 000 enemies, reach the gil limit or get Boco to level 100.
Final conclusions: Most of the cons are not really a big deal. The only two I consider that can actually affect your experience (if compared to the PSX) are the numbers 6 and 7. For con 7, you can just plug in a gamepad and waste five seconds memorizing the button mapping, problem solved. For con 6, not only it pisses you off, but it actually makes Eden Boost unusable, so it really sucks. But if you play the game properly, by the time you get Eden you won't even be summoning GF anymore. Game is great, it is a good experiece. If you miss FFVIII or if you've played every Final Fantasy but never had the opportunity to play this one (just like me), go ahead and buy it! If you've never played any Final Fantasy before, get FF7 first. It is the same price and a better introduction to the series. Or buy both! The series are awesome.
Oh yeah, and just one more thing:

Pros:
-Classic jrpg active time battle system
-Rich story
-Great and memorable characters
-Tons of things to explore and find throughout the world
-Cutscenes still look superb
-Nostalgia high
Cons:
-Graphically, this game has aged horribly, even with the polished character models and higher resolution
-For a jrpg, combat is fairly easy through most of the game with no major learning curve
-Some areas early in the game still have imbalanced amounts of xp earned, leading to easily being levels ahead of your intended level
-Some bugs which existed in original still persist in the pc port, but all are rare and hardly gamebreaking
-Needs to support higher resolutions
As said, you'll get a perfect jrpg experience here and not feel a single penny is wasted if this is your kind of bag.

Some such issues are related to Autolog, which I believe has been long since abandoned which now crashes the game for players, such as myself and requires players to either block certain ports through their firewall or to turn off their internet - just to prevent these problems from happening. Other issues also include the three installs and you're dead situation, where you can only activate the game three times before the key going away, although you can unactivate it, most people either won't remember or won't get the chance ie if their computer dies. Absolutely hate 3rd-party DRMs, developers need to stop and take CD Projekt Red's practices into consideration.
Moving away from technical problems.
The game is brilliant. The amount and quality of content in this game is superb. This game has a massive selection of variety when it comes to cars and tracks. 160 cars is a lot for a racing game and sure you can compare it to games such as Forza 4 at 600 or Gran Turismo (I don't actually know the amount for GT6, I remember GT5 being around 1200) but it doesn't really matter. The car choice in this game focuses on cars that matter in their perspective, which is generally the well known cars such as the Corvette ZR1, Lamborghini Gallardo or Porsche 911 GT3. It doesn't really have any "trash" filler cars as such, apart from the Legends DLC, free on PC, which introduced things like the Mini and the Alfa Romeo Giulia Sprint GTA, which I don't mind, most of the cars are an enthralling experience to drive due to excellent sound design and well made cockpits. There's a view mode that allows the player to not just drive in first person but there's a helmet overlay that feels realistic and the camera moves when approaching a corner. Dials and screens inside cars all light up and work, like the Caterham has a working, although I wouldn't say incredibly realistic Water Temperature monitor which adds to the immersion. Not just this, but full car customization is also put into play. You have full control over tuning and modifying parts for your car. Want to engine swap a Nissan Silvia S15 and take out the SR20DET with a Skyline engine. Sure. It's freedom over car design is a definite plus.
Gameplay consists of a mainly realistic racing experience, not the simulator experience of Assetto Corsa, which puts me off a little bit nor the overly arcade experiences found in your other modern Need for Speed titles since Undercover. It's always intense and if you're like me and turn off every assist, turn up the difficulty, you'll be in for an extraordinary time.
Graphically it's top of the line, 2011 graphics. Yes I'm saying this looks (on MAX settings, which mind you, on my R9 280X only reaches 45-50 FPS on some tracks, strangely) better than most of the games that came out in 2011. The reflections, bloom FX, which I find disorientating at times, textures, etc are just really good.
Campaign is good. Not much to say, it's sort of like an RPG, you level up and with that you get cash, liveries and rims. You do different events for XP and cash, that's pretty much it. And then you can challenge famous drivers and take their highly modified cars.
And finally Tracks. There's a lot of Tracks and variations in NFS Shift 2. Renowned tracks like Silverstone, Brands Hatch, Suzuka Circuit and many others feature in Shift 2 with night variations and different weather variations. Brilliant. Different terrains on different tracks heavily impact your car and it's traction. If you manage to drift offroad and into sand, you're done for. Nothing is holding you back from doing a barrel roll right into the wall. And this has happened to me, most notably in the lighter cars I drive, like the Lotus Elise and the Caterham. With that they come with their own realistic sound effects which again helps boost immersion.
So all in all - it's great. Despite the technical problems it's had, I consider it one hell of a racing game. I find racing in this way more intense than the likes of Gran Turismo.
Pros
- Variety of quality content.
- Truly immersive.
- Car Customization a definite plus.
Cons
- Technical problems related to DRM
- DRM
Rating: 8/10, despite technically issues.

Picked it up for € 3.99 on special offer and boy, was that a deal. People talk about "the graphics", but that's the wrong term actually. Yes, the 3D engine is good for a 2011 game, but what really blows your mind is the LEVEL DESIGN. Screenshots don't do it justice since you really have to experience the diversity & complexity of the world hands-on. The entire visual design of the game is just so masterfully done that I don't even mind the fact that it regularly crosses the threshold of kitsch I can tolerate. Especially the sex scenes could do with a little less stilted moaning & catwalk moves, and instead some more teasing & creativity in general.
So while I'm recounting the downers here's the rest of them:
- Animations (doors, climbing, taking/dealing damage etc.) sometimes lock other movement annoyingly long. Especially casting sometimes gets locked for no apparent reason, so I end up standing like a dork in the middle of battle while hitting the cast button until it finally happens.
- Male characters are quite well done, both visually, substantually and vocally. They are diverse and relate to the world in a meaningful manner. Female characters however seem generally a little more shallow. There are very few meaningful female roles, and all female characters in the game seem to fit a much more narrow blueprint. They look more alike, they act more similar, heck, they even seem to be all the same age. It's like somebody wanted all the women to fit a particular stereotype of "hotness" which gets boring very quickly (I still like Triss though, but she's about the only deep female NPC).
Other than that I really can't think of any more downsides to this game, so since the ups have been discussed in other reviews extensively, it should be clear that this is a SUPER-awesome ARPG.

在玩過機場大亨2(Airport Tycoon 2)後,一直想要找一款機場的遊戲.終於讓我等到了.
無意間發現這款遊戲與SimAirport, 看了外過玩家的評論說Airport CEO的複雜度就像金錢帝國2(Capitalism 2)
所以馬上就下手了.
跟大家分享一下這款遊戲跟Airport Tycoon 2(AT2)的不同點.
1.Airport Tycoon 2 是以Runway當作班機的規劃,而CEO是以Stand(停機坪)當作航班的規劃.
也就是說,只要Runway是空的,就可以讓飛機降落.而CEO是必須有停機坪才可以降落.
這兩個不同的排班,個人覺得並沒有哪個比較好. 只是說以停機坪來排班,就無法創造出地面上飛機大塞車的場景.
2.Check-in Desk specified(指定). AT2可以指定每家航空公司的專屬Check-in Desk.比較類似現實的狀況.
也可以指定冷凍庫使用權. CEO則是系統自動安排.
3.AT2比較沒有注重在Outside建築物.而CEO對於航空站外的道路,公車站,停車場都是有考慮到的.外面道路塞車,物資進不來,你就沒辦法蓋建築物.
4.合約談判(contract Negotiation. AT2的簽約是針對航空公司,而CEO的簽約是針對單一合約.
AT2簽約內容包含停機費,燃料費,飲食費,清理費,一堆費用,但沒有飛機數量限制.也就是一談妥,你只要有飛機起飛/降落,就是按照合約內容收費.
每家航空公司的合約都可以不同.
然而CEO每次的簽約是單一合約.也就是這個合約會有總飛機量與天數的告知,在合約時間內完成就給錢,失敗就賠錢.
以上目前的遊玩心得,畢竟還在開發中,還是建議大家入手.會玩到不想關電腦.

Since the latest patch, a lot of the things that annoyed me were fixed, but there's still a lot of missing features (to be DLC I'm sure) and design choices that I question. Overall, it's certainly not a bad game. But it's not that great either, in its current state anyway. Stellaris has the potential to be another Paradox great, but it's lacking depth right now. I would wait another year, after a few DLC's have come out, then try to pick it up on sale.

In its current state NO I do not recommend this game. The sad part is there are only few reasons for it.
First and the most important one is the empire management. For some weird reason designers have decided that the maximum number of colonies including your starting one is five. When you exceed this number there is an extremely cumbersome sector management mechanic available. If you divide your empire into sectors you cannot manage the individual tiles on those planets though. The game begins the manage them for you automatically and makes a royal mess of it. I do not understand who thought of this absurd mechanics and cannot fathom the reason for it but for me it makes the game unplayable.
Second is the cumbersome help system. There are three levels of help available but the system has no mechanics like "Do not show this again" so each new game you have to go through the same mundane help offers again and again in case you miss something new and important.
Other then these two I have run into few bugs so far but the empire management limitations (Why oh why ?) really broke any apetite I had for this game. In its current condition I sadly but firmly DO NOT recommend this game.

A nice breakout from 'hardcore' FPS games, Paladins is easy to pick up and get started with. If you are BRAND NEW I would recommend 'Pip' as a gret starting character to get familiar with the movement style, ability types and the map layouts.
My advice would be to load up, and play all the available characters up to level 4 to unlock 2 chests each (1 for reching lvl 1, another for lvl 4) and then just take it from there.
I wont lie, some matches/games are frustrating if you end up with an AFK team member, but the truth is that unless you are experiencing TERRIBLE games over and over, it is not a big deal and you will prbably find a game much more in your favour a few matches down the line.
*QUICK TIP*

- don't bother spending 'Essence' on things like cards, weapons or skins etc until you know more about who you like to play with, it's really not worth wasting it early on to get 1 or 2 cards as you will get loads from you chest drops as you lvl anyway.
- learn some fo the friendly the "V key" voice/call-out system buttom combinations, if you use some of these in the spawn at the start of the match you would be surprised at how it can focus the other random team members on the match!
- Don't worry about SALT.
You will loose matches, try not to get stressed.
If your team is getting steamrolled from the start and it looks like hthere is no way to win at all, maybe use it as an opportunity to try s new route to the point or try sneaking up on a specific enemy player, aside from learning new stuff, you would be suprised at how a sudden change in tactics can change the match balance sometimes!

This is a terrible turn-based RPG made with the RPG Maker engine and it's one of the worst games I've played.
I can get past the limited options and visual settings that RPG Maker games suffer from, and I can get past the generic artwork and horrible music, but this game has a horrible combat system and that I can NOT get past.
My main issue with this game is the fact that your enemies level up with you.
This is rarely used in RPGs and with good reason. It's a horrible idea that makes no sense, and makes you want to either:
1. AVOID battles at all costs to keep the enemies low level or
2. Fight in the same area leveling up to 99.
However, WHY would you want to skip battles in an RPG? Why would you want to repeat the same areas if you don't gain an advantage from grinding?
Why do the enemies level up between battles? My team hit level 10 in the first area and the same slimes and flowers were level 10 as well. It's not like they were fighting battles, and this doesn't make sense because in the first area of the game you should not have to be fighting such high level creatures.
I'm not saying this is difficult, I'm saying this is not fun and that's the most important thing.
This game is garbage for this reason, and I would suggest avoiding it no matter how cheap it goes on sale.
Edit: I've learned that it's possible things change later in the game, but based on this being the introduction to the game, I didn't want to continue. This is a very bad way to start off an RPG.

In GalCiv III you play as a race starting on a single planet and expand to rule the galaxy. In classic 4x turn-based style, you explore, expand, exploit and exterminate. There are several victory conditions: conquering every other race, expand your culture across the galaxy, research an ascension gate, transcend by collecting ascension crystals or forming a alliance with all other races.
When Galactic Civilizations III came out it had the engine of a Ferrari but the chassis of a Fiat Punto. It featured a 64bit engine, which allowed for huge galaxies with many stars and civilizations. But the UI was cumbersome and the gameplay was hampered by "constructor spam" which made playing these large maps tedious. After the second major DLC the gameplay has finally caught up with the engine.
It allows for very different play styles. In GalCivIII:Crusade, you can now design your own civilization or download one from Steam Workshop. In my first game, I designed my own Ferungi as a race specialized in Trade and Diplomacy. I won a diplomatic victory without ever building a single military ship! Instead, I used my financial resources to bribe other races into war against my enemies, or hired Mercenaries. Also, since I was ‘the good guy’ other civilizations surrendered to me, thus giving me their remaining planets and assets. To create this financial wealth and diplomatic trust, I used Citizens. These are ‘heroes’ which you get for free every 10 turns.  In my second game, I played as the Yor, an evil race of living machines determined to rid the galaxy of meet-sacks. I conquered every civilization. The new invasion system made this highly convenient. You send a transport loaded with legions, and if a planet has no defending legions you conquer it immediately. This significantly reduced the late game grind, which usually comes with a militaristic play style.
The constructor spam is a thing of the past, as starbase modules are now bought directly. But they now require resources. These resources can be found on planets, mined from starbases or traded with other civilizations.
You can also design your own ships, so if you like to have the USS Enterprise escorted by a swarm of flying hair dryers, this is your game. I appreciate this graphical details, even though I never make use of this feature and use the predefined ships. But you can also export your designs and 3D print it. Your ships also show up on the map, but I usually play on a very zoomed out level, where all ships are displayed by generic icons. I also like that planets consists of tiles which actually show up on the map. E.g. when you zoom in on the night side of a planets, you can see that the lights on the night side trace out the developed parts of the planet.
It is details like this, which show that the developers care for this game. Also, they continue to release updates to the base game several years after release.
There are still thinks, which need some work. The ideology system could need some balancing. E.g. you can chose a perk that increases your trade skill with minor races, but you cannot interact with them in Crusade. Also, tech trading is still cumbersome (but less so than it used to be). Some leaf technologies require you to choose between up to three techs. Then you cannot research the other two. This is unfortunately true even if you acquire the tech via trade. So, if you want to max out on technologies, you constantly have to check between the tech tree and the diplomatic screen.
Overall, I really like this game. If you are interested in 4x games in general, I can recommend it.

I started playing less than 2 weeks ago, and for me it has been the easiest game to get into ever. I had previously tried to play GalCiv 1 & 2, but didn't manage more than 3 hours.
GalCiv 3 (+expansions) was different. The UI was just much more intuitive. The text is a decent size, and easy to read. You can do everything really easily with just the mouse. And the game is just so deliciously absorbing! All the races play slightly differently, and there are many ways to achieve victory beyond simply destroying everyone else.
From looking at the recent game changes, I believe the devs are moving in the right direction. Crusade seems to have taken out a lot of micromanagement. I'm loving that now raw production = population - this was only changed in v2.5, as before that raw production used to be a square root of population. Now it is much more important to increase population. And I find myself redesigning my planets as my population grows. This in turn makes citizens more important; having a scientist/worker/engineer give +31% becomes a big deal with large populations.
Long answer short - this game is amazing - just get it! I am now up to 55 hours gameplay, and am still excited to start my next game!

This game has a good Storyline, and an amazing  Storytelling.
Also a unique shooter experience unlike any other.
Enemies aren't scattered around the map, but rather found in squads of 4-6 (biggest one I found was around 9-10). The enemy AI is wonderful, they chat with each other on the radio planning on how to take you down, or asking for the rest of the teammates to regroup on them to increase their chance of survival, since the half of their squad got slaughtered. They flank, provide supressing fire for their teammates to seek cover, and run away with their tail between their legs if the rest of their squad is down, like, "WHERE IS MY BACKUP!!!", I just love it.
Combat aside, the game "F.E.A.R", doesn't rely on jumpscares, which is something I really love. Instead, it gives you that sense of insecurity, as if you are expecting something to attack you from the corner of your eye at anytime. I can't say this game will be "spooky" to everyone, as it sure is a pretty old game for our generation (still good), so it doesn't have all the technology or the ideas necessary, but it still kept me on my toes at certain parts.
TL;DR: Great Game, I recommend it to anyone who likes FPS/Horror.

I played this game many years back on the PS2 during high school with one of my friends. We would come back home after school and progress slowly through the game. I remember how much we struggled with Mobile Type 8 the first time around  when we thought GFs were the way to go. FF8 was the first FF I played and it is my favorite. I have played every single FF game since FFIII and have always enjoyed the series (not so much the MMO variants). I have lost count how many times I beat this game on the PS2 and later using epsxe. I had save files where I literally maxed every stat on all characters. While I did not go quite that crazy this time around, playing FF8 on steam was a lot of fun. The only aspect of FF8 I wish was different is how easy all aspects of the game (including Omega weapon) are once you have some tricks down. I enjoyed trying the various kick a** combos I had tried in the past. Squall/Rinoa/Zell (or Irvine) make the absolute best team. Nothing beats Rinoa's Angel Wing if she is junctioned properly with 255 magic and only Meteor and curative/support spells she won't cast while in Angel Wing (well unless you can guarantee Squall's Renzokuken goes Lion Heart everytime). Playing around with various character combos was a blast :) While FF8 is not the most popular FF, it is definitely my favorite.

For all you nostalgia seekers out there, this is your ticket to them good old glory days. Anyways.
FF-VII is by far one of the best experiences you can get from a JRPG. Excellent story with a great underlying narrative, rich characters and a deep world to exlpore. Tons of mini-games can be found throughout and many can be revisited. Though I would say some can be time consuming, such as the Chocobo breeding and racing, they have their own rewards for those who really want to invest themselves to get every last drop wrung out of this title. Though the graphics are very dated, the pc port has been lightly polished and performs great. All in all, FF-VII is more than worth the price.
Pros:
-Classic jrpg active time battle system
-Rich story
-Great and memorable characters
-Tons of things to explore and find throughout the world
-Cutscenes still look superb
-Nostalgia high
Cons:
-Graphically, this game has aged horribly, even with the polished character models and higher resolution
-For a jrpg, combat is fairly easy through most of the game with no major learning curve
-Some areas early in the game still have imbalanced amounts of xp earned, leading to easily being levels ahead of your intended level
-Some bugs which existed in original still persist in the pc port, but all are rare and hardly gamebreaking
-Needs to support higher resolutions
As said, you'll get a perfect jrpg experience here and not feel a single penny is wasted if this is your kind of bag.

I purchased Abzu on a sale, knowing that there would come a day where I was bored and just felt like zoning out in an immersive underwater world. Well, that day came and Abzu went above and beyond my expectations.
Featuring gameplay similar to that of Flower, Abzu delivers with visuals that utilize just about every color, in an impressive and unique way. In addition, there is a vast array environments and species, all built / textured with obvious care. But above all else, the musical score in this game is one of the best I have experienced. Featuring an entire ensemble of instruments under the same composer that did Journey, alone the music immersed and entertained me.
Whimsical flute solos as you swim through coral reefs, trembling cello chords as you see a shark, angelic choirs as the sun rays disseminate through the water, and an entire symphony as you swim with schools of fishes. There is no doubt in my mind this game was a product of passion and made in the form of art.
With only a couple hours span, Abzu offers not necessarily a play through, but an interactive experience that deserves to be tried by all.

I've spent way to much time in Europa Universalis 3 and 4. Great games, always something interesting to do and to think about: whom to ally, whom to backstab, where to invade. How to proceed in a tricky tactical situation in a war. When to surrender.
Stellaris is boring. I\'ve started with standard settings and built a  big empire. Now I'll deinstall the game and wait for a couple of upgrades, it\'s just so boring at the moment.
90% of the game consist of waiting for research bars to fill up, waiting for fleets to upgrade, waiting for planets to reach 5 pops to upgrade the ship shelter to a planetary administration and then upgrading the buildings. It's a LOT of micromanagement.
Colonization? Search for a colonisable planet (on the map, there is no list). Find out, which type is is. Find out what size it is. Find out if any of your sector governors built a colony ship as those ships won't appear in your ship list. Find out if you happen to terraform that planet at the time, otherwise the terrraforming process will be canceled upon colonist arrival. Sent ship to colonize.
Colony upgrades: Click through your planets  and look for possible upgrades (there is no list). Upgrade every building manually (there is no "upgrade all" button).
Resource management: Tear down or build gem mines as needed by energy management. Oh, and micromanage your fleets to enter ressource-friendly orbits.
The situation log which was giving missions early on is basically useless right now. One long-term quest chain has apparently been broken, the rest of the list is cluttered with debris from space battles which are not worth to investigate since it stops research for an inappropriate time in exchange for a laughable amount of research points. However, I cannot remove them from the situation log, apparently.
Combat ist boring. Chasing the enemy fleet around, then a battle resembling the "the bowl" level in Destruction Derby of yore (i.e. everyone rushes to the center and starts taking each other apart). There would be some "rock paper scissor" tactics available but since I've never been able to find out in advance what loadout my enemy favours (there doesn't seem to be espionage, not even on this basic level), balanced loadouts seem to be the way to go. Especially since upgrading huge fleets takes forever.
Maybe I am missing something. Maybe there is a hotkey for all the basic UI functionality I would have expected. Hell, maybe there even is a manual. I couldn\'t find it, though. Maybe. There should be one. As it is, the game is lacking a lot of UI functionality resulting in lots of boring micromanagement. On a plus side, at least this distracts from the lack of content...
I am expecting a LOT of FREE upgrades for this game. I definitely won\'t buy as many DLC packs as I have for EU4 and CKII.
Stay away for now, not recommended.

The worst RPG Maker game I've played yet!
I'm one that actually likes RPG Maker games. They take me back to the old SNES era of games that have that certain charm. This game does not have that. At all.
:
- Decent, yet typical story. If you're an RPG lover then you would have probably experienced this story a plethora of times.
:
- Terrible scaling
- Magic. Some magic that cost 200 MP does less damage than magic that does 100 MP
- Corny dialog
- Regular, random battles drag on far too long. It's as if each fight last 2-3 minutes. That isn't welcomed here.
- Troll game. The game will send two fire users (forcefully) to a fire themed area, thus your attacks will be resisted (do a lot less/half damage). At this point you're better off just running from every battle you can just so you can get to the boss while avoiding 4-6 minute random encounters. That's insane and troll-ish.
- Useless treasure chests. Run pass the chest(s) and you'll save yourself from forced encounters/"mimics", random encounters and being disappointed that you got some junk.
I've finished this game just to see how tedious it would get... and it didn't fail, it got even more tedious along the way! Don't torture yourself with this game.

EDIT: I've returned to this review after a brief revisit of Stellaris. I'll keep this short and to the point.
Despite enjoying a good deal of my time with Stellaris, I would NOT recommend it to any undecided buyers. Stellaris is a game with a lot of shallow mechanics, a sort of toybox approach where no single system is too complex. This is great for introducing the game to players, and it makes the game great for LANs, as the party can focus on socialising with the game acting as a light social glue (but then it's competing with other great LAN RTSes).
To me, this meant that I found that a lot of my time with Stellaris evemtually became rote. By far the worst offender of this is warfare system, which seems to just be a case of having a larger number than your opponent.
Overall I think Stellaris is a game of cool concepts and moments, marred by shallow mechanics  that do not feel rewarding to master.

I leave my games running... really!  I did not play over 4,000 hours of Gal Civ III... maybe 2,000 is fair.  Why do I play so much?  Obviously, I like the game.  If you like turn based 4x games and I've tried them all then you should at least try this one.  StarDock's developers have done an awesome job keeping this game interesting by tweaking the game play and adding content regularly.  The developer journals and live-feeds were a great way to keep up with the progression - and they made real progress.
If you ever played WoW for any length of time then you know how active development can really change the game play - nerf something for balance and people cry... dumb-down a raid and people cry... change the game mechanics and a few people quit.  Active development isn't for the faint hearted publisher.  But, StarDock has done this as well as any that I have experienced.  GalCiv III is (should be) a major franchise.
You can play games with thousands of planets and ships, you can have upwards of 30 AI civs competing against you (and others in multi-player) without over taxing my 5 year old Alienware Mx17 R4.  Recently, the developers come back through the code making improvements to speed things up -- that's really refreshing -- as most games just seem to leave their base game alone and keep glomming more content into it until it becomes unplayable.
Design your own civs with unique characteristics.  I also really appreciate all the player developed ships and civs that you can download from Steam - this is really an infinite sandbox.  I once tried a map with myself against 16 other AI's that I tried to make (or found on Steam) as aggressive as possible.  For the most part, they fought each other until they noticed me... and, then...
You should find out.  Try this game.  And, if you want to do me a favor (because I plan to keep playing) then drop a positive note here so that the developers can keep building this great franchise.  Kudo's StarDock, looking forward to more from the gang at St. Joe.

Everyone\'s initial impression of this game is the same, as the game is beautiful in appearance and plays well at the start.  But you quickly become disappointed in the myriad of bugs found.  Say you have a leader who gives a 20% building discount.  Well put him on a world and queue up discounted buildings.  Then move him to the next world instantly since there is no travel time involved and queue up more discounted buildings.  Repeat for each of your planets.  I can understand AI issues arising say in the Sector management, but bugs where you can apply a leadership bonus from one leader across every planet, well that\'s poor quality assurance.  And that is just one such bug.  Want to instantly move two fleets together in a system?  Well just drag a window around them and combine the fleets.  Even though they are weeks away from meeting, now they are instantly combined, no travel time involved to group!  How about quests to scout 6 planets and then you find that 2 of the planets are behind another empire\'s borders and unreachable?  And the auto design optimizer for ships doesn\'t upgrade weapons at all, prefering to just maximize shields and armor while your ships keep the most basic of weapons.  Building frontier outposts is always a risk since it doesn\'t display the area of influence prior to building them, so you may accidentally build it too far out to be part of your empire,
I join everyone else in saying, WAIT 6 MONTHS and this may be a good game by then.  And hopefully without DLC cost for those of us who paid for this untested game out of the box.

While the selling point of this game is the usage of pop culture and historical political figures, they have little necessity to the game itself other than to give a few laughs when you see somthing like "Oscar Wilde holds Washington down in a pool of water, slowly killing him.", only to be followed with the next update being "Wilde decides to go swimming in a pond". What a ruthless SOB that guy is! Of course seeing things like "Trump drowns Putin" feel relevant to world events of today, but are mostly random in this simulation game.
So what is this? Well...it is a simulation survival game in which you are allowed to create hundreds of characters on your own, as well as use the pre-creted ones, and then have them try to survive in an ever increasing world of dangers. The default characters tossed into the game all have their own images like Trump, Putin, Zuckerberg (He was a beast in one of my sims killing about 5 people), Notch, etc., but you can change all thse images to anything you want for their player cards (not sure why you would want to), as well as give them all your own "favorite quote" that you think each may say. You can add as many new players as you want as well. There are about 50 I think, which makes the "Random characters" option for a quick game a bit silly as it requires at least 100 chatracters for the option to work, which means you have to create over 50 more characters yourself for that option to be viable.
After customizing your players to what you want them to be, they are all randomly thrown into the world and randomly interact with it and eachother until their ultimate demise. You can change a few stats on them, but I can't see any real benefit to that so far as I maxed out all of Trump's stats while doing nothing to anyone else (everyone else has a default stat set of 5/10 on all stats), and Trump still wasn't killing people off any better than anyone else, and in my game he actually died trying to escape the arena despite me continually giving him food and watter, while not helping hardly anyone else. (Which may happen when Trump is ultimately impeached after becoming president MIRITE!?)
The characters all appear as tiny little stick men on the screen and if you click on them you can see their player card, which allows you to move, feed, or kill them as well as showing their pictures. You have some other windows that you can pop up to allow you to see who has died and how, see who is teamed up, etc.
You can help some of your favorites by giving them food an water to keep them from dying of hunger and thirst, or just flat out "kill" other players you don't like, but in the end they are all subject to some sort of RNG as to when, or if they will die. Most of the in-sim options to leave care packages don't seem to work that well that I can tell. They seem to sit on the map forever even if you place them right in line with the players as they walk over them. You can start "Events" too like acid rain, weird fogs, etc. that have an impact on all the characters. I only started a few, and it looks as if they are random too because you can't pick which event you want to start. I have no idea how many of these there are, but I hope there are many, and they are all more ridiculous than the last.
For $1.99 I can't say it is too expensive for this, and I generally found it rather entertaining to play. You can make it simulate hundreds of created characters and just let it run at any speeds you like. The defualt is 150x normal speed, but if you want to read all the things that happen early on you should lower it to around 50x or less if you plan to add more than about 25 players to your sim. I didn't find any bugs so far, and it is fun to let it simulate for an hour, or more if you make hundreds of characters, just to see what the results are. I'd like to see more ways to look at the logs and find after game results, but overall it is worthy of the $1.99 price tag and fun enough for a few hours of sim play.
There are trading cards, which currently are worth a fair amount in a 5 card set due to there being some very in demand emoticons such as Donald Trump, Bernie, Hillary, etc., and of course "Awoo!" being the big emote get for $$$ and "yah...i no wut dat iz i'm Rule #^_^". So at $1.99 your 3 card drops can probably be sold for well over $1 total to cut the cost of this game in half if you buy it right away. :P

A true gem! Apart from the obvious "wtf" aspect of the art style (contestant for the best use of Source 2date imo) & the bizarre characters & story, this game has a hand 2 hand combat system that can put 3A titles to shame. While ranged and melee weapons are present the heart of the combat lies in good ol' fist fights, where you have to be thinking on your feet in order to survive. It is amazing how they've managed to make each part of the h2h combat system tacticaly valid, esp block/evade where usualy one option tends to overshadow the other. Hits also have some "weight" to them as opponents will react accordingly to each thumping blow.  Another + is the iclusion of a tower mode where you'll be focusing solely on the combat. Only drawback is the game's length: approx 5 hrs for the sp story. All in all one of the most unique games out there. Def give this 1 a shot!

The gameplay is fairly rough and not very responsive at times. You are forced to use a mouse / keyboard rather than be able to use a gamepad or controller like platform games are meant to be played. Certain button combinations on the keyboard seem to cancel out other buttons, such as when you are climing ladders and want to move to the side. The game seems to only be able to accept one button press at a time.
The art style is very nice and the music is quite good for this type of game. I really enjoy how colorful the game is.
There isn't very much in the way of a tutorial. You get some on-screen tips when you walk past a "?" sign, however, it is very poorly done and missing a lot of information. For example I had no idea why I ran out of bullets. I was constantly out of bullets with absolutely no explanation as to why. No on-screen bullet counter or anything, they just ran out and there was no reload button. Also, there is no way to check what buttons done because this is a bad mobile port and no effort was given in this area. When I got farther on in the game eventually a bullet count icon appeared, barely visible on the left with no explanation. Why wasn't this on the 1st level?
First Impressions / Gameplay Video
While it's definitely not the worst game ever, I still would not recommend it. This game needs to have gamepad / controller support and a far better tutorial. Also, an options screen is required for PC games. Without these things I cannot possibly recommend Combat Racoon.
Perhaps if you really wanted to try it, check it out on your mobile phone.

Despite being a decent update to make the game compatible with modern machines, it's a painful reminder of why some good things are better left on the nostalgia shelf. This game was great for its time, but there are too many design decisions that stick out like a sore thumb and make it difficult to enjoy in modern day.
Even with the improved 3D models, I would still suggest people who want to relive the FF8 experience find a PSX to play it on, as that's the way it was meant to be played. Even if you patch the PSX music into this game (that's right, SE did not update the re-release to use the much-superior PSX soundtrack), it's still a relic of an age past, and the best way to experience relics is to experience them in their original form. Which is on a PSX, with a PS1 controller, with disc swapping, and memory cards that you save your 40+ hour save files onto and live in fear of them randomly corrupting themselves, requiring you to start all over.
This is a good attempt by Square-Enix to make even more profit off products they made in a time when making high-quality games seemed to come naturally to them, but the Square that exists is not the Square that made those games. I would much prefer to see them proving that they can *still* make quality games, as opposed to trying to remind everyone of how much better they used to be.

F.E.A.R. is your standard action plot, based on cliches specific to the genre, while being marvelously adorned with apparently dominating paranormal elements, which grab your attention. By making use of its clever acronym, it promises a tension-fest and often doesn't fail to deliver. While the plot is sometimes left in the background, supernatural events become repetitive and the focus is entirely on its highly realistic shooting gameplay, it remains a decent title even after all these years.
Pros:
+highly accurate and realistic combat
+clever interference of the paranormal in the otherwise quite standardized plot
+most of the environment is destructible. You've got smoke from grenades, holes in the walls, lights that go off when the bulbs are destroyed, blood stains everywhere someone gets shot.
+there is that uncertainity about the border between reality and imagination which makes up a good psychological horror game
Cons:
-repetitive level design; in 90% of the time, you won't be able to distinguish one area from another
-repetitive combat, new enemies are introduced at great distances in the game and they rarely offer a change of pace
-story is pretty disappointing most of the time
Neutral:
+/- a lot of focus on the gameplay and often very little story to go with it. If you're a die-hard fan of shooters, this is clearly something for you. Otherwise, it might ruin your experience.
Overall, it's certainly a game worth trying, especially if you're a fan of shooters. It deserves a 7.5-8/10 in my opinion, mainly due to its unforgivable repetitiveness.

This game has a terrible story, is full of used tropes, has a very basic combat system and no meaningful progression system - besides a Metroidvania set of abilities which allow you to progress, but barely alter gameplay.
Yet it is absolutely amazing.
The story doesn't matter, because what matters is the moment, what matters is the colourful characters and their compelling dialogues and unusual, yet on-point delivery. Yes when you look back on it, that story was bad - but did you reall care while playing?
The tropes don't matter, because they are used well. I'll indulge myself in a stupid fetch quest for an ungrateful character if it allows me to screw him over.
The basic combat system doesn't matter, because the floatiness of it all is exploited and becomes a game mechanics. I'd bet you were not supposed to do half the moves you can accomplish in this game. But they are incredibly satisfying to pull off regardless.
The absence of progression system does not matter, because you will learn by playing that the tools at your disposal from the start can actually accomplish much more than you first thought. You learn by playing, in the moment.
There are a LOT of things in this game that when considered on their own are completely unimpressive. But Dust:An Elysian Tale is the epitome of "greater than the sum of its parts". Everything just fits and works together. I never once looked back and say "uh that wasn't actually that great now that I think about" because I didn't need to. I was too busy enjoying fast-paced combos over a brilliant soundtrack, in a vivid magical world populated by weird species.
If only the final chapter didn't completely crumble, this would have possibly been the absolute best experience I ever had. But as it stands now, it was just amazing.

At first glance Stellaris looks intimidating and daunting. There's such a wide variety of interfaces, choices, customizations and so forth that enables you to truly craft the empire and species of your nerdiest sci-fi dreams. Stellaris is really all of your favorite sci-fi elements and films roled into one package and the combinations are endless. Mass drivers, missles, torpedoes, lasers... you pick, all of these are available for you to focus your empires combat effectiveness.
Also as a side note, one of the most under-mentioned and truly epic pieces of this game, is the amazing soundtrack. You have orchestral and synthetic sounds of superb quality.
After having spent 50 hours the last two weeks binging on stellaris, and having one game run 200 years, I am starting to notice a pattern develop. While every game is truly unique and totally different from the last, Stellaris starts to become much more familiar and easier the more you play it. Much like Crusader Kings 2. You'll be focused on balancing your economy at first, then getting your tech up to snuff. Neglect one and a militant facist religous empire may wipe you off the map in less than 100 years. If you manage to survive into the mid game you'll be faced with a series of choices for your techs that may or may not end the galaxy. The late game as far as I have witnessed is spent trying to clean up an end game crisis and reach that victory condition of 40% control.
The only downside I have for this game is after awhile it feels a bit bare bones. No civilian trade lanes. Combat is basic, your swarm of ships vs my swarm of ships, usually highest value wins. No other victory conditions besides conquest (hard if your a pacifist). Terraforming is very limited. Diplomacy is very limited. Options to bring an empire into your fold are limited and so forth. All of these things have been noted by the community and I have full faith in Paradox that these will be addressed in the future.
I know over time as Paradox always does, this game will be fleshed out and probably end up completely different than it is now in two years. Paradox has started with a great initial package, truly nailing what every nerd has been wanting for so long in a stagnate genre.
8/10. Buy it. The galaxy is yours.

Okay, so as someone who has tinkered with RPG Maker for years, I'm trying to cut this game a little slack, especially since it almost exclusively uses the pre-supplied resources, save for a sideview battle system and various edits of the base character graphics.
I can deal with that, and I can see why it was done. However...
The dialogue drives me up the wall.
Several words are misspelled, punctuation seems random, and the game can't decide between "X-tu" and "xtu".
Also, the obscene amount of exclamation points and question marks used is just obnoxious.
And before I even get to move or look at anything, the game wants to tell me the controls, and that I can press F1 for options (including remapping the controls it just told me about) and F5 for fullscreen/window toggle.
The game immediately tells you about the ninja village you live in, the Kage that sacrificed himself, the sealing of beasts inside of children, the village in the leaves, and then you go to school to meet your friends, the emo kid, the healer, and the one nobody cares about, and your first mission is to retrieve some bells from your sensei.
After that, it's revealed that Orochimaru, a ninja master long thought dead, is actually alive, and is...
...Wait, no, sorry, I got lost there for a moment. I thought I was writing a review for a JRPG, not Naruto.
You'd be forgiven for thinking they're the same thing.
Also, before you see any real action, there is actually a battle tutorial.
It teaches you the complex art of battle, covering topics such as "how to attack", which tells you about the attack button, and how to press it; "hp and you", which teaches you the fundamentals of health points (or sometimes hit points); "skills for the skilled", which covers everything you need to know about selecting attacks that cost MP (I think it's MP anyway, I couldn't be bothered to commit any of this to memory).
But yeah, a battle tutorial. For a JRPG. Yep.
And just in case you forgot, you can press F1 for options, and F5 to switch between fullscreen and windowed.
There are also save points, but those don't matter, because they forgot to disable saving anywhere you want.
While this game has its flaws, it still did one good thing:
it taught me that I can put very little effort into an RPG Maker game, and it will make a few bucks.
You too can be the next big JRPG star! ...or at least make a few bucks on some shovelware. :)
