It's Call of Duty so you get the intense fast paced shooter action with body counts that make the Sack of Carthage look like the actions of the TeleTubbies.  But this was really the first one to make me question whether I should enjoy these games.  First off, let me clarify that I don't play games for the multiplayer.  Crazy as it sounds, I care most about the story, the immersion in the experience, and just having a good time.  Not that I don't enjoy multiplayer and do it on occasion, it's just not my cup of tea.
That being said, given my taste for Cold War era...everything you'd think I'd love this story.  And frankly, well yes I do!  It's got it all, Communists, Cubans, Vietnam, cool space age weapons that actually existed, the frakin SR-71, Rolling Stones, CCR!!  Phenomenal stuff?  So is there a problem?  Well...kinda.  I know it's a shooter and I usually never have a problem with violence in video games provided it fits the story and does not distract from it.  The problem with Black Ops is that I feel it skirts the line and occasionally passes over it of focusing so much on the violence that you lose the immersion.  It just comes across as immature.  It's as if to give a greater shock value or to claim greater "realism" (ugh, I hate when people judge a war game on realism), the developers simply resorted to showing more visceral violence to draw attention to it.  I get it, war is violent.  But I feel like this game is a 12 yr old playing in the back yard yelling about how violent war is and intense and awesome Black Ops people are.  Maybe that's because the target market for this game is 12 yr olds and bros.  Be that as it may, sometimes I feel like a 12 yr old playing war in the woods.  Or a total bro telling his bros he's such a badass becuase he's good at Call of Duty.  If you're feeling like that, put in Black Ops and have a blast, because it's fun!  Play it with a group of people and have fun with it.
If you feel like existentially grappling with the reality of war and violence, you should probably load something else.  But for what it is, Black Ops does it's job very well and I see myself playing it in the future.

The game feels unfinished.
1. It takes 15 seconds to load a battle. What is going on during that time? This is a simple game, and I have a powerful machine. I want to run many battles fast, I don't want to wait 15 seconds between them.
2. The programming part has very little documentation: only a couple of tutorials on the workshop. You have to guess what things like "the default trigger 'TRIGGER'" and "TestTargetAmountInRange" mean. (And how it's different from "Has Target Amount In Range")
3. The AI architecture is a little illogical: why do animations cause actions? Why not make events and actions the center of your program and attach animations later? Why do you need separate code blocks instead of making every action a code block by default?
4. The AI section is not very well organized. I want to look at a screen and understand how my AI works instantly. Instead I have to browse multiple lists and switch between them trying to put everything together in my mind. Animation X is started by condition Y, so I have to go to the list of conditions. Condition Y checks variable Z, so I have to open the list of variables. Then it executes this code block, and I have to switch back and forth all the time.
5. The AI capabilities are limited: the designer tried to predict every single feature that the player will need and make a separate option to provide that feature. Instead of providing elementary building block that can be combined into whatever the player wants. The only nontrivial condition that you can use is if you encounter a bunch of enemies. Is that all that can happen in an RTS? What about "half the pack is dead, so let's retreat"? Or "we have a reinforcement, so let's attack again"? Or a million other things that will likely come up if you play long enough? The designer added a note that you can email him and request a feature, but the system should have enough generality that you could implement everything yourself.

First things first: This is not the worst game I've ever played.
That being said, I can't recommend this game. The game came in a bundle with a few other games for practically pennies to the dollar, so I didn't read into the reviews before purchasing it.
That was a mistake on my part. Always read the reviews.
At first, I didn't know what to think of this game. For the first 10-20 minutes or so, I thought it might be a parody game, something meant to be silly. This is because although the description called the game "heavily inspired by Chrono Trigger, Final Fantasy VI, and the Dragon Quest series," the only series that it is remotely similar to is Naruto. Actually, the game reads like a confusing Naruto fanfiction: it mashes together Eastern-ish and Western themes to the point where its almost funny (your Village's Leader in the about? His name was Kage Alex) and there are a few rediculous moments in the dialouge (CHAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA-), and I think the game could have been hilarious.
The battle mechanics are unbalanced and weird, and though I leveled up at an absurd rate, battles still dragged on to the point of being tedious. To be honest, I only got about 2 hours into this "12 hour RPG" and I had to put it down. The problem was that it just got so repetitive that I completely lost interest, and any investment I might have had in the plot went out the window.
However, I think this game should have been what it feels like it is: A Naruto fan game. I would have enjoyed playing a Naruto RPG, even just for the novelty of it. But they dropped some really big, heavy names in the description, where the only things they have in common in this game are being pixelated turn-based RPGs.
I know this game must have taken a lot of time and effort, and I would hate to see something I spent so much time and effort on be torn apart in the reviews. But my biggest problem with it is that the game's description and About were... misleading. I felt a little tricked, and no matter how little I spend on something I do not want to feel like I'd been fooled into doing it.
I may pick it up later after getting a chance to digest it more, but as of right now I doubt it.

A very wierd but very fun little game.  There aren't alot of first person adventure/fighting games out there - probably for good reason - the mechanics are a bit strange and hard to get used to, but they can be alot of fun once you get into the swing of things.
The real highlight for this game, however, is the colorful and original world it is set in.  The blurb calls it "punk-fantasy," which falls pretty short of quantifying just how oddball this game is.  The strange characters, fantastic creatures, and bizzare weapons all feel like they are referencing a deep and well established mythology - but one that is almost entirely alien to me.
There are a few issues with focus and pacing but overall this is a great game that is worth the $15 sticker price.  8/10

'Zeno Clash' is a debut game by ACE Team, who are the developers who recently released 'Rock of Ages'.
This is an impressive title. Extraordinarily impressive. An FPS focusing mostly on brawling and few weapon mechanics, the gameplay is not only innovative, but stunningly creative and chocked full of potential. The imagination used to create this game is off the charts: it's a cornucopia of color and design. ACE has left no stone unturned when  creating an entirely new world. Not only do they focus on the visuals of the planet but also the unique culture, technology, wildlife, language and the natives that inhabit this strange new land. When it comes to being engulfed in a whole new reality, I've seen few games do it as seamlessly as 'Zeno Clash'.
While the gameplay is unvaried and by no means perfect, this reasonably short foray leaves you wanting MORE. For 'Zeno Clash', this is a good thing. This is one game that will have you chomping at the bit for a sequel.

PC port is horrible. The game crashes often while loading a race, and is not worth the trouble of trying on PC. I'd recommend buying it preowned on a console but not on PC.
But the game itself:
Compared to its main rivals at the time, Forza Motorsports 4 and Gran Turismo 5, Need for Speed: Shift 2 Unleashed offers an immersive Sim-cade racing experience that improves on its predecessor. The game itself is enjoyable, not up to par with FM4 and GT5, but still enjoyable. It's big selling point is a "driver" camera view and night racing. The driver camera view adds a layer of immersion to the game, and the night racing is an aspect to set it apart from the other games, mainly Forza Motorsports 4 which did not have at the time (but GT5 did). Compared to its competitors, Unleashed 2 is immersive and intense. The other two games are rather systematic while Shift 2 Unleashed seemed more theatrical and dramatic. This shows in its visuals and car handling physics. Visually, for being a 5 year old game, looks really impressive. The car handling physics are an improvement of the original Shift, but just don't meet the par that is of FM4 and GT5. The cars fishtale easily while turning and are twitchy. NOTE: I used a controller. The AI seem to have very little spatial awareness and crashed into me often. Car selection is minimal compared to FM4 and GT5, but customization is equivalent to FM4. Upgrading, tuning, and vinyls are available in the game. Track selection is great! From real to fiction tracks, racing was varied and never got dull.
Overall: It's a enjoyable sim-cade racer, but you might as well play Forza or Gran Turismo. They just have more content and adept. Need for Speed: Shift 2 Unleashed is an upgrade from its predecessor, but mediocre compared to its competitors.

For me, I love FS 2013.  I grew up on a farm, I went to an Ag school for pre-vet.  So, it's a fun game, although I don't really consider it a game.  It's a simulator....like any other sim, except with this one, you get to be farmer John.  This sim is a great learning tool.  I play with my kids.  I teach them the value and importance of saving and working.  I start each with 100,000 dollars.  I told them thats all the money they get, and teach them about saving...in this case for needed equipment.   It's actually perfect for this kind of thing.
From a personal standpoint, I'd like to see a few changes.  Since there is now an American farm, it'd be nice to see the weather in degrees, instead of celsius.  I know most probably use Centigrade, however, it'd at least be nice to be able to toggle from one or the other.  Also, since you don't have the means at the start, it'd be nice to be able to buy hay and straw for feeding purposes.  You can buy animals and other placeable buildings, so doing this would enhance the simulation.   Additionally, for the American farm, putting the fields in acres instead of hectares would be a nice change as well.   Lastly, it'd be nice to see the seasons change for a more realistic planting experience.  Example, corn in spring/summer, wheat in winter.  Perhaps color coding the calendar with fall/winter/summer would be a good way to accomplish this.
If you want a "game" that you can kill hours on, and have some moderate fun....this is it.  Keep in mind...it's a sim....about farming.  Those who work, or have worked on a farm understand....there is ALOT of monotony.  Nothing happens fast on a farm...except spending money....and lots of it.

Everyone\'s initial impression of this game is the same, as the game is beautiful in appearance and plays well at the start.  But you quickly become disappointed in the myriad of bugs found.  Say you have a leader who gives a 20% building discount.  Well put him on a world and queue up discounted buildings.  Then move him to the next world instantly since there is no travel time involved and queue up more discounted buildings.  Repeat for each of your planets.  I can understand AI issues arising say in the Sector management, but bugs where you can apply a leadership bonus from one leader across every planet, well that\'s poor quality assurance.  And that is just one such bug.  Want to instantly move two fleets together in a system?  Well just drag a window around them and combine the fleets.  Even though they are weeks away from meeting, now they are instantly combined, no travel time involved to group!  How about quests to scout 6 planets and then you find that 2 of the planets are behind another empire\'s borders and unreachable?  And the auto design optimizer for ships doesn\'t upgrade weapons at all, prefering to just maximize shields and armor while your ships keep the most basic of weapons.  Building frontier outposts is always a risk since it doesn\'t display the area of influence prior to building them, so you may accidentally build it too far out to be part of your empire,
I join everyone else in saying, WAIT 6 MONTHS and this may be a good game by then.  And hopefully without DLC cost for those of us who paid for this untested game out of the box.

At first glance Stellaris looks intimidating and daunting. There's such a wide variety of interfaces, choices, customizations and so forth that enables you to truly craft the empire and species of your nerdiest sci-fi dreams. Stellaris is really all of your favorite sci-fi elements and films roled into one package and the combinations are endless. Mass drivers, missles, torpedoes, lasers... you pick, all of these are available for you to focus your empires combat effectiveness.
Also as a side note, one of the most under-mentioned and truly epic pieces of this game, is the amazing soundtrack. You have orchestral and synthetic sounds of superb quality.
After having spent 50 hours the last two weeks binging on stellaris, and having one game run 200 years, I am starting to notice a pattern develop. While every game is truly unique and totally different from the last, Stellaris starts to become much more familiar and easier the more you play it. Much like Crusader Kings 2. You'll be focused on balancing your economy at first, then getting your tech up to snuff. Neglect one and a militant facist religous empire may wipe you off the map in less than 100 years. If you manage to survive into the mid game you'll be faced with a series of choices for your techs that may or may not end the galaxy. The late game as far as I have witnessed is spent trying to clean up an end game crisis and reach that victory condition of 40% control.
The only downside I have for this game is after awhile it feels a bit bare bones. No civilian trade lanes. Combat is basic, your swarm of ships vs my swarm of ships, usually highest value wins. No other victory conditions besides conquest (hard if your a pacifist). Terraforming is very limited. Diplomacy is very limited. Options to bring an empire into your fold are limited and so forth. All of these things have been noted by the community and I have full faith in Paradox that these will be addressed in the future.
I know over time as Paradox always does, this game will be fleshed out and probably end up completely different than it is now in two years. Paradox has started with a great initial package, truly nailing what every nerd has been wanting for so long in a stagnate genre.
8/10. Buy it. The galaxy is yours.

There are plenty of RPGMaker RPG's (or even non-RPG's like "To The Moon") who are actually good.
Sadly, this is not one of them. Infact, there's nothing redeeming to be said about this title.
Let's start with the story. You fight rouges (who look a lot like rogues instead of mascara, but let's ignore that for the moment) for plot-critical documents... a shopping list for the Kings Wife. Well, there's your plot. The only thing more horrible than it are the dialogues. Even though the best part of a RPG is already ruined, maybe it's gameplay can salvage somewhat?
Well, nope. You fight with 4 people. You can equip them in the city, except, you only get the player at that point so you pretty much need to guess/have identic memory or note down what the hell the other 3 can even wear in the first place. So far the good stuff, combat is pretty much mashing spacebar (using chi or tp has little use), sometimes using right to select another target. Do take care not to press too much while mindlessly battling, as right can also start the combat. And if no action is taken you don't auto-attack or defend or anything, nope you're just have your turn wasted. Great mechanic!
In the starting areas you battle lvl 5-8 enemies, in the following areas too. Well, you are level 15 now, but hey, here are some level 3 rats for this high-level area. Enemies can come randomly (oh noes), out of crates (well, that just sucks) and if you're stupid enough to wander into the random enemies.
Talking about random enemies, they can't actually initiate combat with them, you need to run into them. Leading to many accounts of moonwalking enemies just humping you hoping for you to foolishly walk in their direction. Silly random mobs, who would torment themselves to even more of this combat system?
Well, those underleveled foes become a blessing when the bosses end up, who ARE at your level. 1000HP+ with your attacks doing 10 damage per hit. Have a fun 20 minutes slashing into it. Sure gets that 12 hours there. And once you FINALLY defeat the darn thing (make it end!) ANOTHER boss turns up right after it without chance to save. Sure you can use potions to heal but overall you start with what you got (like no magic). Not that it matters anyway since this second boss is so magic resistant you need to rely on melee attacks. Have another 20 minutes of... "fun"...
Yeah, me? I went for the uninstall button instead. Bad gameplay, bad plot, bad dialogue... Bad game.

This is a really great single player turn based strategy game.  Observations-
- Map sizes range from tiny two player maps to ludicrous 36 player maps.
- Lots of worlds to discover/colonize ranging from dead to paradise to ancient precursor worlds.
- 15 different civs to choose from or ... design your own civ.
- The tech tree is filled out really well.
- Colonies need buildings ... and the build list affords several options.
- Your civilization has to make ethical decisions from time to time as the game unfolds. This has an overall impact on gameplay.  Your society becomes good, neutral or evil ... and the AI reacts accordingly.
- Every 10 turns a Citizen will emerge.  Put him to work as a general, scientist, diplomat, spy, etc.
- Design your own ships or go with what's offered in game.
- Manage each individual world the way you like or don't and let the AI governor do it for you.
Gal Civ has a ton of replayabilty, every game you play will be different.  And just when you think you've won or lost ... in comes a mega event that can shake things up leaving everyone scrambling to regain the advantage.
One more thing worth mentioning.  The devs are awesome.  I like to log onto the forums and usually they'll have posted something looking to get feedback and/or just to let you know what they have planned for the game.

Ah yes, this game spoke to me personally...and I've been there several times in my sad lifetime.  Now, there are actually several ways you can interpret this game, though most may agree on only one being the truth...but I'll save this for a bit later.
is a platform puzzle game much like
except it's easier, more fun, and far less bullsh*t.  Your goal is simple.  Find the bench/girl and find yourself a way to meet your goal.  The gimmick this time, however, is the ability to create shadow clones to repeat the actions you programmed in with your own character's body...the "time travel shadow clones" if you will...which I'm certain I've seen in other games before.  Sometimes there are red barriers you can pass...and others will be black barriers that the girl and shadows cannot pass.  Overall, the experience in it's totality should only take 30 minutes.
The music is the same selection you've heard in the trailer labeled "It's hard to let go" (the name alone sets the mood of the entire game's plot) by Michael Ortega, which is more commonly referred to as "Sad Piano" by other users.  There are also two voice actors, both of which do a great job with the narrated story.
Now...for the story... it involves a boy who meets a girl.  Smitten with her, he tries to meet her, yet she almost always eludes him.  At one point, she disappears and, heartbroken from the abandonment, he gets needy...desperate...creepy.  He feels like he NEEDS to be with the one he loves even if the feelings are not mutual.  As the game goes on, the once sane-seeming boy seems to lose himself with despair and obsession.  I've seen this story in a few friends I've met in life and even in myself...
The plot can be interpretted in various ways....did Michelle ever love the Jake?  Did she only agree to meet him only so that she could find a way to run away from him?  Did she abandon him because of his obsession...or was she the one who is blamed for tempting and abandoning him, leaving him in a worse state than he was initially in?  Did he abuse her?  Was he a stalker?  One may never tell, but I will say that abandonment will bring out the worst in someone.  That's what makes this game's story hit home for me...
So, the obvious question...is it worth the purchase/playthrough?  Well, not for full price ($2), but for a sale, it's $0.50 (well worth that price).  There are no achievements, but there are card drops.  Also, it may occur that Steam and AVG Free may not load this game because they think it's a virus.  Rest assured if this happens, it's a false positive.

This game is absolutely breathtaking!
It's a completely dialogue-free experience. Nobody says anything. Because of this, if you're the type that likes the story of a game to be spoon-fed to you, then steer clear.
The story of the game gave me a Little Nightmares feeling, meaning: put some very detailed things in very precise locations and let the players fill in the blanks.
The graphic is beautiful and all movements are very smooth. While the animals are not as detailed as other games, somehow the movements and the ambient makes them feel more alive than I've felt in any other game.
I would actually say this is not a game as much as it is a visual experience. It is meant to pull you in and make you feel everything you would feel if you were truly there. This isn't something you can do in bits and pieces. You need to take a couple hours and explore and experience everything at your own pace.
The story itself is short, but there is a lot of potential for multiple runs. I would honestly replay the whole story  just for a few of the visuals you get from it.
Last but certainly not least... the music. One word: PERFECT!
Half of this game is the music. The gentle tones will accompany you all throughout this amazing experience, always with the right tempo and the right volume to give you a beautiful background without ever sounding forced. It's not the kind of soundtrack that tells you how you should feel, instead it goes perfectly together with whatever you are feeling.
All in all, I recommend this to everyone who wants to try a gorgeous experience completely different from almost all other games out there. Once again: this is not a survival game, it's not an exploration game, it's not an educational game... it's a visual and auditory experience, and I personally believe that everyone should try it.

I think the primary issue with this game, beyond solveable ones like optimization and gameplay that are being modifed quite literally as I type this, and that no doubt will be perfected through patches and DLC (as is done in all PDX games), is that it recquires a different type of roleplaying to enjoy.
Most PDX grand strategies require roleplaying to enjoy, but with most of them the framework for the player\'s interaction with the world is easy, as its based in actual history. It is much easier to design a scenario where a character plays as Matilda, Duchess of Tuscany and where the player is able to play that role to their satisfaction, as real life has done much of the setting and characterization for them. This is especially notable in PDX\'s primary market, which would be people with an interest in history. With that in mind, having a goal-less game is easier, as the player is really interacting with a history for amusement, rather than attempting to meet some standard set by the game.
Stellaris is different. There are goals set, yes, but they are fairly unimaginative and have very little involvement in game events; they also force you to play as an expansive empire. But, mostly, there is no history to interact with. Everything here is up the player\'s devising. Sure, there\'s references to other space operas, and this game is undeniably a space opera, its just that its so open-ended that, in order to have an experience similar to say, CK2, the player will have to manufacture characters and plots and flavor themselves.
I do this fairly easy. Thus, once they fix mechanics and optimizing and other such things, I will be able to enjoy the game quite a bit. Others, however, will see this as bland and flavorless, and that is their right.
I still reccomend the game, though. This price point, which would have made me balk a decade ago, is now a full $20 less than the AAA industry standard for a base game. The DLC will be expensive as a total, but as with all PDX games the basic features of each will be included in a patch, and much of the dlc will be cosmetic, in this case perhaps new ships and races. One of the best 4x strategy game I have ever played ... and I have played a lot of different 4x games over the past 20 years.
The game was great to start with, but since release the game is constantly improving and new features are still coming in.
For me, the killer feature of this game is the really good AI. Compared to all other current 4x games, this game has by far the best AI. A good AI is really important, but sadly underestimeted, which is why most other 4x games have a really stupid AI which is easily exploited in various ways. Usually the AI compensates its stupidity by insane cheats. But not so in Galactic Civilizations III, here the AI is actually quite smart and really fun to play with. I wish more games would focus on AI like this.
Also, I like the fact that Brad Wardell (the founder and CEO of Stardock) has personally put a lot of programming hours into the game, showing his love and commitment for the game. And this guy really made a difference since he joined the team, increasing the performance of the game, improving the AI and also some nice game design choices.
For the full experience, I can also recommend both of the expansion packs and at least the mega events DLC :)

DOOM 2 is a timeless masterpiece of a game. Even after more than 25 years after its release it's still a really enjoyable game
But 32 levels isn't just all that you can get from this game, if you get the .wad file and download GZDOOM for singelplayer and Zandronum + Doomseeker for multiplayer DOOM, you will be able to play a TON of awesome mods that most of the time look like new full 12+ hour games. Just look these mods up and see for yourself what you can play in this old game:
GZDOOM sourceport:
-DOOM: The Golden Souls 2:
Super Mario and Doom combined into one awesome game. Platforming and shooting at it's absolute finest
-Russian Overkill:
The most badass set of over-the-top weapons, more than 50 weapons to kill everything that moves with the power of a steroid injected bull
-Reelism:
Playing DOOM in an open arena with RNG weapons, effects and enemies. This is decided by a slot machine. After a couple of rounds a boss will appear. This is also playable in Zandronum multiplayer, and loads of fun
-Skulldash:
A mix between speedrunning and DOOM combat. If you're into speedrunning, this is a game for you
I keep calling these mods "games", because they most of the time offer more gameplay and hours of fun than normal games can offer you
Zandronum sourceport:
-Push: I can't find a good link, because some other popular mod uses the name push for one of it's maps, sorry
In this mod you jump really high and can shoot plasma balls and lasers. You win by knocking the other player off the stage, it's like Super Smash Bros. Believe me when I say that this is the most fun multiplayer mod or even game you will ever play
-Serious Sam: The Retro Encounter:
Serious Sam in DOOM, what's not to love? This is my go-to mod when I want to do a deathmatch with my friends. It's just so much fun shooting at eachother with laserguns and grenade launchers.
I think I've rambled on for long enough. My final statement: If you're going to play DOOM 2, absolutely play DOOM 2 mods! If you want to see more mods, check this youtuber out, his whole channel is dedicated to reviewing DOOM 2 mods.
I think that there's a mod for every player in DOOM 2, and I highly encourage you to play those mods. If you really don't want to buy it, there are freedoom wads, these are free for use and so you can experience the DOOM 2 mods FOR FREE!

Final Fantasy VII is easily one of my favourite games of all time. In fact, I'd go as far as calling it a contender for my favourite game full stop. Whilst its age is shown in its graphics, it still holds a prime place in my heart after playing it over and over for many years, and it will continue to do so for the rest of my days.
Obviously, the game isn't without its flaws. No game is. However, FFVII has few of them. The main flaw is its plot holes during some of the flashback sequences. However, these are mostly due to translation errors and censored content outside of Japan, so that's not really the game's fault. However, a vast majority of these relate more to the lore of the world rather than the events of this game in particular, and are explored in more detail throughout the other games in the FFVII collection. The very few that apply to this game in particular can be found within the game, but through optional quests, which isn't too bad. The other big flaw is the occasional use of compulsory, story related minigames that tend to break the pacing a bit. However, it could be much worse, as many games of the time were, when it comes to pacing, as a vast majority of the rest of the game deals with pacing in a relatively superior manner.
Of course, to be a game that many gamers consider the most influential and most iconic JRPG of all time, as well as one of the top 3 PS1 games of all time (according to a poll that PlayStation ran, alongside Crash Bandicoot and Metal Gear Solid), it must do a lot of stuff right, right? That is indeed the case. Here's a list of things that are done really nicely.
-Story - The story is among the best throughout all of gaming history. It's powerful, it's moving, it makes you think... You'll be hard-pushed to find a video game with a better story, even today.
-The characters - The characters are amazing. The main party members are all likeable in their own way, and they are all relatable too. The bad guys are the kind of bad guys that people love to hate, which is why they are popular, and actually good villains. The chemistry between characters is well done too.
-The music - FFVII has a phenomenal soundtrack. The music always matches the mood of the current location and event. The battle themes make the battles feel action packed, especially the boss themes which add tension to the fights. There are also multiple tunes in the game that are moving, and they are used to set the mood beautifully.
-The gameplay - Unlike XIII, this Final Fantasy is not a corridor. Whilst it tells you where to go next, it doesn't force it upon you. It allows you to explore, finding new items and equipment, and even two extra characters. There are also numerous sidequests which you can do, should you fancy a break from the story. The battles are also fun. The battles are turn based, which some might consider a bad thing outside of Pokémon these days. However, in 1997, most RPGs were turn based, with FFVII being no exception, and FFVII has a really good battle system. It's also mildly customisable. You can make it easier and more casual by setting the game to wait for you to make your choices in your turns before attacking you, or you can make it harder by letting CPUs take their turns whilst you select, meaning you have to be faster in making your choices. As well as this, it has a wonderful ability system in the form of Materia, which allows you to customise your characters' abilities easily.
Overall, this game is a masterpiece. This game proves that video games could be considered an art form when done well. With the remake around the corner, I highly recommend this masterpiece so you can see where the worldwide love for Final Fantasy VII first began. The remake will likely be an amazing game, but it won't necessarily have the charm that the original does. Play this game. If JRPGs, or story driven games in general, are your thing, I promise you that you will not be disappointed by this timeless classic.

In 1997, a JRPG like no other took the world by storm and introduced the West to a whole new type of video game. It was upbeat, clever, and full of grand adventure. It was dark, heartbreaking, and full of moments of despair as well as triumph. It was massive, containing a world that took at least seventy hours, if not even more, to fully explore. It was also concise, gathering nine unique, broken but hopeful heroes in a quest to defeat a near unstoppable madman, all ten of whom have since become icons in gaming worldwide. And through it all, a soaring musical score gave them all identity, personality, and relatability in a game with no spoken words.
This game...was Final Fantasy VII.
Like the first six Final Fantasies before it, FFVII is a standalone title with its own story, characters, and universe. As such, you can jump right in without missing anything. In this installment, you take up the massive sword of Cloud Strife, a sullen yet determined young man with more to his initial demeanor than meets the eye. In your very first mission, you join a gang of eco terrorists named AVALANCHE and blow up a city power plant, defying the corrupt energy company that controls most of the planet, but costing untold innocent lives in the process. But soon events spiral beyond your control, and it's up to you to save the planet alongside the brittle AVALANCHE leader Barret, a beautiful flower girl named Aerith, and Tifa, the only friend you have left from your old life...
FFVII plays like most old school JRPGs, with your party wandering a massive world map and encountering monsters and enemies as you go. The combat is turn based, wherein you and your opponents attack in turns with different moves, ranging from attacks with your weapons to magical spells to summoning all manner of creatures and warriors to inflict massive amounts of damage. Each ability you can use is equipped with a gemstone called a Materia, which you can level up for more powerful results by continuously fighting with it equipped. Practicing Materia combinations can result in some incredible strategies, so experiment until you find the combos that work best for you.
Newcomers not used to JRPGs or retro gaming may not immediately click with a game that came out back in 1997. Their initial response is understandable, given that video games and the technology used to make them were very different back then. Personal feelings and the fanbase's nostalgia aside, the character models for the world map and non combat events are very simple and low detail, with their quality improving during battles and cinematic cutscenes. This is also a localized game originally from Japan, and some things tend to get lost in translation. The Steam version is apparently much better than the original Playstation release, but there are occasional odd moments in dialogue. As stated above, none of this dialogue is spoken, which means you're reading everything the characters say via word bubbles.
The plot can be a little hard to follow if not paid complete attention to, and the lore is pretty expansive. Certain moments feel a little jumbled (and one section slightly distasteful), and not everything is always made entirely clear. It can be a real grind to, well, grind up experience for the Materia you need to kill the more powerful bosses, especially towards the end of the game.
But the biggest potential issue that even diehard fans will admit to?
Minigames.
Minigames EVERYWHERE.
However, these gameplay mechanics and designs, these flaws, should not be used as an excuse to not give this game a good ten to twenty hours before quitting. There is a reason so many Final Fantasy fans will declare this game the best of the series and/or their personal favorite, and why Square Enix has finally caved to the years of demands for a full remake on newer consoles. The story here is one of the most powerful you will ever experience, and the extra lengths you go to become stronger make the end battles you fight all the more sweeter to win. Your party almost becomes a little family to you, friends you never thought you'd make. You'll laugh. You'll cry. You'll clench your fist in rage and pump it in the air in triumph.
Because I guarantee that once you've begun Final Fantasy VII, "there ain't no gettin' off this train!"

F.E.A.R is an elegant mix of action and horror. It's vicious, bloody combat is interspersed with moments of gut-wrenching tension. The excellent balance struck between these two elements, and the way they interact with F.E.A.R's surprisingly enjoyable narrative is perhaps the game's strongest aspect. While F.E.A.R's gun-play is a bit dated, it still manages to be a treat regardless. weapons feel great and there is a real sense of power and importance behind every shot. This effect is further enhanced by a bullet-time ability which not only provides the player with another fun tool to play with, but also serves to show off F.E.A.R's beautiful particle effects and gore.
With such good combat, it is a shame that F.E.A.R suffers from poor enemy variety. While there are a handful of special enemy types, you will primarily be fighting similar sets of human enemies throughout the game's duration. In addition, levels have a severe lack of visual variety. I spent much of the game creeping through similar looking offices and ruined buildings. Despite this, I rarely got lost, as the game does and excellent job of guiding you through it's levels while still giving you the freedom to explore, often rewarding you with weapons and upgrades for doing so. FEAR's atmosphere and lighting are also note-worthy, serving to ensure you are always on edge, even during the game's calmer moments.
Interspersed throughout F.E.A.R's combat are moments of intense horror. the game does a great job of directing your attention to just the right spots through the use of clever sound and light cues. while the risk of danger in these scenes are minimal, they do serve to break up what could have been an otherwise tedious string of combat segments. They are paced to perfection, never feeling drawn out or overdone. These scenes also provide a means of engaging narrative delivery, which often left me excited to see what would come next.
F.E.A.R's story is engaging and serves to tie the experience together. It's psychological themes fit together nicely with the game's dark atmosphere. Much of the story is presented through audio logs and radio messages, which allows it to develop without slowing down game-play. unfortunately, the game's voice acting, while not terrible, tended to stick out in the midst of F.E.A.R's more serious tone.
Despite it's flaws, I thoroughly enjoyed F.E.A.R. it's many parts all fit together well, forming a game that I recommend to anyone interested in shooters or horror games and is able to look past many of the game's aging elements.

As a huge racing fan, buying almost every game that releases I have to say that SHIFT 2 is among the best of them across the board.
Unfortunately, it's Steam page is marred by reviews that start with 'excellent game' before proceeding to not recommend due to the DRM policies and performance issues in the Steam client (This was the last game Electronic Arts released on Steam before Origin came along). I, running a mid-range PC on an i5 and a R9 270 with 12GB RAM, have not noticed these issues so far, the main one being crashes to desktop, rendering unplayable unless placed in Origin (Which can supposedly be achieved with a copy/paste of the CD Key you receive). The second issue people see with this is its DRM policy, the game can only be installed on 5 PC's/across 5 system resets before it can be activated no more. If you are someone who intends to reset or purchase a new PC an additional 4 times whilst playing this game, this could be an issue, mind you EA Support is surprisingly good, last time I had issues installing a game they fixed it and gave me a limited edition upgrade on two occasions, but of course they will migrate you to Origin.
When (and if according to these reviews) you get into the game, it is superb. The visuals still hold up incredibly well and the soundtrack within the menus and loading screens is great - composed with the assistance of award-winning composers, one of whom is now doing the Game of Thrones' soundtrack.
The gameplay is immensely intense; you know if you hit the driver in front or brake slightly too late it could all be over in a savage first person crash. At most times this game is more of a survival horror than a racing game, it doesn't feature a rewind feature like most sim-racers of the time and instead of casing you as the car, you are actually cast as the driver, something racing games have never really tapped into. This is achieved by the amazing 'helmet cam', taking you not only into 1st person but direct from the driver’s vision. The cockpit blurs under high intensity, the camera shake is perfect and the tilt as you approach a corner really adds the dynamics and intensity, this is also aided by 'motivational' comms messages at the start of races and Vaughn Gittin Jr. who teaches you the basics and introduces you to events, his spotlight of which is drifting, which I have to say is pretty uncontrollable, the general consensus is that the drift events in the career are near impossible.
The career overall is very good, you start low end in 'Modern D', D class vehicles such as hatchbacks and work your way up to the FIA GT1 World championship, along the way you are given tasters of what's in store such as time trials or 'hot laps' in Bugatti's and Lambo's which occur about 20% through the game alongside difficult and exhilarating championships and invitationals which can earn you McLaren's and exclusive Team Need for Speed/Speedhunters tuned beasts. Overall the career isn’t the longest and you can probably have it done in under 40 hours, but despite this you still won't have anywhere near enough to buy all the cars which you can still work for through quick events, online and seasonal events.
The cars in this game are very detailed and each have fully rendered interiors
, all of them, par a few which are already done up, offer livery choices, including the ability to fully create your own with 100's of stickers which can be placed anywhere on the car, rim options and incredibly open and detailed handling tuning, alongside performance upgrades and body kits for every vehicle. The vehicle range is very varied, especially taking into account that PC players receive the classic Legends and Speedhunters DLC's for free with additional cars and career events. Cars range from classic & retro to hatchback, sport, super, hyper, muscle and open-wheel alongside their respective race versions and tunes from all across the world.
Tracks are also very detailed, but you hardly have the time to look at them when your hitting 200mph and there’s a corner 70yds away - the selection is quite large with almost all the major and quite a few minor tracks from around the world present alongside a few fictional ones too.
Car customisation
Racing intensity and sense of speed is off the charts
Vehicle selection
Free DLC packs for PC
Track range
Visuals still hold up very well
Soundtrack
Career Progression
Pro's only apply if you get the game and it works
EA's DRM policy
Drift events
Can get frustrating
Overall I would 100% recommend this game, unless you plan on restoring your PC an additional 4 times. Drift events are completely avoidable in the career progression.

My "Yes" recommendation has reservations.
The game is very solid. I encountered no bugs or crashes, and the UI, while different from what I'm used to (I've never played a Paradox game before) is relatively intuitive. The graphics are beautiful with no observed artifacts, as are the sounds (although the music gets repetitive.) The tutorial is bare-bones, and there is no manual other than the Stellaris WIki that can be accessed within the game.
I have two real beefs with the game, however: the AI-controlled sector management hides too much important info from the player, and the mid-to-late game crises are often game-endingly brutal.
In the interest of manageability, you are limited to direct control of only 5 planets. You may group additional planets into sectors which are managed by the AI. This is fine except that should you build colony ships in a starbase in one of the AI-controlled sectors, the player receives only a brief notification when the ship is ready for use. This can be critical because colony ships drain energy credits like mad until the colony is created.  Colony ships created on non-sector planets are displayed as Civilian Ships in the Outliner (a quick access menu on the right side of the screen) but sector-created colony ships are not.  If you don't handle the ship when the notification pops up, the player is forced to manually check each starbase until he locates the colony ship, which becomes clumsy and tiresome as your empire grows. Paradox should address this issue in a future patch.
The more serious issue is the inevitable mid-to-late game crisis. As your empire grows, you will encounter one or more older races which are overwhelmingly advanced and xenophobic. Just encountering them is sufficient to provoke a game-ending jihad by an insanely powerful race bent on your destruction. The frustrating part is that you can't avoid these berserkers if you expand, and if you don't expand, your empire will die. So far I haven't figured out how to avoid this seemingly inevitable extinction; I'm usually the strongest empire when I encounter the berserkers but neither I nor my alliance can beat them nor can they be negotiated with. It is just game over...

This game is one of those argument-ending 'Name one' games.
"Games aren't artistic! Name one!"
"PC ports are impossible, and they'll always be faulty. Name one that wasn't!"
"Actio brawlers can't have major plot twists! Name one!"
"Comic relief sidekicks are such a pain. Name one time that they did that right."
Well... this is that kind of game, yes.
The controls are smooth, the voice acting is gorgeous, the soundtrack deserves to be called 'epic,' even the scenery is chewing the scenery, and as for the story? It's the kind of story where you think you know what the twist is going to be early on, but then they throw a curve ball at you and do something pretty unexpected, even unique. All three of the main characters (yes, the sword is a character) are at least interesting, Fidget is downright brilliant on so many levels, and even the shopkeeper has a story.
Yeah, not even kidding. The freaking SHOPKEEPER has a story, and it's not even a bad one.
Probably best played with a controller, because there were instances where I struggled because I forgot you could jump diagonally by holding two keys at once (eheh...) but perfectly serviceable with mouse and keyboard, and its options menu is spot-on. There are features that you wouldn't think even existed.
This game is a classic. It's iconic. And the controls are simple enough for someone new to games to pick up.
Basically, in the spirit of the season, it's a good game for gamers and it's a good experience for non-gamers. All the beauty and heart of a Disney classic mixed with the action of a Nintendo classic. Definitely worth a look.

Without going in to a LONG multipage review, I'll just hightlight the two problems I have with this game.
First I off, I wanted to give this game a thumbs up, I really did, however, as I played on and on, multiple games, and yes I have about 90+ hours game time as of this review, but the more I played the less enamored I became with the game.
There are many good points, but mainly it is solidly built with very few bugs, and just starting out it is truly enjoyable.
However, that quickly fades into the first big problem, after a few hours at 'fastest' game speed, you are BORED out of your mind.  The attempts at AI, sector management, diplomacy, research, etc, all show their faults, as in beyond  scratching the surface they are dumb, shallow, researchable technologies disapearing, and little to no depth, hence BORING.  I tried about 10 games playing many hours to see if anything would change, and no, very little did besides several different responses to events that change with your races traits.
Second is the AI balance for the other empires.  Repeatedly I was beaten by much smaller empires who amassed navies 3-5 times the maximum strength I was capable of given the amount of upkeep it takes for ships/amies.  I would try again, using another strategy, etc..., and failed 8 of 10 times ( with the Fallen races destroying me the other two), also using normal mode.  I've played many RTS' over the years and have never seen it where my 'AI management' was so dismal that an empire 1/4 my size could build and maintain a fleet 3 times the maximum size of mine.  Oh, and they go straight to your homeworld and game over.
Frustration, with other 4xRTS' you can make a mistake or learn fairly quickly with only losing 30 min to an hour of game time, this game you could be at hour 15 and just finished discovering Battleships and Fortresses, and lose it all in 5 min.  Now you have to start over, unless you were lucky enough that whatever you did to anger another empire was before an autosave, in 6 game month increments, and that only worked once for me, the empires would eventually attack no matter what I did.
Overall, I think this is a solid game but little depth as the game progresses.  Also, the AI needs some serious tweaking or at least let me manage or be able to build on the managed sector worlds instead of relying on a pathetic AI.  Maybe I could stand a chance against an empire that can utilize 100% of its resources when my AI does nothing.

I want to like this game, I like Cubicle Quest, but this game, this game has so many flaws!  Also I will say that I've played way more than what it says I have since I played this mainly offline and steam does not track offline play time.  I'm currently on Chap 9 in game
Pros:
-Naruto storyline
-pretty good humor when the grammar isn't atrocious
Cons
-Naruto based storyline
-Every character you can tell relatively early on is a Naruto reference and some chapters if you can't tell by then will quite literally toss that fact in your face
- There is an arbitrary level cap which you WILL hit well before the end of the game
- The enemies lv with you making relatively easy fights becoming incredibly long and tedious by the end game
- Nearly every skill is improperly coded so instead of doing realistic damage they do 1 dmg, every, time.
- There are not only random encounters when walking through a map, but roaming ones you actually see on the map, and if one of those touch you, you can't flee and when you get later on those fights can take upwards of 15 mins to complete especially on chap 8 I believe
- The cast of playable characters you can use is relatively small and out of all of them at end game you will only be using one of them (this game's version of Sakura), and one is completely useless for nearly the whole game (this game's version of Rock Lee)
- Out of all the late game skills you get only one does any consistent or notable damage which is deadly bubbles, which you will spam in EVERY FIGHT
- The music is repetitive to the extreme, This game as well as cubicle quest use the same base sound files, but there it actually sounds nice to me, here it is dull and clashes, the only song that has stuck out to me is the one where you fight all the music ninjas (the games version of the sound 5 from the Sasuke's departure arc) and that song doesn't show up till the end of chap 6 I beleive.
-  the complete and utter lack of real stable pace in game, this is mainly due to how awful nearly everyone is and you have no real control over your party due to plot reasons.  So you can go from having everything falling before you from having bubbles attack, to needing to run from everything knowing that it'll take too long fighting them
- Having both human and enemy units know the same skills but the code is different meaning they work differently, this is a really weird nitpick but some enemies later on down the line know late game skills your party can learn, but unlike for you they actually work for them!  This is especially bad during one of the phantom fights because it uses tsunami which for you does maybe 800 dmg, but when they use it it does nearly 2.5k making it one of the hardest fights in the game.
So yeah lots of problems, need I say more?

: Overall, I'd give this game an 7/10 – Better than most 4X games, but it still feels a bit shallow. I think the genre still has a lot of growth potential. That said, this might be the peak, at least for right now.
A turn-based 4X that feels slightly faster paced than most, filled with familiar faces, to those of us that have played previous games. For those who haven’t, those faces will become familiar enough.
I love the fact the this is a 4X game where you can actually turn your empire on a dime from a cultural powerhouse to a war machine, if needed. No, it won’t be quite as advanced as if you had planned for that from the start, but you won’t just get run over, either. Nobody likes that in 4X games, watching all of their careful planning get plowed through because the RNG placed the game’s version of Klingons on their door step, and their race is optimized for an influence victory. In GalCiv III, it’s actually possible to defend yourself, through diplomacy and through intelligently building fleets that counter your enemy. It’s a nice change from most other 4X games.
You can’t control anything about the fights. The ships simply fight, and that’s that. You can watch, and it’s pretty, but you can’t interact. It seems like, in space, a big part of the fight would be the strategy, but you don’t get to have a strategy. You only get to watch.
Also, it feels like a lot of the game is poorly explained, if at all. For instance, you have asteroids that you can mine. It shows the distance to the nearest planet. It doesn’t show what that means. For example, is there a drop off in benefit? What is the benefit, anyway? You can do some digging to find some vague info, but only after you have built the asteroid mine. Cultural influence is similarly vague, and apparently changed almost entirely with Crusade, so even the answers you find online will conflict with each other. This is a game that needs either tooltips or a user manual, yet has neither, at least not in enough quantity or detail. Also, the game leads in like there is a story (campaign), but that only lasts about 2-3 hours at most. That almost feels scammy. If people are looking for that experience, they’re going to feel pretty let down considering that’s just enough time to not be able to get a refund, and then they’re left to play “sandbox” games because that’s all there is. That said, with many 4X games, that’s all there is, period.
I would recommend it to those 4X players who enjoy turn-based, balanced repetition, that produces clear results. Don’t expect deep storyline or replayability by way of new and interesting surprises, though. The current “Recent Reviews” score of “Mixed” seems way off. This is a much higher quality game than that would suggest.
The $29.99 asking price seems fair to me, considering the infinite replayability, so long as you like the core game mechanics. It’ll take a while to get all the Steam achievements, if nothing else. It also goes on sale fairly often, so if you’re on the fence, you can count on an eventual price cut.
This game is the culmination of decades of hard work and expertise in this genre. Nobody else comes close, when it comes to experience. Unfortunately, any longstanding lore advantages are absent, as the stories of these persistent races are largely forgettable, and so most of us who have played the older games have, in fact, forgotten. I would love for them to port the old games’ stories into the new game engine, just so that we can remember where it all came from, but I know that costs money.
The graphics are decent. The cinematic space battles are especially nice, but seem almost wasted, considering watching them instead of clicking “Quick Battle” is, in essence, a very pretty waste of time. It changes nothing.
The music is good, but there is only so much of it, and it starts to drone pretty quickly. You will switch to your own music soon enough.
Meh. Not great. The space battles are about what you would expect, and destroying a planetary improvement causes a sound that is so irritating that I have to believe the developers wanted to punish us for some reason.
The game is very stable, and seems very polished, now that they have gotten over the few bugs from the initial launch of the new content.
The new updates are very recent, as is the Crusade DLC, so time will tell if they continue to release new, quality content. I hope they do, or get to work on GalCiv IV!
Story-wise, there is none. 4X-wise, there is quite a bit of replayability. It plays just like any other 4X that way, especially if you want to gather all of the Steam achievements.
All things considered, this is definitely a buy for lovers of the 4X genre. For others, maybe not so much, but then again, 4X games are kind of a love ‘em or hate ‘em kind of thing, aren’t they?

I've been seesawing back and forth on this game. I just bought the Crusaders DLC , decided to keep it. As you can see I have some time in this game. Haven't broke 100 hours yet but I probably will eventually. If you ever played Galciv I and Galciv II and you loved both games than this is the best of the three. Especially with the Crusaders DLC which in my opinion should have been a free update. I'll even go further and say all the content it adds should have been in the game in the first place. One problem with this game I will share that I have experienced and many others, both before the Crusaders DLC and AFTER it , is that any map of Immense size or larger with more than , well, I'll say six AI opponents, although I've never used fewer than 8 on that size of a map, anyway the game starts out fast but then as you explore the map and run into even 2 or 3 other civilizations / empires the game starts to slow down. Every turn seems to take forever.  I've got a I7-4790k cpu, a GTX 970 gpu with 4 gigs vram, and 32 gigs of Corsair Vengeance ram at 2400 mhz. My pc is less than a year old. I checked it out on the internet and found that people with even better systems than what I got have encountered the same issue. However, having said all that , I started recently to play the game on Gigantic maps which is beneath Immense with 6 AI opponents and so far so good. The game is fun, it's not perfect, it's not easy but if you loved Galciv I and Galciv II you will truly love this game. Warts and all. So being one of those people I have to recommend it. I don't think there will be another , this one took 2 years to get to this point and it's still got problems. It's not perfect like I said. But it is a fun game. One thing people should know is that you might play a game for over 300 turns and think you're doing good but when you get attacked by another Empire and they wipe out half your colonies in a dozen turns....lol....just start a new game and try again....(they call that replay value....)

Platformy puzzle thing in which you use your unexplained shadow clones to get over everything except your first erection.
The basic mechanic at play is that you perform whatever actions to then have a clone mirror them concurrently to your next run when you trigger it to do so. You can use multiple clones, and I'm not sure that I ever encountered a limit on numbers. This allows you to use the clones as platforms or placeholders to get you to the goal (a clone can also complete the level if necessary). You've seen this done before, surely. There's also a handful of box puzzles, a handful of times you also have to control the girl from the other side of the level or some such.
None of it's ever actually that tricky, because at the most daunting levels you can just spam clones and keep jumping in the direction of your goal (a bench, because you're Forrest Gump) and eventually you or one of the clones will make it to the goal via mounting a stack of shadow chums.
There's never a time limit, and only one or two mild synchronization bits, so what challenge you'll find is all in fiddling with clone placement for jumps and such.
Outside of the story presentation and narration (other reviews can give you an idea), there's nothing really out and out bad about it, but there's absolutely nothing that makes it an essential game to own. It's a short and simple puzzle game.
It evidently has cards that I idled, because I have 5 hours dumped into it, and it certainly didn't take me more than about 40 minutes to actually play through all levels, bonus included.
And, come the end of the journey, Jenny/Michelle doesn't like you anymore and is fed up with you... wait for it... shadowing her everywhere. Go home, Forrest.
Fun tip: it is mildly amusing to have two shadow clones get in a shoving match back and forth with a box.

This Steam version of the much-adored Final Fantasy VII is a bit lackluster. I'll be honest, it falls just a bit short of the original game. However, this does not mean at all that it is a bad game. After all the bugs, glitches, startup issues, and square enix account issues, this game shines quite brightly. If there is no possible way to play this other than on a computer, I highly recommend this game to anyone. However, to anyone who has a PlayStation that is able to run this game and the $50 price sink available, get the game that way. The computer version was made as a way to get others who have not seen how great this game was to see it in all of its glory.
